# Jeremiah 1-20

## THE ARGUMENT

The Prophet Jeremy was a priest, and so an ordinary teacher, (which some other of the prophets were not) before his entrance upon this extraordinary employment. This he began (being in his younger years thereunto called) under a good King Josiah; in times, though bad enough (the main body of the people, notwithstanding all the care and endeavor of that godly governor, continuing still inclined to their former idolatry, and other wonted evil courses) yet nothing so bad, as not long after they proved, when that pious prince was by immature decease taken away, who had kept them yet within some compass of external conformity, and restrained them from the public profession, and open practice of such abomination, while he lived. But the kings that succeeded him, being themselves also addicted to like impieties, and excesses, and complying with the people therein; all things, in short time, grew to such an height of corruption, both in church and state, that the prophet having a long time, as one striving and struggling against the stiff stream of a strong torrent, in vain labored to reclaim them; and having endured much opposition by the false prophets, and sustained much hard measure from the priests, princes, and people, for the faithful performance, and due execution of his office, (under which some expressions of human frailty, at some time, broke from him) he was, at length, constrained to denounce from God, the utter ruin and destruction of that whole state; which, by the Chaldeans, God accordingly made good. Howbeit, withal for the comfort and support of the faithful, he foretells their return after seventy years’ captivity; and the enlargement of the church, by that blessed Branch, the Messias: withal, adjoining divers prophecies against those several nations, that had been either the destroyers, or the oppressors of God’s people.

Upon the surprisal of the city by the Chaldeans, he was by the king of Babylon his special appointment, set at liberty: but was shortly after carried away by force, into Egypt, among the rest of the people, which Prince John, and his complices, upon the murder of Gedaliah, whom the Chaldean king had made governor of the land, for fear of the Chaldeans, against God’s express charge, did thither transport. There continued he prophesying, how long, it is not certain: howbeit, being called unto that office in the thirteenth of Josiah, it could not be less than between forty and fifty years that he spent in that employment. In Egypt it is not unlikely that he ended his days; though how, in what manner, or by what means, is as uncertain, as the time of his abode in those parts.

Some other things seem to have been written by him, which are not now extant, besides the sermons and prophecies recorded in this book: as a solemn Lamentation composed upon the death of Josias, 2 Chron. 35.25. that roll or volume, which Baruc engrossed for him, containing a summary of all his foregoing sermons, Chap. 36.2–18. and the same enlarged with some farther additionals, Chap. 36.32. But the main, yea, in likelihood the whole sum and substance of both these, we have at large in the records of this book. As for that Epistle, that goes under his name, as written to his Countrymen, that either were to be, or were already in captivity at Babylon, (diverse from that specified and recorded here, chapter 29.) it is deservedly deemed a mere counterfeit, as well as those prophecies of Baruc, whereunto it is adjoined.

## CHAPTER 1

**Verse 1.** *{The words of Jeremiah the son of Hilkiah of the Priests, that were in Anathoth in the land of Benjamin.}* The three first verses of this chapter seem to contain an inscription, or title, of the main body of all the prophecies, and sermons, in this whole book recorded: of all in general, in this verse; of those more specially from his first calling, unto the time of the captivity, in the two next verses.

*{The words}* That is, sermons, or prophecies; as, *The word that Esay saw*, Esay 2.1. and, *The words of Amos*, Amos 1.1. and, *The words of the Preacher*, Eccl. 1.1. Some render it, *The book*, and would have it to design no more, than what is delivered from hence, unto the end of the thirty ninth chapter: from whence say they, another book begins: as in the Revelation of John, from the eleventh chapter the like, Rev. 10.9,11. But I suppose the term here to be of larger extent, and to take in the whole volume of prophecies, that bear the name of this prophet. Nor is it probable, that all those ensuing prophecies from chapter 39. should be of later date, than Zedekiah’s captivity; yea, concerning some of them, the contrary is apparent. See chap. 51.59.

*{Jeremiah}* Heb. *Jirmjahu*; and so constantly in this book; as *Jeshajahu*; and *Jechizkijahu*, and the like; though elsewhere also, sometime, *Jirmja*: whereof see on Esay 1.1. The Greeks render it *Jeremias*, Mat. 2.17. & 16.14. we in English, ordinarily, *Jeremy*; as *Zachary*, and *Timothy*, 1 Tim. 1.2. and so our former versions exhibit it. It seems to signify one *raised up by God*, 1 king. 14.17. & 16.2. 1 Sam. 2.7. Psal. 9.13. and was a name, not unusual, among God’s people, as appears, 2 king. 24.18. 1 Chron. 5.24. & 12.4,10,13. Neh. 12.1.

*{the son of Hilkiah}* Added to distinguish him, from others, that might be in those days of that name. Of the groundless conceit of the Rabbines, concerning such denominations of prophets from their parentage; see on Esay 1.1.

*{Hilkiah}* Heb. *Chilkijah*, or *Hilkijah*, as the name is found written, 1 Chron. 6.13,45. or, *Chilkijahu*, or *Hilkijahu*; as here, and Esay 22.20. See there. The Greek, and Latin, ordinarily render it, *Helkias*; as *Benjamin*, for *Binjamin*, Phil. 3.5. and for *Joshijah*, *Josias*, Mat. 1.11. Of this name divers were, as one here mentioned; and another that was high priest under Josias, 2 king. 22.8. whom the Chaldee Paraphrast, the Jewish doctors, divers of them, and not a few Christian writers, with whom the authors of our Geneva Annotations concur, suppose to have been the Father of this our prophet: But hereof there is no great probability; for, to omit all other arguments, that seem to persuade the contrary, the high priest had his house and abode constantly at Jerusalem; whereas this Hilkiah had his dwelling at *Anathoth*, subjoined here, in likelihood, of purpose to distinguish him from that other of the same name, being high priest; yet living, and exercising that function, some space of time, after that Jeremy began at first to prophesy, as appears from 2 king. 22.4. compared with the very next verse of this chapter. Nor seems that of force sufficient to take this off, that of Abiathar the high priest under Solomon, it is said, that he had *fields of his own* inheritance at *Anathoth*, 1 kings 2.26. for albeit, he so had, yet lived he at Jerusalem until Solomon deposed him, and confined him thither; whereas of this Hilkiah there is no such thing read, but that he made his abode at Jerusalem, as his place required, 2 kings 22.4,8.

*{of the Priests that were in Anathoth}* Heb. *Of the priests in Anathoth*. Or, *at Anathoth*, rather; because the name of a Town, or city; as 2 kings 2.28. 1 Chron. 4.28,31. one of the priests that dwelt there: it being one of the cities out of the Benjamites’ lot assigned to the priests, Jos. 21.18. 1 Chron. 6.60. See Esay 10.30.

*{in the land of Benjamin}* In that portion of the land of Canaan, which by lot was assigned unto the posterity of Benjamin, Jos. 18.11. Jacob’s youngest son: Of whose name, see Gen. 35.18. Heb. *Binjamin*: But we follow herein the Greek pronunciation, as in many other names, Acts 13.21. Phil. 3.5. See chap. 37.12.

**Verse 2.** *{Unto whom the word of the LORD came in the days of Josiah, the son of Amon, King of Judah, in the thirteenth year of his reign}* In these words is precisely related the time, and year, wherein Jeremy was called unto this Prophetical function, from being an ordinary priest, to be an extraordinary prophet, and began to execute the same.

*{unto whom the word of the LORD came}* Heb. *whom the word*, or, *a word of the Lord* (as 2 Sam. 7.4.) *was unto him*: a kind of elegant redundancy, in that language, very frequent: The like whereunto, see Gen. 1.11. Psal. 1.4. 2 Sam. 6.22. Now by *the word of the Lord*, here, some understand a *charge*, or *commission*, made out by God unto Jeremy, for the exercise, and execution of his Prophetical employment, and the publishing of these his prophecies; as they conceive the word to be taken also, Hos. 1.1. Lu. 3.2. Joh. 10.35. *word*, for *charge*, or *commission*, or *command*; as 1 Kin. 12.24. Esth. 1.12. & 3.15. and so ch. 26.1. Others conceive it to design the subject matter of his prophecy, or that which was revealed to him, and he enjoined to publish; as, *the word which Esay saw*, Esay 2.1. & Gen. 15.1. *the word*, or, *a word of the Lord was to Abraham*; where no such charge, or commission, is implied: and so *the word of the Lord*, here; and *the words of Jeremy*, v. 1. are in effect, and substance, one and the same; called *the word of the Lord*, because proceeding from him, and delivered in his name, v. 4,7. *the words of Jeremy*; because by him delivered, as *God’s mouth, and messenger*, to his people, ch. 15.19. & 26.12,15. And this latter I incline to, though the word may well comprehend both, since that the former also, together with the revelation, did constantly concur. So Mic. 1.1. Zeph. 1.1.

*{in the days}* The time of the reign. See on Esay 1.1.

*{of Josiah}* Heb. *Joshijahu*; as *Jirmjahu*, v. 1. and sometime *Joshijah*; as Zach. 6.10. for the name (though not the person) is the same. Greek, *Josias*, Mat. 1.10. which our English seems best acquainted with: and it seems to import one *firmly founded*, or *grounded upon God*. See Esay 16.7. & 44.8. Of this good king’s religious reign, but over a people, though by his pious, and sedulous provisions, restrained from their wonted pollutions, and reduced to an outside conformity in public profession, & practice, of the sincere service of God; yet remaining still, in regard of disposition of heart and affection, much unreformed, and unreclaimed. See 2 kings 22. & 23. 2 Chron. 34. & 35.

*{the son of Amon}* Of whose irreligious reign, and how he renewed and restored again those abominations and idolatries, which his father Manasse, upon his humiliation and serious repentance, had abandoned and abolished. See 2 Kin. 21.19,23. & 2 Chron. 33.21,24. The name signifies, *a nurse-child*, Prov. 8.30.

*{King of Judah}* See on Esay 1.1.

*{in the thirteenth year of his reign}* Some five year before the book of the Law found in the Temple, by Hilkiah the high priest, 2 kings 22.3,8. and Josias reigning one and thirty years in all, 2 kings 22.1. it follows hence, that Jeremy prophesied eighteen years under Josias.

**Verse 3.** *{It came also in the days of Jehoiakim, the son of Josiah King of Judah, unto the end of the eleventh year of Zedekiah, the son of Josiah, King of Judah, unto the carrying away of Jerusalem captive, in the fifth month}* As in the former verse was related the beginning of Jeremy’s exercising this extraordinary function; with an intimation of the time of his prophesying under Josias: So in this verse is further related the continuance of it, under his successors, unto the captivity that was under Zedekiah, by the space of two and twenty years, see 2 kings 23.31,36. & 24.8,18. which taking in those eighteen under Josias, make up at least forty: whence it may be that Jewish fable, that God should tell Moses of a prophet to come, meaning Jeremy, that should reprove them on this side, and reprove them on that side; that should prophesy forty year one way, and forty year another way; as if he spent in prophesying, as many years after the captivity, as he had done before it.

*{It came also}* Heb. *and it was*: *It was*; as before, ver. 2. *and*, for *also*; as Prov. 28.16. Esay 6.2,3. he had also Prophetical visions, and revelations in those times. See Esay 1.1. & 2.1. Joh. 1.1. & 3.1.

*{in the days of Jehoiakim}* Here question is moved, why Jehoahaz, and Jehoiachin are not here mentioned, as well as Jehoiakim, whereas the one reigned before him, coming between him, and his father Josias: the other succeeded him, coming between him, and his brother Zedekiah. Whereunto the common answer is, that these two are omitted, because they reigned a little above three months apiece, some half a year only; and that at two several times between them, 2 kings 23.31. & 24.8. 2 Chron. 36.2,9. which answer may well serve for the former: concerning whom also it is uncertain, whether any special prophecy were revealed to Jeremy, or delivered by him, in his days. And for the latter, there was no special cause of naming him, whether ought in that kind came out under him, or no; since that his short reign comes within the compass of the two lists, and limits of time here fixed. See chap. 22.11,24.

*{Jehoiakim}* Of this *Jehoiakim*; and his name, see on chap. 22.18. of his wicked reign, 2 kings 23.34,37. & 24.1,6. 2 Chron. 36.4,8.

*{the son of Josiah}* Of whose issue, see further on chap. 22.11,18.

*{unto the end of the eleventh year of Zedekiah}* Heb. *until the eleventh year of Zedekiah was accomplished*; as Lev. 25.29. where there seems to be some diversity of account between this, and that which follows, where the *fifth month* is named; that which comes short by a whole month of the half, by many more of the whole year. But the answer hereunto is easy, that the *fifth month*, though it ended not the year, in regard of its ordinary set, and standing computation, yet it might end the eleventh year of Zedekiah’s reign, having entered about that time thereinto.

*{the son of Josiah}* 1 Chron. 3.15.

*{unto the carrying away of Jerusalem captive}* Heb. *until Jerusalem* (that is, the people thereof) *departed*; or, *went into captivity*; as Judg. 18.30. *unto the day, that the land departed*, or *was captived*. There are two captivities mentioned; the one under Jehoiachin, 2 kings 24.13. the other, under Zedekiah, 2 kings 25.11. and of this the prophet expressly here speaks. Howbeit, the meaning here is, not that the prophet, at this second captivity, ceased prophesying, for it appears that he prophesied afterward, both in Judah, chap. 40.43. and in Egypt, chap. 44. but that he prophesied so long under the state that then stood, when he entered upon that office.

*{in the fifth month}* See on chap. 52.12,15.

**Verse 4.** *{Then the word of the LORD came unto me, saying;}* Heb. *And the word of the Lord was unto me, saying*; as verse 2,11. Jon. 1.1. yet because this seems to have reference to the time of his first call to this office, verse 2. the copulative is not amiss here rendered, *then*; as Exod. 7.9. Esay 36.3,9,11. A change of the person; as Mic. 3.1.

**Verse 5.** *{Before I formed thee in the belly, I knew thee; and before thou camest forth out of the womb, I sanctified thee, and I ordained thee a Prophet unto the Nations}* The words of God to the prophet, acquainting him with his ancient purpose, and determination, to assign him to that office, which he now called him unto. See Esay 49.1,5.

*{formed thee}* Heb. *molded*, or *framed*, and *fashioned* you; as the potter does the clay, whereof he makes some earthen vessel, Gen. 3.7,8. Esay 43.1. & 44.2. & 64.8.

*{in the belly}* In your mother’s womb: so is the word *belly* used, Esay 46.3. & 49.15. He that at first framed man out of the earth, does still frame man in the womb, upon the earth, Job 10.9. and 31.15. Psal. 119.79. and 139.15,16.

*{I knew thee}* I had you in mind, I took special notice of you, as of one to be thus employed. So Exod. 33.12,17. Rom. 8.29.

*{before thou camest out of the womb I sanctified thee.}* The same thing in divers terms; I designed you to be a prophet before you were either bred, or born. It is no more than what the apostle says of himself, that God had *severed him*, that is, in his secret purpose, set him apart, *from his mother’s womb*, unto that ministry, which afterward he called him unto *by his grace*, Gal. 1.15. See the use of the word *sanctify*, Esay 13.3. chap. 12.3. and 51.27,28. which they strain too far here, who, with the Jewish writers, expound it, of a real and actual sanctification of the prophet, by infusion, and collation of spiritual grace upon him, while he was yet in his mother’s womb: which howsoever concerning John the Baptist, the Evangelist, in the Angel’s words to his Father, seems clearly to aver, Luke 1.15. in regard whereof, it is said of him, by some of the Ancients, that he was *new bred, yet unborn*. Yet I suppose it cannot be with good ground, from Scripture, affirmed of any other.

*{and I ordained thee a Prophet}* Heb. *I gave thee*; I assigned, or appointed you so to be; as Esay 49.6. It is in plainer terms, what he had before said of him: the copulative need not be inserted, being not in the text.

*{unto the nations.}* The Jewish doctors have many odd quirks and questions, here, about Jeremy: where, to let pass, what they say of his parents’ preparation to the begetting of him, and the strength of natural constitution designed unto him, and the prediction delivered to Moses concerning him, whereof somewhat before; and that he should prophesy one while to the Jews, another while to the Gentiles: and as long to the one, as to the other. They first move a question, why God should tell him all this, when he called him, concerning his predestination of him unto, and preparation of him for this office, rather than Esay, or any other of the prophets? and to this they answer, that it was to encourage him, because he hung back, and would have excused himself, ver. 6. which Esay did not, Esay 6.8. and therefore needed no such spurs. But then they move a new question, why did not God use the like motives to Moses, who was as unwilling, as Jeremy, to go on God’s errand, Exod. 3.11. and 4.1,10,13. To which they answer, that Moses was a man of greater wisdom, than Jeremy, and knew it well enough of himself: And besides, he had a power given him to work miracles, which Jeremy had not, Exod. 4.2,8. And true it is, that in all likelihood, God used this speech unto Jeremy, to confirm, and encourage him to that weighty work, which he was now about to employ him in; the rather, in regard of his age, being called to it very young; the consideration whereof, made him so loath to come to it, ver. 5. but God neither is wont, nor is tied to use the same ways and means of encouragement, at all times, and upon all occasions, unto all, which at some times, to some he does. Another question they move, why it is said, that God had given him to be a prophet to the nations, when as he seems rather to have been sent unto the Jews? To this, some of them answer, that by *the nations*, are the Israelites themselves here understood, so called; because they walked after the fashions and courses of the nations, and were in that regard, in no other account with God. See Esay 1.4. Chap. 9.25,26. But others of them answer, with the Chaldee Paraphrast, that therefore he is said to be given for a prophet *to the Nations*; because he was to render unto them the cup of God’s wrath, chap. 25.15. and they add withal, some of them, that the particle *unto*, may here signify *against*, as it does, Psalm 51.4. and 56.3. Job 7.20. and 8.4. and that he did prophesy *against the Nations*, or *Gentiles*, it is expressly said, chap. 46.1. as against *Egypt* in that chapter, and chap. 43.10,13. against *Palestine*, chap. 47. against *Moab*, chap. 48. against *Ammon, Edom, Damascus, Kedar, Elam*, chap. 49. against *Babel*, chap. 50. and 51. Howbeit, we need not conceive this so to be spoken of *the nations*, as to exclude the Jewish people; for howsoever God were pleased thus to speak unto the prophet, to let him know what a large and ample commission he was to have, and how honorable an employment, as verse 10. the like whereunto, see Esay 49.6. yet his meaning was not thereby to exempt the Jews from his charge, but to comprehend them, with other nations, therein; as *Jerusalem, and all the Cities of Judah* are mustered among *the nations*, and set in the Front, whom with the cup he is sent unto, chap. 25.15,17,18.

**Verse 6.** *{Then said I;}* Heb. *And I said*. See on ver. 2.

*{Ah, Lord GOD;}* An interjection of grief and complaint; as Josh. 7.7. Judg. 6.22. chap. 4.10. used here by the prophet, in way of introduction to that speech, which he was to make unto God, requesting to be excused, and discharged of an employment of that nature, as both considering with himself the weightiness of the work, 2 Cor. 2.16. and conscious to himself of his own weakness and insufficiency for the performance thereof, and the discharge of the duties therein required, 2 Cor. 3.5. see chap. 17.16. and of Moses the like, Exod. 3.11. and 4.10,13.

*{Behold, I cannot speak}* Heb. *I know not to speak*; as Esay 29.12. *I know not a book*, for, *I cannot read*. See the like, chap. 6.15. and 8.12. I know not how to deliver your message, in such manner, as I should. For it cannot be conceived simply, as if either, in regard of infancy, or dumbness, procured by some casualty, he were speechless, as Zachary, Luc. 1.20,22. for he could not then have given this answer. Nor does his meaning seem to be, that he had some impediment in his speech, as it seems Moses had, Exod. 4.10,14. or that he complains of some moral defect, or default; as Esay seems to do, Esay 6.5,7. but that he was one unfit to speak by way of instruction, and reproof, and that not to one nation alone, but to many, as was intimated in his charge, wanting gravity, and authority, in regard of his age and years especially. See 1 Sam. 16.11. and 17.12,13,42. Psal. 119.141. 1 Tim. 4.12. Tit. 2.15. see also Exod. 6.12.

*{for I am a child}* Or, *a child I am*; for the pronoun demonstrative very frequently supplies the place of the verb substantive: as chap. 3.12. Hos. 11.9. Mal. 3.6. Here the Jewish masters about Jeremy’s words of himself, are at some variance among themselves: for one of their principal doctors (of whom they use to say, that *from Moses to Moses, this Moses* (for that was his name) *had no mate*) tells us, that the ancient Rabbines have a rule, that *the Spirit of prophecy rests not upon any that is not wise, potent and rich*: and yet I suppose Amos was not very rich, when God called him, from being *a neat-herd*, and *gatherer of Sycamores*, to be *a Prophet*, Amos 1.1. and 7.14,15. but *a child*, or *a youth*, therefore cannot be a prophet; because he carries no power or authority with him: and lest this of Jeremy might deceive us, he tells us, that the word *naar*, here used, does not always signify *a child*, or, *a youth*: for it is used of *Joseph*, when he was *thirty* year old: yea, of *Joshua*, when he was near *threescore* year old, Exod. 33.11. But concerning *Joseph*, the great doctor’s memory failed him; he is so called indeed, when he was *seventeen* year old, Gen. 37.2. and *Benjamin*, when *thirty*, at least, Gen. 43.8. See on Esay 65.20. but of Joseph nowhere, at that age: for, as for the place, which not the doctor himself, but his translator directs us to Gen. 42.22. neither is the word there *Naar*, but *jalad*; whence may come our English, *lad*: nor do they speak there of Joseph, according to the age that he was then of, Gen. 41.46. but according to the years that he was of, when they sold him; but those two places, not advisedly looked into, seem to have bred the mistake: and for Joshua it is indeed generally agreed, that he was, at the time here designed, between fifty and threescore: but that term is there given him, as it is oft elsewhere in Scripture; not in respect of age, or years; but in regard of service, ministry, and employment, under another: so the words themselves lead us, as by the hand, there to understand it, calling him withal, *Moses his Minister*; as one, that then waited, and attended upon him, being about thirty year, by the computation of some, younger than Moses: the like use of the term, without reference to age, see Gen. 14.24. Exod. 24.5. 1 Sam. 25.5. and in a place parallel unto that, Esth. 2.2. But so to expound it here, there is nothing either in text, or story, to induce, much less to enforce. And other of the Jewish writers therefore on this place, herein depart from their great doctor, rightly deeming it to have been spoken by Jeremy, in regard of his years; as in respect thereof, not esteeming himself fit to undertake so great an employment, as having not yet, it may be, been inured much unto speech in public, nor likely, when he should speak to persons of place and quality, and concerning such matters, as God’s prophets were usually sent about, to be by any much regarded; and that God endues young ones, as well as old ones, with the Spirit, and gift of prophecy: they instance in Samuel, 1 Sam. 3.1,10,19. and in Daniel, with his three companions, Dan. 1.17,19,20. to which might be added that of Joel, 2.28. wherein God promises to confer of his *Spirit*, whereby his secret Will should be revealed, to *old men by dreams*, to *young men by visions*: howsoever that great master, in the new Israel, seek to shift off the latter branch, by turning it off to the vain visions, and illusions, or delusions of false prophets; as sottishly and absurdly, as some of our grand Sectaries, and affecters of new-lights among us, do pervert the former; as intimating, that the *old* Teachers should but *dream*, and dote, when as their new upstart *younger* ones should have the clear revelations, and see the divine *visions*.

**Verse 7.** *{But the LORD said unto me}* Heb. *And*: the copulative for the adversative: as Esay 66.2.

*{Say not I am a child; for thou shalt go to all that I shall send thee, and whatsoever I command thee thou shalt speak}* The words may be taken two ways: either as spoken by way of injunction; as if it were said, make no such excuses, nor use any such pretences, but do as I bid you, go whithersoever I send you, speak whatsoever I give you in charge: as Num. 22.20,35. chap. 26.2. Mat. 10.27. for the future tense is oft used in an imperative notion, Exod. 20.3,7,13,17. Mat. 19.8. with Mar. 10.19. or, as delivered by way of prediction and promise, as if God had said, talk not of your years, or your inability to speak, you shall be furnished with sufficiency of ability, both to go whithersoever I shall see good to send you, and to speak whatsoever I shall give you in charge. So Exod. 3.12. and 4.11,12. Judg. 6.14,16. Mat. 10.19,20. Mar. 13.11. Luc. 21.14,15.

*{to all that I shall send thee}* Heb. *upon all that I shall send thee*: that is, upon whatsoever errand, and about whatsoever business I shall send you, Esay 55.11. Acts 26.16. yet the particle is sometime used for *unto*; as 1 Sam. 2.11. Psal. 13.6. Esay 13.1. and then the sense will be, unto what persons soever I send you: as Mat. 10.18. Rev. 10.11. this the rather is mentioned, says one of the Rabbines, not amiss, because he was to go to Jerusalem, which was out of his wonted walk, and there deal with the king, and Peers of the Land, that wherewith he had not been formerly acquainted.

**Verse 8.** *{Be not afraid of their faces}* In the former words God gave the prophet assurance of a sufficient supply of parts, and ability for the discharge of his duty: now he gives him further assurance of protection, security, and safeguard, upon the discharge of his duty: the one, to remove all pretence of disability; the other, to free him from all groundless fears.

*{Be not afraid}* As Absolom to his servants, 2 Sam. 13.28. God much more to his ministers and messengers. So ver. 17. Ezek. 3.9. Acts 18.10.

*{of their faces}* Their stern looks, Ezek. 3.9. the wrathful disposition, and affection of men, discovers itself ordinarily in their looks, and their faces, Dan. 3.19. whence the *face* is sometime used for *wrath*, Psalm 34.16. it may be rendered simply, *Fear not before them*, as it is Amos 2.9. or, *at the presence of them*: as Psal. 68.1,8. either when you come to deliver my message to them: as Psalm 119.46. or, shall come to be convented before them, for the delivery of the same, Mat. 10.18,28. But the word seems here to have some emphasis in it, which our version fully expresses.

*{for I am with thee, to deliver thee, saith the LORD}* God’s presence, with his messengers is a guard, and a safeguard all sufficient, against all opposition whatsoever, Psalm 2.3,6. & 23.4. & 27.1. Earthly princes, and Sovereigns, are not wont to go with those whom they send on embassage; God goes along with those, whom he sends, and is, by his powerful protection, at all times, and in all places, present with them. So Exod. 3.12. Deut. 31.6,8. Josh. 1.5. chap. 20.11. Acts 18.10. Heb. 13.6.

**Verse 9.** *{Then the LORD put forth his hand, and touched my mouth; and the LORD said unto me, Behold, I have put my words in thy mouth}* By these words it appears, that that which the prophet here relates, was done in a vision, wherein God appearing in some visible shape to the prophet, did, by this external sign, confirm and obsign to him, both his mission, and commission, to go upon his errands, and the endowment also of speech, and language, conferred upon him, for the delivery of his messages. See the like, Esay 6.7. but that there done by the ministry of an Angel, this immediately by God himself. For there is no ground, with some Interpreters, to induce the employment of any Angel here. And as for those, who with the Chaldee Paraphrast, by *hand*, understand here the gift of prophecy, because of that phrase, *the word of God, by the hand* of such an one, Hagg. 1.1,3. Mal. 1.1. they seem to be out of the way: the word *hand*, there signifying no other, than *ministry*: as it is well rendered, Hos. 12.10. and as it is also used, Esay 37.24.

*{Then}* Heb. *And*: as v. 6.

*{put forth}* Heb. *sent*: or, *sent out*. So 2 Sam. 15.5.

*{touched my mouth}* Heb. *upon my mouth*. So Esay 6.7. or, reached to my mouth: as Judg. 20.41.

*{Behold}* As you see this outward sign; so assure yourself of the thing thereby signified. So Esay 6.7.

*{I have put my words in thy mouth}* That you may be as my mouth to my people, chap. 15.19. God sends no dumb messengers. See the like form of speech, Num. 23.5,16. chap. 5.14. and another somewhat near it, Psal. 40.3.

**Verse 10.** *{See}* As, *Behold*, before v. 9. repeated again for more certainty. So Esay 65.13,14.

*{I have set thee, this day}* Heb. *the day*, for *this day*: and so v. 18. as Psal. 2.7. So, *the year*, for *this year*, chap. 28.16.

*{over the Nations, and over the Kingdoms, to root out, and to pull down, and to destroy, and to throw down, to build, and to plant}* Jeremy’s mission, in general, was before-mentioned: his commission, and the subject matter of it, together with the object, or parties whom it concerned, are more expressly and distinctly, here specified. The object, and parties, whom it concerned, and to whom it was extended, are whole kingdoms, and nations; as Rev. 10.11. the subject matter of it, is referred to two heads, for evil, or for good, to destroy, or to save; by denunciation, and menaces of wrath, the one; by promises of mercy and goodness, the other: both, by publishing that word, by God, put into his mouth; which should as assuredly be fulfilled, and effected, as if the prophet himself had done it, chap. 44.26. and 55.10,11. chap. 5.14. See God expounding himself to the prophet, chap. 18.7,9. and see the like manner of speech, Exod. 8.5. Most absurd, and ridiculous, therefore are those Popish Parasites, that out of these words would bring the Pope’s power of setting up, and pulling down, of kings and princes, and disposing of their kingdoms and Crowns, at his pleasure: a lively character of *that sinful cast-away creature*, as the apostle styles him, that should *lift up himself above every one that is called God*, 2 Thess. 2.4. It was great pity that poor Jeremy had not some one of them about him, to acquaint them with this his power.

*{to root out, and to pull down}* There is a nearness of sound between these two in the original, which might be imitated in our English, if it were rendered, *to pluck up*, (so the word properly signifies, and is so rendered, chap. 31.12.) *and to pull down*: there is in the one, a metaphor taken from husbandry; from architecture in the other, as by their opposites, in the latter end of the verse appears. See chap. 45.4. These terms of destruction seem to be ranked in the first row, because they were to take up the first place in his prophesying. See v. 12,16.

*{to build up}* See Chap. 12.16,17.

*{to plant}* So Psal. 44.2. and 80.8.

**Verse 11.** *{Moreover the word of the LORD came unto me, saying}* This seems at the same time, in the same vision, to have been represented unto the prophet, as well *the Almond-tree rod*, as also, *the boiling caldron*, v. 13. and both at the time of his first calling unto this employment. Heb. *And* (as Esay 8.1.) *a word of the Lord was to me*, as v. 2,3. So Chap. 2.1.

*{Jeremiah, what seest thou?}* This question God moves to him, to stir him up the rather to attend unto, and take special notice of that that was represented unto him; which otherwise it may be, he would have the less regarded. So Amos 7.8. and 8.2. Zach. 4.2. and 5.1.

*{And I said, I see a rod of an Almond tree}* *I see* (to wit, in vision; as Esay 6.1.) *a rod* (as it is rendered, Gen. 30.37.) or, *a staff*, (as Num. 22.27.) *of an almond-tree*: a visible sign for confirmation of what was to be delivered; as Chap. 19.10. Such *a rod*, or *staff*, in likelihood, as was Aaron’s, with leaves at least, if not with blossoms, or almonds, upon it, as his had, Num. 17.8. and such as the hoary head is compared unto, Eccl. 12.5. otherwise he could not so well have discerned it to be a rod, or staff of such a tree. Thus I rather conceive it to have been, than as some of the Jewish doctors deem, without leaf, or blossom; in regard whereof, God should afterward say, that he had guessed well, wanting that that might have readily informed him of what tree it was: and that it may not seem uncouth, that a branch with leaves and blossoms upon it, should be termed *a rod*, or *staff*, we have elsewhere the like, in a place, as some think, alluding to this, where, as it is said, that *violence is risen up to a rod*, or *staff*; so that this *rod*, or *staff hath blossomed*: and the morning of vengeance is therefore *come*, that destruction is approaching, Ezek. 7.10,11. a good comment upon this place. The old Latin renders it, fondly, *a waking rod*: which yet some Popish writers are pleased to applaud; and one of ours, *a watchman’s rod*, as far as that, from the meaning of the word.

**Verse 12.** *{Then said the LORD unto me}* Heb. *And*, as v. 9.

*{Thou hast well seen}* Heb. *Thou hast done well to see*: *Thou hast seen aright*, as, *do well to play*, for, *play cunningly*, or, *skillfully*, Esay 23.16. Psalm 33.3. Ezek. 33.32. and, as *to do well to be angry*, for *to be very angry*, Jon. 4.4,9.

*{for I will hasten my word to perform it}* Heb. *I am waking unto*, or *watching over my word to do it*: the word implies two things, sedulity, and speed. So Psalm 127.1. *Unlesse the Lord do keep the city, the Warder wardeth, or watcheth, but in vain*: and, *Blessed is the man that is watching at my gates daily*, (that is, early there) *waiting at the posts of my doors*, Prov. 7.37. and, *a Leopard shall watch over their cities*, Chap. 5.6. so Esay 29.20. *the watchers of iniquity*, that is, such as pursue it eagerly & with speed, as the words *σπεύδω* & *σπουδὴ* in Greek (which may not amiss be deemed to come from this Hebrew *shakad*, as from the Greek *λύκος*, the Latin *lupus*) imply either. So that the meaning is, that the Lord was busily contriving an heavy judgment, (resembled by *a rod*, or *staff*: as Esay 10.5.) which he would very speedily, very suddenly, bring upon his people. So Chap. 44.27. and there is in the word an allusion to the Hebrew name of the *Almond-tree*, which in that language, has thence its name: because it is wont to bud and blossom, the earliest of any, as the *Mulberry*, the latest. See Pliny, l. 16. c. 25. The like allusion to the name of the thing, in vision represented. See also Amos 8.1,2. In imitation hereof in that tale of Susanna, Daniel is feigned to descant upon the Greek names of the trees there mentioned, v. 54,55,58,59. whence, by some of the Ancients, it is well concluded, that the story was not written in Hebrew, where the words have no such consonance. See the gracious promise of God to his people, upon their return to him, contrary to the heavy doom here mentioned, and menaced, Chap. 31.27. But what was here threatened, see in part, performed, at the death of Josias, a loss beyond esteem; and after it first by the Egyptian king, that pilled and polled the country of their wealth and treasure, 2 kings 23.33,35. and then by the Chaldeans, Syrians, Moabites, and Ammonites, all joining together against them, to work their destruction, 2 kings 24.2.

**Verse 13.** *{And the word of the LORD came unto me the second time, saying, What seest thou?}* Heb. *A word of the Lord was unto me the second time, saying*; that is, a second word, or further speech, was God, in the same vision, at the same time, pleased to make to me, demanding again of me, what I saw: for there is no article here, in the original: nor is the supply of any, needful. So also, v. 11. nor is the pause between the *second time*, and *saying*; but between *unto me*, and *the second time*, to be joined therefore with *saying*. Of the demand, see v. 12. See also, Jon. 3.1.

*{And I said, I see a Seething pot}* Heb. *a pot blown up*: and so made to boil, Job 41.20. Now this *pot*, thus *seething*, or *boiling* with fire under it, is a resemblance of Jerusalem, and of the grievous condition of the inhabitants thereof, which they should be in, during the siege of the city, Ezek. 11.3,7. and 24.3,5. though some would have the analogy consist in the liquor boiling over, out of the pot; and the inhabitants by violence, cast out of the city: but I suppose rather, the miseries sustained within it, here intended. See somewhat the like, Mic. 3.3. Rev. 16.9,11. And thus the people themselves seem to have understood this passage, when in derision, as pointing at this of Jeremy, they say, *This City is the caldron, and we are the flesh*, Ezek. 11.3. Nor is it the flesh, but the liquor, wherein it is sod, that is wont in boiling to run over. Howbeit, by the *pot* some here understand, not the city of Jerusalem, but the Chaldean Army, that should come in like a seething pot full of scalding water upon them, and not upon the city of Jerusalem only, but upon the whole country of Judea: Nor unlike to those *vials*, or *vessels*, that are said to be poured out upon several persons, and places, Rev. 15.7. and 16.1,4,8,12,17. Yea, one proceeds farther, and would have it to be a deep *hearth of fire*, that the Assyrian, Chaldean, and other Asian kings, with whom the *Fire* was esteemed a deity, and worshipped as a God, were wont to have carried before them, and their Armies, when they went forth upon any expedition. Concerning which, divers authors are by him produced: to which, others also might be added. See on Esay 33.14. But I conceive it much safer, to interpret Scripture by Scripture, and one prophet by another, living especially together some part of their time; and having reference, in likelihood, the one of them, to that which had been delivered before by the other. That which moved these Interpreters to step aside here, shall hereafter be met with in its place.

*{and the face thereof was towards the North,}* The words thus rendered, have no good coherence with the foregoing branch; *I see a seething-pot, and the face thereof was towards the North*; a needless insertion disjoining the text: It would be rendered, as the Hebrew, word for word, yields it; *I see a seething pot, and the face thereof towards the North*, or, *with the face of it Northward*; *and*, for, *with*; as Exod. 1.5. Neh. 12.42. Chap. 2.37. Howbeit, in the last words there is a kind of redundancy in the text; for it is, as if it were said; *from the face of Northward*, or, *toward to Northward*: Much the like is, 1 Chron. 26.17. Psal. 9.17. Amos 4.3. Now by the *face* of the *pot*, some of the Jewish doctors understand the *mouth* of the pot; but that simply considered, cannot so fitly be here meant; for the mouth of a pot standing on the fire, looks plumb upward, not to this side, or that side, as did *the mouth* of the bases on which the lavers were set, 1 Kin. 7.31. Other of them therefore by the *face*, would have meant, that side of the pot on which it has a *lip*, or *notch*, or the like; for the more convenient pouring of ought out of it: another, the *ranges*, on which the pot is wont to be set, that fire may between them be kindled, and burn under it: of which, Psal. 68.13. where the words would be read, *though ye have lien between the ranges*; as scullions oft, for warmth do, when the pot is away; and to this last I incline: yet adding withal, that the *mouth* of the *ranges*, or *furnace* either, rather than the *ranges*, or *furnace* itself, seems by *face* to be here designed: more plainly thus, the *pot* appears *boiling*; there must be fire under it to make it boil; this fire, in likelihood, contained within some *range*, or *furnace*; that range, or furnace, must on the one side, at least, have an open passage, whereby to put fuel in, for the feeding of the fire; this open place, is most fitly termed, the *face* of the *furnace*; and why not of the *pot* also, set upon it, and so fastened to it, that it might well seem one with it, I see not; and this looked *northward*, because from thence they were to come, that should kindle the fire under this pot, and so set it on seething: so v. 14. and this takes away the difficulty, that made those Interpreters interpret this *pot*, not of Jerusalem, but of the Chaldeans.

**Verse 14.** *{Then the LORD said unto me;}* Acquainting me with the meaning of this apparition; as before, v. 12.

*{Out of the North an evil shall break forth upon all the Inhabitants of the land.}* *Out of the North*; that is, from Chaldea, and Babylon, situate North from Jerusalem, Chap. 4.6. & 6.1. Ezek. 26.7.

*{shall break forth}* Heb. *shall be opened*, or *let loose*; as Esay 51.14. Thus wicked persons, though never so powerful, yet are kept under restraint, as in bands, until God please to let them loose for the punishment of others, as bad, it may be, or worse, than themselves, Rev. 7.1,3. & 9.14,15.

*{of the land}* Or, *of this land*; for that is the land here pointed at, ch. 25.9. though it be true, that God gave the whole *earth*, or *world*, in those days and parts commonly known, into the hands of the Chaldean king, who did grievously, in all parts, oppress it, ch. 27.6. Esay 14.16,17.

**Verse 15.** *{For lo I will call all the families of the Kingdoms of the North, saith the LORD,}* Heb. *Lo I calling*, or *am calling*, (See Esay 65.17.) *to all the families of the Kingdoms Northward*; that is, I am, by a secret, but efficacious act, and passage of providence, so disposing of things, that all those of several countries, in the Northern parts, under the command of the king of Babylon, shall come together with him, and be subservient unto him, in the subduing, and destroying of this city, and country. See chap. 5.15. & 6.22. & 10.22. & 25.9,26. for that is the manner of God’s call here spoken of. See Esay 46.11. & 48.13. Zeph. 1.7.

*{families}* That is, *countries*, or people of divers countries. See on Ch. 3.14.

*{and they shall come}* At my call; for they cannot but come, whom God so calls, Esay 7.18,19. and 40.26. and 48.13.

*{and set every one his throne, at the entering of the gates of Jerusalem, and against the walls of it, round about, and against all the cities of Judah.}* The end of their coming, to beset, and surprise the cities of Judah, and Jerusalem itself. See Chap. 5.2,4,5.

*{set}* Heb. *give*; as ch. 6.27.

*{every one}* Heb. *a man*; as ch. 6.3.

*{his throne}* His royal pavilion.

*{at the entering of the gates}* Heb. *at the opening of the gates*: the word is used, sometime, for the *door*, or, *wicket*, that in great gates stand open oft-times, when the double *leaves* are shut: sometime, for the *porch*, or *entry*, before a gate; as ch. 26.10. sometime, for the way that lies before it, and leads to it; as Gen. 38.14. Judg. 9.35. 2 Kin. 7.3. See ch. 43.9. and so it is here to be taken: the *gates* being usually the places, against which Besiegers, and Assailants, are wont to pitch, as well to restrain egress, as to make their assaults, Judg. 9.52. See Esay 22.7. There is another sitting of them, not *at*, but *in* the gates of Jerusalem, now surprised and taken, part of it; mentioned, ch. 39.3. which some, amiss, confound with this. The particle *at*, is wanting here; as also, Gen. 19.11. & 43.19.

*{against all the walls of it round about}* Or, *upon*, as some; as v. 14. but here, *against*, rather; because the siege, rather than the surprisal, is here intended, and the straitness of it intimated. See ch. 4.16,17. & 5.6. & 6.22,23.

**Verse 16.** *{And I will utter my judgments against them;}* Or, *pass sentence*, or, *give judgment upon them*; as it is elsewhere better rendered, chap. 39.5. This some expound of a verbal, or vocal denunciation of judgments, by Huldah, Jeremy, Ezekiel, Zephany, Uriah, and others. But it seems rather to import an efficacious, and actual doom, that God would in his own appointed time, pass upon them, and put in execution, by the Chaldeans. See the use of the phrase, chap. 4.12. & 39.5.

*{touching all their wickedness}* Or, *for all their wickedness*; as chap. 35.5.

*{who have forsaken me}* Or, *because they have forsaken me*, so is the relative used, 1 Kin. 15.13. ch. 13.25. See ch. 17.13. & 29.4. or, *whereby they have forsaken me*; as Deut. 28.20. See Esay 1.4. & 65.11. ch. 7.5. & 16.11. & 22.9.

*{and burnt incense unto other gods,}* Or, *to strange gods*, chap. 7.9,18. & 19.4,13. one part of worship put for the whole; as Esay 65.3.

*{and have worshipped the works of their own hands.}* Idols of their own making, Esay 2.8,20. ch. 16.20. and 32.30.

**Verse 17.** *{Thou therefore gird up thy loins,}* The Lord having acquainted the prophet with the subject matter of his message, enough to dishearten and discourage one of more years, and (it may be) of better parts, and more native boldness of spirit, than he, as yet, had; does now, notwithstanding, impose the charge upon him, enjoins him to go readily, and speedily, about it; and withal, promises to furnish him, with an abundant sufficiency of invincible strength, and impregnable protection, against all power whatsoever, that should by any be raised against him.

*{Thou therefore}* Heb. *And thou*: So chap. 6.11. and 7.16.

*{gird up thy loins,}* Prepare yourself for your employment; address yourself manfully, and readily thereunto: A proverbial form of speech, borrowed from the practice of those, who wearing side, and loose garments, as in those parts they much did, and do still, are wont to truss them up, and gird them unto them, when they are about to undertake some journey, or to set upon some weighty, yea, or but ordinary work, Exod. 12.11. 1 king. 18.46. 2 king. 4.29. & 9.1. Job 38.3. & 40.1. Prov. 31.17. Luk. 12.35. 1 Peter 1.13.

*{and arise}* This word does not imply, either any certain posture, at present, of the party spoken to, or import an alteration thereof; but requires only a present and speedy address unto the employment enjoined, setting all other affairs and employments aside. So chap. 13.4,6. Jon. 1.2.

*{and speak unto them all that I command thee;}* Heb. *shall command thee*, or, *shall give thee in charge*. See v. 7.

*{be not dismayed at their faces}* Or, *before them*, or, *at their presence*. See on v. 8.

*{lest I confound thee before them.}* Or, *lest I break thee to pieces*: the word is the very same with the former; and it signifies, sometime, *to dismay*, or *affright*; as Job 7.14. & 31.34. Hab. 2.17. and, *to be dismayed*, or *affrighted*; as Deut. 1.21. & 31.8. Josh. 1.9. chap. 17.18. sometime, *to break in pieces*; as Esay 9.4. and, *to be broken in pieces*; as Esay 8.9. chap. 50.2,36. and in this latter notion, it may well here be taken. Howsoever, it is, as if God had said, be not afraid of them, so as to forbear telling them out of fear, what I bid you, lest I fright you in a worse manner, than they are able to do, so as utterly to destroy you. See Matt. 10.28. Luk. 12.4,5. So dangerous a matter is it, either for fear, or favor, to conceal God’s errand that he sends us on, and not to dare, or not to do our duty, 1 Cor. 9.16.

*{before them}* In their sight; that which befell Uriah, Chap. 26.23.

**Verse 18.** *{For behold,}* Heb. *And I, lo*; or, *As for me, lo*; As if he had said, do you your duty; do as I bid you; and for my part, assure yourself, that I will not fail to make good, what I do by promise engage myself for, unto you. See the like syntax, Gen. 6.17. 1 Chr. 18.2. Esay 65.11.

*{I have made thee this day}* Heb. *given thee*; as v. 5,15. for the word of *giving*, is, in Hebrew, of a very large extent. See ch. 49.15. Ezek. 3.17. & 12.6.

*{a defenced city}* Heb. *for a city of defense*; as Psal. 108.10. ch. 34.7. that is, to be like a city strongly built, and firmly fenced, supported for the structure of it, not with timber, but with iron columns; and environed, not with stone, but with steel walls. See the like Esay 50.7. ch. 6.27. & 15.20. Ezek. 3.8,9.

*{and an iron pillar}* Heb. *for a pillar of iron*: the word *pillar*, here used, has in it a notion of *standing* upright, firm, and fast, 2 Kin. 11.14. and *iron* is used commonly to denote *strength*: hence, *spears of iron*, Job 40.18. and *bars of iron*, Psal. 107.16. and, *a staff*, or, *scepter of iron*, Psal. 2.9. and, *an horn of iron*, Mic. 4.13. and, *a yoke of iron*, Deut. 28.48. ch. 28.14.

*{and brasen walls}* Heb. *for walls of brass*, or *steel*; as the word is oft taken, Psal. 18.34. chap. 15.12,20. So Zach. 6.1. *hills* of such.

*{against the whole land}* There is the generality of his charge; the land, for the inhabitants of it in general, ver. 14.

*{against the Kings of Judah, against the Princes thereof, against the Priests thereof, and against the people of the land.}* Heb. *unto the Kings of Judah, unto the Princes thereof, unto the Priests thereof, and unto the people of the land*; and so it has reference to the former resemblances, I will make you such, or have made you such, as I have said to all these; and the Lord subjoins this particular enumeration, to the former comprisal of them, in gross; partly, thereby to foreshew him, what he was to expect, to wit, that all sorts, and degrees, would be sure to oppose him, and band together against him; (as indeed they did, ch. 11.19,21. & 20.2. & 26.8. & 36.26. & 38.4.) and partly, to assure him, that though they should all join in one against him, yet he should prove too hard for them; they should no more be able to prevail against him, than as if they should push at an *iron pillar*, or a *steel wall*. See our Savior’s words to his, Luk. 21.17,18.

**Verse 19.** *{And they shall fight against thee; but they shall not prevail against thee:}* Heb. *They shall war upon thee*, or, *against thee*; as Jud. 20.11. The text may well be thus rendered, *For though they fight with thee*, or *wage war against thee, they shall not prevail against thee*, or, *with thee*. Heb. *They shall not be able to prevail over thee*, or, *against thee*. So Esay 16.12. Hosea 13.4. The like syntax, see Esay 50.2. & 58.9. Job 13.15. And see the like promise repeated, chap. 15.20. So Psal. 129.2. Esay 7.1. Revel. 17.14. They shall not be able for all their plots, and practices, to take your life away from you; but you shall survive, to see their ruin, chap. 20.10,11. & 26.24. & 39.11,12.

*{for I am with thee, saith the LORD, to deliver thee.}* And that is security sufficient, though all other fail, and all forsake. See verse 8. chap. 20.10. 2 Tim. 4.17,18. for if God be with us, who can be against us? They must prevail first against him, ere they can prevail against them, that withstand, and oppose those whom he stands by to back and protect, Exod. 14.25. 2 Chr. 14.11. Acts 5.39. Rom. 8.31,37.

## CHAPTER 2

**Verse 1.** *{Moreover, the word of the LORD came to me, saying;}* Whether this were the first sermon, that the Prophet Jeremy did directly preach unto the people, is uncertain, though it be the first here upon record: for the main sum, and substance, of those things, in the former chapter recorded, is most concerning the time and manner of his first calling to the office, and such general instructions, that God was pleased then to give him concerning his carriage in it, and discharge of it: which was yet to be divulged by him, to procure credit and authority, unto what he was to deliver, as from God, and in his name, to his people. But in this, according as by God, he was expressly enjoined, vers. 2. he directs his speech unto the whole body of the state, in the name, and as in the person of God, debating the case, and expostulating with them: minding them of his mercies, and favors showed them, taxing them for their base and unworthy carriage toward him, convincing them of their extreme folly and madness, in bringing mischief and misery upon themselves; and forewarning them of the sorry success they should find, by relying on such, as would not be able to relieve them. For the words of this verse, see Chap. 1.11.

**Verse 2.** *{Go, and cry in the ears of Jerusalem, saying,}* *Go*. Heb. *to go*, or *going*; as Esay 20.2. an interchange, as some, of the infinitive, for the imperative; or, as others, a defect of the imperative; which more fully should be, *going go*, that is, be sure you go. See on Esay 59.13. So ch. 3.12. & 19.1.

*{Cry}* Cry aloud; as Esay 58.1. or, *proclaim*; as Esay 61.2.

*{in the ears}* In the hearing; as Esay 5.9. & 22.14.

*{of Jerusalem}* The inhabitants thereof; as Esay 1.27. there, leaving Anathoth, the place of his former abode, he was now to reside, and to preach unto them. See Chap. 1.1. and 37.12.

*{Thus saith the LORD;}* The prophets’ ordinary preface, showing whose message they came with. So Esay 55.1. Ch. 4.3.

*{I remember thee}* Heb. *unto thee*, or, *for thee*; whence arise various opinions, concerning the end of God’s repetition, and mentioning of the ancient matters, that here he minds them of; for some would have it to be for this end, that thereby they might be put in hope of being received again into favor with him, notwithstanding their disloyal, and unworthy carriages; as chap. 3.1. he retaining still in his mind, his kind and loving affection to them, at first; and they suppose therefore some emphasis to be in the particle here used; as the like may seem to be in that, Neh. 13.22. *this also remember for me*: but the very same form of speaking is found elsewhere used, where no matter of favor is intended; as Psal. 137.7. and not far from the former place, Neh. 13.29. where our translators, not amiss supposing the particle to be a mere expletive, render the places; *Remember me* concerning this; and, *Remember them*; and, *Remember the children of Edom*: the likeliest place, that can be produced, seems that, Lev. 25.45. *I will for them remember the covenant of their ancestors*: rendered there, *for their sake*: as by some, *for thy sake*, here. But others suppose, that God’s main end herein, is to aggravate their unthankfulness, and so to amplify the heinousness of their sin, who had carried themselves so vilely, and unworthily, towards him, who had showed so much kindness, and love, unto them. So Esay 63.7,9. Amos 2.9,11. Mic. 6.3,5. And following this, (which I rather incline to) the verb may be taken in a notion of *mentioning*, or *minding* another of somewhat; in which sense the passive form is very frequently found used: and then, if the particle be deemed an expletive, the text may be rendered; *I will mind thee* of *the kindness of thy youth*; as in that former place of Nehemy; and so Psal. 136.23. or, if it seem to be of some force, *I mention unto thee the kindness of thy youth*: I desire to put you in mind of what love and affection I showed, when I first entered into covenant with you, in the very beginning of your being a people, what time you were, as yet, but a young state.

*{the kindness of thy youth, the love of thine espousals,}* How these words, which in our version hang over-loosely, may be aptly kept knit unto the rest of the context, has already been showed. Some refer both branches to the people, as intimating their affection, and disposition to God at first: and so the words should be read; *I remember thee*, for *the kindness of thy youth*; and *the love of thine espousals*: as Mal. 2.5. but that, the main tenor of the story of those times controls. See Deut. 9.6,24. Esay 48.8. Others, divide them between God, and the people, referring the former to him, the latter to them: but they sever things that are not to be disjoined. They only expound the text aright, that ascribe both unto God: yet not as professing still so to affect them, as some would have it, reading them thus; *I remember thee* with *the love of thy youth*, and *the love of thine espousals*; like that, Psal. 106.4. but as minding them only of what love and kindness, he then had showed them.

*{the kindness of thy youth}* Or, *thy childhood*; as it is rendered, Gen. 8.21. but here, rather, *youth*; because speech is here of this people, as of a damosel fit for espousal; the kindness that I showed you coming out of Egypt: that is the time that is so oft termed, sometime, *the birth*, sometime, *the youth* of this people. See Esay 44.2. & 46.3. & 54.6. Ezek. 16.43,60. Hos. 2.3,15.

*{the love of thine espousals,}* The word here used, is nowhere else found; but comes from a term, that signifies *a spouse*, or *a bride*, vers. 32. the love that I bare and showed unto you, when I entered into a solemn covenant with you, and so espoused you to myself, Exod. 19.5,6. & 24.7,8. Deut. 4.20,32,34. & 5.2. & 26.16,17. & 29.10,15. Chap. 31.31,32. Ezek. 16.8,60. Hos. 2.19,20.

*{when thou wentest after me in the wilderness, in a land that was not sown}* Heb. *thy going after me*: whence some would expound it, of her; that is, this people’s pious affection and disposition towards God, in being content to follow his conduct, and keeping close to him, in that tedious and uncouth passage through the waste Wilderness: To which purpose, also, is that alleged, Deut. 32.12. *and there was no strange god with him*: but this, as was before said, the story itself refells, showing in what manner, with murmuring, and repining, they there went after him, and how even there they went on whoring after idols. See Psal. 106.7,32. Amos 5.25,26. As for that of Moses, it intimates only, that God had no coadjutor in the conduct of them, nor that they worshipped no other god, either with him, or in his stead. See Esay 43.12. The words in our version are not amiss rendered; and sweeter, than as some, *how thou wentest after me*; as Lam. 1.9. there is in the text only a defect of the particle frequently omitted; expressed, Deut. 4.21. & 6.7. but omitted, 1 Sam. 15.7. & 27.8. & 29.6. the goodness and kindness is intended, that God showed, in conducting, safeguarding, feeding, and furnishing them with all necessaries, in that wide and waste place, where there was no tillage, nor sustenance consequently, to be had, for the maintenance of man’s life. See v. 6. Num. 20.5. Deut. 8.2,3. & 29.5,6. & 32.10,12.

**Verse 3.** *{Israel was holiness unto the LORD;}* Consecrated and dedicated to God, as his peculiar, Exod. 19.5,6. Psal. 114.2. chap. 31.44. Some suppose an allusion here, as Zach. 14.20. to the inscription on the high priest’s frontlet, Exo. 39.30. but the term is of larger extent; and reaches unto any time, person, place, or ought else, that is consecrated, and set apart for holy uses, or for God’s service, as in a more special manner his. So it is used, Exod. 31.15. Lev. 21.7. & 27.14,23. Esay 23.18. in all which places, and in the like speeches, *holiness* is put for *holy*: the abstract for the concrete; and so here.

*{and the firstfruits of his increase:}* The *and*, here, would be expunged; for it is not in the text, and it makes the reading ambiguous: for the words so read, may bear this sense, that the first-fruits of Israel’s increase as well as himself, were *holiness to the Lord*: which though a truth, yet is not the meaning of the words here. It would rather be read, either by way of apposition, simply, *the first fruits of his increase*: or, (the note of similitude being inserted; as Esay 62.5. & 66.3.) *as, the first fruits of his increase*: which, as other the holy things, being set apart for God, were not to be eaten by strangers, Exod. 22.29,30. & 34.26. Lev. 22.10. Num. 15.19,21. Deut. 26.2,10. Such are all God’s people, his *first-fruits*, Jam. 1.18. his *first born*, Exo. 4.22. Heb. 12.23. See Hos. 9.10.

*{all that devour them shall offend, evil shall come upon them, saith the LORD.}* The words thus rendered, imply nothing less, than that which is here intimated, and intended. For the drift and scope of this passage, is not to show how the case stood now with them; but how, in former times, it had: and the words therefore would be rendered, as the former branch was, in the time past, *all that devoured them, trespassed*; contracted guilt, made themselves guilty of a trespass against God, and liable to judgment, Exod. 4.23. as those did, that ate or devoured ought that was holy, Lev. 5.15. Prov. 20.25. *evil befell them*: none that then wronged them, escaped without some exemplary punishment, Exod. 17.8,14. Num. 21.23,24,33,35. & 25.17,18. & 31.2. Psal. 105.14,15. & 106.11. And there is in the words thus rendered, a secret intimation, that the case was now altered, it was otherwise now with them; strangers now preyed upon them, and devoured them, at pleasure, as if they were some profane, and common thing, that any one might, without guilt, or fear of control, feed upon, might lawfully enough be dealing with, vers. 14,16. chap. 12.10. & 50.7. See Esay 43.28. & 47.6.

**Verse 4.** *{Hear ye the word of the LORD, O house of Jacob, and all the Families of the house of Israel.}* An introduction usual with the prophets, requiring due attention to what they delivered, as not their own word, but the Lord’s. So Esay 1.10. & 38.14. & 66.5. ch. 7.2. & 17.19. & 19.1. Hos. 4.1. *Jacob* and *Israel*, here, one and the same; as Esay 42.24. & 43.1. and, *the house of Jacob*, and *of Israel*, for his posterity; as Esay 2.5. & 5.7. and *all the Families* thereof, for, all the twelve Tribes; as ch. 31.1.

**Verse 5.** *{Thus saith the LORD; What iniquity have your fathers found in me, that they are gone far from me,}* God having before minded them, what kindness he had, at first, showed unto them, and how chary he had been of them; that the equity of his proceedings may the more clearly appear, if he deal otherwise now with them, than formerly he had done, does here challenge them, to show wherein he had wronged them, or broken covenants with them, or given any just occasion to their forefathers to depart from him, and leave him, as they had done. See the like, Esay 1.2,3,18. & 5.3. Mic. 6.3,4. vers. 31.

*{and have walked after vanity,}* That is, after idols, most vain things, that cannot avail them ought, being nothing, but mere *vanity*: the abstract, for the concrete; as Eccl. 1.2. & 12.8. as noting their extreme folly, in forsaking God, to follow such, 1 Sam. 12.20,21. Esay 41.29. & 44.9. chap. 1.16. & 8.19. & 10.15. See 2 Kin. 17.15. So Rom. 1.21.

*{and are become vain.}* Senseless & sottish, in their counsels and courses; like their idols whom they serve, Psal. 115.8. Jon. 2.8. Rom. 1.21,22. The words would be rendered, *what iniquity did your Fathers find in me, that they went far away from me, and walked after vanity, and became vain*; that it have the better coherence with what follows.

**Verse 6.** *{Neither said they; Where is the LORD that brought us up out of the land of Egypt?}* They did not so much as once think thus with themselves; as chap. 5.24. They regarded not to mind him, or make enquiry after him, who had done so much for them, vers. 8. Psal. 14.2. The deliverance of them out of Egypt, is most frequently mentioned, as one of the most remarkable works, that was ever done for any people; and such, as could not but most deeply, and firmly engage, and oblige both them, and their posterity, to serve him faithfully and constantly, who had manifested, and magnified, as well his might, as his mercy, in working so great and strange a work for them, and to cleave close unto him forever. See Exo. 20.2. Lev. 25.38. Psal. 81.10. Esay 63.9,11,13. Hos. 13.4. Mic. 6.4.

*{brought us up out of}* Heb. *made us to ascend*; as Psal. 135.7. as respecting the situation of that place, lying low, and depressed; so some. Or, *that brought us forth*, simply, without any special reference unto ascent, or descent; as the word is oft used, Ezek. 27.22. ch. 50.9. See Esay 52.4.

*{that led us through the wilderness,}* See vers. 2. Exo. 13.21,22. Num. 10.33.

*{through a land of deserts, and of pits,}* Heb. *a land of wastes*; as chap. 50.12. & 51.43. *and of pits*; as chap. 18.20,22. Prov. 22.14. & 23.27. a place destitute of all necessaries, vers. 2. and full of dangerous passages: yet, the word *pit*, is used oft for the *grave*, Psal. 30.3. & 103.4. which may here also be alluded unto; as if it were said, a place where nothing but death (for want of food) and burial, could be expected. See Exod. 14.9,10.

*{through a land of drought}* Where no water was to be had, but what by miracle God afforded them, Exo. 16.3. & 17.3. Num. 20.2,5. Deu. 8.15.

*{and of the shadow of death,}* A land wherein they were exposed to dangers, daily threatening death; as Psal. 23.4. Luke 1.79. See Deut. 8.15. & 32.10. In the word, *shadow of death*, or *deadly shade*, there is allusion, as some think, unto such passages between hilly groves, in desert places, so overspread, and overshadowed, with boughs of trees, that they strike an horror and dread into such as are to pass through them; the rather, in regard of such harmful creatures, as may lie lurking there, and cannot easily be descried, nor avoided, when discovered: such apprehensions, so powerfully working many times upon men, that they seem dead, even before they die. Others, suppose an allusion to the shadow of some trees, deemed dangerous and deadly, not to plants only, that grow near unto them, (see *Pliny, l. 17. c. 12.*) but to men, or beasts, especially, that lie and sleep under them, *Pliny, l. 16. c. 10. Plutarch,* in his *Symposiacks, l. 3. c. 10.* Others, to that cloudiness, that risen before men’s eyes, as overshadowing their sight, when they lie drawing on to departure; or, to the state of *death* itself, that is compared to *darkness*, and conveys the deceased to a place of *obscurity* and *darkness*, Job 10.21,22. where the phrase itself is used; *a shade of death*, for, *a deadly shade*, such as death brings with it; as, *sleep of death*, for, *deadly sleep*, such as death casts men into, Psal. 13.3. See on Esay 9.2.

*{through a land which no man passed through, and where no man dwelt}* A land extremely desolate, either through which none had formerly passed; much less made abode in, or affording neither fit abode, nor convenient passage for any. So chap. 6.8. & 9.12.

**Verse 7.** *{And I brought you into a plentiful country,}* Or, *Yet I brought you*; as Esay 60.10. & 63.11. A change of the person; as Esay 61.7. & 64.4. Heb. *into a land of Carmel*. See of the term, Esay 35.15. and of the land of Canaan, Num. 13.27. Deut. 8.7,9. & 11.10,12. and God speaks here, as if he were parleying with those, that lived in those times, and directing his speech unto them. See vers. 5,9.

*{to eat the fruit thereof}* To enjoy such commodities, as it afforded. So Neh. 9.36.

*{and the goodness thereof:}* As Esay 1.19.

*{but when ye entered, ye defiled my land, and made mine heritage an abomination.}* Heb. *and ye entred, and defiled my land*. See the like syntax, Gen. 14.14. Esay 30.20. & 35.4. & 65.12. & 66.14.

*{defiled my land}* By idolatries, and other wicked courses, Psal. 78.58. & 106.38. ch. 3.1. *my land*. So Lev. 25.23. *the land is mine, and ye are* but *sojourners with me* in it.

*{made mine heritage an abomination.}* So horribly polluted that land, which I had assigned unto you for an inheritance, Psal. 136.21,22. or, as some, that was as dear unto me, and I was as chary of, as if it were mine inheritance, Deut. 11.12. that it became most abominable, (the abstract, for the concrete; as Esay 1.13. & 41.24. So ch. 6.15. & 8.12.) that I could not but abhor it, Chap. 16.18.

**Verse 8.** *{The Priests said not, Where is the LORD?}* They that should have exhorted, and incited others, to mind me, and seek after me, did not at all mind me, or seek after me, themselves. See vers. 6.

*{and they that handled the law,}* The priests and Levites that should so have done; *did*, for, *should have done*: the indicative form in a notion of duty; as the like, Esay 26.9. that should have opened, and taught it to others, Deu. 33.10. Neh. 8.8. Mal. 2.7. Rom. 2.20.

*{knew me not}* They were ignorant of me themselves, whose office was to bring others to the knowledge of me, Hos. 4.6. Luke 11.52.

*{the Pastors also transgressed against me,}* That is, the Governors, both Civil, and Ecclesiastical, say some; or, the kings, and princes: so the Jewish Commenters here expound it; they that should be unto the people, as shepherds to the flock. See Esay 44.28. & 56.11. ch. 3.15. & 12.10. the princes dealt wickedly, as well as the priests, 2 Chr. 36.12,14. ch. 5.5.

*{and the Prophets prophesied by Baal,}* They became Baal’s prophets; they worshipped idols themselves, and taught the people so to do, 2 Kin. 18.22.

*{and walked after things that do not profit.}* Heb. *went after* such things *as will not profit*; that is, *cannot profit*; as Job 15.3. Lam. 4.17. that is, after idols, that could do them no good; as v. 5,11. 1 Sam. 12.21. Esay 44.9,10. Hab. 2.18. a defect both of antecedent, and relative; as Exo. 23.20. 1 Chr. 15.12. And when priests, princes, and prophets, were all so corrupt, what was the state of the people like to be? See chap. 5.31.

**Verse 9.** *{Wherefore I will yet plead with you, saith the LORD; and with your children's children will I plead.}* This some understand of a verbal *pleading*; and expound it of a course that God intended to take still from time to time, by his prophets, to convince them of their sinful & wicked courses, as he had in former ages done, before he would proceed to execute judgment upon them, and that to render them the more inexcusable, see ch. 7.25. 2 Chr. 36.14,15. Others, understand it of a real *pleading*; as Psal. 74.22. Esay 51.22. by inflicting of evils, and execution of judgment: he would further punish them, as he had done their fathers before them, since that they trod in their steps, Chap. 7.26. yea, not them alone, but their posterity also, either the heinousness of their sins deserving no less, Exod. 20.5. & 34.7. or foreseeing that their issue would walk the same way, that they did; as Moses (says the Rabbine) foresaw, what the people would do after his decease, Deut. 31.29. especially being trained up so, as by their parents they were, ch. 7.18. But the former I conceive here more probable, and more proper sense of the place, especially, if it be applied to God’s present debate with his people, which, I suppose, it does alone concern; for it seems to me, as a passage from that former expostulation, that God had before with them, concerning their fathers, what reason they had to leave him, and desert his service; or what occasion he had given them so to do, vers. 5. unto a new debate with them, upon another ground, vers. 10. which he desires may remain upon record unto posterity, to convince them also of the like extreme folly, if they follow their impiety. So that it is, as if he had said, I have argued the case with your forefathers already, let me debate the matter a little further with you; and let your posterity also consider well what I now say. See Deut. 31.19,21. and so is the same word afterward used, for debating the case or pleading, v. 29.

**Verse 10.** *{For passe over the Isles of Chittim, and see; and send unto Kedar, and consider diligently, and see if there be such a thing.}* A new argument of debate God here enters upon with his people: wherein he challenges them to produce any people, in any part of the world, then commonly known, that had dealt with their idols, as they had done with him: the heathen were more constant and faithful to their idols, than they had been to the true God. See the like argument, Mal. 3.8.

*{passe over}* Or, *go over to*; as Esay 8.8. because they were to pass the sea unto those parts. Howbeit, the meaning is not, that they should either make some set journey, or send some messengers on purpose, to make diligent enquiry, how things there went; but that they should consider seriously what concerning them they knew, by report, or otherwise; and withal intimating, that if they should either by journeying themselves, or by diligent enquiry otherwise, endeavor to inform themselves herein, they would find it to be so as he said. See the like, Chap. 7.12. Amos 6.2.

*{the Isles of Chittim}* *The isles*, or *lands*; as Esay 20.6. & 41.1. chap. 47.1. either situate in the midland sea, or coasting on the other side of it more Northward. See of *Chittim*, on Esay 23.1. *to the isles*; as to *Kedar*: a defect of the particle with either; as 1 Kin. 3.15.

*{Kedar}* *Arabia*, that lay Southward from Judea. See Esay 21.16. & 60.4. as if he had said, go which way you will, to any country, North, or South: Yet some suppose that by the *Chittim*, are understood, the more civil people, such as were the Greeks and Macedonians; by the *Kedarens*, people less civil, and more savage, as those Kedarens were, having no certain place of constant abode, See chap. 49.29. For the Rabbines’ dote and dally here after their wonted manner, when they tell us, that these two nations are here mentioned, because the one worshipped the water; and the other the fire; and yet would not these leave worshipping the fire, though they saw that the water put out the fire.

*{if there be such a thing}* Heb. *if*; or, *whether there have been* such a thing *as this*: a defect of the antecedent; as Judg. 19.30. and it would be in the time past, because of that which follows, vers. 11.

**Verse 11.** *{Hath a nation changed their gods?}* Or, *Whether any nation have changed their gods?* Whether the heathen keep not constant to their country idols. See 2 kings 17.29,33. Mic. 4.5.

*{which are yet no gods:}* Heb. *and they no gods*; but mere counterfeit ones, idols, ch. 16.20. Esay 37.19. Gal. 4.8. *and*, for, *yet*; as Esay 60.10. & 63.11. So vers. 21.

*{but my people have changed their glory, for that which doth not profit.}* Heb. *and*; as ch. 1.7. But my people have, not only changed, but made a most foolish exchange; they have put away, and parted with the true God, who was their glory, Psal. 106.20. of whom they had good, and great cause to glory that they had such a God, Psal. 44.8. & 148.14. & 149.2. and who made them truly glorious, Deut. 4.6–8. Psal. 149.4. Esay 1.10. & 60.13. for that which they had just cause to be ashamed of, vers. 26. for a thing of no worth, for that which could do them no good, could stand them in no stead. See before on vers. 8.

**Verse 12.** *{Be astonished, O heavens, at this, and be horribly afraid, be ye very desolate, saith the LORD.}* Some by the *heavens*, here, would understand the angels, as called upon to stand amazed at the extreme folly, and strange impiety of God’s people. But the celestial bodies seem rather spoken to, by a rhetorical elegancy, and form of poetical and pathetical language, oft used in Scripture; as Deu. 32.1. Esay 1.2. as implying that their courses were such, as might justly fill the whole world with astonishment; and that the very senseless creatures, the heavens especially, those glorious ones, were they apprehensive of such things, would abhor them, be aghast at them, and tremble to think what would be the end and issue of them. So rather, then, as some of the Jewish doctors, who following the Chaldee, would have the meaning to be, as if the heavens were called upon, to bewail and lament the desolation of the land, that was to be, the destruction of the city, and the subversion of the sanctuary.

*{be horribly afraid}* Or, *aghast*, Ezek. 27.35. & 32.10. it signifies properly such *a disturbance*, as a strange storm and tempest is wont to affect those with, that are surprised with it: it has some affinity also with the word, that signifies, *hair*, and *hairy*, or *rough*: whereof, see on Esay 34.14. and may imply such an *horror*, as some horrid occurrent is wont to produce; such as would make one’s hair, as we use to say, stand an end.

*{be very desolate}* Or, *utterly dried up*, and *exhausted*; as Esay 19.5,6. withdraw your lustre, lose your light, be clouded, and darkened; as if you were in some desolate estate, in some dismal condition. See Esay 13.10,33. & 24.23. Ezek. 32.7,8. but especially, Mat. 27.45. where the sun, that glorious light, seemed to be abashed, amazed, and aghast, at that transcendent and matchless impiety committed, in putting of the glorious Lord of life, to an ignominious and accursed death, Acts 3.15. 1 Cor. 2.8. Gal. 3.13.

**Verse 13.** *{For my people have committed two evils;}* Two grand, two most notorious evils.

*{they have forsaken me the fountain of waters.}* A well-spring of all manner of good, yielding water, that runs constantly, and never fails, and one that was such incessantly unto them, while they continued loyal, and dutiful to him, Psal. 36.9. ch. 17.13. & 18.14. Joh. 4.14. & 7.38. Rev. 22.1. Of the word, see on chap. 6.7. it is a metaphor taken from waters, arising, and issuing from a spring, that are wont to hold out all the year long, Esay 58.11. and are, in Hebrew, therefore termed, *living waters*, Gen. 26.15. opposed to such waters, as proceed only from some excess of rain, as land-floods, that, showering down from the hills, run, with a violent torrent, in the winter time; but in the heat of summer, are dried up, and fail, Job 6.15–20.

*{and hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water.}* So is it not amiss rendered the more distinctly to design that second evil of the twain, before-mentioned; as the leaving of God all-sufficient, the ever-living, and incessantly flowing fountain of all good, Jam. 1.17. so the betaking of themselves to sorry base idols, unable to do them the least good, that is, to give them so much as a drop of water, when they want it, chap. 14.22. Zach. 10.1,2.
