Howbeit, the words run, in the Hebrew, *to hew them out cisterns*; as the words are rendered, Deut. 6.11. & Neh. 9.25. *to dig them wells*; as if one having his habitation near a fair and clear spring, affording plenty of water all the year long, should abandon the place upon some groundless dislike, and in a fond humor go and seat himself elsewhere, where if he will have water, he must dig for it; and if by digging, he cannot find it, he must dig pits, to keep what comes by rain, or occasionally otherwise: and that which is subjoined, and makes his condition the worse, these wells or pits, when he has digged them, prove faulty; so as they are not able to keep what is committed to them, but it soaks all away, leaving nothing behind but mire and mud, which usually also breeds therein, and noisome savors withal.

*{broken cisterns}* Or, *pits*; it seems to have been a proverbial form of speech; like that, *wells without water*, 2 Peter 2.17.

*{that can hold no water}* Heb. *that will not hold water*; and so we use to say of a cloven dish, or a broken pitcher; *it will not hold water*: when our meaning is, *it cannot*: so vers. 8. *that will not profit*, for, *that cannot profit*. Such *broken pits* are all idols, unable to afford any relief, or refreshing, unto those, that rely on them, Esay 46.7. and not idols alone, but all outward stays whatsoever; that men, relinquishing God, the only sure stay, trust unto, and so make idols of them, chap. 17.5. wherein also this people were faulty, resting sometime upon Ashur, and sometime upon Egypt, that proved *broken canes* to them, vers. 18,36. See Esay 30.1,5. & 36.6.

**Verse 14.** *{Is Israel a servant? is he an home-bred slave?}* The Lord proceeds to show what condition this people had cast themselves into, by forsaking of him, and putting themselves under the protection of others, unable to do ought for them.

*{Is Israel a servant?}* Some take this to be spoken, as if God should demand of them, whether he had used Israel as a slave, and not rather as a *son*, Deu. 8.5. & 32.6. so it should be, as that afterward, vers. 35. Others, rather referring it, to his evil entreaty, and base usage by others; Is he a *slave*, that he is so slavishly used? like that, chap. 49.1. and the Jewish doctors here not unfitly add; How comes it to pass, that he who was in so great respect and reckoning with God, as was related, vers. 2,3. that he accounted him, as his *first-born son*, Exod. 4.22. should now be left unto such a despicable condition, that every one should at pleasure, wrong him, and domineer over him, as if he were a common slave: Though herein they seem to be out of the way, in that they make this the demand, not of God, as the prophet; but of Israel himself, or of the people, which God, by the prophet, should return answer unto, vers. 17.

*{is he an homeborn slave?}* Such an one, as being born in his lord’s, or master’s family, of one that was his slave before, was, in that regard, *a slave by birth*, Exod. 21.4. Lev. 22.11. alluded to Psal. 116.16. these were with the Latins called *Vernae*. So whereas there were two sorts of *slaves, slaves bought with money*, and *slaves born in the house*, Gen. 17.12,23,27. God seems to have here respect unto either; demanding, whether Israel were so impoverished, that by extreme poverty he had been compelled to sell himself for a slave, Exo. 21.7,8. Lev. 25.39,47. or was born in the family, and under the dominion of them that thus tyrannized over him, as having in that regard, such interest in him, and power over him, Esay 26.13.

*{why is he spoiled?}* Heb. *why is he for spoil?* as c. 49.22. Esay 42.24. what is the reason that strangers make a spoil of him, as if they had a good right to, and interest in whatsoever he were possessed of, as the lord or owner has in whatsoever goods, or state, his slave has. See 1 Kin. 20.3,5,6.

**Verse 15.** *{The young lions roared upon him, and yelled.}* Or, *young lions roar aloud over him*. Heb. *Over him young lions roar, give out their voice*; as Psal. 18.13. Amos 1.2. & 3.4. By *young lions* (of the term, see Esay 30.6.) are understood, the kings of Syria, Assyria, and Chaldea; called *lions*, for their fierceness; and *young lions*, for their strength. See chap. 4.7. & 50.17. said to *roar aloud over him*; as a lion is wont to do upon his prey, or over his prey; either when he comes to seize on it, or is already possessed of it. See Esay 5.29. & 31.4.

*{and yelled}* Heb. *give out their voice*; for there is no copulative in the text: this some understand, as of a general, or commander, giving out a command, or some signal, for assault; and it may seem so taken, Joel 2.11. & 3.16. but it is commonly used for any loud cry in general. See Psal. 45.6. Prov. 2.3. Chap. 22.20. & 48.34. Hab. 3.9. *they roar, utter their voice*, for, *roar aloud*, or, *roar hideously*; as, *they make deep corrupt*, for, *they corrupt deeply*, Hos. 9.9.

*{and they made his land waste,}* Or, *have laid his land waste*. Heb. *put his land unto wastness*, or, *desolation*, ch. 4.7.

*{his cities are burnt without Inhabitant.}* Heb. *burnt from no Inhabitant*, or, *from without Inhabitant*; as chap. 46.19. that is, so burnt, that they lie as a waste wilderness; as chap. 9.12. which none can inhabit; and so chap. 9.10. *burnt from no passenger*, or, *from without any passenger*; that is, so burnt up, that none passes by. See of this use of the particle, on Esay 23.1. & 24.10. See of the desolation here mentioned, Esay 1.7. 2 Chr. 28.5,20,21. & 33.11. & 36.6,7,10.

**Verse 16.** *{Also the children of Noph, and Tahapanes have broken the crown off thine head.}* The Egyptians also they make a spoil of you, 2 Kin. 24.33,35. 2 Chr. 36.3. And he says, the Egyptians *also*, as some would have it, because they were a more effeminate people; as if he should say, not the Assyrians only, a manly, and warlike people; but that womanish nation, the Egyptians, with whom the men do women’s work, as *Herodote, l. 2.* But others, rather, because this people was too prone to confide in them; though they got no help, or good, but much hurt and harm, from them, v. 18,36. Ezek. 29.6,7,16.

*{the children}* Heb. *sons*; that is, the inhabitants, or natives, (as *the sons of Jerusalem*, Esay 51.18,20. and, *the daughters of Sion*, Esay 3.16.) of these two principal Egyptian cities; put here, because royal seats, for the whole kingdom, and land of Egypt.

*{the children of Noph}* As, *the children of Eden*, Esay 36.12. Of this city, see on Esay 19.13.

*{Tahapanes}* Or, *Tachapanes*; a famous and principal city of Egypt, ch. 43.8. Ezek. 30.18. so called, in likelihood, from *Tahpanes*, or *Tachpanes*, in Solomon’s time, queen of Egypt, 1 king. 11.19,20. it stood not far from Pelusium. Whence it is commonly termed by the Greeks, and Latins, *Daphnae Pelusiacae*, to distinguish it from another place of that name near to Antiochia, so named from a grove of *laurel* growing there; as *Loretto*, in Italy, has its name from the like. But they are much out of the way, that would render the same reason of the name of this Egyptian city; because the Greeks corruptly so term it, or dream of any laurel grove in those parts. It is supposed to be the same with that called, also, *Hanes*, or *Chanes*, Esay 30.4.

*{have broken the crown of thine head}* So the Jewish masters expound it, taking the word, in the notion of *breaking* asunder; as it seems taken, chap. 11.16. Mic. 5.6. and, he says, say they, *the crown of the head*; because *wounds* on the head are dangerous, those on the crown of it, especially, as cleaving the head asunder, Psal. 68.21. & 74.13,14. the Chaldee does thus paraphrase it, *They have slain thy men of might, and plundered thy goods*. The Greek renders it, *They have known thee, and mocked thee*; in such a notion, as those words are used, Gen. 19.5. & 39.17. and the old Latin, *They have defiled thee to the crown of the head*; which some expound, of no part left free from their filthy lust; as of the Chaldeans, Lam. 5.11,13. Others, of those idolatries, that they were defiled with in Egypt, as well as in Chaldea, chap. 16.13. & 44.17. Others, of abusing them in base manner, and by cruel oppressions, riding over their head, or insulting over their princes, who are as their heads; that, say they, of the Assyrian reached up to the midst of the neck, Esay 8.8. & 30.28. but this should go over the very crown of the head, Deu. 28.43,44. Psal. 66.12. so that no part should go free, from top to toe, from abuse and oppression, Esay 1.5,6. the heads of the people, the princes themselves not escaping, Lam. 5.12,16. But these lay too much weight upon two vicious versions, rendering the verb in such a notion, as it is nowhere found used. Some late interpreters render it, *They have fed upon the crown of thine head*, taking the word in a notion of *feeding*; as it is used, chap. 3.15. Esay 6.13. or, of *depasturing*, rather; as chap. 6.3. with 12.10. and Esay 3.14. they have fleeced you, despoiled you, and eaten upon you; either *fed upon the crown of thine head*; or, *fed upon thee in the crown of thine head*; that is, say they, in the Southern part of you, that lay toward Egypt, situate South from Judea, Esay 30.6. ch. 13.19. the *head* of a land, by a trope; as the *shoulders* of it, Deut. 33.12. or, rather, they spoil and make havoc of you, in the best and principal part of you; as Esay 28.4. and this last, I conceive, to be the genuine sense of the text: a defect of the preposition; as Esay 32.6. & 57.5. and of the pronoun; as Esay 60.4.

**Verse 17.** *{Hast thou not procured this to thyself, in that thou hast forsaken the LORD thy God, when he led thee by the way.}* The Jewish commenters conceive these words to be, as an answer, by God, returned to the people’s complaint, of their present low, and forlorn condition, and God’s neglect of them in it, v. 14. But they seem rather (for those were God’s words, not theirs) an argument, that God uses, to convince them of their extreme folly, in forsaking him, and thereby plunging themselves into such a doleful, and dismal condition. So v. 19. ch. 4.18.

*{procured this}* Heb. *done this*; as chap. 4.18.

*{in that thou hast forsaken the LORD thy God}* It was not his leaving of them, but their leaving of him, chap. 1.16. vers. 13. who leaves none, till they leave him, 1 Chron. 28.9. 2 Chron. 15.2.

*{when he led thee by the way}* Heb. *in the time*, wherein he was *leading thee on the way*: a defect both of the relative, and of the verb substantive; as Gen. 30.4. That by his providence governed you, and led you on in safety, protecting you from all evils, while you followed his conduct, and would so have done still, had you not forsaken him, and refused to have been conducted by him, Psal. 91.1,13. Esay 58.8,11. or, who prescribed you a way, and course of life, to walk in, which if you had observed, you had been safe and successful, Psal. 81.13,16. Esay 48.18,19. & 64.5. Ezek. 20.10,11. But the former here rather, because it alludes to the conduct of them in the wilderness, Exo. 13.21. Esay 63.12. v. 2.

**Verse 18.** *{And now what hast thou to do in the way of Egypt, to drink the waters of Sihor; or, what hast thou to do in the way of Assyria, to drink the waters of this river?}* God here instances in, and twits them with, two of their cleft cisterns, or broken wells, whereof, albeit, they had proof enough formerly, how little good they had gained, or gotten, by seeking to them, and making use of them, yet they would needs be running after them still. See 2 Chr. 28.16,20. Esay 30.1,7. & 31.1,3. & 36.6.

*{now}* Having before so oft had experience of the ill success of such courses, v. 36.

*{what hast thou to do in the way of Egypt}* Or, *with the way of Egypt*; as the particle is rendered, Psal. 147.20. Heb. *what to thee, to the way!* So 2 Sam. 16.10. *what to me, and to you?* for, *what have I to do with you?* and, *what to me, and to thee?* for, *what have I to do with thee?* 2 kings 3.8. See the like, Mark 1.24. & 5.7. John 2.4. only there is here a defect of the copulative: what need or occasion have you to send, or to travel, into Egypt? like those, Numb. 14.3,4.

*{to drink the waters of Sihor}* Of Nilus, the river of Egypt, Amos 9.5. so called, of its blackness, by reason of the mud and slime, that it brings down with it, wherewith it battels their grounds; Or, as some, by reason of the black color of the grounds and lands it passes through, which yet comes, in effect, home to the former; for such stuff must the river of necessity bring down with it, as is the land that it passes by. See on Esay 23.3. and it seems very strange, that some granting *Sihor*, to be Nilus here, should strain it to be some small rill, or rivulet, elsewhere; as Joshua 13.3. 1 Chron. 13.5. To *drink the water of Nilus* in Egypt, is put here, for to seek help and relief there. But he delivers it, in these terms; as if he should say, that they could have nothing to do there, or no errand thither, unless it were to drink of the puddle water of that river, when they had, or might have had, as good, yea, far better than that, nearer at hand, at home. See chap. 18.14. So 2 Kin. 1.3.

*{or, what hast thou to do}* Heb. *and*; the copulative in a disjunctive notion; as Esay 48.5. & 58.13.

*{in the way of Assyria}* Or, *with it*, is before.

*{to drink of the water}* To seek aid, either of them, or their idols, 2 Chr. 25.14,15. & 28.23.

*{of the river}* Euphrates, the river of Assyria, Isaiah 8.7. in way of eminency so termed, Psal. 72.8. Isaiah 7.20. See Gen. 15.18.

**Verse 19.** *{Thine own wickedness shall correct thee,}* That is, as some, your courses, without any further dispute, or debate, give in evidence sufficient to convince, and condemn you; as Esay 3.9. Hos. 5.5. but the words would rather be read, *Thine own wickedness might correct thee*; your bad courses proving such, as they have formerly done, might be (one would think) sufficient to reclaim you, and amend you, to make you abandon them, and be fearful of returning again to them. See Hos. 2.7.

*{and thy backslidings shall reprove thee.}* You must taste the bitterness of your wicked courses, you must feel the smart of them, before you will wax wise, Esay 28.19. Job 33.14,22. a note of a servile and base disposition, Prov. 20.30. & 29.15. or, rather, as before, *thy backslidings*, or *perverse courses* (as ch. 5.6. & 14.7.) *might reprove thee*, or, *convince thee* (as Job 6.25.) might, by convincing, instruct you, and teach you more wisdom; as ch. 6.8.

*{know therefore, and see}* Heb. *and*, (as Ch. 1.17.) *know and see*; as 1 Sam. 12.17. that is, *take notice*, (as v. 2.) and *consider*: as v. 31. weigh well with yourself, what it is, that has brought all these evils upon you; for by your own experience, you cannot now but know it; as *knowing* is taken, Gen. 22.17. 2 Cor. 5.21.

*{that it is an evil thing, and bitter, that thou hast forsaken the LORD thy God,}* As before, v. 17.

*{evil}* Not in a moral, but in a natural notion; though true in either: but this here, not that, intended; such as procures evil of punishment, and misery: as, *I create evil*, Esay 45.7. and, *evil befell them*, vers. 3.

*{bitter}* Such as brings *bitter*, that is, grievous, distasteful, ill-pleasing things, upon you. So the word, *bitter*, is commonly taken, Ruth 1.20. Prov. 21.6. See ch. 4.18.

*{the LORD, thy God,}* Me, who am the Lord your God: the noun, for the pronoun; as Esay 2.1.

*{and that my fear is not in thee;}* *My fear*, for, *the fear of me*; as, *thy fear*, for, *the fear of thee*, Psal. 5.7. and, *his fear*, for, *the fear of him*, Job 3.11. and, *his knowledge*, for, *the knowledge of him*, Esay 53.11. See ch. 5.22,24. the want of this fear, the ground of all sin, and cause of all evil, Gen. 20.11. Psal. 26.1. Mal. 3.5. Rom. 3.15,18.

*{is not in thee}* Heb. *unto thee*: but so the particle is also used, Gen. 24.45. 2 Kin. 7.12.

*{saith the Lord GOD of Hosts.}* See Esay 1.24. & 10.24.

**Verse 20.** *{For of old time I have broken thy yoke, and burst thy bands; and thou saidst, I will not transgress.}* Or, *when* (as Psal. 72.2. Joel 2.20.) *of old* (as Esay 63.9,19.) Or, *For when of old, I brake thy yoke, I burst asunder thy bands, thou saidst, I will not transgress*. See the like syntax before v. 7. when I brake the yoke that the Egyptians had laid upon you, Exo. 1.11,13,14. and dissolved those bands, wherewith it was so fastened unto you, that you were not able to shake it off, (See Esay 10.27. & 58.6.) when I set you free from the Egyptian bondage, when I brought you out of Egypt, v. 6. Psal. 81.5,6,10. you did then by solemn promise engage yourself to yield obedience to me in all things, and not willfully to transgress my commands, in ought, Deu. 5.27. & 26.17. & 27.10,26.

*{yoke}* For servitude and thraldom, Esay 9.4. Chap. 28.2,10,14.

*{bands}* An allusion, either to such bands, as captives, prisoners, or slaves, are wont to be kept in, Chap. 39.7. & 40.4. or to such as the yoke is wont to be fastened with, unto the neck of the beast that draws in it. See Esay 58.6. Chap. 30.8. Lam. 1.14.

*{I will not transgress.}* Or, *I will not serve*; to wit, any other god, but you alone, Exod. 20.3,23. Josh. 24.16. Psal. 81.9. Ezra 10.12. for there are here two divers readings; arising, as in divers places elsewhere, from the affinity in shape of two Hebrew letters, by the easy mistake of the scribe’s eye, or the sudden slip of his pen, put oft the one for the other. So *Diphath*, for, *Riphath*; and, *Rodanim*, for, *Dodanim*, 1 Chr. 1.6,7. with Gen. 10.3,4. and *Hadareser*, 1 Chron. 18.3. for *Hadad-eser*, 2 Sam. 8.3. the like in this word, see Chap. 15.14. that which our version has, seems the right reading, and is owned by the Jewish critics: for as for the ancient Greek, and old Latin, who following this latter, render the words, *Of old thou hast broken thy yoke, and burst thy bands* (as chap. 5.5.) *and saidst, I will not serve thee*, like those, Psal. 2.3. Luke 19.14. they alter much the rest of the text, where no variety of reading is.

*{when upon every high hill, and under every green tree, thou wanderest, playing the harlot.}* *When*; or, *but*; or, *yet*; as Esay 31.4. & 49.25. Notwithstanding these your engagements to me, you deal most disloyally with me, leaving me to run after your idols, and in every place that you take liking to, and deem fit for your purpose, defiling yourself with them, see Esay 57.5,8. chap. 3.2,6. after the manner of the heathen people, Deu. 12.2. 2 Kin. 17.9,11.

*{high hill}* Where they had their high places, Psal. 78.57,58. Ezek. 20.28,29.

*{green tree}* Or, *flourishing*, goodly, thick, shady, shroudy tree, Eze. 20.28. Hos. 14.13. So 2 Kin. 16.4. Psal. 37.35. & 52.9. ch. 11.16. & 17.2,8. Cant. 1.16. *Our bed is fair and flourishing*. He has an eye as to their high places, so to their groves, Deut. 7.5. & 12.3. & 16.21. See Esay 17.8. & 27.9.

*{thou wanderest}* You go astray from him, unto whom you had by covenant joined yourself, (see on Esay 57.8.) and run on madding, and gadding, after idols: the word signifies, *to travel*, or, *journey*; or, *go to and fro*, Esay 63.1. properly, from one’s own place, or seat, into some strange land, or foreign parts, Esay 51.14. Jer. 48.12. these are all the places where it is found.

*{playing the harlot.}* Committing whoredom: so is idolatry commonly styled in Scripture, ch. 3.1,2. Ezek. 16. & 23. Hos. 1.2. & 9.1. the reason you have before, vers. 2.

**Verse 21.** *{Yet I had planted thee, a noble vine, wholly a right seed.}* I settled you, at first, in a right and goodly church-constitution; both free from all superstitious, and idolatrous services, and so molded, as was most seemly, and sightly.

*{Yet I had planted thee,}* Or, *And I did then plant thee*, Exod. 15.17. Psal. 44.2. & 80.8. Esay 5.2.

*{a noble vine}* The church of God is, in Scripture, frequently, compared to *a vine*, or *vineyard*, Psal. 80.8. Matt. 21.33. Mark 12.1. Luk. 20.9. See Esay 5.1. & 27.2. Howbeit, the word, *vine*, is not here in the text: the Hebrew is no more than *sorek*; which some therefore understand of the place where it was planted. I planted you, in *Sorek*, in *a choice place*; for not vines only, but other things; as silk, or fine linen, such as lawns, and the like, have this attribute given unto them. See Esay 19.9. and that from a place so termed, Judg. 16.4. some choice kind of vines had this name, it is commonly deemed; and the word might be used, as *Carmel*, v. 7. more generally, for other the like: as also it is apparent, that the place is commended for a rich and choice place, wherein God seated his people, Exod. 15.17. Esay 5.2. but the *sorek*, is in the latter place distinguished from the seat, or soil, wherein it was planted. See Esay 5.3. The most therefore refer it, not to the place, but to the plant: and of these, some read the words with a note of similitude; as, *sorek*, as, *a choice vine*. I had as much care, in planting of you, as a man could have of the choicest vine, or plant, that could be, Esay 5.3. & 17.11. & 27.3. Some, *I planted thee for a Sorek*, for *a choice Vine*; I so planted you, that you might prove such an one. Others, lastly, with *sorek*, that is, with plants, or *slips*, of *sorek*; such as come thence: as for choice slips, and plants, curious people are wont to send far and near, Esay 17.10. and such slips are termed *serukim*, as slips of *Sorek*, Gen. 49.11. Esay 16.8. and this best agrees with that parallel place, Esay 5.3. that which I conceive to be meant principally of these ordinances, that God, by Moses, settled among them, when he molded them first into a church, and state. See Esay 44.2.

*{wholly a right seed.}* Heb. *all of it a seed of truth*: *a seed of truth*, for, *a right, true, genuine*, or, *generous*, no bastardly, no counterfeit *seed*; as, *men of truth*, for, *true*, and *trusty*, Exod. 18.21. Neh. 7.2. and God is said to have given his people in Mount Sinai, *ordinances right, and laws of truth, and statutes, and precepts good*, Neh. 9.13. and it is the usual epithet, that the psalmist gives unto God’s word, and ordinances, that they are *all truth*, Psal. 119.142,151,160. and they are the *seed*, wherewith God set, or sowed his church, Matth. 13.24,27,37. Luke 8.5,11. for *seed* is used in a large notion, as well of slips that are set, as of seeds that are sown. See Esay 17.10,11. I suppose therefore the words would be rendered, with *seed all of it right*, or *true*: the particle *with*, is oft suppressed; as Esay 17.10. Yet some read the words, *whose whole seed* might be *truth*; that is, say they, *whose fruit* might *all* be *firm*, or *sure*; from which he might certainly expect good fruit; as Esay 5.4. But *seed*, for, *fruit*, seems to sound here somewhat harsh.

*{How then art thou turned into the degenerate plant of a strange vine unto me?}* By what means is it come to pass, that you are so strangely altered and changed? For it is spoken by God, in way of admiration, as wondering at the sight of so uncouth an alteration. See the like, Esay 1.21. and of this affection attributed to God, Esay 59.16.

*{How then}* Heb. *And how*; as ch. 1.12,14. Esay 40.18.

*{art thou turned unto me?}* Or, *turned me?* for there is an elegant redundancy in the word, *to me*, very familiar, not in Hebrew only, but in other languages also, and in our own. So, *I will go me*, Cant. 4.8. and, *Go thee*, Gen. 12.1. Cant. 2.10. and, *Stay ye*, Gen. 22.5. *he shall flee him*, Esay 31.8. See vers. 22. chap. 5.5. & 12.8. & 16.20.

*{into the degenerate plant}* There is neither *into*, nor *plant*, in the text; but some such supply is needful of either: the term used here, is an adjective plural: it has in it a notion of *revolting*, or, *departing*, ch. 17.13. for it is found only in this form here, and there: it is not amiss rendered *degenerate*, but must have some plural substantive joined with it; it may be rendered *degenerate* slips: so *a strange* vine, or plant, Esay 17.10. where see many instances of the like defects.

*{of a strange vine.}* Strange plants, and seeds, are sometime mentioned, in way of commendation; because such are usually rare, and choice ones. See Esay 17.10. but here, in way of discommendation, not having so much relation to foreign parts, (though in that kind also *strange* fashions, and services, were reprovable in God’s people, Esay 2.6. Zeph. 1.8.) as in way of opposition to such slips, and plants, as God had planted his vineyard with; that slips of *Sorek*, should prove slips of *Sodom*, Deut. 32.32.

**Verse 22.** *{For though thou wash thee with nitre, and take thee much soap, yet thine iniquity is marked before me, saith the LORD.}* Though you use all the means, and courses you can devise, either to cleanse, or to clear yourself; yet the foul blotches of your wickedness, sticking fast upon your soul, will appear still, as fresh, as ever in my sight; nothing will avail you, either to free you from the filth, and guilt of them; or to secure you from my wrath.

*{For though}* Or, *Although*: for so much the two particles jointly signify; and the words seem to be, not so much any rendering of a reason of the foregoing reproof, as a passage unto a further conviction of her, by removal, and rejection of such colorable pretences, as God’s people imagined to purge themselves with.

*{wash thee with nitre}* The Hebrew word used here, and Prov. 25.20. is that, from whence the Greeks, Latins, and we, have the name of this material, of singular use; not only for the scouring of apparel, and taking out of stains, and blotches, from clothes; but for the clearing of the skin, and taking spots and freckles away from the body. Of it, see *Pliny, l. 31. c. 10.* and it is deemed therefore by some, to have its name from a word, that signifies to *loose*, or *dissolve*, Habak. 3.6. because as *vinegar* dissolves it, Prov. 25.20. so it *dissolves*, and *looses*, from clothes, and bodies, any foul and filthy matter.

*{take thee much soap}* Heb. *multiply to thee soap*: *to multiply soap*, for, *to use much soap*: as, *to multiply prayer*, for, *to make many prayers*, Esay 1.15. *to multiply gifts*, for, *to offer many gifts*, Prov. 6.35. *to multiply songs*, for, *to sing many songs*; or, *to use much singing*, Esay 23.16. *to multiply medicines*, *to use many medicines*; much physic, ch. 46.11. *to multiply cities*, for, *to build many cities*, Hos. 8.14. *multiply to thee soap*; that is, *use much soap about thee*; or, *use thee much soap*: by a familiar and frequent redundancy, as our version seems to have taken it: whereof, see on v. 21.

*{soap}* So some of the Jewish doctors, by a foreign term, expound it: But others of them say, it is a kind of herb; (with whom the old Greek, and Latin, concur) which fullers much use, being of the same nature, and efficacy, with *niter*, and *soap*: it seems to be that which the Greeks call *struthium*; the Latins, *radicula*; some later ones, *saponaria*, or, *soapwort*. Of its singular quality in this kind, see *Pliny, l. 18. c. 3.* Howbeit, others suppose it to be a kind of mold, such as we call *Fuller’s-earth*; and one of the Jewish masters would have it to be *alum*; that it was of much use with fullers, for the scouring of clothes, is apparent, by Mal. 3.2. it is called sometime, *bor*; as Job 9.30. Esay 1.25. sometime, *borith*; as in Malachy, and here; from a word that signifies, to cleanse and purify. By these natural means of abstersion, and cleansing, some understand here all rites of expiation, either religious, as ablutions and aspersions, Num. 19.9,10,12,18,19. Heb. 9.10,13. oblations, and sacrifices; to this purpose applying that, 1 Sam. 3.14. Heb. 10.1,2. or superstitious, by the use whereof they imagined their sins to be all wiped away; and themselves made as pure, and clean, as if they had never done ought amiss, Chap. 65.5. & 66.17. Others, all those colorable pretexts, and pretences, whereby they sought to smooth over their wicked courses, and to extenuate, at least, the guilt of them, if not wholly to excuse them. See vers. 23,33,35.

*{is marked}* This word being here only found, is by interpreters therefore very diversely expounded. Some render it, *it is revealed*; it lies open before me, Job 34.21,22. Prov. 15.11. Heb. 4.12,13. Others, *it is written*; it remains upon record with me, Deu. 32.34. Job 14.17. Esay 65.6. Hos. 13.12. but these give no reason why they so render it: the word *cetem*, whence it seems derived, does in Scripture signify, *fine gold*, or, gold of special note, Job 28.16. & 31.24. whence some render the word, *it shineth, it glisters*, like gold: a very unfit form, to express the filthiness and foulness of ought: another therefore, carrying on the sentence, *Though thou wash thy self with nitre, and use much sope about thee, and thine iniquity gild* itself *over, with the finest gold before me*: yet *how canst thou say I am not polluted?* This course of the context should we admit, I should rather conceive the word to be taken in that sense, wherein it is, by the Arabic interpreter, commonly used, for to *conceal*, or to *hide*; Luk. 1.24. 2 Cor. 4.3. *though thine iniquity conceal it self*: though you seek to hide, and conceal it, all that possibly you can, Job 31.33. Psal. 32.3. Prov. 28.13. But I suppose that the context rather runs the other way aright: the word *cetem* therefore has in the Chaldee, and Syriac, another notion, wherein it is among the Jewish doctors very frequent: for it signifies with them, either *a spot, a blot, a blemish*, cleaving to the skin; as Jam. 3.6. in the Syriac version; or, *a mark, a brand*, entering deep into the flesh; as in the same, Gal. 6.17. Hence, some render it, *it is exceedingly*, or, *remarkably foul*, or, *filthy*: the old Greek, and Latin, *thou art bespotted with thine iniquity*; but this the text will not so well bear. Others, *thine iniquity is deeply imprinted upon thee*; as Chap. 17.1. Either of these last, or both (the word it seems to come of comprehending both) may well be received; your iniquity is so exceeding foul, and it cleaves so fast to you, and has entered so deep with you, that no niter, or soap, no washing you with these, or the like, that is able to fetch it off, or get it out. See Job 9.30,31. Howbeit, a learned late writer, rejecting all other interpretations, would have it rendered; *thine iniquity is laid up before me*, producing, and drawing hither, as a parallel place, that of Moses, Deut. 32.34. *This is laid up before me, sealed up in my treasures*; that of Job 21.9. *God will hide* (that is, lay up) *his iniquities for his sons*; that of Hos. 13.12. *Ephraims iniquity is tied up* (as money is in a pouch, or purse) *his sin is hidden*; that is, laid up in God’s mind and memory: the main ground of this interpretation, here, is, because the Arabic word, *chetem*, signifies *to hide*: so found used in the Arabic, Psal. 50.14. Luk. 1.24. & 8.17. 2 Cor. 2.3. Heb. 4.13. And this I shall leave to the judgment of the learned: only adding, that yet, to me, the proportion, and opposition, seems to be more natural, and familiar, between *washing*, and *scouring*; and remaining still *deeply stained*, than between *washing*, or *scouring*, and being *laid up*, or *hid*.

*{before me}* Or, *in my sight*; howsoever, you may, either sooth up yourself in your sin, or delude others with vain pretences; yet you cannot blind, or blear mine eyes. I see your filthiness, as it is, Gal. 6.7. Heb. 12.13.

**Verse 23.** *{How canst thou say, I am not polluted?}* How can you be so shameless, as to offer, or assay once, to clear yourself, when as your wickedness is so evident? See Prov. 30.20.

*{canst thou say}* Heb. *wilt thou say*; but the word is in a potential notion, as other the like, v. 23. Esay 49.15. Ch. 11.12. Yet some render it not amiss, *How darest thou say?* See the like, Esay 10.14. & 36.9. Zach. 1.21.

*{polluted}* As an adulteress, Numb. 5.20.

*{I have not gone after Baalim?}* Or, *I do not go after Baals*; as answering to that charge against her, of running, and gadding to and fro, vers. 20. by way of denial; as after also, vers. 35.

*{Baalim}* Or, *Baals*; the word *Baal*, signifying properly, *a Lord*, *Master*, or *Owner*; and in the next place, an *Husband*, as such to her, that is joined to him in wedlock. See on Esay 46.1. it was a term that they commonly gave unto idols, Hosea 2.16,17. and the name was therefore common unto many of them: hence *Baal-Peor*, Psal. 106.28. and *Baal-Zebub*, 2 kings 1.2. and the like; and in the plural, comprehending the whole crew of them, *Baalim*, or *Baals*, Judg. 2.11. Hosea 2.11.

*{see thy way in the valley,}* God, because she so pleaded not guilty, points her, as with the finger, unto those particular places, where she had with her idols, defiled herself. So Chap. 3.2.

*{thy way}* *way*, for course, or carriage; as Psal. 1.6. Esay 55.7. for those Rabbines seem here to go out of the way, that would here have meant *a path*, that should be made by her frequent passing to and fro.

*{in the valley}* The valley over against Beth-Peor, in the plains of Moab, from whence they went up to worship Baal-Peor, Num. 22.41. & 23.28. & 25.3. So some of the Jewish doctors, following the Chaldee paraphrast. That of the sons of *Hinnom*, say others, where they burnt their children in sacrifice, Chap. 7.31. as pointing her to the bones of them that lay there. But the term seems more large, as was also their practice. See Esay 57.5,6. for the Jewish doctor seems over-nice here, who having moved the question, why God should bid her look to her way in the *valley*, whereas before she was charged with sacrificing on the *hills*, vers. 20. makes answer; First, that a way is not so easily seen on the hill, being oft stony, and rocky, Prov. 30.19. as in the vale; as if paths were not as visible on the one, as in the other: And secondly, that the way in the valley, was for no other end, but to go up to the hills, to sacrifice there: whereas by that place of Esay it appears, that they exercised their idolatries, as well by the brook sides in the vale, and where they had shady trees growing, as well as upon the top of the hills.

*{Know what thou hast done}* Or, *take notice what thou dost*; as v. 19. Ch. 3.13. Prov. 27.23.

*{thou art a swift dromedary, traversing her ways}* Or, to make the context run on the more smoothly; *take notice what thou dost*; how you are as *a light dromedary, that traverseth her ways*: the note of similitude is oft omitted; as Psal. 11.1. Esay 21.8. v. 3. and thus the Jewish doctors, with the Chaldee paraphrast, read it. Or, as some, *O thou swift dromedary, that traversest thy ways*: *her ways*, for *thy ways*; a change of the person, as Job 18.4. *O thou that tearest his soul*, for, *that tearest thy soul*.

*{dromedary}* Of this beast, see on Esay 60.6.

*{swift}* Heb. *light*; as Esay 19.1. and the word may well be here retained, as it is, ch. 3.9. & 4.14. though what the Rabbines here tell us of the female, in this kind, being lighter, and swifter than the male, seems but a fable. Of the female the prophet speaks, for another cause; as the like, vers. 24.

*{traversing her ways}* The word is nowhere else read; that it comes from, signifies *a shoe-latchet*, Gen. 14.23. Esay 5.27. hence some render it, *retaining her ways*; keeping still to her wonted guise; as the latcher, say they, keeps the shoe fast to the foot. Others, *dilating*, or *explicating*, your way; so the ancient Greek, and old Latin: that is, running at large, and ridding your way, at pleasure; as alluding to the loosing of the latcher, Mark 1.7. Others, *latcheting*, or, *delineating*, your *way*; that is, as by your loose latchet, or somewhat that you draw after you, or drops from you; so *marking* the way along, as you go, that you may thereby be traced: that which the Chaldee paraphrast may seem also to hold out, who renders it, *marring*, or *defiling*, your *way*; using a term, from whence, in the Chaldee, is a word deduced, that signifies *dung*, and other like filth. Others, lastly, and so some of the Jewish doctors, *doubling*, or *implicating*, and *entangling*; or, as our English exceedingly well, *traversing thy ways*: as the *latchet*, to fasten the *sandal* to the foot, is drawn over and over; or, as the *shoe-latchet* is tied up in knots, and so drawn several ways, to make the shoe sit fast to, and even on, the foot: and it is an allusion to the manner of the *dromedary*, and other beasts of the like kind, left at large, whose females, in gendering time, being mad for the male, run in a confused manner to and fro after them, and one while after one of them; another while after another: not unfitly resembling the practice of this people, that, being mad upon their idols, thought they could never have enough, or enough of them, and were continually therefore running after some one, or other of them, and much pleasing themselves in variety and change. See vers. 28,36. chap. 11.13. Ezek. 16.25,29. & 23.5,20. I shall subjoin yet, what I find lately in a learned man’s annotations; he would have it to be rendered, either from an Ethiopic word, signifying, *late*, or *at even*, Matt. 28.1. Mark 13.35. *that belateth*, or, *benighteth*, her *ways*; alluding to the nighttime, wherein wild beasts stir abroad, Psal. 104.20. (but that is spoken of beasts of prey; whereof this is none) and loose people look out, Job 24.15. Prov. 7.9. or from an Arabic term, signifying, *a companion*, or, *partner, that maketh her ways common*; like a common harlot, promiscuously admitting all comers, Ezek. 16.25. But these I leave as conjectures to be deemed of by others.

**Verse 24.** *{A wild ass used to the wilderness, that snuffeth up the wind at her pleasure;}* To the former similitude of the dromedary, he adds this of the wild ass, as wild, and as wanton, as the other; and such as there is no restraining of, from her wild vagaries, or surprising of her, save when she goes great with young.

*{A wild ass}* Some, to join this to the former, render the words, *A wild ass* she is; and then, why not rather, as before, *A wild ass* you are; or like *a wild ass*; as, *a lion’s whelp*, for, like *a lion’s whelp*; and, *a strong ass*, for, like *a strong ass*; and, *a serpent*, for, like *a serpent*, Gen. 49.9,14,17. or, following the other version, which need not be rejected, *O thou wild ass*. The word here used, some would have to signify *wild*, in general: and to answer, the Latin, *fera*, as in letters, and sound, it does: and to be applicable therefore, as well to *a wild* man, as *a wild* beast, Gen. 16.12. such as all men are naturally said to be, Job 11.12. but the word seems rather to denote some particular kind of wild beast; which yet the Jewish masters are not wholly agreed upon. Some give us strange names of it, and tell us, it is a beast that sleeps one whole month in the year: some *dormouse* belike they dream of. But the most herein concur, that it is the *wild ass*, called *Onager*: and so the old Latin here renders it, and the Greeks elsewhere, Job 6.5. & 39.5. Psal. 104.11. Esay 32.14. as also the Chaldee paraphrast so takes it; though some take the word that he here uses, more generally, Dan. 4.21. But another question is among them, whether it be the male, or the female, that is here spoken of; about which, both they, and ours, are divided. And the adjectives both, whether nouns, or pronouns, are, some of them, in the masculine form; some, in the feminine: whence some conclude for the one sex, and some for the other: But one of them well observes, that the genders in the names of beasts, as *ox*, *ass*, and the like, are promiscuously used; which in other languages also is not unusual: but the tenor of the context seems to imply, that as *a she dromedary*, vers. 23. so *a female Onager*, is here intended: Yet not, as they here again inculcate, because the female is the better runner of the twain: as of the *hind*, they fable the like, on Psal. 18.33. where the word may be rendered, as well *hart*, as *hind*: as *lions*, where yet the word is *lionesses*; but the participle joined with it, masculine, Zeph. 3.3. See Chap. 4.29.

*{used to the wilderness}* Heb. *taught the wilderness*, that is, inured, and accustomed to it; as ch. 13.23. Hos. 10.11. that runs at large there, Job 39.5,6. for howsoever the word here used, signifies, *a plain* sometime, as well as *a wilderness*, see on Esay 63.13. and a Rabbine would have it so taken here; because running there is more ready, and less subject to impeachment; yet I suppose the word here need not be diverted from its native notion, that of Job, and this so well suiting together.

*{that snuffeth up the wind at her pleasure,}* Heb. *that* (a defect of the relative; as Esay 65.1.) *snuffeth up the wind*, as chap. 14.6. but the *snuffing up*, or rather, the *drawing in of the wind*, there, is not the same (though the words be the same, and the subject the same, and the Rabbines therefore confound them) with the *snuffing up of the wind*, here mentioned: for that is a drawing in of the fresh air, to allay the inward heat, arising from drought: whereas this *snuffing up of wind*, is, as the Hebrew here has it, *in the desire*, or *lust of her soul*; (as Deut. 12.15. *all that thy soul lusteth after*,) when she winds the male, going proud, as of some other creatures we use to speak: & one of the Rabbines therefore observes not amiss, that this *snuffing* appertains to the sense of *smelling*, and is spoken of drawing in the wind, or air, by the nostrils: though he here misapply it, supposing it (wherein some other also concur with him) to be intended here, as done for the more freedom of breath, that she may run the more speedily; shortness of breath, and difficulty of breathing, being a great impediment to speed, which is clean besides the prophet’s intent in this place: as also, that seems no less of some other, who so take it, as if it implied, that she would rather endure hunger and drought in the wilderness, than repair to places habitable, and be serviceable to man.

*{at her pleasure}* Heb. *in her soul’s desire*, or *lust*; when she lusts after, and longs for, the male. There is here a double reading, *his soul*, and *her soul*: and the former, it seems, some more curious, than skillful, scribe, would needs be putting in, because he found the word, *taught*, in a masculine; whereas the word *snuffing*, being in a feminine, might have taught him, to let it stand, as he found it: but the latter is the more generally received. And I wonder much at that learned scholiast, who tearing the text asunder, would not have those words spoken of the *wild ass*, but of Jerusalem, because the former words were in a masculine form; whereas these run in the feminine: but of the promiscuous use of the genders in living creatures, enough before; and we may find both, sometime, used of the very selfsame thing; as Ezek. 2.9. Jon. 1.17. & 2.1. (for what some of the Rabbines dream of two fishes there, is both frivolous, and fabulous) yea, the very like is, by the learned scholiast himself observed in the very next verse; and by one of the Jewish commenters, chap. 3.5. & 4.14. and though Jerusalem, or the Jewish people, be intended in the text; yet it is in an allegorical way, under the resemblance of such a creature, and her usual carriage; besides, that he seems to be as far wide from the prophet’s intendment, when he supposes, that in this passage Jerusalem thirsting after idolatry, is compared to, yea, or resembled by, the *thirst* of *wild asses*; whereof the psalmist speaks, Psal. 104.11. whereas that there touched upon, is no other, than such as is ordinary, and common, with other beasts, to wild asses; nor as that of the *hart*, Psal. 42.1. though extraordinary, yet differing much also from this here; the one proceeding from true want; from mere wantonness the other.

*{in her occasion who can turn her away?}* What the word rendered *occasion*, should here signify, is much questioned. The particle *in*, is not in the text: the most interpreters therefore admit it not. The old Latin knits the first word to the former, rendering the text, *snuffing up the wind of love*, or *lust*, rather: and this would suit well with the subject matter of the place, and the prophet’s intendment here; but neither do the pauses in the original allow it; nor is any ground given for such signification of the word. The Chaldee paraphrast renders it, *as a dragon*; and some of the Jewish doctors following him, *dragon-like*, or after the manner of dragons: they build partly upon that place, chap. 14.6. where it is said, *The wild asses stand in the high places, and snuff up*, or *draw in the wind like dragons*: and partly, upon the affinity of sound, and identity of some letters in either term: but there is no analogy that will fitly deduce, either the one from the other, or both from the same source. Some other of the Jewish doctors would have it taken in a notion of *yelling*; or because it is an *ass* that it is ascribed to, it might better be, *braying*; because a word near it, and of the same stock with it, is used for *wailing*, Esay 29.2. Ezek. 2.5. Some of ours, *a set time*; rendering it, in, or at, her set time. Some, *her course*; her running, and ranging. Some, *her incurse*, or *assault*, running upon the male, to incite him to cover her. Some, *in her occurse*; in the lighting upon, or meeting with, her: and these all from that use of the word, whence it is derived; whereby it signifies, *to cause* ought *to befall one*, or *to meet with one*, Exod. 20.13. Psal. 91.10. Prov. 12.21. The most, *her occasion*, or *opportunity*, or *in her opportunity*, or *occasion*; because the verb whence it comes, is so used, 2 Kin. 5.7. *he seeketh an occasion* (or *picketh a quarrel*) *against me*: and the noun, thence derived, very little differing from this, Judg. 14.4. *he sought an occasion against the Philistines*: he intended to *pick a quarrel* with them: and though that learned scholiast reject this, as a poor, and cold expression; yet to me it seems to suit very well with the prophet’s intent: for it is, as if he had said, when she finds *opportunity*, or takes *occasion* rather, to run thus on madding after the male, there is no staying, or turning of her; do what any can, she will have her will, she will have her way. Thus retaining our version, which I prefer, there is only a supply of the preposition, which is very frequently suppressed; as Esay 44.12. & 48.4. or, if that be omitted, there is a redundancy of the pronoun demonstrative; *her occasion, who can turn it back?* But the former seems the better.

*{all they that seek her will not weary themselves}* So the Jewish commenters, for it would be to no purpose; because it is a creature that will not be taken, or tamed, Job 39.5,8. though that is somewhat too large: But the meaning is, that there is no dealing with her, while she is in this fit, she is so wild and fierce then; there is no taking of her, while she runs thus a madding: Yet some late writers of note render it, to a clean contrary purpose; *all they that seek for her, need not weary themselves*: that is, say they, turning it to Jerusalem, resembled to a common strumpet; all that desire to be naught with her, need not to take pains to seek her out; they may trace her well enough by what falls from her, ver. 23. or they may find her at hand, ready at all times to receive such, ch. 3.2. Ezek. 16.25. and 23.44. but this suits not so well with the similitude.

*{in her month they shall find her}* What some learned interpreters here have of the *monthly* course, (which the old Latin here exhibits, and Popish writers much beat their brains about, devising how to make good) and of the manner of lewd women, admitting loose persons like themselves, without distinction of times, Ezek. 22.10. strangely straining to fetch in hither for the backing hereof, that of Hos. 5.7. and others of the *new moons*, on which for idolatrous services they were wont to meet, Hosh. 2.11. I let pass, because I deem them to be clean beside the intent and scope of the place; which I conceive to be meant of such as hunt for, and seek to take the wild creature here spoken of: And this the most, as well Jewish, as our interpreters also, agree in: of the *month*, only the question is, what *month* should be here meant. And one of the Rabbines tells us, not that the *wild ass*, but that the strange creature, (I know not what, for two strange names he gives us for it, and says, some say it is the one, and some the other) here mentioned, lies fast asleep all one month in the year; and that is the month, in which men may easily surprise her. But that is one of his idle relations, whereof he has not a few. Others, take it for the *month*, or *months*, (the word collectively taken; as *day* for *days*, Gen. 8.6. and *year* for *years*, Gen. 5.4,5,6,7.) wherein she goes great with young, and grows near her time, when she is heavy, and cannot so well shift for herself: the *months*, of which, Job 39.1,2. and this indeed seems the genuine sense of the place: the meaning whereof well may be, as it is applicable to Jerusalem, and the Jewish people; that albeit, there were now no dealing with them, while they were thus in the fervor of their filthy lust, so desperately bent to run after their idols, that they would have their swing whatsoever it cost them, or whatsoever came of it, v. 25,31,33. Chap. 22.21. Yet the time should come, when being in streights, and distresses, they would be less wild and fierce, grow tamer, and become more tractable, and easier to be dealt with, by those that seek after them for their good, v. 27. Hosh. 5.15. and 6.1.

**Verse 25.** *{Withhold thy foot from being unshod, and thy throat from thirst}* That these words contain in them, an wholesome admonition, given either by God, or from God, to this people, is generally agreed on. In regard whereof, some put into the text, *I said*, or, *when it is said unto thee*. See the like defect, Psalm 27.8. Acts 15.5. But about the exposition of them, there is some difference. For some understand the words, as if it were said, do not wear out your shoes, and expose yourself unto thirst, by taking journeys unto remote places through waste wildernesses, where water is not to be had, for the procuring of aids from foreign people. See Josh. 9.13. Esay 36.6. and 57.15. v. 6. Others, do not, by putting off your shoes, (as persons do, when they go to bed) address yourself unto the adulterous bed, Esay 57.7. or do not uncover your feet (as Deut. 28.57. Esay 7.20.) do not prostitute yourself, Ezek. 16.25. forbear your adulterous thirst after idols. See the use of the metaphor, Prov. 5.15,18. Eccles. 26.12. Others lastly, which I conceive to be the right, break off these your wicked and wretched courses, (to wit, in running and gadding after strange people, and strange gods) which will at length, if you go on in them, bring you into captivity, and in it, to extreme beggary and misery. See Prov. 6.26. and 30.16,20. Esay 20.2,4. and 47.2. Chap. 13.22. and 14.10. and 48.18.

*{withhold thy foot}* Or, *withdraw thy foot*. So Prov. 1.25. and 4.27.

*{from being unshod}* That is, that you may not come to be unshod, to go barefoot, and bare-legged, Esay 20.4. and 47.2. without hose or shoes. See Chap. 13.22. and so, *from thirst*; that you may not bring yourself to thirst; that is, to extreme want, having not so much as water, wherewith to quench your thirst, Psalm 107.5. Esay 5.13. See the like use of the particle, Esay 23.1. and 24.10. Ezek. 16.41.

*{but thou saidst}* Heb. *and*; as v. 11. You return a directly cross answer, a plain negative; whereby is confirmed what was before said, of no staying, or turning her, in the heat of her lust, v. 24. See Hos. 5.4.

*{There is no hope}* The word, here used, has a notion of *despair* in it; as appears by the use of it, 1 Sam. 27.1. Eccl. 2.20. And the most read it here, in way of asseveration, rendering it, in a Latin proverbial form, *It is done*: there is an end then, so let it be. Others, *it is desperate*; the case is desperate. Others, *I am desperate*, I am at a point. Others, as our version, *There is no hope*; there is no hope of reclaiming us. Others, which I incline to, as the fittest; *There is no remedy*, as we use to say, *Past cure, past care*: Yet some interpreters of note read it, by way of interrogation: and that, it may be, the rather, because the answer in the like case is found turned in the negative, Esay 57.10. *Thou wert wearied with the length of thy way; and yet thou saidst not, There is no hope*: And they render it therefore, *Should I despair?* Should I grow out of heart, and give over my course, and the way that I am in? and the negative following so close upon it, seems to add some strength to it. I shall leave it to the consideration and censure of the learned. The same is found, Chap. 18.12.

*{No}* Either we will not follow your advice: as Prov. 1.25. Chap. 6.16. and 44.16. or, we are not out of hope, by our own ways, to attain our ends, and sufficiently to defend ourselves, from these, and the like evils, and we are resolved therefore constantly to persist in them, Esay 28.14,15. and 57.10.

*{for I have loved strangers, and after them I will go}* Or, *I love strangers*; mine affection is strongly and firmly set upon strange people, and strange services; and them I will after, whatever come of it, Esay 2.6. Ezek. 23.7. See chap. 18.11,12.

**Verse 26.** *{As the thief is ashamed when he is found; so is the house of Israel ashamed, they, their Kings, their Princes, and their Priests, and their Prophets;}*

**Verse 27.** *{Saying, to a stock, Thou art my Father; and to a stone, Thou hast brought me forth}* That is, says the Chaldee paraphrast, and the Jewish masters after him; As it is with one that has borne the name, and had the reputation of an honest man, when he is taken stealing, and so comes to be discovered, that then shame and ignominy befalls him, by the loss of his former reputation and credit: for an open, or a professed thief, has no shame of ought. In like manner is it with this people, who bearing the name of God’s people, as their fathers did before them; and professing to serve the true God, and him only, may justly be ashamed, when they are taken in such gross and palpable idolatries, worshipping stocks and stones instead of him; yet the meaning, say they, is not, that they were indeed ashamed: had they been so indeed, they would have turned from them, and not gone after them still, but that they had good and just cause so to be, Chap. 3.3. and 5.15. and 8.12. But most of ours, rather; As a thief that hopes to carry the matter so closely and covertly, that he shall go away with his pilferings, and thefts, undiscovered; yet is confounded, and put to shame, when contrary to his expectation, notwithstanding all his slights, and wiles, whereby he made account to escape, he is intercepted, and not only misses of his prey, but is exposed to public disgrace, and made liable to legal penalties: so shall this people, all sorts of them, be put to shame and confusion, when they shall find their idols, whom they now trust to, and rely upon, to fail them, and prove utterly unable to relieve, or deliver them, in their difficulties and distresses, v. 27,28,36. Esay 1.29,31. and 2.20,21. and 20.4,5. Chap. 3.24,24. Hos. 4.19.

*{As a thief is ashamed}* Heb. *According to the shame of a thief*; as, *according to the overthrow of Sodom*, Amos 4.11. See Chap. 48.27.

*{when he is found}* Either upon search made for him, found out, and apprehended, as Achan, Josh. 7.11,18. or, taken in the manner, as we use to say, and as they speak upon a groundless supposition, Gen. 44.12,16.

*{is the house of Israel ashamed}* So most interpreters read the words in a passive notion; and so it is apparently taken, Ch. 46.24. and 50.2. Joel 1.11. yet some late interpreters of note, render it in an active notion; *they have put to shame the house of Israel, them*, &c. or, *made them ashamed*; that is, their idols have so done: and so likewise they render it, Chap. 5.15. and 8.12. and so in this form it is once found used, 2 Sam. 19.5. but the other is the more frequent, and the syntax seems to favor it here.

*{the house of Israel}* See ver. 4.

*{Kings, Princes}* The chief that had better breeding, and should have been exemplary to others. See Chap. 5.5. So Chap. 1.18. ver. 8.

*{Prophets, and Priests}* See v. 8.

*{saying}* Or, *That say*. See Esay 8.12.

*{to a stock}* *A stock*, and *a stone*, for, idols made of the stock of a tree, or of stone, Deut. 28.64. Esay 40.20. and 44.14,17. Dan. 5.4,23. so in contempt he terms them, from the subject matter of them; as their altars also, are termed *bricks*, Esay 65.3. So chap. 3.9.

*{Thou art my Father}* Giving the honor of God (who indeed was their *Father*, Deut. 32.6. Esay 64.8. Chap. 3.4. Mal. 2.10. Mat. 23.9.) to idols; and being so sottish, and senseless, as to take a dead stock, or a stone, void of sense and life, for their *Father*; and so to call or account it, Esay 44.17.

*{Thou hast brought me forth}* Or, *begotten me*: as the word is commonly used, Gen. 4.18. and 10.8. you are my maker: they make stocks and stones, idols, made of such matter, and of their own making, their makers, v. 28. See on Esay 8.12.

*{for they have turned their back unto me, and not their face}* Or, *but they turned their back unto me*: so is the particle used, Esay 30.16. and 49.25. they look after their idols, but they look not after me, but turn their back toward me, Chap. 32.33. Ezek. 8.16. See Esay 1.3,4. Heb. *the hinder part of the neck*, Psalm 18.40. See Esay 66.3. there is in the original, an elegant *antanaclasis*, or diversity of notion in the same terms; as if it were said, *they face me with the back part of the neck, and not with the face*. See chapter 7.24. and 18.17.

*{but in the time of their trouble they will say, Arise, and save us}* Or, *yet*; as Esay 65.20. v. 11. Though they now thus neglect me, as if they had no need of me, v. 31. and run after their idols, relying wholly upon them; yet when troubles come upon them, and they find now to their shame, how little help their idols are able to afford them, they will then be glad to seek to me for succor and safety, Judg. 10.10,15. Esay 26.16. Hos. 5.15. this is that which he said before, *in her month she will be found*, v. 24.

*{Arise, and save us}* The usual note of God’s people, in time of distress, Psalm 3.7. and 7.6. and 10.12. and 44.23. whom these wicked ones would then imitate.

**Verse 28.** *{But where are thy gods that thou hast made thee? let them arise, if they can save thee, in the time of thy trouble}* God’s answer to them, turning them over to their idols, whom forsaking him, they had served, to try what they could do for them, and to seek for relief, and rescue from them. And some therefore put into the text, *Then will I answer them*. So Deut. 32.37. Judg. 9.11,14. 2 kings 3.13. Hos. 13.10. Chap. 11.11,14.

*{But where}* Heb. *And where*; or, *where now*; as Esay 8.7. and 31.3. What is become of your idols now? where are they, that they help you not? as Chap. 37.19.

*{that thou hast made thee}* Or, *that thou madest*, or, *hadst made thee*, Esay 2.20. Chap. 1.16. and 16.20.

*{arise, if they can save thee}* Or, *arise*, and try whether (as Judg. 9.3.) *they can save thee*, or no; a complexive form of speech, such as Esay 28.2. see Esay 47.12,13.

*{arise}* Implying, that they were not able to stir from the place where they were set, and fixed, Esay 46.7. Chap. 10.5.

*{if they can save thee}* Heb. *will*, or, *shall, save thee*: but the word is in a potential notion; as the like, v. 8,11. See Esay 45.20.

*{in the time of thy trouble}* Heb. *of thine evil*: as Psalm 49.5. So before, v. 27.

*{for according to the number of thy cities, are thy gods, O Judah.}* What need you come to me, when you have idols so many, and those so near at hand to go to: enough, and near enough, were they able to do ought for you, or to afford you any succor. So Chap. 11.13.

*{according to the number of thy cities}* A defect of the particle, the note of collation, or similitude; such as the Jewish critics observe, Exod. 14.13. to reconcile the words there with what afterward follows: not *the Egyptians, whom*, but *in that manner, which ye see to day, ye shall never see more*: for it is said, they saw them after lie dead on the shore, Exod. 14.30. So Exod. 34.18. according to *that which I commanded thee*; and Chap. 32.11. according to *the precept, and the ordinances*. They had several tutelar deities for their several cities; after the manner of the heathen, that had every country, and city, an idol, one or more, of their own, 2 kings 17.29,31.

**Verse 29.** *{Wherefore will ye plead with me?}* To what end will you stand out, and offer to debate the matter with me, when the evidence given in is so clear against you? v. 23,34. Chap. 3.2. yet some of the Jewish interpreters turn it another way, expounding it of such *contending*, as gave the name to *Meribah*, Exod. 17.2,3,7. *why do ye quarrel with me*, when mischief befalls you, and demand why I deal so with you? and that they were indeed too prone to, chap. 5.19. and 22.8. But that seems not intended here.

*{Ye all have transgressed against me, saith the LORD.}* Or, *ye have all rebelled against me*: as it is rendered, Esay 1.2. *all*, for all sorts, from the highest to the lowest: see v. 26. so Mal. 3.9.

**Verse 30.** *{In vain have I smitten your children, they received no correction}* I have tried all courses with you, by fair means to win you, by harsher courses to reclaim you; but neither have prevailed to work any amendment with you: see Esay 1.5. and 9.13. chap. 5.3. Amos 4.6,11. Zeph. 3.2.

*{in vain}* Without any good effect; as chap. 6.29.

*{smitten}* As Esay 27.7. *chastised*: as Prov. 23.13,14. or, *wounded*: as 1 kings 20.37. so chap. 30.14.

*{your children}* Whom you train up in such idolatrous ways, as yourselves take to, chap. 5.7,17. and 7.18. and because from the least to the greatest, they were transgressors alike, chap. 6.13. and 8.10. So the Jewish commenters, and some other. But *your children*, seems here rather, as others conceive, to comprehend as well parents, as children, the whole body of the Jewish people: and it seems to me to be no other, than as if he had said, *thy sons*, or *children, O Judah*, whom expressly he named, v. 28. as, *thy sons, O Sion, against thy sons, O Javan*, Zach. 9.13. so *the sons of Judah*, Joel 3.6. and *the children of thy people*, for your people any of them, Lev. 19.18. see v. 16. and chap. 5.7.

*{they received no correction}* Or, *they would receive no instruction*: though they were corrected, they would take no warning by what they suffered: they would not be instructed, that it might have been for their good, Psal. 94.12. So the word is rendered, Prov. 5.12,23. & 6.23. & 8.33. & 12.1. & 13.18. & 15.32. & 24.32. and so it would here be rendered: for though the word primarily signify *chastisement*, as Prov. 13.24. & 23.13. and strictly taken, such *instruction*, as comes by *chastisement*, *correction*, in its native sense, as we term it, Prov. 22.15. yet *instruction* would do better than *correction* here, because the thing by chastising here intended is *instruction*: whereas *correction* is with us most commonly used for the *chastisement* itself. Now as *to receive instruction*, is to yield to what, by admonition, reprehension, or correction is required, and so to be bettered thereby, Prov. 19.20,27. chap. 35.13. so *not to receive it*, is to stand out against it, to refuse to yield to it, or to be bettered by it, chap. 5.3. & 7.28. & 17.23. & 32.33.

*{your own sword hath devoured your prophets, like a destroying lion}* You have been so far from hearkening to admonition, and receiving of instruction, that, in savage and barbarous manner, you have slain those prophets, which called upon you for repentance, that yourselves might not be slain, 2 Chron. 24.20,21. chap. 26.23. Nehem. 9.26. Mat. 23.29,35,37. Luc. 11.47. & 13.33,34. Acts 7.52. 1 Thes. 2.15.

*{your own sword}* Or, *your sword*: yet not as some, the sword that has smitten you, not wherewith you smite, but wherewith you have been smitten: but here rather the other: as Psalm 37.15. and the *sword* here put at large, for any forcible means of taking away life: see Mat. 21.35,36. & 23.37.

*{hath devoured}* Heb. *eaten*: as Esay 1.20. hence the sword is said to have *a mouth*, chap. 21.7. Luc. 21.24.

*{your Prophets}* The prophets that God sent to you: as *Zachary*, 2 Chron. 24.20,21. *Uriah*, chap. 26.23. and others, not a few, 1 Kin. 18.13,14. & 19.10. So the most, both Jewish, and ours: yet some of either would have it, *your Prophets*, as chap. 37.19. and *their Prophets*, v. 26. the false prophets; either as pointing to such executions, as themselves had sometimes done upon them, 1 kings 18.40. 2 kings 10.15. (but that can have no place here) or, as intimating that the same *sword*, that had ranged among them, had taken away, together with them, their false prophets, who had promised them safety, Hos. 4.5. but nor does this seem very probable to be meant in this place.

*{like a destroying lion}* In a cruel and savage manner; as a lion, that kills not only, but rents and tears to pieces, Psalm 72.

**Verse 31.** *{O generation, see ye the word of the LORD}* God here again returns to his former expostulation with them, pressing them to show, what wrong he had done them, or wherein he had carried himself so harshly towards them, as should cause them to leave him, and relinquish his service: see v. 5.

*{O generation}* Some would have the article here, to be a note of demonstration, and knit this and the last words of the foregoing ver. together, thus rendering the text, *like a devouring lion is this generation*: but this too much disjoins the context. Others would have it a note of admiration, and exclamation: as if it were said, *Oh generation!* or, *how strange a generation is this*, what times are we, of this age, fallen into? see Esay 23.8. But others rather a note of compellation; calling upon the people then living, to hearken sedulously to what he said, and pressing that upon them now, which he had upon their fathers before, v. 5. so the article is used, Deut. 32.1. Psal. 9.6. and 114.5. Joel 1.2.

*{see the word of the LORD}* *See*: that is, *consider* seriously; as v. 19. *See the word*: as, *hear the rod*, Mic. 6.9. for the heart has an eye to see the one, as well as an ear to hear the other: there is an inward eye, as well as an outward, Deut. 29.2,3,4. Prov. 20.12. Eccl. 1.16.

*{have I been a wilderness unto Israel?}* Have I held my people to hard meat, as cattle kept upon some bare and barren heath, or wide waste? or, have I not made them *my pasture sheep*, and been careful to provide good feeding, and all other necessaries for them, Deut. 32.13,14. Psalm 23.1,2. & 103.3. Esay 5.2,3,4. Ezek. 34.14,20,31. or, have I been unto you, as that *wilderness*, through which I led you to Canaan? v. 2,6. did not I make that vast and waste wilderness, to be as no wilderness unto you, whatever it was to any other, by furnishing you abundantly with whatsoever was needful for you, during the whole time of your abode in it? Deut. 8.3,4. & 32.10,11. Neh. 9.20,21. Psalm 78.15,16,23,30. or, has my service been unto you, an unfruitful service, like a barren land, which though a man take never so much pains about it, and be at never so much cost with it, yet will yield him nothing answerable to either? Heb. 6.8. as if the service of God those complain, Job 21.15. Mal. 3.14. or rather, have I not dealt at all times bountifully and liberally with you, so long as you followed me, and continued loyal unto me? Deut. 28.1,13. 2 Chron. 19.3,5. & 26.5. & 31.10. & 32.22,23. chap. 22.15. Mal. 3.10.

*{a land of darkness?}* Either by way of apposition to the former: *a land of darkness*, as that waste and wild desert was: or by way of disjunction; the disjunctive supplied, or *a land of darkness*; as some other horrid, and horrible place. The like want of the disjunctive, see Esay 17.6. & 27.7. The word here used, nowhere else found in this form, is diversely rendered: for the old Latin expresses it, by a term, that has in it a notion of *lateness*; as we should say, *a late-ward land*; that is, a land, in which it is long, or late, in the year, ere ought comes up, or attains, at least to any maturity or growth. So is a word of the same root rendered by divers, Exod. 9.32. where it is said, *of the rye*, and *the wheat, they were late-ward*; not so forward as the *flax*, and the *barley*: and of later fruits, the Jewish doctors do commonly use the word: as also the Chaldee, Eccl. 11.6. and those that go this way, thus paraphrase the place; Have I been to you as a wilderness that yields no fruit at all? or, as a late-ward land, that comes up very slowly with ought? have I been either barren towards you, or backward with you, in doing for you, as occasion required? and not rather bountiful, and forward, in conferring upon you whatever your hearts could desire, Psalm 37.4. & 81.10. But the most, both Jewish, and other, go another way, as our version also does. The root it comes of, is very commonly used for *darkness*; properly a *thick, misty, palpable darkness*, Exod. 10.22. chap. 23.12. Joel 2.2. Amos 5.20. Zeph. 1.15. Yea, hither do also some refer that, Exod. 9.32. of those kinds of grain, that they were yet hid in the ground, they lay *in the dark*; but as the simple word is used of that palpable *darkness*, that overspread Egypt, Exod. 10.22. so the word, thence deduced, much of the same making with this, is used of that black, cloudy *darkness*, that God set between the Egyptians and the Israelites, at the red sea, to keep them asunder, Josh. 24.7. and to add a further degree unto it, the syllable *jah*, containing one of God’s names, whereof see on Esay 26.4. is, as the Jewish critics well observe here, annexed unto it; as if it were said, *land of darkness of God*; that is, of extreme darkness: as, *a flame of God*, for a most vehement flame, Cant. 8.6. where a term of the same frame: and, *a trembling of God*, for a very dreadful trembling, 1 Sam. 14.15. and *a sleep of God*, for *a very deep sleep*, 1 Sam. 26.12. Of the like form of terms, see on Esay 6.13. and 19.24. By the word then thus resolved, is here meant, either a land of extreme misery; *darkness* put for misery, as Lam. 3.2. So Esay 8.22. & 9.19. or rather, a land continually possessed with *extreme darkness*, receiving no light at all from heaven, or any of those celestial creatures: and consequently, unfit to afford abode for man or beast, and unable to produce ought that may be useful to either: and which therefore no marvel if people should abandon, to seek some place of better abode elsewhere, Psalm 107.4,5. It is then, as if God had said, Have I been such to my people, that their wants and streights with me, should enforce them to leave me? Some late writers of prime note, derive the word from another root, that signifies *to fall*, or *to shed*: and render it, *a land that sheddeth*, or *spilleth* her fruit, Esay 1.30. & 28.1,4. wherein nothing comes to maturity, but falls ere it be ripe, and fit for food: or, *a land that casteth down* her inhabitants; makes them fall, and fail, either for want of food, which it yields not; or, through excessive pains, wherewith it tires, and wears them out in tilling of it: as Num. 13.32. and it is true, that the Jewish critics tell of a twofold pointing of the word, in divers books; but neither suits well with this notation, unless we leave out a letter.

*{a wilderness, and a land of darkness}* For, *as a wilderness*, and *as a land of darkness*: as v. 3,23.

*{wherefore say my people, We are Lords, we will come no more unto thee?}* If my people cannot thus justly complain of me, or my service, what is the reason then, why now they think they are grown great, they withdraw themselves from me?

*{say}* Entertain such thoughts; as Psalm 14.1. & 30.6. v. 25.

*{my people}* Those that I took to me, when they were in a very low condition, to make them my peculiar people, Deut. 4.20,34. & 7.6,7. & 32.9,10.

*{we are Lords,}* The word here used, is by divers diversely rendered. The Chaldee, as spoken in way of complaint, *We are expelled, cast off*, or *cast out*: as from an Arabic term, says one, that signifies *to expel*. One of the Jewish commenters, *we are separated from thee*: to which purpose also the old Latin, *we are gone, have departed*, or *withdrawn our selves*: as God complains of them, chap. 5.23. The ground hereof is deemed to be from the use of a word so signifying in the Talmud: but that is of another form than this here; nor is ever so used in Scripture. But it may rather seem to have been in relation to another root, whereunto also some of the Jewish critics refer this: which albeit it properly signify, *to descend*, or *go down*, Judg. 19.11. yet is frequently used, without any such special intimation of *descent*, for *to go*, or *to depart*. See Esay 30.2. & 31.1. & 38.8. A late learned annotator gives a twofold exposition of it, diverse from any of the former: He would have it rendered, either, *we will*: it is our pleasure; we are resolved upon it, that we will come no more at you, we will have nothing any longer to do with you: from an Arabic word that so signifies; as he would have this also so to do, Gen. 27.40. & Hosh. 11.12. or, if that like not, *we have mourned*; as the word (though in another form) is used, Lam. 1.9. as if the people should complain of God, that they never had merry day, but matter of mourning, from time to time, so long as they served him. See chap. 44.17,18. But some other of the Jewish doctors, whom most of ours follow, and our version concurs with, take the word in a notion of *ruling*, both here, and Hos. 11.12. as also, another of near affinity with it, does most frequently import, Lev. 26.17. Esay 14.2. and they render it therefore, *we rule*, or *we lord it*: as the apostle seems to speak, 1 Cor. 4.8. *Ye lord it without us*: We are grown up to a goodly kingdom, furnished with princes and potentates; we have gotten that strength, that we have no further need now of your support: and this seems to suit best, both with the scope of the place, and the use of the word elsewhere. See chap. 22.21. Hos. 8.4. The ancient Greek renders it, *We will not be ruled*: as v. 20. *I will not serve*: but that version puts in the negative, which is not in the text, and turns the verb out of its active form into a passive.

*{we will come no more unto thee}* Or, *at thee*: we will be ruled no longer by you; we can do well enough without you; we will live no longer under your strict government. So Deut. 32.15. ch. 22.21. See too much of this in Uzziah, 2 Chron. 26.15,16. a tang of it in David, Psalm 30.6. in Ezekiah, 2 Chron. 32.25.

**Verse 32.** *{Can a maid forget her ornaments? or, a bride her attire?}* God proceeds to discover, not the unthankful carriage only, but the extreme folly of this people, who though God had not only been no such fruitless land to them, as was formerly said, v. 31. but an ornament, an honor, a dignity unto them, the main matter of their glory, (see ver. 11. Esay 60.2,3,15,19. and 62.2,3.) that made them to be of high esteem and repute, in the eyes and minds of other nations, Deut. 4.7,8. 2 Sam. 8.10,13. 1 kings 8.41,42. 2 Chron. 32.23,30. Psalm 148.14. & 149.9. Ezek. 16.10,14. yet they were more regardless of him, than a young maid, or a bride would, or could be, of her jewels, or such her attire, and ornaments, that might grace her in the eyes of those that beheld her, Esay 62.10.

*{Can a maid forget?}* Heb. *will a maid forget?* But it is here not amiss rendered, as in a potential notion; as the like, v. 23. and so would that be rendered, Esay 49.14.

*{her ornaments}* Heb. *ornament*, or *array*, Ezek. 16.11. See on Esay 49.18.

*{or}* A defect of the disjunctive: as ver. 31.

*{a bride}* *A bride*, and *a young maid*, says the Rabbine, are here one and the same: for no bride, but a young maid, is so wont to be set out, nor any other young maid ordinarily; and would have a glance here, to be had unto God’s espousal of her at mount Sinai, ver. 2. but this seems too nice. See Esay 49.18. and 62.10.

*{her attire}* Heb. *her bindings*; the Greek and Latin, *her breast-band*, or *stomacher*: but it would rather be, *her headbands*. See Esay 3.20.

*{yet my people have forgotten me.}* Or, *but my people have forgotten me*. Heb. *and*: as Esay 22.20. ver. 1,27.

*{my people have forgotten me}* Have given over my service, and neglect me; do no more regard or look after me, than as if they had clean forgotten me, or had never known me, Deut. 32.15,18. Psalm 106.21. Hos. 8.14. So Psalm 44.17,20.

*{days without number}* That is, as we use to say, *time out of mind*: not now alone, but for a long time past, Esay 48.8. Mal. 3.7. Heb. *days*: whereof *there is not number*: so Cant. 6.8. a defect of the relative: as ver. 24.

**Verse 33.** *{Why trimmest thou thy way to seek love?}* Heb. *Why dost thou do well in thy way*, or, *make good thy way?* as chap. 7.3. whence divers interpretations arise. The most received, both with Jews, and other: Why do you use so many tricks and devices to gain love, and to draw foreign people unto you, whom you hope for help by? See chap. 4.30. The word is used, as well of *evil*, as of *good*: as Mic. 7.3. and it is used of Jezabel’s dressing her head, 2 kings 9.30. See Esay 23.16. where the word is likewise used. Others, Why do you use vain pretences, to varnish, and smooth over your wicked courses, as hoping thereby to regain favor, and get in with God again, and as if it were possible to delude him? as Esay 78.36,37. cha. 3.4. or thereby making account to excuse your courses, as if it were only for fear of some enemy, when it is indeed for satisfaction of your filthy lust, that you seek to them. See ver. 35. Some other, in the last place, Why do you take such long and tedious journeys, to draw lovers, spiritual adulterers, to you. See Esay 57.9,10. which may serve for a comment upon this place: and this I take to be the genuine sense of it. It is well observed by a Rabbine, who yet goes the former way, that the word is used generally to be *earnest, eminent*, or *excessive*, in ought: so, *to do well in play*, is to *play skillfully*, Psal. 33.3. Ezek. 33.32. *to do well in anger*, or, *to make anger good*, for to *be very angry*, Jon. 4.4,9. *to do well in evil*, for *to do evil, sedulously, earnestly, effectually*, Mic. 7.3. so here, *to do well in thy way*, or, *to make a good way*, is *to travel hard*: to take a long, a tedious journey; to go a great and wearisome way.

*{therefore also hast thou taught the wicked ones thy ways.}* There are two readings, both here, and chap. 13.21. The one reading has it in the first person; *I have taught*: which those that retain, expound the words, as spoken by God concerning himself. I have acquainted foreign people with the wickedness of your ways, that they may come in to execute judgment upon you for them, chap. 1.15,16. & 40.2,3. Lam. 4.15. But the other reading is the more generally received, and seems the right: and one of the Rabbines who retains it, renders the words, *Thou hast inured*, or *accustomed* yourself *to the worst of ways*: as the word was used, v. 24. See chap. 13.23. But this, though one of ours approve it, seems somewhat forced.
