Others rather, with whom our version agrees, you are so lewd in your courses, that wicked women (for the word is feminine) harlots themselves, may learn of you; you go in your filthiness so far beyond them, ch. 5.28. 2 Chron. 33.9. Eze. 5.6,7. & 16.31,33,34,48.

*{Therefore}* Or, as one of the Jewish commenters, *surely, verily*: whom one of ours following, would have this particle to be also so taken Gen. 4.15. chap. 5.2. Hos. 2.16. which may do not amiss here: so *acen*, and *lacen*, should in those places be the same.

**Verse 34.** *{Also in thy skirts is found the blood of the souls of the poor innocents}* You are guilty not of spiritual adultery, idolatry alone, but of murder also, and that of poor innocents, which you have added thereunto: the marks and evidences whereof are so fresh upon you, that it cannot be either concealed, or denied.

*{Also}* Over and above, or beside your idolatry, Ezek. 16.20,21. 2 kings 21.16.

*{in thy skirts}* Heb. *in thy wings*, Psalm 91.4. Esay 18.1. whence some would have it to be an allusion to fowls of prey, eagles, or puttocks, that having seized upon chickens, pigeons, partridge, or the like, and torn them in pieces, have their wings, and feathers, all over stained with the blood of them. See chap. 12.9. But neither is the word in this form, used of them: and the text seems rather to look another way. The word *wing*, is used commonly for the *skirt* of a garment, Num. 15.38. 2 Sam. 24.4,5,11. and *wings*, for *skirts*, Deut. 22.12. in this form especially: and it is rather therefore an allusion unto such, as having been killing people, and shedding of blood, have their garments stained and defiled with gore blood, Esay 63.2,3. For that learned scholiast seems to me strangely to torture the text, who expounds it of *blood* concret, drawn from such, as she should hire to commit filthiness with her: so *blood* here should be somewhat like that, John 1.13. and *garment*, such as Jude 23. but the notion is too obscene, and the exposition forced.

*{the blood of the souls of poor innocents}* That is, either simply the blood of such: *souls*, for *persons*, as Exod. 1.5. 1 Pet. 3.20. or, their *life-blood*, as we use to say: for some blood may be let out, and drawn from one, and yet life left: *soul*, for *life*, as chap. 19.9. and 34.20. the former I suppose the right; but the form makes the speech the more pathetical.

*{of the poor innocents}* Or, *of poor innocents*: for there is no article in the text, which, as it is here rendered, might very well be understood of their children, which they slew in sacrifice to their idols, 2 kings 16.3. and 21.6. Psalm 106.37,38. chap. 7.31. and 19.5. Ezek. 16.20,21,36. and 23.37. but according to the usual course of construction in Hebrew, wherein the manner is to place the substantive before the adjective, it should rather be rendered *innocent poor ones*: and so comprehend (though not excluding those) all the blood, that by oppression, and evil practices, was shed in Jerusalem: Of the abundance whereof, see 2 kings 21.16. and 24.4. Esay 1.15,23. and 59.3,7. Ezek. 7.23. and 9.9. Lam. 4.14. For otherwise, that of the poorer sort of men they used to make sacrifices when they could come by them, is not by any testimony of Scripture so evident; that of Hos. 13.2. is ambiguous.

*{I have not found it by secret search, but upon all these.}* There needs no search be made for the discovery of it: it is apparent to be seen upon all parts of your apparel.

*{by secret search}* By narrow search, or, *by privy search*: as we use to speak. Heb. *by digging*: through walls, Ezek. 8.8. and 12.5. or, *by breaking open*: of doors, or houses, Exod. 22.2. One of the Rabbines, whom a late learned writer also follows, reads the words, *Thou didst not find them breaking up of houses* (or, *with such a tool*, as thieves are wont to carry about them, and to make use of for that purpose) *but because of all these things*, did you slay them: to wit, because they reproved you for them, and would not do as you did. But this offers over-much force to the text: from which the old Latin strays not a little in the former branch, that renders the words, *I have not found them in ditches*: that is, say they, that follow it, in obscure cells and caves: such as harlots had wont to lurk in out of sight: but you exercise your fornications, in open, public, and eminent places, Esay 57.7. Ezek. 16.24. true indeed, but nothing to the prophet’s purpose in this place: and the Greek as far in the latter branch, rendering the words, *but upon every tree*, or *oak*; which some of the ancients expound of the *trees*, under which they slew them in sacrifice, v. 20. And a late learned writer of the *oaks*, or *trees*, that they found those poor souls climbing up to get food, when they seized on them, to make sacrifices of them: but the error arises from a gross mistake of the word, which the Latin discovered, and the interpretation is so unworthy so worthy an author.

*{but upon all these}* *But*; as v. 27. *upon all these*: to wit, the skirts of your garments: as if he should say, your garments are all over stained with blood: not your hands only, as Esay 1.15. See 1 Kin. 2.5.

**Verse 35.** *{Yet thou saidst, Because I am innocent, surely his anger shall turn from me.}* Heb. *And*: as ver. 27,32. But it may well be read in way of interrogation, *And saidst thou*, or, *Canst thou say*, or, *Darest thou say*, (yet after all this, have you the face to say it) *I am guiltless? sure his anger will turn from me*. See ver. 23.

*{Because}* Or, *That*: as Esay 52.5,6. But I suppose the particle here redundant: *thou saist that I am clear*, for *thou saist I am clear*: as Rev. 3.17. *thou saist that I am rich*, for *thou saist I am rich*.

*{I am innocent}* Clear, guiltless. So she Prov. 30.20.

*{his anger shall turn from me}* Heb. *is turned from me*: but the time past is used oft in a future notion. So Mic. 7.8. *I have risen*, for *I shall rise*. God has no cause to be angry with me: God’s *anger* is said *to turn away*, when he ceases to manifest it, Esay 5.25. and 9.11.

*{behold, I will plead with thee, because thou sayest, I have not sinned}* For this very cause I will plead with you, because you plead not guilty; and by pleading not guilty, do redouble your guilt. So the Rabbine, *The denial of a fault, is a doubling of it*.

*{I will plead with thee}* Or, *I will proceed in judgment against thee*. Heb. *I will be judged with thee*: as Esay 66.16. chap. 25.31.

*{because thou sayest, I have not sinned.}* Because you stand upon your justification, ver. 23,29. and will not be brought to acknowledge your sin, chap. 3.13. though the proofs and evidences of it are so pregnant against you, ver. 20,23,34. I will, without any further debate, proceed to pass sentence upon you, and put it speedily in execution, chap. 1.18. One of the Jewish doctors knits to this verse, the last words of the foregoing, ver. 34. as having reference to this clause, thus reading the text: *For all these things, and because thou saidst, I am not guilty—I will enter into judgment with thee*. But these words seem rather to have reference to what went before there, as was above showed.

**Verse 36.** *{Why gaddest thou about so much to change thy way?}* To what end do you run to and fro in this manner, one while one way, another while another way, to seek succors abroad? Esay 57.10. v. 18,25. chap. 14.10. like a trader that haunts marts and markets, repairing now to one, then to another, Ezek. 27.19. where the same word is used; one while sending to the Assyrians, 2 kings 16.7. 2 Chron. 28.16. Hos. 5.13. another while to the Egyptians, Esay 30.2. and 31.1. chap. 37.5. Hos. 12.2.

*{to change thy way}* Or rather, *changing thy way*: for this was not the end of her gadding, to change her way; but the manner of her gadding rather, that she did in gadding, change her way: or, did so gad to and fro, that she was oft taking a new way: so the particle is used, and in this form would be rendered, Gen. 3.22. Exod. 14.11. Num. 5.6. Deut. 9.18. See Esay 3.8. & 10.2.

*{thou also shalt be ashamed of Egypt, as thou wast ashamed of Assyria}* You shall receive no more succor, or relief from the one, than you did formerly from the other.

*{thou also shalt be ashamed of Egypt}* *Thou*, as well as others, that resort to Egypt for succor, Esay 36.6. so the words thus rendered, may seem to import: but that is not the genuine intendment of them. They would rather be rendered, as they lie in the original, *Of Egypt also thou shalt be ashamed*, or, *thou shalt be ashamed of Egypt also*: that the collation may appear to stand between Egypt and Assyria, not between other people, and themselves.

*{of Egypt}* As they were, Esay 20.5. and 30.5. and 31.5. chap. 22.22. and 37.7. 2 Kin. 24.7.

*{of Assyria}* Who distressed them, rather than delivered them, 2 Chron. 28.20.

**Verse 37.** *{Yea, thou shalt go forth from him, and thine hands upon thine head}* Your ambassador shall return from Egypt, whither you had sent them for succor, v. 18. with heavy hearts, and in a dejected habit; having their expectation frustrate, and failing of those ends, which from thence you hoped to obtain. Thus the most: Howbeit, one of the Hebrew commenters renders it, *Thou shalt go from hence*, from the place where you now are, into captivity: nor shall all aids you can procure from Egypt, or any other, be able to save you, chap. 37.7,10. And this I conceive to be the genuine sense of the place.

*{from him}* Heb. *from this*; to wit, place; as, *in this*, for in this place, Num. 22.19. 1 Sam. 14.34.

*{and thine hands upon thine head:}* Or, *with thine hands upon thine head*: for so is the copulative oft knitter of notions together, so Esay 35.10. *they shall return, and come to Sion, and joy upon their heads*, for *with joy upon their heads*: and chap. 1.13. *I see a boiling pot, and the face of it North-ward*, for *with its face North-ward*.

*{thy hands on the head}* A lamenting gesture, used commonly by women, importing extreme grief, and anguish of heart and spirit. See an instance of it in Tamar, ravished by her brother Amnon, 2 Sam. 13.19. and well suits with one expelled her country, and going out into captivity.

*{for the LORD hath rejected thy confidences}* *Rejected*; as Esay 41.9. or, *refused*; as Job 34.33. where opposed to *choosing*. Thus if we take it here, we may, with the Rabbine, read it, *The Lord hath rejected thee for thy confidences*. God, because of your resting upon foreign forces, and not relying upon him, (2 Chron. 16.7.) has rejected, and cast you off, chap. 6.30. and 7.29. a defect of the pronoun: as Esay 51.23. and 60.15. of the particle *for*; as Mal. 2.5. or, the word may signify, as it does frequently, *despised*: as it is rendered, Psalm 53.5. Judg. 9.38. Esay 33.8. or, *abhorred*: as Job 7.16. And referring it, as our version does, to the *confidences*, I suppose it may well be rendered, *the Lord disalloweth*: for what we reject, or refuse, we disallow: or, sets *light by them*: for so we do what we despise: or, as some render it, *the Lord abhorreth* them: he cannot abide such perfidious dealing, God approves not of these your courses, that you take for the securing of yourself: he protests against them by his prophets, Esay 30.1,15. or, he *setteth light* by them, he scorns them, and your folly, in imagining to secure yourselves by them, Esay 30.6. and 31.2,3. Either of these will well fit with the words of the text. I incline to the first.

*{and thou shalt not prosper in them.}* Or, *therefore thou shalt not prosper* by them: so is the copulative oft used, chap. 1.17. ver. 9. No courses can prosper, that God approves not, Psalm 1.6.

## CHAPTER 3

[Source gap: the beginning of the commentary on Jeremiah 3:1 is absent at this join in the supplied scan. The text resumes below.]

them to the former, is that wherein they are much puzzled. This first word may seem to imply, that the discourse should begin with a continuation of the former argument; and those that so deem, render it, as indeed it signifies word for word, *saying*; as Chap. 2.1. Yet among these again, there is some difference, as there was about the sense of the last clause of the foregoing discourse: for one of the Jewish doctors supposes, that God in the speech subjoined, renders a reason, why he must needs reject Jerusalem; to wit, because his own law had said, that if a man should take again his wife, that had been separated from him, and had been joined to another, the land would be defiled by it; and therefore he could not without some aspersion, and dishonor to himself, receive her again, who had left him, and joined herself to idols, until he had given her up into the hands of her enemies, and by a long and tedious captivity under such, made her to forget those her lovers, whom she had adjoined herself unto. Some of ours, and those of note, suppose the coherence to be this, God rejects the courses that you trust to, and will frustrate them, and turn them to your evil, because of your obstinacy; saying, that if you did repent indeed of them, he would receive you again, though an husband in such case by the law might not do it; but that there is no such matter with you; for you persist still in your wicked wonted courses, vers. 2,5. A learned scholiast coming after them, though in rendering the text he concur with them, yet receiving no satisfaction (it seems) from these their expositions, says only, that the coherence is obscure, and so leaves them, and it. And indeed most interpreters here leave them, supposing this passage to make entrance into a new argument, whereby God yet professes a willingness to receive the Jewish state again into grace and favor, notwithstanding their manifold forepassed abominations, upon their sincere acknowledgment thereof, and serious repentance for the same; albeit, in the like case, an husband so used, by the law might not so do: and they render the word, some, *It is said*, some, *They say*, some, *It is said*; but the case, as we say: That which our ancienter versions seem to have followed. The old Latin, *It is commonly said*; whence some gather, that it was grown to be a vulgar, or proverbial speech, common in men’s mouths, when they would intimate some irreconcilable matter; A woman that is gone from her husband, and has been joined to another, may not again be entertained: and this indeed seems to be the right notion of the term here, though none of them, that so express it, either give instance of it, or show any ground for it. It is in the Hebrew only in the infinitive mood, in a gerundial notion, with a particle prefixed, and knit to it, *saying*, or, *In saying*: but these infinitives are frequently used in an emphatical, but defective form of speech: whereof, see instances not a few, on Esay 59.13. Of this word, in this very form with the particle, see Esay 44.28. where it is as here, *In saying to Jerusalem*, for, *That in saying say of Jerusalem*; as the foregoing words, v. 26. where the verb finite is expressed, do plainly show; as also, Esay 9.9. which comes full home to this, *In saying out of the pride and stoutness of hearts*. *In saying*, they say, for, they say commonly, or they use to say. So is it more fully with the participle, Chap. 23.17. *They are saying saying*, that is, they are still, commonly, or continually *saying*; and with the verb finite, Ezek. 28.9. *wilt thou* in *saying say*, for *wilt thou still say?* Our received version therefore may well be retained, *They say*; for the speech is indefinite; though the Latin be more full; and our English might so also be, if it were rendered, *They say commonly*, or, *They use to say*: and we need not have recourse to such strained and forced connections, as those other interpreters are enforced to flee unto. The like syntax is also, Isaiah 44.14.

*{If a man put away his wife, and she go from him, and become another man's, shall he return unto her again?}* In this form it may be, that this proverbial speech was used among them, when somewhat was pressed upon them, that their stomachs went against, as to be reconciled to one, whom they conceived to have deeply wronged them, or against whom they had conceived some deadly feud; Should a man entertain a wife again, that he had cast off, when she has been another man’s? Howsoever it is apparent, that the interrogative here has the force of a negative, which it adds also some emphasis unto, and the law expressly forbids it, Deut. 24.1,4.

*{a man}* Any man; as Chap. 5.1.

*{put away}* Heb. *send*, or, *send out*; as Gen. 8.7,8. or, as we use to say, *dismiss*, and it is commonly used of such *dismission*, or *divorce*, as is here intimated, Deut. 22.19,29. & 24.1,3,4. Esay 50.1. Mal. 2.16.

*{become another man's}* Heb. *be to another man*. So Lev. 22.12. Deu. 24.2.

*{shall he return unto her again?}* That is, may he entertain her to be his wife again? No, he may not; for so the words of the law are, *He may not return to take her* (that is, *receive her again*) *to be his wife*, as before she had been. Howbeit, it may seem that these words have not so much an eye to the inhibition of the law, as to the usual disposition of men’s minds in such cases: and it is not therefore said, *It is said in the Law*, as our Savior says, *It is written in your Law*, John 8.17. or, *The Law saith it*; as the apostle, *Doth not the Law say it?* 1 Cor. 9.8. but, *They say*; it is that which men commonly use to say: and the words therefore may well be rendered, *will he*, or *would he return to her again?* That is, would he be reconciled again to her? for that is the usual notion of *turning*, in such terms, Esay 63.17. Zach. 1.16. & 8.3. would any man take such an one into favor again? could he set his affection so again upon her, as to be reconciled to her, and entertain her again? albeit, that there were no law, that inhibited the doing of it.

*{shall not that land be greatly polluted?}* Or, *should not that land be exceedingly profaned?* Heb. *in being profane, be profaned?* for these geminations of the word have much emphasis in them. So *polluting pollute*, Lev. 13.44. for so the words there are. The land, or state, wherein such base and abominable courses should be suffered, that women should go to and fro interchangeably, in such manner forward, and backward, from man to man, would become vile, and much looseness, and dissolute carriage would be, in it, thereby occasioned: and this is deemed to have respect to those words of the law; *It is a thing abominable in Gods sight, and thou shalt not make the land to sin*. Deut. 24.4. and by such promiscuous couplings, *lands* are said to be *defiled*, Levit. 18.27,28. the same word, and form of speech, concerning a *land*, or state, see Num. 35.33. Psal. 106.38. Esay 24.5. Yet there want not that read, and render the words; *Is not that land profaned*, or, *polluted?* That is, is not the land that this people dwell in exceedingly profaned and polluted, by the manifold abominations that they commit, and exercise in it? vers. 2,9. But I go rather with the former.

*{But thou hast played the harlot with many lovers:}* Heb. *and thou hast committed fornication with many friends*, or *companions*; and according to the latter exposition of the former branch, the copulative may well be in his proper sense retained, carrying on the demand; Is not *the land* (wherein you dwell, or, *which the Lord thy God giveth thee for an inheritance*, Deut. 24.4.) extremely profaned, or polluted, by you? *and hast not thou committed fornication with many thy mates?* or, *by thy committing fornication with many mates?* as the copulative is used, Chap. 1.13. & 2.39. Howbeit, following the former; which the pauses seem to favor, it is well rendered, *but*; as Chap. 2.11,25. or, may not be amiss, *but though*; for the copulative sometime not implies only, but includes, those particles; as Isaiah 65.12. & 66.14. Chap. 2.7,20. Hosea 12.2. Zach. 12.3. although you have thus egregiously defiled yourself, not with one only, which yet were sufficient by law to debar you from all hope of return to an husband again; or were enough to make a breach irreconcilable between such a wife and her husband; but with a multitude of loose and base ones, like yourself, idols, and others, in whom you trusted, so that you have made yourself as a common strumpet. See Chap. 2.20,23,36. vers. 2. Ezek. 16.31,16. Hos. 2.5.

*{yet return again to me, saith the LORD.}* Heb. *and returning*, or, *in returning return again to me*: a defect of the one verb, to be necessarily supplied; as in the beginning of the verse. So it is fully, 1 kings 9.6. *if in turning ye turn*, & 22.28. *if in returning thou return*, for, *if ever thou return*; *returning return*, that is, return sedulously, and seriously, and not feignedly. See vers. 10. Chap. 4.1,2. and if you so do, there shall be free access for you unto me again. I will dispense with mine own law, I will do that in favor of you, which I have inhibited others in the like case to do; and that scarce any man could endure, though there were no law to inhibit it; upon your hearty repentance, I will be reconciled again unto you, and receive you into grace and favor again. For so much is here intimated, as is more fully expressed, Zach. 1.3. Mal. 3.7.

**Verse 2.** *{Lift up thine eyes unto the high places, and see where thou hast not been lien with.}* This is subjoined, to confirm, and to convince her of the truth of the charge given in against her, concerning the multitude of her whoredoms, v. 1.

*{Lift up thine eyes}* A phrase commonly used in Scripture, when persons are called upon to view a thing considerately. So Gen. 13.14. & 31.12. Esay 49.18. & 60.4.

*{to the high places}* So the word properly signifies, Esay 49.9. Chap. 14.6. God pointed them to the places, where they had abused themselves with their idols; as Chap. 2.23. but as there in the vale, so here on the hills; on which their idolatrous services were most frequently exercised, 2 king. 17.9,29. & 21.3. & 23.5,8,15,19. v. 6. Howbeit, we are enforced here to make a stand; for a learned late writer herein controls all our interpreters, and the Jewish masters with them, who the best and soundest of them expound the word here used, as we do *high places*; whereas this cross man will needs have it to signify *valleys*, or *plains*, because in the Syriac the word is so used, Luke 3.5. but it seems no such strong argument, to confirm the use of an Hebrew term, from the like in the Syriac, no more than of an ancient Greek word from the modern Greek, or of some Latin term from the present Italian; unless the places where it is found used in the Hebrew text will attest also thereunto. This the author of this new interpretation foreseeing, instances in a place, wherein he supposes it must of necessity so signify; for it is said of Balaam, Num. 23.3. that (to try if he could meet with God) *he went to Shephi*, that is, says he, *to the plain*; for *to the hill*, or *high place*, it cannot be, because he was on the *high places of Baal* already, Num. 22.41. But to let pass the divers interpretations of the word in that place, the uncertainty whether it be the attribute there of any place or no, and the improbability of his going down into the vale, or the plain, there to meet God; who would not imagine, that, I say not, Balaam might, but that he should rather, though being already on the high places whereon they used to sacrifice, yet step aside to some *cliff*, as some not amiss render it; or to some place somewhat higher and more eminent, than that where he and the rest then were? so that this place little helps to strengthen this new conceit; and that, Esay 13.1. where the Hebrew use and notion of the verb original, plainly discovers itself in an attribute given to an high mountain; besides, those other places where it is used, both here, and elsewhere, in this prophecy; as vers. 21. Chap. 4.11. & 7.29. & 12.12. & 14.6. do seem clearly to carry it the received way; as when we come to scan them, shall be showed. It is true, that the Chaldee oft-times renders it *streams*, or *floods*; and from him one of the Jewish commenters (but none of the soundest) in this place so expounded it: but *streams*, though they run in the valleys, yet they come down thither from the hills, Psalm 104.10. and *streams of water* are promised on the *lofty mountains*, Isaiah 31.25. as well as in *the valleys*, Esay 41.18. see on the place. The ancient Greek, and old Latin, here, as also elsewhere, render it *right forward*, little regarding how it suits with the sequel.

*{see where thou hast not been lien with}* Implying, that there was scarce any place free from her pollutions, Esay 57.5,8. Chap. 2.20. vers. 6,13. Of the word here used; as also, Deut. 28.30. (in which place, as in this, the over-mannerly Masorets have been pleased to check the penmen of Scripture, and appoint an honester term to be read in the room of that they found written.) See on Isaiah 13.16.

*{in the ways hast thou sat for them, as the Arabian in the wilderness:}* You have carried yourself, like some strumpet, that is wont to sit by the highway side, waiting and watching for customers; the manner of such, that of Tamar shows, Gen. 38.14. See Ezek. 16.24,25,31.

*{sat for them}* That is, *sate* looking, or waiting, *for them*; to wit, for those your companions, and copesmates, vers. 1. a complexive form of speech; as Chap. 2.28.

*{As the Arabian in the wilderness}* The Greek renders it, *as a Crow in the wilderness*; because the word for a *Crow*, in Hebrew, has the same radical letters with this; but the vowels differ much: nor is the form the same in either. The old Latin has, *as a thief in the wilderness*: and the Arabians are indeed to this day noted for people that live much upon pillage: which trade, such as follow, are wont to lie in wait by the highway side, in waste, or woody places, especially to passengers, to spoil them, Judg. 9.25. Hos. 6.9. Luk. 10.30. But others rather, and so the Jewish writers, conceive it to have reference to another usage of that people, who dwelling in tents, and inhabiting those deserts, by which merchants used to pass with wares and commodities, were wont to pitch their tents near to the places of their ordinary passage; and there to wait their coming, to truck and trade with them. See Gen. 37.25. Job 6.19. Esay 15.7. & 21.13. and so the resemblance agrees very well; she waited for her customers, (as they for their chapmen) whom she drove a trade with. See the same collation laid the other way, Esay 23.17,18.

*{in the wilderness}* As those of *Arabia the desert*: who are hence also by some thought to have their name. See Esay 21.13.

*{and thou hast polluted thy land with thy whoredoms, and thy wickedness.}* Or, *profaned thy land* (as vers. 1.) *with thy whoredoms, and thy naughtiness*; as with your idolatries, so with other your wicked courses, and oppression and murder, Chap. 2.34. See Chap. 16.18. Ezek. 36.17.

**Verse 3.** *{Therefore the showers have been withholden;}* You have been chastised with drought, Deut. 28.23,24. Esay 5.6. See Chap. 9.12. & 14.1,2,22.

*{Therefore}* Heb. *And*; yet so the copulative is taken, Ch. 1.17. & 2.19. but I suppose here rather; as vers. 1. (See there) *And though*; for God’s purpose is here to note out her incorrigible disposition, that by no gentle chastisement would be brought to shame of, or sorrow for, her sin, Chap. 2.30. and 3.5.

*{the showers}* That is, say the Jewish doctors here, *the former rain*, that falls usually in the eighth month, called *Marcheshvan*, or *Bull*, 1 king. 6.38. containing part of our October, and part of November; and was requisite for the bringing up of their seed; called therefore the *seed-rain*, Esay 30.23. to which purpose also, was the violence of rain in those regions, being hotter, and the ground generally drier than with us, required; and in regard whereof it is said, Joel 2.23. that God will give them *the former rain in justice*, or, *unto justice*: which our version renders *moderately*. Some other, *duly*, in his due season, Deut. 11.13. I should rather say *plentifully*, or, *liberally*; as Psal. 68.9. in just and full measure; as Psal. 72.3. Hos. 10.12. and it is therefore also here so called, by a term, that has a notion of *muchness*, or *multitude* in it; used also, Deut. 32.2. (where it is distinguished from the smaller rain, that distilled down, as thin *as an hair*) Psal. 65.10. & 72.6. Chap. 14.22. Mic. 5.7. though it have another name more peculiar to it elsewhere: whereof see Chap. 5.24. and Isaiah 30.20. as also in regard hereof, that month wherein it usually falls, is said to be called the month of *Bull*, from the abundance of rain then falling, as making a *deluge*: and this the rather seems probable, because it is distinguished here from the *latter rain*: though the word otherwise be more general.

*{have been withholden}* To wit, from you: and from your land, Amos 4.7. The reason, see Chap. 5.25.

*{and there hath been no latter rain}* Heb. *latter rain was not*: the latter *rain*, is that which falls in the first month, Joel 2.23. called *Nisan*, by a Syriac term, Neh. 2.1. *Abib*, by an Hebrew, Exod. 13.4. containing part of our March, and part of our April: this was much desired for the filling of their corn, being then in the ear, and the fitting of it for harvest; for from *the corn* then *eared*, has that month its name in Hebrew. See Job 29.23. Prov. 16.15. And this *latter rain* seems to have its name from a word found once only, Amos 7.1. where it is commonly deemed to signify the *latter hay*, or *grass*; by the Latins called *foenum cordum*, so not a few render it; but I conceive it rather with one of the Rabbines, (whom yet I find none that follow) to signify that which the Latins call *culmum*, and *stipulam*, the *corn*, says he, *grown up unto its cane*, or *reed*, that is, *stem*, or *stalk*: Before which, while it is yet in the blade, it is oft, either cut down for, or eaten down by cattle, where it grows over-rank: A course not unusual, at this day with us, for the foiling of stoned horses; and such, in likelihood, were *the King’s horses*, for which such corn was cut.

*{and thou hadst a whores forehead, thou refusedst to be ashamed.}* Some others, *but*; as Ch. 2.25. I rather, *yet*; as Ch. 2.35. For all my chastisement of you, in this manner; yet you would not be drawn to take shame to yourself, to acknowledge your sin with shame; as Ezra 9.6. or to be ashamed of what you have done, and to repent you of the same; but like a common strumpet, that is ashamed of nothing, but to seem ashamed of ought; you have persisted in the open practice of your former uncleannesses, Ch. 6.15. & 8.12. Amos 4.7,8. Zeph. 3.5.

*{a whores forehead}* A proverbial form; shame appears in the face, Psal. 69.7. Dan. 9.8. and none more shameless, than common harlots, whence Babylon has her title, telling what she is written in her *forehead*, Rev. 17.5.

**Verse 4.** *{Wilt thou not from this time cry unto me, My Father, thou art the guide of my youth?}* There is a twofold reading in the original. The one runs thus; *Have not I cryed unto thee*, to wit, by my prophets, *that thou shouldest say of me, Thou art my Father, and the guide of my youth?* But this both forces, and fetches the text beyond reason, or due regard. The most, both Jewish, and ours, follow the other, which our version also exhibits; yet do they differ much in the exposition of it: For some take it, as spoken in the time future; will you not at length, learning wisdom by those chastisements, wherewith you have already been exercised; and finding by woeful experience, how little relief you can get from those, on whom you relied, repent you of your folly, and seek again to me? Chap. 8.4,5. Esay 1.5. & 9.12,13. Some, in the time present, as intimating her shamelessness, vers. 3. as if it were said, dare you yet, after all this? Or, have you the face to cry unto me in such terms as these, & ask whether I will ever retain wrath towards you? when as you go on still to give me just occasion so to do. Others, again, in the time past, rendering the words, *Didst thou not from this time cry unto me?* Or, *Hast thou not from this time cryed unto me?* That is, did you not yet all this while make show, as if you had not left me, but did still continue loyal and faithful to me? for in the deepest of their idolatries, they would seem still to retain God’s service. 2 king. 17.32,33,41. Chap. 7.9,10. Ezek. 23.38,39. Zeph. 1.5. Or, Have you not since your rain has been restrained, and you have been punished with drought and dearth, in fawning, but false-hearted manner, sought unto me, imagining thereby, though without reformation, or amendment of ought amiss, to pacify my wrath, and obtain some releasement of the present evil? Chap. 2.35. & 36.6. Psal. 78.34,37. Esay 48.1,2. & 58.2,3. Hos. 5.15. & 6.1,4. & 7.14. and this exposition, the form of the verb favors, being in the time past, and is more probable, than that of some other, who (either not regarding the negative particle here, or taking it only for a note of interrogation, as in Greek sometime it is; and as some other of note also do, Mal. 1.10.) render the words, *Dost thou*, or, *wilt thou still cry unto me*, in this manner? as the speech of God, reproving them, for repairing, or seeking to him, whom they had formerly cast off, to run after idols, and others: not unlike that, Judg. 10.13,14. Psal. 50.16. Chap. 2.26. Ezek. 20.39.

*{Wilt thou not cry?}* Or, *Hast thou not cried?*

*{from this time}* Wherein I now admonish you, Chap. 2.25. or, wherein I have chastised you, vers. 3.

*{cry to me}* Or, *call me*; as Esay 2.19. Ch. 33.16. Hos. 2.18. for in this syntax, the particle is oft redundant.

*{O my Father,}* Lamenting as a child to his father offended; as Luk. 15.21. Chap. 31.18. not unlike that of David, to Saul, 1 Sam. 24.11. or, *My Father*, by way of apposition; *call me* as I command you, and would have you to call me, vers. 19. and as you ought to do: call me your father; so account, and so acknowledge me, vers. 19. that is, one that have loved you as a father, carried a fatherly affection towards you, Deu. 8.5. Psal. 103.13. Mal. 3.16. or that has been your maker, Esay 43.1. & 44.2. & 64.8. for what one upon the place suggests, that the manner was among the Jews, that the bride delivered over to the bridegroom, used then to call him *her Father*; because she was then *to leave her Father*, and *cleave* wholly to *him*, Gen. 2.24. and he thenceforth, to be as a father to her, seems groundless, and nothing probable.

*{the guide of my youth}* Because the old Latin has it, *the guide of my virginity*: therefore some would have this, to respect the name of *Father*, before, given unto God here: for the father, say they, has the care and charge of his daughter’s virginity, until she be joined unto an husband, Deut. 22.15,16. But this conceit has no place here; and some other, though acknowledging the right reading, yet by *guide of my youth*, understand one, that has fostered, and brought me up from my youth, *my foster-father*, as we use to say. But the words, which in the original are expressly, as we have them, contain in them, the ordinary style of an husband, Prov. 2.16. especially such an one, as has married a wife, in her youth, or younger years, Mal. 2.14. as God did this people, Cha. 2.2. and to him, in divers respects, are these two relative titles given; the name of a *Father*, as he made them a people, a church, and a state, Esay 64.8. the name of an *husband*, as by entering into covenant with them, he espoused them to himself, Ezek. 16.8. See Esay 54.5. the words may be read, as the former, in way of compellation also, if we so take them, *O thou the guide of my youth*; as the words of a wife, seeking for reconciliation to her husband, being justly displeased with her, 1 Cor. 7.11. or, as they are in our version, calling upon God, in such terms, as he likes, and allows, Hos. 2.16.

**Verse 5.** *{Will he reserve his anger for ever? will he keep it to the end?}* These words, the Jewish doctors make the prophet’s words, by an interrogation, implying an undoubted negative; as if he had said, would you but thus seek unto God, God (you need not doubt of it) would no longer retain his wrath, but would be at one with you again, vers. 12. Deut. 4.29,31. & 30.1,3. 2 Chr. 7.13,14. But others, the most, and best, rather understand them, as the words of the people, running on in a continued tenor with the former; and those either enjoined them to use, and required to be used of them; as Hos. 14.2,3. Joel 2.17. or used indeed by them: and complaining unto God (though not in sincerity) as God’s own people are oft wont to do, when some breach has fallen out between him and them, lamenting and complaining of the continuance of his wrath and indignation, and laboring to pacify, and appease it again. See Psal. 77.7,9. & 85.5. Esay 64.12.

*{reserve his anger for ever}* A defect of the noun, for the verb to pass unto; as Gen. 42.33. *take*, for, *take* food; *gather*, for, *gather* grapes, Lev. 25.11. *eat*, for, *eat* bread, Chap. 16.7. *tread down*, for, *tread down* their enemies, Zach. 10.5. and in the present notion very rife. So Lev. 19.18. *thou shalt not reserve against the children of thy people*, Psal. 103.9. He *doth not reserve*, or *retain, for ever*, Nah. 1.2. *he reserveth for his enemies*: and hereafter again, *I will not retain for ever*, vers. 12. now the Jewish doctors here insert to make these full, *thy sin*, I will not always keep in mind your sin, Esay 43.25. chap. 31.34. and indeed so it seems, to be not unfitly made up in that place of the law, *Thou shalt not revenge nor retain*, keep in mind a wrong or unkindness done you; which some of the Jewish thus explain. *Simeon* comes to *Reuben* to borrow an ax of him, and he denies it him, some time after *Reuben* comes to *Simeon* to borrow of him a ladder. If *Simeon* answer him, *I will not lend you my ladder because you would not lend me your ax*, he revenges; if he say, *though you would not lend me your ax, yet I will lend you my ladder*, he retains: thus they. Howbeit, in the most places, and so here, the word *wrath* seems to do best.

*{to the end}* Or, *perpetually*, without end, *for ever*; for it is in notion the same with the former. See Esay 13.20. & 25.8. So 2 Sam. 2.26. Psal. 9.19.

*{Behold, thou hast spoken, and done evil things, as thou couldest.}* Here we meet with a double reading again: for some copies have it, *I spake*, or, *I have spoken*. I God’s prophet, or, I the Lord, by my prophet, have spoken to you, and admonished you of these things, endeavoring to reclaim you, vers. 4. Chap. 2.25. but you persist still in your wicked courses, and will not be reclaimed. But the other reading, which our version exhibits, is most generally received; yet with some variety of exposition; for some render the text, as here we have it, *Thou hast spoken, and done evil things as thou couldest*: what you have spoken of your desperate resolution, Chap. 2.25. that you make good by your wicked actions, obstinately persisting in the practice of evil; all that possibly you can, Chap. 8.6. Or, as some other, *Thou dost* both *speak, and do evil* still, *and prevailest*; to wit, by your obstinate wickedness against my goodness, that I cannot remit, or slacken my wrath. See Chap. 15.6. & 44.22. Rom. 12.21. Others again, supposing the foregoing words to be the speech of the people, thus *thou hast spoken*, *but* (as Ch. 2.11,25.) *thou didst wickedly* still all *thou couldest*; as Hosea 7.14. *they cry not with their heart to me, when they howl on their beds; they assemble themselves*, to seek to me *for their corn, and their wine*, but *they rebel* still *against me*. So Esay 58.2,3. And this last exposition seems to me very probable.

*{as thou couldest}* Heb. *and thou couldest*: which some render, *thou prevailest*, or *hast prevailed*; which they seem to expound diversely; one, of their persistence in evil; what you resolve on, you go on in, and there is no stopping, or restraining of you. Chap. 2.24. & 8.6. Another, of prevailing against God’s gracious disposition, and restraining him, from showing favor to them, as otherwise he would, Chap. 5.7,9. Another again, of prevailing with God, upon her repentance; and he renders the text, *Hadst thou* thus *said, though thou hast done evil things, yet thou shouldest have prevailed*: and so indeed is the word used, 1 Kin. 22.22. Ch. 38.22. But here it seems rather to go in its most ordinary sense, and the text to run with it most smoothly: *and thou couldest*, that is, either, *when thou couldest*: so the copulative is used, Ch. 3.4. when you can get any opportunity of putting your wicked plots and purposes in practice, Mic. 2.1. Or, *as thou couldest*; what you could, as far as you were able, or had power in your hand; as Mic. 2.1. If you did not always what you had determined to do, it was for want of ability; not for want of goodwill. So is the copulative used, Job 21.33. & 34.3. and so it answers that, Gen. 44.1. *as they can carry*, that is, *as much as they are able to bear*. The Jewish critic observes here, that the former two verbs are feminine; this masculine; which to solve, he says, that the former has reference to the word *congregation*; the latter, to the word, *people*. See the like, Esay 27.7,8. But of the promiscuous use of the genders, see on Esay 15.1. and on Chap. 2.24,25.

**Verse 6.** *{The LORD also said unto me, in the days of Josiah the King;}* Here, as most agree, begins a new sermon wherein the Lord, by the prophet, first relates Israel’s revolt from him, and how thereupon he had dealt with them: Then taxes Judah, and that as herein worse than Israel, in having not taken warning by what had befallen Israel: yet invites both to repentance, promises restitution, upon repentance; and a reuniting of both people under the Messias; which gracious invitation the faithful party accept of, and make their addresses unto God.

*{The LORD also}* Heb. *And the Lord*; as Chap. 1.3. or, *Moreover*; as Chap. 1.11. or, *Again*; as Esay 8.1. because it begins a new sermon.

*{said unto me}* Acquainted me by revelation, to this purpose, with his mind. So vers. 11. Chap. 11.6.

*{in the days of Josiah the King}* Under the reign of King Josiah, Ch. 1.2. See vers. 10.

*{Hast thou seen that which backsliding Israel hath done?}* Have you not taken notice of the idolatrous courses, that those of the ten tribes took?

*{Hast thou seen?}* Or, *Hast thou not seen?* as 1 Sam. 2.27,28. *did I appear?* for, *did I not appear?* and, *did I choose?* for, *did I not choose?* See Chap. 31.20.

*{seen}* Considered, or taken notice of; as Ch. 2.19,23,31. for whether Jeremy ever saw what was done among those people, is uncertain; that he should see what had been done by them, before their deportation, being yet unborn, was not possible.

*{that which}* Or, *what*: for there is no *that* in the text. So Exod. 19.4. Mic. 6.1.

*{backsliding}* Or, *revolting*; as it is rendered, Chap. 5.23. So v. 8,11,12. See Hos. 4.16.

*{Israel}* The ten tribes, so termed, as the greater part of Israel’s posterity, after their revolt from the house of David, upon the death of Solomon, 2 Kin. 11. in way of distinction from Judah. See Esay 7.1.

*{hath done}* Or, *did*: for he speaks of things, long since past, and done before their deportation, 2 Kin. 17.7,12.

*{she is gone up upon every high mountain, and under every green tree;}* Or, how *she went up*: a defect of the particle, *how*; as Exo. 19.4. See Ch. 2.20. 2 Kin. 17.10.

*{and there hath played the harlot.}* Or, *and committed fornication there*. See vers. 1. Some render the words, *where thou committest fornication*, or, *playest the harlot*; as if in these words God should turn his speech unto *Judah*: and the word in its regular form does so import: but as yet there is no address at all to Judah: and the like irregular form is found in some other words, Deut. 32.18. Chap. 18.23.

**Verse 7.** *{And I said, after she had done all these things}* Or, *yet I said* unto her. *And*, for, *yet*; as Ch. 2.35. v. 3. and a defect of the pronoun; as Esay 37.22. & 66.12. I did not yet presently cast her off; but sought to reclaim her, and invited her by my prophets to repentance, 2 Kin. 17.13. Hos. 12.6. & 14.1. So v. 1,12.

*{Turn thou unto me}* Or, *Return unto me*; as v. 1. to wit, by repentance, and reformation, Esay 57.6,7. Acts 3.19. & 26.18,20. Heb. *Thou shalt return*: the future indicative, for the imperative; as, *Thou shalt love*, Deut. 6.5. and, *Thou shalt not withhold*, for, *withhold not*, Psal. 40.11.

*{but she returned not}* 2 Kin. 17.14. Hos. 7.16. & 11.2,5. Heb. *and*; as Ch. 2.11. v. 1.

*{and her treacherous sister Judah saw it.}* *Judah*; the other two tribes, Judah, and Benjamin, which continued still conjoined, when the other ten revolted: the name imposed from the principal of the twain, that enjoyed the sovereignty, thereby to distinguish it from the other ten. See Esay 1.1.

*{sister}* Israel, and Judah, are, in regard of consanguinity, being both of the lineage of Jacob, termed *Sisters*, Ezek. 16.46. & 23.2,4.

*{treacherous}* Or, *perfidious*, having violated her faith plighted unto God, when the whole body of that people entered into covenant with him at first, Deut. 5.2,3. & 29.10,13. which she had professed to continue in, and keep inviolably, after the revolt of the ten tribes, 2 Chron. 13.9,10. yea, had oftentimes renewed, 2 Chr. 15.12–15. & 23.16. & 29.10. & 34.30–32. but again still violated, by returning eftsoons to her former abominations, 2 Chr. 21.6,10,11. & 24.17,18. & 28.2,3. & 33.2,9. and at present, howsoever she would seem still to continue constant in the service of God; yet all being but counterfeit, her ways being otherwise very lewd and wicked, Chap. 6.19,20. & 7.9–11. Howbeit, the same term is afterward given, as well to the one, as to the other. See vers. 20.

*{saw it.}* *Saw*, that is, *knew*; as Psal. 37.25. & 40.3. with 34.2. could not be ignorant; could not but take notice, both of what her sister had done; and how she had been invited by me to return: for by the same prophets God had sent to them both, 2 Kin. 17.13. a defect of the pronoun, *it*; as Esay 44.19.

**Verse 8.** *{And I saw,}* The sequel of the context in the ensuing discourse, being somewhat obscure and intricate, has much troubled the interpreters, and enforced them to take divers tracts. One of the Jewish commenters gives me an hint of that, that may serve as a thread to lead us through this labyrinth. He observes well, that the *seeing*, here spoken of, has a special reference unto that which comes after, vers. 10. concerning the return of the Jewish people unto God, in the religious reign of Josiah, that for the generality of it, it was not sound and sincere; that which, though Jeremy, and many others, could not discern; yet God, who tries and searches the heart, saw, 1 Sam. 17.7. 1 king. 8.39. Psal. 7.9. Prov. 15.11. & 17.3. & 21.2. chap. 17.10. and the file of the context is therefore to be continued from this to that; which I conceive may most conveniently be thus done, without straining, or forcing the text, as many here do. *And I have seen*, or *see*, that *though for all this, wherein revolting Israel had committed adultery, I had dismissed her, and given her a bill of divorce; yet her perfidious Sister Judah was not afraid, but she also went, and committed fornication*; (*for so it was, that with her notorious fornication she polluted the land, by committing adultery with stones, and with stocks*) and that *for all this her perfidious Sister Judah hath not returned unto me with all her heart, but counterfeitly, saith the Lord*. But we shall examine, and explicate the words apart, as they lie in order in the text.

*{And I saw}* Or, *have seen*, or *do see*; as if he had said, I asked you before, whether you had not seen, how it had been with Israel, vers. 6. I shall now tell you what I have seen, and do still see in Judah; and more it may be than you do, that as they have not taken warning by Israel’s fall, but have been as notoriously lewd, as they; so their external reformation has not been cordial, but counterfeit; *I see*: as Chap. 23.13,14. Some others, *And when I saw*. Others, *And it seemed good unto me*. Others, otherwise; according to which they attemper the several versions of the words ensuing: wherein our version fails, leaving the words hanging in suspense, as if it had been rather, *she saw*, than *I saw*. And the old Latin indeed seems so to have rendered it; for it knits the words following unto the last clause of the verse foregoing: and so some Greek copies also seem to have had it. But that the Hebrew, which the Chaldee also concurs with, controls: whilst yet some interpreters of prime note, though rendering the text themselves otherwise, yet in the exposition run unto.

*{when for all the causes whereby backsliding Israel had committed adultery, I had put her away, and given her a bill of divorce,}* Others, *when I saw that for the actions, wherein she had committed adultery, I must dismiss her*, I *gave her a bill of divorce*. Others, *It seemed good to me for all these causes—to dismiss her, and give her a bill of divorce*.

*{when}* Or, *though*; as Esay 12.1. & 64.6.

*{for all the causes}* Or, *for all*; or, *because of all*: for that is all the word signifies, Gen. 21.11,25. Num. 12.1. & 13.24. Judg. 6.7.

*{whereby backsliding Israel had committed adultery}* Or, *wherein*. Heb. *which*: but herein little difference. Of the terms here given her, see before, vers. 6. what is there termed *fornication*, is here called *adultery*; as also, vers. 9. Ezek. 16.37. because *fornication*, and *adultery*, in a wife, are all one, Matt. 19.9. and this her adulterous carriage, was the cause of her abdication, Ezek. 23.5,8.

*{I had put her away,}* Heb. *dismissed her*. See vers. 5. *to dismiss her*; or, that I must *dismiss her*, suit not well with the text.

*{and given her a bill of divorce;}* Heb. *a book of her divorce*, or, *her book of divorce*; as we use to say, *make*, or, *give him his mittimus*. Of the term, see on Esay 50.1. and God is said to have dismissed, and divorced her, by putting that state from under the wings of his protection, Ruth 3.9. and delivering it up into the hand of the Assyrians, who utterly ruined it, and carried away the main body of her people, and placed them in foreign parts, 2 king. 17.6. Ezek. 23.9. what the Rabbines here debate about the different cases of Judah, and Israel, see on Esay 50.1.

*{yet her treacherous sister Judah feared not}* Or, *that yet her perfidious sister was not afraid*: for the particle, *that*, very frequently suppressed; as Esay 7.1. & 36.1. must of necessity be supplied, either after *I saw*, or in the front of this clause: otherwise the members of the sentence will have no good coherence. Of *Judah*, and the style here given her, see v. 7.

*{but went, and played the harlot also}* Heb. *and* (as v. 1,7.) *she went, and committed fornication*; or, *she also went on whoring*: as, *he went and wept*, for, *he went weeping*, Psal. 126.6. there is an emphasis in the pronoun here expressed, and not therefore to be omitted. See on vers. 7. & Hos. 4.15. & 11.12. She that had retained the profession of God’s service, when her sister had wholly shook it off, and for her idolatries was divorced; yet was not deterred from running out into the like excesses, for which her sister had so suffered, Ezek. 23.11. See 2 king. 17.19.

**Verse 9.** *{And it came to passe through the lightness of her whoredom, that she defiled the land:}* Or, *For so it was, that by her notorious fornication, she profaned*, or *polluted, the land*. This passage, some understand of Israel; some of Judah; some partly, of the one, and partly of the other: which last, seems more improbable, than either of the former: of which twain, I conceive the latter to be the genuine; and the whole verse should be enclosed with notes of intersertion, as above.

*{And it came to pass}* Heb. *And it was*; as 2 Kin. 4.6. & 6.30. or, *For so it was*; as Gen. 12.1. Esay 65.15.

*{through the lightness of her whoredom}* *Lightness*: So the old Latin seems to have taken it; as coming from a word, that signifies *light*, Esay 19.1. Chap. 2.23. and we use indeed to term such as here are intended, *light women*. The Jewish doctors, with the Chaldee, seem to refer it to the same root, but as it has a notion of *contempt*, and vileness, 1 Sam. 2.30. and so it should be, *through the vileness*, or *baseness, of her whoredom*. But the word seems not to come from that root; nor is it ever found used in either of those notions: it signifies commonly *a noise*, or *sound*: but not seldom also, howsoever some have questioned it, *a fame*, or *report*. So it is taken, Gen. 45.16. Cha. 44.15. & 50.46. thus here understood, by *the fame of her whoredom*; will be meant, the report of it blazed abroad; or, as some other, by an *hypallage*, or inversion of the words, not unusual, *the fame of her whoredom*, for, *her whoredom of fame*; that is, *her famous*, (or infamous rather) her *notorious whoredom*; as, *silver of shekels*, for, *shekels of silver*; or, *silver shekels*, Lev. 5.15. and, *the greenness of the tender grass*, for, *the tender grass of greenness*; that is, the *green tender grass*, Psal. 37.2. and it may be so termed, not only in regard of the *fame*, and *bruit*, spread abroad of it; but in regard of the notoriousness of it, in itself; such as does of itself proclaim and publish the shame and filth of the practice: as foul and heinous sins are said to have *a voice, and* to *cry aloud* even to heaven itself, Gen. 4.10. & 18.20. and this the words following, seem to confirm. Now being thus taken, (which I take to be the right) some conceive it to be spoken of Israel: as also, some going the former way of this syntax, render the words, *notwithstanding the report*, or *fame of her whoredom*; that is, although the report of Israel’s idolatry, dwelling so near her, could not but come to her sister Judah’s ears, Ezek. 16.46. But I find not where the particle, here prefixed, is so used. Others, who take the latter, and (as I suppose) righter way, render it, *for her famous*, or *notorious whoredom*; to wit, *it came to pass, that she defiled the land*: which I conceive to be the genuine sense of the words; though more fitly expressed, if instead of *for*, we say *with*, or *by*, or *by reason of*: for the particle is here a causal; as Psal. 18.12,15. Esay 21.3. & 33.3. & 63.17. but that which they fail in, is the misapplication of it; in that they understand it, as spoken of Israel, whereas the course of the context aright conceived, and duly considered, will evidently show it to be intended of Judah, who in the very next words before going, is said to have *gone a whoring*, vers. 8. and concerning whose whoredoms, and the notoriousness thereof, he speaks further in this verse.

*{that she defiled the land}* Heb. *and she profaned*, or *polluted the land*: so is the copulative in this form of speech very frequently used, Esay 22.20. & 37.26. & 65.24. & 66.18. See the same before, Chap. 2.7.

*{and committed adultery with stones, and with stocks.}* With idols made of either. See Chap. 2.27. or, *by committing adultery* with such: as *stand and feed*, for, *stand feeding*, Esay 61.5. See vers. 8. Some render it *for she committed adultery*. But the causal is not needful here.

**Verse 10.** *{And yet for all this, her treacherous sister Judah hath not turned unto me with her whole heart, but feignedly, saith the LORD:}* Or, *And* that *for all this yet*; as having relation to what was before said in the person of God, vers. 8. *I have seen*, or, *I see*, that neither Judah took warning by what had befallen her sister for her impieties and idolatries; for after that she fell into them afresh in the reign of Manasses, 2 Chr. 33.3–9,22. as also that although they seemed to make goodly shows, and fair semblances of returning again to me, in the days of good Josiah, 2 Chr. 34.29,33. & 35.1–18. yet were they never thoroughly converted, or cordially turned from their former idolatrous courses, as appeared by their sudden relapse, and return again to them, presently after his decease, 2 Kin. 23.32–37. & 24.9,19. 2 Chr. 36.1,2,14.

*{yet for all this}* As vers. 8.

*{her treacherous sister Judah}* See vers. 6,7.

*{hath not turned unto me with her whole heart}* Though Josiah himself so did, 2 Kin. 23.25. yet the people, and generality of them had not so done: *with the whole heart*, that is, entirely, sincerely, Psal. 119.2,10. ch. 24.7.

*{but feignedly.}* Heb. *in falsehood*, falsely, counterfeitly: as those, Psal. 78.36,37.

**Verse 11.** *{And the LORD said unto me,}* Or, *The Lord also said unto me:* as Chap. 1. 3.

*{The backsliding Israel hath justified her self more than the treacherous Judah.}* Israel is not so bad as Judah; Israel's sin is not so heinous as is the sin of Judah: both in regard of her perfidiousness, that would seem to retain God's service still with her, and renewed covenants oft with him; (which Israel never did) but broke them as fast again, see vers. 7. and partly, also, because she would not be warned by the sight of that, which had in such idolatrous courses befallen Israel, vers. 8–10. See the like, Ezek. 16. 47, 51, 52. & 23. 4–12.

*{justified her self}* Heb. *her soul;* as Num. 30. 5. *so, his soul,* for *himself,* Job 18. 4. *my soul,* for, *my self,* Psal. 7. 2. *thy soul,* for, *thy self,* 1 Sam. 20. 3.

*{more than treacherous Judah.}* Heb. *from,* or *in regard of;* as if he had said, Israel may go for an honest woman in comparison of Judah; she is so far the worse. The like form, see Esther 2. 17. Prov. 22. 1. Eccl. 7. 1. Isa. 54. 1. and in the like argument, Luke 18. 14. Of the terms given to either, see vers. 6, 7.

**Verse 12.** *{Go, and proclaim these words towards the North,}* God hereupon, the rather to shame Judah, and to entice her to repentance; bids the prophet, turning towards those parts, wherein those of the ten tribes remained captive, to proclaim a gracious invitation of them, to return again to him, with a promise of mercy and favor, to be showed unto them, when they should so do; together with a secret intimation, that it would sometime be so done; and that under the kingdom of the Messiah the reserves of either family should be reunited.

*{Go}* Heb. *Going.* Either the infinitive for the imperative, or the imperative suppressed. *Going go;* that is, go out of hand, presently, setting all other affairs apart. So Chap. 2. 2. & 13. 1. Howbeit, as the Jewish commenter well observes, God's meaning was not that the prophet should travel into those countries where that people then abode; but to address himself unto the performance of the duty enjoined him, setting his face that way; as the like is enjoined Ezekiel, Chap. 20. 46. & 21. 2. and the word therefore (says he well) is to be taken in a notion of address: as Eccl. 2. 1. Jon. 1. 7.

*{and proclaim}* Heb. *and thou shalt cry.* See the like, Chap. 2. 2. & vers. 7.

*{toward the north}* Because the regions of Assyria, and Media, into which those of the ten tribes were transported by Tiglath-Pileser, and Shalmaneser, 2 Kings 15. 29. & 17. 6. lay northeast from Judea. See Chap. 50. 3, 9. as on the contrary part therefore Ezekiel being among the Jewish captives in Chaldea, lying north likewise from Judea, Chap. 1. 14. is willed to look southward, when he was to prophesy against Judah, and Jerusalem, Ezek. 20. 46. & 21. 1. So that he was to utter these words, in the hearing of those of Jerusalem; as ch. 2. 2. but with his face toward the places where Israel was in captivity, so speaking, as if he were parleying face to face with them.

*{and say}* Heb. *and thou shalt say;* as before, *thou shalt cry.*

*{Return, O thou backsliding Israel, saith the LORD.}* The subject matter of that which he was to proclaim; a new summons of Israel to repentance. See v. 6, 7, 14. ch. 31. 22.

*{and I will not cause mine anger to fall upon you.}* I will not proceed further in wrath against you.

*{cause mine anger to fall}* Heb. *make my face to fall:* *face,* for, *anger,* or, *wrath,* as Psal. 34. 16. Lam. 4. 16. because anger discovers itself in the countenance; *to fall:* a metaphor, either, from those that fall in fight upon their foes, Josh. 11. 7. or rather from storms and tempests, that fall from above, to the spoiling and destroying of people, and other creatures here beneath, Gen. 19. 24. Psal. 11. 6. Rom. 1. 18. See Chap. 30. 23, 24. and the Jewish doctors supply here not amiss from the clause following, *for ever,* because it had in the dispersion of them fallen in part, and that heavily, on them already.

*{for I am merciful, saith the LORD}* Or, *pious, pitiful,* Deut. 4. 31. Psal. 86. 15. & 103. 8. & 145. 8.

*{and I will not keep anger for ever.}* I will cease to be further wroth with you, Psal. 103. 9. See on v. 5.

**Verse 13.** *{Only acknowledge thine iniquity,}* No promise of pardon, but upon condition of repentance, Isa. 1. 19, 20. & 55. 7. nor sincere repentance, without serious sight, and ingenuous acknowledgment of sin, Prov. 28. 13. Heb. *yet;* as Psal. 73. 1. *know,* that is, *take notice of,* or *acknowledge;* as Psal. 51. 3. Isa. 59. 12. See chap. 2. 23.

*{that thou hast transgressed against the LORD thy God,}* And have therefore been justly delivered up into captivity, 2 Kings 17. 18.

*{and thou hast scattered thy ways to the strangers under every green tree,}* Running sometime one way, & sometime another, after strange gods, and foreign people, 2 Kings 17. 4, 9, 10. v. 6. See the like, ch. 2. 23, 25. The Rabbine perverts it, when he expounds it, of *the opening of the feet,* Ezek. 16. 25.

*{and ye have not obeyed my voice, saith the LORD.}* Heb. *ye have not hearkened unto my voice;* calling upon you, by my prophets, for reformation of these your wicked ways, and miscarriages, 2 Kings 17. 13, 16. vers. 7.

**Verse 14.** *{Turn, O backsliding children, saith the LORD;}* Or, *Return, Turn again,* as v. 12.

*{for I am married unto you}* Or, *I have married you:* for the verb is active, and is in that form used ever of the man, Deut. 21. 13. & 24. 1. Isa. 54. 5. & 62. 5. Mal. 2. 11. of the woman perpetually in the passive form, Gen. 20. 3. Deut. 22. 22. Prov. 30. 23. Isa. 54. 1. & 62. 4. I am your husband that have married you; I took you at first into covenant to me, and you did enter into the same with me, and plighted your faith unto me among the rest of my people, Deut. 29. 1, 15. and I am ready, notwithstanding your long continued revolt, upon your sincere, and serious repentance, and return to me, to entertain you, and to renew my covenant again with you, Hosea 2. 19, 20. v. 1. Some of the Rabbines render it, *I am your Lord;* and it is not for mine honor, that my people should be in the hands of their enemies, Isa. 52. 5. Ezek. 36. 20. and the word indeed in its first and proper notion so signifies. See chap. 2. 22. but in this place, the constant tenor of the context, comparing this people to a disloyal wife, carries it rather the other way. For as for that, which one of them tells us of a conceit of his fathers, that it should be rendered, *I have been vexed,* or *grieved by you,* or *am grown a weary of you;* or, *I loath,* and *abhor you:* for so the word signifies, whereby he expresses it, Gen. 27. 46. Lev. 20. 23. Num. 21. 5. Isa. 7. 16. withal adding, that the word does always so signify, where the particle *let,* follows it; it seems to me unworthy of any consideration: nor had I mentioned it, but that I find some writers of note, taking notice of it, and some great critics inclining to it, if not approving of it. It is true, that God is said to be vexed and grieved, and wearied with the sins of his people, Isa. 43. 24. & 63. 10. ch. 15. 5. Ezek. 6. 9. but this in no wise sorts here with the sequel of the context: and for that of the particle, it is nowhere found in construction with this verb, save here, and chap. 31. 32. a place parallel to this; and no such judgment therefore can be built thereupon; and it seems to me, to have no other use in either place, than it has in the like syntax, with divers other verbs in that language, with which it is generally deemed to be redundant.

*{and I will take you one of a city, and two of a family, and I will bring you to Zion.}* Our interpreters generally expound this of the paucity, or small remnant of those, that should be reserved, and return, whether into their own country, as they suppose some did with those of Judah, at the dissolution of the Babylonian captivity; or unto God, being converted, and adjoined unto his church, according to those foregoing prophecies, Isa. 11. 11, 12. & 17. 6. & 14. 13. On the other side, some of the Jewish doctors carry it beyond all reason wider another way; as if the meaning were, that if there were but *one* true convert *in a city,* that whole city should be reduced, together with that one: and so if but *two* only such *in a family,* that whole family should, together with those two, be brought back; and so they should all at length return to their own country again. But I see not how the words can admit of such a sense. The former, it is true, they may well bear: howbeit, so taken, they seem not so well to suit with the persons spoken to. The revolted Israelites are invited to *return;* and God promises, if they so do, to *take them;* whom? but the Israelites that do return? some one out of a city, consisting of such; and not the whole city rather, if there were an whole city of such? or one out of a city, consisting of Israelites, among all whom yet but one such should be? I suppose it not probable, that there were any such cities consisting of Israelites only. I embrace, therefore, that here, that one of the Jewish commenters suggests, whom a learned late writer follows; That God would make such an exact search for them, in looking after them upon this their sincere and serious return, in all places, in which they had been dispersed; that though there should be but some *one* only of them, *in a city,* or some *two* only *in a whole country,* yet they should not be neglected, but should be culled out and reduced. It is a plain parallel place unto that of Isa. 27. 12. See the note there. And whereas it may seem to be somewhat improper to say, *one out of a city, and two out of a family;* (for so it would for the fuller expression be rendered) as if a family were of a larger extent than a city. To this, the Rabbine answers not amiss, that the word *family* is in Scripture sometime used for a *country,* or the people of a country; as chap. 1. 15. Gen. 12. 3. (compared with, chap. 22. 18. where for *families,* in the former place, is *nations,* in the latter) Zech. 14. 17, 18. and may well so also be used in this place.

*{I will bring you to Zion}* Either join you unto Judah again, that you may worship God at Jerusalem with them, chap. 3. 18. Ezek. 27. 21, 22. or join you unto my church, whereof Zion is a type; that so *all Israel may be saved,* Rom. 11. 26. See Isa. 56. 7. & 66. 20. See also vers. 18.

**Verse 15.** *{And I will give you Pastors according to my heart, which shall feed you with knowledge and understanding.}* As God promises upon their repentance, to reduce, and restore them; so to settle a government among them, for the continuance of them, in a right and religious course and carriage, and such rulers over them, as should not either mislead them or oppress them, which others formerly had done, Isaiah 13. 11. Chap. 23. 1, 2. Ezek. 34. 2–4, 10. but should rule and govern them in a religious manner, with a wise and discreet regard of their good, Isaiah 60. 17, 18. Chap. 23. 4.

*{I will give you}* It is God that gives governors, whether good or bad; as a blessing, the one; as a chastisement and exercise, the other, Hos. 13. 11. Act. 13. 20, 21. Ephes. 4. 11.

*{Pastors}* rulers, either in the state, as some, Chap. 12. 7. Mic. 5. 5. or in the church, as others, Ephes. 4. 11. or in both, Isa. 56. 10, 11. See Chap. 23. 1, 4.

*{according to mine heart}* Such as I like and approve of, and know to be faithful, and such as shall govern you according to my will and desire, 1 Tim. 1. 12. an allusion to God's testimony of David, 1 Sam. 13. 14.

*{which shall feed you}* As John 21. 15–17. 1 Pet. 5. 2. or, *rule you,* cha. 23. 2. Ezek. 34. 2. Act. 20. 28.

*{with knowledge and understanding}* This clause either respects the manner of their ruling in skillful and discreet manner, Psal. 78. 72. 1 Pet. 5. 2. or the subject matter of their feeding, the food wherewith God's people were to be fed, the spiritual food of sound knowledge, and right understanding of God's truth, Deut. 33. 19. Neh. 8. 8, 12. Mal. 2. 7. Eph. 4. 11. 1 Tim. 3. 2. 2 Tim. 4. 2. But I suppose, that it has respect here to the former.

**Verse 16.** *{And it shall come to pass when ye are multiplied and increased in the land, in those days, saith the LORD, they shall say no more, The Ark of the Covenant of the LORD; neither shall it come to mind, neither shall they remember it; neither shall they visit it, neither shall that be done any more.}* This place seems as pregnant as is possible, for the utter cessation and abolition of those visible pledges of God's special presence among his people, which before had by God himself been to that purpose sanctified, set apart, and settled among them, after the enlargement and growth of his church under the Messiah. Which yet the Jewish masters, though acknowledging the Messiah his times here to be intended, labor, by a very sorry shift, to put off: for the meaning, say they, is, that in those times they shall not need to think of sending for the Ark of God, to be with them in their camp, or of carrying it out with them into the field, as in times past they had done, Josh. 3. 3, 6, 11. & 6. 8, 13. 1 Sam. 4. 4, 5. & 14. 18. 2 Sam. 11. 11. & 15. 24. because all shall then be quiet, there shall be no war, after the expedition of Gog and Magog is once over, Isaiah 2. 4. But besides that we read not that after the temple was once built, the Ark, once therein seated, was ever removed, brought out again, or any such use at all made of it: the words are very general, and very express, that it should not at all be sought to, or once minded, or any use at all made of it. And yet this, as light a shift as it is, is by a learned late writer also held forth, and approved. Nor want there other of ours, and some of chief note, that will not suffer this Scripture to go the way before mentioned; but turn it another way; some expounding it, that whereas formerly the Jews herein gloried over Israel, that they had the Ark of God with them, a pledge of his special presence among them, which the other had not, 2 Chron. 13. 9, 10. such a conjunction and concord, should be now between them, that Judah should no more glory herein, God should be alike present with either. Other again, that after their restitution, the Jewish people themselves should not so much trust unto, and rely upon, those outward pledges of God's favor toward them, and presence among them, the Ark, and the temple, as formerly they had done, Chap. 7. 3. But these considerations, as well as the former, do all come far short of, and are a great deal too narrow, to reach the large and wide extent of the expressions of God's Spirit in this place. That which some others have, that therefore no regard should in those times be had of the Ark, because the whole city should be deemed equally holy with it; for whereas the Ark was as God's throne, or chair of estate before, (see on Isa. 37. 16.) and the temple in regard of it, Chap. 14. 21. & 17. 12. Ezek. 43. 7. now Jerusalem, the whole city should be so esteemed, vers. 7. it fits well with the state and condition of the church; but could not consist with the ordinance of God, so long as a temple, whether with an Ark, or without an Ark, allowed and approved of by God, in its peculiar use and force stood. For as concerning what some others say, That in the second temple there was no Ark at all; and would have this Scripture to intimate as much: It is first a great question, whether it be a truth, and not a Jewish fable: the grounding of it on that defect of a letter in a word, Hag. 1. 8. is without doubt, both frivolous, and ridiculous. But whether it were so or no, it cannot concern this place: for if there were no Ark in it, it was a defect; and that such as was not by any means extraordinary otherwise supplied: and it is esteemed by the Jews themselves as a blemish; whereas the want of an Ark; the use of it, and regard to it, here implied, is mentioned as no small benefit and dignity to the church, of the times here intended; they should have no need now of such an ordinance; they should not miss it, they should find no want at all of it.

*{it shall come to pass}* Heb. *it shall be:* as vers. 9.

*{when ye are multiplied and increased}* Heb. *and have fructified,* or, *are grown fruitful,* Gen. 26. 22. Exod. 1. 7. both words are oft joined together, but the latter here usually in the former place elsewhere; as Gen. 1. 22, 28. & 9. 1, 7. chap. 23. 3. but as here, so Ezek. 36. 11. a place parallel to it: and it seems to imply, that they should be fruitful in converting of many from abroad, and bringing them in unto the church. See vers. 17.

*{in the land}* An eye to the land of Canaan, resembling God's church; called therefore the *holy land,* Zech. 2. 12.

*{in those days}* Or, *times;* as Chap. 1. 2, 3.

*{they shall say no more}* Or, *it shall not be said;* as Chap. 16. 14. So Ch. 31. 29. there shall be no more talk of it.

*{The Ark of the Covenant of the LORD}* So is the Ark commonly called, Numb. 10. 33. Deut. 10. 8. & 31. 9, 25, 26. Heb. 9. 4. as also other whiles, *The Ark of the testimony,* Exod. 25. 22. & 30. 26. & 31. 7. and the ground of either style is the same, to wit, because the two tables of the law; wherein the covenant made between God and his people, was contained, Exod. 34. 28. & 40. 35. Deut. 9. 9, 11, 15. and were therefore a testimony of the same, 2 King. 11. 12. Isa. 8. 20. were reserved in the Ark, Exod. 25. 16, 21. & 40. 20. and as the Ark is therefore so called in regard of them, as made principally for them, 1 King. 8. 9. so is the tabernacle also called *the Tabernacle of the Testimony,* as intended chiefly for them, and it, Exod. 30. 26. & 38. 21. Act. 7. 44. the Ark therefore containing them, being seated in the innermost, principal, and most sacred place, both of the tabernacle, and the temple, Exod. 40. 21. 1 King. 8. 6. Heb. 9. 3, 4. And if the use of this chief and principal pledge of God's presence, after the coming of the Messiah, and the church consisting of Jew and Gentile under him settled, was utterly to cease; much more the place designed for it, with the whole furniture thereof, service restrained to it, and rites appertaining thereunto, John 1. 17. & 4. 23. Col. 2. 17. Heb. 10. 1, 8, 9.

*{neither shall it come to mind}* Heb. *ascend,* or, *go up, upon the heart.* Men shall not mind it; they shall not so much as once dream of it. See Isa. 65. 17. So Ch. 7. 31. 1 Cor. 2. 9.

*{neither shall they remember it}* Or, *neither shall they mention it,* or, *make mention of it:* for the syntax here seems to lead unto that notion of the word; it shall not be remembered, or mentioned any more: for the verb is indefinite, as that before, *they shall say,* for, *it shall be said:* and also in the next branch,

*{neither shall they visit it}* That is, *it shall not be visited;* there shall be no more repairing unto the place of its residence, to pray, and worship there before it, as now there is, Deut. 12. 11–14. 1 Sam. 7. 2. 2 Sam. 7. 18. 1 Kin. 8. 29, 30, 33, 34. 1 Chr. 13. 3. Psa. 42. 2. & 84. 7. & 95. 2. & 99. 5.

*{neither shall that be done any more}* No such visitation of it shall any more be used; or rather, as some other render it, *neither shall it any more be magnified:* it shall not be in any repute, or esteem; so the word seems to import, Deut. 32. 6. 1 Sam. 12. 6. The Spirit of God using here so many pregnant expressions, and so seriously and instantly inculcating, in such variety of terms, one and the same thing, seems to have foreseen how loath and backward people would be, this people especially, to admit of, and assent unto, the matter here foretold; and how prone and forward by sleights and subtleties, to writhe and wrest this prediction to some other intent and purpose; and to have delivered it therefore in such express and precise terms, as might cut off all ambiguity, and meet with all such devices as human wit should invent, either to elude, or divert it.

**Verse 17.** *{At that time they shall call Jerusalem the Throne of the LORD}* Or, *Jerusalem shall be called;* for such indefinite forms are by the passive best expressed. So vers. 16. Mal. 1. 4. *Jerusalem,* God's church, whereof that was a type; Gal. 5. 26. Rev. 21. 2. *shall be called;* shall so be, and be so accounted; as Isa. 60. 14. & 61. 6. *the Throne of the Lord;* in regard of his constant residence, and sitting in state and power, by his ordinances, and by the exercise of them there, together with his Spirit accompanying the same. See Ch. 14. 21. & 17. 12. & before on v. 16.

*{and all the nations shall be gathered unto it;}* That so Jacob's prophecy may be fulfilled, concerning *the gathering of the nations unto Shiloh at his coming,* Gen. 49. 10. and the word here used, is the same with that, Gen. 1. 9. where God says, *Let the waters under heaven be gathered together into one place:* as also it is said in that parallel place, Isa. 2. 2. *the nations shall flow into it;* as intimating both their multitudes, and their forwardness, or eagerness, rather forcing, than forced in, Psa. 110. 2, 3. Matt. 11. 12.

*{to the name of the LORD to Jerusalem}* To the place which God shall make choice of, to place his name there, Deut. 12. 11. which was sometime *Jerusalem,* Psal. 122. 3, 4. is now *the Church,* 1 Tim. 3. 15. Rev. 21. 2, 3. but Jerusalem now without Ark or temple; for those things are now past and gone, vers. 16. Rev. 21. 22. Yet some read it, *for the name of the Lord to Jerusalem.* But the former I approve rather, as precisely answering the particle, used twice here in the text; which though it be sometime indeed so used, as in the former place they would have it, as Gen. 2. 23. yet why it should here swerve from its most proper notion and use, I see not. See Isaiah 60. 9.

*{neither shall they walk any more after the imagination of their evil heart.}* Neither the Israelites, nor the proselyte Gentiles, shall take such evil courses, as before times they did; but shall live according to the prescript of God's will and word, Isaiah 2. 3.

*{the imagination}* The word here used is very frequent, both in this prophet, Chap. 7. 24. & 9. 13. & 11. 5, 13. & 16. 12. & 18. 12. & 23. 17. and elsewhere, Deut. 29. 19. Psal. 81. 12. but concerning the native and genuine sense of it, there is much difference among the learned, as well Jewish as others: for some render it, *stiffness, obstinacy, stubbornness;* deriving it from a term commonly used among the Talmudists, implying *firmness,* and *fastness.* Others,

*pravity,* and *perverseness;* deducing it from a word that signifies the *navel,* and the knotty *wreaths* of it, Ezek. 16. 4. Job 40. 16.
