Others, *wriness,* or *obliquity.* Whence *enemies* are deemed by them to be so termed; because they *look awry* on those whom they are at enmity with, Psal. 5. 8. & 27. 11. & 54. 5. & 56. 2. & 59. 10. though rather, because they have either a cautious, or an insidious eye on them, they *observe* and *watch* them to do them a shrewd turn, 1 Sam. 18. 9. Psal. 56. 6. Chap. 20. 10. Other lastly, as ours here, *imagination,* or *cogitation,* or *contemplation,* or *thought,* or *sight:* which last seems most genuine; because all those that thus diversely render it, yet herein concur, that they hold it to rise from a root that signifies *to see,* or *to view,* Num. 23. 9. & 24. 17. yet herein may some difference arise, in that *sight* applied to the soul, sometime respects the mind and its imagination, judgment and approbation of aught; as Psal. 17. 2. *let thine eye-lids see the right;* that is, consider and approve it: and so *the imagination of the heart* should be, what the mind conceives, resolves and approves of: sometime, it respects the will and affection; as Psal. 66. 18. *if I see iniquity with my heart:* if mine heart hang after it; if I affect it, and have a desire to it: so it should import here *the desire of the heart:* according to either it may be rendered, *the sight of the heart:* they shall not follow what their corrupt heart likes and loves; what it approves and affects. See the like phrase, Num. 15. 39. Eccl. 11. 9. Isa. 57. 17.

**Verse 18.** *{In those days shall the house of Judah walk with the house of Israel,}* Some render it, *The house of Judah shall go to the house of Israel.* So the ancient Greek, and the old Latin; that is, say some, The one shall go to the other, that they may return jointly in company home together: and so is the particle used, Isa. 22. 15. and in the latter part of this verse: And these suppose an allusion in these words to the return from the Babylonian captivity, Judah said to go to Israel, because Cyrus his proclamation did principally concern them, abiding in Babylon, and other parts of Chaldea: But that they should send to, and invite those of the ten tribes remaining in Assyria and Media, to come and go along with them: whereof, though we find no record, yet it is not unlikely that divers of the other tribes did, whether invited by them or no. Or, as others, there shall be free and open passage from the one to the other, that they may have mutual trade and commerce the one with the other; as Isa. 19. 23, 24. contrary to that which had formerly been, Luk. 9. 53. John 4. 9. But the Chaldee, and the Jewish commenters, whom some others also follow, read the words as our Version has them, *Judah shall walk with Israel:* and they point us to places where the particle is elsewhere so used, Exod. 35. 22. 1 Sam. 20. 8. Isa. 7. 2. Ezek. 16. 37. Mic. 7. 13. the meaning then is, they shall be reconciled either to other, and shall converse in familiar and friendly manner the one with the other: for that is usually designed by the term of *walking together,* Psal. 55. 14. Amos 3. 3. the enmity that had been formerly between those two houses, shall then cease: the ten tribes being then reunited to the other two tribes: and the other two joining in amity with them, and both walking in one way together with those proselytes, v. 17. See Isa. 11. 13. Ezek. 37. 19, 22. Hos. 1. 11.

*{the house of Judah, with the house of Israel}* Of these *two houses,* see Isa. 8. 14.

*{and they shall come together out of the land of the North}* From Chaldea, and Assyria, the places of their captivity, both from Judea northward: See vers. 12. Chap. 1. 13. & 31. 8. The spiritual deliverance, and restitution of them, by Christ, with the constitution of them in the body politic of his church, being shadowed out in these prophetical sermons, by those temporal deliverances and restaurations, that to either of those two people, or any considerable party of either, God was pleased to afford. So Isa. 11. & 54. & 60. Chap. 31. & 33.

*{to the land that I have given for an inheritance unto your fathers.}* Or, *that I gave.* Heb. *which I caused your fathers to inherit,* or *to possess,* as an inheritance, Psal. 44. 2, 3. & 78. 51. & 135. 12. & 136. 21, 22. the land of Canaan, see v. 16.

**Verse 19.** *{But I said, How shall I put thee among the children, and give thee a pleasant land, a goodly heritage of the Hosts of nations?}* Some read these words in the time past, *How did I put thee among the children, and gave thee a pleasant land,* &c. as if God should relate what he had formerly done for this people; as Esa. 63. 7, 8. Amos 2. 9, 11. but the most conceive them as the words of God, relating what he intended to do for them, upon condition of their repentance, and continuance in loyalty to him.

*{But I said,}* Heb. *And I said,* which some also here retain. Others, *I said indeed;* as Isa. 30. 20. As if he had said, I had such thoughts as these with myself, for he speaks after the manner of men, in dealing and discoursing with men. See Isaiah 63. 8.

*{How shall I}* Or, *should I.* The voice of God either admiring, and devising with himself, as some, by what means a people brought so low, and worn out with long captivity, might or could be restored to a flourishing state and condition again, like that, Ezek. 37. 3. *Can these bones live?* or, as others, rather, not so much wondering, as demanding of them, how he should do that for them, which he had before said, he would do, to wit, bring them home, and settle them in their land again, vers. 18. such an one, as is here related, when as they had dealt so perfidiously with him in times past, and had so defiled it before, vers. 6, 9, 13, 20. Somewhat like that, Hos. 6. 4. & 11. 8.

*{put thee among the children}* Or, as some, *among my children:* a defect of the pronoun possessive; as Job 13. 18. Isa. 49. 16. how should I reckon or account you as one of mine adopted ones, Hos. 1. 10. The syntax will not admit that of a learned late writer, *I will make thee sons:* that is, says he, I will bless you with a plentiful issue, Isa. 44. 3, 4. v. 16.

*{and give thee a pleasant land}* For a child's portion; a possession, among my people, who are as children to me, Exod. 13. 11. Psa. 16. 6. & 136. 21, 22.

*{a pleasant land}* *A desirable,* or *delightful land.* Heb. *a land of desire,* or *delight.* So is the land of Canaan termed, Psal. 106. 24. Zech. 7. 14. Of the phrase, see Isa. 2. 16.

*{a goodly heritage}* Heb. *an heritage,* or *possession of goodliness,* or *beauty.* Of the term, and form, see on Isa. 4. 2. & 13. 19. & 24. 16. & 28. 1, 4, 5. It is an attribute given oft to the land of promise, 2 Sam. 1. 19. Ezek. 7. 20. & 25. 9. Dan. 8. 9. & 11. 16, 41, 48.

*{of the Hosts of Nations}* Somewhat to this purpose, the Greek; and the Latin, just so renders it: but the Greek, and some other, insert the word, *God;* the land of the God *of Hosts,* the almighty ruler *of the Nations.* Others, insert the word *land* only, supplied from the former branch, and they expound it, some, a land of *hosts of nations;* that is, a land held by people that were strong and mighty, Num. 13. 28, 29, 32, 33. Deut. 4. 38. Amos 2. 9. or warlike, and ready to wage war with those that should offer to invade them, Num. 21. 23, 33. But the Chaldee Paraphrast, with whom the Jewish doctors here concur, expounds the word here used, to the same effect with the former, as they may well both belong to the same root, and may well import the same thing, save that the one is singular, the other plural: and it is by them two ways rendered, either *the heritage of the delight of delights,* or *deliciousness of deliciousnesses of the nations;* that is, the most goodly, pleasant, and most delightful country, that any nation is possessed of: Or, a land *of the desires of the nations;* that is, such a land as all nations much affect and desire; the word coming from a root that in the Chaldee, or Syriac tongue rather, signifies, *to will,* or *desire,* Dan. 5. 19. & 7. 19. and this latter notion seems in this place the genuine. See Ezek. 20. 6. where this land is styled by the former term here used, *the goodly one of all lands;* that is, the goodliest and most desirable of any.

*{and I said, Thou shalt call me my Father, and shalt not turn away from me.}* Or, as some, *further I said;* as Chap. 1. 11. & 2. 1. I should rather render it, *yet I said;* as vers. 7. As if he had said, After such cross thoughts as might dissuade me, from showing such grace and favor unto this people, I yet at length resolved to do it, upon condition, that they would take me for their protector, and continue loyal to me.

*{call me my Father}* So account me, and so acknowledge me, vers. 3, 4. Psal. 89. 26. Mat. 23. 9.

*{shalt not turn away from me}* From following me (as Matt. 16. 24.) to go after strange gods, Deut. 7. 4. Heb. *from after me;* as 1 Sam. 15. 11.

**Verse 20.** *{Surely as a treacherous wife departeth from her husband; so have ye dealt treacherously with me, O house of Israel, saith the LORD.}* Concerning the connection of these words with the former, there is some diversity of opinion among interpreters, whence the initial particle is diversely either rendered, or supplied. For some read as our Version, *Surely;* and the word here used most usually so signifies, Gen. 28. 17. Exod. 2. 14. vers. 23. Yet some render it, *But;* and so it seems to be used, Psal. 66. 19. & 82. 7. Zeph. 3. 7. and this last place may seem parallel to the present: for God there tells, what he presumed and promised to himself of them, and expected from them: but withal there relates, what contrary courses they took; and it may be deemed, that God does the like here: and this suits well with the exposition of those, who understand the foregoing verse, of the time past; to wit, of God's seating and settling them at first in that land. But others, some render it with the supply of a causal, *For surely,* which I conceive to sort best with the sequel of the context: as if God should in these words have rendered a reason, why he would have her engage herself unto such future loyal carriage; because she had in this kind been very faulty before, vers. 6, 13. the like defect of the causal, see Gen. 42. 18.

*{as}* The note of similitude is wanting; as Job 7. 9. but it may here be included in the particle expressed; as in other the like oft it is, see Isa. 29. 16. & 64. 9.

*{a treacherous wife departeth}* Heb. *a woman dealeth disloyally;* a *woman,* for, *a wife,* as Ch. 16. 2. *dealeth disloyally,* for *dealing disloyally departeth:* or in disloyal manner leaves, and *departs from her husband,* Prov. 2. 17. a complexive form, like that, Isa. 38. 17. *thou hast loved my soul from the pit;* that is, *out of love* delivered, or saved *my soul from the pit;* as Psal. 103. 4.

*{from her husband.}* Heb. *friend;* as Hos. 3. 1. either her husband, whom she has in a solemn legal manner been joined to, or to whom she has otherwise engaged herself; as that Levite's concubine, Judg. 19. 1, 2.

and that Samaritan woman, John 4. 17, 18. a learned man observes here, that the word comes from a term, that signifies to *consort,* or keep company with one, Prov. 29. 3. and that thence an Ethiopic word derived, is used for a *bridegroom,* Mat. 9. 15. and would have this so taken here.

*{so have ye dealt treacherously with me, O house of Israel}* Or, *so ye house of Israel* (you Israelites) *have dealt disloyally with me;* unto whom you had solemnly plighted yourselves, as in a conjugal bond, v. 14. see vers. 8.

**Verse 21.** *{A voice was heard upon the high places weeping, and supplications of the children of Israel.}* This voice divers interpreters understand of a lamentation, and outcry, made by the people, in regard of their grievous pressures, and sore calamities, either breaking in upon them, as those that apply it unto Judah and Jerusalem, surprised and sacked, as some, by the Babylonians; as other, by the Romans; (who seem to be clean out of the way) or continuing still with them, and lying heavy upon them; as those that apply it unto Israel, whom questionless it concerns. But others rather, and so the Jewish commenters, expound it, of a bewailing of their sins, and acknowledgment of them, with a seeking unto God for mercy and pardon: and this the term of *supplications* leads us unto. The like, see Zech. 12. 10.

*{A voice was heard}* So the Greek, and the old Latin, whom most follow: Yet some late writers, *shall be heard:* but it should rather be, *A voice is heard:* for, as the Jewish critic well observes, it is not a verb, but a participle of the present tense; as the like is, Chap. 31. 15. a place parallel to this: and it is, as if the prophet had said, Methinks I hear such a voice already, see Isa. 13. 4.

*{upon the high places}* The Greek here, by a gross mistake, renders it, *A voice from the lips:* The old Latin, *in the ways;* as Amos 5. 16. But the right of it is, as the Jewish commenter well expresses it, *in the eminencies,* or *high,* and *eminent* places; as Chap. 7. 29. which some understand, *on the housetops:* where in public calamities, lamentations, and outcries, were sometime made, Isa. 15. 3. & 22. 1. Chap. 38. 28. Others, suppose it an allusion to the manner of those that keep sentinel in places erected for that purpose; or that having some business of importance to impart unto others, get up into such places, or repair to some higher ground, from whence they may the better, and by the more, be heard, Deut. 27. 12, 13. Judg. 9. 7. Isaiah 40. 9. whether way in that regard we take it, the phrase seems to import, either *a loud* cry; as Chap. 22. 20. or an *open* cry; as our Savior uses the like term, Matth. 10. 27. with reference to such places, from whence such cries may be loudest and farthest heard: for I cannot concur with that learned man, that would have it rendered, *in the low places,* or *in the plains,* see on vers. 2.

*{weeping and supplications}* According to this reading, there is a defect of the copulative; as Isa. 30. 33. & 32. 13. which the Chaldee supplies: and they are found so conjoined, Chap. 31. 9. but the words in the original seem here to run in another syntax, thus; *A voice of weeping of supplications;* that is, *of weeping in supplications,* or, of *supplication tears;* of *weeping,* or, *mournful supplications;* of supplications joined with weeping. So Ezek. 7. 16. Zech. 12. 10. Ch. 31. 18. sorrow for sin, and the expressions of it, should be somewhat proportionable to the heinousness of it; Peter when he had fallen foully, *wept bitterly,* Matt. 26. 75.

*{for they have perverted their ways, and they have forgotten the LORD their God.}* This some take as rendering a reason of their present calamity, the ground that had given them this cause of lamentation, Chap. 2. 17, 19. & 30. 15. vers. 25. Isa. 59. 14. Others, rather conceive it as the subject matter of their lamentation; they bewailed their sins and forepassed transgressions, as Ephraim, the same with Israel, Chap. 31. 18. to which purpose also some of the Rabbines supply the word of *confession;* confessing, *that they have perverted their ways:* but that is not necessary: for the text without it, runs smoothly enough thus; *A voice of weeping in supplications,* or *supplications* joined with *weeping, that they have,* or *because they* perverted *their ways;* that is the thing that in their prayer they lament and bewail: it is not unlike that, Lam. 5. 14. *Woe worth us, that ever we thus sinned:* the particle is in either place the same.

*{perverted their ways}* See Lam. 3. 9.

*{forgotten the LORD their God}* Hos. 2. 13. & 8. 14. See Ch. 2. 32.

**Verse 22.** *{Return ye backsliding children——Behold we come unto thee.}* In these words the prophet seems to personate both the ministers of God, that should invite this people to return unto God, in the former branch; and the people wrought upon by their ministry, returning an answer unto their call, in the latter branch; for the better clearing whereof, some insert these supplies, *Return ye backsliding children;* shall the Lord say; and, *Behold we come unto thee,* shall they say; or, *Return ye backsliding children,* says he; *Behold we come unto thee,* say they; for the prophet speaks it in a prophetical strain, as of a thing present. See the like, Psal. 27. 8. 2 Sam. 18. 3. Isa. 26. 19. Ch. 2. 25.

*{Return ye backsliding children;}* God's gracious invitation of them, by his ministers, and messengers, Act. 2. 38. & 3. 19. 2 Cor. 5. 20. See v. 14. Hos. 14. 1.

*{and I will heal your backslidings.}* Or *revolts:* all the breaches made between you and me, shall be salved and made up again; I will pass them all by, and be reconciled again to you; yea, I will remove all those evils, and repair all those ruins, which by your revolt from me, you had brought upon yourselves, see Isa. 57. 18. Ch. 32. 40. Zech. 10. 6.

*{Behold, we come to thee:}* Their answer, as ready to return at God's call; as Psa. 18. 44. spoken rather in the person of the people of Israel, to shame Judah: not unlike to that, 2 Sam. 19. 11, 12. than, as some would have it, the speech of God, putting such words into their mouths, as he would have them to use to him, v. 4, 5. Hos. 14. 2, 3. reading the words, say, *Behold we come to thee.*

*{for thou art the LORD our God.}* You are he that has right to us, and are best able to save us, Isa. 55. 7. Ch. 14. 22.

**Verse 23.** *{Truly in vain is salvation hoped for from the hills, and from the multitude of mountains:}* The reason why they repair to God, and seek unto him; because they now find the vanity and inability of all other stays, and that he alone is able to save them. The Hebrew is concise; *in vain from the hills, the multitude the mountains;* but the supply is from the next branch: the like whereunto, see Psal. 20. 7.

*{Truly}* Or, *Surely;* as vers. 20.

*{in vain}* Heb. *in,* or, *unto falsehood,* or, *a lie,* or, *vanity.* So Cha. 8. 8.

*{from the hills}* By the *hills* and *mountains,* some here understand the strength of their hills and forts; those especially about Jerusalem, or those of Samaria, and others in those parts, which they formerly had much relied upon, and trusted unto, Ch. 5. 17. & 21. 13. Psal. 125. 2. Amos 6. 1. or the aids that they expected from beyond the hills, Psa. 121. 1. & 60. 11. by *mountains* especially, the helps of great kings, as the Assyrian and Egyptian, Hosea 5. 13. & 7. 11. & 12. 1. & 14. 3. But others, and so the Jewish commenters, their idols, whom they had worshipped upon the hills and high places, vers. 6. Chap. 2. 20. but now found altogether unable to afford them any relief, or delivery, Ch. 2. 11, 13. & 10. 5, 14, 15. Isaiah 46. 7.

*{and from the multitude of mountains;}* Or, *from the multitude in the mountains;* that is, the multitude of idols that were worshipped on the mountains: for the Jewish critics observe, that the former word does not lean upon the latter, but is in a form absolute and entire, and a defect there is of the particle *in,* to be supplied; as Deut. 22. 21. 2 Kings 12. 11. Howbeit, a learned man would have the word rendered *mountains,* to be not a noun, but a verb, that signifies *to lift up,* or *to offer,* whence the word for an *oblation,* Isa. 40. 20. and he thus renders the whole sentence, *Surely in vain it is from off the hills to offer a multitude,* to wit, of oblations, or many oblations; or because the word *hamon* signifies, as well *noise,* or *tumult,* as *multitude,* Psal. 65. 7. *to offer with noise,* or *tumult,* a defect of the particle; as Isa. 33. 5, 7. as having reference to the mountains on which they were wont to sacrifice to their idols, v. 6. Ch. 2. 20. The words will admit either.

*{truly in the LORD our God is the salvation of Israel.}* Or, *surely,* as before. It is the true God alone whom we were sometime joined unto, that is able to save us. Psal. 3. 8. & 44. 7. & 130. 7, 8. Isa. 43. 11. & 45. 15, 17. & 63. 1. Jon. 3. 8.

*{the salvation of Israel}* That is here, *our salvation:* the noun for the pronoun; as Isaiah 2. 1. but they speak so the rather, in regard of the promises made by God unto Jacob, concerning himself, and his seed, and God had by that name taken them unto himself, and into his protection, Psal. 135. 4. Isa. 41. 8, 14. Chap. 14. 8.

**Verse 24.** *{For shame hath devoured the labour of our fathers from our youth, their flocks and their herds, their sons and their daughters.}* Our idols have brought nothing either to us, or our fathers, but damage and detriment, both in their state, and their issue; yea, destruction on either.

*{For}* Heb. *And;* as Isa. 65. 15.

*{shame}* *Shame,* say some, that is, *sin;* for sin brought in shame, Gen. 2. 25. & 3. 7. and is that alone whereof men justly may, and ought to be ashamed, Ezra 9. 6. Chap. 2. 26. vers. 3, 25. Ch. 8. 12. Ezek. 43. 10, 11. Rom. 6. 21. Eph. 5. 12. Phil. 3. 19. or, *that shameful thing,* as some not amiss render it, that is, say they, their idol Baal, Cha. 11. 13. Hos. 9. 10. whence *Jerubbaal,* Judg. 6. 32. is termed *Jerubbesheth,* from the word here used, 2 Sam. 11. 21. a name used, as *Baal,* Chap. 2. 23. for their idols in general, as being all most base and shameful things.

*{hath devoured}* Or, *consumed;* wasted and destroyed (as Isa. 9. 18. Joel 1. 19.) all these things here reckoned up, being either wastefully spent upon them, Ezek. 16. 16, 21. Hos. 2. 8. or, wasted and consumed by God's just judgment upon them for the service of such, Hos. 2. 3, 4, 9, 12. Cha. 5. 17.

*{the labour of our fathers}* The fruits of the earth, and the wealth, gotten by their industry and painful labor. So Psalm 128. 2. Isa. 45. 14. Chap. 5. 27. & 20. 5. See Ezek. 23. 29. Hos. 2. 9. & 8. 7.

*{from our youth}* Or, *childhood;* as Gen. 8. 21. from time to time, as far as we can remember, or have been able to observe aught, we find that nothing has thrived, but all has gone backward, and been wasted with our fathers, and ourselves; or ever since the time that we were first a nation, as Isa. 48. 8. so Chap. 2. 2. & 22. 21. yet here it may seem to be taken the former way. See vers. 25.

*{their flocks and their herds}* Their cattle of all sorts; the less, as sheep and goats, both which the former word comprehends, Exod. 12. 5. and the greater, as beeves, which the latter properly signifies, Isa. 65. 25. either being spent in sacrifices to their idols, Amos 4. 4, 5. or destroyed by the enemy, or the curse of God otherwise upon them, for their idolatry, Ch. 5. 17.

*{our sons and our daughters}* Either their idols requiring them also for sacrifice, on whom they spared not to bestow them, Psal. 106. 37. 2 King. 17. 17. or taken away from them by the sword, plague, and famine, sent in upon them by God for these their idolatries. See Deut. 28. 51, 57. Hos. 2. 4. & 9. 11, 16.

**Verse 25.** *{We ly down in our shame, and our confusion covereth us; for we have sinned against the LORD our God, we and our fathers, from our youth unto this day, and have not obeyed the voice of our God.}* We have likewise brought abundance of shame and confusion upon ourselves, by treading continually in the wicked steps of our forefathers.

*{lye down in shame}* As a man that being in straits, or discontent, and knows not which way to help himself, is wont to cast himself down upon his couch, 1 Kin. 21. 4. or as sick men, not able any longer to hold up the head, are compelled to betake themselves to their bed, 2 Sam. 13. 5. 2 Kin. 1. 4. or as some sluggards, that lie over head and ears, wrapped up, and buried (as it were) in their bedclothes; as the Apostle, of the wicked of the world, that lie wallowing, as swine, in mire and dirt, that they *lye down in wickedness,* 1 Joh. 5. 19. and the Latin proverbial form, of some, that they lie all in leaven, as over head and ears in it.

*{confusion covereth us}* As Psa. 44. 15. *the shame of my face covereth me;* an allusion here to the coverings that men have cast over them, when they lie in bed, Isaiah 28. 20. we have nothing but shame to wrap ourselves in; nothing but confusion to cover ourselves with: by the like similitude, it is said of Babel, *the worm is spread under thee, and the maggot over thee,* Isaiah 44. 11. such shame and confusion have those shameful things our idols brought us unto, vers. 24.

*{for we have sinned}* Or, *because we have sinned,* Isa. 64. 5. ch. 6. 13. vers. 21.

*{against the LORD}* Heb. *to the Lord.* So Deu. 1. 41. Judg. 10. 10. 1 Sam. 7. 6. Psa. 51. 4.

*{we and our fathers}* A sinful race of us, Isa. 1. 4. So the servants of God ordinarily in confessing their sins, not excusing themselves by them, or by their examples, justifying their own evil courses; as those, Jer. 44. 17. but humbly acknowledging the guilt and evil of either, Ezr. 9. 7. Neh. 1. 6. & 9. 3, 33, 34. Psa. 106. 6. Isa. 64. 6. ch. 14. 20. Dan. 9. 16.

*{from our youth}* See on vers. 24. for this may well be taken the latter way there mentioned.

*{unto this day}* See Deu. 9. 7. & 29. 4. 2 Kin. 17. 34, 41. Ch. 7. 25. & 32. 31.

*{have not obeyed the voice of the LORD.}* See vers. 13.

## CHAPTER 4

**Verse 1.** *{If thou wilt return, O Israel, saith the LORD, return unto me:}* Whether this chapter begin another sermon, or continue the former, is somewhat doubtful: as also, whom the two first verses concern, whether the ten tribes, or the other two.

*{O Israel}* Those that conceive this to be the beginning of a new sermon, by *Israel* understand *Judah,* mentioned after, v. 3. and so is Judah sometime termed, as being, though not the greater, or larger, yet the better, and more principal part of Israel, Gen. 49. 10. So is it styled, 2 Chr. 12. 1. & 15. 17. & 21. 2, 4. & 29. 21, 24. But those that continue this with the former (whom, upon due consideration, I rather concur with) by *Israel,* understand the ten tribes, as before, were invited to repentance, ch. 3. 12.

*{If thou wilt return, return unto me.}* The words run thus, word for word in the original; *If thou wilt return, O Israel, saith the Lord, unto me, thou wilt,* or *shalt return:* Which divers interpreters diversely render. Some, as our Version, *If thou wilt return, return to me;* that is, turn not this way, or that way, from one idol to another, or one foreign friend and helper to another, or one evil course to another, as bad or worse than it, Chap. 2. 36. but home to me, as you profess to do, Chap. 3. 22. and do it heartily, not feignedly, as your sister Judah has done, chap. 3. 10. *to me,* I say, chap. 3. 7. that *search* and *see the heart,* 1 Sam. 16. 7. Prov. 15. 10. & 16. 2. chap. 17. 10. Others, *If thou wilt return to me,* (as you profess to do) *return:* do it sincerely, with your whole heart, as Josias did, 2 King. 23. 25. not *with an heart, and an heart,* Psal. 12. 3. with a *double,* Jam. 1. 8. or, *a divided heart,* Hos. 7. 14, 16. this reading, the stops in the text favor, making a short stay, at *unto me:* they come in effect much to one, and either of them fit well with the latter part of the foregoing chapter, where a large profession is made in the person of Israel, or the people of the ten tribes, of their return to the true God, the God of Israel, their God; which they are here admonished to see to, that it be sound and sincere, as chap. 24. 7. and for the latter word, being no other than the former again repeated; it is not unusual, that the future indicative form be used for the imperative; as in this very word, chap. 15. 19. Prov. 1. 23. But it may well be rendered, suspending the sentence, *If thou wilt return to me, wilt return;* I say. The same thing emphatically repeated; as Isa. 27. 5. & 57. 19. or, as some again, and so some of the Jewish commenters, *If thou wilt return to me, thou shalt return;* to wit, from your captivity again, as God had formerly promised, Deut. 4. 29, 31. & 30. 2, 5. chap. 3. 14. and this way the Chaldee Paraphrast goes. Howbeit, some others, both Jewish, and ours, take the word here in the latter branch, not in a notion of *returning,* but of *resting,* and abiding quiet. Of which use of the word, see at large, on Isa. 30. 15. as also, somewhat hereafter, on chap. 30. 10. of these, some expound it, *thou shalt rest,* applying it to Judah; that is, you shall quietly abide in your land, where now you are, and shall not *wander,* or go out of it into captivity; as they understand the next branch: or, as some, understanding it, as spoken by way of admonition, as Isa. 7. 4. keep yourself quiet, and look not after this course, and that course, for your own security and safety, but rest upon God alone, Isaiah 28. 16. But I take it here rather in the former notion; and as a branch of the condition.

*{and if thou wilt put away thine abominations out of my sight, then shalt thou not remove.}* Heb. *and wilt not,* or *shalt not wander:* And here again interpreters run several ways; some referring it to Judah, as our Version renders it, *then thou shalt not wander;* that is, go out of your land into captivity, 2 King. 21. 8. Lam. 1. 8. or, *then thou must not wander,* or, *then do not wander;* for both come to one: if putting away your idols, you will return to me, you must not wander again after them, or any other, but keep close unto me, Chap. 2. 25. & 14. 20. Deut. 4. 3, 4. & 30. 20. Psal. 81. 8, 9. *and,* for *then;* as Isa. 40. 19. chap. 2. 21. thus they fit Israel as well as Judah. And I suppose they may be thus rendered in a continued, but still suspended, sentence, *If thou wilt return to me, and if thou wilt put away thine abominations, and wilt not wander:* this is word for word the text.

*{put away}* As Hos. 2. 4.

*{thine abominations}* Your idols, which my soul loathes and abhors, Deut. 27. 15. Ezek. 11. 18. & 20. 7, 8. Of the term, see on Isaiah 66. 3, 17.

*{out of my sight}* That is, says the Jewish doctor, out of every place wheresoever they are, for God's eye is in every place, Prov. 15. 3. much more out of his land, which he has a special eye upon, Deut. 11. 12. and most of all, out of his house, his temple, which he has a continual eye unto, 1 Kin. 8. 29. & 9. 3. in which yet they had placed their abominable idols, 2 King. 21. 7. & 23. 4, 6. 2 Chr. 36. 14. Ezek. 8. 5, 6. thus applied and restrained unto Judah. Others, more at large, out of all places, as well public, as private also, Deut. 27. 15. Isa. 44. 13. Ezek. 8. 12. or not out of your houses only, but out of your hearts; for there also I see them, Ezek. 14. 3, 4. chap. 17. 1. vers. 14.

**Verse 2.** *{And thou shalt swear,}* As by way of injunction, as Deut. 10. 20. where *swearing by the name of God,* is made a part of God's religious worship. Or, *And wilt swear,* as carrying on still the condition. See Isa. 19. 18.

*{the LORD liveth}* Or, *by the life of the Lord;* as, by *the life of Pharaoh,* Gen. 42. 15, 16. the ordinary form of an oath used in those times, 1 Sam. 14. 39, 45. & 19. 6. if you will, when you do swear, swear by the Lord, Psal. 63. 11. Isa. 65. 16. not by Baal, or any idol whatsoever, Josh. 23. 7. Ch. 5. 7. & 12. 16. Zeph. 1. 5.

*{in truth, in judgment, and in righteousness.}* In sincerity, not in hypocrisy, in a true, right, and religious manner: not falsely, feignedly, fraudulently; as those, Isa. 48. 1. Ch. 5. 2.

*{in truth}* Or, *truly;* as Judg. 9. 15, 16, 19. 1 Sam. 12. 24. swearing nothing, but what is agreeable to truth: not abusing God's name, to attest an untruth, Exod. 20. 7. Lev. 11. 12. Zech. 5. 4. & 8. 17.

*{in judgment}* Or, *considerately,* Psal. 112. 5. well weighing, and advisedly considering, what it is that you are to swear, and who it is by whom you are to swear; that you neither profane his name, and make it common, by light usage, or upon light occasions, Mat. 5. 34, 37. Jam. 5. 12. nor make use of it unadvisedly; but use it reverently, religiously, in matters of weighty concernment, Josh. 9. 14, 15. Mat. 14. 7. though some refer it to matter of *judicature;* as Prov. 16. 10. & 24. 23. but the word *judgment,* is of a far larger extent. See Isa. 56. 1.

*{in righteousness}* Or, *righteously;* as Psal. 72. 2. Isa. 63. 1. binding yourself unto nothing by oath, but what is equal and just; not making an oath a bond of iniquity, 1 Sam. 25. 22. Matt. 14. 7. swearing with a full purpose, to perform what you do by oath oblige yourself unto; and being careful accordingly to make the same good, Psalm 15. 4. Mat. 5. 33.

*{and the nations shall bless themselves in him, and in him shall they glory.}* Or, *then;* as chap. 1. 4. See vers. 1. for the Jewish doctor well observes, that this comes in here, as an effect, and event, that should ensue upon Israel's performance of the foregoing offices: though he carry it not along, as I conceive he should do: the copulative running along in the original, in speeches of this nature, through each branch the same, makes it uncertain sometime where the condition ends, and where the matter, ensuing upon the performance of it, begins. Hence mistakes in not settling the connection aright, and breaking off the condition too soon. So in Jacob's vow, Gen. 28. 20. *If God will be with me, and will keep me, and will give me food and raiment;* 21. *and I return in safety to my fathers house, and the Lord will be my God:* 22. *and this stone which I here pitch shall be Gods house; and of all that thou shalt give me I will tithe out unto thee:* where they break off the condition amiss in the midst of vers. 21. rendering the words, *then the Lord shall be my God:* whereas it ought to be carried on unto the end of that verse, and the note of engagement fixed at the beginning of vers. 22. *then this stone shall be Gods house,* &c. In like manner here is the condition needlessly interrupted, which might well be carried on without intercision from the beginning of the chapter, to this branch; *If thou O Israel wilt return to me; and if thou wilt put away thine idols, and wilt not wander; and wilt swear by the Lords life, in truth, and judgment, and righteousness; then shall the nations bless themselves in him, and in him shall they glory;* That is, when you shall thus religiously demean yourself, then shall other people moved by your example, come in also unto God, and worship him, together with you, Psal. 47. 8, 9. that which was before hinted, ch. 3. 17.

*{shall bless themselves in him}* The word indeed is thus actively and reciprocally used, Deut. 29. 19. yet sometime only passively; as Gen. 22. 18. & 26. 4. compared with chap. 12. 3. it is somewhat ambiguous, whether way it be taken, Psal. 72. 17. *they shall bless themselves by him,* or, *they shall be blessed in him.* Now the Jewish doctors take it here; some, the former way; some, the latter; but both applying it not to God, but to Israel: the former thus expound it; *they shall bless* either *themselves,* or any other, *in him;* that is, in Israel: as for example, say they, when a man blesses his son, he shall wish, or pray, that he may prove like such or such an Israelite. See somewhat the like to this, Isa. 65. 16. The latter render it, *they shall be blessed in him;* that is, in Israel, the seed of Abraham, and Isaac, in whom all nations should be blessed, Gen. 22. 18. & 26. 4. And because the change of *thee* to *him,* the second person to the third, might be objected, as indeed it may well, they answer, That in Scripture such passage from person to person is not unusual, which is true indeed; for we find the like in the place a little before cited, Gen. 28. 21, 22. where there is a manifest change of the person from *he* to *thee,* from the third, back to the second: but to make such changes needlessly, there is little ground, or reason, where the text, as it is read simply, runs on smoothly without, as here it does. *In him,* therefore is no other here, than that God, by whom they were to swear, and unto whom, being invited by him so to do, they were to return; in him the nations, coming after their example in to him, and being his as well as themselves, and finding gracious acceptance and entertainment with him, chap. 3. 17. shall *bless him,* Psal. 103. [reference obscured]h. 1. 3. and *be blessed in him,* and *bless themselves for him,* that ever they came to know him, and have interest in him. See Psal. 72. 17. & 117. 1. Rom. 15. 10, 11.

*{and in him shall they glory}* Not in Israel, but in God. The verb here, as the former, is in a reciprocal form, whence it is sometime not unfitly rendered, as in such a notion; *he that boasteth himself of a false gift,* Prov. 25. 14. and, *boast not thy self of to morrow,* Prov. 27. 1. But oft-times it does not fitly admit that reciprocal sense; and in this case sometime it signifies, as in its first form, *to praise:* but in a more than ordinary, in an eminent manner; for these forms imply an intention of the thing designed, and add weight to it. So Psal. 56. 4, 10. that which is rendered, *In God will I praise his word;* would rather be, *I will greatly praise God,* for, or because of (supplied, as Mal. 2. 5.) *his word:* that is, his promise: or, *I will glory in God;* as it is rendered, Isa. 45. 25. *In God shall all the seed of Israel glory;* and, *Let him that glorieth, glory in the Lord,* Chap. 9. 24. 1 Cor. 1. 31. 2 Cor. 10. 17. So it may well also be rendered, Psal. 34. 2. & 44. 8. They shall exceedingly praise his name, having had pregnant proof of his goodness, 1 Chr. 16. 10. Psal. 105. 3. and they shall glory now, having a part among his people in him, Psa. 106. 5. as before they did in their idols, Psal. 97. 7. for he is the praise, and the glory of his people, Psa. 89. 16, 17. & 106. 47. & 148. 14.

**Verse 3.** *{For thus saith the LORD unto the men of Judah and Jerusalem;}* From this place, the prophet leaving Israel, turns to Judah, and directs his speech unto them, calling upon them for repentance, and reformation of heart and life, and exhorting them to solemn and serious humiliation, for the averting of God's judgments, vers. 3, 8, 14. discovering the near approach of them, vers. 6, 7, 9. blaming the false prophets for promising them peace, ver. 10. convincing the people to be guilty by their wicked courses of their own ruin, vers. 18. bewailing their folly, that would take no warning, vers. 19, 22. and the calamities that for the same would shortly befall them, by the fierce and furious access of a potent and enraged adversary, vers. 11, 13, 15, 17. and by the horrible waste and havoc made of the whole land by him, vers. 23, 31.

*{For}* So is the particle rendered, Ch. 3. 25. & 6. 13. But I suppose it would rather be rendered, *Moreover;* as it is by interpreters of good note, Isa. 15. 8. & 16. 9. because it begins a new discourse, directed to another person; but entered upon with the same admonition in effect, that before had been given unto the other, Chap. 3. 12, 14, 22.

*{thus saith the LORD to the men of Judah, and of Jerusalem}* What before he called upon Israel for, he calls upon you of Judah now for the like. Heb. *to man of Judah,* (*man,* for, *men,* as Isa. 5. 3. or, *man,* for, *each one;* as Ezek. 20. 7, 8.) *and to Jerusalem;* or, as some, with a supply from the former, *to* the men *of Jerusalem;* and may as well be, to the inhabitants of *Jerusalem;* as it is, Isa. 5. 3. and v. 4. Of *Judah* and *Jerusalem,* see on Isa. 1. 1.

*{Break up your fallow ground, and sow not among thorns.}* Heb. *Fallow your fallow,* or *fallow ye a fallow:* if these terms at least do well suit with, and fitly express, the notion of the Hebrew term; for the noun *nir,* seems to signify a *plough-land,* rather than a *fallow:* (as where it is said, much food is in *the plough-land of the poor,* Prov. 13. 23.) and the verb by *ploughing,* to break up such grounds, which therefore to the sense our Version well yields; and might not amiss also be rendered, *plough up your plough-land:* and the Jewish commenters so expound it; and so Hosea 10. 11. where the same advice is given to Israel, that is here unto Judah. Rid your heart and lives by sincere repentance, and serious reformation of your inordinate lusts, distempered affections, impious carriages, and abominable practices, which as noisome weeds, or as briers and brambles, so long as your hearts are pestered, and your lives overgrown with them, will suffer no seed of wholesome admonition or instruction to prevail with you, nor aught to thrive or come to any good issue, that is either by yourselves undertaken, or by any other for you; for the speech is of far larger extent, than of preparation of the heart for the receiving of the word, though in particular applicable thereunto: whereof see Matt. 13. 7, 25. Luk. 8. 14, 15. Jam. 1. 21. but it is not, lest the prophets of God sow their seed among thorns with you; but that you yourselves sow not among thorns, lest by continuance in your wicked courses, you cause that all your endeavors should yield you no more benefit, than your grain cast on the ground overspread with thorns would do, Prov. 14. 31. A metaphor taken from grounds that are to be broken up for tillage, which had never been to that purpose employed before, or that having been formerly so employed, having lain long fallow, and being overgrown therefore with weeds and thorns, are not fit to receive seed, which would but be cast away, being cast upon them, until they be broken up with the ploughshare, and rid of that trash; which wicked courses, are compared unto, Heb. 6. 8.

*{sow not among thorns.}* Or, *upon thorns.* Heb. *unto,* for, *upon;* as 1 Sam. 17. 49. Chap. 35. 17. It seems to have been a proverbial form among them; *to sow upon thorns,* as, *to sow upon stones,* Amos 6. 12. Matth. 13. 5. Luk. 8. 6. both used of fruitless labor. As all things thrive with the godly, Psal. 1. 3. Rom. 8. 28. so nothing prospers with the wicked, Chap. 2. 37. and 16. 21.

**Verse 4.** *{Circumcise yourselves to the LORD, and take away the foreskin of your heart,}* Circumcise not your flesh alone, but your hearts also; get you the spiritual circumcision, Deut. 10. 16. & 30. 6. Col. 2. 11. and content not yourselves with the carnal alone, wherein you so much glory, Act. 11. 2, 3. Gal. 6. 14. Eph. 2. 11. Phil. 3. 5. for the one will nothing avail you without the other, chap. 9. 25, 26. Rom. 2. 25. The same thing in effect with the former, but delivered in another notion, to meet with their vain confidence in the flesh, Phil. 3. 4.

*{Circumcise yourselves}* Heb. *Be circumcised;* as Gen. 34. 24. but these passives are oft reciprocal. So, *be hidden,* for, *hide your selves,* Ch. 36. 19. See the like, Isa. 1. 6. & 5. 8.

*{to the LORD}* With that circumcision that he requires, regards, takes notice of, and approves, Deut. 10. 16. Rom. 2. 29. Phil. 3. 3. *to the Lord,* or, *for to me:* the noun, for the pronoun; as ver. 2. Gen. 19. 24. 2 Tim. 1. 18.

*{the foreskin of your heart}* The sinful body of the flesh, Col. 2. 11. the obstinacy that grows like a thick skin over your hearts, Ch. 6. 10. Ezek. 44. 9. Act. 7. 51.

*{ye men of Judah, and inhabitants of Jerusalem:}* Heb. *man;* as v. 3. Isa. 5. 3.

*{lest my fury come forth like fire, and burn that none can quench it, because of the evil of your doings.}* That the wrath of God, by your evil courses incensed against you, do not in so fierce a manner break in upon you, that there will be no pacifying, or appeasing of it again, until you be consumed by it.

*{my fury}* Or, *wrath:* see Isa. 51. 22. & 63. 5.

*{come forth}* As Judg. 9. 20. or, *go forth;* as Isa. 55. 11. Hos. 6. 5. as fire out of a cloud, Psal. 18. 12. or, as that from the Lord that smote Nadab and Abihu, Lev. 10. 2.

*{like fire}* Zeph. 2. 2. So Deut. 32. 22. Psal. 79. 5.

*{that none can quench it}* Heb. *and* there be *no quencher:* So Chap. 21. 12. Amos 5. 6. but these enunciatives have oft a potential notion. So Chap. 2. 23, 32. and the like denunciation, Chap. 17. 20, 27. *and,* for, *that;* as chap. 14. 19. a defect of the pronoun *it;* as Isa. 9. 9. & 21. 3.

*{because of the evil of your doings.}* Or, *for;* Heb. *from the face of.* So chap. 7. 12. It is sin alone that incenses God's wrath, Isaiah 64. 5.

**Verse 5.** *{Declare ye in Judah, and publish in Jerusalem, and say, Blow ye the trumpet:}* Give warning throughout the whole country, and at Jerusalem especially, of the enemies' approach, vers. 16. And this the prophet subjoins to his former admonitions, to show, that it is high time for them to go about that, which therein he required of them; and withal, to intimate, in what kind and manner it was, that the wrath of God was ready to break in upon them; not by a pestilence, as Psal. 106. 29. or famine, as Psa. 105. 16.

but by a foreign invasion; the last and worst of evils; and that which usually draws those other two at its heels, Levit. 26. 25, 26.

*{Declare and publish}* Or, *Declare* it, and *publish* it: the like defect with that, v. 4. *publish,* Heb. *make to hear;* as Isa. 48. 20.

*{Blow the trumpet}* To give warning of the enemies' approach, Chap. 6. 1. Ezek. 33. 2, 3. and to call men either to assemble and arm, 2 Sam. 20. 1, 2. 1 Cor. 14. 8. or to retire out of the fields, and repair to the towns and places of strength, chap. 8. 14. & 10. 17.

*{cry, gather together; and say, Assemble yourselves, and let us go into the defenced cities.}* The speeches and courses of people at their wits' end, unable to stand before, much less to make head against the forces breaking in upon them, and resolving therefore by flight, and repair to places of strength, to make what shift they can to save themselves.

*{cry, gather together}* Heb. *cry,* or *call, fill,* that is, *cry with full* mouth; see ch. 12. 6. or, *call a full* assembly: so, *a fullness,* for a *full* assembly; or, a company, *a multitude,* Isa. 31. 4. & *to fill,* for, *to follow fully,* Num. 32. 11, 12. and, *to gather all together,* or, *to make all ready,* chap. 51. 11. *call all together;* or, *call all to come together; call full,* for, *call to fill;* as, *rose early corrupted,* for, *rose early to corrupt,* Zeph. 3. 7.

*{Assemble yourselves}* So ch. 8. 14. Heb. *be assembled,* or *gathered together;* as Gen. 49. 1. Ezek. 39. 17. as, *be circumcised,* v. 4. or, as some; *Retire, betake your selves;* as the word is used, Lev. 26. 25. Num. 30. 11, 20. 2 Sam. 17. 13. But in those places is still subjoined, an expression of some place to be retired unto; whereas here the word is put absolutely: and that act is intimated in the next clause, to which this coming together, is as a preparative; as if it were said, *get ye together,* as many as you desire should be in safety, and repair to some place of strength.

*{let us go into the defenced cities.}* For shelter and succor, against the invading enemy. So Judges 9. 51. Chap. 36. 6. Matth. 24. 16. Heb. *cities of fortification,* or *defense;* as Chap. 1. 18. & 34. 7.

**Verse 6.** *{Set up the standards towards Zion;}* Heb. *standard;* as ver. 21. nor need it be altered; though the authors of this Version seem to have conceived it, as spoken of the Chaldeans coming in, & marching with their banners and ensigns displayed against Jerusalem: but they seem rather the words of the prophet in the person of the Jewish people, showing what they will then do, or require to be done; and to be a continuation of their advice, in part, delivered, vers. 5. And this way interpreters, as well Jewish, as others, do most generally take them: *towards Zion;* that is, as some, *in Zion;* in Jerusalem, and in Zion the highest place of it, whence it may be farthest seen: so, *to the ground,* for, *on the ground,* Gen. 28. 12. *toward Babel,* for, *in Babel,* chap. 29. 15. *toward the North,* for, *in the North,* Chap. 46. 6. Or, as others rather, *set up a standard towards Zion;* that is, whereby men may be admonished to repair *unto Zion,* or to make *towards Zion;* to Jerusalem, their chief city of strength; as Zion the strongest place in it, 2 Sam. 5. 6, 7. so ch. 50. 5. a defective or complexive form of speech, like those, Psa. 31. 17. *let them be cut off into the grave,* for, cut off, and thrown *into the grave;* Isa. 14. 12. *thou art cut down to the ground,* for, *cut off,* and thrown *down to the ground;* Isa. 38. 17. *thou hast loved my soul from the pit,* for, *out of love to my soul,* kept it *from the pit.*

*{retire}* Some render it, *strengthen your selves;* as if it came from that verb, that has a notion of *hardening,* or *strengthening,* Prov. 7. 13. & 21. 29. but it seems rather to come from another root, that signifies, *to retire,* or *get away;* as Exod. 9. 19. Isaiah 10. 31. Chap. 6. 1.

*{stay not}* Heb. *stand not;* as Deu. 5. 31. Chap. 51. 50. Hasten each one, without delay, to flee for his life from the danger approaching, Luk. 17. 31. Hitherto was the speech of the people, such as they should use amidst that fear and confusion, that the Chaldean forces, breaking into their land, should bring upon them. Now follow God's words, by the prophet, relating the occasion and ground that should be of this terror.

*{For I will bring evil from the north, and a great destruction:}* Heb. I (the Lord) *am bringing* (so Chap. 5. 15. & 6. 19. as of a thing in doing; and so it is well rendered, 2 King. 21. 12.) *evil* (a devastation of your land, Chap. 1. 14.) *from the north* (from Chaldea, Chap. 1. 13, 15. & 6. 22.) *and a great breaking;* or *even* (as Isa. 56. 5, 7.) *a grievous destruction;* as Isa. 30. 23, 24. v. 20. Chap. 6. 1.

**Verse 7.** *{The lion is come up from his thicket,}* The *lion* (Nebuchadnezzar, the king of Babylon, 2 King. 24. 1. so termed for his force and fierceness, Prov. 30. 30, 31. the like whereunto, see chap. 2. 15. & 5. 6. Ezek. 19. 2. Dan. 7. 4. 2 Tim. 4. 17.) *is come up* (or, *come forth,* or *come on;* as Isa. 7. 1, 6.) *from his thicket;* *his covert;* as Chap. 25. 38. because such is commonly in the forest among the thicket, Isa. 9. 18. that is, from Babylon, his strongest hold, and stateliest seat; his principal place of constant residence and retire, Dan. 4. 30.

*{and the destroyer of the Gentiles is on his way:}* Or, *a destroyer of nations;* for here is no special distinction between Jew and Gentile intended: one, by whom God has already destroyed many nations, 2 King. 24. 7. Isa. 14. 17. Chap. 50. 23. & 51. 20. and intends to destroy you, Chap. 23. 7. *is on his way;* or, *is set forward;* as Num. 10. 18, 22. is on his march for Jerusalem, Ezek. 21. 21, 22.

*{he is gone forth from his place}* From his place of residence, Babylon, as before.

*{to make thy land desolate}* Heb. *to put thy land into desolation;* or, *to make it a desolation;* that is, very desolate; as Isa. 13. 9. Chap. 2. 15.

*{and thy cities shall be laid waste without an inhabitant.}* Or, as some, that *thy cities may be overgrown* with grass: for the Jewish critics are divided about the notion of the word here used. Some deriving it from a word, that signifies *dryness,* and consequently *wasteness,* Ch. 2. 6. Others, from a verb signifying, as they conceive, *to sprout* out with grass, or the like; as the bodies of fowls do with feathers; because the letters of it come near to those words that have either of these notions: and hence the twofold rendering of the verb here; as the like of the participle, 2 Kin. 19. 25. & Isa. 37. 26. for the word is nowhere else found in either notion, which makes it the more ambiguous; but whether way it be taken, the sense is the same; for places lying waste, are so usually overgrown, Isaiah 5. 6. & 32. 13, 14.

*{without inhabitant}* As chap. 2. 15. & 9. 11. or, *because there is no inhabitant* in them: for in these, and the like forms, the particle here used, has the nature of a causal; as Num. 14. 16. chap. 10. 6. & 19. 11.

**Verse 8.** *{For this gird you with sackcloth, lament and howl:}* Or, *Because of this;* or, *Therefore;* as Psal. 32. 6. Lam. 5. 17, 18.

*{gird you with sackcloth}* Heb. *gird sacks:* the wonted garb in great and grievous mournings, public especially, in those times among that people, 2 King. 6. 30. Isa. 3. 24. & 22. 12. chap. 6. 26.

*{Lament and howl}* Some suppose that the former word imports properly the expressions of grief, by outward gestures of the body, as wringing the hands, beating on the breast, and the like, chap. 2. 37. Nah. 2. 7. Luk. 18. 13. the latter, by weeping, complaining, crying out, and the like, Psal. 32. 3. Isa. 38. 14. & 59. 11. Hos. 7. 14. See on Isa. 32. 12.

*{for the fierce wrath of the LORD is not turned back from us}* Or, *because* (as ch. 3. 21, 25.) *the fierce wrath of the Lord will not turn from us;* until it have done that which God intends by it, ch. 30. 24. see Isa. 9. 12, 17. & 13. 13.

**Verse 9.** *{And it shall come to pass in that day, saith the LORD,}* As ch. 3. 16, 17.

*{that the heart of the King shall perish, and the heart of the Princes, and the Priests shall be astonished, and the Prophets shall wonder.}* The effect of the report of the enemies' irruption, arriving at Jerusalem, and the people's flocking thither for shelter and safety; to wit, that the great ones, who should have encouraged the meaner sort, and those who had promised them peace and security, should then themselves be utterly dismayed, and at their wits' end.

*{the heart of the Kings, and the Princes shall perish}* They shall be clean out of heart: so Psa. 73. 26. *my heart faileth;* and *it is withered like grass,* Psa. 102. 4. and *melted as wax,* Psa. 22. 14. but here more than all that, it is *perished;* clean destroyed, utterly gone; as Psal. 12. 1. Isa. 57. 1. Mic. 7. 1. as it is said of the Canaanites, that upon the report of the Israelites passing Jordan, *there was no spirit any more in them,* Josh. 5. 1. so with these it would be upon this occasion, as if there had been no heart at all in them.

*{the Priests, and the Prophets}* The false prophets; that prophesied nothing but peace, ch. 6. 14. & 8. 11. See vers. 10.

*{shall wonder.}* Or rather, *be amazed;* as the word is rendered, Isa. 13. 8. or, *astonished;* as Job 26. 11. but that this was before used, to express another term of the same notion: for *wonder* here, is too slight, and slender; since that the meaning is not, that they should wonder to see their prophecies prove false, which they knew well enough to be no other, than vain devices of their own coining, ch. 23. 26, 27. but they should be dismayed, as well as the rest, for all their confidence that they had before made show of; and endeavored to work into others; and that the rather, because, then to their shame, they would be discovered, and generally in disgrace; yea, even abhorred by those, whom formerly by their lying prophecies, they had deluded, see chap. 37. 19.

**Verse 10.** *{Then said I;}* Heb. *And I said;* as ch. 2. 21.

*{Ah Lord GOD, Surely thou hast greatly deceived this people; and Jerusalem, saying, Ye shall have peace whereas the sword reacheth unto the soul.}* The prophet having made mention of those false prophets, vers. 9. does here thereby take occasion to complain of their deluding the people, by promising them, as from God, peace and safety.

*{Ah Lord GOD;}* As Chap. 1. 6. and see the prophet's grief, for the people's being thus deluded by these false prophets, chap. 23. 9.

*{Surely, thou hast greatly deceived this people,}* Or, *much deceived.* Heb. *deceiving deceived:* not that God indeed had so done, or that he had promised peace and safety; but that the false prophets had in his name, and as from him, so prophesied to them, chap. 23. 17, 25, 31. & 27. 9, 14, 15. & 28. 2, 11. and the people believed them, chap. 23. 32. and that God should indeed have deceived them exceedingly, if he had sent them upon any such errand unto his people, as they pretended; but which indeed he had not done, Chap. 23. 16, 21, 26, 27, 32. Howbeit, some expound it, *thou hast deceived this people;* that is, *suffered them to be deceived;* as Isa. 63. 17. & Ezek. 14. 9. by giving them up, and leaving them unto those their false prophets' delusions; because they loved not, nor listed to listen unto his truth, but desired, and delighted, to be flattered, and soothed up with such lies, as those their prophets preached to them, 1 King. 22. 8, 23. Isa. 30. 10, 11. chap. 5. 31. Mic. 2. 6, 11. & 3. 5. 2 Thess. 2. 11, 12. Others, and so some of the Jewish doctors, *Thou hast showed this people to be greatly deceived: to deceive,* for, *to show to be deceived:* as, *to know,* say some of ours, for, *to make to know,* Gen. 22. 12. Deut. 13. 3. God by his judgments upon them, made it to appear, that their false prophets had deluded them. But the words may well here read by way of interrogation; *Hast thou indeed thus deceived this people?* as if he had said; Is it possible you should promise them peace, and hold them in an expectation of it, as these prophets in your name do, when you intended nothing less? implying it to be a thing altogether impossible that God should so do, Num. 23. 19. Tit. 1. 2. The note of interrogation, in the Hebrew, oft wanting, makes divers places the more ambiguous: as Job 13. 15. Hos. 4. 14. Mal. 1. 8.

*{ye shall have peace}* All shall be well; or all shall go well with you; for that is the usual signification of the term in such forms of speech; *is it peace?* or, *Is all well?* 2 King. 9. 11, 17, 19, 31. and, *enquire of their peace;* that is, *whether all be well with them,* Gen. 37. 14. 1 Sam. 17. 18. Chap. 15. 5. and this was the false prophets' usual note to the people, chap. 11. 18. & 23. 17. Ezek. 13. 10, 16.

*{when as the sword reacheth unto the soul.}* Strikes to the heart, vers. 18. wounds deadly, even to the taking away of life: *soul,* for, *life;* as vers. 30. 1 Sam. 26. 24. Matt. 16. 25, 26. Luk. 14. 26. So David, *the waters come in even unto the soul,* Psal. 69. 1.

**Verse 11.** *{At that time it shall be said unto this people, and to Jerusalem, A dry wind of the high places in the wilderness toward the daughter of my people, not to fan, nor to cleanse.}* Tidings shall in those times come to the men of Judah, and those especially of Jerusalem, of a stormy wind coming toward them, that shall sweep all away before it.

*{At that time}* When the King of Babylon shall be on his march, vers. 7.

*{it shall be said to this people}* News shall be brought them, v. 5. as Zeph. 3. 16.

*{and to Jerusalem}* As vers. 3.

*{A dry wind}* Or, as some, *A clear wind:* and so the Chaldee, because the word is sometime used for *clearness,* Isa. 32. 4. or, *A fair wind;* without wet; the word being used for *serenity,* Isa. 18. 4. and these two come much to one: and such usually the north wind is, Job 37. 22. Prov. 25. 23. and they suppose the word *hath* in it some glance to that coast, from whence the enemy was to come, vers. 6. which yet is more probable, than that which some of the Rabbines have, who because the word sometime applied to men's persons, signifies, *fair,* and *white,* Cant. 5. 10. Lam. 4. 7. expound it of the Chaldean army, that they should be all goodly, and sightly, the men, their horses, their apparel, their armor, and arms, Ezek. 23. 12, 15. But the meaning is rather, as our Version well renders it, and as other of the Jewish writers well interpret it, *a dry,* or, *a drying wind:* and the old Latin not amiss, *a parching,* or *a scorching wind;* a wind that brings no rain or moisture with it to water the grounds, but that blasts, and parches, and burns up all, and makes all the land to be for drought, like a desert. So is the word used, Psal. 68. 6. Isa. 58. 11. Ezek. 24. 7, 8. & 26. 4, 14. It is a resemblance of the Chaldean army coming in swiftly and fiercely, like a sore tempestuous wind, making spoil and havoc of all. So Ch. 13. 19. & 30. 23, 24, 28.

*{of the high places in the wilderness}* Or, *upon the high places in the plain:* for so also is the word used, see Isa. 63. 13. chap. 9. 10. a defect of the preposition: as Isa. 26. 18. & 48. 4. Some interpreters put in the verb, *bloweth:* I should rather, if any supply be deemed needful, the participle, *blowing:* for the sentence is not consummate in this verse, but continued, and carried on to the next: *a wind on high ground,* and *in a plain,* in a champaign, where it is wont to be most powerful and prevalent, there being no shelter against it, nor aught to break the force of it, as in other places oft there is, Isaiah 21. 1. Chap. 13. 24. Some think an allusion to those mountains, plains, or wastes, that lay between Chaldea, and Judea, by which the enemy was to march, in his expedition against them, vers. 12. But a learned man would not have the word rendered *high places,* either here, or elsewhere, so to signify; but *champaign,* or *plains,* or *valleys,* rather; in which, says he, lying between hills, the sunbeams, by reflection having the more force, make the wind the more scorching; but it seems to be not the parching or scorching only, or so much as the scattering and carrying away of all before it, that is here most principally intended, which in higher places the wind has more power to do, than in lower; and I see not therefore, why the received Version (which the best of the Jewish commenters constantly attest to) should be waived, either here, or elsewhere: see on Isa. 13. 2. ch. 3. 2.

*{toward}* Heb. *in the way of the daughter of my people;* as Num. 14. 25. & 21. 4, 33. where there is a defect of the particle *in,* as here: and the words would be rendered, as here; *toward the red sea,* and *toward Bashan.*

*{the daughter of my people}* As, *the daughter of Zion,* Isa. 1. 8. See there; *my people,* for beauty and delicacy, like a young *damsel;* and as dear to me as a darling *daughter.* So Chap. 9. 1.

*{not to fan, nor to cleanse}* Not such a wind as they use to fan with, and by fanning, to cleanse the grain, by severing the chaff, and such like lighter trash, from the good corn, and weighty grain, and carrying away the one, but leaving the other, Matt. 3. 12. for such wind, must not be any stiff, or boisterous wind: but this wind is such an one, so fierce, so furious, as scatters, and carries all together away with it. See Isa. 27. 8. chap. 15. 7. & 18. 17. & 51. 1. Ezek. 5. 2. & 21. 3.

**Verse 12.** *{Even a full wind from those places shall come to me.}* Even *a full wind:* the particle supplied; as Job 42. 16. or, *A full wind,* I say; as Isa. 35. 4. & 51. 22. for the sentence from the foregoing verse is continued in this, *a full wind,* that is, *a wind full* of a curse and calamities; a pestilent wind, says one of the Jewish commenters: but rather, as another of them, *a stiff, a strong wind;* as 2 Kin. 9. 24. *Jehu filled his hand with a bow,* that is, as our Version not amiss reads it, *drew a bow with full strength:* and so here, *a full wind:* a wind blowing in its full strength, having nothing to oppose it. See on vers. 11. But there seems somewhat more in it, than the Jewish critic here takes notice of: for the particle subjoined, is commonly a note of comparison: *great from,* in Hebrew, is *greater,* Gen. 48. 19. *good from; better,* Prov. 22. 1. Eccl. 7. 1. *Strong from; stronger,* 2 Sam. 1. 23. Psal. 18. 17. in which places also it should be so rendered: that therefore which is here rendered *from those* places, as having reference to the *high places in the plain,* or *waste,* before mentioned, vers. 11. some other interpreters conceive rather, to imply some matter of collation, than of station, or motion, from place to place: and they render the words *a fuller,* that is, *a stronger than they:* which they refer to the persons before mentioned, vers. 9, 11. that should be carried away with it: as if it were said, a wind stronger than they are able to endure or withstand: but that seems to look too far backward. I rather conceive it to have reference to such winds, as they used to fan, and cleanse their corn with, in the latter end of vers. 11. in the words next before going; and suppose it would be rendered therefore, *fuller and stronger,* in fuller strength, *than those,* to wit, winds wherewith we use to winnow and cleanse your corn, Isaiah 30. 14.

*{shall come to me}* Or, *cometh to me;* that is, as some, *against me;* as chap. 3. 25. Psal. 51. 4. & 56. 3. So the Jewish doctors; the prophet, say they, speaking in the person of the people; or rather, relating the words of the people, what in those times they should say, ver. 11. But ours most understand it, as spoken in the person of God, *shall come for me;* that is, by commission from me, at my command, to do my works, to fulfill my will; as of wind and storm it is said, Psal. 148. 8. So Isa. 6. 8. *who shall go for us?* and this they suppose confirmed, by what follows: but thereof there is no necessity; and the course of the context seems to carry it rather the former way; unless we will take it for an elegant redundancy, very common, not in Hebrew only, but in other languages, as well learned, as vulgar. So Gen. 12. 1. *Go thee out of thy country:* Num. 22. 6, 11. *Curse me this people,* Exod. 30. 24. *Take thee Spices:* Gen. 27. 13. *Take me a kid:* Cant. 4. 6. & chap. 5. 5. *I will go me,* and the like: which if we admit, it will then be no more than such a wind as has been described, *cometh me:* for in the present tense, I suppose, it ought to be rendered; because it is not a speech of prophecy, foretelling what shall be, or what will come; but a speech, reporting at that time, when the enemy is on his way, what there is coming towards them.

*{now also will I give sentence against them:}* Heb. *will I speak,* or, *utter judgments with them.* Of which phrase, see chap. 1. 16. when this storm comes, which they shall then be told of, vers. 11. The very report whereof shall amaze, and amate, the mightiest, and most confident among them, vers. 9. then (for he speaks of it, as of a thing present) will I put in execution that doom, that I formerly passed upon them: it would therefore be rendered, *now,* (to wit, at this time, by this stormy wind) *will I also,* or, *even* (as Isa. 57. 6, 7.) *I will do execution upon them.* See chap. 39. 5.

**Verse 13.** *{Behold, He shall come up as clouds}* Another resemblance, setting forth the manner of the enemies coming in upon them, ushered in with a note of admiration in the front of it. So Isa. 10. 33. & 66. 12.

*{he}* Nebuchadnezzar, and his forces.

*{shall come up}* Or, *come marching.* See Isa. 7. 1. v. 7.

*{as clouds}* As clouds driven with the wind, for swiftness; as Isa. 19. 1. or, with forces, for multitude, as thick as clouds, Isa. 60. 8. Heb. 12. 1.

*{and his chariots shall be as a whirlwind}* See Isa. 66. 15.

*{his horses are swifter than eagles}* An hyperbolical form of speech, used to express eminent, or extraordinary swiftness, chap. 48. 40. Lam. 4. 19. Dan. 7. 4. Heb. *lighter;* as Isa. 19. 1. chap. 2. 23. vers. 24.

*{woe unto us, for we are spoiled.}* The people's voice, in their distress; or the prophet's, beforehand lamenting the spoil that would be made of them. See the like, Lam. 5. 16.

**Verse 14.** *{O Jerusalem, wash thine heart from thy wickedness, that thou}*

*{mayest be saved.}* A serious admonition and exhortation, to sincere repentance and reformation, as well of heart, as of life, for the preventing and averting of this threatened destruction: the same, in effect, with those former, v. 3, 4. but delivered in a new notion, and expressed by a divers similitude.

*{O Jerusalem}* You inhabitants of Jerusalem, and people of Judah, in general, v. 3, 11. so ch. 6. 8.

*{wash thine heart}* As *circumcise thy heart,* vers. 4. that your repentance being hearty, it may be sound and sincere, not feigned and counterfeit, as formerly, chap. 3. 10. cleanse not your hands alone, (as by external rites you oft do, Mark 7. 3, 4. Heb. 9. 10. alluded to, Psal. 26. 6.) but your hearts also, Jam. 4. 9. Act. 15. 9. Heb. 10. 22. 1 Pet. 1. 22. otherwise all your ceremonial washings will stand you in no stead, chap. 2. 22. Matt. 23. 25, 26. no more than Pilate's complemental washing of his hands, freed him from the guilt of Christ's blood, Matth. 27. 24. It may seem an allusion to such physical lotions, and potions, wherewith the inward parts of the body are wont to be purged and cleansed; which so long as they remain foul, all bathings, and scouring of the skin, or topical medicines, applied to the outward parts, are in vain used: it requires, questionless, the true inward washing, whereof the outward washings were all but types, and mere shadows, without substance, where the inward was wanting, 1 Cor. 6. 11. So Isa. 1. 16. See chap. 13. 27.

*{from thy wickedness}* Not from your bodily soil, but from your spiritual filth, that makes you loathsome in God's sight, Prov. 30. 12. 2 Cor. 7. 1. Heb. 9. 13, 14. Jam. 1. 21. 1 Peter 3. 21.

*{that thou mayest be saved.}* Not as the Apostle says, *baptism saveth,* 1 Pet. 3. 21. though such spiritual washing and cleansing, as the prophet here speaks of, be the way and means to attain that salvation too, 2 Thess. 2. 13. Tit. 3. 5. but *that thou maist be saved,* that is, delivered from those evils and miseries, that will otherwise to your utter destruction befall you. See v. 4.

*{how long shall thy vain thoughts lodge within thee?}* Heb. *thoughts of vanity;* as Zech. 10. 2. how long will you feed yourself with vain thoughts, and hopes of succor and safety, from foreign forces, or other means, that are not able to relieve you, chap. 2. 5, 37. or, *thoughts of iniquity,* or *mischief;* wicked and mischievous thoughts: as Prov. 6. 18. Isa. 59. 7. and so one of the Rabbines here expresses it; thoughts of violence and oppression. See Isa. 55. 7. But I rather conceive the word here to signify, (as natively and usually it does, and as in the very next verse it seems to do) *affliction;* your *thoughts of affliction;* such thoughts of yours, as will bring nothing but affliction, misery, and mischief upon you: as, *prophecies of expulsions,* Lam. 2. 14. so called, not from the subject matter of them, but from the effect of them; not because they threatened them with expulsion, but because by promising them peace, (which the people relying on, repented not) they were the means of bringing expulsion upon them. Howbeit, there are two other readings: for because the verb is singular; and again may be as well of the second person masculine, as the third feminine: from the former consideration, some of our interpreters, of prime note, render it; *How long shall it* (to wit, your wickedness) even *thy thoughts of vanity lodge in thy mind?* but it is common to have a noun plural, in way of distribution, joined with a verb singular: and the sense is, any one of those your such *thoughts:* the like, see Isa. 26. 19. Psal. 119. 103. Prov. 14. 1. & 28. 1. From the latter, one of the Rabbines would have them thus read; *How long wilt thou lodge in thy thoughts of affliction?* that is, says he, persist and continue in them? as, *mine eye lodgeth,* that is, continues *in bitterness;* Job 17. 2. So, *the world lieth in evil,* 1 John 5. 19. all the difficulty, in this reading, is, that the form is here masculine, in the rest feminine; which he thus salves, that in this the congregation is respected, in the other terms the people. See Chap. 3. 5.

*{within thee}* Heb. *in the midst of thee:* as Nah. 3. 13. Deut. 18. 2. & 19. 10.

**Verse 15.** *{For a voice declareth from Dan, and publisheth affliction from mount Ephraim.}* As if he had said; It is high time for you thus to do; for reports are coming to you thick and threefold, of the enemies coming on apace toward you. Heb. there is *a voice reporting,* and *making to hear:* the verbs are the same that were before, v. 5. and that is related as done here, that was either enjoined, or advised there: *a voice,* for, *a rumor,* or *a report:* as Gen. 45. 16. Chap. 50. 46. and this report is said to come from *Dan;* because that was the utmost bound of the land of Israel northward, towards the land from whence this evil was to come, vers. 6. and from *mount Ephraim,* because that nearest to Judea, whither the enemy was bound: and the subject matter is *affliction;* as the word is well rendered, Job 5. 6. and so it is used, Job 4. 8. & 15. 35. Compared with Prov. 22. 8. Psal. 7. 14. Isa. 59. 4. See Isa. 1. 13. Chap. 20. 18. and this is the first and native sense of it; for it comes from a term, that has a notion of *grief,* and *mourning,* Isa. 3. 26. & 19. 8. Hos. 9. 4. though in the second place, also, *wrong;* because by it, men are *afflicted, grieved,* and made to mourn. And thus the Jewish Rabbine, whom most of ours follow, expound this place, which is confirmed, also, by that which is said, Chap. 8. 16. *the neighing of his horses is heard from Dan.* Howbeit, the Chaldee Paraphrast, understands it of *the voice* of God's prophets, acquainting them, with what affliction was to befall them, for the worshipping of the golden calves; the one, at Dan; and the other, at Bethel; and the idol that Micah of mount Ephraim made, Judg. 17. 1, 4, 5. & 18. 29, 31. 1 King. 12. 28, 29. But we read not the worshipping of those calves objected to Judah, but to Israel only, Hos. 8. 5, 6. & 13. 2. Some other therefore late interpreters, of special note, render it; *For a voice declareth,* or there is *a voice* that *declareth greater iniquity,* or, *the iniquity* to be *greater, than* that of *Dan; and that publisheth more grievous,* or, that *publisheth* it to be *more* grievous, *than* that in *mount Ephraim:* as if he had said; It is as notorious, as if it were proclaimed, that the wickedness of Judah, in idolatry, especially, is greater, and more grievous, than that of Israel, committed at Dan and Bethel, with the golden calves there. I am not ignorant, that the particle here used, is, commonly, employed in comparisons, as was before observed, on vers. 12. as also, that the noun here used, is usually, in many places, rendered *iniquity,* (for which, there is another word, in Hebrew, more proper, though in sound near to this, yet of a diverse notion, and notation) where I suppose it might better be rendered *wrong;* as Job 34. 5, 22. Psal. 5. 5. & 6. 8. & 14. 4. as also, that the word in the former branch may well, and is oft supplied from the latter: as Isa. 13. 13. & 18. 7. & 30. 17. and that in such collations, the subject matter, wherein the collation consists, is not seldom in the one member concealed: of which, see on Isa. 5. 29. vers. 31. and with all these favorable helps admitted, that sense may be made up from the words, that these worthy writers give unto it: Nor can it be denied, but that Judah was, in some sort, far worse, and more condemnable, than Israel. See Ch. 3. 11. But it seems needless to me, thus to wring a text for a new sense; where it does, of itself, freely afford one so suitable to the course of the context, and the main drift of the place. Nor does that sense, which another learned annotator gives, seem to flow so naturally from the place, though one of the Rabbines, from whom he seems to have received it, have somewhat to that purpose, to wit, that the report of that *affliction* which had befallen them for their idolatry, *at Dan and Bethel,* should have admonished Judah; and been a warning to her: and so indeed should it have been, Ch. 3. 8, 10. but every truth is not in every place taught: nor seems this here to be implied.

**Verse 16.** *{Make ye mention to the Nations, behold, publish against Jerusalem, that watchers are come from a far Country, and give out their voice against the cities of Judah.}* This likewise tends to give warning, or notice at least, to those of Judah and Jerusalem, of the enemies' march towards them; though some understand it of the summoning of the Chaldeans and other nations with them, to come on against them.

*{Make ye mention to the nations,}* The subject matter, says one of the Rabbines, of the *voice,* or *rumor,* before mentioned, vers. 15.

*{Make ye mention,}* Or, *Put them in mind;* as Isaiah 43. 26.

*{to the nations}* Those of Judah, say some: *concerning the nations,* say others: the Chaldeans, and their complices, 2 King. 24. 3. so the particle is oft used, Gen. 20. 13. and 26. 7.

*{publish}* Heb. *make to hear;* give them to understand; as v. 5.

*{against Jerusalem}* Or, *to Jerusalem;* as Exod. 20. 3. *to my face:* 1 Sam. 2. 11. *to Ramah.* See v. 5. or, *concerning Jerusalem,* as Isa. 1. 1. & 2. 1. Some of those that retain that which our Version exhibits, do thus render the words: *Mind* them *of the Nations, tell* them, *behold, against Jerusalem watchers are coming.*

*{watchers}* So the word is used, 2 Kin. 17. 9. hostile forces; which why so termed, see v. 17.

*{come}* Heb. *coming;* behold them coming: as if they might see them on their way, and did point with the finger to them; as Isaiah 65. 17.

*{from a far Country}* From Babylon, Isa. 39. 3.

*{and give out their voice against the cities of Judah}* Or, *that give out;* the copulative for the relative; as Isa. 44. 7. & 49. 7. that threaten ruin to them: or, *that will give out;* that will with loud shouts assault them. See Ch. 2. 15. & 12. 8.

**Verse 17.** *{As Keepers of a field are they against her round about}* *Are they;* or, *will they be, against her;* to wit, Jerusalem, mentioned, vers. 16. An intimation of a strait siege to ensue, they will lie round about Jerusalem, Isa. 29. 3. Zech. 12. 2. As those that are set to watch a field, or a vineyard, and the fruit in it, so strait, that none can be suffered, either man or beast to get in, that may annoy it, or commit waste in it, Isa. 27. 3. and there is deemed by some to be a bitter taunt in the term: for both *watch* indeed: but the one to keep from going in, the other from coming out: the one watch that nothing go in that may hurt or annoy; the other, that nothing come in that may help or relieve, 2 Chron. 16. 1. 2 Kin. 6. 24, 25. & 25. 1, 3. Yet some suppose the similitude to be taken, from such as are set to watch wild beasts, or deer, enclosed in a wood, to keep them from breaking away, and making escape. But the former is the more probable; for *field,* and *wood,* are in Scripture commonly opposed. See Chap. 5. 6.

*{because she hath been rebellious against me, saith the LORD}* The ground of all their misery, as themselves acknowledge, Lam. 1. 18, 20. So Hos. 13. 16.

**Verse 18.** *{Thy ways and thy doings have procured these things unto thee;}* Heb. *Thy ways and thy doings* (or, *Thine* own *ways* and *thine* own *doings;* to make it the more vigorous, as Ch. 6. 19.) have *doing* done *these* things *to thee:* of which manner of speech, both defective and redundant, see on Isa. 59. 13. The same matter, see before, Ch. 2. 17, 19. so Isa. 50. 1. Psa. 107. 17. Ch. 5. 25.

*{this is thy wickedness;}* Or, *this* has *thy wickedness* done, or procured; supplying it from the former branch: as the like, Genesis 1. 16.

*{because it is bitter}* Or rather, *that,* as the particle is also frequently used, Neh. 4. 1. Job 11. 6. & 22. 3. Isa. 52. 5, 6. *that it is bitter.* See Ruth 1. 20. Amos 8. 10. So Ch. 2. 19. for their wickedness was the cause of the bitterness; not this of that.

*{because it reacheth unto thine heart.}* Or, *that it reacheth unto thine heart;* that it goes to the very heart with you. See vers. 10, 19.

**Verse 19.** *{My bowels, my bowels;}* These words some would have to be the people's, crying out in their distress; thereby to maintain the common reading of the foregoing words, which they rent from the former verse, and thus knit unto this; *Because it is bitter,* and *reacheth to thine heart;* therefore shall you say, *My bowels, my bowels.* Such defects and supplies, it is true, are not unusual: see on Chap. 3. 22. but needless here: the right reading of the foregoing words, was before showed.
