The most rather conceive these words to be the prophet's own, very pathetically bewailing the calamities of his people, and expressing his extreme sorrow and inward grief for them. So Ch. 9. 1. Isa. 22. 4.

*{My bowels, my bowels}* He cries out, as a woman in sore and hard travail; or as one torn and tortured with wind in the bowels, that can find no vent. See Isa. 26. 17, 18. and the ingemination of it adds no small emphasis to it; for those that are in pain are wont to double their words: so, *My head, my head,* 2 King. 4. 19. and, *My leanness, my leanness,* Isaiah 24. 16. See the like affectionate and passionate repetitions, 2 Sam. 18. 33. 2 King. 4. 13, 14. Prov. 31. 2.

*{I am pained at the very heart;}* Heb. *at,* or, *in,* (a defect of the particle, as 2 Chr. 21. 16.) *the walls of my heart;* the *walls* of the heart; that is, the *sides* of it, say some: Others rather, the *bowels* that lie round about the heart; as enclosing and fencing it, situate in the midst of them, Psal. 22. 13. as if his very heart were beset and straitened, as the city in the siege, v. 17. or were surprised as its walls were, Ch. 5. 10. Lam. 2. 8, 18. which he may well allude to: a defect of the pronoun; as Ch. 3. 19.

*{my heart maketh a noise in me;}* Or, *with me.* Heb. *to me.* Of which form of speech, see on vers. 12. the like redundancy, see Psal. 144. 2. Cant. 1. 6. & 8. 12. *my heart soundeth with me;* as Isa. 16. 11. though some render it, *my heart worketh,* or, *is troubled:* as it is rendered, Ch. 31. 20. (as the sea is said *to work,* and to be *troubled,* Ch. 5. 22. & 51. 55. Isa. 57. 20. Jon. 1. 13.) and is *unquiet within me;* it cannot rest. So the word seems to be taken, Psal. 46. 6. Cant. 5. 4. where the word *moved,* is too slender; *stirred,* at least, had been better. My bowels round about my heart are so full of pain, that my heart flutters to and fro, and cannot rest. See the like, Job 30. 27. Lam. 1. 20. & 2. 11.

*{I cannot hold my peace;}* Heb. *I will not;* or, *shall not, be silent:* but such potential notions are frequent. See Ch. 2. 23, 32. It is as if one being in pain, and willed to be quiet and still, should answer those that so speak to him, My pain is such, that I cannot be quiet, I cannot forbear speaking. See Job 7. 11. & 10. 1. & 13. 19. & 16. 6. Isa. 22. 4.

*{because thou hast heard, O my soul, the sound of the trumpet, the alarm of war.}* There is a twofold reading, the one in the margin, the other in the text, *I have heard, O my soul,* says the one; *thou hast heard,* or, *dost hear, O my soul,* says the other. This latter is the more received, and is the more emphatical of the twain: as the like, Judg. 5. 21. Psal. 103. 1. & 104. 1. The reason why his heart cannot rest; because he is so affected, as if he had the noise of the enemies' warlike trumpeting, and shouting, continually in his ear, Job 15. 20, 21. he says not, as the Rabbine well observes, *O mine ear,* but, *O my soul:* for the matter was not in being, but his soul, by the Spirit of prophecy, hearing and seeing it, as present, did as much affect him, as if he had with his bodily eye seen the enemies' approaches, and assaults; and with his bodily ear, heard their hideous shouts. See vers. 21. So John 8. 56. *Abraham saw my day, and rejoiced.*

*{the trumpet}* Not his own people's, but the enemies'. So vers. 22.

*{the alarm of war.}* Or rather, *the shout of battle:* as the word is better rendered, Chap. 20. 16. for the *alarm* is properly that sound, or noise, by which men are roused up, and called upon, to betake themselves *all* to their *arms;* whereas that here intended, is the shout that is made in joining battle, or in assault. So Chap. 49. 2.

**Verse 20.** *{Destruction upon destruction is cried.}* Heb. *Breach upon breach* (as v. 6.) *is cried,* or *proclaimed.* A further reason of this his extreme grief: there is yet a further noise in the ear of his soul, a grievous cry of one mischief and calamity, coming upon the neck of another: as Deut. 32. 23. Psal. 42. 7. Ezek. 7. 26. That is, say some of the Jewish writers, the captivity of Judah, after the deportation of Israel. But other, and so ours, most of them, rather, (because the prophet speaks of things to come, and concerning his own people) the death of Josiah, 2 Chr. 35. 24, 25. the deposition and deportation of Jehoahaz, of Jehoiakim, Jehoiachin and Zedekiah, successively, and the utter spoil and ruin of their land and state in this last, 2 Chro. 36. 2, 20.

*{for the whole land is spoiled}* Or, as some, *because;* or, as I conceive it, *that,* or, *so that,* (as v. 18.) *the whole land is plundered:* so v. 27. See hereafter this general devastation most rhetorically described, vers. 23, 26.

*{suddenly are my tents spoiled, and my curtains in a moment.}* The *tents* of my people, and their *curtains,* whereof those tents consist, Cant. 1. 5. Chap. 49. 29. that is, their strong cities, lofty palaces, and stately houses; or their habitations in general, Isa. 54. 2. Ch. 10. 20. are as easily, and suddenly overturned and ruined, as some shepherd's, or other like sorry tent, Isa. 38. 12. Lam. 2. 6. an allusion either to the ancient manner of that people's dwelling, while they abode in the wilderness, Num. 24. 2, 5. and in other parts before, Gen. 33. 18. Heb. 11. 9. and the ordinary habitation of divers people at that day, Hab. 3. 7. or to the overthrow of a camp consisting of tents, Judg. 7. 13, 14. Chap. 6. 3.

**Verse 21.** *{How long shall I see the Standard, and hear the sound of the trumpet?}* Or, *How long shall I see the standard?* how long *shall I hear the sound of the trumpet?* The interrogative supplied from the former branch: as Psal. 94. 3. The prophet seems to have been so affected, as if he had the sight of the one continually in his eye, and the sound of the other in his ear. See vers. 19. and withal, by this manner of speech, implies the long continuance of this evil; that albeit the whole land were suddenly plundered and spoiled, yet the war was drawn out at length, as well in the surprisal of city after city, as in the several surprisals and sackings of Jerusalem, under her three last kings. See on vers. 20. and the like forms of speech, vers. 14. Chap. 13. 27. & 47. 6.

*{shall I see? shall I hear?}* Or, as some render it; *am I compelled to see? am I compelled to hear?* as Hab. 1. 3.

*{the standard, the trumpet.}* By *standard,* and *trumpet,* some understand their own, either giving warning of the enemies' approach; or calling people together, to repair to places of strength, or to join together in a body, and arm, to make head against the enemy, vers. 5, 6. Others rather, whom I concur with, the enemies' *standard,* marching on, and coming to make assault; and his *trumpet,* inciting his forces, either to join battle, or to make assault, and to proceed eagerly in either, Isa. 31. 9. & 33. 23. & 59. 20. Josh. 6. 5, 16. 2 Chr. 13. 12.

**Verse 22.** *{For my people is foolish, they have not known me; they are sottish children, and they have no understanding:}* Or, as some render it; All this is, *Because my people is foolish:* as Psal. 38. 3, 5. My people, by their own folly, and stupidity, have brought all this evil and mischief upon themselves, Chap. 2. 17, 19. vers. 18.

*{For}* Or, *Because;* as Ch. 3. 25.

*{my people}* God speaks it, yet owning them, that had cast off him. So Ch. 2. 13, 31, 32.

*{is foolish}* Or, *are* (because the word is collective, and plurals follow; as Isaiah 5. 26.) *foolish.* So Deut. 32. 4. Isaiah 44. 18, 19.

*{they have not known me}* Or, *they know me not,* Isaiah 1. 3. Ch. 9. 3.

*{they are sottish children}* So Ch. 5. 21. *a sottish people: children;* as Isa. 1. 4. & 30. 1. the verb deduced from the noun here used, see 1 Sam. 13. 13. 2 Sam. 24. 10. the pronoun demonstrative, is here put for the verb substantive; and so in the next branches: as Isa. 60. 21. Ch. 9. 3.

*{they have no understanding}* Heb. *they are not understanding.* So Deut. 32. 28. Isa. 27. 11.

*{they are wise to do evil; but to do good they have no knowledge.}* They have no wit to anything, but what is evil; that to plot and practice, they are cunning enough, Luke 16. 8. See Chap. 9. 3. the contrary hereunto, the Apostle requires, 1 Cor. 14. 20.

*{they are wise}* Heb. *wise they are:* the pronoun, for the verb, as before.

*{to do evil}* Either to others, or to themselves: for all their projects and policies were such, as tended to their own ruin, by carrying them from God, and driving him from them, Isaiah 30. 1, 14. and such, indeed, is all human wisdom naturally, Rom. 8. 6, 7.

*{but to do good, they have no knowledge.}* Heb. *and* (as Chap. 3. 7.) *to do well, they know not:* for well-doing, they have no skill. See Chap. 13. 23. the contrary lesson God would have them to learn. Isa. 1. 17.

**Verse 23.** *{I beheld the earth; and lo it was without form, and void: and the heavens, and they had no light.}* The prophet proceeds, here, to describe the lamentable effects, that should ensue this hostile invasion, which as they were in a spiritual rapture represented to the eye of his mind; so he endeavors, by a very rhetorical delineation, to set forth at large, and to set a most rueful spectacle, as in a lively map of extreme devastation, and desolation, before their eyes, if the foresight of these their miseries, which otherwise would ensue, might so affect them, as to move them unto the timely entertainment of those counsels and courses, whereby the same might be prevented.

*{I beheld}* Or, *I saw,* or, *I see,* (as speaking of a thing present, and in view) in spirit; as Col. 2. 15. but here more than so, in a vision, or apparition: as Dan. 7. 2, 13. Act. 10. 11. & 11. 5. Revel. 1. 10, 12. Or, *when I look upon the ground, it is shapeless,* or, *unsightly,* and *empty;* and so in the rest: the like syntax, see Ch. 2. 7, 20. & 5. 7.

*{the earth}* The land of Judea: but aright rendered, *the earth;* because it has a glance unto Moses his words, Gen. 1. 2.

*{it was without form, and void.}* Or, it is *without form,* and *void:* not only without habitation, or inhabitants; but despoiled also, of all its former goodly furniture, and laid utterly waste and desolate: insomuch, that the earth might seem reduced unto that original chaos, or confused mass, that at first it was, Gen. 1. 2.

*{and the heavens}* Or, *I saw,* or, *I see the heavens:* by a supply from the former branch; as Gen. 1. 16. 2 Chron. 10. 11. vers. 21. Heb. *to the heavens.* But a Jewish critic deems the particle here redundant; as Psalm 2. 7. else it should be rendered, I look *to the heavens.*

*{and they had no light}* Or, *have they are without light;* (as Exod. 19. 4. Psal. 119. 159.) as if that primordial darkness were returned, that possessed the heavens, and overspread the surface of this lower world at first, Gen. 1. 2. A sad and solemn expression in Scripture, very frequent of utter desolation, or extreme distress. See Isa. 8. 21. & 13. 10, 13. & 24. 23. Ezek. 32. 7. Joel 2. 10. & 3. 15. Amos 8. 9. Some expound it here of the smoke of the houses; yea, whole towns and cities, fired and burnt down by the enemy, obscuring the air, and darkening the sky: as Gen. 19. 28. Josh. 8. 20. Judg. 20. 40. Isa. 9. 18. & 35. 9, 10. See 2 King. 25. 9. Ch. 37. 10. & 38. 23. & 39. 8. & 52. 13.

**Verse 24.** *{I beheld the mountains, and lo they trembled; and all the hills moved lightly.}* *I saw,* or *I see;* as before, vers. 23. *the mountains* (to wit, of Judea, Chap. 3. 23. & 9. 10.) *how, lo, they tremble,* (Heb. *are trembling) and the hills move lightly,* or, *swiftly:* *lightly,* says a Rabbine, as being lightened of their burden; the trees growing on them, or edifices built upon them, being burnt up and destroyed: but *swiftly,* rather; yea, exceeding swiftly: for the verb is in a redoubled, and withal, a reciprocal form: as if he had said, *the hills all apace bestirred themselves:* *light,* for, *swift;* as Isa. 5. 26. vers. 13. He speaks, as if the calamity were so hideous, and God's wrath revealed therein so fierce, vers. 26. that the very senseless creatures might seem to tremble and quake exceedingly at the apprehension of it. So Psal. 18. 7. & 114. 4, 6, 7. Isa. 5. 25. Hab. 3. 10. For that seems too slender, that a learned late writer has, of their shaking, with the multitudes of people passing over them. This hideous spectacle, concerning rather the spoil of the enemy made of, and in the land after the surprisal of it, than their march either unto it, or in it. Some render it, *they are destroyed,* from a term usual in the Talmudists' writings. But the received notion of *concussion,* or *shaking,* another backs from the Ethiopic use of the word, Matth. 24. 29.

**Verse 25.** *{I beheld, and lo there was no man;}* Or, *I look, and behold the men are gone.* Heb. *the man is not.* So Isa. 6. 12. Ch. 6. 8. & 7. 20. the people are either killed, or captived, or fled, and the land left without inhabitants, v. 7.

*{and all the birds of the heavens were fled}* Or, *the birds of heaven,* (see Isa. 1. 2. for it is but one heaven, at most, the birds abide in, Gen. 1. 20.) or, *of the air* (as Matth. 8. 20. & 13. 32.) *are fled:* as Psa. 11. 1. or, *wandered away;* as Prov. 27. 8. either falling down, or scared away, says one, with the cries of the soldiery: or rather, having forsaken the land, for the extreme desolation of the country, become like a wilderness, v. 26. See the like, Ch. 9. 10. Zeph. 1. 3. for of such birds, or fowl, it is meant, as either being tame, are kept, or fed, in or about the house; or that use to haunt places inhabited, and peopled, and to build, and feed, about, or near thereunto: not of such as haunt, and abide, in deserts, and places, by men abandoned, Isa. 13. 21. & 34. 14, 15.

**Verse 26.** *{I beheld, and lo the fruitful place was a wilderness;}* Or, *I look, and behold the tilled land* (Heb. *carmel.* See Isaiah 29. 17. & 33. 9.) is become *a wilderness.* See Chap. 9. 12. & 12. 10. & 22. 6.

*{and all the cities thereof were broken down,}* Or, *all his cities,* (the cities of my people, vers. 22.) or, *its cities* (the cities situate in such places) *are broken down,* or *demolished,* Isaiah 1. 7. Chap. 33. 4. & 39. 8.

*{at the presence of the LORD, and by his fierce anger.}* Heb. *from the face of the Lord* (that is, *his wrath;* as Chap. 23. 12.) *from the heat,* or *fervor, of his nose,* or *anger.* See vers. 8. Hereby intimating, that it was not so much through the enemies' rage, as from the wrath of God, justly incensed against them for their sins, that so heavy a judgment was to befall them, 2 Kings 24. 3. 2 Chr. 36. 17, 20. Ch. 9. 22, 23.

**Verse 27.** *{For thus hath the LORD said}* Or, *Thus saith the Lord;* as Cha. 2. 5.

*{The whole land shall be desolate}* Or, *This land shall be very waste,* or *very much wasted.* Heb. *shall be wasteness:* as Isaiah 1. 7. See vers. 20.

*{yet will I not make a full end,}* Or, *yet* (Heb. *and;* as Cha. 3. 7, 9.) *will I not make an utter consummation,* Chap. 5. 10. & 31. 11. For God would yet reserve himself a remnant, Isa. 1. 9. & 24. 13. according to that which he promised in the law, Levit. 26. 44. Howbeit, some expound it, *and yet I have not made a full end* with them: all this shall not serve, to satisfy my wrath; but I will inflict further penalty upon them, and afflict them yet more grievously before I have done; as having an eye to their ensuing captivity, and those grievous and tedious afflictions, that for so long a time, during it, they should endure, Lev. 26. 36, 39. and to this purpose, this form may seem to sound, Ch. 5. 18. where it is said, *Notwithstanding, in those days, I will not make a full end with you:* but neither is the syntax the same here, and there: and that place also may well be deemed to look rather the former way.

**Verse 28.** *{For this shall the earth mourn, and the heavens above be black:}* They shall wear blacks as mourners use to do, Isaiah 30. 23. Psal. 38. 6. & 42. 9. Chap. 8. 21. & 14. 2. See v. 23. Ezek. 32. 15.

*{because I have spoken it, I have purposed it; and I will not repent, neither will I turn back from it.}* What I have resolved upon and said, I will do, Num. 23. 19. Isa. 14. 24, 27. The particle *it,* is supplied; as Chap. 3. 7.

*{I will not repent}* Ch. 15. 6. Zech. 8. 14.

*{neither will I turn back}* See v. 8. Ch. 30. 24.

**Verse 29.** *{The whole city shall flee for the noise of the horsemen and bowmen:}* *The whole city;* the inhabitants of Jerusalem, all sorts of them *shall flee* for fear (Chap. 39. 4.) *of the horsemen* (Heb. *horseman;* as Ezek. 26. 10.) *and bowmen.* Heb. *him that throweth,* or, *shooteth* out arrows *with a bow;* as Psal. 78. 9.

*{they shall go into thickets,}* There to hide themselves for fear; as Gen. 3. 8. 2 Chr. 33. 11. So the Chaldee, whom some of the Rabbines follow, and the ancient Greek. Yet some of the Rabbines render it, *they shall go up to the thick clouds;* as the word is oft used, Job 20. 6. Isa. 44. 22. an hyperbolical speech, says the Jewish doctor, that is, into the highest hills, that seem to reach the clouds; *into the high places;* says the old Latin: or as if they would climb up to the clouds, Chap. 49. 16. Amos 9. 2, 3. but the word signifies, *thickness* in general; and the former is more probable.

*{and climb up upon the rocks}* Or, *to the cliffs,* Job 30. 6. that are as the branches of the rocks; for so the word primarily imports, Job 15. 32. See the like, Isa. 2. 21.

*{every city shall be forsaken, and not a man dwell therein.}* Or, as some, *the whole city;* as before: but the pronoun in the clause requires the received reading; the meaning is, that their cities generally should be ruined, and left without inhabitants, vers. 25, 26.

**Verse 30.** *{And when thou art spoiled, what wilt thou do?}* Heb. *And thou spoiled;* which some render, *thou* that are *to be spoiled;* as Psalm 137. 8. *destroyed,* for, to be destroyed: as sure to be spoiled, as if you were spoiled already; or, *spoiled,* that is, *ready to be spoiled:* as, *perished,* for, *ready to perish,* Isa. 27. 13. But we need not depart from the received Version; *what wilt thou* being *spoiled do?* or to make it the more emphatical; *And thou being spoiled, what wilt thou do?* that is, *And,* as for *thee,* (for the pronoun seems to be put here absolutely; as Isa. 65. 11.) *when thou art spoiled, what wilt thou do?* But there is an irregularity in the syntax, not unlike that Chap. 2. 24. for the pronoun and verb are feminine; the prophet here again turning his speech unto Jerusalem, or Zion, vers. 31. and speaking unto her as to a woman, and that an harlot, as before, Chap. 2. 20. & 3. 10. whereas the participle passive is masculine. This to salve, the Jewish critics, some of them would have it to be a defective form of speech, and the note of similitude to be supplied; *And thou* that are, or, *when thou* are *as one spoiled, what wilt thou do?* So it should be like that, *Thou hast broken to pieces Rahab, as one slain,* or *thrust thorough,* Psal. 89. 10. But another of them has recourse to his wonted refuge, that the one has reference to the congregation, the other to the people. See Chap. 3. 5. & 4. 14. but the genders are very oft in this prophet found promiscuously used, as in the places pointed to, has been showed.

*{though thou deckest thee with ornaments of gold, though thou rentest thy face with painting, though thou clothest thyself with crimson, in vain shalt thou make thyself fair; thy lovers will despise thee, they will seek thy life.}* These words some annex to the former, thus rendering the context; *And thou,* who are *to be destroyed,* (or are near unto destruction) *what dost thou,* (or mean, or intend you) *that* (as vers. 18.) *thou thus deckest thy self?* &c. as if he should say; Is this a time for you, when you are threatened with destruction, thus to *adorn yourself,* when it were more seasonable for you, to lay your rich attire aside, Exod. 33. 4, 5. and to put on sackcloth rather, and to humble yourself in the sight of God for your sins. Thus some of the Rabbines, paralleling this place with that, Isay 22. 12, 13. But the close of the verse shows, that the words run rather another way. And a learned writer of ours has well observed, that the particle here used, includes oft a twofold notion; whereof, see on Isa. 29. 16. & 54. 9. & 61. 5. Chap. 10. 21. & 12. 5. and so in this place: where it may therefore well be rendered: *For though thou clothest thy self,* &c. All your whorish attires and designs, tricks of enticement, and arts of allurement, will stand you in no stead, will not avail to save your life; to retain your lovers with you, or to keep them from loathing and growing weary of you, yea, and helping to work your ruin.

*{clothest thyself with crimson}* A wear of much account in those days, as well as in these times, 2 Sam. 1. 24. where it is rendered, *scarlet;* by some learned, there and here, *a double-dye;* but of the word, see at large, on Isa. 1. 18. See also, Revel. 17. 4.

*{deckest thyself with ornaments of gold}* Array yourself in the richest and most gorgeous manner that may be, 2 Sam. 1. 24. where the same word is used, that is here rendered *ornament:* whereof, see also Isa. 49. 18. Chap. 2. 32. See Psal. 45. 13. Ezek. 16. 13, 17. 1 Tim. 2. 9. Rev. 17. 4. & 18. 16.

*{and rentest thy face with painting}* Noted as an whorish practice; in Jezebel, 2 King. 9. 30. in Aholah, and Aholibah, Ezekiel 23. 40.

*{rentest}* With excessive use of such counterfeit stuff; paint and parget so much and so oft, till at length you crack the skin of your face with it.

*{thy face}* Or, *thy cheeks.* Heb. *thine eyes;* and so also, 2 Kin. 9. 30. Ezek. 23. 40. but the *eyes* are sometime put for the *face;* as 1 Sam. 16. 12. Isa. 1. 15. as the *face* also for the *cheeks,* or the *eyes,* Isa. 25. 8. compared with Rev. 7. 17. See Isa. 3. 16. though some would have the *eyes* here taken for the *eyelids,* or *eyebrows,* as if that kind of counterfeit here mentioned, had been used, either to dilate the one, as some, or as others, to make black the other: neither of both very probable. See the next note.

*{with painting}* Or, *paint.* Heb. *puc,* or *phuc;* whence both the Greeks and Latins have their *φῦκος* and *fucus:* which though some would make a mineral, yet most agree to have been a sea-plant, wherewith a kind of red color was ordinarily dyed; whence also wanton women made use of it therewith to counterfeit red, as with *ceruse* white. See more hereof, on Isa. 54. 11.

*{in vain shalt thou make thyself fair}* Strive to improve your beauty, by adorning and setting out yourself; as you do your idols, Ch. 10. 4. and as harlots use to do, 2 Kin. 9. 30. Ezek. 23. 40. to gain love, and draw lovers to them, Chap. 2. 33.

*{thy lovers will despise thee, they will seek thy life.}* Those that formerly affected you, will grow out of love with you; and not so only, but now loathing you, and waxing weary of you, after they have satisfied their filthy lust with you, will not stick to work your ruin. See Amnon's affection, 2 Sam. 13. 14, 15. and Jehu's practice, 2 Kin. 9. 30, 33. and of the Romish Babylon, Rev. 17. 13, 16. & 18. 3, 9. that is, Those whom leaving God and his protection, you have formerly relied upon, and that professed to be in a league of amity with you, Chap. 22. 20. Hos. 2. 5. will then not leave you only, but join with the enemy against you, Lam. 1. 2. See 2 King. 24. 3. Chap. 27. 3.

*{thy lovers}* Or, *paramours:* for the word is never used but of wanton and lascivious lust, rather than love; found here only, and Ezek. 23. where it and its offspring are nine several times used: it is not unfitly expressed, by a Greek term used of the Romish Babylon and her paramours, Rev. 18. 9. the pronoun is wanting in the original; as Isaiah 60. 4. but it may stand without it, and be taken more generally; no paramours will now look after you, one or other: you will be as an harlot out of date. See of Tyre, Isaiah 23. 15, 17.

*{despise thee}* Set light by you; or, *reject thee;* or *abhor thee.* See on Chap. 2. 37.

*{seek thy life}* Heb. *thy soul;* as vers. 10. Chap. 11. 21. and 19. 7.

**Verse 31.** *{For I have heard a voice as of a woman in travail, and the anguish as of her that bringeth forth her first child; the voice of the daughter of Zion, that bewaileth her self, that spreadeth her hands, saying}* The prophet as before he seemed to hear in his spirit the hideous shouts of the enemies' forces assaulting and surprising Jerusalem; so now to hear in like manner the doleful lamentation that Jerusalem herself makes, proceeding from that extreme anguish of soul, wherewith she is surprised, to see her people, her children so savagely butchered, and no end made of the massacring and murdering of them. See 2 Chr. 36. 17. Isa. 29. 7, 8. & 46. 6.

*{For}* As confirming what was said in the close of vers. 30. of their *seeking her life.*

*{I have heard}* Or, *I hear;* as before, *I see,* ver. 23. methinks I now hear.

*{a voice as of a woman in travail}* Heb. *a voice as* a travailing *woman;* for, *a voice as* the voice of one *that is in travail.* See the like, Isa. 5. 29.

*{a woman in travail}* A similitude in Scripture very frequent, to express extremity of anguish and grief, Psa. 48. 6. Isa. 13. 8. & 21. 3. & 26. 17, 18. Ch. 6. 24. & 30. 6. & 49. 22, 24.

*{the anguish as of her that bringeth forth her first child}* Or, *a voice of anguish like the anguish of one being in travail with her first birth:* a *voice* must be supplied; because it has reference to somewhat heard: and *anguish* repeated; as *voice* before: *one being in travail with her first birth.* Heb. *making her first birth;* straining to be delivered of it: and this adds to the force of the resemblance, and the extremity of the grief and anguish thereby resembled. Women in such case having usually hardest labor, and (having not been enured unto, or acquainted with pains of that nature before) the less patience, for the most part, in that regard to endure it.

*{the voice of the daughter of Zion,}* That is, of Jerusalem. See Esay 1. 8.

*{that bewaileth her self}* Or, *how fetching deep sighs, she bewaileth her self;* for that is the proper notion of the word. See Psal. 27. 12. a defect either of the relative, as Chap. 2. 32. or of the particle *how,* as Psal. 55. 2.

*{that spreadeth her hands, saying,}* Or, how *spreading her hands,* she says: either *stretching* them *out,* as for relief and succor, to those from whom she expects it; as Esay 1. 15. or *wringing her hands,* and *displaying* them, out of grief and anguish; as the manner of women in extremity of pain or sorrow, joined with impatience and impotency of spirit, is wont to be. See Chap. 2. 37. Lam. 1. 17.

*{saying}* Or, *saith;* a necessary supply, as Esay 58. 3. and 62. 11.

*{woe is me now}* Heb. *Woe now to me.* So Lam. 5. 16.

*{for my soul is wearied because of murderers,}* I am weary of my life; as Rebecca speaks, Gen. 27. 46. but this word is not there: or, *my soul fainteth,* or, *is faint:* as the word is well rendered, 1 Sam. 14. 28, 31. and so it would be, Chap. 31. 25. See Lam. 5. 17.

*{because of murderers.}* Or, *for* (so the particle is used, as noting the cause or ground of aught, Exod. 10. 14. Mal. 2. 3.) *murderers;* the Chaldeans, mine enemies, that murder my people without mercy, 2 Chr. 36. 17. and that much enhances her anguish, that her *lovers,* her *paramours,* are now become *murderers,* and have their hands in her blood as deep as any, vers. 30.

## CHAPTER 5

**Verse 1.** *{Run ye to and fro in the streets of Jerusalem, and see now and know, and seek in the broad places thereof, if ye can find a man, if there be any that executeth judgment, that seeketh the truth, and I will pardon it.}* Whether this chapter cohere, as some think, with the former, is somewhat uncertain. Howsoever, God in it by the prophet proceeds to complain of the general corruption of all estates and degrees among them, their gross abuse of his mercy, their strange obstinacy under his judgments, their extreme folly and stupidity manifested to their damage and destruction in either, which by the Chaldeans he threatens them with.

*{Run ye to and fro}* In this verse he implies the great paucity and rarity of righteous ones in Jerusalem, when he makes offer to spare it, if by going to and fro, and making enquiry in the streets and places of most concourse and confluence of people, they could meet with, and light upon, but any one such.

*{Run to and fro}* Or, *Go to and fro;* or, *up and down,* as Num. 11. 8. 2 Sam. 24. 2. Job 1. 7. for there is no notion of *running* in it, either in the notation, or the common use of the term; but in this form it is constantly used of going to and fro for enquiry and search, 2 Chr. 16. 9. Dan. 12. 4. Amos 8. 12. Zech. 4. 10. the word is in the plural number, as spoken not to the prophet alone, but to any other, that would undertake the employment; as if he had said, make the search who will, it shall be all one who does it: for they narrow it overmuch, that would restrain it to Jeremy, and Baruch.

*{in the streets of Jerusalem}* As Chap. 7. 17. the word is general, and comprehends as well *lanes,* as *streets,* as well the narrower, as the broader passages in a town or city, 1 Kin. 20. 24. See Cha. 6. 11. yea, sometime more generally, all places, either without doors, in town, or city; or without town or city, *the country,* as we term it, rendered therefore *the fields,* Prov. 8. 26. and so it would be rendered, Psa. 144. 13. that *our sheep may bring forth thousands——in our fields,* or *villages:* in the *country,* where the cattle are kept; distinguished from *the streets,* that is, the *towns,* or *cities,* where men abide, in the next verse; *no outcry* (so would it be rendered) *in our streets:* thus if it be here understood, the meaning will be, go up and down, both in city and country also, about Jerusalem. But I take it rather in the former sense; as ch. 14. 16.

*{see and know}* As, *know and see,* Chap. 2. 19. So 1 Sam. 23. 22, 23.

*{seek}* Make diligent enquiry; as Deut. 13. 14.

*{in the broad places thereof}* Heb. *in the streets;* as Lam. 2. 11, 12. Zech. 8. 4. so called in Hebrew, from the *breadth,* or *broadness* of them. See Gen. 26. 16. as also *streets* have thence their name both in Latin and Greek, in which language also, they have another term, for *narrower lanes,* to distinguish them from the broader: these he mentions the rather, because the greatest numbers of people are usually in the broader streets; that which makes them, says one, sometime to lose their name: places of meeting and convention, either for market, or merchandise, being commonly in such: and there therefore one being most likely not to lose his labor, what sort of people soever he were to look after.

*{if ye can find a man}* Some descant here upon the word *man,* that is, say they, one that deserves the name of *a man;* as the Cynic sometime went up and down at noonday with a lantern and candle in his hand, amidst a press of people in the market-stead, searching, as he said, for *a man:* and as one of the ancients, who delighted too much in dallying with Scripture, would pick mysteries out of that form, as it is in the original, Exod. 36. 4. Levit. 15. 2. *a man, a man;* that is, says he, a man both ways, in regard both of the outward and inward man: for there are some *men men,* and some *men beasts,* Psal. 49. 12, 20. Eccl. 3. 18. chap. 10. 8, 14. the notion is good: but the Scriptures are wronged: for *a man,* or, *a man man,* is no more than *any one,* or, *any* simply, in the one place; and *every one,* or *each one,* in the other. So is the word commonly used. See Isa. 8. 11. & 57. 1. & 36. 6. & 40. 26. & 66. 13. ch. 4. 29.

*{if there be any}* The word *any,* is not here in the text, but is not amiss inserted, as supplied from the former branch; and because the next term is singular, some render it, *any one:* that admitted, here is a very large offer made concerning Jerusalem, larger far than that which God made unto Abraham concerning Sodom. God came so low there, as to promise to save Sodom, if *ten righteous* at least, might be found in it, Gen. 18. 32. whereas here he promises, as is deemed commonly, to spare Jerusalem, if but any one righteous one could be met with in the streets of it, being in all likelihood a city larger and more populous, I say not than Sodom; but than that, and the other three cities joined to it, that perished with it; yea, than all those four cities added to it, that should have been destroyed together with it: But of this more hereafter.

*{that executeth judgment, that seeketh the truth}* Heb. *doing judgment, seeking truth;* (as Prov. 12. 17.) or, *fidelity;* 2 Chron. 34. 12. *to do judgment,* is, *to deal justly, uprightly,* Isa. 56. 1. as *to do truth,* or, *fidelity;* is, *to deal truly, faithfully,* Prov. 12. 22. 1 Joh. 1. 6. *To seek truth,* or, *fidelity,* is seriously to apply oneself unto true and faithful dealing; as, *to seek righteousness,* is, to apply oneself in like manner, unto just and upright dealing, unto the practice of righteousness, Zeph. 2. 2. So that the meaning seems to be, if there can be any one found, that is careful to deal uprightly, and faithfully. Where arises a very great and difficult question, wherewith interpreters are much troubled; for was not Jeremy himself in Jerusalem? was not Baruch his scribe there? there is more than one, there is two at least then; nor were there wanting such in likelihood among those princes, elders, and people, that rescued Jeremy out of the hands of the cruel priests, and false prophets, and the scum of the people, chap. 26. 8, 16, 17, 24. or, among those that dissuaded the king from burning the book, chap. 36. 16, 25. not to add Ebedmelech one of King Zedekiah's courtiers, chap. 38. 7, 9. Now to this there are divers answers; For first, some of the Rabbines answer, that the command is to search in the *streets;* but that such godly ones as were then in the city, were not there to be found, because they did keep within doors, and dared not come abroad for fear, chap. 36. 19, 26. but this is not probable, and the places before related disprove it: Others, that there was none to intercede, or deal with God in the behalf of the city, because the wicked ones slew them, and dealt so cruelly with them; as an enemy, should he surprise the city, could not do worse: to add some strength to this, the last clause might be read, *that I may spare it:* if any such may be found, that will intercede with me not to destroy it: the copulative for the infinitive, as Esay 61. 3, 4. but it is not likely, that the godly party were so hard-hearted any of them; but of Samuel's mind rather, *Far be it from me, that I should sin against the Lord, in ceasing to pray for you,* 1 Sam. 12. 23. And of Jeremy's, that prayed unto God constantly for them, even after that by God he was forbidden so to do: See on chap. 7. 16. Some other salve it, by reading the last branch; *and I will spare him,* will deliver him out of the common destruction, as I did Lot sometime out of Sodom, Gen. 19. 29. 2 Pet. 2. 6, 7. such an one shall have his life for a prey, chap. 21. 9. & 39. 18. & 45. 5. And this would do well, if the text would bear it; but the affixed particle here is not masculine, but feminine, which shows it to have reference not to the just one, but to *Jerusalem.* Others therefore again answer, that the words are spoken to Jeremy, and Baruch, and therefore they are included: and besides, that Jeremy was not of Jerusalem, but of Anathoth, chap. 1. 1. and Ebedmelech a Chushite, chap. 38. 7. But these neither seem of weight: Of ours some of chief note thus salve it. God by the prophet, say they, deals with the main body of the people apart, setting aside those faithful ones, whose number was not great, and were not comprehended in that body of the people, whereof he speaks. But neither does this seem to satisfy: for to say, see if you can find any righteous or religious ones, except it be of, or among those that are such, (and so in effect it must be) seems to be but a trifling manner of speech: they come nearer home, who expound it, *one,* that is, very few; *one,* for *a few;* as *one days,* (so the Hebrew is) for, *some few days;* or, *a few days,* Gen. 47. 44. & 29. 20. So Isaiah 30. 17. *A thousand shall flee at the rebuke of one,* and *one of a city,* chap. 3. 14. But the truth is, *one* is not in the text, much less but *one;* as *one,* for, *one only,* Eccles. 4. 8. Nor go they far from this, who conceive the meaning to be, *any:* that is, any considerable number, in regard whereof God should spare the city, as he would have done Sodom sometime. And this sense the words may very well bear; *any that doth,* for, *any that do;* any, as we say, worth the speaking of: or, if we will restrain it to an individual notion, and understand it strictly of one single person; the meaning may be, and that I conceive to be the right, That the people of the city were generally so corrupt, that a man might go to and fro, from street to street in it, for a long time together, and yet not light on any man, one or other, that were sincerely righteous, that were truly religious; See ch. 6. 28. & 9. 2, 4. and the like generality of corruption complained of, Gen. 6. 1. Psa. 12. 1. & 14. 2, 3. Isa. 64. 6, 7. Mic. 7. 1, 2.

*{and I will pardon it,}* Or, *spare it.* As Lam. 3. 42. For that one, or, those few righteous ones, I will spare the whole city and not destroy it, as Gen. 18. 24, 26, 29, 31, 32.

**Verse 2.** *{And though they say the LORD liveth, surely they swear false.}* Whereas it might be objected that they might meet not a few, that would seem very devout, had God's name oft in their mouths, and used to swear not by idols, as others, but by the only true God; vers. 7. ch. 12. 6. Isa. 48. 1. this objection to meet with, God tells the prophet, and them by him, that though they so did, yet that they do is not sincerely, ch. 12. 2. & 44. 26. Psa. 50. 16. Matt. 23. 14, 23. 2 Tim. 3. 5. For even then when they swear calling God solemnly to witness, they have no regard of truth, they swear falsely, and do it but to deceive, ch. 4. 2. 5, 20.

*{And though}* Or, *For,* (as ch. 3. 24.) *though;* Heb. *if,* as Job 14. 7, 8. or, *when;* as Psa. 63. 6. Amos 7. 2.

*{The LORD liveth}* The usual form of an oath, See ch. 4. 2.

*{surely}* Heb. *unto so,* or, *even so,* as ch. 29. 28. Even when they do so swear; but that which our Version has, may well be retained: for the word is sometimes used as a note of asseveration. See chap. 49. 26.

*{they swear falsely}* Heb. *unto falsehood;* or, *a lie;* as Isa. 42. 4. *unto truth;* or, *in falsehood;* as *in vanity,* or, *in vain,* ch. 2. 30. So Lev. 6. 3. ch. 7. 9. See Isa. 48. 1. Matt. 23. 23.

**Verse 3.** *{O LORD, are not thine eyes upon the truth? thou hast stricken them, but they have not grieved.}* The prophet turns his speech to God, complaining of their hypocrisy, which he could not but descry, and their extreme obstinacy under his hand.

*{are not thine eyes upon the truth?}* Or, as some, *dost not thou respect truth,* or, *fidelity?* that is, true, upright, and faithful dealing (which in these men is wholly wanting) do not you respect it, expect it, require it, delight in it; as chap. 22. 17. *thine eyes are not, but upon thy lucre only;* that is, you regard and look after nothing but that. But *thou affectest,* or, *delightest, in truth in the inward parts,* says David to God, Psal. 51. 6. Howbeit, by *truth,* or, *fidelity,* some understand here men of *truth,* or, *fidelity;* that is, men *true* and *faithful;* as *strength,* for, men of *strength, strong* men, Isa. 3. 25. and *wisdom,* for, a man of *wisdom;* a *wise* man, Mic. 6. 9. and it is true, that such alone God respects, and regards, Psal. 11. 5, 7. & 35. 15. So David of himself, *Mine eyes are upon the faithful in the land,* Psal. 101. 6. that is, those they are that I respect and regard: yet the former, seems to be the proper sense of the place. And others again, *Thou descriest truth;* your eyes see and discern, whatsoever shows men may make, where sincerity is, and where it is not, and you know therefore well enough, how hollow-hearted these men are; that which also is true as well as the former: for *his eyes behold,* and his *eyelids try,* or, *discern the children of men,* Psa. 11. 4. and, *he pondereth their spirits,* Prov. 16. 2. And both of them, I deny not to be here intimated, and to flow necessarily from the text, and the drift of the place; but the first I conceive to be the precise sense of the terms.

*{thou hast stricken them, but they have not grieved}* *But* (Heb. *and,* as ch. 4. 22.) *they are not grieved,* they are not affected with aught, that hitherto has been inflicted upon them; either by the hand of Sennacherib, Isa. 10. 5, 6. & 36. 1. or, by Pharaoh Necho, 2 Kin. 23. 37. or, by the forces of the Chaldeans and their complices, under Jehoiakim, and Jehoiachin, 2 King. 24. 2, 13. they take nothing to heart, they are like Solomon's drunkard, Prov. 23. 35. Isa. 42. 25. Amos 6. 6.

*{thou hast consumed them, but they have refused to receive correction}* Or, *thou hast wasted them;* but (as Prov. 11. 23.) *they refuse to receive instruction.* See ch. 2. 30. Zeph. 3. 2. corrected they have been with a witness, but instructed they will not be; they have been grievously wasted, and yet will they not be warned; they are never the better, or more reformed, for aught that has befallen them, Isa. 1. 5, 6. & 9. 13. Amos 4. 6, 11.

*{they have made their faces harder than a rock}* *To harden the face;* in Scripture, is to grow obstinate and impudent, Prov. 21. 29. So, *they made their hearts as adamant,* as it is rendered, Zech. 7. 12. Heb. *hard from a flint;* that is, *harder than a flint,* as Ezek. 3. 9. but there used of firmness and unmovable constancy.

*{they have refused to return}* Or, *they refuse to return;* they go on still in their wicked courses, chap. 8. 5. & 9. 3. and refuse by sincere repentance and serious reformation, to turn from them, and return unto God; notwithstanding that his hand has been so heavy upon them, to reclaim them, and bring them home unto him. See ch. 3. 1, 12. & 4. 1.

**Verse 4.** *{Therefore I said}* *And I said:* but the copulative is sometimes used for the illative; as ch. 3. 3. & 7. 16. Howbeit, I suppose here it need not be altered, unless it be for a discretive; *but,* or, *yet I said;* that is, *I thought* with myself, as Psa. 39. 1. Isa. 63. 8. chap. 3. 19.

*{Surely, these are poor, they are foolish; for they know not the way of the}*

*{LORD, nor the judgment of their God.}* Or, *these;* (to wit, that swear by the name of God falsely, v. 2. and persist in their wicked courses, v. 3.) *are poor* ones *only;* as the particle is used, Gen. 18. 32. or, *peradventure* (as Psa. 39. 11.) *they are poor* ones; the pronoun demonstrative, for the verb substantive, as ch. 4. 22. It may be they are of the meaner, and poorer sort only, that are thus faulty; poverty putting them upon evil courses, Prov. 30. 9. which they make the less conscience of, in regard of their ignorance, because they are not so well acquainted with God's word, and ways, Judg. 1. 10. John 7. 49. *they are foolish,* (as Esay 19. 13. chap. 50. 36.) or, *they do foolishly,* (as Num. 12. 11.) *because* (as Chap. 3. 21, 25.) *they know not the way of the Lord, nor the judgment of their God:* the same thing in divers terms, See chap. 8. 7. *judgment,* for *course, custom,* or *manner* of dealing, in general, 1 Sam. 2. 13. & 8. 11.

**Verse 5.** *{I will get me unto the great men, and will speak unto them; for they have known the way of the LORD, and the judgment of their God}* I will try whether it be any better with the great ones, peradventure I may find it otherwise with them, being better acquainted with God's will, and his ways; because they have had better breeding, and more abundant means of instruction, than those of the meaner sort, Prov. 4. 3, 4.

*{I will get me.}* Heb. *I will go me;* as Cant. 4. 6. See chap. 4. 12.

*{they have known}* Or, *know;* as vers. 4.

*{but these have altogether broken the yoke, and burst the bonds}* But these also generally, as well one as another (Psal. 14. 3.) have cast off the yoke of God's law, and the bonds of loyalty and obedience to him, Psal. 2. 3. Lam. 3. 27. Matt. 11. 29, 30. Luke 19. 14, 27. they that should have ruled and directed others, and have taught them better things, are as bad, if not worse, than any other, themselves, ch. 6. 13.

**Verse 6.** *{Therefore a lion out of the forest shall slay them}* Nebuchadnezzar and his forces, resembled here by divers similitudes; compared to a lion for his strength, a wolf for his ravenousness, a leopard for his swiftness, as some, or for his slyness, and watchfulness, rather.

*{a lion out of the forest}* As, *a boar out of the forest,* Psal. 80. 13. See chap. 4. 7.

*{shall slay them}* See 2 King. 25. 7, 18, 21. chap. 52. 10, 24, 27. Heb. *smite them:* as chap. 40. 14, 15. & 41. 2, 3. See Isaiah 66. 3.

*{and a wolf of the evenings shall spoil them.}* So the Chaldee, the old Latin, and the most, both Jewish, and other, the Greek only excepted, who are clean out of the way here: yet the plural, from the word that signifies *Evening,* is, in this form, nowhere else found: the singular is, being there also applied unto *wolves;* whereby these Chaldeans are also resembled for their fierceness, Hab. 1. 8. as are the judges, among this people, for their rapacity, Zeph. 3. 3. *wolves of the evening,* or, *evening wolves:* so termed from the time, wherein beasts usually look out, range abroad, and lay about them for prey, Psalm 104. 20. being then especially the more eager upon it, when they have been all day before without it. See Gen. 49. 27. yet some in those two places render it, *Wolves of Arabia,* as they suppose the word to be used, chap. 25. 24. and would have it also to be so understood here; but that other place in this prophet is questionable; and the form being plural, will not here admit it. That is more probable, which some other of the Jewish have, who render it, *the wolves of the deserts:* for so the word is oft used, chap. 50. 12. & 51. 43. because there commonly they keep: or, *of the plains;* for so also is the word used, Deu. 34. 1. ch. 39. 5. because, for prey, they there usually haunt.

*{a leopard shall watch over their cities, every one that goeth out thence shall be torn in pieces.}* To a *leopard,* is the Babylonian king and his forces compared, as for swiftness, Hab. 1. 8. so here for slyness, watchfulness, and lying in wait: as Hos. 13. 7. and it is here said of them, that they shall so strictly beset & begirt their cities, & have so watchful an eye upon them, that not any one shall be able to peep out of them, but shall fall into their clutches. See chap. 4. 16, 17. The words may be read with supply of the note of similitude oft wanting: as Gen. 49. 9, 14, 21, 27. *As a lion——shall he slay them; as a wolf——shall he spoil them; as a leopard——shall he watch over their cities:* *he shall,* that is, God *will;* or indefinitely, one *shall.* See Hos. 13. 7.

*{because their transgressions are many, and their backslidings are increased.}* Or, *are multiplied:* as Psa. 40. 5, 12. & 60. 4. the same thing twice in several terms, with a defect of the copulative: as v. 4, 5. yet the Chaldee, ancient Greek, and old Latin, render it, *are strengthened,* or *grown strong.* But the constant use of the word well observed, carries it rather the other way. See on Esay 16. 14. & 31. 1. & cha. 30. 15.

**Verse 7.** *{How shall I pardon thee for this?}* Or, *how can I,* or, *how should I* (as chap. 2. 23. & 3. 19.) *spare thee* (as v. 1.) *for this?* as Gen. 22. 23. Mal. 2. 3. How can I without some aspersion and disparagement to mine honor and justice, pass by and pardon such foul abuses? So v. 9.

*{thy children have forsaken me}* Your citizens, or inhabitants: *thy children;* as ch. 2. 30. have forsaken me, deserted my service, ch. 1. 16. & 2. 13.

*{and sworn by them that are no gods,}* By idols, false and counterfeit gods, chap. 16. 20. Gal. 4. 8. such they *swear* by, chap. 12. 16. Zeph. 1. 5. contrary to that inhibition, Josh. 23. 7. but here to *swear* by them, is put more largely for the service of them, and performance of religious worship unto them: one kind of it used to imply all the rest. See chap. 4. 2. Heb. *by not gods:* a defect of the pronoun demonstrative, the relative, and verb substantive: the like is, 2 Chro. 13. 9.

*{when I fed them to the full, they then committed adultery, and assembled themselves by troops in the harlots' houses.}* Thus idolatry and adultery, spiritual filthiness, and corporal uncleanness, go usually hand in hand the one with the other, Num. 25. 1, 2. Hos. 4. 12, 14. Amos 2. 8. Rev. 2. 20. & 9. 20, 21. & 17. 5. Fullness of bread, through man's abuse, breeds filthiness and looseness of life, Ezek. 16. 49. And the more love and kindness God shows to corrupt man, the more liberty he thereby takes to live loosely and lewdly, and the more freely to offend, Deut. 32. 15. Esay 26. 10. Hos. 4. 7. Rom. 2. 4, 5. Jude 4.

*{When I fed them to the full, they then committed adultery}* When I fed them plentifully, and gave them their fill. Heb. *and I satiated them* (as Psal. 81. 16. ch. 31. 25.) *and they committed adultery.* See the like former, ch. 2. 7, 20. the *then* in the latter branch may well be spared: as Esay 66. 14.

*{assembled themselves by troops}* Heb. *trooped themselves:* as Mic. 5. 1.

*{in the harlots' houses.}* Heb. *in the house of an harlot:* in the brothel houses: a defect of the preposition; as Job 11. 3. *house,* for *houses;* as Prov. 14. 11. and *harlot,* for *harlots;* as Prov. 6. 26.

**Verse 8.** *{They were as fed horses in the morning; every one neighed after his neighbours wife.}* Their excess of uncleanness, and the generality of it, is further taxed, and amplified with a similitude taken from the unruliness in that kind of stallions, or stone-horses full fed. See Ezek. 23. 23.

*{as fed horses}* About the epithet here used, there is great variety of opinions: The Chaldee renders it *wild horses;* as ch. 2. 24. *a wild ass:* The Greek, and Latin, *mad upon mares;* as deriving it from the word that has a notion of *fornication,* or unclean couplings: but this the analogy will not admit. The Jewish critic-masters would have it so read, as if it signified *armed,* or *barbed horses;* such as this people for their willful running headlong into sin, are compared unto, ch. 8. 6. which some of their commenters follow, as drawing it from a term that signifies *armor,* or *arms,* Deu. 23. 13. & 1 Kin. 22. 38. as some think. But the most, both Jews, and ours, render it *fed,* or *well fed:* from a word that signifies *to feed,* found in the Syriac, of Daniel, chap. 4. 12. in the Chaldee Paraphrase very frequent: whence also the word for *food,* or *victuals,* in Hebrew, Gen. 45. 23. 2 Chro. 11. 23. Dan. 4. 12. as also, if our critics may be credited, a word that signifies a *victualler,* or *hostess;* as, say they, Rahab was, Josh. 2. 1. and our English byword, of *provender-pricked,* besides common experience, enforces unto us, that horses well fed, are wont to grow the more wanton and unruly; alluded unto, Deut. 32. 15. and the masters of husbandry, advise to keep stallions high fed, when they intend them for that use.

*{in the morning}* About this word, there is no less diversity of exposition, than concerning the former. Some of the Jewish doctors would have it to be a Gentilish term from the country called *Meshec,* of note, say they, for horses, stallions especially; and for horses, indeed, it seems that the land of Togarma, one of the same lineage with Meshech, was famous, Gen. 10. 2, 3. Ezek. 27. 13, 14. as were also the *Mazaces;* of whom Oppian, in his *hunting poem,* l. 1. v. 170. Nor does the exception against this seem valid; to wit, that then it should be not *Maschim,* but *Maschijim:* for the one *jod,* is in such Gentilish terms oftentimes omitted: as in *Jehudim* and *Sidonim,* Deu. 3. 9. Esther 8. 9. But of any such note of that country for horses, some better proof would be had: for that Oppian's *Mazaces,* and the *Meshecites,* or *Masacites,* were the same people, is not easy to prove. Some of the Greek interpreters render it *drawing;* as if it were *horses of draught,* or *draughts:* and the verb from whence they seem to have drawn it, is used of *sowing,* Amos 9. 13. and the noun from it of *seed,* Psal. 126. 6. and so it might be deemed, to import beasts used for tillage: but if it be taken for a participle, the analogy rejects it; if for a noun, the syntax refuses it: and the notion suits not with the subject matter. Howbeit, to help this, a learned late annotator, would have it to be a participle, in a Chaldee, or Syriac form: the like whereunto he finds, Dan. 3. 16. & 5. 25. Mark 14. 37. 1 Cor. 4. 11. 1 Thess. 2. 9. 1 John 2. 20. conceiving that they understood it, of *drawing* out at length that part, or member, not named, because not so fit or needful to be expressed; and supposing withal, that they read the word in a passive form, otherwise vowelled than we now have it. But this sense of the word here, he himself approves not. A learned late writer would have it rendered, *a stallion,* that is, an horse kept and maintained on purpose for breed. So he says the Syriac translator has expressed it: and the same he supposes, that the old Latin intended. Nor seems the Chaldee otherwise to have taken it, rendering it in a word by the Talmudists used to signify the *gendring* of camels, and taken from their peculiar manner of coupling, as dogs do; which yet may peradventure be of larger extent; for that a term near it, differing but in an *he,* for an *het,* or a *chet,* seems to have a notion of somewhat about *horses:* whence they have a term for a *quiry,* or a *Master of horse.* But some of the Rabbines here expound it, as our Version has it, *in the morning:* as also some suppose the Chaldee did; but that the text is now corrupted, which had *Shacharin,* that is, *seeking in the morning* at first: and this interpretation is most generally received; as, say some, the *morning dew,* is by the same word expressed, Hos. 6. 4. whereunto they add that in the morning, horses having been full fed overnight, and rested well in the night, are more frolic and lusty. Against which it is objected, that the word is singular in Amos, but here it is plural; whereof more hereafter. And whereas it is by some in defense of the former interpretation alleged, that the singular and plural contracted are sometime the same, as in *tannim,* and *tannin,* for *tanninim,* and *tanninin,* Job 30. 29. Psal. 44. 19. Esay 34. 13. & 35. 7. & 43. 20. ch. 9. 11. & 14. 6. & 10. 22. & 49. 33. & 51. 37. Lam. 4. 3. Mic. 1. 5. To this the learned annotator before mentioned excepts, That in all those places, the word is singular: as Ezek. 29. 3. though collectively understood; which yet to affirm of so many places, seems somewhat hard. The ground of the mistake, in these misexpositions, he conceives to be, that the interpreters refer, that to the horses, which is meant of the men, wherein I concur with him, though I go not otherwise his way. He understanding it of the men, would have it rendered, *going forth:* for so, says he, *to draw out,* to wit, the feet, or one's self, is used for *to go forth,* Gen. 37. 29. Exod. 12. 2. Deut. 21. 3. Judg. 4. 6. & 20. 37. Job 31. 33. and for the form, he has recourse, as before, to the Chaldee: Howbeit not seeming herein satisfied himself, he adds another conjecture, that it may be rendered, not *going out,* but *looking out,* as loose and lascivious persons are wont after those whom they affect and are taken with; from a word, that in the Chaldee and Syriac does so signify, and is so used in either, Gen. 19. 28. Num. 23. 9. Act. 28. 4. and because the middle letter is not alike pointed in that, and this here; he adds, that the like variations are found in some other words, Esay 3. 16. vers. 30. chap. 23. 14. & 29. 17. But these conjectures, to me, seem somewhat overstrained, and far fetched: let other learned deem of them, as to them shall appear. Meanwhile, amidst this diversity of opinion, I shall make bold to propound my thoughts, and so leave them to the learned. I take the word in the received, common, and well-known sense, *of rising early:* or, as it is also not unusually taken, *of setting sedulously,* and eagerly, upon aught. So God says, that he called upon his people *rising early, and speaking, and sending, and protesting, and teaching,* ch. 7. 13, 25. & 11. 7. & 25. 4. & 26. 5. & 29. 19. & 32. 35. & 35. 14, 15. that is, doing sedulously and earnestly all this: and the prophet of himself professes to have in like manner done his duty, ch. 25. 3. and yet nearer to the present, it is said of his wicked people, Zeph. 3. 7. *they rose up early, corrupted all their actions:* that is, *rising early, they corrupted,* or, *they rose up early to corrupt all their actions:* they were early, eager, and earnest upon it: and I conceive the word of *rising early,* is here attributed, not to the horses, but to the men here compared to them, thus rendered precisely, according to the words and pauses in the text, *Fed horses rising early they are:* for the note of similitude is not in the text, and it is oft omitted. See on vers. 6. here the rather, to make the speech the more emphatical; as ch. 2. 23, 24. So that as it is said of drunkards, and riotous persons, Esay 5. 11. they *rise early to follow strong drink;* so here of those unclean and adulterous persons, they are in the morning so soon as they are up like fed stallions, or stoned horses, as eager and earnest to look after their whores, as those other to look after their liquor. All that can be objected against this is, that the participle is singular, which I acknowledge, the verb plural, which in distributive notions is a thing most frequent. See on Esay 2. 20. & 3. 12. & 26. 19. and hereafter, v. 26. and that to express more fully, rendered it may be, As *full fed horses they were rising early* each one of them: as in that former place it is put into the text. The very next words confirm it; where the noun is singular, *a man,* for *each one;* as Ezek. 20. 7, 8. as also, the pronoun, *his neighbor;* and the noun, *wife:* yet the verb plural, *they neigh.*

*{every one neighed after his neighbours wife.}* This one of the Jewish doctors slyly expounds, of their coming abroad with jollity, when they come out in a morning from their adulteress's bed; as shamelessly glorying in their sin and shame; like horses, says he, that having fed well in the night, use to neigh in the morning: but the prophet's purpose here, is not to express the disposition or carriage of these loose and lewd persons, when their filthy lust is satisfied; but rather their earnestness and eagerness in seeking after those, with whom they may satisfy their unbridled lust; nor is the *neighing* here alluded to the *neighing* of an horse, out of alacrity or courage, whereof, see Job 39. 19, 25. but his *neighing* upon the sight or scent of the mare, proceeding from unquietness, until he can come at her. Of the generality of this corruption among them, see chap. 9. 2.

*{neighed after}* That is, *neighing* sought *after:* as, *lamented after,* for, *lamenting* sought *after,* 1 Sam. 7. 2.

**Verse 9.** *{Shall I not visit for these things, saith the LORD?}* Or, *Should I not?* Should I suffer such things to go unpunished? I might well then be deemed a favorer of them, as such wicked ones conceive of me, because I forbear them a while, Psalm 50. 21. Mal. 2. 17. *to visit,* for, *to punish;* as Psalm 89. 31. Esay 26. 14. & 27. 1. See chap. 6. 6. because visitation and due cognizance ought to go before execution of justice, Deut. 13. 14. and to show, that God never proceeds to execution of judgment, but upon sure and certain knowledge, Gen. 18. 20, 21. Zech. 1. 12. *for these things;* as Chap. 1. 18.

*{and shall not my soul be avenged on such a nation as this?}* Or, *should I not avenge my self?* as Esa. 1. 24. *my soul,* for, *my self;* as Psa. 3. 2. and, *his soul,* for *himself,* Amos 6. 8. But *my soul,* makes the speech here more emphatical; as Psal. 11. 5.

**Verse 10.** *{Get ye up upon her walls and destroy,}* God's words, as signing or giving out a commission to the Chaldeans, to surprise and sack Jerusalem, and to make havoc of her people. See on Esay 10. 6. See also, chap. 34. 22.

*{but make not a full end}* That is, as some, but stay not there; go on to waste the whole country, to destroy the whole nation, chap. 4. 23, 27. but the meaning rather is, that God would not have them utterly destroyed. See chap. 4. 27. & 30. 11. and the ground of this restriction, in the like case, Matth. 24. 22. Heb. *and* (or, *yet;* as chap. 2. 7, 19.) *a full end ye shall not make;* as implying a providential passage, fixing a limit how far they shall proceed, and no further: as with Job 1. 12. & 2. 6. and of the sea, Job 38. 10, 11. vers. 22. but, though no less be implied, yet the future indicative seems put for the imperative: as chap. 3. 7, 19.

*{take away her battlements}* Break down her walls from the top to the bottom; the battlements whereof were appointed for safeguard, Deut. 22. 8. yet of the word here used, there is some question made; for though some of the Rabbines expound it, as our Version renders it, calling them the *teeth* of the wall. Yet, because it is not found elsewhere used, but of the *branches* of a vine, Esay 18. 5. where the same verb is joined with it that is here, and Jer. 48. 32. one of them would have it also to be so here: as if Jerusalem were compared to a vine, whose branches were to be cut off and spoiled; as of Moab, Esay 16. 8. and this further to put on, he would have the former word also rendered *walls,* to signify the *rows, alleys,* or passages between the vines in the vineyard; of which also, or the like, some expound that, Job 24. 11. but the term of *scaling,* suits ill with such. The Chaldee renders the former, *her cities;* this, *her palaces,* Esay 32. 14. But these neither of them carry any great probability; the *battlements* seem to have had that name given them; because they shot up like branches above the main body of the wall.

*{for they are not the Lords.}* The pronoun for the verb substantive; as vers. 4. God owns them not, either them or their city; they are out of his protection, their shield is gone from them; they have lost their best bulwark, Numb. 14. 7. See chap. 12. 7.

**Verse 11.** *{For the house of Israel, and the house of Judah, have dealt very treacherously against me; saith the LORD.}* Both houses, as well the ten tribes, as the other two, chap. 2. 4. have dealt very disloyally and perfidiously with me, chap. 3. 1, 6, 10. Heb. *in dealing disloyally have dealt disloyally;* as Esay 24. 10. Howbeit, the words may be meant here of the two tribes only, and be read, as by way of explication with some emphasis, thus; *the house of Israel, even the house of Judah;* as Ezra 1. 8. chap. 4. 6. and to this I incline. See vers. 15. & Esay 31. 6.

**Verse 12.** *{They have belied the LORD}* Or, as some, *denied* him, as Josh. 24. 27. Job 8. 18. & 31. 28. Prov. 30. 9. or, *They give the Lord the lie;* they make him a liar: as he speaks, 1 John 5. 10. See Esay 59. 13.

*{and said}* Or, *in saying;* or, *saying:* as Gen. 24. 60. So Gen. 18. 15.

*{It is not he:}* The prophets speak not from him, but fright us with tales of their own devising, 1 King. 22. 24. chap. 29. 26, 27. & 43. 2. For as for that which a learned late writer has from one of the Jewish commenters, that they deny God to be the ruler of the world; that which God should afterward refute by two instances, the one in his ruling of the sea, vers. 22. the other, in disposing of the seasons of the year, v. 24. seems clean besides the drift and purpose of the prophet in this place.

*{neither shall evil come upon us,}* See Esay 28. 14, 15.

*{neither shall we see sword nor famine.}* Heb. *and sword and famine* (or, *or famine;* as chap. 2. 18.) *shall we not see;* that is, *feel,* or suffer; as chap. 43. 14. & 44. 17.

**Verse 13.** *{And the Prophets shall become wind;}* Their words are but wind; their prophecies shall pass into the wind; shall prove windy, vain, and of none effect: a proverbial form of speech, very common, not with the Greeks and Latins only, but in Scripture also very frequent, Job 6. 26. & 15. 2. Prov. 11. 29. Eccl. 5. 16. Esay 57. 13. Hos. 8. 7. & 12. 1. 1 Cor. 14. 9.

*{and the word is not in them}* Or, *neither* (as v. 12.) *is the word* (to wit, of God) *in them.* They speak not from God, as they pretend to do; nor does God or his Spirit speak by them, or in them, chap. 43. 2. 2 Cor. 13. 3. See v. 12.

*{thus shall it be done unto them.}* The evils wherewith they threaten us, shall befall themselves, 1 Kin. 22. 24, 27.

**Verse 14.** *{Wherefore thus saith the LORD God of hosts;}* Esay 22. 15. & 28. 16.

*{Because ye speak this word}* Because you speak on this wise; *word,* for, *words;* as 1 Sam. 30. 31. or, for, *thing;* as ch. 7. 23.

*{Behold; I will make my words in thy mouth fire, and this people wood;}*

*{and it shall devour them.}* I will out of hand make it to appear, that the word that I have spoken by you my prophet, (for to him abruptly, as men use in passion, he turns his speech. See the like, ver. 19.) to be no vain word, Deut. 32. 47. but such as shall speedily be put in execution, and take hold on them, as fire on sear-wood, utterly to consume them, Psal. 83. 14. Esay 9. 18, 19. ch. 6. 11. See cha. 4. 4.

*{Behold I will make}* Heb. *Behold* (as chap. 1. 9.) *I am giving;* as chap. 32. 3, 26. *giving,* for, *making;* as Ezekiel 3. 8, 17.

*{my words in thy mouth}* Which I have put into your mouth, cha. 1. 9, 15, 16.

*{fire}* By the effect of it, ch. 23. 29. See Ezek. 5. 2, 4.

*{this people wood}* Fuel for it. See the like, Zech. 12. 6. Obad. 18.

*{and it shall devour them.}* Heb. *eat them;* as Esay 26. 11.

**Verse 15.** *{Lo, I will bring a nation upon you from far, O house of Israel, saith the LORD}* Heb. *Behold I am bringing:* as chap. 4. 6. & 11. 11.

*{from far}* From Chaldea; as Chap. 4. 16. Deut. 28. 49. Esa. 39. 3, 6, 7.

*{O house of Israel}* You people of the Jews, who are of the lineage of Israel; and the chief part thereof: for they alone are the people here threatened; the other ten tribes were in captivity already. See on ch. 4. 1. So v. 20. ch. 6. 9.

*{it is a mighty nation, it is an ancient nation;}* Heb. *a mighty nation it is, a nation from of old,* or, *from antiquity,* (as Esay 63. 16. chap. 2. 28.) *it is;* the pronoun for the verb substantive: vers. 4, 10. Eccl. 1. 10. that has been a potent people ever since Nimrod's days, the first founder of Babylon, Gen. 10. 10. Esay 23. 13.

*{a nation whose language thou knowest not, nor understandest what they say.}* For the Babylonians spoke the Syrian tongue, Dan. 2. 4. as did also the Assyrians: which the Jewish people generally understood not, having not been accustomed thereunto, Esay 36. 11. that which was long since threatened, Deut. 28. 36, 49. who will be the more stern and savage to you, because you shall not understand what they say to you, nor you know how to entreat them. See Esay 28. 11. and 33. 19.

*{knowest not}* That is, *understandest not:* as Psal. 81. 5.

*{nor understandest}* Heb. *hearest;* as Esay 26. 11. & 33. 19.

*{what they say}* Heb. *what he shall say;* but the word *nation* is collective. So v. 16.

**Verse 16.** *{Their quiver is an open sepulchre}* Heb. *his quiver;* or, *whose quiver* (the demonstrative for the relative; as Esay 47. 4. vers. 11.) *is an open sepulchre:* a proverbial form of speech. See Psal. 5. 7. Prov. 1. 12. the *quiver* said so to be in regard of the arrows, *sons of the quiver,* as they are termed, Lam. 3. 13. that shall be deadly to destroy and devour, or consume many. See Esay 13. 18. such shall their arrows be, as shall not miss what they aim at, like the Benjaminites' sling, Judg. 20. 16. and Jonathan's bow, 2 Sam. 1. 22. and where they light, they shall wound mortally, they shall pierce to the heart; as Psal. 45. 5.

*{they are all mighty men.}* The pronoun for the verb substantive; as Esay 60. 21. So vers. 17.

**Verse 17.** *{And they shall eat up thine harvest, and thy bread, which thy sons and daughters should eat; they shall eat up thy flocks and thine herds: they shall eat up thy vines and thy fig trees}* They shall consume and devour all your provisions, as well the fruits of the earth, as your cattle. See Deut. 28. 30, 31, 33, 51.

*{thine harvest}* Your crop, Lev. 26. 16.

*{which thy sons and thy daughters should eat}* *The childrens bread,* Matt. 15. 26. and he says, *thy bread,* that *they should eat;* rather than *the bread* that *thou shouldest eat:* because unto tender-hearted parents, it is a greater misery to want food for their children, than to want it for themselves, Lam. 2. 12, 11. Heb. which *thy sons and thy daughters shall eat:* a defect of the relative; as chap. 4. 31. and, *shall eat,* for, *should eat:* as, *shall reign,* for, *should reign,* 2 Kin. 3. 27.

*{thy flocks and thine herds}* See chap. 3. 24.

*{thy vines and thy fig trees}* That is, the fruit of them; as Esay 36. 16.

*{they shall impoverish thy fenced cities, wherein thou trustedst, with the sword:}* By cutting off, and destroying the people in them. See Deut. 28. 52.

*{fenced cities}* Heb. *cities of fences:* as, *cities of fence,* ch. 34. 7. your strongest and best defended cities: for these plurals exaggerate. See on Esay 58. 11. & 64. 6.

**Verse 18.** *{Nevertheless in those days, saith the LORD, I will not make a full end with thee.}* Heb. *And also;* or, *Yet even.* *And,* for, *Yet,* as vers. 10. *also,* for, *even:* as Esay 57. 6, 7. Of the meaning of the words, see on chap. 4. 27. and before here, vers. 10.

**Verse 19.** *{And it shall come to pass, when ye shall say, Wherefore doth the LORD our God all these things unto us? Then shalt thou answer them,}* Heb. *And it shall be;* as chap. 4. 9. *and thou shalt say to them,* for, *When ye shall say,——then thou shalt say to them:* or, *that when they shall say,——thou shalt say to them;* as Deut. 30. 1, 3. a passage from person to person; as vers. 14. See chap. 3. 2.

*{Wherefore doth the LORD our God all these things unto us?}* Or, *hath he done.* Thus wretched and sottish creatures, as if they were to be taught and told that, as a thing that they had never heard of before, which by the prophets of God had so oft been foretold them; or as if they had cause to question, why God should deal so with them, when as they had dealt so disloyally and perfidiously with him, v. 21. See the like expostulations of wicked ones with God, Esay 58. 3. Ch. 13. 22. & 16. 10.

*{Like as you have forsaken me, and served strange gods in your land; so shall ye serve strangers in a land that is not yours.}* See Deu. 28. 47, 48.

*{forsaken me}* Ch. 1. 16. ver. 7.

*{strange gods}* Heb. *gods of a stranger;* or, *strange people.* So Josh. 24. 23. See the like, ch. 8. 19.

*{in your land}* Or, *in your own land:* to make it to answer the other branch more fully: as, *to your own hurt,* ch. 7. 6.

*{in a land that is not yours.}* Heb. *in a land not yours:* as, *for not bread,* Esay 55. 2. *by not Gods,* vers. 7.

**Verse 20.** *{Declare this in the house of Jacob, and publish it in Judah, saying;}* *Declare and publish;* as ch. 4. 5. *the house of Jacob,* and *Judah;* one and the same: as *Jerusalem* and *Zion,* Esay 1. 27. & 2. 3. See vers. 11.

**Verse 21.** *{Hear now this, O foolish people, and without understanding, which have eyes and see not, which have ears and hear not.}* *Hear now;* as Esay 7. 13.

*{O foolish people}* Or, *sottish;* as it is rendered, ch. 4. 22.

*{without understanding}* Heb. *to* whom *heart is not;* as Hos. 7. 11. a defect of the relative: as vers. 17.

*{which have eyes and see not, which have ears and hear not.}* See Esay 6. 9. & 42. 20. Ezek. 12. 2. Heb. *eyes are to them, and they see not; ears are to them, and they hear not:* or, *but they see not; but they hear not:* the copulative for the discretive, or adversative; as Esay 29. 13. Chap. 12. 2. and the demonstrative for the relative, as vers. 16. and a passage from person to person; as chap. 2. 6, 7. vers. 19.

**Verse 22.** *{Fear ye not me? saith the LORD; will ye not tremble at my presence? who have placed the sand for a bound of the sea, by a perpetual decree, that it cannot pass it; and though the waves thereof toss themselves, yet can they not prevail: though they roar, yet can they not pass over.}* The folly and sottishness of this people is hereby evinced, in that neither the apprehension of God's powerful greatness manifested, in bounding that vast and violent body of the sea, which no might or slight of man is able to master, when it rises and rages, with a bank of sand, and so keeping it within compass, that it cannot stir an inch further than he has set and assigned it; will enforce them to fear him, and stand in awe of him: nor the consideration of his gracious goodness, Act. 14. 17. manifested, in crowning the year with his blessing, Psal. 65. 9, 11. and giving seasonable times for the ripening and receiving the fruits of the earth, induce them to serve and observe him for their own benefit and behoof, vers. 24.

*{Fear ye not me?}* Heb. *Will ye not fear me?* and so it would be rendered to suit with the next branch; unless we render that also in the present; will you not be ruled by me, who am able to rule and overrule the most unruly creature of all others, Job 7. 12. the sea, Psa. 65. 7. & 93. 4.

*{tremble at my presence}* As Psa. 114. 7.

*{who have placed the sand for a bound of the sea}* Heb. *set the sand a bound to the sea.* See Psal. 104. 9. Job 26. 10.

*{by a perpetual decree}* Or, *an ancient decree.* Heb. *an ordinance of perpetuity;* as Exod. 29. 9. or, *of antiquity,* as vers. 15. Hab. 3. 6. if we take it the latter way, it has reference unto the antiquity, either of God's disposition, at the creation, Gen. 1. 9. Job 28. 10, 11. or of his determination after the flood, Gen. 8. 21. & 9. 11. if the former way; which the words following seem to lead unto, it must be understood of the continuance of it. Whereof, see Gen. 9. 11. Job 26. 10.

*{that it cannot pass it}* Or, *which it cannot pass.* Heb. *will not,* or, *shall not pass;* as Psa. 104. 9. the copulative and demonstrative for the relative; as Esay 46. 11. & 48. 8. and the indicative in a potential notion; as ch. 2. 23, 32.

*{and though the waves thereof toss themselves, yet can they not prevail;}* Heb. *and* (or, *so that,* as chap. 14. 19. or, *though;* as Esay 10. 5.) *the waves thereof toss themselves,* (as ch. 46. 7, 8.) *and* (or, *yet;* as ch. 3. 7.) *they cannot,* (to wit, get over; supplied from the next branch) or, *they shall not prevail;* as Gen. 32. 28. 1 Sam. 26. 25. that is, *they cannot;* as before: two copulatives diversely used, in a twofold notion; connexive, and concessive; the former, the like whereunto, see Exod. 19. 4. v. 26. in a single discretive notion; the latter; as v. 10. So in the next branch;

*{though they roar, yet can they not pass over.}* Heb. *and they roar,* or, *rage;* (as it is rendered, Psa. 46. 6.) *and they shall not pass over: and,* for, *though,* and, for *yet;* as Job 8. 7.

**Verse 23.** *{But this people have a revolting and rebellious heart; they are revolted and gone.}* *But.* Heb. *And;* as ver. 3.

*{a revolting}* Or, *refractory.* See v. 3, 6. they are of a refractory spirit, wholly bent unto, pitched and fixed upon rebellious courses, Psal. 78. 8.

*{revolted and gone}* From my law, which the sea itself observes, vers. 22. as some: the wretched and rebellious condition of mankind, who alone of all the creatures transgress the law which God has prescribed them; go beyond the bounds that he has assigned them, Psa. 119. 90, 91. & 148. 8. or, *revolted and go on;* persist in their revolt and rebellious courses, and will not be reclaimed, v. 3. ch. 8. 4, 5. Heb. *they are gone aside;* (Psal. 14. 3.) *and go,* or, *will go,* ch. 2. 25. Hos. 2. 10.

**Verse 24.** *{Neither say they in their hearts;}* They think not once with themselves; as Psal. 14. 1. ch. 13. 22. Zeph. 1. 12.

*{Let us now fear the LORD our God}* Let us serve and worship him; let us observe and obey him: *to fear,* for, *to serve;* as 2 King. 17. 25, 41. because all our *service* of God ought to proceed from *fear,* Deu. 10. 20. 1 Sam. 12. 24. and to be mixed with *fear,* Psa. 2. 11. Heb. 12. 28. Let us serve him for his goodness, Deu. 28. 4. Hos. 3. 5. and for our good, Deu. 5. 29. & 6. 24. & 10. 13. ch. 32. 39.

*{that giveth rain}* Deut. 28. 12. Amos 4. 7. Matt. 5. 41. which neither the idols, nor the clouds of themselves can give, Job 38. 25, 28. chap. 14. 22. Zech. 10. 1. and which if it be withheld, the sky will be as brass over our heads, and the earth as iron under our feet, Deut. 28. 23. *rain,* says the Rabbine, to water their gardens, and for other uses, both for man and beasts; the other two sorts subjoined, principally for their corn: but this seems but a nicety; the other two seem to particularize rather this general, as being the rains chiefly desired.

*{both}* Heb. *and;* on which the Jewish critic would ground his former nicety; but it is rather a particular explication of what *rain* he intended: *and,* for, *both,* as chap. 17. 26. or, *even:* as chap. 52. 13.

*{the former and the latter}* Heb. *yoreh* and *malqosh;* So Deut. 11. 14. for the word *geshem,* for rain, before used, comprehends both, Hos. 6. 3. Joel 2. 23. the former called here *yoreh,* and elsewhere also *moreh,* Joel 2. 23. is termed the former; not because it came first, according to the more general account of the year, and the ordinary ranking of the months whereof it consisted; for that which is here rendered the latter, came in the first month, Joel 2. 23. this in the eighth: but in reference to their husbandry, and the order thereof; the former falling shortly after their seedtime, the latter, sometime before their harvest, in regard whereof, also the year for civil contracts began at the month *Tisri,* in account otherwise the seventh, See Lev. 23. 24. & 25. 9. and it had its name *yoreh,* or, *moreh,* from a word that signifies *to pour down,* Prov. 11. 25. Hos. 10. 12. See Esay 30. 20. ch. 3. 3. In which latter place also, see of the latter rain, called *malqosh* both here and there.

*{in his season}* In the months above mentioned, Lev. 26. 4. So Deu. 11. 14.

*{he reserveth unto us the appointed weeks of the harvest}* Or, *and keepeth;* or, that *keepeth for us the weeks appointed for harvest:* a defect either of the copulative, as vers. 5, 6. or, of the relative, as chap. 4. 31. vers. 17, 26. That continues unto us the seasons of the year, each in his turn and due time, Gen. 8. 22. or, that keeps the times of harvest fair and dry for us, so that we have weather of either sort seasonably; for rain in harvest is unseasonable and hurtful, Prov. 26. 1. See 1 Sam. 12. 17, 18. Esay 18. 4.
