**Verse 22.** *{Is there no balm in Gilead? is there no physician there? Why then is not the health of the daughter of my people recovered?}* The words contain an implication of evils and calamities, so grievous, so desperate, that no power, or skill of man, was able to overcome, and ease them of.

*{no balm in Gilead}* A place famous for the most sovereign balsam, see Gen. 37:25. ch. 46:11. Howbeit, the Greek, and the old Latin, following it, renders the word, both here, and Gen. 37:25. & 43:10. *rosin*; and from the word here used, the name of *rosin*, both in Greek and Latin, seems to have descended; ours in English, also, coming nearer to it, than either; which some retaining, affirm to be meant of such a kind of liquid *rosin*, or *turpentine*, as we term it, as issued from the *Terebinth* tree, which yields the best balsam, and is highly commended for the closing up of wounds. See of it, Pliny in his *natural history, l. 14. c. 20. & lib. 24. c. 6.*

*{is there no physician there?}* Or, *is there no chirurgeon there?* For the word includes both: the place being so famous for such a sovereign confection, it is not unlikely that there would be many artists there, of either profession to direct the use of it; as with us at the Bath: the prophet therefore demands, as one that should wonder at it, that there should be no balm at all to be had at Gilead, no one chirurgeon at all to be found there: but withal implying, that though there were there never so much store of the one, or great number of the other; yet all would not serve to cure a mortal wound, to recover a patient altogether incurable; and that the state and condition of the people was such: for what some speak here of spiritual physicians, priests, or prophets, at Gilead; as Elias, 1 Kings 17:1. See Hos. 6:8, 9. seems to swerve from the genuine sense of the place.

*{why then is not the health of the daughter of my people recovered?}* Heb. *why is no cure*, or *healing of the daughter of my people gone up*, or *come?* of which form of speech, see on ch. 30:17.

## CHAPTER 9

**Verse 1.** *{Oh that mine head were waters, and mine eyes a fountain of tears, that I might weep day and night for the slain of the daughter of my people.}* The prophet in this chapter proceeds to lament the grievous calamities that were to befall his people; together with their wickedness and general corruption, the procuring cause thereof, vv. 1, 16. incites others to the like solemn lamentation, verses 17, 22. and labors to bring them off from their vain confidence, either in natural and worldly parts and abilities, as strength, wisdom, and wealth, verses 23, 24. or external rites, as circumcision, verses 25, 26.

*{Oh, that mine head were waters}* Or, *water*; for the notion is singular, though the form plural; so Gen. 24:13. 1 Sam. 7:6. Ps. 119:136. Heb. *who will give*, or, *make*, (as Hos. 11:8.) *my head water?* a usual form of wishing, in Hebrew: so Deut. 5:26. Ps. 55:6. Mal. 1:10. for so I suppose that place also would be rendered. So also verse 2.

*{and mine eyes a fountain of tears}* Heb. *tear*; as Ps. 80:5. & 116:8. Isa. 25:8. the very same word in Hebrew signifies both an *eye*, and a *spring*, Gen. 16:7. Neh. 2:13.

*{that I might weep day and night}* Heb. *and I will weep*: the copulative for the finitive: as Josh. 24:9. Mal. 1:9. *day and night* without intermission; as Lam. 2:18, 19. as if he could never lament or mourn enough. See the like, Isa. 22:4. ch. 4:19. & 8:18. & 14:17.

*{for the slain}* Heb. *the slain*: *weep the slain*, for, by *weeping bewail the slain*. So Deut. 21:13. *she shall weep for her father and mother*; that is, *weeping bewail them*: *slain*; that is, *ready to be slain*: as, *destroyed*, for, *to be destroyed*, Ps. 137:8. *perished*, for, *ready to perish*, Isa. 27:13. as sure to be slain, as if slain already. So Gen. 20:3. Job 3:12. ch. 32:24. Ezek. 21:24. So also, ch. 35:5.

*{of the daughter of my people}* My dear countrymen; as ch. 8:19, 21, 22.

**Verse 2.** *{Oh that I had in the wilderness a lodging place of wayfaring men, that I might leave my people and go from them.}* A second wish, that he might withdraw himself from his people and live in any solitary desert, and in any sorry lodge or shed there, rather than among them, whose wicked lives were such a continual eyesore, and heart-sore to him: as were the Sodomites to Lot, 2 Pet. 2:7, 8.

*{Oh that I had}* Heb. *Who will give me?* as verse 1.

*{in the wilderness}* In the most solitary waste, Ps. 55:7. and among the wild beasts, not so much to escape danger from them; as Elias, 1 Kings 19:3, 4. or to avoid molestations by them: as Prov. 21:19. Ps. 120:5, 6. Eccl. 25:18, 22. as hoping to find better entertainment with the wild beasts, than with them; as those faithful ones, Heb. 11:38. or, that his soul might not be continually vexed with the sight of their sinful courses, as the words ensuing show. See David's affection in the like kind, Ps. 119:136, 139, 158.

*{a lodging place of wayfaring men}* Or, *a traveler's lodge*; any such sorry shed, as is wont to be erected in solitary places where no housing is, for travelers to rest, and repose themselves in, by the way: see Isa. 24:19.

*{that I might leave my people}* Heb. *and I will leave*: see on verse 1. so Ps. 55:6. *that I might flee away, and be at rest*.

*{for they are all adulterers}* The reason why he would rather retire himself to any place, were he at his own choice, than live among them, such as they were.

*{all adulterers}* For the generality of them, see ch. 5:8. So Hos. 7:4.

*{an assembly of treacherous men.}* Or, *a company of perfidious dealers*; not a holy *congregation*, for which the word is commonly used, Lev. 23:36. Num. 29:35. Deut. 16:8. but a whole rout, or pack, of perfidious wretches, Isa. 1:4. See ch. 3:10. Howbeit, because the word is used commonly for a holy *meeting*, or a day of *restraint* from civil employments, Lev. 23:36. Some read the text here, *dealing perfidiously* in the day of *restraint*; as if they dealt never more wickedly, than on those days, wherein they ought to have been most strict, and to have demeaned themselves most devoutly: see Isa. 58:3, 4. Ezek. 23:38, 39. And another, because the word it comes of signifies sometime *to rule*, 1 Sam. 9:17. 2 Chr. 14:11. and another derivative very near to this, *regiment*, or *dominion*, Judg. 18:7. would therefore have this here to signify, *a kingdom of perfidious ones*. But the first is as the most received, so the most familiar, and most free.

**Verse 3.** *{And they bend their tongue like their bow for lies;}* Heb. *And they tread their tongue their bow to falsehood*: *to tread*; the usual term, in Hebrew, for *to bend*; because by treading on it, the bow bends: so ch. 46:9. & 50:14. & 51:3. one of the rabbins tells us, that it came so to be used, at first, from an engine, not unlike to our crossbow, that used to be bent with the foot: *their tongue their bow*, that is, their tongue which is as their bow, or which they use as a bow to shoot out lies, to the impeaching of others, in their name, state and life: the tongue is, in Scripture, compared oft to *a bow*, and words to *shafts*: so Ps. 64:3. & 120:1, 2. verse 8. and this *bending of the tongue* like *a bow*, may seem to be that which the psalmist calls, *devising of mischief with the tongue*; that is, of mischievous matter to be uttered by the tongue, Ps. 52:2. See Ps. 64:3, 4. For that construction of a great man seems somewhat overharsh; *they bend their tongue; their bow is a lie*: the *lie* should be the *shaft* rather: see verse 8.

*{but they are not valiant for the truth upon the earth:}* The text is here by divers diversely both distinguished and interpreted. The Greek takes somewhat from the former clause, and fastening it unto this, renders the words, *falsehood and not faithfulness prevaileth upon earth*. But this the text will not bear. The old Latin on the other side pulls somewhat from this, and affixes it to the former, reading them thus; *they bend their tongue as a bow of falsehood, and not of truth*: but neither does this suit well, either with the pauses in the Hebrew, or some terms in the text. The Chaldee, whom the Jewish commenter concurs with, has the same in effect that our version exhibits, save that those last words, *upon the earth*; which might seem to answer our English phrase, *in the world*: as if it were said, *for the truth they have no courage in the world*: as the like, Isa. 26:18. *no deliverance upon earth*; (of which, see there) they seem rather to understand of *the land* that they lived in; that they did not put out themselves, or make use of their strength for the maintenance of truth and equity *in the land*; but for the wronging of the weak. So Isa. 59:4. and this I take to be the native sense of the place: *and*, for, *but*; as ch. 8:15. though the copulative may well be here retained. Howbeit, some late writers of note render it, *and not according to faithfulness*, or *by neglect of faithfulness*, (that is, by falsehood and unfaithful dealing) *they grow strong upon earth*, Ps. 73:12. ch. 5:27, 28. & 12:1, 2. But this to me seems somewhat to force the text.

*{for they proceed from evil to evil}* Or, *but they proceed* (as Ps. 118:17.) *from evil to evil*; from one evil to another; or from one degree of it to another: they grow daily worse and worse, ch. 7:26. So 2 Tim. 3:13.

*{and they know not me, saith the LORD.}* This comes last, as the main cause of all the former; the principal ground of all evil is in Scripture assigned, as sometime to the want of the sincere fear of God: as Gen. 20:11. Ps. 36:1. Mal. 3:5. Rom. 3:18. so otherwhile to the want of the sound knowledge of God, as here, so Judg. 2:10, 11. 1 Sam. 2:12. ch. 4:22. Hos. 4:1, 2. and indeed the former follows upon this latter; for where no knowledge of God is, no fear of God can be: what a man knows not, he cannot fear.

**Verse 4.** *{Take ye heed every one of his neighbour; and trust ye not in any brother: for every brother will utterly supplant; and every neighbour will walk with slanders.}*

**Verse 5.** *{And they will deceive every one his neighbour, and will not speak the truth}* They are generally so corrupt, that a man can hardly find, or light on any one honest and faithful, whom he may trust, though he be never so near to him in nature, or pretend never so much friendship or fidelity to him, Ps. 12:1, 2. Prov. 20:6. ch. 5:1. & 12:6. Mic. 7:5, 6.

*{his neighbour}* Or, *friend*: as it is well rendered, 2 Sam. 13:3, 7. and 16:17. 1 Kings 4:5. and so would be here, and verse 5. for there is here an emphasis in it: nor is it barely as in that common phrase, ch. 22:8.

*{will utterly supplant}* Or, *will surely supplant*. Heb. *supplanting supplant*; overreach, go beyond, and cheat his own brother: the word signifies properly *to trip up one's heels*; a figurative speech taken from the practice of runners, or wrestlers, an allusion to the name of Jacob thence so termed, Gen. 25:26. & 27:36. Hos. 12:2. See the contrary enjoined, 1 Thess. 4:4.

*{every neighbour}* Or, *friend*; as before.

*{will walk with slanders}* Carrying tales to and fro, and spreading abroad false reports. So ch. 6:28. a wicked practice, inhibited, Lev. 19:16. such friends as speak a man fair to his face, will be detracting from him, and traducing him behind his back. So ch. 12:6. & 18:18. See Prov. 26:20, 22.

*{they will deceive}* Or, *mock*, and delude; as Job 13:9. or, *beguile*: as Gen. 31:7.

*{every one his neighbour}* Heb. *a man his neighbour*, or, *his friend*; not simply, *one another*; as v. 20. Zech. 8:10. but each one his nearest and dearest friend, as v. 4.

*{and will not speak truth}* See the contrary enjoined, Zech. 8:16. Eph. 4:25.

*{they have taught their tongues to speak lies;}* Or, *they have enured*, or, *accustomed*, them; as the word is, ch. 2:24. Hos. 10:11. where it would also be so rendered; they have got such a habit and custom of lying, that they cannot leave it. See ch. 13:23.

*{and weary themselves to commit iniquity}* They take pains to do wickedly, and tire out themselves in it, Ps. 7:14. Isaiah 5:18.

**Verse 6.** *{Thine habitation is in the midst of deceit}* God's speech to the prophet. You my prophet live among a company of deceitful and falsehearted people, and have need therefore to walk warily, ch. 12:6. or, as others, there is little hope therefore that you should do any good upon them, they are so wedded to their deceitful ways: and this the words following seem to confirm. See ch. 8:5.

*{Thine habitation}* Heb. *Thy sitting*; that is, *Thine abode*: as Exod. 16:3. Deut. 6:7. & 11:19.

*{in the midst of}* Or, *among*; as ch. 39:14. & 40:5.

*{deceit}* That is, *deceitful persons*: *deceit*, for, *men of deceit*; as Ps. 109:2.

*{through deceit they refuse to know me, saith the LORD.}* They are so addicted to their deceitful courses, that they will rather stick to them, though to their own ruin, than return to me for their good, ch. 8:5. or, that their strong affection to them, makes them altogether unwilling and averse unto the knowledge of me and my will, because contrary thereunto, Ps. 36:3, 4. or, as others, they so trust to their frauds and falsehoods, to their wiles and guile, whereby they make account to secure themselves, that they regard not me, or ought that comes from me, Job 21:14. Ps. 52:7. Isa. 28:15. & 30:15. But I adhere rather to the former.

*{they refuse to know me}* A further degree than the former, of *not knowing*, verse 3. a refusal to know; implying a willful, affected, obstinate ignorance; a rejecting of means offered them, whereby they might come to knowledge. See Ps. 82:5. 2 Pet. 3:3, 5.

**Verse 7.** *{Therefore thus saith the LORD of hosts; Behold, I will melt them, and try them.}* I will melt them, as the finer does his ore, or metal, in the furnace and fire of affliction, to consume the wicked as dross out of them, and to refine the residue, Isa. 1:25. & 4:4. & 49:10. Dan. 11:33. Mal. 3:3. or, as some of the Jewish commenters, I will try them by some lesser and lighter afflictions, whether they will be brought home to me, or no, before I proceed to an utter destruction. That which a late learned writer exhibits in the time past, rendering the words; *I have melting them tried them.* I have by milder castigations assayed to amend them; but to little purpose, ch. 6:29. But the sequel of the context, and the illative in the front of the verse, carries it rather the first way.

*{I will melt them, and try them}* Heb. *I am melting them and I will try them*; that is, I am about by melting to try them. See the like, ch. 6:27.

*{for how should I do for the daughter of my people?}* Or, *what else*

*should I do for the daughter of my people?* that is, as some, what could I do less? understanding it of the time past: or, as others, what other course can I take with them, being generally grown so desperately evil? as, *How can I do this great evil?* Gen. 39:9. See Isa. 5:4, 5. Hos. 11:8. it may well be rendered; *How should I deal* (as Hos. 6:4.) otherwise, (as the particle here used seems to be taken, Ps. 68:2. Mic. 1:4.) *the daughter of my people*: or, as one of the Jewish doctors not amiss, *because of* the wickedness *of the daughter of my people*, as verses 1, 3. and there seems to be, as he well observes, an emphasis in it; as if God had said, how can I endure to see, or suffer, to mine own extreme dishonor, such horrible abominations to reign among those, that are called and counted my people. See verse 9.

**Verse 8.** *{Their tongue is as an arrow shot out;}* The *tongue* was before compared to *a bow*, verse 3. here, *to a shaft*: to *a bow*, in regard of the fitting of it for the uttering of falsehood by wicked contrivances; to *a shaft*, in regard of the speech passing from it to the wrong and prejudice of others; as Ps. 64:3. Prov. 25:18. There is concerning the attribute here assigned to this *shaft*, or *arrow*, a twofold reading in the original: for some copies had it *a slaying*, or, *slaughtering shaft*: (for the ancient Greek and old Latin rendering it, *wounding*, and some other *cutting*, come far short of the true notion of the term) and *arrows* are mentioned as *instruments of death*, and of *destruction*, Ps. 7:13. Deut. 32:23. Ezek. 5:16. others, *a shaft drawn out*, as the word is used, 2 Chr. 9:15, 16. of *gold drawn out*, or, beaten out into plates; which those that follow, expound, either of a shaft *drawn out* of the quiver: or, *shot out* from the bow; (and this our version follows) or, *drawn over* the whetstone to sharpen it: according to that, *they have whet their tongues like a sword*, Ps. 64:3. *and they have sharpened their tongue like a serpent*, Ps. 140:3. and this last the Chaldee also exhibits: but neither do any of these expositions suit well with that use of the word concerning *gold*, and the notion of it thereby in that place expressed: for in that notion, or in any other, save that of *slaying*, it is nowhere else found: yea, some of those Jewish doctors also that retain this latter reading, bring it fully home to the sense of the former, affirming the word to be, not a passive participle, though it have the form of such an one, but a *toar*, as they term it, or a noun adjective; alleging such an one of the same stamp used for an *oppressing* person, Prov. 28:17. whereunto may be added, that as in Greek and Latin, and with us also from the latter, some such passive forms have yet an active notion, as when we say, *a considerate*, and, *a circumspect* man; so in Hebrew also, their *Pauls*, as they term them, have sometime the like, Prov. 7:10. *a woman*, not *reserved*, as some; but as some other, *circumspect*; or, as others again, *cautious*: as our version, *subtle*: word for word, *observant*, or, *watching* warily to entrap and ensnare foolish youth: and whether reading therefore for the frame of the word we follow, this may well be, and I conceive to be the true sense of the words; *A slaying* (that is, a pernicious and mischievous) *shaft* (for the two terms in Hebrew have some consonancy with them) or, *arrow, is their tongue*: for the note of similitude (that which makes it the more emphatic; as ch. 6:8.) is not in the text. Some late writers of prime note, instead of *a shaft* here, give us *a knife*; and it is true, that a wicked tongue is compared sometime to *a sword*, Ps. 57:4. & 59:7. and to *a razor*, Ps. 52:2. but these learned interpreters do not show us, where the term here found is ever used for *a knife*; nor does any such place appear.

*{it speaketh deceit}* Or, *fraud*; it utters nothing less than what in truth they intend: as it is reported to have been a common byword concerning one of the popes, and a base son of his, that the one of them *never spake what he meant*, and the other, *never meant what he spake*: and this *deceit*, or *fraud* is commonly pernicious or mischievous, as the Latin word for *fraud* is used for either; in regard whereof, *the false tongue* is said to be as *the razor* of such a guileful barber, as pretending to trim a man's hair, instead thereof cuts his throat, Ps. 52:2.

*{one speaketh peaceably to his neighbour, with his mouth; but in his heart he layeth his wait}* Or, *with his mouth will a man talk peaceably*, or *kindly*, (Heb. *speak peace*; as Ps. 35:20. and 85:8. Est. 8:30. & 9:3.) *with his neighbour*, or *friend*, (*with another*; as Zech. 8:16, 17.) *when inwardly*, or, *in his heart*, (Heb. *in the midst of him*; as ch. 3:14. See Ps. 5:9.) *he layeth wait for him*. Heb. *and*, for, *when*; as ch. 6:14. and, *his wait*, that is, *wait for him*: as, *his snare*, and, *his gin*, for, *the snare*, and *the gin*, set for him, Job 18:10. when they speak a man fairest, they then mind him the most mischief. So Gen. 34:13. 2 Sam. 3:27. & 13:26. & 20:9. Ps. 5:9. & 28:3. & 55:22. Prov. 26:23, 25.

**Verse 9.** *{Shall I not visit them for these things? saith the LORD? shall not my soul be avenged on such a nation as this?}* Or, *Should I not punish?* See the same, ch. 5:9.

**Verse 10.** *{For the mountains will I take up a weeping and wailing, and for the habitations of the wilderness a lamentation; because they are burnt up, so that none can pass through them, neither can men hear the voice of the cattle; both the fowl of the heavens, and the beast are fled, they are gone.}* The prophet's words returning to his lamentation again; as before, for the multitude of the people slain, verse 1. so now for the utter devastation of the whole country, as well hill, as vale; left destitute of all living wights. See ch. 4:23, 26.

*{the mountains}* For Judea, about Jerusalem especially, was much of it hilly, Ps. 87:1. & 125:2. Isa. 14:25. ch. 17:3. & 33:13. Ezek. 36:1, 8.

*{the habitations of the wilderness}* Or, *pastures* (as the word is used, Joel 2:22.) *of the plain*, or, *vale*. See Isa. 63:13. thus the whole country is divided into *hill* and *vale*, ch. 17:26. & 33:13. Ezek. 36:4, 6.

*{a lamentation}* As ch. 7:29. Ezek. 19:14. So hereafter, v. 20. and, *to take up a lamentation*; as Ezek. 19:1. & 26:17. & 27:2. & 28:12. & 32:2. Amos 5:1.

*{burnt up}* Or, *desolate*: so wasted and spoiled, as if they had been burnt up with fire. So verse 12. ch. 46:19. See Joel 2:3.

*{so that none can pass through them}* Heb. *from no man passing*; that is, either *because none passeth* to and fro by them; for through want of passengers, ways become waste, Lam. 1:4. or *so that none passeth through* them, they are so waste and uncouth: so extremely are they wasted, that not only there is no dwelling in them, but no passing by them. So ch. 2:6. v. 12. *man*, for, *any one*; as ch. 5:1. and a defect of the pronoun; as ch. 8:10.

*{neither can men hear the voice of the cattle,}* Heb. *nor do they hear the voice of the cattle*; that is, *nor is the voice of cattle heard* there. See Isa. 62:10. the lowing of oxen, or bleating of sheep, Judg. 5:16. 1 Sam. 15:14. that had wont to feed and graze there. See ch. 33:10, 12, 13. a defect of the particle *there*, or, *therein*: as ch. 6:16.

*{both the fowl of the heavens and the beast are fled}* Heb. *from the fowl of heaven and unto the beast they are fled*: as Gen. 7:3. ch. 50:3. See ch. 4:25.

*{they are gone}* Because nothing is left that may sustain either, ch. 12:4.

**Verse 11.** *{And I will make Jerusalem heaps, and a den of dragons;}* Heb. *I will give* (as verse 1.) *Jerusalem unto heaps*: as Job 15:28. The city shall be ruined. So Ps. 79:1. See Isa. 25:2. & 37:26.

*{a den of dragons}* As they made God's house a den of robbers, ch. 7:11. Heb. *an habitation*, or, *dwelling place*: as Ps. 90:1. and so it is rendered, ch. 51:37. where the same things are said of Babylon. See Isa. 34:13. ch. 10:22.

*{and I will make the cities of Judah desolate, without an inhabitant}* Heb. *the cities of Judah I will give*, (or, *make*, as before) *desolation*; that is, *utterly desolate*. So ch. 4:27. & 10:22.

*{without inhabitant}* Or, as some, *because there is no inhabitant*. So ch. 4:7. See v. 10.

**Verse 12.** *{Who is the wise man that may understand this; and who is he to whom the mouth of the LORD hath spoken, that he may declare it?}* The prophet having related the dreadful devastation that the whole land should undergo, does now incite men to consider seriously with themselves, what might be the procuring causes of so great and grievous evils.

*{who is the wise man that may understand this}* Heb. *Who the man the wise, and he will understand this*: but the copulative is oft used in a finitive notion, as before, vv. 1, 10. as if he had said, Is there never a wise man among you, who vaunt so much of your wisdom, ch. 8:8. to understand and take notice of the procuring causes of these evils? See the like, Ps. 107:43. Hos. 14:9.

*{and who is he to whom the mouth of the LORD hath spoken, that he may declare it?}* Or, *or*; (as ch. 5:12.) *to whom the mouth of the Lord hath spoken*. Heb. *whom the mouth of the Lord hath spoken to him* (as Ps. 1:4.) *and he will tell it*; as before: or, if there be none so wise among you, that is able of himself to conceive it, is there never a prophet among all those with you, that profess themselves to be such, ch. 2:7, 16, 18. whom God has acquainted with his mind herein, that he may, from him, at least make it known to you?

*{for what the land perisheth, and is burnt up like a wilderness that none passeth through?}* Or, *wherefore is the land perished?* See verse 10. ch. 2:6.

**Verse 13.** *{And the LORD saith;}* Or, *Therefore saith the Lord*: the copulative, for the causal; as ch. 6:11. & 7:16, 28. if there be none among you, that can tell wherefore all this comes upon you, God himself, by me, will inform you of the cause of it: so ch. 5:19. & 16:10, 11. & 22:8, 9.

*{Because they have forsaken my law, which I set before them, and have not obeyed my voice, neither walked therein;}* Or, *Because they have left my law, which I set* (Heb. *gave*; as Dan. 9:10.) *before them*, (see ch. 26:4.) *and have not hearkened to my voice* (as ch. 3:25.) *nor walked therein*; to wit, in, or according to my law; for to that it has reference: see Dan. 9:10, 11, 14.

**Verse 14.** *{But have walked after the imagination of their own heart.}* Heb. *And* (as verse 3.) see ch. 7:24. & 15:8. so 2 Pet. 3:3.

*{their own heart}* As, *their own face*, ch. 7:19. and, *their own way*, ch. 4:18.

*{and after Baalim}* See ch. 2:23.

*{which their fathers taught them.}* Or, *as* (Lev. 7:26. ch. 48:8.) *their fathers taught them*, or *accustomed them*; as v. 5. training them up in such idolatrous practices, as themselves exercised: see ch. 7:18. 1 Pet. 1:18.

**Verse 15.** *{Therefore thus saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel,}* God pursues still his answer to the former demand. The same style, see ch. 7:21.

*{Behold, I will feed them, even this people, with wormwood, and give them the water of gall to drink.}* Heb. *Behold, I am feeding*, (that is, *about to feed*; as ch. 8:17.) *them, this people*; as Exod. 2:6. *and she saw him, the child*, ch. 27:7. *that shall not serve him, Nebuchadnezzar*; pronoun and noun both together, for the more emphasis; and our version therefore well inserts, *even*.

*{with wormwood}* That the word here used, is the name of some herb or plant, is not doubted: and it seems to appear by Deut. 29:18. but what herb it should be, the Jewish doctors themselves seem as uncertain as we: it is a kind of herb, says one; a bitter herb, says another: and that not unlikely, by the allusion in likelihood to that place of Moses, Acts 8:23. & Heb. 12:15. and more evidently by Prov. 5:4. and therefore *wormwood*, say some, because *bitter*, Rev. 8:11. but a third adds, that it is a plant, or *simple* (so I render the word *sam*, because larger than our *spice*) not of life, but of death; that is, not vital, or wholesome, but mortal, hurtful even to death, a deadly poison, as well as the other here joined with it: which epithet the Chaldee also in that place of Moses gives it; and then surely not *wormwood*: for that is no unwholesome, or hurtful, though nothing toothsome or pleasant, much less a venomous or poisonful plant; as this is acknowledged to be: and may well be deemed to have its name, as an *accursed* herb, or plant, from the Arabic word, that signifies *to curse*. Said to be used in that version, Gen. 3:17. & 12:3. Mark 11:21. and I suppose therefore the text might better be rendered; *I will feed them with wolfsbane, and drench them with water*, or, *juice of hemlock*: or using the names of some other like poisonful plants; for *water of gall*, seems no fit phrase: but of this latter, see before on ch. 8:14. they are both joined together, as here, so Deut. 29:18. ch. 23:15. Lam. 3:19. Amos 6:12. but this apart without that, Amos 5:7. & Lam. 3:19. where this people complain, that God had given them to drink such a quantity of it, that they were even drunk withal; so that the same thing is mentioned as their meat here; as their drink there: and the meaning is, that God would bring such grievous afflictions upon them, that should put them to such torture and torment, as rank poisons would do, had they no other thing either to eat or drink but such.

**Verse 16.** *{I will scatter them also among the heathen, whom neither they nor their fathers have known;}* That which God by Moses had long before threatened them. Deut. 28:64. See ch. 15:4, 7.

*{and I will send a sword after them, till I have consumed them.}* So Lev. 26:33, 38, 39. See ch. 42:16. and 43:11. and 44:12, 27.

**Verse 17.** *{Thus saith the LORD of hosts;}* Because this people were so strongly possessed with a spirit of security, which their false prophets confirmed them in, pronouncing them assured peace and safety, that they little regarded the prophet's doleful lamentations, as of one, whom they conceived to be but either a mad or a melancholic man. ch. 5:12, 13. The prophet now tells them, that God himself did invite them unto solemn lamentation, to try whether that would work upon them or no. So Isa. 22:12.

*{Consider ye}* As ch. 2:10. or, *understand*, as Isa. 1:3. either conceive aright what your condition is, and suffer not yourselves any longer to be therein deluded; or consider with yourselves seriously of it: I incline to that rather.

*{and call for the mourning women, that they may come; and send for cunning women that they may come;}* Heb. *call for mourning ones*, (but in the feminine form, as the next also,) *and they will*, or, *shall come; and send for wise ones, and they shall*, or, *will come*; the copulative in a finitive notion, as Isa. 53:2. vv. 1, 2. and *wise*, for *cunning*, or, *skillful*; as Exod. 31:3, 6. Such there were among the Greeks, and Latins, and were for the most part women, by a peculiar term in Latin, called *praeficae*, that professed an art and skill of mourning, and making exquisite lamentation; to which purpose also they were wont to be hired at solemn funerals, where going along with the corpse, they made much more semblance usually of lamentation and wailing, than those did that mourned indeed, and such it seems there were also among this people; such at least as were skillful in composing of doleful poems and ditties, that might raise up and enhance affections of that kind in others. See 2 Chr. 35:25. Job 3:8. Eccl. 12:5. Amos 5:16.

**Verse 18.** *{And let them make haste and take up a wailing for us, that our eyes may run down with tears, and our eyelids gush out with waters.}* These words would thus rather be knit to the former, *that they may come, and take up speedily a wailing for us*; the syntax, as before, v. 17. *to haste and take up*; for *to take up hastily*, or, *speedily*; as, *to haste and come*, for, *to come hastily*, 1 Sam. 4:14. *to haste and take*; for, *to take speedily*, without delay, Est. 6:10. *to haste and forget*, for, *eftsoon to forget*, Ps. 106:13.

*{that our eyes may run down with tears}* Heb. *and* (as before) *our eyes shall descend with tears*. So v. 1. ch. 14:17.

*{gush out}* Or, *flow down*; as showers from the sky, Job 36:28. Isa. 45:8. or, as streams from a spring, Ps. 78:16. Isa. 48:21. See verse 1.

*{with waters}* Or, *with water*, as v. 1. a defect of the particle, *with*, both here and before, as Isa. 61:8.

**Verse 19.** *{For a voice of wailing is heard out of Zion; How are we spoiled!}* Or, as some render it, *will be heard out of Zion*: that is, out of Jerusalem. Yet the present tense may be retained, it being as sure to be heard, as if heard at present, and as sounding in the prophet's ears already, as ch. 4:19, 20. & 6:24. & 8:16, 19.

*{we are greatly confounded, because we have forsaken the land, because our dwellings have cast us out.}* We are at our wits' end; because we are compelled to leave our land, (see Isa. 2:11, 12. & 6:12.) and are violently cast out of our dwellings. See Job 15:33, 34. Deut. 29:28. but the form of speech is very pregnant; *our dwellings* themselves *cast us out*; as being weary of us for our impurities, and even spewing us out, Lev. 18:18. & 20:22. the speech of the people, either enforced to retire to Jerusalem, abandoning the places of their former abode, or of those of Jerusalem, expecting ere long, to undergo the like. A defect of the pronoun; as Isa. 37:4. Howbeit, some of the Jewish commenters, whom some of ours also follow, read the words, *they* (that is, the enemy) *have cast down our dwellings*, to the ground: as Ezek. 19:12. and then no supply needed.

**Verse 20.** *{Yet hear the word of the LORD, O ye women; and let your ear receive the word of his mouth;}* Or, *For hear*, etc. because it is a further confirmation of what was before said, v. 17. that God himself invites them to it, and enjoins it. See the like exhortation, Isa. 32:9, 11. and the phrase, Job 4:12. if you regard not what I say, yet weigh well, and take to heart what God says.

*{ye women}* Because affections of this kind more rise and flee usually with that sex; in such calamities and distresses especially; as being less able to shift for themselves. See on Isa. 32:9.

*{and teach your daughters wailing,}* Learn them beforehand some doleful ditties, that may express your grief, and affect others also with it.

*{and every one her neighbour lamentation.}* Heb. *and a woman her friend*, or, *familiar*; that is, *one teach another*: as Gen. 11:2. Isa. 34:15, 16. a supply of the verb from the former branch; as Gen. 1:16. Implying, that so great should be the calamity, and such cause of mourning on all hands, that no lamentation might seem sufficient. See Amos 5:16. Lam. 1:12. & 2:13.

*{a lamentation}* As ch. 7:29. v. 10. from this is Cain deemed, by some, to have had his name; but his mother's words seem to carry it another way, Gen. 4:1.

**Verse 21.** *{For death is come up into our windows; and is entered into our palaces; to cut off the children from without, and the young men from the streets.}* Destruction creeps in so on every side of us, that there is no possibility to avoid it; as Ezek. 21:14. *it entereth into our privy chambers*, or, *closets*: nor can our strongest places keep it out, ch. 6:5. & 17:25. Lam. 2:5. an allusion, as some, to an enemy scaling, and surprising a city, 2 Sam. 5:8. ch. 5:10. as others, to the stones and fire-works, that by engines were thrown into the city. See ch. 6:6. as others again, to the heaps and piles of dead bodies reaching up to the very windows, and the enemy by them climbing up to them. See ch. 33:5. others, to thieves, that break in, or steal in, at windows, Joel 2:9. John 10:1. and these would have it to imply, not so much the unavoidableness, as the suddenness, and unexpectedness of it; for in great and high buildings, say they, the doors commonly in the nighttime are shut, but the windows are left open, there being no fear of danger by them, in regard of their height. But the former is more probable, and seems to allude to a city taken by assault.

*{to cut off the children from without, and the young men from the streets}* Or, *it proceedeth to cut off the children without, and the young men out of the streets*: so that there is no safety for any, either without doors, or within. See 2 Chr. 15:5. Lam. 4:18, 19. nor regard of any age, see ch. 6:11. Some such word must of necessity be supplied to make the sense full: for to say, that it enters in by the windows into the great houses, to cut off them in the streets, seems not to sound so well; *children from without*: whither they are wont to run and steal out, and where wont to play together, Zech. 8:10. and *young men from the streets*: where they are wont to meet together, not desirous, or enduring commonly to be cooped up much in the house, ch. 6:11. & 49:26. both words here used are of the same notion, and signify *streets*; though the former seem the more general. See ch. 5:1.

**Verse 22.** *{Speak, Thus saith the LORD;}* I conceive with some learned interpreters, that these words are to be read by way of parenthesis; and those that follow, to be thus knit unto the foregoing sentence: *it proceedeth to cut off the children from without doors and the young men out of the streets; (Speak it, the Lord so saith*, or, *it is the Lord's saying) and men's carcasses shall lie as dung upon the open field.*

*{even the carcasses of men}* Heb. *and* (which need not be inserted) *man's corpse*, or, *the carcass of man*: but both taken collectively; as ch. 7:33.

*{shall fall as dung}* Or, *shall fall* (that is, *be slain*; as ch. 6:15. & 44:12.) *and lie* (a double notion in the same term: as Isa. 14:24.) *as dung*. See ch. 8:2. there is an elegant consonancy in the original, between the noun *carcass*, and the word *fall*: as the like is also in Greek.

*{upon the open field}* Heb. *on the face*, or *surface, of the field*, as 2 Kings 9:37.

*{and as the handful after the harvestman}* Or, *as the sheaf* (as Amos 2:13.) *from after*, or, *behind the reaper*: which the hired reaper, either forgetting, or not regarding, lets lie, and leaves behind him. See Ruth 2:7.

*{and none shall gather them.}* Or, *where there is none to gather*, or, *take it up*, (so, *and they shall serve*, for, *where they shall serve*, Gen. 15:13.) as having relation to the sheaf let fall, or left behind. Heb. *and no gatherer*; the meaning is, none to afford them sepulture, Ps. 79:5.

**Verse 23.** *{Thus saith the LORD, Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither let the mighty man glory in his might, nor the rich man glory in his riches.}* God by the prophet here labors, to beat them off from those vain confidences, either in public, or private stays and shelters, whereby they made account sufficiently, to secure themselves against those evils, that the prophets of God threatened them with. For the public, they made account they had many wise counselors, and politic men, to manage as well military, as civil affairs, ch. 8:8. and store of warriors, and men of valor, to execute great matters; and they wanted not treasure if need were, to hire forces with from abroad, and so be well enough able to withstand the Chaldeans, if they should come in upon them, Isa. 30:6. ch. 37:5. Again, many among them made account if it came to the worst, yet they should shift well enough, either by their shifts and sleights, or by their might, or by their money, wherewith they might ransom themselves, Ps. 49:6. & 52:7. Prov. 10:15. & 13:8. & 18:11. Isa. 28:15. & 30:2. & 31:1. But God here assures them, that it is in vain to glory in, or rely upon any of these, power, policy, or wealth, for not any of these should avail, to deliver them from death or captivity, when God should bring the judgment now denounced upon them, Ps. 33:16, 17. Prov. 11:4. Eccl. 9:11. Isa. 28:17. & 30:3. & 31:2, 3. Ezek. 7:19. Amos 2:14, 16.

**Verse 24.** *{But let him that glorieth, glory in this, that he understandeth and knoweth me, that I am the LORD that executeth kindness, judgment, and righteousness in the earth}* If they will glory in ought, or rely on ought, let it be in, and on me, who alone am able to save and secure them, Ps. 20:7, 8. Isa. 43:11. & 45:25. & 63:1. 1 Cor. 1:31. 2 Cor. 1:9, 10. & 10:17. and in the sound and saving knowledge of me, (whom this people refuse to know, to their own ruin, vv. 3, 6. Hos. 4:6.) and of my goodness and faithfulness, to those that do sincerely rely on me, which will be the only means to secure them, Ps. 9:10. & 32:10. & 34:22. & 37:40.

*{understandeth and knoweth me}* The Jewish doctor thus distinguishes these two, that the former signifies an intellectual or contemplative knowledge, by which we conceive aright of the nature of God, his attributes, and his works; the latter an active or practical knowledge, whereby men do so know him, that they imitate him in heart and life, and live according to his law; whether the words are so to be distinguished, I much doubt, yet make no question but that the conjunction of these two words together, as if it were said, *in knowing me skillfully or understandingly*, (for that I conceive to be the true sense of the phrase, *in understanding and knowing me*) does intimate such a sound and solid knowledge of God, as does not float in the brain, but sinks down into the heart, and so works upon the affections, that it works them unto God and his will, the efficacy whereof appears, and is expressed in the life; all other knowledge of God being but knowledge falsely so termed, and no true or sound knowledge at all, 1 Tim. 6:20. 1 John 1:6. & 2:4.

*{that execute kindness, judgment and righteousness}* Heb. *that do*, or, *doing*, (as Exod. 20:6. ch. 32:18.) *kindness*, (and goodness, in favors and blessings exhibited to the godly, Ps. 5:12. & 25:10. & 103:17, 18.) *judgment*, (which he executes upon the obstinate wicked; and *righteousness*, (whereby he maintains and defends the faithful, Isa. 1:27. & 51:4, 5.) or, *goodness* in general, whereby he deals kindly with all that reject not him, and his *kindness*; *uprightly* and equally with all in general, Ps. 92:15. & 97:2. & 99:4. & 105:8, 9. for so *judgment* and *justice* are usually taken where they are thus coupled together. See Isa. 56:1. ch. 5:1. and in this sense rather do I take the words here for that which follows.

*{for in these things I delight; saith the LORD,}* Both in doing them myself, and in seeing them done by others, Ps. 5:4. and 11:5, 7. & 15:1, 2. & 24:3, 5. & 99:4. Isa. 33:15, 16. & 61:8. Mic. 6:8. & 7:18.

**Verse 25.** *{Behold the days come saith the LORD, that I will punish all them that are circumcised with the uncircumcised,}* The Lord here endeavors to take this people off from another privilege, which they relied much upon; as formerly from the *temple*, ch. 7:4. and their *temple-service*, ch. 7:21. so here, from their *circumcision*, whereby as the genuine seed of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, (with whom, and their posterity in that line, the covenant, whereof *circumcision* the sign and seal, Rom. 4:11. was continued) they were distinguished from other nations that were without it; and this prerogative they stood not a little upon, and presumed much on it, Gen. 34:14. Acts 11:2, 3. Rom. 3:1. Eph. 2:11. Phil. 3:3, 5, 9. Now this the Lord, to take them off, as a sorry stay for them to trust to, tells them here, that he intends very shortly and suddenly, to hold a visitation, wherein he will proceed against wicked persons and people, as well circumcised as uncircumcised, without any regard had to that external rite, promiscuously and impartially one with another. See Rom. 2:25, 27. Phil. 3:3. Heb. *the days are coming*, (as ch. 7:32.) *and* (as ch. 3:9.) *I will visit upon* (as ch. 5:9. & 21:14.) *circumcision with uncircumcision*: as Rom. 2:26, 27. Gal. 2:7, 9. For the Jewish Talmudists are here most absurd, expounding it of such as having been formerly circumcised, to renounce their circumcision, drew on again their foreskin: (of which practice, see 1 Cor. 7:18.) as, say they did *Ismael*, and hence the corner ones here; *Esau*, and thence here the Edomites; the issue of Lot, whence the *Moabites* and *Ammonites* here; the *Egyptians*, that had in Joseph's days received circumcision, but after his decease, abandoned it again; and *Jehoiakim* king of Judah, to please the king of Babel. But these are no other than their own groundless fictions and fables; the meaning of the text is plain enough, God himself by the prophet, explaining it in the words next ensuing.

**Verse 26.** *{Egypt, and Judah, and Edom, and the children of Ammon, and Moab, and all that are in the utmost corners, that dwell in the wilderness.}* He seems to begin with the Egyptians, because this people relied much upon them, Ezek. 29:6, 7, 16. and to them in the next place he subjoins the Jews, reckoning them up without distinction, among the nations uncircumcised, the reason whereof is afterwards given. And concerning those here mentioned, there is no great doubt or difficulty, save only about the last, described not by any peculiar name, but by some remarkable circumstance, and the place of their abode; that they are of the Kedarens, and the kingdom of Hazor, seems to appear from ch. 49:28, 32. but why so styled, as both here and there, that is the question; the Hebrew is, word for word; *cut off to the corner*, or, *polled by the corner*, which the Jewish commenters expound, of the country they lived in, as if the meaning were, that they lived as *cut off* from other people, in the utmost *nooks*, and remotest parts of the wilderness. But the Chaldee, ancient Greek, and old Latin expound it, of the manner of their cutting of their hair off, by the *corners*, or sides of the temples, which was the manner of some people, but forbidden God's people; and which Herodotus, *lib. 3.* affirms to have been the Arabian fashion; and this seems the more likely; the place of their habitation *in the wilderness*; to wit, in part of Arabia the desert, is noted apart here: now that these several people were by Nebuchadnezzar to suffer, together with the Jews, appears plainly by that other prophecy, where they are related with others added unto them, ch. 25:18, 19, 21, 23, 24.

*{for all these nations are uncircumcised, and all the house of Israel are uncircumcised in the heart.}* Or, *in heart*; as Ezek. 44:7. for the article is superfluous here, nor is in the text. In these words God renders a reason, why he ranked the Jews among the uncircumcised ones; to wit, because they were such in heart, as the other were in their flesh; whence it appears, that the Edomites, though descended from Isaac by Esau, who was doubtless circumcised as well as Jacob, had abandoned the use of this rite, which yet Hyrcanus in the times of the Maccabees, enforced them to resume. See Joseph's *antiquities, l. 13. c. 17.* for *these nations*, says he, are *all uncircumcised*; though that no way either backs that Talmudic fancy concerning the sense of this place, or adds force to their figments, which they fabulously adjoin concerning some others. But hence it appears that the generality of Isaac's posterity were at that present uncircumcised, either in the one kind, or in the other: his whole issue by Esau having cast off the outward circumcision; and the main body of Jacob's posterity, then in being, (*the whole house of Israel*, as well Judah, as the other ten tribes) wanting the inward circumcision of the heart; without which, the outward rite in the flesh is of no force or worth in God's account. See ch. 4:4. Amos 9:7. Rom. 2:28, 26. Gal. 5:6. & 6:15.

## CHAPTER 10

**Verse 1.** *{Hear ye the word which the LORD speaketh to you, O house of Israel.}* The Lord by the prophet in the former part of this chapter, (for the latter is of a far diverse subject) dissuades and dehorts this people from attending to, or at all regarding those heathenish practices of astrology and idolatry: for he couples them both together, vv. 1, 16. and this former part, as to me seems, principally concerns those of the former captivity, under Jeconiah, who already were in Babylon; the latter, those that remained yet in the land under Zedekiah. See ch. 24.

*{Hear ye the word}* The like entrance, see ch. 7:2. Amos 3:1.

*{which the LORD speaketh}* Not I, but the Lord, Isa. 1:2. 1 Cor. 7:10.

*{O house of Israel}* As ch. 2:26.

**Verse 2.** *{Thus saith the LORD, learn not the way of the heathen}* Because the Jewish people, were a great part of them to go in captivity into Babylon, and other the regions adjacent, yea, many of them in likelihood were there in captivity already, (see verse 11. ch. 24:1. & 29:1, 2.) God by the prophet endeavors to confirm and strengthen them, the pious especially among them, (for such also there were there of them, ch. 24:5. Ezek. 11:16.) against those superstitions and vanities that were rife in those parts; and they might be in danger, being exiles and captives in a strange land, to be strongly tempted unto: Heb. *Learn not to the way*: where either the particle is superfluous, omitted therefore, Ps. 106:35. ch. 12:16. or else it may be rendered, *Accustom not yourselves to the way of the heathen*; and so some render it; *do not imitate them*, see ch. 9:5. their *way*; that is, their superstitious courses, Lev. 18:3. & 20:23.

*{and be not dismayed at the signs of heaven}* The first head of superstitions, which he begins with, is *astrology*, a study and practice so rife among them in those parts, Isa. 47:13. that the professors and practicers of it, not with them alone, Dan. 2:2. & 5:7. but among other nations also, are generally designed by the name of *Chaldeans*. See Strabo l. 17. Cicero of *divination* l. 2. Pliny l. 6. c. 26. *Astrology*, I say, not that which we commonly term *astronomy*, whereby the true nature and notion of the celestial bodies are by grounds of reason, and rules of art thence taking their rise, inquired into, and discovered; but that *judiciary astrology*, as it is usually styled, whereby men take upon them, from the postures and aspects of them, to foretell the issue of humane affairs, either public, or private, and what casual events, shall befall either persons or people: a practice grown of late with us into great esteem, being either countenanced or connived at, by those in authority with us, though having entered themselves, and caused others with them, to enter into a religious bond of a solemn *oath* and *covenant*, to endeavor the *extirpation* of all those things among us, that are *contrary to sound doctrine, and the power of godliness*, whereof this is none of the least. For the original whereof, (since it has not, nor can be showed to have any ground from the light of nature, or natural reason) we shall not need to go far to find it out. We have a blind, but insolent, buzzard (I may well so term him) among us, one that professes himself no small doctor in these impostures, and dotages (wherewith he has bewitched not a few with us, esteeming his predictions, as no other than divine oracles) and takes upon him by the stars, to steer the affairs of our state, pretending to *read in the book of heaven*, all that he writes, who will sufficiently inform us herein. Now this man to justify the warrantableness of this his practice, tells us, that *the good angels of God in former ages, at first by personal conference, acquainted the sons of men with this learning of the stars; and those holy men*, (says he) *so instructed, living many years, and in purer airs, where they curiously observed the planets and their motion, brought this art to some maturity, without the least hint of superstition. But as the sons of men fell from God in divine worship, so in flitting and shifting their habitations, they forgot the purer part of this art; and in some countries added superstitious conceptions.* The holy angels then belike by this man's relation, did at first inform those holy men, which they could not otherwise have known, of the nature of the planets; to wit, that *Saturn* was *a melancholic malignant* planet, *Mars, a choleric and litigious* one, *Mercury, a thievish, Venus, a lascivious and wanton* one: and that they do accordingly affect and dispose such people, or persons, as are either bred under them, or whom they have special relation unto. For these, and the like ridiculous fopperies, and impious calumniations of those glorious creatures, are with them, as the Popish *purgatory* with the Papists, the main grounds and principles of their whole art, which being taken away, the whole fabric and frame of their superstitious superstructures, will presently fail and fall flat to the ground; as with those other, all their masses, dirges, obits, pardons, and indulgences, if you deny them their purgatory; which because they can produce no clear Scripture for, they run with these men to their forged revelations. But whence these frivolous conceits, and irreligious surmises concerning those celestial bodies, (which if you question, you shake the ground of all their conjectural skill,) had their original, may well be conjectured from the very names, the heathen imposed upon them, being borrowed from their counterfeit deities, whom they deemed so qualified: assure ourselves we may, that God's holy angels never raised any such foul aspersions and groundless defamations, upon those pure and spotless creatures, far from, and wholly incapable of the tincture of such vicious dispositions. But all that this man relates, we may if we please, and be so silly as so to do, take upon his credit; for he tells us not what times those were, wherein it was thus, or who those holy men were, unto whom the holy angels at first revealed those things; or out of what records he has these relations, concerning such pretended revelations. And as little reason have we, to engage our faith to his antagonist, another fowl of the same feather, that flies yet somewhat higher than he, and pretending *his predictions to be grounded on art and nature*, tells us (that we may not misdoubt or question his art) that *this art was deduced from God to Adam, to Seth, to Abraham*; for proof whereof, he refers this to a knight of note, for his studies in this kind; who in favor indeed of this art, which he was overmuch addicted to, and besotted with, affirms in part what he says, but bringing no better proof of it, than a tale of Joseph the Jew, who in his *Antiquities l. 1. c. 3.* tells us, that *those of Seth's issue living long and without disturbance, gave themselves to the study of heavenly things, and the constitution or administration of them; and because Adam had foretold a twofold destruction of the world that should come, the one by water, the other by fire; they left the sum of what they had, of that kind of learning observed, engraven on two pillars of brick the one, of stone the other*: but neither is any word in the Jew of this their *judicial astrology*, nor of any skill in this kind, or any other by God imparted unto Adam, which they yet father upon him: and the whole relation of the *two pillars* seems as true, as that which he adds of the continuance of the latter of them in Syria unto his time. And indeed, if any sons of Adam ever had any such immediate communion, either with God himself, or his holy angels, it must be those ancient patriarchs, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and those prophets of God among his people unto whom God used sometime immediately, sometime by the ministry of angels, to impart his mind, concerning future events, as well public, as private: but nowhere in Scripture read we, that God did this, either by the natural course of the celestial signs, or, as from thence to be observed; nor undoubtedly had any such art and skill, been taught the godly ones among God's people, whether by God himself, or his angels; would they either have concealed it from them, or much less committed it unto Paynims, and pagans, and by such, have transmitted it unto posterity; for from such in corrupt times, it crept in among Christians, being yet ever among them liable to censure; nor was any in the ancient church, that had professed such arts, admitted into the profession of Christianity, unless that first they renounced those damnable practices, and recanted such their superstitious conceits. But men may easily guess what angels they were, that acquainted men at first with these things, and set them on work to busy their brains about such matters, as neither light of nature, nor grounds of reason, were able to inform them of, but must have some revelation; either divine, or angelical, or diabolical rather, for the finding of them out. So far are God himself and his prophets from taking notice hereof, as some such heavenly discovery, or giving any approbation thereunto, that God by them sometime derides it, Isa. 44:25. and 47:13. and sometime dissuades and condemns it, as a heathenish practice, not befitting his people to heed; as here, so elsewhere, Deut. 18:10, 14. From the prince of the air therefore, it may justly by this man's own grounds and grants, be deemed to have proceeded; at first by him taught the heathen that were ruled and swayed by him; and from them, together with the worship of them in their idols, conveyed unto God's own people. For what of further observation he subjoins; to omit, that those ridiculous principles must first be made good, ere any observation can be grounded upon them: the like did the heathen magicians report of their charms, and other superstitious divinations by the flight of fowls, and from the bowels of beasts; to wit, that observations had been made of them, for many hundreds of years. See Pliny l. 28. c. 2. and this and those may well go together, one with the other, unto him, that was the first founder of them, *the father of lies*, John 8:44.

*{and be not dismayed at the signs of heaven}* As if the event of things, or the issue of your affairs depended upon them; which those fond *stargazers* bare people in hand, and took upon them thereby to determine and foretell, what good or bad success men's designs should have, Isa. 47:12, 13. Howbeit, *signs* there are of two sorts; first, natural, and ordinary, the stars themselves being set in the skies, to distinguish the times and seasons of the year; to which may be added, the conjunctions of them one with another, or oppositions of them one to another, whence the eclipses of some of them, at sometime do proceed; and these are those signs, which coming in a constant course, and continued tenor, (in regard whereof men skillful therein, are able either going backward, to tell how it has been with them for thousands of years past, or looking forward how it will be for as many, if the world itself should so long continue:) God would not have his people to be affected or affrighted with, as if in regard of them, or from them, any evil in the success of their affairs could betide them: other *signs* there are extraordinary, in dreadful apparitions, besides the ordinary course of the creature, by which the Lord does sometime give notice unto his people, of his displeasure, and warning of ensuing wrath; and these God does not inhibit his people to be affected with, and taking of them unto heart. See Joel 2:30, 31. Luke 21:11, 25.

*{for the heathen are dismayed at them}* Or, rather, *though the heathen be dismayed at them*. Though they be so silly or superstitious, as to be therewith thus affected, yet ought you not so to be. So is the particle very frequently used, in our versions also not seldom expressed, Gen. 8:21. Josh. 17:18. Ps. 23:4. Isa. 12:1. Dan. 9:9. Mic. 7:8. Hab. 3:17.

**Verse 3.** *{For the customs of the people are vain}* Heb. *The statutes*, or, *ordinances of the people* (that is, the courses of this nature, which people of several countries herein concurring do, as if it were some sacred or divine ordinance, very precisely and superstitiously observe) *vanity itself*; i.e. *are each of them exceeding vain*, as vain as vanity itself; and a matter therefore very ill-beseeming such as profess themselves to be God's people, as did the Jews then, and as Christians at this day do, to be taken and carried away, with such frivolous and ridiculous fancies and fopperies: the pronoun, for the verb substantive, as ch. 6:16, 28. the abstract, for the concrete, as verse 15. Eccl. 11:8, 10. and the singular distributively joined with the plural, as ch. 5:8.

*{For one cutteth a tree out of the forest (the work of the hands of the workman) with the axe.}* From their astrology, he passes to their idolatry; and these two, say some, he joins together, because those Eastern people had a conceit, that the images of those celestial bodies which they worshipped, had a secret efficacy conveyed unto them from those celestial bodies, whom by them they adored. But the connexion to me, seems to be apparent from the context itself: you must not be afraid of the signs of the heavens, though heathen so be, for their courses are full of folly and vanity; and that they are so, does further appear by their idols, which though they either made themselves, or caused to be made by some other, yet they worship and stand in awe of. The words would rather be read without any parenthesis, *A tree is cut down out of the forest, for the work of the hands of the carpenter*, or, *carver, with the axe*; that is, for the carpenter to exercise his handiwork on it with the axe; for the *axe* here seems not to be mentioned, as the instrument of felling the tree, but of framing the image out of the wood, or timber of it. So that here the sorriness and baseness of their images is intimated, by the matter of it, a piece of wood; the maker of it, a poor man that works upon it for his penny, and the instrument wherewith he frames it, *his axe*. See the like, Isa. 40:20. & 44:12, 17. Heb. *a tree cutteth he out of the forest*; the verb used indefinitely, and most fitly therefore expressed by the passive: as, *he planteth an ash*; for, *an ash is planted*, Isa. 44:14. the pronoun redundant, as Isa. 8:13. & 45:9. the particle *for* supplied, as v. 9. Mal. 2:5. of the word rendered *workman*, see on Isa. 40:20. of *axe*, Isa. 44:12.

**Verse 4.** *{They deck it with silver and with gold}* Or, *It is decked*: the verb being taken indefinitely, as verse 3. Heb. *make it fair*, or *beautiful*: to add some grace to it, having no beauty otherwise of itself, but what by such means they give it, see Isaiah 40:19. and 46:6.

*{they fasten it with nails and with hammers, that it move not}* Or, *it is fastened with nails and with hammers*, as before; that is, as some, the joints of it, one to another, that they may not fall asunder; but the image he speaks of, seems carved out of the main trunk or timber of the tree, verse 5. as others, the silver and gold plates to the wooden stock, that they may sit close to it: but he seems here to speak only of such wooden gods, as were only made beautiful, with some leaf-silver and gilt; of others afterward, verse 9. and others therefore rather, to the wall, pillar or post, that it is nailed to, that it may stand fast and not *stagger*, (so the word properly signifies, Isaiah 28:7. Neh. 2:10.) and fall. See Isaiah 40:19. and 41:7. and 46:7. Heb. *and it shall not* (as ch. 9:1, 2.) *stir*, or, *stagger*; as before: goodly gods, about whom so much cost must be used to make them handsome, so much care must be taken, as with children to keep them from a fall.

**Verse 5.** *{They are upright as the palm tree, but speak not}* They stand bolt upright like a palm, or a pillar, and cannot move or bend; or they stand upright, as one that stands up to speak, but are not able to utter ought, Ps. 115:5. & 135:16.

*{They are upright}* Heb. *They are firm work*, or, *massy matter*, carved out without joints, as works of massy metal beaten out of a main piece. So the word is commonly taken, Exod. 25:18, 31, 36. the pronoun for the verb substantive, as verse 3.

*{as a palm tree}* That grows straight and even up to the top, without knots or boughs, scaled only, and the flaggy leaves, which are the only branches of it; at the top of the trunk, or, *as a pillar*; for so the word also is used, Cant. 3:6.

*{they must needs be borne, because they cannot go}* Heb. *bearing borne they shall be*; or, *carrying they are carried*; which some understand, of their carrying them about in their solemn processions, either in chariots, or on men's shoulders: but it may be understood more generally, of bearing them from place to place; either at the first seating of them, or upon any occasional removal. See Isa. 45:20. & 46:1, 7.

*{because they cannot go}* Ps. 115:7. much less help, or hurt.

*{be not afraid of them}* No more than of the signs of heaven; though these sottish people fear as well these, as those, v. 1.

*{for they cannot do evil, neither also is it in them to do good.}* Heb. *they will not*, or, *shall not, do evil*; but the verb is taken potentially, as ch. 2:23, 32. See Isa. 41:23.

**Verse 6.** *{Forasmuch as there is none like unto thee, O LORD, thou art great, and thy name is great in might}* Unto these vain and base idols, the prophet opposes the true God, (whom he turns his speech unto) as indeed in regard of his incomparable might and majesty, alone worthy of all fear and dread, Ps. 86:8, 10. & 89:7, 8. & 145:3. Heb. *from none being like thee*; the particle in a causal notion, as ch. 4:6. That which some suppose to have reference unto what went before, v. 5. concerning the inability of idols, to do good or evil; because not like to the true God: but others rather to what follows, verse 7. concerning reverence and due regard to be given unto the true God; as showing the cause, why he ought to be so reverenced and regarded.

**Verse 7.** *{Who would not fear thee, O king of nations?}* These words make up an entire sentence with those of the former verse: and might therefore not unfitly be annexed unto them. Of the title therein given unto God, together with the ground of it. See Mal. 1:14. Rev. 15:4. Ps. 47:7. and 103:19.

*{for to thee doth it appertain}* Or, *since that* (as ch. 8:14.) *it agreeth to thee*; as Gen. 34:15, 22. *fear* and *reverence* sorts and suits well with you, not with them; the noun supplied from the verb foregoing, Ps. 76:7, 11. & 89:7. or, as some; *the kingdom*, implied in the word, *king*, 1 Chr. 29:11, 12. Matt. 6:13. but the former rather, this being the cause of that.

*{forasmuch as among all the wise men of the nations, and among all their kingdoms, there is none like unto thee}* Heb. *for in all the wise of the nations, and in all their kingdoms, because none being like unto thee*: the particle in a causal notion, as before, verse 6. and there is a twofold particle; either the one being redundant, but added for the more emphasis, or some supply to be made, as some conceive, rendering it; *for among all the wise of the nations, and in all their kingdoms*, you are great, or the greatest; *because there is none like unto thee*: and he mentions the *wise* ones and the *kings*, says the rabbin, because the wiser sort among the heathen knew well enough, that there was but one supreme power, and if they worshipped any other, it was but as mediators between him and them; and that no kingdom was perpetual, but God's alone: and *kings* that conversed with, or made use of such, knew as much also, Dan. 4:3, 32, 37. But I concur rather with those, who conceive these two to be mentioned, the rank of *wise*, and of *royal*, (for it is *kingdom*, not *kingdoms*) because of these two sorts the heathen used to deify after their death; some for their wisdom, some for their royalty. See Isaiah 46:1. ch. 50:2. among either of which, either for wisdom or prowess, there is none comparable to God, 1 Sam. 2:2. Ps. 18:31. 1 Cor. 1:25. 1 Tim. 1:17. & 6:15. And to cut off these difficulties for matter of syntax, I suppose the words may well thus be rendered, *even among all the wise of the nations, and all their royalty, because there is none like unto thee*: the first particle being taken not as a causal, but as a note of asseveration, or amplification, as the same is apparently found so used, Isa. 32:13. *kingdom*, or, *royalty*, for, *kings*: as, *government*, for, *governors*, Isa. 60:17.

**Verse 8.** *{But they are altogether brutish and foolish:}* Heb. *And* (as ch. 9:13, 14.) *in one they are brutish and foolish*. Which the Jewish commenters expound with reference to the wise men mentioned verse 7. that though in other things they were wise, as in acknowledging one supreme power; yet herein they dealt foolishly, in teaching the people to worship stocks and stones, Rom. 1:21, 23. But this exposition narrows the text too much: our version renders it, *altogether*; and a form somewhat like it, is used for, *together*, Ezra 2:64. & 3:9. and would so be rendered Ps. 82:7. but the word *one*, is there masculine; here, feminine: nor is the particle the same. I suppose it may well be rendered, *at once*: and so it is rendered, though, as I conceive, not aright, Prov. 28:18. but so the very same form is used in the Greek, Luke 14:18. which will come well home to what our version exhibits: for it is as if he had said, not of some special ones, but of all idolaters in general; as verse 14. (unto whom with their folly, and brutish stupidity, he now returns again) Take them all *at once*, or *altogether*; they are even as brutish and senseless, as those very stocks and stones they worship, Ps. 115:8. & 135:18. See Isa. 41:29. & 44:18, 20.

*{the stock is a doctrine of vanities.}* Either that which the idols teach, is nothing but mere vanity and falsehood; as they are said to be *teachers of lies*, Hab. 2:18. Zech. 10:2. (and images then surely ill laymen's books) or those things, that are taught and received, or believed concerning them, are most vain things, as the idols themselves are, verses 3, 14. See Isa. 44:10, 20. Heb. word for word; *an instruction of vanities, wood it is*: the pronoun positive for the verb substantive; as v. 3. for all the cost bestowed upon it, and pains taken about it, it is but a piece of *wood*, or a stock still. See Isa. 10:15. & 44:15, 17.

**Verse 9.** *{Silver spread into plates is brought from Tarshish, and gold from Uphaz, the work of the workman, and of the hands of the founder.}* He comes in this passage to the better and richer sort of their idols, and such as were most sumptuously and gorgeously set forth: because with such sottish people are wont to be more taken, than with those sorry ones of wood or stone; and shows, that these also, for all their rich materials and their bravery, were as far from any divine power or efficacy as the former.

*{Silver spread}* Heb. *drawn out*, or, *dilated*: beaten out into plates, Exod. 39:3. Num. 16:13. to cover their images with, that were not all of massy metal. See Isa. 40:19.

*{from Tarshish}* From beyond sea; from the *ocean*; either Eastern, or Western, or, as some, from *Tartessus*, Ezek. 27:12. See on Isa. 2:16. & 23:1.

*{gold from Uphaz}* Where the finest gold seems in those times to have been, Dan. 10:5. this some suppose to be the same with *Paz*, or *Phaz*, Job 28:17. Ps. 21:3. See on Isa. 13:12.

*{the work of the workman}* Or, *for the work of the workman*; as v. 3. for the *carver*, or *carpenter* there; so, for the founder, or goldsmith here, to exercise his art and skill upon: for the word has here reference not to the work done about it formerly, in beating it out into plates, but unto the work further to be done, for the framing of an image out of it. See Isa. 40:19.

*{and of the hands of the founder}* The former word was more general, comprehending any skillful workman, working in wood, stone, or metal; this those that work in the last only, and such properly as exercise their skill thereupon, by casting, melting, and refining with fire, alluded to, Ps. 66:10. Mal. 3:2, 8.

*{blue and purple is their clothing}* With garments of such costly stuff, and gorgeous colors, they were wont to adorn, and set out their idols. See Isa. 30:22. Ezek. 16:17, 18. Hos. 2:3.

*{blue}* Stuff, either silk, linen, or woolen, dyed of that color; which the Jewish doctors of greatest repute say was a *sky color*; yet some of them say it was dyed with a *worm*. Others, with the blood of a fish; and those suppose it to have been *yellow*; these blue. The Greek renders it an *hyacinth*, or *violet* color: whatsoever color it were, it appears that it was much worn by kings, and great personages, Est. 8:15. Ezek. 23:6. and used for hangings in kings' courts, Est. 1:6. it was used also about the furniture of the tabernacle, and the priestly robes, Exod. 25:4. & 26:21. & 28:5, 6. and about the temple, 2 Chr. 2:7, 14.

*{purple}* For the term here rendered *purple*, the rabbins tell us it was a *red* color; and some of them, that it was that which the Arabians call, *kermes*, we *crimson*, whence some gather that this was the foreign name of that which the Hebrews called *tola*, and *tolaat*: whereof, see on Isaiah 1:18. but of this latter conceit, there is no probability; for these two are distinctly mentioned in the work of the tabernacle, where the one is rendered *purple*, and the other *scarlet*, Exod. 25:4. and howsoever it be true, that these two come so near the one to the other, that they seem to be used sometime promiscuously; whence the garment that the soldiers in mockage arrayed our Savior with, is rendered *a scarlet robe*, Matt. 27:28. and *a purple robe*, John 19:3. yet there is no doubt, but that they were two distinct colors, the *scarlet*, or *crimson* dyed of *a grain*, or *a worm*, or both, which in these times we call *cochineal*, (see on Isaiah where before) the *purple* of the *blood*, or *matter* of a shellfish, at this day out of use and unknown. See Pliny in his *natural history, l. 9. c. 35.* Howsoever, that this *purple* was anciently the wear of kings and great persons, appears not by the sacred records alone, Judg. 8:26. Est. 8:15. Luke 16:19. Rev. 17:4. but by the foreign histories of several nations of all ages, ancient and modern. The former and this, are oft joined together in divers of the places above recited, and very frequently in relating the work of the tabernacle, and the priests' vestments.

*{they are all the work of cunning men.}* Heb. *the work of wise ones all they*, or *they all*; *wise*, for, *cunning*, or *skillful*; as ch. 9:17. a defect of the subject, as before, verse 7. and the pronoun for the verb substantive; as vv. 3, 8. Both the idols themselves, and all their furniture, are the workmanship of sorry people, unable to give any deity, or divine power and efficacy unto them, which they have not themselves. See Isa. 37:19.

**Verse 10.** *{But the LORD is the true God}* To this base trash he again opposes Jehovah, the true God, a God of another manner of might and majesty, power and efficacy, than these sorry counterfeits. Heb. *And* (as v. 8.) *Jehovah God truth*; rendered generally, as our version in the margin exhibits it, *a God of truth*; as he is also expressly termed, Ps. 31:5. But it may seem that it should rather be rendered, *Jehovah God*, or *God Jehovah is truth*: for the word *Elohim* here is in an entire, not in a contracted form, the usual form of regiment; and albeit, the entire form be sometime found used instead of the contract, as Ps. 80:7, 19. yet the commanding accent here making a stay at *Elohim*, seems to require the other reading. Howsoever the attribute of truth, in the abstract here ascribed unto God, as to the Word of God, Ps. 119:142. John 17:17. does intimate God to be, not *true* only, but even *truth* itself. Nor do I conceive that this term is here given unto God, as in that place of the Psalm, in regard of his *veracity* and *fidelity*, because he speaks nothing but *truth*; *he cannot lie*, Num. 23:19. 1 Sam. 15:29. Titus 1:2. and *he keepeth his truth for ever*, Ps. 146:6. but in regard of the *verity* and *truth* of his essence; as of our Savior it is said, that he is *true God*, or very God, 1 John 5:20. and so is the phrase used, 2 Chr. 15:3. *the God of truth*, for, *the true God*; that is, no counterfeit one, Phil. 2:6. whereas those idols were all of them but mere counterfeits, having nothing of the nature or essence of God, ch. 16:20. Gal. 4:8. Nor do I mislike therefore the judgment of that learned man, who reads it with supply of the preposition, in it; *Jehovah is God in truth*, or *truly*; as Deut. 13:14. and 17:4. where the word so taken, the copulative shall not need to be inserted.

*{he is the living God}* As Ps. 42:2. both endued with *life* himself, and being the *fountain of life*, Ps. 36:9. from whence all life is in any kind or degree derived unto any: whereas these idols are but dead things, verse 14. and in that regard inferior unto the worst and meanest living creature, wholly destitute of all life themselves, and altogether unable either to impart it in the least and lowest degree unto others, or to maintain and preserve it in others, Isaiah 46:7. as the name of God is here in a plural form, so is the attribute also plural; as the like, Josh. 24:19. and the same, ch. 23:36.

*{and an everlasting king:}* Heb. *a king of eternity*; as, *Father of eternity*, Isa. 9:6. another manner of king than either these idols, whom they call their *kings*: see on ch. 8:19. or their *kings*, that set them up to be worshipped, Dan. 3:1. for these are both of them corruptible creatures; verses 11, 15. Ps. 146:3, 4. they and their kingdoms lie down in the dust together, Isaiah 14:9, 19. Ezek. 32:18, 32. whereas the true God is an eternal king, and his kingdom endures forever, Ps. 93:2. & 103:19. & 146:10. Dan. 4:34. 1 Tim. 6:15, 16.

*{at his wrath the earth shall tremble,}* Or, *trembleth*. His angry look, his frown alone, is able to shake the main body of the earth, Ps. 18:7. & 68:8. & 77:18. & 104:32. & 114:4, 6, 7. Hab. 3:6, 10. Other manner of works, and effects, than their poor puppets were able to produce.

*{and the nations shall not be able to abide his indignation.}* Heb. *shall not sustain*: the verb is so used, ch. 6:11. Amos 7:10. but it is here in a potential notion, as the like, v. 5. All the people of the world being put together, are not able to sustain his wrath, that is, either to withstand his wrath, or to stand before him when he is wroth, Ps. 76:7, 8. Isa. 40:15, 17. Dan. 4:35.

**Verse 11.** *{Thus shall ye say unto them}* Or, *on this wise*. This verse is conceived not in pure Hebrew, but in the Syrian dialect, in which also some other passages and portions, either in, or of the Scriptures of the Old Testament were penned (see Dan. 2:4. Ezra 4:7.) because that was most generally spoken among the Chaldeans, with those especially at Babylon: whence it is observed, that when Cyrus had taken Babylon, he caused it by his heralds to be proclaimed through the whole city in the Syrian tongue, that every man, upon pain of death, should keep within doors, Xenophon, l. 7. In this dialect therefore, is this passage conceived, that they might have it at hand to stop the Chaldeans' mouths in their own language, when they should be enticing of them unto idolatry; for neither did the Chaldeans well understand the pure Hebrew, nor the Jews the Syrian, which both the Assyrians, and the Chaldeans also used. See Isa. 36:11. ch. 5:15. The Chaldee paraphrase seems to intimate, that this should be the sum of a letter, that Jeremy should write and send unto the Jews, that abode in captivity at Babylon; wherein some other control him, and say, That it was written rather beforehand to confirm them against they came thither. And true, indeed, it is, that this is not that epistle that Jeremy is reported to have sent unto Babylon, unto those that with Jehoiachin or Jeconiah, had been carried thither before the reign of Zedekiah, 2 Kings 24:14, 16. See ch. 29. But it may well be, nor is it unlikely, that this prophecy was penned as well for the behoof and use of such as were there already, as for those afterward that were, with Zedekiah, to be brought thither, ch. 52:11, 15. See v. 1.

*{The gods that made not the heavens, and the earth, even they shall perish from the earth, and from under these heavens.}* The peculiar character of the true God, to be creator of heaven and earth, Gen. 1:1. Ps. 146:6. Isa. 37:16. & 44:24. & 48:13. Rev. 10:6. and it is observed, that it was a usual speech among some Greeks that held one supreme deity, *Let him that saith he is God, make another world*; and some of the ancient fathers advise Christians living among Paynims, to say, when they would press any strange god upon them, *Let him make me a world, and he shall be my God.*
