*{the gods}* In the heathen language, as *the gods*, Dan. 2:11. and, *a son of the gods*, Dan. 3:25. ill rendered there, *the Son of God*, whom the heathen king never dreamed of: termed *gods*, because by the heathen so called and accounted, Ps. 96:5. 1 Cor. 8:5, 6.

*{that made not the heavens and the earth}* Or, *the heaven and the earth*; as it is rendered, Gen. 1:1. See Isa. 1:2. the word used for the *earth* in this former branch is nowhere else found in Scripture: and it seems to have been a term of some peculiar dialect in the Syrian language, that used to turn *Ayin* into *Koph*, as the other Syrians did the Hebrew *Tsade* into *Ayin*; from whence the Hebrew word for *earth* in the next clause. Howbeit the Jewish doctors, as one of them here tells us, make it a Hebrew term, to make up four names in Hebrew for the *earth*, very fondly applied by them to the four seasons of the year, the *spring, summer, autumn*, and *winter*; and that here respecting this last.

*{even they shall perish}* These words, *even they*, are neither of them in the text, nor are needful here, unless the pronoun in the close of the verse be fetched in hither, which then must be omitted there. See v. 15. Isa. 2:18.

*{from off the earth}* A diverse word here from that before, deduced from the Hebrew, and of more frequent use in the Syriac, Dan. 2:35, 39. Ezra 5:11. *from off the earth*; as Ps. 21:10.

*{from under these heavens.}* Or, *this heaven*; or, as some, *heaven*, simply: if we read it, *this heaven*, it must be understood, as if they should speak it, pointing up to heaven; as some suppose that our Savior did to his own body, when he said, *this temple*, John 2:19. this heaven, which the true God made, see the like, ch. 7:4. but some of note refer the word, *these*, not to the *heavens*, but to the counterfeit gods, *These shall perish from off the earth, and from out of* the regions *under heaven*; for so they, with some others, supply the text here; as Deut. 9:14.

**Verse 12.** *{He hath made the earth by his power;}* After this admonition, by way of advice, given them, which some interpreters enclose as a parenthesis, he returns again to relate some of those works of the true God, wherein his incomparable might, wisdom, and majesty, most appears. The whole passage contained in this verse, and the next, is found the same, ch. 51:15, 16. The first, is the creation of the earth ascribed to his power. The next, his settling the habitable part of it, ascribed to his wisdom. The third, his constitution of the heavens in a way of wondrous skill. The last, his disposition of wind and rain, with the appurtenances attending either. *He hath made*, Heb. *making*; or, It is he (to wit, the true God, v. 10.) *that made*; as Ps. 146:6. and so in the ensuing branches.

*{the earth}* The main body and bulk of it, Gen. 1:1.

*{by his power}* A work requiring an infinite power to produce a frame of that vast and immense bigness, ch. 31:37. Job 38:4, 6.

*{he hath established the world by his wisdom}* Or, *that hath prepared*, (as the word is rendered, Ps. 147:8.) or, *settled* (as Ps. 65:6.) *the world* (that is, the habitable part of the earth, Ps. 24:1. & 93:1. See Isa. 13:11. & 14:16.) *by his wisdom*. So disposing in most wise manner of it, that there might be a conveniency, and sufficiency of room, for the sons of men, and other land creatures, to dwell upon; that which at first he did by causing the waters to quit a great part of the surface thereof, and retire unto such places as he had assigned them; and afterward, from time to time, as by continual keeping them within the bounds before assigned them, so by framing inlets for them into the land, and disposing of springs and streams, for the several parts thereof, whereby it might become the more useful, both for man and beast, Gen. 1:9. Job 38:8, 11. Ps. 104:6, 11, 34. ch. 5:22.

*{and stretcheth out the heavens by his discretion}* Or, *and that stretched*, or, *spread out the heavens by his understanding*, or *skill*: for so the word properly signifies, Exod. 36:1. Job 12:13. Prov. 21:30. an unconceivable measure of art and skill has the Lord showed, in framing and drawing out that goodly canopy of the sky, so gloriously adorned, and embellished, with unexpressible variety of resplendent lights, over the whole circumference of the earth, Isa. 42:5. & 44:24.

**Verse 13.** *{When he uttereth his voice, there is a multitude of waters in the heavens;}* Heb. *at his giving a voice*, (of which phrase, see on ch. 2:15.) or *at the voice of his giving*; or, *at whose giving out a voice* (the possessive, for the relative, as Isa. 48:2.) That is, say some, at his will, at his pleasure; for his Word is his will, and his will his work, Ps. 105:31. & 119:3. & 135:6. Dan. 4:35. But others rather, when he causes it to thunder, (for that is commonly called *God's voice* in Scripture, Ps. 18:13. & 77:18. Exod. 20:18. and is, indeed, a most majestical voice, Ps. 29:3, 10. & 68:33. which some wretched tyrants have endeavored to imitate, some of the most impious of them have been exceedingly afraid of) abundance of rain usually follows, Job 37:2, 5. or, as some render the words, *there is a noise of waters* (and the word may signify either, see Isa. 63:15.) *in the heaven*, that is, *in the air*; as Ps. 8:8. & 18:11. See 1 Kings 18:41.

*{and he causeth the vapors to ascend from the ends of the earth}* Or, *and that*, or, *who causeth*, etc. a defect of the relative; as ch. 8:13. See the same, Ps. 135:7. ch. 51:19.

*{vapors}* Heb. *elevations*; it is rendered *clouds*, Prov. 25:14. but the Jewish critics tell us, it is more general, comprehending as well dry exhalations, the matter of wind; as moist vapors, the matter of rain.

*{to ascend}* Or, *go up*; because unless they go up, no rain can come down, Gen. 2:5, 6.

*{from the ends of the earth}* Not, as the Jewish doctor, from those remote Northern, and Southern parts, which he conceives not to be inhabited; but from all parts of the earth, especially from the sea at the lands-end, Ps. 72:8. to water the earth, and to feed and maintain the springs, from which the rivers stream, Ps. 104:10, 13. & 147:8. Eccl. 1:7. Howbeit, we need not to render the words therefore with the Jewish critic; *after that he hath made the vapors to go up*: though the copulative seem so used, Lev. 9:22. or with another learned late writer, to read the text, *At* (that is, so soon as he gives out) *his voice*, whereby *to set a multitude of waters in the heaven, he causeth the vapors to go up from the ends of the earth*, The same reason they give both, because the ascent of vapors goes before rain: but the copulative in its proper sense may well stand here; for the prophet does not tie himself to any such strict method here, as that one member of his discourse must be so riveted into another, but relates the several works of God apart one from another, and this, together with those that follow, in that order, as to his hand he found them recorded by the psalmist, Ps. 135:7.

*{he maketh lightnings with rain}* So is the particle used, Ezra 1:5. & 2:63. yet in this very passage, Ps. 135:7. it is rendered, *lightnings for rain*: and so it is used, Ezra 10:14. ch. 7:18. either may well stand; for lightning, by rending the clouds, makes way for rain, which goes commonly along with it, Job 38:25, 26. neither of which any idol is able to do, ch. 14:22. Zech. 10:1, 2. nor are the heavens themselves of themselves, Job 38:28, 34, 35. ch. 14:22.

*{and bringeth forth the wind out of his treasures.}* Heb. *treasuries*, or *storehouses*, as 2 Chr. 11:11. Neh. 13:12. Joel 1:17. God has his storehouses, as well for *wind*, as for *water*, Ps. 33:7.

**Verse 14.** *{Every man is brutish in his knowledge;}* Or, as some other, *by his knowledge*; that is, as some, man deals then most brutishly, when he thinks to do most wisely, Job 11:12. Rom. 1:22. Or, as others, restraining it to those idol-god-makers, they deal most brutishly in abusing their *knowledge*, that is, their art and skill, to the making of idols, and in giving such honor to that that is of no worth or use, Isa. 44:9, 20. But others render the words, *Every man is become more brutish than to know*; that is, than to understand and take notice of the palpable folly and vanity of such silly courses as these are; they are so bewitched and besotted therewith, Isaiah 44:18. Others again, *from knowing*, for, *more than to know*; as, *from speaking*, for, *more than to speak*; 1 Sam. 25:17. *from reckoning*, for, *more than to reckon*, Ps. 40:5. Or, *Every man becometh brutish*, falling *from knowledge*, or having lost his understanding, and his wits, as we say; as Hos. 9:1. *Thou hast played the harlot from thy God*; that is, falling or departing *from thy God*. But I conceive the genuine notion and construction of the words to be this; *Every man is become brutish for want of knowledge*: for this particle oftentimes implies a defect of the thing spoken of. So Ps. 109:24. *My flesh faileth from fatness*; that is, *for want of fatness*; and Lam. 4:9. *these pine away from the fruits of the earth*; that is, *for want of the fruits of the earth*. So the meaning is plain, It is for want of knowledge and understanding, that people, all sort of them, even these among the rest that would seem wiser than the rest, are become so brutish, and so stupid, Isa. 44:18. verse 8. for what difference is there between a man and a brute beast, when he wants that that should distinguish him from a beast? Job 35:11. Of the heathen idol-makers and worshippers he speaks, whose follies he does here again return unto. See the same again, ch. 51:17.

*{every founder is confounded by the graven images;}* Or, *shall be confounded*, or *may be confounded for*, or *ashamed of the graven image*; which he causes to have it afterward graved, and polished, to make a handsome god of it: or, as others, for which he casts silver plates to cover it with, that it may be more gorgeously set out: ashamed of them, at present, they may be, and one day shall be, Ps. 97:7. For as for those learned late interpreters, that would have the word rendered actively, not *is*, or *may be*, or *shall be confounded*, or *ashamed*, but *maketh confounded*, or *ashamed*: it is beside the ordinary use of the word; and as I conceive has no more place here, than in ch. 6:15. & 8:12. where they also so render it. Nor do I conceive that the word will well bear that sense, which some other give it here, who render it, *is grown infamous*; the *graven image*, for, any at large; as Isa. 42:17. as the *molten* follows after.

*{for his molten image is falsehood.}* Heb. *his melting*; as Isa. 41:29. *falsehood*, or *a lie*; as Isa. 44:20. having nothing of that which they conceive it to have, or attribute unto it. See v. 8.

*{and there is no breath in them}* Heb. *and wind*, or, *spirit is not in them*: there is no breath of life in them, Ps. 135:17. sorry dead things they are, altogether unlike *the living God*, v. 10.

**Verse 15.** *{They are vanity}* Heb. *Vanity they*, for, *are they*. See verse 3.

*{and the works of errors}* Or, *a most deceitful work*; either proceeding from an unsound and erroneous judgment, Rom. 1:28. or, tending to nothing but deceit, and leading into gross errors, v. 8. Hab. 2:18. Howbeit, because the verb is used sometime for *to mock*, or *delude*; as Gen. 19:14. some render it, *works of illusions*, or, *mere mockeries*: such as people are strangely deluded with, 2 Thess. 2:11. and deserve rather derision and mockery than fear, or reverent regard, verse 5.

*{in the time of their visitation they shall perish.}* As v. 11. that is, says the rabbin, when the day of Babylon's visitation comes, (see the phrase, ch. 11:23.) then will God destroy her idols together with her, Isa. 46:1. See Jer. 51:18.

**Verse 16.** *{The portion of Jacob is not like them:}* The true God, who is said to be the *portion* of his people, Deut. 32:9. Ps. 16:5. & 73:26. & 119:57. is not like unto these vanities; but one that is able to protect and save his, Gen. 15:1. Ps. 18:31. & 84:11. Isa. 41:11. & 63:1.

*{and Israel is the rod of his inheritance}* They are his possession, as he is theirs, Deut. 26:17, 18. ch. 12:7. Zech. 2:12. a metaphor taken from the manner of the division of land, as by *lot* and *line*, or *cords*, Ps. 16:5, 6. so by *rod*, or *reed*, also, Ps. 74:2. Ezek. 48:21.

*{the LORD of hosts is his name.}* So Isa. 47:4. It is he that has all the creatures in heaven and earth at his command, Gen. 2:1. Ps. 119:91. Dan. 4:35. See this passage the same, Jer. 51:19.

**Verse 17.** *{Gather up thy wares out of the land, O thou inhabitant of the fortress.}* The latter part of this chapter, as it consists of a far different subject from the former; so it seems to me to be the sum of another sermon. See on verse 1. and the like hereunto, ch. 22:20. In it the prophet from God threatens this people with extreme distress and dispersion, for the brutish stupidity of them and their rulers, verses 17, 22. himself bitterly bewails that heavy doom, and makes suit for mitigation of so sore a sentence, verses 19, 23, 25. In the entrance into it, the prophet calls upon those his countrymen that abode in any place of strength, to get in whatsoever they had in any place abroad, as the usual course of people is in times of invasion, Judg. 9:51. ch. 4:5, 6. and 8:14. So rather, than as those, who suppose it spoken to such as had got into Jerusalem, as advising them to pack away from thence, and get them out of the land of Judea; as ch. 6:1. Ezek. 12:3. Matt. 24:16, 18. Luke 17:31.

*{gather up}* Or, *withdraw*; as 1 Sam. 14:20. otherwise, *gather up out of the land*, should be a complexive form, for, *gather and get out of the land*: as, *thou hast loved my soul from the pit*; that is, *loved and kept it from the pit*, Isa. 38:17.

*{thy wares}* Or, *merchandise*; for it comes from a word that signifies *a merchant*, Job 41:6. Isa. 23:8. in times of public invasion, the manner of such being to betake themselves, and the commodities they trade in, unto places of most security; put here generally for all goods, chattel, or chattels whatsoever.

*{out of the land}* That is, from the country abroad, where they lie open and exposed to pillage and plunder by the enemy.

*{O thou inhabitant of the fortress}* Heb. *Inhabitress*: as chap. 21.13. for in a feminine form the prophets use to speak both of, and unto, companies of people that live as in a body together, in some city, or whole country, whence the names of *virgin*, or *damsel*; and *daughter* so frequent with them. See Esay 1.8. & 37.22. & 47.1. chap. 9.1. This one of the Rabbines restrains unto Jerusalem the strongest fort in Judea: and it may well be, that the Jews there abiding, should hereby among the rest (for the words seem more general) be admonished to get in what provision they could from abroad, as expecting a strait and tedious siege. But another of them transfers it to Babylon, as advising her to gather together all those spoils, which from other nations she had pillaged, and to betake her to flight with them out of her own country; which all her idols and magicians could not be able to secure against the Medes and Persians her enemies. But this is many miles from the Prophet's meaning.

**Verse 18.** *{For thus saith the LORD; Behold I will sling out the inhabitants of the land at this once; and will distress them that they may find it so.}* Heb. *Behold I am slinging*; I am out of hand about, by the Chaldeans, to cast this people out of their land into Babylon, as easily and readily as a stone is cast out of a sling, 1 Sam.17.49. & 25.29. See ch.16.14.

*{at this once}* Or, *as at one cast*: not making any long work of it; but slinging or flinging them all out at once, 2 Chr.36.17.

*{and will distress them that they may find it so.}* The text here has no more than, *that they shall*, or, *may find*. The old Latin here inserts a negative, rendering the words, *that they may not be found*: and so it should have reference to the term of *slinging*. I will so cast them out, and in that manner disperse them, that they shall not be found; as stones thrown far with a sling, are not easily found. But there is no negative in the text, nor reason to insert it: neither is the verb in a passive form. Others understand it of the strait siege of them in Jerusalem; *I will straiten them that they* (that is, their enemies) *may find* them. Others, *I will put them to* such *straits*, or, *afflictions, that they may find*, and receive the reward of their wickedness. So the Chaldee, and some other, *that they may find*, by discovery, the folly and vanity of their former courses, as also of their idols, and other lying helps, that they formerly relied upon: or, as others lastly, which to me seems most likely, *that they may find*, by woeful experience, that word of God to be true, which they will not now believe, cha.5.13,14. Ezek.6.10. & 33.33.

**Verse 19.** *{Woe is me for my hurt; my wound is grievous}* One of the Jewish doctors knits this verse by a supply thus to the former, *I will afflict*, or, *straiten them, until they shall find*, and say, *Wo is me for my hurt*, &c. wherein also some late interpreters of special note follow him. But such forced connections seem not to do so well. I conceive them rather with others, to be the words of the Prophet, either himself bewailing, or in the person of the people bemoaning that grievous condition, that by their security and stupidity, they had brought upon themselves, v.18.

*{woe is me}* An ordinary form of lamentation: as ch.4.31.

*{for my hurt}* Heb. *my breach*; as ch.6.14. & 14.17.

*{my wound is grievous}* Heb. *my stroke*. So chap.14.17. and 30.12. Nah.3.19.

*{but I said, Truly, this is a grief; and I must bear it.}* Some conceive these to be the Prophet's words so delivered in the person of the people, as teaching them to take notice of, and acknowledge God's hand in their sufferings, and humbly submit to the patient enduring of it: not unlike that, 1 Sam.3.18. Lam.3.17,18. Mic.7.9. and they render the words, *But I said, Surely this is my infirmity*, (that which God has allotted me) *and I must*, or, *will bear it*. Others take it, as spoken by the Prophet of himself, as making account sometime that he should overcome his grief; but finding himself now unable to master it, ch.8.18,21. or in the person of the people with himself, as having sometime made account that it was an infirmity, that might well enough be borne, a fit of sickness that would easily away again; but that they found it now to be far otherwise, ch.6.14. & 8.16. and these read the words, *Yet I said, It is but such an infirmity, and I shall bear it*; or, *that I may bear*.

*{But}* Heb. *And*: as ch.10.10. or, *Yet*: as ch.7.26.

*{I said}* Or, *I thought* with myself; I made account; as Psalm 39.1. & 77.10.

*{Truly}* Or, *Surely*: as Psa.73.1. as if it were a note of certainty: or, *Yet*, or, *But*; for it seems here rather to be a note of diminution: as verse 24.

*{this is an infirmity}* The pronoun demonstrative for the verb substantive; as Psalm 25.12. some render it, *my infirmity*; as Psalm 77.10. but the pronoun possessive is not here.

*{and I will bear it}* Or, *which I may bear*: as ch.5.22. or, *that I may bear it*, as ch.14.19.

**Verse 20.** *{My Tabernacle is spoiled, and all my cords are broken}* By *Tabernacle*, or, *Pavilion*, is here meant the city of Jerusalem; or the state of Judah: as Esay 33.20. & 54.2. See chap.4.20.

*{cords}* Wherewith the curtains of their tents, or pavilions were fastened to the pins, or stakes: all the stays of city and state. See Esa.3.1,2. & 33.20.

*{my children are gone forth of me, and they are not}* They are gone into captivity, and are as if they were not, being past hope of all recovery; as ch.31.15.

*{there is none to stretch forth my tent any more, and to set up my curtains}* He persists in the similitude of a tent or tabernacle, consisting of curtains erected, or stretched out, by help of poles, cords and pins, or stakes. See Esay 54.2. chap.4.20. & 49.25. There is none that may help to raise and set up my state again. See Esay 51.18.

*{and to set up}* Or, *or to set up*: as ch.9.12.

**Verse 21.** *{For the Pastors are become brutish, and have not sought the LORD:}* The main cause and ground of all these evils, the brutishness and stupidity that was generally among them, (for if the rulers were such, the people much more. See ch.5.4,5.) and their total neglect and disregard of God.

*{For}* Or, *Because*; as chap.6.13. or, *For, because*: for the particle has sometime a twofold notion included in it; as Deut.31.20. ch.4.30. & 12.5.

*{Pastors}* Rulers, as well civil, as ecclesiastical, both magistrates and ministers, Esa.56.10,11. So is the word taken, ch.3.15. Num.27.17.

*{brutish}* As v.8. Psa.73.22. & 92.6.

*{have not sought the LORD}* Or, *seek not the Lord*; do not look after him, Psa.14.2. Esa.9.13. Zeph.1.6. neither consult at all with him, or take advice from him, Esa.31.1.

*{therefore they shall not prosper;}* Because they neglect him, without whom nothing can prosper, Esay 30.1,6. & 54.15,17. chap.2.37.

*{and all their flocks shall be scattered}* Heb. *their pasture*, (so the word constantly signifies, Psalm 95.7. Esay 49.9. Hosh.13.6.) for, *their sheep*: or, *the sheep of their pasture*; or, *their pasture sheep*, as it is more fully expressed, Psalm 74.1. & 79.13. & 100.3. chap.23.1. Ezek.34.31. See chap.25.36. The people committed to their charge, shall all be dispersed. See chap.13.26. chap.50.6,17. Zach.13.7.

**Verse 22.** *{Behold the noise of the bruit is come, and a great commotion out of the North country, to make the cities of Judah desolate, and a den of dragons.}* The Prophet's words, as if he saw the Chaldean army marching forward to invade and overrun Judea, and heard not the report of their approach alone, but the noise that they raised before them. See chap.4.7,19,20. Heb. *a voice of hearing*: as, *a word*, or, *speech, of hearing*; that is, *a word*, or, *speech, heard*, Heb.4.2. or, *of report*, or, *rumor*, (as 1 Sam.2.24. ch.49.14,23. that is, *a loud rumor*; or, *a loud report*: as, *a voice of cry*, for, *a loud cry*, ch.8.19.) *behold it cometh*; as Ezek.21.7. See ch.4.16. & 8.24.

*{and a great commotion}* Or, *concussion*; or, *shaking*: as Esay 14.16. Hag.2.7,21. or, *noise*; rattling of chariots, and clattering of arms; for thereunto it is usually applied, Esa.9.5. & 29.6. ch.47.3. Ezek.3.12. Nah.3.2. See ch.8.16.

*{out of the North country}* Or, *of those that come from the North-country*; that is, from Babylon, ch.1.15. & 5.15. & 6.22. and some such supply must be to make the sentence entire.

*{to make the cities of Judah desolate, and a den of dragons.}* See cha.9.11.

**Verse 23.** *{O LORD, I know that the way of man is not in himself; it is not in man that walketh to direct his steps.}* The Prophet turns his speech unto God; acknowledging that warlike affairs do not depend upon the power or policy of man; but upon his providence and disposal: and that therefore, though the Chaldeans were never so powerful and ireful; yet it is not in their power to do what they list, but what he is pleased to give way unto; who is able for all their power and policy, wrath and rage, to restrain them at his pleasure, and to turn them which way he will, Psalm 78.10.12. Prov.21.1. Esa.37.29. Some conceive it to have reference to a secret hand of God, in directing Nebuchadnezzar to shape his course toward Jerusalem, when he was at a stand, and in debate about another way, Ezek.21.21. They that expound it as concerning free will, are beside the meaning of the text.

*{that the way of man is not in himself}* Heb. *that to man his way is not*; or, man's way is not his own; he is not master of his own way: *his way*; that is, *his own way*; as Esa.53.6.

*{it is not in man that walketh to direct his steps}* Heb. *it is not to man walking*, (or, *the man that walketh*; it is not a thing in his power,) *and to direct*, or, *settle his goings*: *that he should* (as Isaiah 53.2. Mal.1.9.) *directing direct*, or *settling settle*, that is, with any certainty *direct*, or, *order* (as Esay 9.7.) that is, *settle* and establish (as 2 Sam.7.12.) *his goings*: to carry them on, and give such success to them, as himself pleases, Psalm 37.23. Prov.16.9. & 20.24. & 21.30,31. of such defective, yet emphatical, forms of speech, see Esay 59.13. ch.6.11. for the verb is an infinitive, in a gerundial notion.

**Verse 24.** *{O LORD, correct me, but with judgment; not in thine anger, lest thou bring me to nothing.}* The Prophet's supplication in behalf, and in the person of his people, as if seeing the approach of Nebuchadnezzar's forces he should say, Lord we know well, that this army could not come in upon, nor prevail against us, but by your permission and your provision; but since that you are resolved thereby to chastise us, we beseech you in wrath remember mercy, Habb.3.2. and with such moderation correct us, that we may be able to bear it, 1 Cor. 10:13. not with such extreme anger, as utterly to consume us, Isa. 57:16.

*{but}* Or, *Yet*. See verse 19.

*{with judgment}* Heb. *in judgment*; that is, *with moderation*, in measure, Isa. 27:8. ch. 30:11.

*{not in thine anger}* Ps. 6:1. not according to that which our sins, whereby we have provoked you unto wrath, Isa. 64:5. ch. 7:18, 19. do most justly deserve, Ps. 103:10, 14.

*{lest thou bring me to nothing.}* Heb. *diminish me*, Ezek. 29:15. so diminish me, that I should no more be a nation. See ch. 30:11. and 46:26.

**Verse 25.** *{Pour out thy fury upon the heathen that know thee not, and upon the families that call not on thy name:}* Let the fierceness of your wrath be set against the heathen, that do not acknowledge or worship you, and not against your own people, Ps. 74:1, 2. See the same, Ps. 79:6.

*{pour out}* See Isa. 42:25. So ch. 6:11. & 7:20. Lam. 2:4. and 4:11.

*{thy fury}* Or, *wrath*, as it is rendered, Ps. 79:6. See ch. 4:4.

*{know thee not}* As Exod. 5:2. or, *acknowledge thee not*, as their God; as Isa. 10:11. & 37:10.

*{families}* That is, countries, or, kingdoms: as ch. 1:15.

*{that call not upon thy name}* That do not acknowledge your sovereignty in seeking to you by prayer, Ps. 14:4. & 53:4. invocation a special note of such acknowledgment, Ps. 50:15. & 116:13. 1 Cor. 1:2. 2 Tim. 2:9.

*{for they have eaten up Jacob, and devoured him, and consumed him, and have made his habitation desolate.}* Turn the rigor of your wrath against them to take vengeance upon them for the mischiefs they have done to your people, Ps. 79:7, 10, 12.

*{for}* Or, *because*; as verse 21.

*{eaten up Jacob, and devoured him, and consumed him}* Heb. *eaten Jacob, and eaten him, and consumed him*. Which would rather be rendered, *eaten up Jacob, even* (as ch. 6:5, 19.) *eaten him, and consumed him*; that is, so eaten him up, that they have clean consumed him. See ch. 50:7, 17.

*{have made his habitation desolate.}* This some of the Jewish interpreters understand of the temple; and would have it read in the future: They will lay the temple waste. But this forced exposition is needless, when the words are of themselves plain enough: as *Jacob*, for, his posterity God's people: so, *his habitation*, taken collectively, for the land and cities of their abode. See ch. 8:16. & 9:11. verse 22.

## CHAPTER 11

**Verse 1.** *{The word that came to Jeremiah, from the LORD, saying,}* See ch. 1:1. The time when this message was delivered by God to the prophet, as well as of those foregoing, ch. 10:1, 17. is uncertain; they might very well be much about the same time. See verse 9.

**Verse 2.** *{Hear ye the words of this covenant}* He is willed to mind them of the covenant which in Moses his time, they had with God entered into, and to call upon them for the due observation of it; withal taxing them and their ancestors for the willful breach of it, and obstinate persistence therein, vv. 8, 10. for which they are threatened with destruction, vv. 11, 17.

*{Hear}* That is, consider, regard, obey, observe: as vv. 3, 7.

*{the words}* Or, *matter therein contained*: as ch. 7:27. and 36:32.

*{of this covenant}* Long since plighted between God and them, Exod. 24:3, 8. Deut. 29:10, 22. and it is not unlikely, that the prophet held out the book, or volume of the law, wherein the covenant was engrossed, and recorded, then in his hand.

*{and speak unto the men of Judah, and unto the inhabitants of Jerusalem}* Heb. *and ye shall speak*, or, *speak ye*; as 2 Kings 1:6. whence some suppose that this message should be delivered unto Jeremy, to impart unto the priests, withal charging them, according to their duty, Deut. 31:12, 13. & 33:10. to acquaint the people with it. And they therefore render the whole verse thus; *Hear ye*, to wit, O priests, *the words of the covenant, that ye may* (as ch. 10:18.) *speak them to the men of Judah*, etc. But the words following, *And say thou*, or, *thou shalt say*, verse 3. seem to control this. Others rather, and so some of the Jewish doctors conceive, that some other prophets of those times were to join with Jeremy, in the delivery of this message, either Zephany, if it were in the days of Josiah, Zeph. 1:1. or Uriah, if it were in the days of Jehoiakim, ch. 26:20. But I suppose we need not have recourse unto either of these helps. The Scripture does oft pass from number to number; as it does apparently in this place: for in the next verse the charge is in the singular given to the prophet, unto whom alone doubtless this message was delivered, v. 1. but the plural number is here used, as I conceive, to intimate, what God would have his ministers and messengers press especially upon his people, to wit, the keeping of covenants with him; and to let the prophet know, that this part of his message was no other, than others in his place, were from time to time, as occasion was, to be dealing in with his people. See v. 4.

**Verse 3.** *{And say thou unto them;}* Heb. *And thou shalt say* (as v. 2. *ye shall speak*) *unto them*; to wit, *to the men of Judah, and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem*, v. 2. See Isa. 1:11.

*{Thus saith the LORD God of Israel}* The Lord God that made his covenant with Israel, Deut. 5:2.

*{Cursed be the man that obeyeth not the words of this covenant}* Heb. *cursed be the man*; evil betide him, Deut. 27:26. *that heareth not*, as Ps. 81:11, 13. So verse 2. *the words of this covenant*. See verse 2.

**Verse 4.** *{Which I made with your fathers, in the day that I brought them forth out of the land of Egypt from the iron furnace,}* Egypt is called *an iron furnace*, or, *furnace of iron*: as here, so Deut. 4:20. 1 Kings 8:51. in allusion unto such *furnaces*, wherein ore or metal is melted and tried, Isa. 48:10. and it is called *an iron furnace*, not in regard of the matter, whereof such are wont to be made; for furnaces and melting pots are not made of metal, but of *earth*, Ps. 12:6. but in regard of the ore or metal therein to be melted; a stronger matter being required for the making of such a furnace, wherein not gold or silver, tin or lead, but iron, either ore or metal, is to be melted and cast, and a far fiercer fire to be used about it, than with any of those other. God hereby intimating the grievousness and extremity of that affliction, which his people sustained in Egypt, and out of which he delivered them, by bringing of them from thence, Exod. 1:13, 14. Of the rest of the verse, see ch. 7:22.

*{saying, Obey my voice, and do them, according to all that I command you; so shall ye be my people, and I will be your God;}* Exod. 19:5, 6. Lev. 26:3, 12. See ch. 7:23.

*{do them}* To wit, my commandments, or the *things* contained and contracted on your parts in the *covenant*, vv. 2, 3. See v. 6. the pronoun for the noun; as ch. 4:9. and a passage from number to number; as verse 2.

**Verse 5.** *{That I may perform the oath which I sware unto your fathers, to give them a land flowing with milk and honey, as it is this day.}* Heb. *That I may confirm*, or *establish, the oath, which I sware unto your fathers*, by making it good unto them, Deut. 7:12. & 8:18. & 9:5. Ps. 105:9, 10. The end of God's requiring obedience on their part, not for his own behoof, but for their benefit, that he may do them good.

*{to give them a land flowing with milk and honey;}* Abounding with plenty of all good things, as well for necessary sustenance, as for pleasure also and delight, Exod. 3:8, 17. Lev. 20:24. Num. 13:27. Deut. 6:3. & 11:9.

*{as it is this day}* Or, *as this day* appears. So Deut. 8:18. ch. 44:6.

*{Then answered I, and said, So be it, O LORD.}* Heb. *And* (as ch. 4:10.) *I answered* (as Isa. 21:9.) *and said, Amen, O Lord*: which some expound with reference to God's command, as if he had said, Lord, what you have enjoined me, I will do, and incite others of my rank, priests and prophets, likewise, unto the doing of the same. Others conceive it, as spoken in the person of the body of the people, as obliging themselves under a penalty unto the due observation of God's commands; as Deut. 27:15, 26. Ps. 106:48. I conceive it rather to be the speech of the prophet, speaking in his own person, taking hold of, and having respect unto, those gracious words in the close of his speech, and putting his *Amen* thereunto, as if he had said, So Lord let it be, that this people being careful to keep covenant with you, may enjoy still that land, which you did by oath bind yourself to settle them in. See ch. 8:6.

**Verse 6.** *{Then the LORD said unto me;}* Heb. *And*; as v. 5. which need not here be altered. Or, *Again*; as ch. 1:11. For it is a repetition of the former injunction.

*{proclaim all these words in the cities of Judah, and in the streets of Jerusalem;}*

*{Proclaim}* As ch. 7:1.

*{all these words}* As ch. 7:27.

*{in the cities of Judah, and in the streets of Jerusalem.}* See the reason, verse 13.

*{Hear ye the words of this covenant, and do them.}* Action and practice the main end of hearing, Deut. 6:3. See v. 2.

**Verse 7.** *{For I earnestly protested unto your fathers; in the day that I brought them up out of the land of Egypt, even unto this day, rising early and protesting, saying, Obey my voice.}* See ch. 7:23, 25.

*{earnestly protested}* Heb. *protesting protested*, 1 Sam. 8:9. as, *charging charged*, Gen. 43:3.

*{I brought them up}* As ch. 2:6.

*{rising early}* See ch. 5:8. & 7:13.

**Verse 8.** *{Yet they obeyed not, nor inclined their ear; but walked every one in the imagination of their evil heart.}* See ch. 7:24.

*{therefore will I bring upon them all the words of this covenant, which I commanded them to do; but they did them not.}* Heb. *and* (as ch. 7:28.) *I brought upon them*: and so it would be rendered as ch. 22:7. I brought upon them all those menaces or judgments threatened in the law against the willful transgressors and violators of the covenant plighted between me and them, Deut. 28:16. & 29:19, 20. a twofold defect of the pronoun after the verb; as Gen. 43:24. ch. 9:10.

**Verse 9.** *{And the LORD said unto me;}* Or, *Again*; or, *Moreover*; as verse 6.

*{A conspiracy is found among the men of Judah, and among the inhabitants of Jerusalem.}* Because it might be said, what is all this to those that now live, if their forefathers in former ages broke covenant with God, and smarted then for the same? God therefore tells the Prophet, that the main body of the Jewish people, and those of Jerusalem, among the rest, had made a general revolt from him, and betaken themselves unto those idolatrous courses, that their forefathers took before them. And hence the Jewish commenters, not without some good probability, gather, that this prophecy was delivered in the reign of Jehoiakim; what time they fell back from God's service and worship, restored with them, and settled among them, in the days of good Josias. See chap. 14. 1.

*{A conspiracy}* Or, *combination*, or, *league*, 2 Kin.15.30.& 17.4. a defection from God, as by a general consent of all sorts of people throughout the land and state. So Ezek.22.25. a conspiracy among the prophets.

*{is found}* That is, say some, is detected: as, the King of Assyria found conspiracy in Hoshea, 2 King.17.4. and, as a thief is found, when he is taken in the manner, Jer.2.26, but it may after the usual phrase of Scripture, be understood simply, A conspiracy is found, that is, there is a conspiracy, See the like, Est. 1.5. Esa. 13.15, Luke 17.18,

*{among the men of Judah, and among the inhabitants of Jerusalem}* Heb. *in the man of Judah*: but man, for, men; as Esa. 5. 3. among the main body of the Jewish state: for whereas one of great note understands it of a conspiracy, between the men of Judah, and those of Israel the ten tribes: as if, though being at enmity otherwise, they had now conspired together in a revolt from God, he seems not to have observed the precise terms of the text: in, for, among; as Esay 66.19.

**Verse 10.** *{They are turned away to the iniquities of their forefathers which refused to hear my words:}* Being not warned, nor amended, by those judgments which for their disobedience befell them, ch.7.26, v.8.See ch.13.10, Heb. *they have returned upon*, or, *unto*; as Prov.26.11. with 2.22. ch.6.9,.

*{Forefathers}* Heb. *first fathers*: first, for, former; as Eccl.7.10.Esa. 61.4. 1 Tim.5.12.Rev.1.4.

*{and they went after other gods to serve them:}* This thus rendered, may seem to be meant of their ancestors, But it seems rather by the emphatical expression of the pronoun in the text, to have reference unto those that then lived, the present conspirators and late revolters; and would therefore, to take away all ambiguity, be rendered, and they, or they also (as ch.3.6.) are gone after other gods, See ch.7.9. & 13.10.

*{the house of Israel and the house of Judah, have broken my covenant which I made with their Fathers.}* As well Judah, as Israel; the other ten tribes, have broken covenant with me, See ch, 3.6,8.&5.11, Howbeit, it follows not hence, that the conspiracy mentioned, v.9. was there intended between the two houses, as that learned writer supposes to be from this clause made good. Of the two houses, See on ch.3.18.

**Verse 11.** *{Therefore thus saith the LORD}* The sin in breach of covenant was before, v.9, 10, the denunciation of judgment for it, now follows,

*{Behold, I will bring evil upon them, which they shall not be able to escape.}* I will deal with them, as I did with their fathers before them, v. 8. Heb. *I am bringing*, (as ch. 4.6. & 6.19.) *evil to them*, (For, *upon them*, as Ezek.7.16.) *which they shall not be able to get out of*, as Psalm, 88. 8. and such a redundancy, as verse 12. that shall entangle them in such difficulties and perplexities, as they shall not be able by all their might or slight, to wind themselves out of, See the like, Mic. 2, 3.

*{and though they shall cry unto me, I will not hearken unto them,}* I will deal then with them, as they deal now with me; I will then refuse to hear them, as they now refuse to hearken to me, verse 10, Zach. 7.11,13. Heb. *and they shall cry unto me, and I will not hearken unto them*, the like syntax, See Esay 53.9. chap. 7.27. and 8, 4,

**Verse 12.** *{Then shall the cities of Judah, and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, go and cry unto the gods unto whom they offer incense.}* Let them seek then for succor to them, whom now they serve, Deut.32.37,38. Judg. 10.14, See ch.2.28,

*{Then}* Heb. *And*, as verse 5.

*{shall go and cry}* Or, *let them go and cry*; as, *let them arise*, chap. 2.28,

*{the cities of Judah}* The inhabitants of them, as Esa.40.9.

*{to which they offer incense.}* Which they worship; one part of religious worship put for the whole, as ch. 7.9, Heb. which they are burning incense to them, an usual redundancy, as Psal.1.4, Prov.2.15, and before, v. 11.

*{but they shall not save them at all in the time of their trouble.}* Heb. *and* (as chap. 10. 10.) *they shall not saving save them*, (that is, *be able at all to save them*, as Esay 45.20.) *in the time of their evil*, of that evil, which I am bringing upon them, verse 11,

**Verse 13.** *{For according to the number of thy cities were thy gods, O Judah, and according to the number of thy streets, O Jerusalem, have ye set up altars to that shameful thing, even altars to burn incense unto Baal.}* See ch.2.28,

*{that shameful thing}* Heb. *shame*, as ch. 3.24. Hos.9.10,

*{burn incense to Baal}* See ch.7.9.

**Verse 14.** *{Therefore pray not thou for this people, neither lift up a cry or prayer for them.}* See ch.7.16. So ch.14.11.

*{for I will not hear them, in the time that they cry unto me for their trouble}* As v.11. nor thee for them, as ch.7.16.

**Verse 15.** *{what hath my beloved to do in my house}* These words are by divers diversely expounded. One of the Jewish commenters makes them the Prophet's speech, speaking of God, what should my beloved (that is, God, whom I love, as Esa.5.1.) do any longer in my house? to wit, his Temple, which I as constantly frequent as mine own house: So Anna, Luke 2, 37. One of ours, (who seems to have taken his rise from the Rabbine) makes them: God's speech speaking of the Prophet; what should my beloved (thou my dear Prophet) do any more in my house? frequent my Temple any longer, there to preach to this people, or to pray for them, when as there is no good to be done, either upon them by the one, or for them by the other, verse 14, Another of ours expounds them, as a speech of God the Father, speaking of Christ his beloved Son, Matt. 3.17. & 17.5, Eph. 1.6. who had wont to manifest himself, in his word and power in the Temple, Exod. 23.20. & 33. 14. Ezek. 1.26, and 10.2. Mal. 3.1. But the Chaldee, whom another of the Jewish commenters concurs with, understands it as spoken by God of his people. What hath my people, whom I heretofore so entirely affected, and so dearly loved, Esay 5.1. ch.12.7, Hos. 3.1.& 11, 1. Mal. 1.2, any more to do in mine house, when she has so grievously played the harlot? Esa.1.12,21, ch.7.9,11. And the entendment of it seems to be, to cut them off from hoping to prevail with God by prayer, and repairing for that end to his Temple, where he had promised to hear them, while they continued loyal with him; or when they returned sincerely to him, 2 Chr.7.14,15. Heb. *what to my beloved in my house?* as Esa.22.16.

*{seeing she hath wrought lewdness with many}* Heb. *in her committing vileness with many*; a defect of the preposition, as well before the verb, as the noun; when she takes such vile and lewd courses with so many, either wicked ones, heathen, whom she joins with, as some; or idols rather, after whom she goes a-whoring, so others: as if she were some common strumpet; what should she do any more in my house, to make my house no better than a brothel-house? Chap.7.30. See Chap.2.20, & 3.1,2. verse13. There is in the Hebrew a passage from gender to gender whereof see ch.2.14. A learned late writer would have it rendered, *her doing*, (that is, her doings, or deeds;-the verb for the noun) *is extreme lewdness, O ye great ones*: the article in a vocative notion, as Deut. 32.1, Joel 1.2. let others consider of it, I concur with the former.

*{and the holy flesh is passed from thee}* These words have almost as many interpretations, as interpreters, Some by holy flesh, understand the faithful people among them clean wasted and gone, Psalm.12.1. Esay 64, 6,7. Chap. 5.1. Mic.7.1. flesh; for, people, as Psalm.65.2, Esa. 40.5. to pass away; for, to perish, and be gone, Job 6.15.& 9. 26. Some the circumcision, which they bare in their flesh, as a seal of God's covenant, and the sign of an holy seed, Gen. 17, 11,13. Ezra 9.2. which by reason of their profaneness and ungodliness otherwise, was become as uncircumcision unto them, chap. 9,26. Rom. 2, 25,29. The most of the flesh of such beasts, as were slain for sacrifice, to be offered either unto idols, or unto God. And among those that thus take the word flesh; some read the words, as uttered by way of interrogation; some as by way of enunciation: of those that follow the former manner of reading, one expounds them of their idolatrous sacrifices, the flesh whereof, says he, is called holy, by a contrariety of speech, as unholy and impure; as the Greek *ἅγιος*, and the Latin *sacer*, is sometimes used; and the Hebrew *Kaddesh*, Lev. 6.29. Deut.22.9. but herein I suppose this author goes alone, and so I leave him. Others of them, and so the ancient Greek, and old Latin, and those many that follow either, understand it of the sacrifices offered to God in the Temple, called flesh of holiness, as Hag.2.12, as sanctified by the altar on which it was offered, Mat.23.19, and they render the words shall, or, can, the holy flesh cause thy wickedness to pass away from thee, wherein thou dost glory? do ye imagine, that your sacrifices are able to expiate your sins, when ye are so far from being humbled for them, that ye glory in them, See chap. 7. 9,21. But this exposition the words will not bear, for the verb is not here in an active or transitive, but in a standing or immanent form or notion; it signifies not to put away, but to pass away; and so the best interpreters reading the words enunciatively, render them; the holy flesh hath passed, or, is passed away, from thee. Which some expound of their utter neglect of God's altar, and the sacrifices to it belonging, which they disregarded and no more looked after, than as if they were matters that had never been enjoined them, as 2 Chr.28. 24. Esay 57.5,6. but this seems not so probable. Others rather, that their devotions and holy performances, were all past away, in regard of any acceptance they found with God, or benefit that redounded thence to themselves; See Esay 1.11,15. and 66, 3. Or that they were so profaned, that the holiness of them was utterly gone; though holy in themselves, yet not holy to them, Hos. 2.13, 14. Tit.1.15, or, lastly, that they had no more right now to the holy flesh, than the priest's daughter that had played the harlot, or joined herself to a stranger, Lev. 21.9. & 22.12. The last of these I best like of. Howbeit, I shall crave leave after all this variety, to subjoin mine own thoughts: The words in the text run thus, *and the holy flesh, they shall pass away from upon thee, or, with thee;* or, in plainer terms, *from thee,* as 2 Chr. 33.8. compared with, 2 Kin. 21.8. and the meaning, as I take it, is; the holy flesh of your sacrifices, which you now so profane, shall be wholly taken away from you; the Temple wherein they were to be offered, being utterly defaced and destroyed. See on Esay 29.1. this comes freely from the words without force, only I would for *and,* put, *therefore;* so is the copulative oft used and rendered, v. 11. ch. 1.17. & 2.19. & 3.3. & 6.11. & 7.14,16. *therefore the holy flesh shall pass away from thee:* as having reference as well to the wickedness before mentioned, as to her delight in it, or security under evils denounced or imminent, in the next words related; there is in the text a noun singular, *flesh,* joined with a verb plural in relation to the sacrifices, the flesh whereof was intended: so Isaiah 25.3. *the city of the terrible nations shall fear:* where the city is singular, the verb fear plural; and a passage as before from gender to gender, so from person to person, not unlike those, chap. 2.6,7. & 5.19. & 6.17. and so vers. 16. and both these irregularities, each one of the readings and interpretations before mentioned acknowledge, as well as this now given.

*{when thou doest evil then thou rejoicest}* Heb. *when thine evil,* or, *because when thine evil, then thou rejoicest:* which some understand of evil of sin and wickedness: so most interpreters; you are so far from sorrow for sin, and repenting thereof, that you rather rejoice and glory therein, as Prov. 2.14. yet some understand it, of the evil of penalty and affliction, procured by, and inflicted for sin, as v. 12. and they read the words, *when thine evil is at hand, then doest thou rejoice;* that is, when you are admonished of those evil courses, and have warning given you of evils approaching for the same, you slight all admonitions, and set light by all warnings, and give yourself to nothing but sensuality and jollity, as Isaiah 22.12,13. This latter I incline unto. See ch. 5.3. only whether of the twain we take to, I should conceive the particle prefixed here to include, as oft it does, a twofold notion, as Exo. 18.16. chap. 4.30. & 10.21. & 12.5. and should therefore render it, *because when thine evil is,* or, you are in your evil (be it of sin or penalty) *then thou revellest it;* See Isaiah 22.2. The sum of the whole verse then is this, What has my people to do any more in my Temple, seeing that with so many idols, they in most vile manner pollute themselves? therefore shall the sacred rites be all shortly taken away from them, the rather, because that notwithstanding those calamities, that for these their wicked courses, they were told would shortly seize upon them, yea had seized upon them in part already; they go on still in following their delights and their jollity, and take nothing to heart.

**Verse 16.** *{The LORD called thy name a green olive tree, fair and of goodly fruit.}* What was before intimated of God's love to his people, is here more particularly expressed, in the fruits and effects of it, together with the evil likewise before hinted, which God for their wicked and unthankful carriage towards him, was now resolved to bring upon them.

*{The LORD called}* Or, *The Lord that called;* as, *the Lord that planted,* vers. 17. a defect of the relative, as chap. 6.20. and 8.13.

*{called thy name}* That is, had sometime called you, as Isaiah 8.3. *call his name,* for, *call him;* and, *called thee,* that is, *made thee,* as, *the Lord of the whole earth shall he be called,* for, *shall he be,* Isa. 54.5. and, *thy land shall be called married,* that is, *thy land shall be married;* as in the same place it is expounded, Isaiah 62.4. See the like, Matth. 5.9.

*{A green olive tree}* Or, *a fresh and flourishing olive tree,* Psal. 52.8. and so fresh oil, Psa. 92.10. such a tree, as keeps his verdure all the year long, as the olive and some others do: an emblem of constant and continued prosperity and excellency, Psa. 1.3. & 37.35. ch. 17.8. Hos. 14.7.

*{fair and of goodly fruit}* Heb. *fair of fruit of form,* or, *fashion;* that is, as the Jewish critics expound it, fair both to sight and for fruit, or, *a goodly tree, with goodly fruit:* that which some understand morally of their well-doing, and good works: but I suppose to be meant rather, as those other before cited parallel places, of that external prosperity, flourishing condition, and prosperous successes, that God had been pleased to bless that people with, while they continued faithful to him. See chap. 12.2.

*{with the noise of a great tumult hath he kindled fire upon it, and the branches of it are broken}* That God who formerly blessed you, and made you so prosperous and glorious, has determined to bring in those upon you, that shall waste and destroy you. There is in the words a passage again, from person to person, as Isa. 1.29. vers. 15.18.

*{with the noise of a great tumult}* Or, *an exceeding streperous,* or, *tumultuous noise:* the word is found nowhere save here; and Ezek. 1.24. such a noise is intended, as soldiers are wont to make in the storming of a city. See Isaiah 5.29. yet some would have the word here used, to be of the same notion with *Milah,* that signifies a word, or, speech, and so our English renders it, Ezek. 1.24. *a voice of speech:* and according to this notion they expound this place, *God with a word will kindle a fire.* But neither does that version in Ezekiel, suit well with the other resemblances there adjoined, of the rushing of many, or, mighty waters, and, the noise of a camp: nor does the epithet *great,* here annexed to it, so well sort with it in this place; *with,* as chap. 2.18. or, *at,* as Numb. 16.34.

*{hath he kindled a fire}* Or, *hath kindled a fire,* or, *will kindle a fire:* the Lord, who called you, etc. as before: *will now kindle a fire,* is now resolved to set you on fire, to waste and consume you with fire and sword, ch. 17.27. & 21.14.

*{upon it}* Or, as one of the Jewish critics renders it, in the branches thereof, so the word is used, Nehe. 8.15. and it may stand not amiss here.

*{and the branches of it are broken down}* Heb. *and they shall break the boughs of it:* but the verb is put indefinitely, and is therefore by the passive not amiss rendered, as Mal. 1.4. Luke 12.20. the word rendered branches; used also, Ezek. 31.12. is deemed properly to signify, high and lofty boughs, and by it therefore the Rabbines here would have understood, the king's palace, and God's Temple, and some others, their princes, as by the former the people.

**Verse 17.** *{For the LORD of hosts that planted thee, hath pronounced evil against thee, for the evil of the house of Israel, and of the house of Judah, which they have done against themselves to provoke me to anger, in offering incense unto Baal.}* In these words the Prophet does more plainly unfold, what in the former verse he had spoken concerning this people, and the evil that was to befall them, in the great change of their estate; withal, pointing them to the principal procuring cause of it, their idolatrous practices; whereby they had provoked God to wrath, and jealousy against them.

*{For}* Heb. *And;* as ch. 5.2.

*{that planted thee}* As Isa. 5.2. ch. 2.21.

*{hath pronounced evil against thee}* Heb. *spoken evil against thee,* or *concerning thee;* passed a doom of penalty upon you. See chap. 26.13,19.

*{for the evil of the house of Israel, and of the house of Judah}* Which they have learned the one from the other, and wherein the one has imitated the other; for the house of Israel is here mentioned only, as the former in defection to idolatry, whom the other afterward did perfidiously follow. See cha. 3.6,10,11. & 5.11. vers. 10.

*{against themselves}* See ch. 7.19. or, as others, between them, see on v. 9,10. But I conceive it to be no other than an elegant redundancy in the Hebrew language very frequent: *the evil that they have done them.* So Gen. 12.1. *Go thee out of thy country,* Exo. 20.23. *Ye shall make ye no gods: Make thee a serpent.* Num. 21.9. & Ezek. 37.11. *we are cut off us.* See ch. 7.8.

*{to provoke me to anger}* See ch. 7.18.

*{in offering incense unto Baal}* As vers. 13.

**Verse 18.** *{And the LORD hath given me knowledge of it, and I knew it: then thou shewedst me their doings.}* In the latter part of this chapter, is a discovery made by God to the Prophet, of a secret conspiracy that his own countrymen the inhabitants of Anathoth, vers. 21. had entered into against him, vers. 18,19. the Prophet's reference of his cause unto God, who had revealed it to him, with a demand of justice against them for it, v. 20. and God's just doom past upon them, for such their design against his faithful servant the Prophet, vers. 21,23.

*{And}* Or, *Moreover;* as ch. 1.11. & 8.4.

*{the LORD hath given me knowledge of it}* Or, *the Lord informed me,* or, *gave me notice.* Heb. *made me to know;* as Exod. 33.12.

*{and I knew it}* Or, *so I knew it;* as Isa. 50.9. by that means I came to the knowledge of it, which otherwise I could not have done: God's care of his Prophet's safety. So Act. 23.12,24. & 26.21,22. A defect of the pronoun *it;* as Gen. 28.16.

*{thou shewedst me}* Heb. *madest me to see;* as 2 Kin. 8.20. a passage from person to person; as before, v. 15,16.

**Verse 19.** *{But I was like a lamb, or an ox, that is brought to the slaughter;}* I was as ignorant of their evil intentions, as a sheep or an ox; that is leading to be sacrificed in the Temple, or slain in the shambles, when he thinks he is going to the field; or to the fold, the one; to the stall, the other, Prov. 7.22. Isa. 53.7. neither aware, nor suspicious, of any such evil from them, as not being conscious to myself of any wrong that I had done them; but having ever sought their good, ch. 15.10. & 18.19.

*{But}* Heb. *And;* as vers. 12.

*{I was}* The pronoun for the verb substantive; as Psalm 92.10.

*{a lamb, or an ox}* Heb. *a sheep* (as Hos. 4.16. where a lamb does not so well) *an ox*: the disjunctive is wanting, as Esa. 38.14. chap. 2.31,32. Howbeit, some make the latter to be an attribute only to the former, rendering it, some, a tame, or gentle; some, a taught lamb; or a lamb taught and brought to hand; because the root signifies, sometime, to teach, Job 15.1. & 33.13. and another, a friendly; or familiar lamb; because the word seems so taken, Psalm 55.13. Mic.7.5. and is in Arabic for a *friend* frequently used. But hereof, let others judge.

*{that is brought to the slaughter}* Heb. *led to sacrifice*, or to *slay*; as Lev.9.4. a defect of the relative; as Isaiah 53.7. chap.8.13.

*{and I knew not that they had devised devices against me, saying;}* A necessary supply, as Psalm 105.15. Chap.4.31. See Chap.18.18.

*{Let us destroy the tree, with the fruit thereof;}* The Chaldee, ancient Greek, and old Latin, whom interpreters, Latin and Greek, not a few, follow, render these words, as if the text said, *Let us cast wood into his bread*; which they expound, Let us kill him, by mingling the juice or powder of some poisonful plant or wood with his meat: because the word, *bread*, includes all kind of food, 1 King.4.22. Neh.5.18. or, as some, *Let us give him wood to eat instead of bread*; as the Prophet complains in the person of God's people, That God had fed them with such gritty bread, that had rather worn out their teeth, than nourished their bodies, Lam.3.16. Prov.20.17. Let us kill him with hunger, starve him to death, shut him up where he shall have nothing to feed on, unless he can eat timber and stones. But because the word, in the Hebrew, signifies, *to destroy*; as chap.6.5. Some of them would have the text read, *Let us spoil his meat with wood*: And others, *Let us spoil wood*; that is, make powder of it, to put into, or mingle *with his meat*. But these seem all forced readings; and a *tree* or *wood*, for *poison*, is nowhere found: for whereas some of them point us to, Exod.15.25. the tales they tell of the tree there mentioned, are of equal weight with this their exposition of the word in this place. A learned late writer, rejecting as over-harsh and hard all the former; thus renders the text, *Let us break wood upon his body*. This to fetch about, he tells us, that the word rendered *bread*, is used both in Arabic, and in Hebrew, also, sometime, for *flesh*, (or for *meat* rather in general) Lev.3.10,11. & 21.8. Job 6.8. And another near to it, for the *flesh* of man's body, Job 20.23. Zeph.1.17. and the word rendered *wood*, for a *staff*; as 2 Sam.21.17. Esay 10.15. and so the meaning should be, Let us beat him, or bang him, with staves, or cudgels, till we break them again. That which to me seems not unlike that of the Talmudists, who expound that speech of Adam, Gen.3.12. *The woman gave me of the wood*; that is, banged me with a bough of the tree, and so enforced me to eat: and to sound no less harshly, than any of those other. The words run plainly enough in the text, *Let us destroy the tree with its bread*; where by *destroying*, some understand hewing down, as Deut.20.19. by *tree*, the *stock* of a tree, as chap.2.27. and by *bread*, the *fruit*, that it affords for man's sustenance, Gen.1.29. Some other, by *tree* the *stalk* of a plant, as of corn; and by *bread*, the *grain*: whereof bread is made; as Esay 28.28. and it seems to have been a proverbial form of speech, *Let us destroy stock and fruit*, or *stalk and grain together*; that is, Let us make an utter riddance of him, that nothing of him, or his doctrine, name, mention, or memory, may remain. So the words following expound this branch; for that which some of the ancients dream of Christ and his cross; and Popish expositors prate of Christ in the host, are but frivolous fancies, not at all touching the text.

*{and let us cut him off from the land of the living}* Let us make away this Jeremy, that we may hear no more of him, nor he trouble us any more. So Psalm 52.5. Esa.38.10,11.

*{that his name may be no more remembered.}* Heb. *and his name shall be no more remembered*; as chap.6.5,10. So Psalm 9.5,6. & 83.4. Some suppose that it has some reference to the abolition of the name and memory of such as were condemned for false prophets; as they sought, and thought, to have Jeremy dealt with. See the like, John 16.2.

**Verse 20.** *{But, O LORD of hosts}* The Prophet's words, committing and commending his cause unto God, and craving justice at his hands. So ch.15.15. & 18.19. & 20.12.

*{that judgest righteously}* Heb. *judgest justice*; as Psa.9.4. that is, *with justice*; as Psa.9.8. & 96.13. & 98.9.

*{that triest the reins, and the heart;}* Or, *searchest*, ch.6.27. Psalm 7.9. 1 Sam.16.7. 1 Chr.28.9. chap.17.10. & 20.12. Rev.2.25. a twofold metaphor; the one, taken from the trying of ore or metals, Psa.26.2. & 66.10. the other, from the bodies of beasts slain for sacrifice, which being broken up, their entrails lie all open to the eye, Heb.4.12. and they seem over-nicely to distinguish, who by the *reins*, would have understood men's desires; by the *heart*, their designs.

*{Let me see thy vengeance upon them;}* So Psalm 79.10. A speech proceeding, as most deem, from a prophetical spirit; which some therefore would have delivered rather by way of prediction, than of imprecation; as Psalm 59.10. & 92.11. rendering the words, *I shall see thy vengeance upon them*; as if he had said, It shall surely befall them, and I shall survive to see it: but it seems rather a direct prayer, or bill of complaint, wrung from him, by the contemplation of their extreme malice against him, and commenced at God's tribunal, craving justice against them, as against persons grown incorrigible: and that not without some mixture of human frailty, as those other, chap.15.15. and 17.18. and 18.21,24.

*{for unto thee have I revealed my cause.}* Or, *do I reveal my cause*; that is, commit it; as 1 Pet.2.23. because those that desire to commit their cause unto any, are wont, before they so do, to open it to them, and acquaint them with it.

**Verse 21.** *{Therefore thus saith the LORD of the men of Anathoth, that seek thy life;}* God's answer follows to the Prophet's bill of complaint.

*{the men of Anathoth}* The place of the Prophet's ordinary abode. See chap.1.1. and these seem to have been the forwardest men in informing and incensing the priests at Jerusalem against him, chap.20.10.

*{seek thy life}* Heb. *soul*; as ch.4.30. & 19.7.

*{saying, Prophesy not in the name of the LORD, that thou die not by our hand:}* Prophesy not unto us, in that manner as you do, menacing us with plagues and judgments. So Esa.30.10. Amos 2.12. & 7.16. Mic.1.6,11.

*{that thou die not by our hand}* Heb. *and thou shalt not die*. So verse 19. *and his name shall be no more remembered*; *by our hands*; by our means, some one way or other; as 2 Sam.21.22. If you do, we will dispatch you ourselves, and never trouble them of Jerusalem with you: a desperate speech, expressing a great height of rancor and malice, that they were grown unto against God's Prophet, which in likelihood they began more openly to discover, when they perceived that he had some notice of their clandestine plots and projects, though they knew not how he should come by it.

**Verse 22.** *{Therefore thus saith the LORD of hosts, Behold I will punish them:}* Heb. *visit upon them*; as ch.9.25. & 13.21. the complaints and imprecations of God's prophets, though proceeding sometime from heat of passion, are oft seconded with very dreadful and dismal effects. See 2 Kin.2.24.

*{the young men shall die by the sword,}* To wit, of the enemy, either in fight, or in surprisal of the city, 2 Chr.36.17.

*{their sons and their daughters shall die by famine.}* A death more grievous than the former, Lam.4.9.

**Verse 23.** *{And there shall be no remnant of them}* That which they intended against you, v.19. shall be inflicted upon them; a just retaliation, Deut.19.19. Yet see on ch.16.3.

*{for I will bring evil upon the men of Anathoth; even the year of their visitation}* Or, *when* (as Joel 2.20.) *I shall bring evil* (as v.11.) *upon the men of Anathoth* (v.21.) *in the year* (as Neh.1.1. & 2.1.) *of their visitation*; what time I shall come to take vengeance upon them, v.22. So ch.10.15. and 23.12.

## CHAPTER 12

**Verse 1.** *{Righteous art thou, O LORD, when I plead with thee:}* This chapter which seems to have some connection with the former, consists of three parts; 1. A disceptation between God and the Prophet, concerning some passages of his providence, verse 1,6. 2. A renewed lamentation of the sad condition of God's people, justly deserted by him, and given up to be destroyed for their sins, verse 7,14. 3. A denunciation of wrath against their bad neighbors, that had joined with the enemy against them; yet with a promise of restitution, upon their reformation, verse 15,17.

*{Righteous art thou, O LORD, when I plead with thee:}* Or, *Righteous art thou* (the pronoun supplying also the place of the verb substantive: as ch.11.19.) *though* (as ch.2.22. & 10.2.) *I should contend with thee*: as Esa.50.8. chap.2.21. you would appear so to be, if either I, or any other mortal creature should presume to enter into debate with you, concerning the justice and equity of any of your proceedings. A learned late writer would have it read by way of interrogation, *Should I dispute with thee?* and so the particle seems to be used Esa.29.16. & 36.19. which may here also be well admitted. Howsoever, the Prophet fixes this in the first place, as a ground not to be once questioned, much less doubted of, or denied, that God is just and upright in all his dealings, though weak man be not able to conceive himself, or render to others, a reason of whatsoever he does. So Psa.51.4. & 73.1. & 92.15. & 119.75,137. & 145.17. Rom.9.14.

*{yet let me talk with thee of thy judgments.}* Give me leave yet to argue a little with you, concerning some of your proceedings, that I may be the better informed, and more fully satisfied, concerning the ground and reason of them. Heb. *Let me speak judgments with thee*: yet is not *speaking of judgments* here taken in that sense, wherein this form of speech is used, for to *pass*, or *execute, a judiciary doom*, or *sentence*, ch.1.16. & chap.39.5. nor yet, as some other would have it expounded, for *speaking moderately*; because the word *judgment* has sometime a notion of *moderation* in it, chap.10.24. Psalm 112.5. but for arguing and debating a case or cause, for the better clearing of truth and right, as in judiciary courses is wont to be done.

*{Wherefore doth the way of the wicked prosper?}* This consideration of the prosperity of wicked men, and their thriving by wicked courses, has at sundry times much molested the minds of many godly ones. See Job 21.7,13. Psalm 37.1. & 73.2,12. & 94.3,4. Hab.1.4,5. and the wicked thereby take encouragement unto evil, and of nourishing impious conceits in their hearts, concerning God and his providence, Job 21.14,15. Psalm 10.3,6,11,13. & 14.1. & 94.7,8. Mal.2.17. & 3.15.

*{wherefore are they all happy, that deal very treacherously?}* Heb. *are all the perfidious practisers of perfidiousness* (that is, such as use the most perfidious practices, or that most of all practice perfidiousness. See Esay 24.16.) *at ease?* (So Lam.1.5.) they live at ease, and free from troubles, Job 12.6. & 21.9. Psalm 73.5. Zach.1.11. chap.48.11. (for that is the proper notion of the word here used, Job 3.25. & 16.12. & 20.20. & 21.23. chap.49.31.) the interrogative is supplied from the former branch; as Job 3.11,23.

**Verse 2.** *{Thou hast planted them; yea, they have taken root, they grow; yea, they bring forth fruit.}* They thrive and prosper as much as may be: a tree may be planted, and yet not take root; and then it cannot stand firm, or long continue: it may take root, and yet not thrive or grow, by reason of some inward defect, or outward accident, as the leanness of the soil, or the sharpness of the air: it may thrive and shoot up, and yet not fructify; make a goodly flourish with leaves, and blossoms, yet all be blasted, and yield no fruit: but the state and condition of the wicked here mentioned, is described by the resemblance of a tree, that being set in a rich soil, and having taken firm root, thrives exceedingly and shoots up in height, and spreads in breadth; and is not only clad with a garnish of green leaves, and goodly blossoms; but is laden also with great abundance of fair fruit; than all which, what can more be desired? See ch.11.16. Ezek.31.3,9. Dan.4.11,12,20,22.

*{Thou hast planted them}* The same God that plants his people, Psalm 44.2. & 80.8. does plant the wicked also: that is, assign them unto, and seat them in the places of their abode; he casts out others before them, and plants them in their room, Deut.2.5,9,12. Act.17.26.

*{they have taken root}* Heb. *rooted*. So Esa.40.24.

*{they grow}* In wealth and power, ch.5.27,28. Heb. *go on*; as Gen.26.13.

*{bring forth fruit}* See the like, Esay 37.31. Heb. *make fruit*; as Gen.1.11,12. Hos.9.16.

*{thou art near in their mouth, and far from their reins.}* They profess you in word, but deny you in heart and deed, Psalm 14.1. & 53.1. Tit.1.16. They make show of drawing near to you, as a people in league and covenant with you, and have you and your name oft in their mouths; but they have no heart, love or affection at all to you, their hearts are wholly estranged from you, Esa.29.13. & 48.1. & 58.1. Psalm 50.16. & 78.34,37.

*{and far}* Or, *but far*; as Esa.29.13.

**Verse 3.** *{But thou, O LORD, knowest me, thou hast seen me, and tried mine heart towards thee.}* That this disceptation of the Prophet, with God, had some reference to the carriage of his malicious townsmen before-mentioned, chap.11.21. and other his spiteful enemies towards him, appears by this passage; wherein, as other God's faithful servants in the like case, he appeals unto God himself for the sincerity of his heart and carriage, in the discharge of his duty. So Job 13.15,16. & 23.10. & 27.2,6. Psalm 7.3,10. & 17.3. & 26.1. chap.15.15. & 17.16. 2 Cor.1.12. See Chap.11.20.

*{knowest me}* Having taken trial of me: not that God did not before trial taken, know how he stood affected, Prov.15.11. but that in that regard he may the more boldly appeal unto God, who had taken such trial of him, Gen.22.12. Psalm 17.3.

*{toward thee}* Heb. *with thee*; as 2 Kin.10.15.

*{put them out as sheep for the slaughter, and prepare them for the day of slaughter.}* A petition of the same nature with that before, cha.11.20. whereof see there. Howsoever this intimates, what the issue and upshot will be of all the prosperity and tranquility of the wicked, which for a time they here enjoy, Jam.5.5. by consideration whereof, the faithful godly yet recover and gather strength against the temptation before related, Psa.37.2,20,36,38. & 73.17,22. Job 21.17,21. Mal.3.18. & 4.1.

*{prepare them}* Heb. *Sanctify them*, as Esa.13.3. ch.6.4. a borrowed speech taken from such rites as were used about the preparing either of beasts for sacrifice, or of persons to partake in a sacrifice, Exod.12.3,6. 1 Sam.16.5. 2 Chr.30.17,19. Job 1.5.

**Verse 4.** *{How long shall the land mourn, and the herbs of every field wither, for the wickedness of them that dwell therein?}* Concerning the sense of these words, there is no great doubt or difficulty: the question is only concerning the connection and coherence of them with the rest of the context: that which most interpreters either take no notice at all of, or fetch it so far about, that first to unravel their resolutions, and then to discuss them, would prove a work over-tedious. I concur with those, who conceive, that in these words, the Prophet renders a reason, why he desires to have the prosperity and tranquility of these wicked wretches to be cut off, and themselves removed and taken away, to wit, that the whole land might not fare the worse for them, and the godly party, among the rest, suffer in those general calamities, that at present lay heavy upon the main body of the land, being procured by their impieties.

*{How long shall the land mourn}* A land is said to *mourn*, when it lies waste, stripped, and despoiled of its wonted verdure and bravery, in grass, corn, plants, and fruits, wherewith it was formerly clad and adorned, whether through extremity of drought, 1 King.17.1. & 18.5. or spoil and havoc made of all, by storm and tempest, Prov.28.3. or by vermin, Joel 1.4. & 2.3. or by the irruption of an enemy, Esay 1.7. as being now in a mourning weed. So Esay 24.4. & 33.9. chap.23.10. Lam.1.4. Joel 1.10. Now this some would put off to the waste that was to be made by the Chaldean invasion, chap.4.20. verse 10,11. but they show not what may consist here with the current of the context. It seems rather to be meant of the present dearth, by means of a long continued drought lying heavy upon the land at present. Whereof, see at large, ch.14.1,2.

*{herbs}* Heb. *herb*, or *herbage*: as might well be rendered: and so rather than *grass*; as it is, Psalm 72.16. & 92.7. for the word is more general.

*{for the wickedness of them that dwell therein.}* So Psalm 107.34.

*{the beasts are consumed, and the birds:}* Or, *the cattle* (as Psa.50.10.) *and the fowl*. Such cattle and fowl as are wont to be kept about men's houses, which in times of extreme drought and dearth for want of food, either perish, or stray the one, and fly away the other. See cha.4.25,26. & 9.10. & 14.5,6.

*{because they said, He shall not see our last end}* This impious speech of those wicked ones, some understand as a denial of God's providence and prescience, like that, Psa.73.11. and they render the words, *He seeth not our latter end*. God himself does not know, what our end shall be. Others, as spoken in way of presumption; that whatsoever the prophets might say, God would not bring those evils that they threatened upon them; and these render the words, *He will not see our latter end*: he will not suffer such an end to be made of us, as they say. But I conceive rather, that these words were spoken by them of Jeremy; though redounding and reaching to God himself, whose messenger he was, and whose messages he delivered to them; as if they had said, This Jeremy tells us what at length will befall us, and that all our present prosperity shall end in extreme misery: but his words are but wind, he will never live to see any such matter befall us; we shall sooner see an end of him, than he any such end of us. See ch.5.13. So Gen.19.14.

**Verse 5.** *{If thou hast run with the footmen, and they have wearied thee, then how canst thou contend with horses?}* Hitherto was the Prophet's speech to God. Now follows God's speech, whether in way of answer to the Prophet, or leaving him, directed to the people, is much controverted. Some, both Jewish commenters and ours, conceive it as an answer returned to the Prophet's expostulatory complaint; and either checking him for it, or meeting with the root and ground of it. Some suppose, that in it God checks and controls the Prophet's curiosity and presumption, in taking upon him to inquire into those things that were far beyond the reach of his shallow capacity: and they thus expound the similitude of *horse* and *foot*. If you are not able to discover the privy plots and projects of men, that stand on even ground with you, and are silly creatures like yourself, as that conspiracy of your own townsmen against you, chap.11.18,19. how is it, that you take upon you to search into, or suppose that you may be able to comprehend the reasons and grounds of God's secret counsels, concerning the administration of the affairs of the world? Others, (which is more probable) are of the mind, that the Lord considering from what ground this disceptation of the Prophet proceeded, to wit, from some inward disquiet of mind, that the wrongful and spiteful carriage of his townsmen had possessed him with; and animating him unto a quiet and patient undergoing these brunts of their malicious demeanor, by intimating unto him, that there were other manner of conflicts and oppositions to be dealt with in the further process of his prophetical function; against which he was to arm himself. As if he had said, if these meaner men of Anathoth, that are but as *foot*, do so molest you, that you are almost tired out with them; how will you be able to bicker with those great masterful ones at Jerusalem, that are in regard of them, as *horse* to *foot*? Thus they that understand it as God's speech to the Prophet. But divers, whereof the Chaldee also gives some hint, would have it to be the speech of God to the people; demanding of them, to control and quell their vain confidence and security, how they will be able to make their part good with the Chaldean, so potent an adversary, when as far meaner than they have at divers times put them to so much trouble. It seems to have been a proverbial form of speech among them; as one not unlike it, is found in Greek authors, *A footman running with a Lydian-chariot*: and, *foot fighting with horse in a plain*.

*{if thou hast run with the footmen and they have wearied thee,}* Or, *if* (as Deut.12.21. Esay 36.7.) *when thou runnest with footmen they weary*, or, *tire thee*. See the like construction, chap.7.27. & 8.4. & 11.11.

*{then how canst thou contend with horses?}* Heb. *and* (as chap.8.9.) *wilt thou mingle*, or, *close*, (as chap.22.15.) *with horses?* that is, *with horsemen*; as Deut.20.1. for whom we also use the word *horse*: the verb is in a potential notion: as ch.2.23,32.

*{and if in a land of peace,}* whereunto *thou trustedst*, they wearied you, *then how wilt thou do in the swelling of Jordan?* The insertions in this our version, are taken from the former part, all save that of the relative, which is not unfrequent; as chap.8.13. & 11.19. Yet some insert a divers clause, thus rendering the words, *and if when thou trustedst in a land of peace*, you were deceived, *how wilt thou then do in the rising of Jordan?* For sense they come much to one; I suppose our version the better. These apply it to the Prophet; who, if in his own native habitation among his kindred and acquaintance, he did not deem himself safe, or free from opposition and molestation, he had less reason to look for a quiet life among those haughty and lofty ones at Jerusalem. Others apply it to the Jewish state, which if it were so much annoyed with her bad neighbors the Moabites, Ammonites, and Edomites that were allied to her; she would much less be able to secure herself, when the Chaldean forces, like a strong stream of some great river, surrounding its banks, should break in upon her. See the like, Esay 8.7,8. & 59.19. chap.46.7. & 49.19. and some of these omitting those former insertions, thus read the words; *and though* (as Esa.30.20.) *in a peaceable land thou mayst confide*, or, *be secure*; *yet* (Heb. *and*; as chap.7.26.) *what wilt thou do in the swelling of Jordan?* though you seem now safe while all is as yet quiet with you; yet you will find it to be otherwise, when a potent adversary shall overrun your country.
