*{in the land of peace}* Or, *a land of peace*; that is, say some, *a land of friends*, or, *a friendly land*: as, *a man of peace*, for, *a confederate*, or, *a friend*, Psalm 41.9. others, *a land of peace*; that is, *a quiet, and peaceable land*: as, *an habitation of peace*, for, *a peaceable habitation*, Esay 32.18. for that which a great man has; *a land of peace*, for, *a land of no defense*, or, *strength*, to withstand or keep out an enemy: as, *a land of war*, for, a land well fortified and fitted for war; a land of defense, seems to carry here no probability at all with it.

*{in the swelling of Jordan}* Which in harvest time uses to rise up above his banks, and overflow all the lower grounds bordering upon it, Josh.3.15. 1 Chron.12.15. and there want not, who suppose some allusion here to Nebuchadnezzar's forces that were to pass over Jordan in his expedition against Judea; and others again to the lions and leopards that had their dens thereabouts; or in mount Lebanon, where the head of it was, Cant.4.8. chap.49.19. and 50.44. Zach.11.3. But these things seem over-far fetched.

**Verse 6.** *{For even thy brethren, and the house of thy father, even they have dealt treacherously with thee; yea, they have called a multitude after thee:}* The men of Anathoth, your countrymen, allies and nearest kindred, though they make fair shows of love and good liking to you outwardly, yet are covertly plotting your death, informing and exclaiming to the state against you, and inciting them to work your ruin, chap.11.21. & 20.10. or if it be referred not to the Prophet, but to the people; your confederates, O Judah, and in regard of descent, your brethren, the issue of Lot, Psalm 83.8. the Moabites and Ammonites, Gen.19.37,38. and the issue of Isaac, the Edomites, ch.35.29. & 36.1. Mal.1.2. though they may seem at present to comply with you, chap.27.3. yet are inwardly falsehearted, and will join with the enemy against you, ch.4.30. v.14. 2 Kin.24.3. See ch.4.30.

*{have called a multitude}* Or, *a full assembly*. Heb. *full*. So, *a fullness*, Esay 31.4. or, *they cry*, or, *will cry, full*, or, with *a full* throat, *after thee*: a defect of the subject here, as of the adjunct in the like form, Esay 58.1. so, *a full*, for, *a full cup*, Psalm 73.10. Of the Edomites' cry against Jerusalem, see Psalm 137.7. *to cry after thee*, seems here to be no other than, to cry unto, or upon others, to prosecute you with hue and cry, as some notorious malefactor.

*{believe them not, though they speak fair words to thee}* Trust them not, though they speak you never so fair; for they mind nothing less than what they speak, ch.9.4,6. Prov.26.15. *fair words*. Heb. *good words*, or, *things*. So ch.52.32.

**Verse 7.** *{I have forsaken mine house;}* God having done with the Prophet, and hinted unto him what he must further expect and prepare himself for, as before, chap.1.17,18. does now return to tell, what he intends to do, not with the men of Anathoth only; as chap.11.22,23. but with Jerusalem, and the whole state of Judah.

*{I have forsaken my house}* I am resolved to leave, and abandon my Temple, that has been hitherto as my palace, my court, the place of my special residence, Psalm 78.68,69. and 132.13,14. ch.7.14. & 11.15.

*{I have left mine heritage}* Or, *possession*. My people, that were sometime my peculiar possession, and as dear unto me, as any man's inheritance is to him, ch.10.16. & 50.11.

*{I have given the dearly beloved of my soul into the hands of her enemies}* My people, that were sometime so dear to me, so deep in mine affection. See ch.11.15.

*{the dearly beloved of my soul}* Or, *my dearly beloved*: *my soul*, for myself; as Psalm 3.2. so, *his soul*, for, himself, Amos 6.8. but the word *soul*, makes the speech the more emphatical: as Psalm 42.2. Cant.1.2. & 3.1. Heb. *the love of my soul*. See 1 Sam.20.17.

*{into the hand}* Or, *power*: as Judg.6.13. ch.20.5.

**Verse 8.** *{Mine heritage is unto me, as a lion in the forest; it cryeth out against me, therefore have I hated it.}* Because that this might seem strange, that those whom God had so entirely affected before, he should now deal so harshly with, as to deliver them up unto the power and pleasure of their utter enemies; the Lord shows here, that the cause and ground of this so great an alteration in his affection toward them, and dealings with them, proceeded not from himself, but from them: they who were sometime his *sheep*, Psalm 77.20. and 100.3. were now become fierce *lions* roaring against him, and rending his messengers, chap.2.30. Matth.23.37. Acts 7.51,53. and that is it that has turned his love into hatred, Isaiah 63.10. for what the Jewish doctors here have of men's leaving their way upon the hearing of lions roar; and of the cry of oppression, Isaiah 5.7. and of idolaters in the service of their idols, 1 Kings 18.26,28. is all beside the intent of the place.

*{Mine heritage is}* Or, *is become*, as Isaiah 1.21. to intimate a change.

*{a lion in the forest}* That is, *a lion of the forest*: as, *mountains in Gilboa*, for, *mountains of Gilboa*: 2 Sam.1.21.

*{it cryeth out against me}* Or, *yelleth aloud*; as ch.4.15. Heb. *hath given out her voice*: as ch.4.16. Joel 2.11.

*{have I hated}* Or, *I hate*; as Mal.1.2.

**Verse 9.** *{Mine heritage is unto me as a speckled bird; the birds round about are against her;}* By another similitude, God seems here to set out the cause of his disaffection towards his people: because they were become, as like ramping lions, so like ravenous fowls; for which cause also the Lord was resolved to beset them with enemies, that as birds of prey, should in like manner prey upon them, as they had done upon others; and call those in upon them, who as wild beasts should devour them. Some read the words as by way of interrogation, joined with admiration, *Is mine heritage become thus unto me? are the birds round about against her?* Others, by way of enunciation, as our version exhibits it: the Jewish critics, and the use of the particle, carry it the former way; which I therefore also incline unto: yet so, as that I conceive a defect of the negative in the text; which in such interrogations is not unusual. So 1 Sam.2.27,28. Job 20.4. See chap.31.20. and I suppose the words may well be rendered, *Is not mine heritage* such a *bird to me? are not the birds*, or, *shall not the birds, be round about against her?* and thus our ancienter English exhibited it: which in effect also, comes home to the present version. I shall subjoin a learned writer's version, with his exposition; and so leave it; *O ye coloured birds*, (you birds of what color soever you be,) *mine heritage is mine*; (and I may dispose of it, as I please, as ch.27.5.) *O ye birds be round about against her*: come and beset her on every side; and bring the beasts along with you. I adhere still to the former, as better suiting with what went before, verse 8. for the former branch at least, though not wholly rejecting what is here exhibited, for the latter.

*{as a speckled bird}* The word here used, and not elsewhere in this form found; comes from a root, which though nowhere used in the Hebrew text of Scripture, yet is found in the Syriac of Daniel, Dan.4.15,23,33. and 5.21. as also in the Syriac and Arabic versions of the New Testament, Matt.20.23. Luk.7.38. and it is of the same notion with another very near it in Hebrew, both signifying *to dip*, *to bedew*; and by consequence, *to dye*, or *color*; the word that is used for *a ring*, issuing from the one; and *the finger* that wears it, from the other: now because a term springing from this root, seems to signify a *tincture* of some remarkable color, or variety of color, Judg.5.30. hence it comes to pass, that the old Latin renders it, *a bird dyed*; and our English, *a speckled bird*: and hereby, say some of the Jewish writers, is meant a kind of *owl* red with black spots, which other birds cannot abide, and are wont therefore to flock about her, and beat her. Others would have it a *peacock*, Job 39.13. or some other bird as curiously feathered, as if she were painted, or dyed, Psalm 68.13. which other birds therefore for her beauty, use to gaze upon and admire; nor want there those that further drive on this conceit, supposing an allusion to birds kept in a cage, partly, for their goodly shape, and sightliness; and partly for their pleasant note, which men are wont to take much delight in; that such had this people been unto God, till they changed their note; and did not now *sing as a bird*, but *roar as a lion*, verse 8. so one: or, till they became, of tame ones *wild*, like those that live abroad *in the woods*, verse 8. says another. So expounding the word *speckled*, as if it signified *wild*, or none but wild ones were such: or *is become wild*, that is, fierce, as some render it. See verse 8. which hither also they draw: but these things seem either fabulous, or forced. Some of ours conceive no special kind of bird to be intended, but any *speckled*, or *pied* fowl to be designed: and that this people are here so styled, because not contenting themselves with God's livery, and the simplicity of his service, they had put themselves into a garb patched up as a parti-colored coat, of divers sorts of superstitious rites and practices, taken up as strange fashions from foreign nations, Ezek.8.5,10,11,16. And this seems more probable than any of the former. Howbeit, some of the Jewish writers, by *a bird dyed*, or *stained*, understand here a fowl besprinkled with blood; as garments therewith besprinkled, are said to be *dyed*, or *stained*, Esay 63.1,2. that which frequently befalls birds of prey: and some of them conceive it to be spoken of God's people; as if it were said, *Are the bloody*

*{birds of prey}* with *mine heritage? are the birds of prey*, I say, gotten *round about her?* This, it is true, offers too much violence to the text: but yet I suppose it hints us the true notion of the term. I conceive therefore the meaning near the same in effect, that was before intimated, verse 8. *Is not mine heritage become to me as a stained, or bedewed bird of prey?* for such fowl does the word here used properly signify, as both the general use of it shows, Gen.15.11. Job 28.7. Esay 18.6. Ezek.39.4. as also the notation of it confirms; for the word it comes of, signifies, *hastily*, or *fiercely, to fly*, or *fall upon* ought, 1 Sam.14.33. & 25.14. and it is not amiss therefore rendered, *a ravenous bird*, Esay 46.11. God's people then are said to have been *a ravenous bird*, or, *a fowl of prey*, in regard of that rapine and oppression, that was grown so rife among them. See chap.6.6. and not so alone, but such an one all *stained*, or *bedewed* with gore blood; that by their cruel courses had been shed among them, wherewith their garments are said to be all over besmeared, chap.2.34. and this I take to be the genuine sense of the place. To which also will in effect come home, what some late interpreters of prime note have; who, because from the same root with this arises a word signifying *a finger*, would have the word here used to signify *a fingered bird*, or, *a taloned fowl*; that is, a fowl with great *talons* like *fingers*: and it is true, that Pliny, lib.11. cap.47. sorts birds or fowls into two ranks; some *fingered*, some *palm-footed* ones: but this term is much more general, comprising as well sparrows and wrens, as eagles or falcons: and the derivation hereof in the original, is nothing so familiar and free as the former, unto which therefore I adhere. In the text there is a defect of the note of similitude, but such as renders the sentence more emphatical, as ch.5.8. and as I conceive an elegant redundancy in that form; *unto me*, as if it were said, *is become me*; as, *I will go me*; Cant.4.6. See on chap.11.17. What this people were become to him and his prophets, or to him in his prophets, he had showed before, verse 8. here what they were among themselves one towards another.

*{the birds round about are against her?}* Or, *Are not the ravenous fowl round about against her?* the word *fowl* in the Hebrew is, as before, singular, but here in a notion collective, as all agree, and we also commonly so use the word, *fowl*; and it may well be rendered in the time present, according to the prophetical strain, as foretelling what in God's purpose, already resolved on, should be; So verse 10,12. or, as some render the words, not in way of interrogation, or of enunciation, but in way of invitation; *O ye ravenous birds* fly in *on every side against her*. Howsoever we read it, it is as if he had said, as she is become like a ravenous bird, so with a company of ravenous fowl, therein like herself, shall she be on every side beset, that shall prey upon her, destroy her, and help to devour her; and by these ravenous fowls are questionless designed Nebuchadnezzar and his forces, that should begirt and take Jerusalem; as Cyrus and his army are resembled by the like, Esay 46.11.

*{come ye, assemble all the beasts of the field, come to devour.}* An invitation of wild beasts to come in upon them, either as wolves; and the like into a flock of sheep to worry them, and prey upon them, as Esay 56.9. or, as wild boars into a vineyard, to root up and spoil all, as Psalm 80.13. or as ravenous beasts into a field, where many carcasses of men slain lie, to feed upon them, as chap.7.33. and 15.3. Rev.19.17,18. and this last the Jewish commenters pitch upon; withal rendering a reason why the *fowl* are first mentioned, because they first commonly, from afar off, discover their prey, Job 39.29,30. Matt.24.28. Luk.17.37. and the beasts usually come after them. But this seems over-curious: certain it is, that, by ravenous birds and beasts, such as are wont to prey upon the less, and more feeble of either kind, and to destroy and devour them, are here represented, those forces consisting of many several nations, as the Chaldeans, Assyrians, Syrians, Ammonites, Moabites, Edomites, and others, that under the conduct of the King of Babylon, should make such spoil and havoc of God's people, 2 King.24.2,3. chap.1.15.

*{Come ye}* Or, *Go to*: Go your ways, and get you about it; for it is a term commonly used, to express a setting or inciting of any to go about some employment, as Josh.2.16. 2 Kings 1.2,6. chap.7.12. and some conceive it, as spoken to the fowls both to come in themselves, and to bring along with them the beasts also. Howsoever, it is as if God were setting some on work, to go and summon people, as wild beasts, to come in upon his people.

*{all the beasts}* Heb. *every beast*; as Psalm 50.10. wild beasts of all sorts, that use to prey upon man or beast. See the like, Esay 56.9.

*{come}* Heb. *make*, or, *cause to come*; for the injunction is not directed to the beasts themselves, but to those that should bring them together.

*{to devour}* Heb. *to eat*; as ch.10.25. Rev.19.18.

**Verse 10.** *{Many Pastors have destroyed my vineyard,}* The kings and princes that serve under Nebuchadnezzar, so termed before, Chap.6.3. have destroyed, that is, shall destroy (as sure to be done as if done already) God's people, his vineyard, Esay 5.7. a similitude borrowed from shepherds, or neat-herds, that turn their cattle into vineyards. For they seem to turn it a wrong way, that expound it of the governors of God's people, either civil, or ecclesiastical, who by their misgovernment had ruined the state, Esay 59.9,11. chap.10.21.

*{they have trode my portion under foot}* The word signifies any *portion* of land, or the like, 2 Sam.14.30. 2 King.3.19. taken from the manner of dividing possessions, and inheritances, and assigning each one his peculiar share, or *portion*; Josh.13.7. and 18.10. Prov.17.2. So God's people are said to be God's *portion*, or, *possession*, Deut.32.9. as before his *heritage*, verse 8,9. and his *vineyard*, verse 10. as also the land wherein they lived, Lev.25.23,24. this the enemy is said to tread down, as beasts do a pasture ground, or a garden, where they spoil as much with their feet, as with their feed, Esay 5.5. & 63.18.

*{they have made my pleasant portion a desolate wilderness.}* This aggravates the mischief and misery done by them, that they have made such spoil, not of some common field, or an ordinary pasture, but of a curious and choice paradise, which they have so spoiled, that they have left it like a wild waste, Joel 2.3.

*{made}* Heb. *given*; as ch.9.10.

*{my pleasant portion}* Heb. *my portion of desire*, or, *delight*, as ch.3.19. See Psa.16.6.

*{a desolate wilderness}* Not such a wilderness wherein cattle use to graze, and people, some at least, inhabit; as 1 Sam.17.18. & 25.21. Luk.1.80. but such as are wholly abandoned, in regard of the barrenness of them, to wild beasts, Deut.32.10. Esay 30.6. ch.2.2. Mark 1.13. Heb. *a wilderness of desolation*; that is, *a most desolate wilderness*, as Joel 2.3. & 3.19.

**Verse 11.** *{They have made it desolate}* Heb. *He hath put it into desolation*; as Zeph.2.13. He, that is, God, say some, v.12. but it is God that speaks it: Nebuchadnezzar, or the people that come with him, say others not amiss. Howbeit, it may well be rendered simply, the verb being indefinite, *It is made utterly desolate*; as afterwards. See the like, ch.10.4.

*{and being desolate it mourneth unto me.}* It affords me a very sad and rueful spectacle; See v.4. for they seem to stray from the intent of the place, who expound it of the people's mourning to God, and his not regarding them, ch.11.14.

*{the whole land is laid desolate}* So ch.4.20,27.

*{because no man layeth it to heart.}* Because no man lays to heart God's menaces, that they may take some course, by repentance and reformation to prevent them, chap.5.3,12,13. and 11.15. and 18.18. or, *yet*; (as the particle is taken, Job 5.7. Esay 9.1.) *no man layeth it to heart*; few, or none amidst these grievous calamities, do seriously consider and apprehend aright, the grounds of this dreadful judgment, and the procuring causes of it, See Esay 42.25. chap.9.12. Hosea 7.9. Heb. *there is not a man putting it upon heart*, as Deut.11.18. a defect of the particle, *it*, as chap.6.11.

**Verse 12.** *{The spoilers are come upon all high places through the wilderness.}* Or, *In the plain*; as Esay 63.13,14. Lam.4.19. either that lay in the way, between Chaldea and Judea, chap.4.11,12. or those within the land of Judah, chap.3.2,21. & 7.29. No place of fortification or defense, such as high places naturally are, in regard of their situation and the difficulty of access unto them, is able to stay or to withstand them; See Habb.1.10. See also chap.7.29. where, as here also, a learned man would have the word rendered; not *high*, but *low* places, or, *plains, in a wilderness*. Whereof see there.

*{for the sword of the LORD shall devour, from the one end of the land, even to the other end of the land}* The sword of the enemy, called the *sword of the Lord*, because drawn, and coming by his appointment and secret design (as Esa.34.5,6. chap.47.6.) runs through the whole land, from end to end (Heb. *from the end of the land, and unto the end of the land*, as Deut.28.64. cha.25.33.) and destroys all before it. Heb. *eateth*, as verse 9. 2 Sam.11.25. chap.2.30. and 46.10. and it is spoken as a thing present.

*{no flesh shall have peace}* Heb. *there is not peace* (that is, *safety*; as 1 Kings 8.27,28. chap.4.10.) *to all* (that is, *any*; as Gen.3.1. Job 1.11. & 8.12.) *flesh*, *all flesh*; for, *any flesh*, as Psalm 143.2. Rom.3.20. and, *any flesh* here, for, any of that people, as chap.45.5. Mat.24.22. those that promised to themselves and others, security and immunity, shall then find it to fare far otherwise with them, than they expected or hoped for, Esa.28.15,17,18. chap.4.9,10. and 6.14,15. and 8.11,12.

**Verse 13.** *{They have sown wheat, but shall reap thorns:}* According to that curse, Gen.3.18. Deut.28.38. no good fruit shall come of all their labor, Gen.4.12. Job 31.4. Mic.6.15. Hag.1.6. no good issue of all their vain endeavors whereby they hope to help themselves, ch.2.37. & 3.23.

*{but shall reap thorns}* Or, *but* (Heb. *and*, as verse 2.) *reap thorns*: There is an elegant consonancy in the words of *reaping* and *thorns*, in the original; as if it were said, *reap riffraff*; nothing that is good for ought.

*{they put themselves to pain, but shall not prevail:}* They may tire themselves out with plots and projects, and this course and that course, to wind themselves out of the difficulties and straits, that they have cast themselves into, but all will be to no purpose, ch.2.26,37. & 11.11. For the Rabbine that understands it of their crying unto God, until their hearts ache again, and not prevailing with him, as Psa.18.41. is as much out of the way, as the same of some other, on verse 11.

*{and they shall be ashamed of their revenues}* Heb. *of your revenues*: a passage from person to person, as ch.11.15,16,19. They shall be ashamed to see how little good comes of all their labors, Eccl.5.16. See Esa.17.10,11.

*{because of the fierce anger of the LORD.}* Which shall blast all their proceedings, as chap.51.45. Of the attribute, see Isa.13.9. ch.4.8,26.

**Verse 14.** *{Thus saith the LORD against all mine evil neighbours, that touch the inheritance that I have caused my people Israel to inherit;}* This prophecy is shut up for the stay and support of the small remnant of faithful ones, mixed here and there among the main corrupt body of the Jewish people with a comfortable close, promising restitution to them, vindication of the wrongs by their bad neighbors done unto them; together with a gracious offer of mercy also to them, if they turned unto God, and joined with his people in the true and sincere service of him.

*{against all mine evil neighbours Against}*, or, *concerning*, rather; as ch.18.8,10. & 49.1,7. *mine*; not the Prophet's, as may seem, but God's, in whose person he speaks it, as by the words following appears: and *his neighbours* he terms them, because they bordered upon his *portion*, verse 10. thereby understanding, not the Chaldeans, as some, (for they are still spoken of as a remote people, Esa.39.3. ch.5.15. & 6.22.) nor the Egyptians neither, as some other, (for Palestine lay between Egypt and them) but the Philistines, Syrians, Phenicians, Moabites, Ammonites, and Edomites, who bordering upon God's people, had invaded and annoyed them, by their present distracted and distressed condition taking occasion so to do, 2 Kin.24.2. Psa.137.7. ch.41.9. Obad.11,14.

*{that touch the inheritance}* That is, as some, that border upon it, are contiguous unto it: but as others rather, that wrong, hurt, and annoy them, in the least degree; for there is an emphasis, in the term of *touching*. So Job 1.11. Psa.105.15. Zach.2.8.

*{which I have caused my people Israel to inherit}* Psa.135.12. and they therefore have no right, nor can make any just claim unto, Judg.11.23,24. ch.49.1.

*{Behold, I will pluck them out of their land;}* I will deal with them, as they have dealt with my people: as they have dispossessed my people of their land; so will I cause them to be dispossessed of theirs. See ch.30.16. that which was also done by Nebuchadnezzar into whose hands they were likewise given, ch.25.20,22. and 47. and 48. and 49.1,27.

*{and pluck out the house of Judah from among them.}* I will deliver my people, as by main might, snatching them out of their hands, that have possessed themselves of them, and bringing them back from those places where in captivity they shall abide, Deut.30.3. Esa.11.11,12. & 27.12,13. cha.32.37. Ezek.20.37,38. and there is an elegant diversity and disparity of notion in the same word of *plucking out* here used in this branch, and the former: the like whereunto, see ch.34.17.

**Verse 15.** *{And it shall come to pass after that I have plucked them out}* Heb. *it shall be*; as ch.3.16. So v.16. *after that I have plucked them out*; not my people only from among them, but them out of their own countries also, verse 14.

*{I will return and have compassion on them,}* Or, *I will again have compassion on them*; as Psa.71.20. & 85.6.

*{and bring again every man to his heritage, and every man to his land.}* Reduce them to their own country, and restore them to their several possessions again. See the like promises, Esa.18.7. & 19.22,24. and 23.17,18. & 24.22. ch.49.6,39.

*{every man}* Heb. *a man*; as ch.5.8.

**Verse 16.** *{And it shall come to pass, if they will diligently learn the ways of my people, to swear by my name, The LORD liveth: as they taught my people to swear by Baal; then shall they be built in the midst of my people}* The gracious promise of restitution is not made to these people, but upon condition of relinquishing their former idol-services, and embracing the services of the true God, having learned it from his people abiding among them, as God's people had formerly learned the service of their idols, by intermingling of themselves with them, Num.25.1,2. Psa.106.35,36.

*{diligently learn}* Heb. *learning learn*.

*{the ways of my people}* That is, the manners, fashions, customs, and practice of my people: as, *the way of the nations*, ch.10.2.

*{to swear by my name}* Not, *to my name*; as giving up their names, and by a solemn oath of allegiance engaging themselves to me, as Isa.19.18. but *swear by my name*; that is, *by me*, as Isa.48.1. *swearing by him*, being here put, as a principal part of religious worship, for the whole service of God, as Deut.10.20. ch.4.2. as the *swearing by Baal*, and idols in general, for the superstitious and idolatrous service of them, ch.5.7. Zeph.1.5.

*{the LORD liveth}* Or, *by the life of God*: the most usual form of an oath in those times, ch.4.2. & 5.2.

*{then}* Heb. *and*; as ch.4.1,2.

*{built in the midst of my people}* Or, *among my people*; as Deut.13.1. & 18.15. ch.9.6. that is, as some, they shall dwell quietly, as before in vicinity or neighborhood with my people: or rather, they shall be firmly settled in the places of their former abode, (as the term of *building* is used, 2 Sam.7.27. Job 22.23. chap.33.7. Mal.3.15.) and shall, withal, have a share among my people in such spiritual privileges as they enjoy. See Isaiah 19.23,25. and 56.5,7.

**Verse 17.** *{But if they will not obey, I will utterly pluck up and destroy that nation, saith the LORD.}* Heb. *And* (as verse 12.) *if they will not hear* (that is, *obey*, as Psalm 81.11. chap.7.23. if any of them shall refuse to yield hereunto) *and* (or, *then*, as verse 16.) *I will plucking up pluck up, and will destroy that nation*; that shall refuse so to do. See Isa.60.12.

## CHAPTER 13

**Verse 1.** *{Thus saith the LORD unto me,}* In this prophecy, or sermon, (which seems to have been delivered in the reign of Jehojacin: see v.18.) partly by the type of a girdle rotted and become fit for no use; and partly by the type of bottles, full of liquor, dashed one against another; God sets before the eyes of his people, how he purposed to deal with them; and that principally for the contempt of his admonitions and menaces, and their willful obstinacy and persistence in their evil courses, which by continued custom they were become so inured unto, that nothing could withdraw them from them.

*{Thus saith}* Or, *said the Lord unto me*; for he tells them of an errand, not that God now was sending him, but had sometime before sent him on.

*{Go, and get thee a linen girdle, and put it upon thy loins, and put it not in water.}*

*{Go}* Heb. *Going*; as ch.2.2. & 3.12.

*{get thee}* Or, *buy thee*, as ch.19.1. & 32.6. *get thee*, or, *buy thee*: as *go thee*, Gen.12.1. See ch.11.9.

*{a linen girdle}* Heb. *a girdle of flaxes*, or, *linens*: as, *a garment of linens*, Lev.13.47. and it seems to intend, not an ordinary girdle, either leathern, or woolen, such as were commonly worn, 2 Kin.1.8. Mark 3.4. but such an one as the better sort of persons wore, Isa.22.21. Ezek.44.17.

*{put it upon thy loins}* The wonted place of wearing girdles, 2 King.1.8. Isa.11.5. why he was to do this, is afterward showed, verse 11.

*{and put it not in water.}* Or, *but*; as chap.12.2. do not wet it: do nothing yourself to it, that may cause it to rot: thereby implying, that neither God, nor ought from him, had been any cause of the general corruption, and consequently of the destruction of this people, by that girdle resembled, verse 9,11. Hosea 13.9. & 14.1. Nor can I assent unto that learned late writer, who conceives, that the Prophet was forbidden to lay it in water for the softening of it, that it might remain stiff; resembling that people's stiffness of heart and neck, Isaiah 48.4. and much less with those Jewish doctors, who would have the meaning to be, that though with long wearing it in the place of sweat Ezek.44.18. it would grow sweaty and nasty, yet he should not wash it, that it might rot the sooner.

**Verse 2.** *{So I got a girdle according to the word of the LORD, and put it on my loins}* I did as God bade me, I got me such a girdle and wore it, as men use to do. Heb. *And*: (as Ezek.3.14.) *I got*, or, *bought*; as chap.32.9. *word*, for, *command*: as Jonah 3.3.

**Verse 3.** *{And the word of the LORD came to me the second time saying;}* Heb. *was to me*; as ch.1.13.

**Verse 4.** *{Take the girdle that thou hast got, which is upon thy loins,}* Or, *Take the girdle that thou boughtest*; and which you wear.

*{and arise, go to Euphrates, and hide it there in a hole of the rock.}* Whether this were actually done, or in vision only, it being so long a journey for the Prophet to take, is very doubtful: and both the Jewish writers and ours seem divided about it. I incline with the most, to the judgment of those, who suppose it to have been done in vision, only so far forth as concerns his journey, as well for the carrying of it thither, as for the fetching of it back again, v.7. not unlike that journey of Ezekiel, from out of Chaldea to Jerusalem, and from thence back again to the captivity in Chaldea, Ezek.8.3. and 11.24.

*{arise,}* As ch.1.17. See there.

*{go to Euphrates}* Heb. *Prat*, or, *Phrat*, Gen.2.14. and it is made one of the limits, or boundaries of the promised land, Deut.1.7. & 11.24. Josh.1.4. The journey thither with this girdle thus enjoined, some would have to signify, that destruction which should befall them for their traveling into Assyria, seeking unto, and relying on, the King of Assyria, whose country bordered upon that river, as safe under his protection, 2 Kin.16.7. ch.2.18,36. Others, with whom I rather concur, that they should be removed out of their country, and carried captive unto Babylon, situate upon that river, Psa.137.1. See on Esay 21.1. Ezek.1.1. & 3.15.

*{hide it there in the hole of the rock}* Thus the Jewish commenters expound the word here used, as our version renders it, *an hole*, both in this place, and elsewhere; where people are said to be hid in the like, chap.16.16. Isa.7.19. and so both the ancient Greek and old Latin exhibit it. Howbeit, the Chaldee renders it, *on the smoothness of the rock*; using the same term, both Ezek.26.14. & Isa.57.6.

in which latter place, the Hebrew has, *the smooth pebbles of the brook*: Whence it may be deemed, that the paraphrast conceived, that it should lie hid among the beach; to which purpose, a learned writer of ours supposes, that it should be laid in some place, where by the washing of the river it might be corrupted: but that were rather to lay it where it were to be washed away with the current of the stream; and not to be found at his return again. Some other late commenters of note, render it, *in the projecture*, or, *overhanging of the rock*; to gain thereby some strength to their former conceit of this people's for safeguard, putting themselves under the Assyrian king's protection, which should be hereby designed: but neither is the signification of the word probable; nor needed that straining of the term here for their purpose; *holes* of rocks, as well as brows and prominences, being for security commonly repaired unto. See Isaiah 2.19. and indeed where should a girdle be hid out of sight, but in some hole? and why in the hole of a dry rock, rather than in the moist ground, but that nothing from without might help to rot it, if it did rot, but its continuance there of itself?

**Verse 5.** *{So I went and hid it by Euphrates, as the LORD commanded me.}* How this is supposed to have been done, see on verse 4.

*{So}* Heb. *And*; as verse 2.

*{by Euphrates}* The Greek and Latin render it, *in Euphrates*; but the words of the injunction confirm our version: and the particle is so used, Josh.1.25,26,32. where *in Shechem*, is, by it, beside it, or near to it: and so, *in Bezek*, Judg.1.4. and 1 Sam.11.8. and, *in Anathoth*, ch.32.7. See ch.20.2.

**Verse 6.** *{And it came to pass after many days, that the LORD said unto me, Arise, go to Euphrates, and take the girdle from thence, which I commanded thee to hide there.}* Heb. *And it was from the end of many days, and the Lord said unto me*: as Gen.4.3. & 8.5. that is, a long time after: as Lev.15.25. Num.9.19.

*{take from thence}* Or, *fetch from thence*: *take*, for, take and bring; as Genesis 27.9. So, *take*, for, *take* and heap, Prov.25.22. *receive*, for receive and give. Psalm 68.18. So chap.36.14,21.

**Verse 7.** *{Then I went to Euphrates, and digged, and took the girdle from the place, where I had hid it;}* Of this second journey, see as before on verse 4.

*{Then}* Heb. *And*; as ch.11.5. or, *So*: as v.5. because the next verse begins with, *Then*.

*{digged}* Either having before stopped up the mouth of the hole, where he hid it, that it might be there the safer, or, finding it by some other means obstructed. So Ezekiel dug in a vision, Ezek.8.8.

*{where I hid it}* Heb. *which*, or, *in which, I hid it there*: that which, though it may seem a redundancy, as the like is found, Gen.2.11. and 3.23. yet the relative may have reference to the *hole*, or the *cave*, and the adverb of place, to the *rock*, wherein that hole, or the region near the river, where that rock was situate.

*{and behold the girdle was rotted, it was profitable for nothing}* An emblem both of that unprofitable condition, that this people by corrupting themselves and their ways, had brought themselves unto; Psalm 14.1,3. Isa.1.4. Mat.5.13. Rom.3.12. Tit.1.16. and of that vile and sorry condition, that by their captivity in foreign remote parts, and their long continuance therein, they should for their wickedness be justly reduced and brought unto, Lam.3.45. Ezek.33.10. & 37.11.

*{it was profitable for nothing}* Or, as we say, *it was good for nothing*; and so is it well rendered, v.10. Heb. *it would not thrive*, or, *be useful*, (so is the word here used, Ezek.15.4.) *for all*; that is, *for ought*. See on chap.12.12. So Gen.14.23.

**Verse 8.** *{Then the word of the LORD came unto me, saying,}* Heb. *And*, &c. as ch.1.12. v.3.

**Verse 9.** *{Thus saith the LORD, After this manner will I marre the pride of Judah, and the great pride of Jerusalem.}* I will by the Chaldeans, who shall overrun the land of Judah, surprise and sack Jerusalem, overthrow the whole state, carry the people away captive, and detain them a long time in captivity far from their own country, utterly spoil all that pomp and power, wherein at present they so much pride themselves. See Lev.26.19. Isaiah 2.11,17. and 23.9.

**Verse 10.** *{This evil people, which refuse to hear my words, which walk in the imagination of their hearts, and walk after other gods to serve them, and to worship them, shall be even as this girdle, which is good for nothing.}* The cause why God would thus deal with them; because by their refusal to be led and guided by him, and abandoning themselves to the service of their own hearts' desires and devices, and the worship of base idols, they had already made themselves nought-worth and good for nothing, chap.2.5. Isaiah 57.6.

*{refuse to hear my words}* That is, *to obey* them. See chap.11.10.

*{walk in the imagination of their heart}* See ch.9.13. & 11.8. and the same again, ch.16.12. & 18.12.

*{and walk after other gods to serve them, and to worship them}* Heb. *and that will walk after other gods, to serve them, and to bow down to them*: the gesture used in adoration, put for adoration, or worship in general. So Exod.20.5. Numb.25.2. 1 King.19.18. See chap.11.10.

*{shall be even as this girdle}* Heb. *and it*, to wit, *this people* or, *they*, (because the word *people*, is collective) *shall be as this girdle*: nor is there any need at all to alter the native syntax; reading the foregoing part of the verse, as by way of apposition joined to the words, next before, *I will marre the pride of Judah and Jerusalem*; *this evil people that refuse to hear my words, and they shall be*, or, *so that they shall become, as this girdle*; for so also is the copulative frequently used. See ch.5.28. 6.5,10. & 11.19,21.

**Verse 11.** *{For as a girdle cleaveth to the loins of a man; so have I caused to cleave unto me, the whole house of Israel, and the whole house of Judah, saith the LORD; that they might be for a people, and for a name, and for a praise, and for a glory: but they would not hear.}* The reason why he compared this people to a *girdle*; because he had taken them unto him, to be as near about him, and to sit as close unto him, as a man's girdle does to his loins, Deut.30.20. Psalm 109.19. & 148.14. and that for this very purpose, that as some rich and goodly girdle, not lying out of sight, or laid up in a chest, but being put on and worn abroad in open view, becomes thereby conspicuous, has notice taken of it, of the costly materials of it, and curious workmanship about it; and is consequently a matter of grace and ornament to him also that wears it, (see Exod.28.8. & 39.5.) So this people, by this their vicinity, nearness and inwardness of conjunction to him, and communion with him, might become famous and glorious in the eyes of all nations, Deut.4.6,8,32,38. & 26.19. chap.33.9. Esay 62.7. and that he himself also might be magnified and glorified in them, Esay 43.21. and 60.19,21. and 61.9,11. and 63.12. and withal, the reason why he would now so deal with them, that they should be like some rich girdle, loosed from a man's loins, cast aside into a corner, or some remote and obscure place, to lie therein out of sight, unregarded and not looked after, till it rot there, (see Lev.26.39.) to wit, their willful disobedience, whereby they inconsiderately opposed and crossed God in his designment intended for their good. See Psalm 81.8,16. a pregnant comment upon this place.

*{For}* Or, *Because*; as chap.13.10. & 10.21. because it carries on the reason rendered of the foregoing passages, unto the very last words of the verse.

*{the whole house of Israel, and the whole house of Judah}* The whole posterity of Jacob. See ch.2.3,4. & 3.18. & 5.11.

*{a people}* A peculiar people, Exo.19.5,6. 1 Pet.2.9,10.

*{a name}* *Name*, for, *renown*; as Gen.6.4. & 11.4.

*{but}* Heb. *and*; as ch.11.2. v.2.

*{they would not hear.}* That is, *obey*; as v.10. Heb. *they heard not*: as Esa.66.4.

**Verse 12.** *{Therefore thou shalt speak unto them this word; Thus saith the LORD God of Israel;}* Or, *Moreover*, (Heb. *And*: as ch.1.11.) *do thou speak this word to them*; or, *tell them this* from me: *this word*, for, *this thing*: as Dan.1.14. See chap.7.8. & 26.2. & 36.2. For at these words, the Lord, having done with the former type, passes on unto another, whereby he would have the Prophet make known unto them, and set further before their eyes, what he intended to do with them.

*{Every bottle shall be filled with wine}* Another type the Prophet is now enjoined to tell them of: a type taken from that they much loved, liked and looked after: for they loved and *looked after the flagons of wine*, Hos.3.1. and those prophets best pleased them, that *prophesied of wine and strong drink* to them, Mic.2.11. God therefore sends his Prophet to them with a prophecy of *wine*, but other wine than they expected. See v.13.

*{and they shall say unto thee, Do not we certainly know, that every bottle shall be filled with wine?}* Or, *and when they shall say unto thee, Do not we know well enough* (Heb. *knowing know*; as ch.26.15. & 40.14.) without your telling, *that every bottle shall be filled with wine*: (little deeming what manner of wine the Prophet meant, and dreaming of nothing but mirth and jollity; like those, Esa.22.13. their security and sensuality being herein glanced at) *Thou shalt say unto them*, or, *Say thou then to them*, &c. v.13. The like syntax is very frequent, Gen.14.14. Pro.3.24. Isa.30.20. chap.8.4. & 11.11. & 12.5. and hereafter, verse 16.

**Verse 13.** *{Then shalt thou say unto them; Thus saith the LORD, Behold I will fill all the inhabitants of this land, even the Kings that sit upon David's throne, and the Priests, and the Prophets, and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, with drunkenness.}* Since that you are so addicted to wine and excess, Isa.5.11,12,22. & 22.13. You shall have wine to your fill. I will fill all sorts among you from the highest to the lowest, with another sort of wine than that you so much affect and delight in, until you be stark drunk with it. I will pour you out so largely from the cup of my wrath, the wine of terror, of anguish, of perplexity and astonishment, that you shall be at your wits' end, and shall no more know what to do, or which way to turn yourselves, than men that are deep in drink: Of which *wine*, see Psalm 60.3. & 75.8. & 107.27. Esay 51.17,21. chap.25.27. & 48.26. & 51.7,39.

*{Behold, I will fill}* Heb. *Lo I am filling*: as, *Lo I am bringing*, Chap.11.11.

*{even the Kings}* Heb. *and* (as chap.10.25.) *the Kings*; either the Kings themselves successively; or, *Kings*, for, King and Princes: as ch.17.20. & 19.3.

*{that sit on the throne of David}* Heb. *that sit unto David* (that is, as some render it, *in stead of David*, as his successors: others, *of the stock of David*, being his issue. So also chap.22.4.) *upon his throne*; as cha.17.25. & 22.2. which should not secure them; notwithstanding that promise of perpetuity made to it, Psal.89.29.

*{the Priests}* That scorned to be ranked among the promiscuous multitude; but were to fare alike with the rest, Esa.24.1.

*{the Prophets}* The false prophets, that preached peace and safety to them; and bore the people in hand that all should be well. See ch.4.9,10. and 8.10,11.

**Verse 14.** *{And I will dash them one against another, even the Fathers and the Sons together, saith the LORD:}* I will set them together by the ears amongst themselves by intestine dissensions, and cause them to fall foul one upon another, as men in drink are wont to do, as Esay 9.19. & 19.2. or, I will break them all together to pieces as earthen bottles full of wine dashed one against another; or like a confused company of people in drink, by the violence of the enemy breaking in upon them, ch.6.11,21.

*{dash them one against another}* Some render it, *I will scatter them one from another.* So the old Latin: and the word here used does oft signify to *scatter*; as 1 Sam.13.11. Esa.11.12. and 33.3. but as oft, to *dash*, and by dashing to *dissolve, dissipate*, or, *break to pieces*, Psal.137.9. Esa.27.9. chap.22.28. and it is so applied to *potters ware*, Psal.2.9. to earthen *pitchers*, Judg.7.19. to *bottles*; as here, so ch.48.12. and so it must here be taken: for the syntax admits not the former.

*{one against another}* Not, *one from another*. Heb. *a man to*, or, *against* (as Judg.2.11. Esa.23.11.) *his brother*: as ch.25.26. Esa.19.2. or, *one with another*; as after, *all together*. So is the particle frequently used, ch.25.26. Lam.3.41. Ezek.16.26.

*{even}* Heb. *and*; as verse 13.

*{the fathers and the sons together}* No regard being had of natural bonds, relations, or affections, Isa.3.5. Mic.7.6. ch.6.21.

*{I will not pity, nor spare, nor have mercy, but destroy them.}* Heb. *from destroying them*; that is, *so as not to destroy them*, or, *that I should not destroy them*: as, *from seeing*, for, *so as not to see*; or, *that they may not see*, Psalm 69.23. and, *from rescuing*, for, *so that I cannot rescue*, Isaiah 50.2. an expression of the same thing in various terms, to imply the certainty of it, as a matter irrevocably resolved. So Isa.27.11.

**Verse 15.** *{Hear ye, and give ear, be not proud, for the LORD hath spoken.}* Or, *Hear and hearken*; (to good advice when it is given you, and while it may be for your good) *be not haughty*. So the word properly signifies; and so it is well rendered, Esay 3.16. persist not in your contumacy, and vain self-confidence, Prov.3.5,7. Rom.11.20. abate of your haughtiness, the highness of your hearts, and the stoutness of your stomachs, before God pull down your pride, ver.9. for it is he that threatens to do it. See the like admonition, Isa.28.14,22.

**Verse 16.** *{Give glory to the LORD your God}* By acknowledgment of your sins, Josh.7.19. and humbling yourselves under his hand, Jam.4.7,10. 1 Pet.5.6. v.18.

*{before he cause darkness}* Before he bring a night of affliction and calamity upon you, Esa.8.22. Lam.2.1.

*{and before your feet stumble upon the dark mountains,}* Either upon the mountains, whereunto you shall betake yourselves for refuge and relief, while you hope by that means to escape, Psal.11.1. Mat.24.16. or the mountains over which you shall be carried away captive into Chaldea, and other foreign parts, v.17. Heb. *mountains of twilight*, or *evening*, Prov.7.9. Isaiah 59.10. the time of darkness approaching after sunset; wherein men are prone to stumble, in such places especially, not without much prejudice and danger, Psa.35.6. Joh.11.9,10. 1 Joh.2.11.

*{and while ye look for light, he turn it into the shadow of death, and make it gross darkness.}* And while you promise to yourselves peace and safety, chap.4.10. & 6.14. and expect from foreign parts such aids, as you imagine will sufficiently secure you, chap.37.5,6. God turn all another way, and wrap you up in such inextricable difficulties, as you shall not be able by any means to wind yourselves out of, chap.8.15. and 14.19. Esay 59.6. Amos 8.9. 1 Thess.5.2. Heb. *and ye expect light, and he make it the shadow of death*; as above, verse 12,13.

*{the shadow of death}* Darkness so dreadful, that the very horror of it is enough to damp a man's spirits, and strike him even stark dead, Psal.23.4. ch.2.6.

*{make it gross darkness}* Heb. *put into gross darkness*: as, *put into desolation*, chap.2.14. See Esay 60.2. So Joel 2.2. Zeph.1.15.

**Verse 17.** *{But if ye will not hear it, my soul shall weep in secret places for your pride; and mine eye shall weep sore, and run down with tears, because the Lords flock is carried away captive.}* All the Prophet can do, when he cannot prevail with them, to bring them to any serious consideration of God's messages delivered unto them, inviting them to sincere humiliation and abatement of their haughty minds, is this, that out of his tender affection, he shall, apart by himself, much bewail their foolish arrogancy, and the miseries, that by captivity and deportation will for the same befall God's people. So 1 Sam.15.35.

*{But}* Heb. *And*; as v.2,11.

*{if ye will not hear it}* This has reference to v.15. the advice now given you, v.16.

*{my soul shall weep}* *I shall weep*: as, *my soul refused*, for, *I refused to be comforted*, Psal.77.2. but the phrase makes it the more affectionate; as Psa.42.1,2. & 63.1.

*{in secret places}* Or, *secrecies*. So cha.49.10. for sorrow commonly shuns company, affects retiredness and privacy. See ch.15.19. Mar.6.16,18.

*{for your pride}* Verse 16. Heb. *from before your pride*; as chap.4.4. and 9.7. foreseeing what the issue of it will be, and what a fall your haughtiness is sure to have, Prov.15.25. and 16.18. and 18.12.

*{mine eye shall weep sore}* Heb. *shedding tears shed tears*: the verb is nowhere found but here, and is doubled to express the grievous lamentation he should make. See ch.9.1.

*{run down with tears}* Heb. *descend with tears*; as ch.9.16. & 14.17. Lam.1.2,16. & 2.18.

*{the Lords flock}* His peculiar people, Psal.100.3. See chap.10.21. vers.20.

**Verse 18.** *{Say to the King, and to the Queen}* By the *King*, the Jewish commenters here generally understand Jehojacin, or Jeconiah; and by the *Queen*, the Queen Nechushtah his mother, who seems to have swayed much in regard of her son's minority; and was, together with him, and a great party of the great ones, and other of the people, taken by Nebuchadnezzar, and carried captive to Babylon, 2 King.24.12,16. chap.29.2. Whence also they gather, that this prophecy was published in the time of his short reign, that did last but three months, 2 King.24.12. For what a late writer has here of persons living delicately, as *Kings* and *Queens, Lords* and *Ladies*, are wont to do, Prov.30.4. Mat.11.8. and of *Bridegroom* and *Bride*, that should sometime be so termed: of whom, chap.7.34. and 25.9. they are his private, not probable, opinions.

*{Say}* God's words to the Prophet, say some: But says the Jewish commenter, not spoken to any particular person, but to any one indefinitely, that might say it to them; as Esay 35.4. *Say to the fearful hearted*: and it is, indeed, as if it were said, *Let this*, or *Be this, said*, or *spoken* to them. So, *Say to the righteous*, Esay 3.10. and, *Say to Archippus*, Col.4.17. Let it be as spoken to them, for them it concerns.

*{the Queen}* Or, *Madame*: the word properly signifies *Lady*; as 2 Kin.5.3. or, *Mistress*, Psa.123.2. Prov.30.23. Esa.24.2. but it is used in a peculiar notion for *Queen*, the King's wife, 1 Kin.11.19. 2 Kin.10.13. or, *Regent*; as 1 Kin.15.13. 2 Chr.15.16. where it is said of Maacah, the Queen-mother, that Asa her son removed her from being *Regent*; for so might the word there well be rendered, that is, from having any *power* of authority in the State, as the notation of the word imports.

*{Humble yourselves, sit down:}* So there should be a defect of the pronoun; as Esay 57.9. but it may well jointly be rendered without any such supply. *Sit below*: Come down from your thrones, or chairs of estate, and sit down upon the ground, or the pavement. See the like to Babylon, Esay 47.1. and to Dibon, chap.48.18. Heb. *Make low*, or, *Lay low, sit down*, for, *Sit low*: as, *Make deep to dwell*, for, *dwell deep*, chap.49.30. and, *made deep corrupted*, for, *deeply corrupted*, Hos.9.9.

*{for your principalities shall come down, even the crown of your glory.}* Heb. *your pillows*, or, *principalities is come down*: the word comes from a root that signifies an *head*, and is used in a plural form always, but in a singular notion for a *pillow*, or *bolster*, or ought that supplies the place of such, Gen.28.11,18. 1 Sam.19.13,16. and 26.7,11,12,16. and the Jewish doctors here expound it, as our version yields it, *Your kingdom*, or, *Kingly State*: but some late writers, *Your head attires*, which may be not improbable: the head being the place, whereon the ensign of royalty is usually worn, Psal.21.3. The Rabbine notes it to be used in the plural, to imply, that their princely state, every jot of it should be gone, that they should be led captive, as other ordinary persons: but it may well be, because the word has no other form than plural, as the word, *heaven, water, virginity, childhood*, and others. The ancient Greek, and old Latin, render it, in one continued tenor, *the crown of your glory is fallen from your head.* But the former version seems the better.

*{the crown of your glory}* Or, *your crown of glory*, or *goodliness*. So it would rather be rendered, than *crown of your glory*; as the like is rendered, Esay 62.3. (for both the latter term, and the syntax, is the same in either) that is, *your glorious*, or *goodly crown.* See Lam.5.16.

**Verse 19.** *{The cities of the South shall be shut up, and none shall open them:}* This the Jewish commenters, and those that tread in their track, understand of the cities of Judah, so called, say they, because Judah lay south from Babylon; whence the enemy is said to come from the north against it, vers.20. as also because it was so situate, in regard of the most part of the land of Israel, Josh.15.1,3. and said here to be *shut up*, and *none to open* them, either because so straitly besieged, that no going in or out for fear of the enemy, Deu.28.52. chap.5.6. or, because depopulated, and left without inhabitants to go in or out, ch.9.11. See Esa.24.10. But some of ours, whom I rather concur with, understand it of the cities of Egypt, which lay south from Judea, Esa.30.6. which by the Chaldean forces lying between the Jews and them, should be restrained, either from entertaining of them, or sending any considerable relief, or succor, to them. See 2 Kin.24.7.

*{open them}* The pronoun wanting, as ch.11.8.

*{Judah shall be carried away captive, and all of it shall be wholly carried away captive.}* Heb. *Judah is carried away captive all of her; she is carried away captive with a captivity of entirenesses*: the noun is to be supplied from the verb. So, *an entire captivity*, Amos 1.6,9. This began in Jeconiah's captivity, 2 Kin.24.14,16. and was completed in Zedekiah's, 2 King.25.10. See chap.52.28,30. A writer of prime note renders the last words, *the city of the peaceable ones shall be carried away captive*; alluding, says he, to the name of *Jerusalem*, and the *perpetuity of peace* and prosperity, which they promised to themselves: but neither do I find the word ever so used; and it is apparent, that Judah is in either member intended.

**Verse 20.** *{Lift up your eyes, and behold them that come from the North.}* That is, the Chaldeans by whom this was to be done, chap.1.14. & 6.21. The Prophet speaks it, as if he saw them coming; and they might also, if they would, but look up, or look out, as Esay 60.4. and it is not unlikely, that even at the very time of the delivery of this prophecy, they were well onward on their way. See on v.18. The old Latin version here goes by itself, rendering the words, *Ye that come from the North*; as if the Chaldeans were called upon to view Jerusalem: but the course of the context runs directly contrary hereunto.

*{where is the flock that was given thee, thy beautiful flock?}* Heb. *thy flock of goodliness*; as, *your crown of goodliness*, v.18. He seems to speak this to the king: What is become now of that goodly flock, God's people, that were committed to your charge, and in whom you did overmuch pride yourself? See Num.27.17. 2 Sam.24.1,2,17. Prov.14.28. ch.10.21. v.9. Howbeit, because the pronoun is feminine, he seems rather to direct his speech unto the State, speaking to it, as to a woman entrusted with government: to which purpose, the reading in the text exhibits both the verbs in the foregoing branch in a singular feminine form, though the received lection read them in the plural.

**Verse 21.** *{What wilt thou say?}* As Joshua, Josh.7.8. and Ezra, Ezr.9.10. *What shall I say?* not unlike that of Job, *What shall I do?* Job 31.14. speeches importing such a perplexity, as makes persons at their wits' end, not knowing what to say, or do, vers.13.

*{when he shall punish thee?}* Heb. *when he shall visit upon thee?* as cha.11.22. *he*, that is, God, say some. Nebuchadnezzar, and the Chaldeans, say others, coming from the north, v.20. because of them he speaks in the very next words: or, God by them, say others, including both, ch.5.9,10.

*{(for thou hast taught them to be captains, and as chief over thee.)}* You by seeking, and in base manner submitting yourself unto them, craving aid from them, and inviting them, by rich presents to you, have showed them the way, how to come, not to assist and relieve you, but to overmaster and subdue you, and make a prey and a spoil of you. See 2 King.16.7,8. For that which a late learned writer here has, as if it were spoken to the king; charging him to have been the procuring cause of all these evils, by being a leader of them unto idolatrous practices, 2 King.24.9. the words, though never so much forced, will not admit. Heb. *and*, (for, *for*, as ch.8.16.) *thou hast taught them against thy self, captains to*, or, *for head*, or, *chief*: *taught them against thy self*; that is, to your own damage and detriment: as Gen.42.36. *all these things are against me*: *taught them captains*; a defective form; for, *taught them* to be *captains*: as, *from a King*, for, *from* being *a King*, 1 Sam.15.22. *from a Regent*, for, *from* being *a Regent*, 1 King.15.13. *predestinated, conformable*, for, *predestinated* to be, or, become, or, be made, *conformable*, Rom.8.20. *chosen, rich in faith*, for, *chosen* to be *rich in faith*, Jam.2.5. *to an head*, or, *for an head*; as Judg.10.18. & 11.8,9,11. or *upon the head*: as Gen.49.26. Deut.33.16. the Jewish doctor not amiss carries it thus on with the former, making the same supply in either; *thou hast taught them against thy self* to be *captains*, to become *the head*; or, *thou hast taught them* to be *captains*, to be *head over thee*: for either way it may be read; but the former seems the better: you have by your inconsiderate courses brought that judgment upon yourself, that God long since threatened to inflict upon you, in case of willful and obstinate disobedience, Deut.28.13,44. See Lam.1.5.

*{shall not sorrows take thee as a woman in travail?}* Or, *will not pains surprise thee, as a travailing woman?* Heb. *a woman of birth*; an emblem of extreme anguish and distress, Psal.48.6. Esa.26.17,18. and 37.3. ch.6.28. & 22.23.

**Verse 22.** *{And if thou say in thine heart}* If such thoughts as these shall arise within you; as Deu.7.17. & 8.4. & 18.21.

*{wherefore come these things upon me?}* As ch.5.19. & 16.10.

*{for the greatness of thine iniquity}* The answer to their question, pointing as with the finger, and directing them to the main cause and ground of all their misery; *for the greatness*, or, *for the multitude*, (as it is rendered, ch.30.14.) *of thine iniquity*; the word will well bear either, as Psal.19.13. & 25.11. so here.

*{are thy skirts discovered, and thine heels made bare}* You are brought to extreme shame and servitude; an allusion to the manner of captives, that are led along without hose or shoes, barefooted, and barelegged, having scarce raiment wherewith to cover their nakedness, which in women captives (and to such an one is Judah compared here) is the more shameful and grievous. See Esa.3.17. and 20.4. and 47.3.

*{are thy skirts discovered}* You are compelled to tuck up your clothes about you, as being to go through thick and thin, Esa.47.2. or, you are exposed to public shame, as women captives oft are, Esay 3.17. and so the Chaldee renders it; See vers.26.

*{thine heels made bare}* Your shoes being forcibly plucked off from your feet; for so the word implies, as Lam.2.6. and the text may be rendered, *and thine heels being violently used*, discovered, or, *by violent usage* made bare, See ch.2.25. There is in either branch a figurative speech; for to speak properly, not the *skirts* of the garment themselves *are discovered*, but the flesh of the body for want of them; whether trussed up, turned up, torn away, or cut off; as 2 Sam.10.4. nor are the *heels* themselves *violently plucked away*, but the shoes being violently plucked away, the heels by means thereof, come to be made bare and discovered. Howbeit in the latter part as some render it, the phrase may be proper enough: *thine heels are spoiled*; being, say they, left bare of that covering, which in modest persons, those of fashion and state especially, such as she is here compared unto, by means of the skirts or borders of their side garments they formerly had; so that this branch should be but the same in substance with, or at most, but an effect or consequent of the former. So the Greek, *thine hinder parts are discovered, and thine heels exposed to shameful view.*

**Verse 23.** *{Can the Ethiopian change his skin? or the leopard his spots? then may ye also do good, that are accustomed to do evil.}* God being now to pass a peremptory doom upon this people, of utter dispersion, and destruction, does in these words render a more full reason of it, their incorrigible and incurable condition: they were by custom and continuance so habituated in evil, that it was become as a second nature in them; no means would prevail with them, to work it out of them, or work them to any good; as soon might a blackamoor be with washing made white, or the leopard's spots be taken from him, as this people brought to ought that was good, and it is in vain therefore to take any further pains with them: See 2 Chro.36.16. cha.2.30. & 5.3. & 6.29,30.

*{can the Ethiopian change his skin}* Heb. *will*, or, *shall the Cushite change his skin*; that is, the hue, or color of it: but the verb is taken potentially, as the like, Esay 10.19. 2 Sam.23.6. Lam.3.7. Amos 6.12. And it is a proverbial form, used among the Greeks also and Latins, with whom, *the washing of an Ethiopian*, or, *a blackamoor*, is commonly used as an emblem, of *labor in vain*: Heb. *a Cushite*, as Num.12.1. and from hence, as also from Amos 9.5. it appears that the *Cushite*, the posterity of *Cush*, the son of *Cham*, and brother to *Misraim*, the father of the Egyptians, Gen.10.6. were a people generally noted in those times for their black hue, above any other; as also, have the Ethiopians been from time to time successively in all ages, whence also that name was by the Greeks given them, importing as much, and thereby distinguishing them from all other people, as of a deeper dye than any other in that kind; which the rather would be observed, because it confirms the received judgment, from all antiquity transmitted unto us, (though by some learned men of great note, without ground sufficient, as to me seems, of late controlled) that the *Cushites* are no other than the Ethiopians, and the Ethiopians of Africa that now are, the posterity of Cush. Nor does that which they allege concerning the ancient seat of the Cushites in Asia, in some part of Arabia, bordering upon the Red Sea, any way cross ought herein received, concerning these black Cushites; the very name and memorial of whom is by these men's own confession, now lost in those parts, since that it is well known, how frequent the transmigrations of people have been, from the places of their first abode: as also how ready the passage might be over that shoaly sea, into the upper parts of Africa, is very easy to apprehend: and whereas some to shift off the force of this place, tell us that the *Kedarens* were black people, and therefore had their name, forcing in to that purpose that passage in the Canticles, Cant.1.5. and the Chaldee paraphrast, who renders *Kedar* there *Cush*; as also that the *Arabians* may seem to have had their name from the like hue, as being the color either of the *night*, or of the *raven*: because the Hebrew term for *Arabia*, and another for the *evening*, and a third for a *raven*, are referred all to one root, neither makes much to this purpose. Since that it is not denied, but that these Cushites had anciently their seat in those parts. But exception sufficient it is, for to enervate the force of any argument, against the received opinion from these forementioned allegations; that what is said of the former, to wit, the name of *Kedar*, is groundless; it being apparent that from *Kedar* one of Ishmael's sons, Gen.25.13. that people had their name: nor are the people themselves, but their *tents*, noted for *blackness*, in that place of the Canticles, and there is for the latter concerning Arabia, as little probability: with equal ground they might be deemed, to have been not of a *black* color, like a *crow*, or, *raven*; but of a *fallow*, or, *willow* color; because a word rising from the same root, signifies a *sallow*, or, *willow*-tree. See Esay 15.7. & 21.13. But the *Cushites* and the *Kedarens*, seem in Scripture still distinguished, and the *Arabes* from either: besides, that one of those learned writers, who goes stiffly this way, acknowledges those Arabes, whom he would have to be these Cushites, to be rather of a *brown*, or, *tawny*, than a *black* hue.

*{or the leopard his spots}* Heb. *and*; as ch.6.20. & 9.12. the word rendered *leopard*, both here, and ch.5.6. is supposed to signify, that wild, fierce, and wily creature, the male whereof the Latins call *Pardus*, the female, *Varia*, in regard of the great variety of spots all over the body of either. See Pliny l.8. c.17. the Greeks call both by the name of *Pardalis*. So Aristotle l.9. c.6. for the other name, I find not in any ancient Greek author; it is here rendered a *leopard*; which word, found in Latin authors of an inferior age, should signify a mongrel creature bred of a *Pardus*, and a *Lioness*; whereof see also Pliny where before. But the Hebrew word here used, as also the Greek *Pardalis*, and the Latin *Pardus*, and *Varia*, seem to design no other, than that which we commonly call an *Ounce*, and some, a *Cat-a-mountain*, because it seems of a middle nature, between a Lion and a Cat; as our Caius describes him, in an Epistle to Gesner, of the bigness of a Mastiff, for head and face like a *Lion*, for body, tail, foot, and nails, liker a *Cat*; the word rendered *spots*, not elsewhere found, signifies properly *dark spots*, such as arise in the body of one that has been beaten, as we say, *black and blue*, Prov.20.30. Esa.53.5. and of a blackish color are the Ounce's spots.

*{then ye also}* Or, *then ye*: This some would restrain to *the King*, and, *the Queen*, mentioned, v.18. but it seems to be more general, and to reach the main body of the state and people.

*{accustomed}* Heb. *taught*; as ch.9.5. & 31.18.

**Verse 24.** *{Therefore will I scatter them as the stubble, that passeth away by the wind of the wilderness}* Heb. *And*; as chap.11.8. yet may the copulative here be retained, if we read the 23. verse as a parenthesis interjected between the 22. verse and this. In that was intimated their captivity; in this, their dispersion into divers several regions and countries, far remote and distant one from another; that which should make their captivity much more grievous and uncomfortable, when they should be thus severed one from another, Deu.4.27. & 28.64. ch.9.16.

*{as stubble}* So Psa.83.13. Esa.40.24. Hos.13.3. Zeph.2.2.

*{by the wind of the wilderness}* Heb. *unto the wind* (that is, to be carried away with the wind, as Ezek.5.2.) *of the wilderness*, or, *the plain*; as Esa.63.13. See ch.4.11. The Rabbines suppose, that the Prophet herein had some eye to the wilderness, that lies between Jerusalem, and Babylon; but of that there is neither any necessity, nor much probability.

**Verse 25.** *{This is thy lot, the portions of thy measures from me, saith the LORD.}* This is your share, the state and condition that God has assigned you, the sad doom that he has passed upon you. It is a borrowed form of speech, taken from lands measured out by line, into several portions and parcels, according to the number of those that are copartners therein, and then divided by lot, that each one may have that part, that the lot has assigned him. So Job 20.23. Psal.11.6. & 16.5,6. Mic.2.5. This denunciation a learned writer restrains to the Queen-mother, mentioned, ver.18. But therein he goes alone, and seems to narrow the text too much. God speaks by the Prophet to the Jewish state, as in the person of a woman, So ver.19,21,26,27.

*{because thou hast forgotten me}* As chap.2.32. Heb. *that*, or, *which hast forgotten me*; as, *which dwelt in Egypt*; Exod.12.40. but the relative is oft used in a causal notion, as 1 King.15.13. chap.1.15.

*{and trusted in falsehood}* Or, *in a lie*: either in idols, as some; chap.2.17,18. & 10.14. or, in vain courses, that cannot stand you in stead, but will fail you in time of need, cha.3.23. and 7.8. & 23.16,17.

**Verse 26.** *{Therefore will I discover thy skirts upon thy face, that thy shame may appear.}* Or, *I will discover*, (Heb. *make bare*; as Esa.47.2. & 52.10. chap.49.10.) by casting up *thy skirts upon thy face, thy shame, that it may be seen*; that that which natural shame and modesty seeks to conceal, may lie open to sight; See on vers.22. & Nah.3.5. where the speech is defective also, as the same here; not unlike that, Psalm 89.39,44. I will expose you to open shame and ignominy, that as your sin has been open and public, so your shame also may be such. See Esay 3.17. & 20.4. Ezek.16.37. and 23.29.

**Verse 27.** *{I have seen thine adulteries, and thy neighings, the lewdness of thy whoredom, and thine abomination on the hills, in the fields.}* Or, as the words lie in the text, *Thine adulteries, and thy neighings, and thy lewd whoredom* have been, or are *upon the hills, and in the fields: I have seen*, or, *I see thine abominations.*

*{adulteries}* Idolatries; as chap.2.20. & 3.1. Ezek.16.31. & 23.44,45.

*{neighings}* That is, says the Jewish doctor, your rejoicing in your wickedness, ch.11.15. but that is clean besides the intention of the Prophet in this place: it is parallel to that, chap.5.8. save that there this *neighing* is of the male winding the female, because speaking of men: here of the female, the mare, when she runs a madding after the male; because the speech is of the Jewish State, as in the person of a woman: as in that other passage of a wild ass, therein parallel to this, ch.2.24.

*{the lewdness of thy whoredom,}* Or, *thy lewd whoredom*, chap.11.15.

*{on the hills in the fields}* *On the hills* (and high places abroad) *in the fields*, ch.3.2. Esa.65.7. Or, *on the hills*, and *in the fields*: no place is free from them, Esa.57.5,7. ch.2.20. & 3.6.

*{I have seen}* Or, *I see thine abominations*: I see them, and take notice of them, though you think I do not; as chap.7.11. Hos.5.3. & 7.1,2. Of the term here rendered *abomination*, see on Esay 66.16.

*{Woe unto thee, O Jerusalem, wilt thou not be made clean? when shall it once be?}* In these words, the Prophet closes up this sad sermon, with an affectionate compellation of the Jewish State, under the title of Jerusalem, the head city thereof; lamenting her willful continuance in her spiritual filth; with an obstinate refusal of being reclaimed and cleansed from it, after means for so long a time tendered unto her, and pressed upon her, to that purpose. See cha.4.14. Ezek.24.13.

*{Woe unto thee}* Spoken not by way of denunciation: as Esa.5.8,11. but of lamentation: as Lam.5.16.

*{when shall it once be?}* Heb. *after how long yet*, or *still*? To wit, will you cleanse yourself? say some: but as I suppose rather, Will you persist and continue in your filth and folly, refusing to come out of it? for the term, by some rendered, *yet* here has a notion of continuance. See the parallel place, chap.4.14.

## CHAPTER 14

**Verse 1.** *{The Word of the LORD that came to Jeremiah concerning the dearth.}* The title prefixed before this sermon, or prophecy, acquaints us with the occasion of it, a dearth caused by drought; but not with the time when this dearth or drought was: Whence arises some diversity of opinion among interpreters, concerning the time of it. Some supposing it to have been in the time of the siege of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar, in the reign of Zedekiah, chap.52.6. but this famine was not in the city alone, as that was, for want of bread; but over the whole country, for want of rain, vers.4,6. Others would have it to be in the beginning of Zedekiah's reign, some good space of time before that siege. I suppose it to have been rather in the reign of Jehojakim: the ground of my conjecture is, because I find chap.36.9. that in the fifth year of Jehojakim, a solemn fast was proclaimed throughout all Judah, which might well be, upon this occasion; and the rather may be conceived so to have been, because God, in his speech to the Prophet, intimates, that they either had already held, or were about to hold a fast, to implore God's favor and mercy, for the removal of this evil, vers.12. as also, the Prophet seems to imply as much in his speech to God, vers.2. Add hereunto the opinion of the Jewish doctors, who suppose the former prophecy contained in chap.11. & 12. to have been delivered in Jehojakim's reign. See on chap.11.9. and it may well be deemed from chap.12.4. that such a drought then was, as is here described.

*{The word of the LORD that came to Jeremiah}* See ch.1.2. & 7.1. This *word* seems to begin at v.10. for the foregoing part of the chapter, seems to have been the Prophet's speech unto God, bitterly bewailing the sad condition of the whole State, by reason of this great drought, v.2,6. and earnestly, with much affection, making suit unto God, for the removal, or mitigation, at least, of this evil, v.7,9. See the like inscription ch.32.1. & 40.1.

*{to Jeremiah}* That is, *to me*; as ch.13.1. but the noun is here for the pronoun: as Esa.2.1.

*{concerning the dearth}* Or, *drought*. Heb. *concerning the words* (that is, the *matter*; as Esth.9.31. Psal.65.3. chap.17.8.) *of the restraints*: to wit, of rain, as chap.17.8. where the same is in the singular number. Hence some would pick out two several *droughts*, at two several times: but *droughts* rather, for a drought of long continuance: the plural often in Hebrew, implying an eminency, or enhancement, of the thing specified. So *wisdoms*, Prov.14.1. *evennesses*, Esa.26.7. *righteousnesses*, Esay 45.24. *droughts*, Esa.58.11. *strengths*, Esa.63.15. Again some would have it here denounced only, none at all in present being. But the whole current of the context, seems to run strongly against that conceit. See the close of it, vers.22. Howbeit, a learned interpreter (therein I suppose going alone by himself) supposes no mention of drought or dearth at all, either present or future, to be here mentioned: for he expounds those words of the text, *concerning the words of cohibitions*; that is, concerning the prayers and supplications commenced by the Prophet, and other godly ones, for the staying of God's wrath denounced against the State: who also therefore supposes both this, and all the foregoing sermons, to have been delivered in the reign of Josiah, 2 King.23.26,27. but though it be true, that the Prophet's prayer seems to have occasioned the prophecy; yet the present *drought* appears plainly to have occasioned the Prophet's prayer.

**Verse 2.** *{Judah mourneth}* The Prophet's complaint of the rueful and distressed condition of the whole State, by reason of the present dearth: *Judah* (the whole land) *mourneth*; not Jerusalem alone, as in the siege. See ch.12.11.

*{and the gates thereof languish}* That is, her *cities*; as Exod.20.10. Deut.16.5. ch.15.7. Lam.1.4. and the inhabitants thereof: so called, because the gates were the ordinary places of public assemblies, and means of keeping in, or letting out, Ruth 4.1,2. 2 King.7.1,20. Psal.127.5. when the country fails through drought, the cities must needs faint through dearth, Eccl.5.9.

*{they are black unto the ground}* Going in black, as mourners, Psa.38.6. & 42.9. Mal.3.14. or looking black in the face, through grief and famine, Lam.4.6. Rev.6.5. for faintness they hang the head, or sink and fall down *to the ground*: for it is a defective, or comprehensive form of speech; not unlike those, Psa.74.7. & 89.39,44. Esa.14.12. Lam.2.19. & 3.53.

*{and the cry of Jerusalem is gone up.}* That is, the cry of the people out of all parts of the country there assembled, to seek God in his sanctuary by solemn prayer and supplication to have the present restraint removed, and the heavens opened again to them, 1 Kin.8.35,36. See ch.36.9. v.12. So 1 Sam.5.12. *the cry of the city went up to heaven.*

**Verse 3.** *{And their Nobles have sent their little ones to the waters, they came to the pits, and found no water, they returned with their vessels empty; they were ashamed and confounded, and covered their heads.}* Or, *When their Nobles had sent their meaner ones to the waters*, and *they coming to the pits found no water*, but *returned with their empty vessels; they were abashed, and confounded, and covered their heads.* Of this syntax, see chap.13.12,16.

*{Nobles}* The great men; who if they were driven to such straits, for want of water, the poorer sort much more. See Esa.5.13.

*{sent their little ones}* Or, *meaner ones*. Some of those of the meaner sort: their menial or domestic servants. See Psal.119.141.

*{to the waters}* To those places where water was wont to be had. So Judg.7.6. or, *for water*; that is, to seek for water, where it might be found; as 1 King.18.5.

*{to the pits}* Places hewn out, or dug, for the receiving and keeping, either of spring water derived unto them, or such rain water as fell from above, Esa.7.3. & 22.11. ch.2.13.

*{found no water}* As Esa.41.17. the rain being restrained, and the springs also that were therewith fed, dried up, 1 Kin.17.7.

*{they returned with their vessels empty}* As they carried them out; not as Naomi, Ruth 1.21. Heb. *they returned their vessels emptily*, or, *in vain*; without effect; as 2 Sam.1.21. for the word is an adverb, and so in that of Ruth; either a defect of the instrumental note, *with*, which our versions supplies; or the verb in an active notion, as some Jewish critics, *they brought back*, or *returned, their vessels empty*. So 1 Sam.23.6. either, *he came down with an Ephod in his hands*; or, *he brought down an Ephod in his hands.*

*{they}* This most expound of the servants sent; I rather, of their masters that sent them, and expected water by them, but were frustrated of their expectation.

*{were ashamed and confounded}* Or, *abashed* (which precisely answers the term in the text) *and appalled*: for it is not so much shame, as dejection and perplexity of spirit, that is wont to surprise persons in such cases.

*{covered their heads}* As in much grief and sorrow the manner was in those times to muffle up head and face, scarce leaving any space free for sight, much after the manner of close mourners with us. See 2 Sam.15.30. So v.4.

**Verse 4.** *{Because the ground is chapt; for there was no rain in the earth, the plowmen were ashamed, they covered their heads.}* Or, *Because the ground* (that peculiarly which is wont to be tilled, Esa.1.7.) *is chapt* (Heb. *is broken*, or *is wasted and spoiled*, as ch.48.20.) *for that no rain hath been* (or *hath fallen*) *upon the land*; (to wit, of Judah, as 1 Kin.18.1.) *the husband-men* (as chap.31.24. for the word is larger than that of *plow-men*, Psal.129.3.) *are abashed*, (so Joel 1.11.) *they covered their heads*, as v.3.

**Verse 5.** *{Yea, the hind also calved in the field, and forsook it, because there was no grass.}* *Yea* (as cha.10.7.) *the hind also calved* (Heb. *brought forth*; as Job 39.1,2.) *in the field* (not in the wild waste) *and forsook it* (to wit, that which she brought forth, her *young*, Job 39.4. (Heb. *forsaking forsook*, as Eccl.4.2. & 8.9. & 9.11. Esa.43.8. & 59.13. and a defect of the pronoun *it*, as chap.12.11.) *because there was no grass*, or *tender*, or *green, herbage*, Psal.23.2. Esa.66.14.
