So great is the drought that the very brute beasts, who by instinct of nature are very affectionate unto, and exceeding chary of their young, (in which kind, concerning the *hind*, see Pliny, l.8. c.32.) have been enforced, though calving in the fields, where herbage usually is not wanting, to leave their young, their milk being dried up for want of moisture, and wander to seek for water, or some green thing, where they can find either. Thus the Prophet relates to the Lord, the poor brute beasts' misery suffering for man's sin and iniquity; if in behalf of the guiltless creature, at least, God may be moved to show mercy to wicked man. So Joel 1.20. See Jon.4.11.

**Verse 6.** *{And the wild asses did stand in the high places, they snuffed up the wind like dragons:}* Or, *The wild asses also* (as chap.3.6.) *stood in the high places, and snuffed up the wind*; or, *stand in the high places snuffing up the wind*: as, *stand and feed*, for, *stand feeding*, Esay 61.5. instead of water thereby endeavoring to allay their inward drought and heat thence proceeding: another kind of their *snuffing up the wind*, from that mentioned, chap.2.24. this for want of moisture, that out of wantonness. And to this purpose, therefore, they are here said, to repair and get up to the *high places*, in which if anywhere, fresh and cool air and gales of wind are to be had, that might that way give them some refreshing, which in the lower grounds and valleys, neither breathes so freely, and is more heated with the reflection of the sunbeams from the higher grounds; and this place alone therefore may sufficiently control that learned man's conceit, who would have the word here used to signify *low* places, or *plains*, especially being compared with what himself has on, chap.4.11. See there.

*{like dragons}* Whose inward drought, because it is not easily slaked, such of them as live in hot and dry deserts, where usually they most abound, are therefore continually drawing in the air; wherewith also alone some of them can continue long, when they have nothing else to relieve them. See Aristotle, l.8. c.4. and Pliny, l.10. c.72. and of the word here used, see on Esa.27.1. & 34.13.

*{their eyes did fail}* Or, *their eyes fail*; being sunk in their heads, or with faintness; for famine causes faintness, and makes the sight fail. See 1 Sam.14.29. Lam.5.17.

*{because there was no grass.}* Or, *because there is no herbage*: nothing green or moist, to relieve or refresh them. Of the word, see on chap.12.4.

**Verse 7.** *{O LORD, though our iniquities testify against us, do it for thy names sake;}* The Prophet's complaint went before: his prayer now follows, wherein he entreats God, that although for their manifold great and grievous sins they justly deserved what they endured, yet that he would for his own name's sake show mercy unto them, in removing of this heavy judgment. The only remedy for removal of judgments, repentance and prayer: so ver.20,22. Lam.3.40,41.

*{though}* Or, *albeit*. Heb. *if*; as ch.5.2.

*{our iniquities testify against us}* Give in sufficient evidence against us, to convince and evict us, as deservedly sustaining whatsoever we endure. Heb. *answer*; as Gen.30.33. So Exod.20.16. see Esa.3.9. & 59.12.

*{do it for thy names sake}* Take pity on us, and relieve us, if not for our own sake, yet for the honor of your mercy, and the glory of your name: so Psalm 25.11. & 115.1,2. Esay 43.25. & 48.11. *do it*, a defect of the pronoun, as vers.5. *forsook it*: so Psal.39.9. or, *work for thy names sake*, as Ezek.20.14. and then there needs no supply.

*{for our backslidings are many, we have sinned against thee.}* Or, *though our revolts are many*, or *great*, whereby *we have sinned against thee.* So the particle is used, Gen.8.21. Josh.17.18. Psal.23.4. and so would it be rendered in those places parallel to this, Psal.25.11. *For thy names sake, O Lord, pardon mine iniquity, though it be much*, or *great*; and, *heal my soul* (that is, *heal me*) *though I have sinned against thee*, Psal.41.4. the defect of the relative is not unusual: so cha.8.13. & 11.19.

**Verse 8.** *{O the hope of Israel, the Saviour thereof in time of trouble, why shouldst thou be as a stranger in the land, and as a wayfaring man that turneth aside to tarry for a night.}* To the Prophet's earnest supplication in the words beforegoing, in this verse, and the next, he subjoins a passionate, yet submiss expostulation, that he whom alone his people had to rely upon, and who had wont to relieve and deliver them in their distresses, should now fail them, carrying himself towards them, as one that had little or nothing to do with them, no more regarding them, nor seeming to care what became of them, than some mere stranger, of a place, that he has no relation to nor settled abode in; or than a traveler of the inn, where he lodges only for a night, and cares not what become of it, when that is over, and he gone.

*{the hope of Israel}* Chap.17.13. & 50.7. Psal.22.4. For the Talmudic doctor does but dally with the text, who because the word here used, does sometime signify any *place, sea, lake, pond*, or *pool*, wherein waters are gathered together. Gen.1.10. Exod.7.19. Lev.11.36. Esay 22.11. would have it here rendered, *the pool of Israel*, in which they are purged from their filth; according to that, Zach.13.1. for *hope*, or *expectation*, the word is frequently used, 1 Chr.29.15. Ezr.10.2.

*{the Saviour thereof in time of trouble}* Psal.9.9. & 46.1.

*{as a stranger}* Or, *sojourner*; as Exo.12.48. Lev.19.33.

*{that turneth aside}* So Jael to Sisera, *Turn in to me*, Judg.4.18. and, *let us turn into this city*, Judg.19.11. whence the Latins call an inn, *diversorium*, that is, a place to turn aside into: there is in the text a defect of the relative, as ch.11.19. & as v.9.

*{to lodge for a night}* Heb. *to lodge*: but so much is implied, as Judg.19.11,13. and it seems to have a glance at that promise of God, whereby he had engaged himself (but that engagement was conditional) to settle his abode among them forever, 2 Chr.33.7,8. Psal.132.14.

*{for a night}* That is, but *for a night*, or, *for a night* only; as, *yesterday*, for, but of *yesterday*, Job 8.9. and, *a moment*, for, but *a moment*, Psa.30.5. and, *one*, for, *one* only, or *one* alone, Eccl.4.8,11. but the word *night*, is not at all in the text, which yet may well be rendered with the like supply, *to lodge* only, or but *to lodge*: *lodging* being here opposed to constant abode.

**Verse 9.** *{Why shouldst thou be as a man astonished, as a mighty man that cannot save?}* The word used in the former branch, is nowhere found else in Scripture, and is by divers therefore diversely expounded: the ancient Greek renders it *asleep*, as if they had read *nirdam* for *nidham*: the old Latin, *a wanderer*; on what ground I cannot guess. Others, as our version, *astonished*, or, *amazed*; *struck dumb*, says one, as if this, and the Hebrew *dum*, whence our *dumb*, were of an affinity: *terrified*, or, *affrighted*, says another; as the word *daham* is used in the Arabic version, Mat.24.39. though another, grounding it seems upon the same place, renders it, *coming upon*, and expounds it, as one that coming in upon one that is in danger, and expects help from him, either does not, or dare not, or cannot rescue, or relieve him. Others lastly, as one that *fainteth*: and so one of the Jewish critics, affirming that in the Kedaren, or Arabian language, the word *nidhum*, which comes very near this, signifies one, that with some grief, or sickness, has his heart quailed: nor does this swerve much from that which our version has, and seems to me most probable.

*{as a mighty man that cannot save}* His power being spent; as Esay 10.18. & 40.30. that which with God, being of infinite power, is impossible. See Esay 40.28,29. & 50.2. & 59.1. the relative is wanting, as ver.8.

*{Yet thou, O LORD, art in the midst of us}* *Yet* (Heb. *and*; as Chap.7.26.) *thou art among us*: as Chap.17.6. & 39.5. having your Temple, the place of your special presence and residence, as your court or palace, with us, ver.21. Psal.46.5. Zach.2.5.

*{and we are called by thy Name}* We are accounted your people, Deut.26.18. Psal.135.4. and the evils therefore that befall us, redound to your dishonor, Ezek.36.20. See Numb.14.13–16. Heb. *thy name is called upon us*: as Deut.28.10. Esay 63.19. Chap.15.16.

*{leave us not.}* Withdraw not your aid from us in this our distress, Psal.27.9. & 38.21. & 119.8. or do not utterly cast us off: as God seemed to threaten; this heavy judgment being by the Prophet apprehended, as a presage and forerunner of a far greater ensuing evil. See chap.6.8.

**Verse 10.** *{Thus saith the LORD unto this people;}* Or rather, *concerning this people.* So is the particle used, Gen.20.13. Esth.3.2. Psal.91.11. Esay 8.12. & 27.2. & 56.4. and here begins the word mentioned, ver.1. as in way of answer to the Prophet's suit and complaint. See the like, chap.42.7. In it the Lord tells the Prophet, that since this people are so addicted to defection from him, and going astray after others, either idolaters, or idols; he will not only at the present disregard them, and not hear them, or return any gracious answer to them, notwithstanding all their fastings and external humiliations, by removal of the present judgment; but that he is resolved to proceed further in judgment against them, and by sword, famine and pestilence, two other evils added to this at present upon them, to consume and destroy them: and forbids the Prophet therefore any further to solicit him in their behalf.

*{Thus they}* This people, whom you move me for, ver.8,9. and he says *this people*; as those, whom God seemed now not to own as his. So ver.11.

*{have loved to wander}* Or, *love to wander*: all their delight is in wandering, in running to and fro, this way and that way, after their copesmates and their idols, chap.2.23–25. and since they love wandering so well, they shall have their fill of it, cha.15.4,7. Hos.9.17.

*{they have not refrained their feet}* Or, *they will not refrain*, or, *withhold*, as (chap.2.20.) or, *withdraw*, (as Prov.25.17. though the word there be not the same) *their feet*; to wit, from running after strange gods, and strangers, chap.2.25.

*{therefore the LORD doth not accept them}* Heb. *and* (as chap.13.24.) *the Lord* (the noun for the pronoun; as ver.1.) *accepteth them not*: as Hos.8.14. or, *hath no favor*, or, *affection*, to them, Psal.44.3. & 85.1. or, *taketh no pleasure in them*; as Psal.147.11. and 149.4. for the same word is used in all those places. See Esay 57.6. and 65.5.

*{he will now remember their iniquity, and visit their sin.}* Or, *he doth now remember their iniquity*; he calls it to mind: which God is said to do, when by some sign he makes it to appear, that he does bear it in mind, though he forbear for some space of time to discover his displeasure, 1 King.17.18. Psal.25.7. and 109.15. cha.44.21,22. *and will visit their sin*, that is, punish them for it: as Exod.20.5. cha.11.21.

**Verse 11.** *{Then said the LORD unto me}* Or, *Moreover, the Lord said unto me.* Heb. *and*; as chap.1.11. and 8.4.

*{Pray not for this people for their good.}* Heb. *make not supplication in behalf of this people*, (see on ver.10) *for good*: as Neh.5.19. & 13.31. See the like inhibition, cha.7.16. and 11.14.

**Verse 12.** *{When they fast, I will not hear their cry;}* Or, *Though* (as cha.12.1.) *they fast*, (see cha.36.9.) *I will not hear their cry*; whereof, see ver.2. The like reason of the same inhibition, see rendered, chap.11.14. and the people's expostulation upon God's refusal in such case to hear them, Esay 58.3.

*{and when they offer burnt offering and an oblation, I will not accept them:}* Or, *and though* (as before) *they offer* (Heb. *make to ascend*, Esay 56.7.) *sacrifice*, or (as cha.13.23.) *oblation*, (see Esay 1.11,13.) *I will not show them any favor*; as Psal.85.1. for the word *them*, may have reference as well to themselves, as to their presents and services. So chap.6.20. & 7.21. Esay 1.11–15. *sacrifice*, and *oblation*, collectively, for *sacrifices*, and *oblations*: but there is an emphasis in it, as if it were said, not any sacrifice, or oblation, whatsoever it be, never so goodly, never so costly, shall prevail with me to obtain any favor, or removal of evil, in their behalf. See 1 Sam.3.14.

*{but I will consume them by the sword, and by the famine, and by the pestilence.}* By further judgments added to what at present they endure. Three grievous evils, any one of them alone sufficient to eat out a numerous nation, 2 Sam.24.12–14. but usually concurring, and oft jointly threatened, chap.29.17,18. and 32.24,36. & and 34.17. Ezek.5.17. and 6.11. and 7.15. and 14.13–21. See ver.18.

**Verse 13.** *{Then said I}* Heb. *And I said.* So chap.13.7,8.

*{Ah Lord GOD, Behold, the Prophets say unto them; Ye shall not see the sword, neither shall ye have famine;}* See the like complaint of the Prophet to God, concerning these false prophets deluding the people; and pitying the poor people deluded by them, chap.4.10. and 23.9.

*{see}* That is, *suffer*, or *endure*; as chap.42.14. Psal.89.48. Joh.8.51,52.

*{neither shall ye have famine}* Heb. *famine shall not be to you*; no such famine shall befall you, as these prophets threaten you with, by the enemies wasting of your country, and the siege of your city, chap.27.8. and 38.2.

*{but I will give you assured peace in this place.}* Thus these wicked wretches speak as in God's name, as if God himself spoke by them, chap.23.17,31. See chap.4.10.

*{assured peace}* Heb. *peace of truth.* See Esay 39.8. and of these false prophets promising the people *peace*, that is, prosperity and safety, chap.6.14. & 8.11. & 23.17.

**Verse 14.** *{Then the LORD said unto me:}* Heb. *And*; as ver.13. which may well be here retained. God's answer follows to this complaint of the Prophet concerning those false prophets, charging them with falsehood and abuse of God's name, ver.14. and threatening destruction both to them, ver.15. and to those that are deluded by them, ver.16.

*{the Prophets prophesy lies in my name,}* Heb. *falsehood*, or, *a lie*; as chap.27.10. See chap.23.16,26. and 29.21.

*{I sent them not, neither have I commanded them, neither spake unto them;}* Or, *I neither sent them, nor commanded them, nor spake unto them*; that all may run in one tenor, as in the original it does. I sent them not on any such errand, nor gave them any such matter in charge to deliver as from me; as chap.1.17. See chap.23.21,32. and 29.9.

*{they prophesy unto you a false vision and divination, and a thing of nought, and the deceit of their heart.}* Heb. *a vision of falsehood*, or, *a lie*, (as in the former branch, and Zach.10.2.) *and a divination, and a thing of nought, and the deceit of their heart*; or, *and a divination nought worth*, (as *a cloud and smoke*, for, *a cloud* of *smoke*, or, *a smoky cloud*, Esay 4.5. *and, a sign and a witness* for, a witnessing *sign*, Esay 19.20. *and, peace and truth*, for, *peace* of *truth*, as ver.13. or, *assured peace*, Esay 39.8.) *even* (as chap.13.13.) *the deceit*, or, *deceitful device*; (as Dan.11.25.) *of* their own (as Esay 56.11. and 57.17. chap.13.10.) *heart.* So chap.23.26.

**Verse 15.** *{Therefore thus saith the LORD concerning the Prophets, that prophesy in my name and I sent them not,}* Or, *when as I sent them not*, as cha.6.14.9.8.

*{Yet they say}* Heb. *and* (as ver.9.) *they are saying*: this is that which they are still telling the people; the pronoun demonstrative including the verb substantive; as cha.17.15.

*{sword and famine shall not be in the land}* Neither war, nor famine procured by it, or accompanying it: as chap.42.14.

*{by sword and famine shall these Prophets be consumed.}* They themselves shall suffer and perish by those evils with the first, from which they promised immunity and security to others. See the like commination, chap.6.15,30. So chap.20.6. 1 King.22.25. See also, chap.42.16. and 44.12.

**Verse 16.** *{And the people to whom they prophesy shall be cast out in the streets of Jerusalem, because of the sword and the famine, and they shall have none to bury them, their wives, nor their sons, nor their daughters.}* The people deluded by them shall perish together with them, and find too late by woeful experience, what wicked impostors they were. So chap.20.6.

*{cast out}* For, lie *cast out*; as 1 King.13.24,25. *was cast in the way*, for, lay *cast in the way*. See on Esay 14.12.

*{in the streets of Jerusalem}* In the time of the siege; or at the surprisal of the city. See ver.18.

*{because of the famine and the sword}* Heb. *from the face of the famine and the sword*; as chap.4.4,26.

*{none to bury them}* So chap.8.2.

*{your wives, nor your sons, nor your daughters}* This is added to aggravate their grief and misery. See the like, chap.5.17. and 6.21. and 11.22.

*{for I will pour their wickedness upon them.}* That is, the punishment due to it: as Gen.4.13. chap.2.25. of the term of *pouring*, see on Esay 42.25. and chap.10.25. Heb. *and*; as chap.13.21.

**Verse 17.** *{Therefore shalt thou say this word unto them;}* Heb. *And* (as ver.10) *thou shalt say this word*; that is, *Say thou*, or, *speak, on this wise to them*: as Chap.13.12.

*{Let mine eyes run down with tears night and day, and let them not cease;}* Or, *mine eyes shall run down with tears night and day, and shall not cease.* Let them know that howsoever the false prophets feed and flatter them with vain promises of assured peace and safety; and bear them in hand that all shall go well with them, ver.13. Yet that you foreseeing, and being well assured of what evils were preparing for them, and would certainly surprise them, if not speedily prevented, can do no other than abandon yourself unto an incessant mourning for them; if you may thereby provoke them unto the like. See Chap.9.1. & 13.17. Lam.1.16. & 2.18.

*{cease}* Heb. as some, *be silent*: as if tears had a voice: Others rather, as our version, *surcease*, or, *give over*. So Lam.3.49.

*{for the virgin daughter of my people}* Of this form, see on Esay 23.12. & 47.1. *for*, or, *because*; as chap.10.21. and 13.17.

*{is broken with a great breach,}* Or, *will be broken*; but he speaks in the prophetical form of things future as present. See chap.4.20. & 6.14. and 8.11,21. the instrumental particle is in either member wanting: as chap.30.14.

*{with a very grievous blow.}* See chap.10.19. and 30.12. So Neh.3.19.

**Verse 18.** *{If I go forth into the field, then behold the slain with the sword; and if I enter into the city, then behold them that are sick with famine.}* The Prophet to show them what cause he had thus to lament, speaks as already present at the siege of the city; and as if, whithersoever he betook himself, he had nothing but sad spectacles, and objects of much grief in his eye; without the city, of men slain by the enemies' sword; within the city, of people perishing for want of food; See ver.12,15,16. Chap.15.2. and 33.5. and 38.2,9. so Deut.32.25. Lam.4.9. Ezek.7.15.

*{then behold}* Heb. *and*; as ver.13. and so in the next branch.

*{slain with the sword}* Heb. *slain of the sword*; as Esay 22.2. Lam.4.9.

*{them that are sick with famine}* Heb. *sicknesses*, or *diseases, of famine*: for the word being a substantive properly signifies, 2 Chron.21.19. chap.16.4. the adjunct for the subject; as Prov.14.1. Dan.9.23. there is in the original an elegant consonancy between the terms of *sick*, and *slain*: the word *slain*, is used of the famished also, Lam.4.9.

*{Yea both the Prophet and the Priest go about into a land that they know not}* Heb. *yea*, (as ver.5.) *also Prophet, also Priest*, that is, as well the false prophets as the priests, who had both conspired together in deluding the people, and in opposing God's true prophets, (chap.5.31. and 26.6.) shall be led captive into a remote land, into a strange country where they had never been before, chap.15.14. This, say the Jewish doctors, was fulfilled in the captivity under Jehoiacin; of whom the like is said, chap.22.26,28. for with him were the most of any note in the State carried captive to Babylon, 2 King.24.14,16. and that there were some of these false prophets among the rest; (for of the priests need no doubt be made) they suppose to appear, nor seems it improbable, by what we find chap.29.8,15,21. and then indeed it is not unlikely that this was in part executed; though more fully under Zedekiah afterward accomplished. See cha.20.6. and 52.24. and it is said, say they, *Go about*, to note the length of the way, and the remoteness of the place, whither they were to be carried: for those that take long journeys, cannot always go straight on, but are enforced oft to fetch a compass, and to go far about: and according to this exposition, (which I conceive to be most probable) the copulative in the last clause should be used for the relative; as oft-times it is: (see Esay 49.7. chap.4.16.) for the Hebrew is, *and they know not*, or, *knew not*, or, *shall not know*. Whence some expound it, admitting the former interpretation for the residue of the text; *and yet for all this, they shall not understand*, or take notice of God's just judgment upon them for their wicked courses, (as Esay 42.25.) but persist still in the same, chap.29.8. Others, they shall wander up and down the country seeking for relief and refuge; being at their wits' end, and not knowing what to do; as Esay 8.21. See chap.4.9. Howbeit, because the word here found is used frequently for *merchants*, Gen.23.16. Esay 23.8. so called, because they go to and fro from place to place with their wares. Some read the words, *they shall go up and down trading* in a strange land: and some others of prime note, *they make merchandise* (not unlike the phrase that the Apostle uses, 2 Cor.2.17. that is, to eat upon the people, and make a prey of them, pretend to have visions and revelations from God, chap.23.25–27,30–32. Mic.3.5.) *against the land*; as the particle is used, chap.1.19. and 15.20. to the ruin and destruction of it, Lam.2.14. *and they know it not*: the people are not aware of it, apprehend it not, take no notice of it: or, because the verb is indefinite, *it is not known*: their knavery is not discovered. But this seems a more forced interpretation than the former. Thus they that expound this of the wicked priests, and false prophets. Yet because it may seem to be no matter of grief, such especially as the Prophet should so much bewail, that priests and prophets so qualified, should sustain what they most justly deserved; a learned late writer would have it meant of God's true prophets, as Ezekiel and Daniel, that were also carried away captive into Chaldea, Ezek.1.1–3. Dan.1.3,6. or of the priests only, but those of two sorts; such of them, as were employed most about sacrifice and prayer, called here priests; and such of them, as were taken up with song and matter of praise, termed prophets both here, and 1 Chr.25.1. But I see no reason of relinquishing the foregoing interpretation; since that the Prophet might very well intermix together with the miseries of his people, which justly also befell them, being the main matter of his grief, the deserved judgment of God, which should be inflicted upon those by whom they had been seduced, as God himself in his speech to him had before joined them together, ver.15,16. Howbeit a learned late writer, understanding this passage of the present famine, renders it, *even the Prophet, even the Priest*, (whom for their place and employment, should of all others be relieved and supplied with all necessaries) *go to and fro in the land*, (seeking for relief) *and men know them not*; that is, they are not regarded, nor notice taken of them; the famine is so general, and so great: the verb taken indefinitely; and rendered therefore passively; as the like, Job.7.3. but the sword joined with the famine here, confirms me in my first judgment.

**Verse 19.** *{Hast thou utterly rejected Judah}* The Prophet after his professed lamentation for the calamities of his people, impendent and imminent, but which he beheld and considered as incumbent and present; does now return again unto God, directing his speech unto him, as before, ver.7–9. by way of complaint, expostulation, confession of sin, supplication for mercy in the behalf of his people, and profession of a constant purpose of dependence upon him, as in the person of the better sort among them. Thus the Prophet yet ceases not to solicit God for them, notwithstanding that inhibition, ver.11. as did Moses before him, Exod.32.10,11,31. *Hast thou utterly rejected Judah?* or, *wilt thou utterly reject Judah?* Are you resolved to deal with Judah, as you have done with Israel, the other ten tribes? chap.3.8. Heb. *Hast thou rejecting rejected?* or, *wilt thou rejecting reject?* Lam.5.22. See Psal.89.38.

*{hath thy Soul loathed Zion?}* Or, *Doth thy soul* (that is, *dost thou?* as chap.6.8. and 12.7. and 13.17.) *loathe* (as Zach.11.8. Psal.11.5. Esay 1.14.) *Sion*; the place that you formerly so much delighted in, Psal.132.13,14. but the people here principally intended. See chap.15.1. and this threatened, Lev.26.30.

*{Why hast thou smitten us, and there is no healing for us}* Or, *so that there is no healing for us?* as chap.11.19,21. or, *that there can be no curing of us*; as chap.15.1. See chap.8.22. and 15.18.

*{we looked for peace, and there is no good; and for a time of healing, and behold trouble.}* See the same, chap.8.15. see also, chap.13.16. Lam.4.17.

**Verse 20.** *{We acknowledge, O LORD our wickedness, and the iniquity of our Fathers; for we have sinned against thee.}* In these words the Prophet, as some conceive, would teach the people and prescribe them a form of prayer, which they might use, humbling themselves in the time of their distress; as Hos.14.2. But I suppose it rather the Prophet's own prayer at present conceived in the person of the godly, which the Lord had among that people, as a small quantity of good grain intermingled with, and buried in an huge heap of chaff and trash. See the like confessions, Chap.3.25. Psal.106.6. Dan.9.8.

*{We acknowledge}* Heb. *We know*; as Psal.51.3. Esay 59.12. So chap.3.13.

*{for we have sinned against thee.}* As it is rendered also, Psal.41.4. or, *We acknowledge, that we have sinned against thee*: as the particle is used, chap.4.18. and 11.19.

**Verse 21.** *{Do not abhor us for thy Names sake;}* Though for our sins (we confess it) we deserve that you should. See on ver.7.

*{abhor us}* Or, *it*; to wit, Sion, ver.19. because speech of the Temple follows; howsoever, a defect of the pronoun; as Esay 37.19. chap.15.14.

*{do not disgrace the Throne of thy glory}* Or, *thy throne of glory*; as, *thy hill of holiness*, Psal.15.1. that is, *thy glorious throne*, as 1 Sam.2.8. Esay 22.23. Either Jerusalem the seat of David's throne, chap.3.17. called also the Throne of God, 1 Chr.29.23. or rather the Temple and the Ark in it, the place of God's special presence among his people; and his chair of state, Psal.80.1. ver.7. See chap.17.12. though we by our sins have deserved to be destroyed, yet suffer not your own throne to be disgracefully used, and yourself to be disparaged and dishonored therein. See Esay 63.18. and 64.10,11. Psal.74.3–8.

*{remember, break not thy covenant with us.}* *Remember* your congregation; as Psal.74.2. or, your *covenant*, from the next branch; as Psal.74.20. and 106.15. *break not thy covenant with us*: as they complain, Psal.89.39. Howbeit, God never breaks covenant with those that continue loyal, and are careful to keep covenant with him, 1 King.8.23. Psal.103.17,18.

**Verse 22.** *{are there among the vanities of the Gentiles that can cause rain? or can the heavens give showers?}* Neither are any of the heathen idols, Zach.10.2. nor the creature above of itself, able to afford the earth a drop of rain, unless God please thereby to give it. See Job 38.25–29. Deut.28.23,24.

*{vanities of the Gentiles}* Their vain idols, chap.8.19. and 10.15.

*{that can cause to rain}* Heb. *that make to rain*: no, that is God's peculiar prerogative, Deut.28.12. Psa.147.8. ch.5.24. Amos 4.7. Mat.5.45.

*{or}* Heb. *and*: as ch.9.12. v.12.

*{can the heavens give showers?}* Without your provision, or permission? God must hear the heavens, ere the heavens can the earth, Hos.2.21. Heb. *shall*, or, *will, they give showers?* but the word is in a potential notion; as the like, chap.13.23. Of the word *showers*, see chap.3.3.

*{Art not thou he, O LORD our God?}* Either, *Art not thou, O Lord, our God?* the pronoun for the verb substantive; as Psal.44.4. you alone are our God, who in all our necessities we are to repair unto, and who alone are able to relieve us, Psal.65.2,5. or, *Art not thou he* that gives rain, or that makes to rain? supplied from one of the former branches; that can give it, and supply our want of it when you please, 1 Kin.17.1. & 18.1.

*{therefore we will wait upon thee}* Heb. *and*; as vers.10,16. we will seek to no other but to you for it, in this our present want and distress, Zach.10.1. and wait patiently until you be pleased to afford us this mercy, Esa.8.17. & 30.18.

*{for thou hast made all these things.}* Rev.4.11. and having at first made them, do at your pleasure dispose of them, Psal.135.6,7. they being all at your command; Psal.119.91. & 148.5,6,8. or, *thou dost*, or, *workest*, (as vers.7.) *all these things*: you restrain rain, and give it, when and how you see good, Psal.65.9,10. & 147.8. See Zach.11.12. And this whole passage evidently evinces, that this prophecy was delivered in the time of a great drought.

## CHAPTER 15

**Verse 1.** *{Then said the LORD unto me; Though Moses and Samuel stood before me, Yet my mind could not be towards this people:}* The dependence of this chapter upon the former (for they make up both one continued discourse) stands thus: The Prophet had complained to God of the grievous judgment of drought then present, and moved him in his people's behalf, for the removal of it, chap.14.2,9. God hereupon tells the Prophet, that he was so far from granting what he requested for them, that he was resolved for their leaving him, to leave them, to expel them out of their land, ver.10. and instead of removing the present judgment, to consume them by other additionals to it, v.12. and forbids the Prophet therefore to move him any further for them, vers.11. The Prophet nevertheless returns to his wonted course of soliciting God earnestly for them; entreating him, that he would not yet utterly cast them off, or loathe and abhor them, vers.19,21. And to this branch of his suit the Lord here returns this answer, containing a close, but flat denial of his suit; that his affection is so alienated from them, that though Moses and Samuel, persons so gracious with him, that at their request he had oft spared this people, and granted what in behalf of them they desired, Psal.99.6,8. were now surviving, and should intercede for them, yet they should not prevail to win or turn his heart to them; and it was in vain therefore for the Prophet to solicit him any further in their behalf. See the like, Ezek.14.14. Such an height of disaffection toward persons and people, may God be wrought and brought unto, by their obstinate persistence in cross and crooked courses, after all means used to reclaim and reduce them from the same, that no intercession of any shall avail, to find favor, or obtain mercy, at the hand of God, for them. See 1 Sam.2.25. & 3.14. Esa.22.12,13.

*{Then}* Heb. *And*; as ch.14.13,18.

*{Though}* Heb. *If*; as ch.14.1.

*{Moses}* Of whom, see Exo.32.11,14. Num.14.19,20.

*{and Samuel}* Or, *or* (as chap.14.22.) *Samuel*. Of whom, see 1 Sam.7.9.

*{stood before me}* A form of speech, having sometime a notion of ministry and attendance, 1 King.10.8. and 17.1. Dan.7.10. here importing the gesture used commonly in prayer, Gen.18.22. & 19.27. Matth.5.5. Mark 11.25. Luk.18.11. but yet more specially here of one that by prayer, as an intercessor or advocate, pleads or deals for another, Deut.5.5. Psalm 106.23. chap.18.20.

*{yet}* A defect of the conjunction; as Esa.44.11.

*{my mind}* Heb. *my soul*; as ch.6.8.

*{could not be}* Heb. *is not*, or, *were not*, or, *will not be*; as chap.14.19.

*{to this people}* As not owning them now. See ch.14.10.

*{cast them out of my sight, and let them go forth.}* Or, *let them be gone*: see vers.2. as importing that God could no longer endure so much as the sight of them: a speech borrowed from the practice of men, who are wont to throw aside such nasty and loathsome things, as they list not to see, or cannot brook the view of, into some obscure nook or hole, where it may lie out of sight, Psalm 31.22. 1 King.9.7. 2 King.23.27. The Prophet is said to do, what by him God declares and denounces to be done: see chap.1.10. and 6.11.

**Verse 2.** *{And it shall come to pass, if they say unto thee, Whither shall we go forth? then shalt thou tell them; Thus saith the LORD, Such as are for death to death; and such as are for the sword to the sword; and such as are for the famine to the famine; and such as are for the captivity to the captivity.}* To that heavy doom passed upon this people, vers.1. the Lord here subjoins, what the issue and effect of it should be when they should be thus cast out of God's gracious sight, and gone out of his protecting presence: as Gen.4.16. to wit, that they should be exposed to those formerly denounced evils, some to one kind of them, some to another, accordingly as God had designed them thereunto, chap.14.12. see chap.43.11. Ezek.14.21. and these four, say the Rabbines, rise by degrees: the sword more grievous than the pestilence, 2 Sam.24.13,14. the famine than the sword, Lam.4.9. captivity than any of them, being an evil of more length, and exposing to all kind of calamity, Lev.26.39. Deut.28.48,65,67.

*{it shall come to pass}* Heb. *it shall be*, as ch.3.16.

*{if they say}* Or, *when they shall say*; as ch.5.19. where the particle is the same.

*{whither shall we go forth?}* Or, simply *go*; as Gen.4.16. & 10.11. 2 Kin.5.26. Zach.6.8.

*{for death to death}* *Death*, for, *the pestilence*; distinguished from those other kinds of death, by the *sword* and *famine*; as also, Revel.6.5. so chap.14.12. Matth.24.7. *death* by *diseases*; as chap.16.4. diverse from *death* by *slaughter*, Ezek.28.8. See chap.18.21.

*{for the sword to the sword.}* *The sword*; because a principal and most general weapon of offense, put for all other of that kind; as Gene.27.40. and death by the sword, for a violent death from the force of an enemy, by what means soever effected; as Esay 1.20.

**Verse 3.** *{And I will appoint over them four kinds, saith the LORD; the sword to slay, and the dogs to tear, and the fowls of the heaven, and the beasts of the earth, to devour and destroy:}* *I will appoint*, or, *set over them*; as Lev.26.16. a borrowed speech from officers set over people, or persons, and appointed how to handle them, and deal with them, Exod.1.11.

*{four kinds}* Of penalties. Heb. *four families.*

*{dogs to tear}* Heb. *to draw*, or, *drag*, ch.49.20. used of a corpse or carcass, ch.22.19.

*{fowls of the heaven}* Heb. *fowl*, collectively: and *heaven*, for, *air*, as ch.4.25.

*{beasts to devour, to destroy}* Heb. *beast*; as, *fowl*, collectively: here for wild beasts, such as are wont both to assail and worry living persons, even unto death, and to prey also upon the dead. So Deut.28.26. Esa.18.6. see 1 Kin.14.11. & 21.23,24. 2 Kin.9.35,36. ch.12.9. Lev.26.22. Ezek.14.15.

**Verse 4.** *{And I will cause them to be removed into all Kingdoms of the earth}* Heb. *I will give them for a removing.* So chap.24.9. & 29.18. & 34.17. Ezek.23.46. See Deut.28.25. for those that render it, *wandering*; as from Gen.4.14. chap.14.10. mistake the root. The former threatening concerned those that were designed to death; this, those that were to go into captivity, vers.2. that they should be dispersed into several regions and countries one from another. See chap.9.16. & 13.24. vers.7. Deut.28.64. Ezek.5.12. & 12.14.

*{because of Manasseh the son of Hezekiah King of Judah, for that which he did in Jerusalem.}* That is, say some, such sins as his were; to wit, idolatry and murder, 2 King.21.2,7,16. See chap.2.28,34. so it should be like that, 2 Pet.2.15. Jude 11. or rather, as others, the sins that Manasses did himself commit, and the people partook with him, and imitated him in, 2 Kin.21.9,11. and which albeit he repented of, 2 Chr.33.12,13. yet the people were never truly humbled for, chap.44.10. nor sincerely reclaimed from them, ch.3.10. see 2 King.23.26,27. & 24.3,4. See the like of Jeroboam, 1 King.14.15,16.

*{the son of Hezekiah}* But one altogether unlike his father, and that reversed what had been by him well done, 1 King.21.3.

**Verse 5.** *{For who shall have pity upon thee, O Jerusalem? or, who shall bemoan thee? or who shall go aside to ask how thou dost?}* So Esa.51.19. Nah.3.7. intimating, that she should be left in a forlorn condition, friendless, helpless, and comfortless, deserted by all, and failing even of such offices, as men are wont to afford even to mere strangers in misery. See Lam.1.2.

*{For}* Or, *But*; as some: and so is the particle used, ch.14.12,13. or, *yet*; as Job 5.7. Esa.49.25.

*{have pity on thee}* Show any favor or mercy to you. See 2 Chron.36.16,17.

*{bemoan thee}* Condole with you, and seek to comfort you, though they cannot otherwise help or relieve you: as Job 2.11. So Nah.3.7.

*{go aside to ask how thou dost.}* So much as turn in, as they pass by, to inquire how it fares with you. Heb. *to ask of thy peace*; as 1 Sam.25.5,14. 2 Sam.8.10. For they mistake the form, who understand it of *praying for her peace*, Psal.122.6.

**Verse 6.** *{Thou hast forsaken me, saith the LORD,}* See the same plea against them, ch.1.16. & 2.13,19,32.

*{thou art gone backward.}* See ch.7.24.

*{therefore will I stretch out mine hand against thee, and destroy thee}* Heb. *And*; as ch.14.16,22. See ch.9.16. Job 6.9.

*{I am weary with repenting.}* Or, *of repenting*; as Esa.1.14. I am weary of reversing or staying the execution of such dooms and denunciations, as from time to time have been passed upon you for your wicked courses; and reprieving you, from the destruction pronounced against you, upon your formal reformation, and feigned repentance. I am now resolved to forbear and spare you no longer. So Gen.6.3,6,7. Psal.78.36,38,56,64. ch.4.28.

**Verse 7.** *{And I will fan them with a fan in the gates of the land;}* Or, *into* (as Esa.30.29.) *the gates of the earth*; that is, of the wide world: that *gates* are here put for *cities*, or, *coasts*, as ch.14.2. is agreed. But those that follow the former version, suppose the place designed, from whence they should be driven away and removed, to wit, out of the cities and coast of Judea: and so there may seem an allusion to the place where men use to fan or winnow their grain, to wit, in the door usually of their garners, or barns. Those that take to the latter, (wherein they have the Chaldee, and the Jewish doctors, going before them) conceive reference to be had unto the places, into which they were to be driven and dispersed, to wit, into the cities, regions, coasts, and quarters, of the wide world; as vers.4. see Lev.26.33. chap.9.16. & 10.18. howsoever, they seem to be wide here, who would have the *fanning* here spoken of, to be a cleansing only, and purging fan, by which God had assayed to sever them and their wickedness, but in vain, the one from the other, chap.6.29,30. that this was no such fanning, but such a fanning as should carry all away before it: see chap.4.11. such as that, ch.51.2.

*{I will bereave them of children, I will destroy my people;}* According to this reading, the pronoun is wanting, to be supplied from the former branch, as chap.13.19. but the text without it may well be read, *I will bereave*, or, *waste, and destroy this people*: *bereave* of their children, as Gen.42.26. Hos.9.12. (though that be not in the text) or, *waste* and *consume*: for the word is of a far larger extent. See Lev.26.22. (where, *of your children*, is groundlessly put in, as here) Deut.32.25. (where it is extended to old as well as young, and it is rendered, *destroy*) Lam.1.20. Ezek.5.17. & 14.15. in all which places it is rendered without that addition, either *bereave*, or *spoil*: *I will waste and destroy my people*; or, waste them until they be destroyed: see ch.14.15,16. vers.3,6.

*{my people}* Not, *this people*; as before, vers.1. to let them know, that that privilege of being called and accounted his people, should not secure them, nor save them from destruction, See chap.12.7.

*{sith they return not from their ways.}* Or, *because they return not from their ways*, from their wicked courses, but persist obstinately in them, chap.8.4,5. the particle is wanting, which some therefore otherwise supply, rendering the text, *yet* (as chap.15.1.) *they return not from their ways*, and the words foregoing in the time past; *though* (as chap.3.1.) *I have fanned them, and wasted, and destroyed them, yet* (as vers.10.) *they return not*; they are not reclaimed, they are never the better, for all that has been done to them already; So Esay 1.5,6. chap.5.3. And this those Jewish doctors that go this way, understand of the ten tribes carried away captive by Salmanaser, 2 Kin.17.6. by whose ruin, the other two should have taken warning, but would not, chap.3.10. but this is very improbable. Others, with more probability suppose it to have reference to those calamities, that had befallen them by Pharaoh-Necho at the death of Josiah, when many of them in likelihood were destroyed, and the land afterward pillaged, 2 Kings 23.29,33. or to the evils that they sustained by Nebuchadnezzar, under Jehojakim and Jehojacin, 2 Kings 24.2,16. but neither do we read of any such dispersion, as is here intimated, effected either by the Egyptian, or by the Chaldean under Jehojakim, and for that deportation under Jehojacin, it is supposed to have been later than the date of this prophecy. See chap.14.1.

**Verse 8.** *{Their widows are increased to me, above the sand of the seas.}* Heb. *are many*, or, *more* in number (as Psal.40.5,12. & 69.4. their husbands being either slain, or otherwise destroyed, chap.18.21.) *than the sand of the seas.* A proverbial form of speech, in an hyperbolical or excessive expression, intimating a numberless number, or exceeding great multitude of ought, not easy, if at all, to be numbered. So Gen.22.17. & 32.12. & 41.49. Psal.139.18. Esa.10.22. The words, as the former, vers.7. are conceived in the time past, but if so rendered, it must of necessity be understood after the Prophets' usual manner, speaking of things future, as past or present; for we read not of any such havoc in Jeremiah's time made of this people, before that under Zedekiah, for they seem to run too high, that would carry it up to *Ahaz* his time, 2 Chron.28.5,8. as do some of the Jewish writers: nor see I therefore, why the words may not be rendered here in the future, as well as in the verse foregoing: as, *I will fan, I will bereave*, or, *waste; I will destroy* there: so here, *their widows shall be more* in number, *than the sand of the seas*; as the Red Sea, the Midland Sea, and the like, Psal.104.25. & 114.3.

*{to me}* That is, say some, *from me*; by my just judgment executed upon them: as, *blessed of*, or, *from the Lord*, 1 Sam.23.21. and, *salvation is of*, or, *from, the Lord*, Psal.3.8. for the particle is in these places the same. Others, *before me*, or, *in my sight*. But I conceive it rather, to be only an elegant redundancy and fineness of speech, the like whereunto, See Gen.12.1. compared with Act.7.3. Exod.18.27. Cant.4.6. Esa.22.5. ch.22.6.

*{I have brought upon them, against the mother of the young men, a spoiler at noonday.}* Howsoever these words be read, as they are diversely rendered; that they are meant of Nebuchadnezzar, is in a manner generally agreed, which may be good direction unto us, for the right rendering of the former passages.

*{I have brought}* Or, *I will bring*; as chap.49.8. Ezek.14.21.

*{upon them}* Heb. *to*, or, *unto them*; as Obad.5. that is, either *upon them*, as Esa.3.26. & 26.9. or, *against them*; as chap.3.25. Howbeit, it may be no other than a redundant elegancy, as that in the foregoing branch.

*{against the mother of the young men}* Heb. *young-man*, or, *a young-man*; and here the interpreters are divided, and go divers several ways: Some render it, *against the mothers of the young-men*, taking both *mother* and *young men* collectively, and they thus expound it; the women shall be deprived of their husbands, and the young men of their mothers: others *against the assembly of the young-men*, chap.6.11. because from the word *mother*, come some terms that signify *company, family*, or, *people*. So the Chaldee, and some Jewish commenters treading in his steps; others, *against the mother*, and, *the young men*; that is, against both parents and children, 2 Chr.36.17. chap.6.11. & 13.14. & 14.16. Others; *against the mother of the young-men*, as our version renders it, that is, against Jerusalem that has heretofore bred many choice young men, Esay 51.18. Others, *a spoiler of young men*; one that shall spoil and make havoc of them, drawing in hither the word following, but by a trajection overharsh. Others lastly, *against the mother*, (that is, against Jerusalem, the *Metropolis*, or, *Mother-city*; as Esay 50.1. alluded to Gal.4.26.) *a young-man*, or, *a choice young-man*; as the word originally intimates, ch.49.19. & 50.44. Where it is used of Cyrus as many conceive. So is Nebuchadnezzar here termed, because he seems to have been in the flower of his youth, and at the height of his strength, when he came against Jerusalem. See chap.4.7. and this last I concur with, because the words of the text do most freely yield it, and the points or pauses also go with it.

*{a spoiler at noonday}* One that shall assail it; not as a thief by night in the dark, ch.49.9. 1 Thess.5.2. Rev.3.3. & 16.15. but as a highwayman that robs openly at noonday, chap.6.4. Zeph.2.4.

*{I have caused him to fall upon it suddenly, and terrors upon the city.}* These words are likewise very diversely rendered. I shall omit some versions, because they cannot be fitted to the terms of the text: the main difficulty and difference in the rest, is about the word rendered *city*, as it most usually signifies, which signification those that retain, here render the text, either as our version does, *and terrors* upon *the city*; or, because the words lie otherwise in the Hebrew, as other, desolation of *city*, or, *cities, and terrors*. But because this latter makes somewhat an uncouth insertion, as the former seemed to do an overharsh trajection. Some would have the word *city* to be absolutely, rendering the words, as for *the city*, there shall be *terrors*; that is, the city shall abound with, or be full of terrors; as *it is all oppression*, that is, it abounds with, or is full of oppression, chap.6.6. But because those also seem somewhat forced, others therefore seek some other signification for the word rendered *city*: and here the Jewish critics suggest us, two divers senses of the word; the former from those places, where the word in the plural form at least, has the notion of *an enemy*, 1 Sam.28.16. Psal.139.20. Dan.4.19. and these render the text, *I will cause to fall upon her suddenly, an enemy and terrors*, as, *the spoiler is fallen upon thy fruits*, chap.48.32. and *terror and trembling is fallen upon me*, Psal.55.5. the latter, because the word comes of a root that signifies *to raise*, or, *rouse*, Chap.6.22. & 25.32. would have it rather to signify, *a tumult*; and this some interpreters of the best note with us follow; instead of *enemy*, rendering it *tumults* and *terrors*. To these two, a learned late annotator adds a third, he conceives the word here used to be a Chaldee term, by change of a letter, framed from an Hebrew word that signifies *pain*, or, *torment*, Esa.21.3. & 13.8. and of such interchange of letters he gives some instances, in this very word; for an *Angel*, or, *Messenger*; Dan.4.13. from the Hebrew term, for a *messenger*, Prov.25.13. chap.49.14. Obad.1. and in that for the *earth*, chap.10.11. Hence he renders the text, *I will cause to fall upon her pain*, or, *torment, and terrors*. And these three last seem least of any to force the text; all that can be objected against them is, that the word itself is nowhere found in either of the two latter notions, nor the singular form at all in the first. I shall therefore take the boldness amidst this variety and diversity, to subjoin mine own conjecture; the word precisely the same is used for *a watcher*, Dan.4.13,23. and to the same effect with a very slight alteration, Cant.5.2. Mal.2.12. I suppose therefore that the text may well thus be rendered, *I will cause to fall upon her* (that is, upon Jerusalem the mother-city) *suddenly a watcher and terrors*; that is, such a watcher, or such watchers, (the word being collectively taken) as shall fill them with affrightment; that the Chaldean forces set down before Jerusalem, are compared to *watchers*, and are so styled, though by another term, See chap.4.16,17. & 5.6. and of the *terrors* that upon their approach should surprise them; See cha.4.9. & 6.25.

**Verse 9.** *{She that hath born seven languisheth, she hath given up the ghost.}* Jerusalem, that formerly had bred up so many children, (*seven*, for many, as Lev.26.18,24,28. 1 Sam.2.5. Job 5.19. Psal.119.164.) now faints and fails, is clean spent; both bereaved of those she had, and unable to breed any more; See 1 Sam.2.5. Esay 23.4. & 51.18,20.

*{given up the ghost}* Or, *gaspeth*: Heb. *puffeth out her soul*, as Job 11.20.

*{her sun is gone down, while it was yet day}* Or, *the sun is set with her while it is yet day*; before the day is at an end, or the time of evening yet come. Amidst the height of her prosperity, and imaginary security she is suddenly fallen. So, *the Sun shall go down with them at noon-day*, when they least dream of, or look for any sunset, any fall, Amos 8.9. See also Esay 13.10. and 59.10.

*{she hath been ashamed and confounded}* Or, *she is abashed and confounded*; as ch.2.26,36. & 3.25. & 14.3.

*{and the residue of them, I will deliver to the sword before their enemies, saith the LORD}* That is, Judah and Benjamin, the two tribes that remain of that stock, says one of the Jewish commenters, ch.13.11. their children, as the word is used, Esay 14.22. says another, those that are not carried captive, says a third; applying it to those put at Riblah to death, in sight of the Chaldean tyrant, ch.52.10,27. as some other, to those that were slain with Gedaliah, 2 King.25.25. chap.41.3. of ours, those, say some, that fell not in the first encounter; others, such of them, as escaped the famine and pestilence, by which many perished in the siege of the city, shall be exposed to the enemies' sword: and this last seems the most likely. See chap.14.12. vers.2.

**Verse 10.** *{Woe is me my mother, that thou hast born me, a man of strife, and a man of contention, to the whole earth:}* The latter part of this chapter is spent in a communication or conference between God and the Prophet; not unlike to that, chap.11.20.12.9. It begins with the Prophet's complaint, (not wholly free from some tang and taint of discontent and distemper thence arising) of the general harsh usage and cross carriage that he had met with, for no other cause, than for the free and faithful discharge of his duty in the work of his ministry. See the like, chap.17.15.18. and 20.14,18.

*{Woe is me,}* An usual form of lamentation. See Chapter 4.31.

*{that thou hast born me}* Or, *that ever thou didst bear me*, chap.20.17,18.

*{a man of strife and a man of contention to the whole earth}* Or, *land*, rather; as chap.3.1. vers.14. not, *a man of strife*, that is, a *contentious* person, a man given to strife and contention; one that strives and contends with every one: as Esay 41.11. Job 31.35. but one whom the people do all generally oppose, whom the whole land strives and contends with. So Judg.12.2. the lot, as of Christ himself, when he was here upon earth, Psalm 2.1,2. Luke 2.34. Act.4.27. so of his ministers and messengers, Luke 21.17. Acts 28.22.

*{I have neither lent on usury; nor have men lent to me on usury, yet every one doth curse me}* Or, *I have not lent* to them, or, to any of them, *nor have they lent to me*; for the word is more general, extending itself unto any creditor or debtor, on any terms whatsoever. See Deu.15.2. & 24.10,11. 1 Sam.22.2. 2 King.4.1. Esa.24.2. and so the Jewish doctor here expounds it: for *usury* among themselves was forbidden the Jews, Deut.23.19. there has been no such pecuniary contracts or dealings in money matters between me and any of them, as are wont to breed difference and controversy between man and man.

*{yet every one of them curseth me.}* Heb. *is cursing me*; a defect of the discretive, as ver.1. or of the particle foregoing in the same notion, as it was there used, as Esa.10.20. and so it may also here be rendered, *that every one of them* should be *cursing me*; as daily they do.

**Verse 11.** *{The LORD said;}* God's answer to the Prophet, comforting and encouraging him against these his troublesome distracting, and disquieting thoughts.

*{verily it shall be well with thy remnant}* Heb. *if it be not well*; a defective speech in the nature of an oath; and the like in the next branch: as if he had said, Let me not be deemed a God of my word, or true and faithful in what I say or promise, if it be not so. See the like, 1 King.20.23. Psal.89.35. & 95.11. & 131.2. Esa.5.9. & 14.24.

*{with thy remnant}* Heb. *if thy remnant*, or, *residue, be not to*, or, *for, good*: by his *remnant*, or, *residue*, understanding not his issue; for it is not likely that he had any, chap.16.2. but the remainder of his life, as some; or the end and close of it, as others. See Psal.37.37. Esa.3.10. for they may justly be deemed to stray far from the intendment of the text, who would have by *his remnant*, here meant a remainder of God's people, which God would have reserved for himself, in that general destruction, Esa.7.3. & 10.20,21. *thy remnant*, say they, as, *thy wealth*, vers.13. But the truth is, there appears not any mention of *remnant* at all in the text. There was, it seems, some variety in copies here anciently: the *Cetib*, as they term it, can nothing be well made of, the *Keri*, which the critic masters has substituted in the room of it, goes evidently another way: neither of them afford the term that signifies a *remnant*; and where neither yields it, small reason seems to admit it, no necessity enforcing to it. Some therefore of the Jewish commenters following their Masorets' corrected reading, render it, *If I loose thee not*; from a word that signifies *to loose*, Dan.5.16. and, as some also, Job 37.3. and they apply it to that of Nebuzaradan's loosing Jeremiah from his bands, chap.40.14. as a promise of God to procure liberty for him, from such restraint and bands, as by his people he might endure. Which exposition, as it suits well with the complement of God's promise, so it removes the ground of those former difficulties.

*{verily I will cause the enemy to entreat thee well, in the time of evil, and in the time of affliction.}* Heb. *if I do not cause*, &c. as before; the word *well*, is not in the text: yet may not amiss be supplied from the foregoing branch; but is not necessarily required. In the words God may seem to meet with and prevent a doubt, that might arise in the Prophet's mind; to wit, that if this general evil threatened befall the whole State, the Prophet must of necessity bear his share in it with the rest. Now this to remove, God undertakes to the Prophet, to secure him from that fear, by assuring him, that he will so manage the matter, that he shall find better entreaty, when that time of public calamity shall come, at the hand of the enemy, than he had formerly found at the hand of his own people: for those draw it too far, that beyond Jeremiah's own person, extend it to any other, of whom, though in part true, chap.39.17,18. & 45.5. & 52.31,34. (as formerly promised, 1 Kin.8.50.) Psal.106.46. Dan.2.48,49. yet it is not here intended.

*{cause the enemy to entreat thee}* That is, says one of the Rabbines, understanding it of the Jews, I will make those of your own people, who are now your bitter enemies, to come and seek unto you in the time of their distress; as also they did, ch.21.1,2. so it should not be much unlike that, Rev.3.9. But the most rather understand it of the Chaldeans. To which purpose another of them; I will cause the enemy to propound the question to you, and put you to your choice, whether to go along with him, or to stay in the land with Gedaliah, chap.40.4. or, as it may well be rendered, *I will intercede for thee with the enemy*; as the word is used, Esa.53.12. chap.36.25. I will so deal in your behalf with the enemy, that he shall entreat you kindly, he shall use you no otherwise than well, chap.39.11,12. I shall adjoin my conjecture concerning the place, and so leave it: they make all (as to me seems) a needless trajection in the text, where the words lie in order thus; *I will intercede for thee in the time of evil, and in time of affliction the enemy*, or, *with the enemy*. I conceive that there is a defect of the preposition *from*, not unusual. See Exod.15.19. & 19.12. Esay 32.2. & 33.6. & 40.21. I read it therefore, *of affliction* from *with the enemy*, or, simply, *from the enemy*: as, *from the Lord*, Gen.19.24. where the particle is the same with that here expressed; referring *the enemy*, not to *intercession*, as the object of it, but to *affliction*, as the efficient of it, with which it stands also joined in the text: all that can be objected against this is, that the particle here used, is commonly prefixed to the party with whom intercession is made, Gen.23.8. ch.7.16. & 27.18. & 36.25. Job 21.15. another mostly, to the party in whose behalf; as Gen.23.8. Esa.53.12. and I shall leave it therefore to the decision of the learned.

**Verse 12.** *{Shall iron break the Northern iron and the steel?}* There are divers expositions given of these words: to pass by those that mistaking a letter in the text, and so misled by another in shape very like it, do of necessity swerve very far from the genuine sense of it, and scarce give any good or fit sense at all. Some of those that retain the right, suppose the verb here used, to come from a root, that has a notion of *confederacy*, or *friendship*, Prov.13.20. & 22.24. and they, with the old Latin, render the word, *Shall iron be confederate*, or, *joined, together, with iron from the North, and steel?* as if it were said, There is no hope that this obstinate people, and the Chaldeans, should ever be brought to an accord, (that it seems they had been sometime tampering about, see chap.51.59.) no more than iron can be glued unto iron, or to steel: Which they suppose to be spoken by God to the Prophet; some, to free him from that fear that Jonas was possessed with, of being accounted a false prophet, things falling out otherwise than as he had denounced, Jon.4.1,2. Others, (because this conceit is crossed by the Prophet's constant course of dealing with God in a contrary way, chap.9.1. & 13.15,17. & 14.7,8,19,21. & 28.6. vers.18. to assure him, that there was no hope or possibility of having any accord between them and the enemy; that he might no more be troubled with it, nor trouble himself with soliciting of God, to no purpose, about it, that business being now as past cure and care. But neither does this sense seem to fit well with the place; nor is any such form, as that here, found anywhere springing from that root. The most, therefore, both Jewish, and ours, take the word here, as our version does, and as it is frequently taken in the form here used, Job 34.24. Psal.2.9. chap.2.16. & 11.16. but they diverse ways apply it: Some, to God's counsels, and purposes; and they read the words thus, *Can one break iron, the Northern iron, and the steel?* as if it were said, *Can such iron be broken?* the verb being taken potentially, as chap.13.23. and indefinitely, as chap.8.4. that is, say some, shall any power be able to cross my proceedings, or to hinder the execution of my word and purpose, being of greater strength by far than iron, even the strongest and toughest of it, than steel itself? chap.23.29. Or, as others, shall any might or malice of the adversary be able to prevail against you my Prophet, whom I have made to be as such? chap.1.18. vers.20. Others, retaining the received reading, which our version exhibits, expound them, some of the Chaldeans, said to come from the north, chap.1.14. & 4.6. This people, seem they never so strong in their own conceit, chap.21.13. shall never be able to match those northern forces, that I shall send in upon them, vers.8. Others, of the Prophet himself, as if he had said, Though this people that thus oppose you, be in regard either of their inward obstinacy, or outward might, as hard and tough as iron, or the like metal, Esay 48.4. chap.6.28. yet shall they be no more able to crush you, or prevail against you, than ordinary iron is able to break such tough iron stuff that the northern parts yield, or than the firmest and strongest steel. See chap.1.18,19. vers.20. See also, Ezek.2.7,8,9.

*{Northern iron}* Heb. *iron from the North*, that is, such as is brought from the countries, that lie northward, out of which regions the strongest and toughest iron came to them: for the Chalybes, who were anciently most famous for ironworks, and their skill in tempering thereof, and from whom both with the Greeks, and Latins, the *steel* had its name, were a people of Pontus, neighboring upon the Paphlagones, and their country northward from Judea. See Strabo, l.12. Mela.l.1.c.20. Eudoxus in Steven the Byzantine, and Virgil of husbandry, l.1.

*{and steel}* That is, says the Jewish doctor, *iron and steel*, mixed together: and some other suppose an allusion to those words, chap.1.18. *a pillar of iron, and a wall of steel*; implying the Prophet to be as both, which though they might seem able to prevail against him, in regard of the one, yet should be sure to fail in, when they come to the other: but the words I conceive would rather be read by way of disjunction: *Northern iron*, or, *steel*; as the like. ch.10.20. & 14.22. Of the word, *steel*, see ch.1.18.

**Verse 13.** *{Thy substance, and thy treasures, will I give to the spoil without price:}* God in these words either continues his speech concerning the Chaldean forces, and their invasion of the land according to those, who of them expound the foregoing words, vers.12. or as the most, who conceive them to concern the Prophet, turns his speech from him to his people, foretelling what should become of all their wealth, wherein they prided themselves, ch.9.23. it should all become a prey to the Chaldeans, ch.17.3. as in conquest is wont to be, Esay 10.14. & 45.3.

*{without price}* Not regarding loss, or gain, but execution of my justice only, Psa.44.13. Esa.52.3.

*{and that for all thy sins, even in all thy borders.}* That is, as the most, for your sins that have been committed throughout the whole land, from the one end of it to the other, Chap.2.28. & 3.2. & 11.13. Heb. *and in* (that is, *for*; as chap.18.18.) *all thy sins and* (as chap.14.14.) *in all thy borders*: where because the particle is the same in both members, a learned interpreter would have the latter read, *and for all thine ends*, that is, evil projects and purposes: but neither is the word so used in Scripture; and the former interpretation is confirmed by chap.17.3. where the selfsame thing is repeated.

**Verse 14.** *{And I will make thee to pass with thine enemies into a land which thou knowest not.}* Or, *I will cause thee to serve thine enemies in a land, that thou knowest not*: for there is a double reading here, as also, chap.2.20. arising from the near affinity for shape of two Hebrew letters, *dalet* and *resh*: and from the like interchange of letters, is that variety of version in the same argument, *he was seen*, 2 Sam.22.11. and, *he did fly*, Psa.18.10. the latter reading (which the Chaldee follows) seems to receive some strength from cha.17.4. Howsoever, there is a defect of the relative in the latter limb (supplied itself, chap.17.4. by a copulative, chap.14.18.) of the pronoun in the former, which may as well be supplied, *it*, as *thee*, with reference to the *wealth* or *substance*, mentioned, verse 13. it shall all be carried away into a strange country, into an unknown land; as Esay 8.4. & 15.7. & 39.6. For as for that learned scholiast, who to reconcile those two places that seem parallel, would have the words rendered, *I will cause thine enemies to pass over thee*; that is, says he, to tyrannize, or rule imperiously over you; as they complain, Esay 26.13. Psal.129.1,3. and as the word, says he, is used, Job 13.13. *let what will pass to me*, or, *pass over me*, that is, *betide me*, as himself there renders it: it seems too much forced, and the place pointed too impertinent: nor seems the old Latin to come anything nearer home to the genuine sense of the place, who renders it, *I will bring thine enemies from a land that thou knowest not*, or, that learned man, who yet more regarding the particle, yields it, *by a land*, or, *through a land that thou knowest not*, or, *which thou knowest not*, which way they should come to you, being so remote from you.

*{for a fire is kindled in mine anger, which shall burn upon you.}* A defect of the relative, as in the former branch, and chap.14.8. see chap.17.4. see also, Deut.32.22. Esay 42.25. chap.4.4. and 17.27.

**Verse 15.** *{O LORD}* The Prophet returns here to the prosecution of his former complaint, v.10.

*{thou knowest}* You know me and mine integrity, Psal.139.1,23. or, you know how it fares with me, their malice and mine innocency; and that I complain not without cause, ch.11.18. see ch.12.3.

*{remember me}* Think upon me for good, Neh.5.19. & 13.14,22,31. Psal.106.4. Esa.38.2. see chap.18.20.

*{and visit me}* In mercy; as Ruth 1.6. Psal.106.4.

*{and revenge me of my persecutors}* See of this chap.11.20. See chap.17.18. & 18.21. See also, Psal.119.84. 2 Tim.4.14.

*{take me not away in thy longsuffering:}* Or, as some, *according to thy long-suffering, take me not away*: forbear to deal harshly with me; as chap.17.17. or suffer me not to be taken away by the malicious practices of my perfidious enemies: So is the particle taken, Psalm 119.91,154. As others, *After thy long forbearance take me not away*; to wit, among the rest in the common calamity that shall befall this people, when your forbearance shall have an end, 2 Chr.36.16. chap.44.22. so is the particle used, Esay 38.17. Others, *take me not away in*, or, *by*, or, *through thy long-suffering*. Heb. *the length* (that is, the dilation, or delay) *of thine anger*: not unlike that, Exod.34.7. Num.14.18. save that the word is there in an adjective notion, here, as seldom, if ever elsewhere, in a substantive. Suffer me not to be taken, and perish by mine enemies' malicious and mischievous projects, while out of your long-suffering, and slowness to wrath, you forbear to right me on them. See on Esa.48.9. So is the verb used, Ezek.33.4,6. and so the particle, Neh.13.27. ch.5.2. Somewhat to this purpose, the Chaldee, and Greek, seem to suggest, as if a speeding of justice, without longer delay, were desired; as Psa.29.10,11.

*{know}* That is, *take notice*; and make it appear that you so do: as ch.2.19. & 3.13.

*{that for thy sake I have suffered rebuke.}* Or, *I sustain*. Heb. *my sustaining of* (as Psalm 89.50.) *reproach*, Psalm 69.7. See chap.20.8. and it concerns you to right those that suffer for you, Psal.44.22,26.

**Verse 16.** *{Thy words were found, and I did eat them; and thy word was unto me the joy and rejoicing of my heart:}* Or, *when thy words were found, I did eat them*; as Prov.25.16. *Hast thou found honey? eat of it what sufficeth thee*: and Ezek.3.1. *eat what thou findest*: and there seems here a defect of the pronoun, *were found* by me; as Esay 29.6. that is, When as your messages came at first to me, I received and entertained them, as readily, as willingly, as an affamished man does his meat. So Job 23.12. John 4.34. Of the syntax, see ch.13.12,16. Of the phrase of *eating*, Ezek.2.8. & 3.2,3. Rev.10.9.

*{found}* Some put an emphasis upon this term, and that two diverse ways; the one, as if the Prophet should intimate, that he had not sought this employment, but had, unlooked after, been called unto it; as Esay 65.1. the other, as if he should thereby signify, that he had been well assured, that the messages he came with, were the undoubted word of God: as Eccl.7.29. but these constructions I conceive to be overnice: the sense seems plain; as before. See Ezek.3.1.

*{thy word was unto me the joy and the rejoicing of my heart; for I am called by thy Name, O LORD God of hosts.}* Heb. *thy word was unto me, to*, or, *for, joy, and to*, or, *for, gladness of my heart; that thy name was called upon me.* According to our version, the sense should be, as divers give it, that God's Word, though otherwise harsh, and like to be so unto others, yet was to him, because it was his word, delightful, grateful and pleasant; not unlike that profession of the Psalmist, Psal.19.10. & 119.103. or, as one of the Jewish doctors, I was at the first much taken with the messages that I was sent with, hoping that the people would repent thereupon: and so the words following should come in as a reason to induce God to regard him, as being one that had been willing and ready to undertake that office, which he professed to have special care of, Psal.105.15. But neither of these seem to reach the intent of the Prophet. Which seems rather to be that which another of them suggests, agreeable to the words as they run in the original, to wit, that that word or commission given him by God, (whereof, see chap.1.1,5.) whereby he had been called to bear God's name, to be called his Prophet, (of which phrase, see cha.14.9.) was a great rejoicing unto him, and that which encouraged him cheerfully to set upon the work of his ministry, howsoever it proved afterward, v.9. See Ezek.3.3. Rev.10.10. *to joy*, or, *for joy and gladness of heart*, for, *great and hearty joy*, simply; as Zach.8.19. Esa.30.29.

**Verse 17.** *{I sat not in the assembly of the mockers, nor rejoiced:}* Thus the most interpreters, yea, all that I meet with, as if the Prophet should profess, that he had shunned the company and society of profane persons, such as scoffed and mocked at God's messages and menaces. Of which sort were not a few among this people; and that especially among the great ones, Esa.5.19. & 28.14,22. chap.5.13. & 20.7,8. and so it should be the same with that, Psal.1.1. and 26.4,5. Heb. *secret*, for, *assembly*; as Psal.111.1. Ezek.13.9. See chap.6.11. and according to this sense, the next member would rather be rendered, *nor reveled it*; as Esa.22.2,13. But this seems not to be so congruent a profession for the Prophet to make, that he had not kept company with loose and debauched persons, and reveled it together with them. I render the words, *I have not sat in the assembly*, or, *meeting, of those that make merry*. So is the word frequently used. So Eccl.3.4. there is *a time to make merry*; and, *better is grief than mirth*, Eccl.7.3. and, *they prepare bread* (that is, victuals) *to make merry* with, Eccl.10.19. and 2 Sam.6.5. & 1 Chro.13.8. *all Israel made merry before the Lord, with all their might, with singing, and with harps*; yea the word is in this very prophecy twice precisely so rendered, chap.30.19. & 31.4. The Prophet's meaning then is plainly this; that howsoever he did at first cheerfully entertain that employment that God had called him unto; and a place of that dignity to be so near unto God, and be ranked among those that were reckoned his Prophets, seemed much to affect him, yet he had found little joy of it, when he came to the execution of it; for that he met with nothing but matter of grief, and had been therefore far from joining himself with such that met together to make merry, as friends, acquaintance, and neighbors oft do, to partake with them in their mirth; but had rather abandoned himself to a retired and solitary course of life, in private continually bemoaning himself, in regard of those heavy and sad messages, that he was from God sent with to his people, and the evil success that his errands found with them, chap.8.18. & 9.1,2. & 13.17. & 20.7,8. This I doubt not to be the genuine sense of the place, confirmed both by what follows here, and by God's words also to the Prophet, chap.16.8.

*{nor rejoiced}* Heb. *and rejoiced*, that is, *to rejoice*; to partake with them in their mirth; as, *Balack arose and warred* (that is, *to war*) *against Israel*, Judg.24.9. otherwise, the negative must from the former member be supplied: as Psal.9.18.

*{I sat alone because of thine hand}* *Alone*, or, *solitary*; withdrawing myself from company, as persons full of grief and heaviness are wont to do, Psal.102.7. chap.13.17. Lam.3.18. so rather, than as some, being deserted and forsaken of all: as Psalm 88.8,18. But this seems rather to imply a voluntary and affected privacy; *because of thine hand*, that is, as some, because I am at hand with you, and yield constant obedience unto you, in the faithful discharge of my ministerial employment; in regard whereof, they refuse to have any society with me. So, *hand*, should be for ministry: as Mal.1.1. but, *because of thine hand*, seems here rather to import, in regard of your injunction, and those messages which you send by me, full of menaces, and dreadful denunciations of calamities and destruction to befall my people. So Ezek.3.14. *I went with bitterness heated in my spirit, but the hand of the Lord was strong upon me.*

*{for thou hast filled me with indignation.}* Either with *indignation* from this people, who for your messages, are generally incensed against me, vers.10. or with *indignation* at this people, for their obstinacy tending to their destruction, chap.9.1,2. or with *indignation*, which from you I denounce against them, being sent daily upon errands of wrath and indignation to them. See Chap.23.33. the particle is wanting, as chap.9.18. this last seems the best.

**Verse 18.** *{Why is my pain perpetual, and my wound incurable, which refuseth to be healed?}* Why should I continue perpetually in this sad and disconsolate condition, without hope or expectation of any change and alteration thereof for the better: a speech proceeding from human frailty, as conceiving no great likelihood of the before-promised amendment of it, v.11.

*{is my pain perpetual}* Or, *should my pain continue* (as Dan.1.21.) *for ever*; as Amos 1.11. and there is a defect of the particle; as Psal.13.1. or, *should my pain be* a pain of *perpetuity*, or, *eternity*; that is, *a perpetual, an everlasting* pain: as, *pleasures of perpetuity*, or, *eternity*, for, *perpetual*, or, *everlasting delights*, Psalm 16.11.

*{my wound incurable}* Heb. *my stroke* (that is, wound, or sore, caused by some stroke; as chap.10.19.) *grievous*, or *deadly*: so chap.30.12,15.

*{which refuseth to be cured}* A metaphor taken from such wounds, or sores, with which no plaster or medicine can either produce cure, or procure ease, and there is a figurative notion in the word *refuseth*; like that, Jon.1.4. *the ship thought*, or, *made account, to be drowned*: for to speak properly, *the wound*, or, *sore*, can no more refuse ought, than a *ship think* ought: and according to our version, there is a defect of the relative; as ver.14. but some supplying the interrogative from the foregoing branch, read the words, *Why refuseth it to be cured?* whether way we read it, it is not much material; only the word, *incurable*, would be altered, if it be rendered the former way. See Psal.77.2. ch.8.18.

*{wilt thou be altogether unto me as a liar, and as waters that fail?}* Or, *Why* (repeated from the former; as Job 3.23.) *shouldest thou be altogether* (*being be*; as Gen.18.18.) *unto me as a deceitful* (Heb. *lying*) well, or fountain, or spring, (a defect of the subject; as Esay 5.4. & 17.5. Ezek.13.11.) *as waters that fail?* Heb. *that are not faithful*, or *firm*. See Esa.33.16. such as are dried up, and fail in the heat and drought of summer, when men have most need of them, Job 6.15,20. Why should you fail me, and not make your word good unto me, but give me up to undergo such distress and difficulties without end or ease? Such fits of diffidence have the best and strongest of God's saints and servants been at some times surprised with. See Psa.13.1,2. & 31.22. & 77.7,9. & 116.10,11. 1 Sam.27.1.

**Verse 19.** *{Therefore thus saith the LORD;}* Or, *Notwithstanding* (see chap.30.16.) *thus said the Lord.* Albeit, that the Prophet had in this his discourse and dispute with God, much want of that courage and confidence that ought to have been in him, and betrayed a great deal of human frailty; yet the Lord was pleased to stoop so low, as to return a gracious answer unto him: partly admonishing him in a mild and gentle manner, to shake off and abandon these distrustful and discontented thoughts; and to go on constantly in the faithful discharge of his duty; and partly again further confirming him therein, by renewed promises of assured protection and safeguard, vers.20,21.

*{If thou return, then will I bring thee again, and thou shalt stand before me;}* These words some interpreters expound of the people; unto whom God should promise restitution, and confirmation upon their sincere return to him by unfeigned repentance; as chap.3.1. & 4.1,2. & 26.6,7. & 31.36. & 33.26. & 35.19. Zach.1.3. But the most rather of Jeremiah; yet diversely; some, as if God spoke in way of approbation to him, thus rendering the words; *since that thou dost convert thy self, as I do convert thee*; that is, since that you do apply yourself diligently unto those things that I enjoin you, and direct you unto: or, as others, *since that thou dost turn from*, that is, withdraw yourself from the society of those profane ones, vers.17. *I will reduce thee*, that is, free you from those evils whereof you complain, and retain you in my service. Others, by way of admonition; *if thou* be careful to *convert* this people from their wicked ways; that which is the office of a true Prophet of God to labor in, chap.23.22. taking the word in an active notion; which yet it will hardly here bear. But the most and best understand them in way of admonition indeed, but taking the word in a neuter notion; If you turn from, and cast off, these distrustful thoughts and discontents, and apply yourself cheerfully and constantly to the work of your ministry, I will continue and confirm you in your prophetical function.

*{then will I bring thee again}* Or, *then* (Heb. *and*; as v.1.) *will I restore thee*: as Psal.23.3.
