*{and thou shalt stand before me}* Or, *that thou mayst stand*, or, *to stand, before me*; as my servant and attendant in the room and place of a Prophet: as 1 King.17.1. Zach.3.7. a defect of the infinitive particle, as Esa.63.13. and 64.2. Howbeit, the whole passage may well thus be rendered; *If thou wilt return*, (as ch.4.1.) *and wilt be reclaimed by me*, (Heb. *and I shall have reclaimed thee*) *before me shalt thou stand*. So run, and so lie, the words in the text: and I suppose this to be the genuine sense of the place.

*{and if thou take forth the precious from the vile; thou shalt be as my mouth:}* Or, *if thou wilt sever* (Heb. *make to go forth*) *the precious from the vile*. This some expound of doctrine only, if you be careful to teach nothing but the pure truth of God, 1 Pet.2.2. without mixture of other base and vile stuff; such as the false prophets are wont to mingle it withal, ch.23.26,28. Others rather, of persons: that which the latter term does necessarily carry it unto, being used of persons only: If you shall draw out the precious from the vile, by converting those that are vile, that is, wicked ones, from their wickedness, and making precious ones of them, which God's ministers are ministerially said to do, Dan.12.3. ch.23.22. Mal.4.6. Luk.1.16. or, (which seems the genuine sense of the text, and is by the most and best approved) If in your teaching you put a difference between the godly and the wicked, by confirming and comforting the one, and by sharply reproving, convincing, and menacing the other. See ch.20.27. contrary to the practice of the false prophets described, Ezek.13.19,22. & 22.26.

*{thou shalt be as my mouth}* Or, as some, *according to my mouth*: you shall be such an one as I would have you, and have commanded you to be: as, *according to his heart*, 1 Sam.13.13. *thou shalt do all my pleasure*, Isaiah 44.28. or, you shall thereby show yourself to be *my mouth*, to speak from me, chap.23.22. or what you do speak, shall be as if I myself had spoken it, 2 Cor.5.20. & 13.3. See Exod.4.16. and I will be sure to make it good. See 1 Sam.3.19,21.

*{let them return to thee, but return not thou to them}* Heb. *return shall they to thee; and* (for, *but*; as chap.13.17.) *thou shalt not return to them.* Which some therefore conceive, as spoken by way of prediction, or promise. They shall come and seek to you; but you shall have no need to seek to them; fulfilled, say they, when they repaired to him for advice upon the murder of Gedaliah, chap.42.2. to which might be added that before, chap.21.2. But the most conceive them spoken rather by way of admonition, or injunction; (for the future is frequently used for the imperative; as chap.3.7. & 5.10.) Some more narrowly, with reference to those scoffers, mentioned, as they suppose, vers.17. but of that there. Others, more generally, of the main body of the people, whom he was to deal with; Let them (this people, vers.20.) conform if they will, to you; but be not you overinduced either by their force or flatteries, (for they will be both ways tempting you) to come over to them, to comply with them, to soothe them up in their sins, with vain hopes of better things, as their false prophets do, or to conceal ought from them, that I give you in charge concerning them, cha.1.17. & 23.30,31. & 26.2.

**Verse 20.** *{And I will make thee unto this people as a fenced brasen wall;}* Heb. *I will give thee* (as ch.1.5,18.) *for a fenced wall* (that is, to be such an one, or, like such an one, as v.16. Psal.31.2.) *of steel.* See vers.12. If you do go on constantly and courageously in the faithful discharge of your duty, not relenting or yielding at all unto them, (for this seems to depend upon the last clause of the foregoing verse) I will arm you with such power, as they shall not be able to prevail against you. See ch.1.18. & 6.27. v.12.

*{and they shall fight against thee; but they shall not prevail against thee:}* Or, *So that though they war with, or, against thee,* (as Judg. 20.11.) *yet they shall not prevail with thee;* to take your life away from you. See chap. 1.19. & 20.11, 12. so that he might well say, as they do, Psal. 129.1, 2.

*{for I am with thee to save thee, and to deliver thee, saith the LORD.}* I will protect you sufficiently against all their might and malice. See chap. 1.8, 19. & 20.12. So Act. 18.10.

**V. 21.** *{And I will deliver thee out of the hand of the wicked; and I will redeem thee out of the hand of the terrible.}* *Hand,* for, *power;* as Isa. 3.6. *to redeem,* for, *to rescue;* as Psal. 107.2. *of the terrible,* or, *violent ones,* Isa. 25.5. such as you might most fear. See chap. 26.23, 24.

## CHAPTER 16

**Verse 1.** *{The word of the LORD came also unto me, saying;}* Or, *Moreover, the word of the Lord came unto me;* as some of our former versions, and as chap. 1.11. Heb. *And the word of the Lord was unto me:* as chap. 1.1, 2. Where it may be questioned, whether this chapter be one continued discourse with that chap. 15. or this introduction to it be the title of a new revelation at some other time delivered. Whether of the two it be, the Lord in it forbids the Prophet to contract marriage, or breed issue, the times ensuing should be so bad, ver. 2, 4. or to mourn with any for the dead: for better die than live, as the times should be, ver. 5, 7. or to make merry with them; for it should be no time for mirth, ver. 8, 9. informs him, and wills him to inform the people of the ground of such evils as were to befall them, ver. 10, 13. yet annexes a gracious promise of future restitution after these dreadful judgments executed upon them, ver. 14, 18. whereunto the Prophet subjoins an humble profession, as in the person of God's people, of the acknowledgment of God's gracious and powerful protection, and their expectation of the Gentiles coming in to them, ver. 19. all shut up with an expression of God's present indignation against his people, for their idolatry; for which, he would make them, by penalties inflicted upon them, to know and acknowledge his might, v. 21, 22.

**V. 2.** *{Thou shalt not take thee a wife, neither shalt have sons nor daughters in this place.}* Or, *Do not take thee a wife, nor have sons, or,* (Heb. *and;* as Exod. 21.15. Ezek. 14.20.) *daughters.* The future for the imperative; as chap. 15.19. Exod. 20.13, 17. So ver. 5. intimating, that so great & grievous should the calamities of that place in those times be, that wife and children would be but an heavy burden amidst them, and means of much aggravating his grief that had them. So Hos. 9.13, 14. Mat. 24.19. Luk. 23.29. 1 Cor. 7.26.

*{in this place}* That is, in Anathoth, says the Jewish Doctor: but he seems rather to mean Jerusalem, whither this prophecy was delivered unto him: see ver. 3.

**V. 3.** *{For thus saith the LORD, concerning the sons, and concerning the daughters that are born in this place, and concerning their mothers that bare them, and concerning their fathers that begat them in this land;}* All alike to be involved in the same calamities one with another; that which should make the condition of each one of them the more grievous, chap. 13.14. & 14.16.

*{in this place}* This again, the Rabbine groundlessly restrains unto the men of Anathoth, who together with their whole issue were so, says he, to be rooted out, that there should be no remainder of them, chap. 11.23. But here they meet with a difficulty that they find Ezra. 2.23. *of the men of Anathoth,* 128. that returned from the captivity: Which to salve, they say, that some of them did afterward repent, though God did not reveal so much to the Prophet: But the truth is, that neither that former denunciation reached unto all the inhabitants of Anathoth, but to those of them only that maliciously opposed the Prophet, as it is there expressly mentioned: nor is this place Anathoth a poor town in comparison, Esay 10.30. but Jerusalem intended; as also, ver. 9. and as appears by the adjection in the next member; the whole land, to wit, of Judah, whereof that the head city, chap. 15.8. so chap. 7.7.

**V. 4.** *{They shall die of grievous deaths:}* Heb. *death of diseases,* or, *grievances;* as 2 Chron. 21.18. by the plague, or the pestilence, chap. 14.12. see chap. 15.2.

*{they shall not be lamented}* No solemn lamentation shall be made for them, Job 27.15. Psal. 78.64. chap. 22.18. and 25.33. either because they shall be deemed happier that are gone, and taken away from the present evils, than those that survive, chap. 8.3. and 22.10. Rev. 14.13. or because every one shall be so taken up with their own particular and personal fears, cares, and calamities, that they shall have no lust, or leisure to look after their deceased, or to use any wonted solemnity about them. See Ezek. 24.16, 23. Amos 6.10.

*{neither shall they be buried}* See chap. 14.16. & 22.19. & 25.33.

*{but they shall be as dung upon the face of the earth:}* Heb. *for dung:* of which form of speech, see on chap. 15.20. so Psal. 83.10. chap. 8.2.

*{and they shall be consumed by the sword, and by famine;}* Some by the one, and some by the other, chap. 14.15. and 15.2.

*{and their carcases shall be meat for the fowls of the heaven, and for the beasts of the earth.}* chap. 7.33. and 34.20.

**V. 5.** *{For thus saith the LORD;}* Or, *Therefore;* as chap. 9.20. for the particle seems to be here an illative, (as Psal. 116.10. *I believed therefore I spake,* 2 Cor. 4.13.) inferring, and making way, to a further injunction, grounded upon the former denunciation, v. 3, 4.

*{Enter not into the house of mourning, neither go to lament, nor bemoan them:}* Heb. *thou shalt not go in, nor go;* as ver. 1. *into the house of mourning.* Concerning the genuine notion of this term, there are divers opinions, and the Jewish critics themselves are at some variance. Some of them say it signifies *mourning,* and this way most of them seem to go: though some of them would have it signify, not *mourning,* but *a mourner;* withal rendering a ridiculous notation of the word, not worth the relating. But this interpretation, as well the one, as the other, is crossed by that place of Amos, 6.7. where it is rendered *banquet,* and must of necessity import matter of mirth: And so would a late learned annotator have it here to import, understanding it of banquets made for merriment; the rather, because such are mentioned, ver. 8. But the main current of the context, evidently crosses this conceit. Howbeit, by collation of those two places together, it plainly appears, that the word of necessity signifies something at least common as well to mirth, as to mourning. To which purpose, one of the Jewish Doctors tells us, that it signifies in the Arabic tongue, a *shouting,* or lifting up of the voice, whether out of joy, or out of grief; for such outcries are common to either: see chap. 48.33. but hereof no proof is brought. Another of them, therefore, says, it signifies *a feast,* or, *a banquet;* for which he alleges a place out of one of their Talmudists' writings; and it is so found used in the Chaldee Paraphrast, Num. 25.1. Now *feasts,* or, *banquets,* we know, are usual as well at burials, as bridals: and this seems to be backed by that which follows, ver. 7. for as for that which some learned late writers here suggest, that the word should signify such a person, as by the Latins is termed *designator,* one that did give directions for the marshalling and ordering of matters at burials; it seems a groundless conjecture, nor could *the house of mourning* be so fitly termed the house of such an one. I suppose the words may well be rendered, *the banquet-house,* as the old Latin has it; or for fuller explication, *the funeral banquet,* or, *banqueting house.*

*{nor go to lament or bemoan them.}* To lament for the deceased, or to condole with the survivors; as chap. 15.5. By these forbearances, as Ezekiel, chap. 24.24. the Prophet was to foreshow them, how it should be with them amidst those calamities that should shortly surprise them.

*{for I have taken away my peace from this people, saith the LORD, even loving kindness and mercies.}* For I am resolved to take from this people whatsoever benefits of plenty, prosperity, or safety, (for all these, *peace* includes, Psal. 85.8. and 119.165. Esay 48.18. chap. 8.11.) and whatsoever good thing out of my free favor and mercy I had formerly conferred on them, and they had sometime enjoyed.

*{have taken away}* Or, *I will take away.* Heb. *gather up;* as Psal. 85.3. chap. 10.17.

*{even loving kindness and mercies.}* Or, *my loving kindness, and my tender mercies.* See Esay 63.7. a defect of the pronoun, as chap. 4.19.

**V. 6.** *{Both, the great, and the small, shall die in this land: they shall not be buried; neither men lament for them;}* Or, *when great or small,* (*and,* for, *or;* as ver. 2.) *shall die in this land, they shall not be buried, nor shall any lament for them;* as chap. 14.15. Nor need we, as some, to insert, *Therefore.* See of this menace, on ver. 4. where the active here indefinite, is expressed in the passive, *they shall not be lamented;* no lamentation shall be made for them: only here there is a more large extent of it; showing that no regard should, in this kind, be had of the great ones, more than of the meaner sort: see chap. 22.18, 19.

*{nor cut themselves, nor make themselves bald for them;}* Courses in such cases usually practiced among the Heathen, whom the Jewish also did herein oft imitate, though forbidden so to do, Lev. 19.28. Deut. 14.1.

**V. 7.** *{Neither shall men tear themselves for them, in mourning to comfort them for the dead;}* According to this version, the meaning should be the same with that before, of *cutting themselves,* ver. 6. and so some of the Jewish Doctors also take it: but the word is there in a reciprocal form, whereas this here is not; nor is the word here ever elsewhere found so used. Some other of them therefore by change of a letter into another, though in shape diverse, yet for sound in a manner, if not altogether the same) expound it of stretching out the hands, or smiting them one against the other; to which purpose, one version renders it: *they shall not stretch out* their hands, and our ancienter version, *they shall not wring* their hands, as in wailing people oft-times do, chap. 4.31. Lam. 1.17. But others of them, which seems the true and genuine sense of the place, understand it of such provisions of food, as friends, neighbors, and acquaintance, used to send home unto those, that were in heaviness for the loss of parents, children, or other of the family near of kindred, or otherwise dear unto them, taken from them by decease; to the end, that repairing to them, and eating and drinking with them, they might endeavor to comfort them, and help to put away their grief; alluded unto, Deut. 26.14. and this exposition, as the words following confirm; so the use of the word elsewhere does further also help to clear: for so is the word used, Esay 28.7. *to deal thy bread to the hungry:* and Lam. 4.4. *the young children ask*

*bread, and there is none to deal it to them:* to which purpose the text may well be rendered, *Neither shall they deal them bread, in mourning, to comfort any for the dead:* bread, being put for any provision of food in general, as in the places before pointed to, chap. 5.17. & and Luk. 14.1. as also, Ezek. 24.17. a place parallel to this, where the Prophet is inhibited upon the death of his wife, *to eat the bread of men,* that is, such as men used in such occasions of mourning, to partake in with others that came to visit them; by which term it is also in our ancientest English version here rendered. This sense both the ancient Greek, and old Latin, express. Whence also some gather (nor seems it altogether improbable) that the Greek interpreters, in whose steps the Latins trod, did in the Hebrew, for *lahem, to them,* which we now have, read, *lechem,* or *lehem,* (whereof *Beth-leem*) that is, *bread,* and deem this latter the better reading; the rather, for that the pronoun in the latter place is singular, not *them,* but *him,* that is, says the Rabbine, for any of them, though rendered, as taken collectively in the plural. Howsoever, if the word *bread,* be not expressed, as in those other places before produced it is, yet is it to be supplied, *deal* bread, or food; as in the like, Gen. 42.33. where it is said only, *take for your families;* that is, *take* bread or food, *for your families;* as our English well supplies it: and *they came out to draw,* Gen. 24.43. that is, *to draw* water: as it is aright supplied there from ver. 13.

*{neither shall men give them the cup of consolation to drink for their father, or for their mother.}* Heb. *neither shall they make them drink* (as chap. 8.14.) *a cup of consolations* (that is, *a consolatory cup: consolations;* as Esay 66.11.) *for his father, and* (for, *or;* as Exod. 21.15. ver. 2.) *for his mother:* to comfort any orphan, for the loss of his father, or his mother: the word *them,* put distributively for *any of them;* and so might well be expressed, both in the former branch (if the received reading be retained) and (howsoever for that) in this: Of such *consolatory cups* tendered to persons in grief and heaviness, see Prov. 31.6, 7. The meaning is, that all such neighborly and friendly offices on such occasions formerly used, should in those calamitous times be wholly neglected, as others also more requisite, for the reasons before recited. See on ver. 4.

**V. 8.** *{Thou shalt not also go into the house of feasting, to sit with them to eat and to drink.}* Or, *Neither do thou go* (as ver. 2, 5.) *into* (the particle supplied, as chap. 14.18.) or, *unto* (as chap. 34.3.) *the house of feasting* (as Eccl. 7.2, 4.) *to sit* there *with them to eat and to drink:* to make merry with them, Exod. 32.6. Heb. *And thou shalt not go;* as ver. 13. Before he was forbidden to repair with them, to their mournful and funeral banquetings; now is he charged not to keep company with them, at their merry meetings, or bridal banquetings; for at such times feastings were ordinarily used, Gen. 29.21, 27. by his abstinence, and refusal to join therein with them; intimating what should shortly and suddenly befall them, to wit, that they should be utterly deprived of all occasions and matter of such mirth and jollity, ver. 9.

**V. 9.** *{For thus saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel;}* As chap. 7.3, 21. & 9.15.

*{Behold I will cause to cease out of this place in your eyes, and in your days, the voice of mirth, and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom, and the voice of the bride.}* I will quell and quash all your mirth, by sending such evils upon you, as you shall have little joy of ought. See the like, Esay 24.7, 8. Ezek. 26.13. Rev. 18.22, 23. and the very same, chap. 7.34. & 25.10.

*{this place}* The city of Jerusalem; as ver. 2, 3.

*{in your eyes, and in your days}* Or, *in your sight;* While you, who think it will never come, chap. 5.12, 13. or, it will be long before it come, Ezek. 12.27. shall yourselves survive to see it: as Psal. 79.10. chap. 20.4. Ezek. 13.28.

**V. 10.** *{And it shall come to pass, when thou shalt shew this people all these words, and they shall say unto thee,}* Or, *it shall come to pass* (Heb. *it shall be,* as chap. 4.9.) *when thou shalt tell this people all these things,* (as chap. 11.6. & 36.32.) *if* (as Job 10.15. chap. 18.8.) *they shall say unto thee.*

*{Wherefore hath the LORD pronounced all this great evil against us? and what is our iniquity? or what is our sin, that we have committed against the LORD our God?}* Thus pertinacious and presumptuous are wicked men, in endeavoring to smother, and either deny, or excuse, their sins, though never so notorious, and conspicuous, chap. 2.22, 23, 25. and choosing rather to charge God with iniquity, as if he punished them without cause, than to acknowledge their own iniquity, and perfidious carriage towards him, whereby they had deserved much more, than he either threatened them with, or inflicted upon them. See the like demand, chap. 5.19. & 22.8.

*{or what}* Heb. *and what;* as ver. 2.

**V. 11.** *{Then thou shalt say unto them}* Or, *Then;* (Heb. *And;* as chap. 15.19.) *say thou unto them;* as ver. 8.

*{Because your fathers have forsaken me, and walked after other gods, and have served them, and worshipped them, and have forsaken me, and have not kept my Law,}* See chap. 2.5. & 7.24, 25.

**V. 12.** *{And you have done worse than your Fathers.}* So chap. 7.26.

*{for behold ye walk every one after the imagination of his evil heart,}* See chap. 9.13. & 11.8. & 13.10.

*{that they may not hearken unto me.}* Or, *that ye may not hearken unto me;* a change of the person; as Isaiah 1.29. chap. 2.6, 7. & 17.1. See chap. 7.27. & 8.9. & 11.10. Zach. 7.11, 12.

**V. 13.** *{Therefore I will cast you out of this land,}* Chap. 10.18. that which God had long before threatened, Deut. 4.26, 27. & 28.63. Heb. *And I will cast you;* as chap. 14.19.

*{into a land that ye know not, neither ye, nor your fathers;}* Heb. *ye and your fathers;* as ver. 8, 10. So, *ye and your children,* chap. 35.6. that neither you, or they ever saw, or had been in before. See chap. 14.18. & 15.14. See also, Isa. 42.16. but there the phrase used of a providential passage in mercy and favor, here of an effect of God's wrath and displeasure, in aggravation of the judgment.

*{and there shall ye serve other gods day and night}* Or, *where ye shall serve;* as Gen. 15.13. where you shall have your fill of serving strange gods; such as neither you, nor your fathers had known or served before, Deut. 26.64. but with little ease, or rest from those, under whom you shall serve them, Deut. 28.47, 48, 65, 66. whence the Chaldee; whom also some, both Jews, and others, here follow, renders it, *Ye shall serve such people, as serve other gods:* but that is more than is in the text.

*{Where I will not shew you favour.}* Heb. *in which* (to wit, place; as Gen. 21.19. Ruth 1.17. only here a defect of the particle, *in;* as chap. 5.7. & 11.23.) *I will not give you rest;* that which by Moses was threatened, that they should find no rest in those places into which God in wrath should drive and disperse them, Deut. 26.65. which yet the Jewish Doctor expounds, according to that which our version exhibits, *I will not have mercy on you;* as Isa. 27.11. chap. 13.13. Hos. 1.6. & 2.4. but proceed in rigor of judgment against you, chap. 14.16. & 15.14. ver. 5. or, *I will give you no favour in the eyes of your enemies,* but suffer them to exercise much cruelty upon you, Isa. 47.5. contrary to that which at other times he had done with his people, Psal. 106.45. and with some of the godly also did at the same time, chap. 15.11. Dan. 1.9. but this is spoken of the main body of the obstinate wicked: Howbeit, there want not writers of great note, who render the words, *So long as I shall not shew favour unto you,* or, *have mercy upon you;* to release you out of captivity, which after seventy years I will, by Cyrus, do for you, chap. 25.12. But the sense first delivered, seems genuine.

**V. 14.** *{Therefore behold the days come, saith the LORD;}* To these dreadful comminations, yet for the support and comfort of the faithful, is a gracious promise of a strange and remarkable restitution subjoined, to be exhibited to such a remnant as God should please to reserve, after the execution of the judgments here denounced upon the rest.

*{Therefore}* Or, *Notwithstanding* rather: as this particle is necessarily, both here, and elsewhere, to be rendered. See Isa. 51.21. chap. 30.16.

*{behold the days come}* Heb. *coming;* as chap. 7.22. and 9.24.

*{that it shall no more be said, The LORD liveth, that brought up the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt:}*

**V. 15.** *{But the LORD liveth that brought up the children of Israel out of the North, and from all the lands whither he had driven them.}* Thereby intimating, that the captivity in Babylon should be so grievous and tedious, and their deliverance out of it, by the ministry of Cyrus, so strange and great, that it should seem, in some sort, to abolish with them the memorial of the deliverance out of Egypt. See the like, Esay 43.18. But much more should it so be with them, in regard of the spiritual deliverance & liberty from the servitude of sin and Satan, by Christ purchased for them. See chap. 3.16. & 23.7, 8. where of the Messias his times the same is said.

*{that it shall no more be said}* Heb. *and it shall no more be said;* as chap. 3.7. & 7.32.

*{the LORD liveth}* Or, *as the Lord liveth;* the usual form of an oath. So chap. 38.16. *the Lord liveth,* or, *as the Lord liveth* that made us these souls.

*{that brought up}* Heb. *made to ascend,* or, simply, *brought,* and so ver. 15. for there is of no necessary notion of any ascent in the use of the word. See Judg. 15.13. Isaiah 11.11, 16. & 30.1. chap. 2.6. & 39.5.

*{out of the North}* From Babylon, and out of Chaldea, chap. 6.1, 22.

*{from all the lands whither he had driven them.}* Heb. *which he had driven them thither;* as chap. 23.3, 8. see Isa. 11.11, 12. and 27.12, 13. and 49.12. chap. 31.8. and 32.37.

*{and I will bring them again unto the land that I gave unto their fathers}* Or, *for* (as Isa. 13.8. and 16.2. chap. 13.21. and 14.15.) *I will bring them again,* &c. chap. 24.6. & 30.18. nor can I accord with that interpreter, who would have the copulative here rendered, *if;* (though it seemed but rarely, to be so used: see before, ver. 10.) as if the Prophet spoke not affirmatively, but conditionally, if God ever should deliver them; intending only to aggravate their miserable condition during the time of their captivity, not to give any assurance of delivery out of it.

**V. 16.** *{Behold, I will send for many fishers, and they shall fish them; and after will I send for many hunters, and they shall hunt them from every mountain, and from every hill and out of the holes of the rocks.}* In these words, the Lord seems to return to what he had menaced, concerning the destroying of them in their land, ver. 4. or the carrying of them away out of it, ver. 13. showing further by what means he would effect either, to wit, by such forces, as he would send in upon them, that should so environ them, as fishermen do fishes; to make havoc of them, that they should be wholly at their mercy, either to slay or to save, and withal should so pursue, and ferret out, those of them that should either flee into, or lie hid in, any place of retirement, or refuge, that none should be able to escape their hands.

*{I will send for many fishers}* Or, as some render it, *to many fishers;* and so there should be a defect of the word *message: I will send* a message to them: as Gen. 27.47. So chap. 23.38. or, *I will send many fishers,* as chap. 40.2. *and he took Jeremy;* where the same particle is used. Heb. *behold I am sending;* as chap. 25.9. & 43.10. And howsoever we read or render it, the meaning is, that God would by a secret instinct, and enticement, as by a solemn messenger or message sent unto them, cause them to come in upon this people. See Esay 5.26. & 7.18, 19. chap. 1.15.

*{fishers and hunters}* Who should hereby be meant, interpreters differ. Some say, the Egyptians and the Chaldeans; the Egyptians termed *fishers,* because they fed much upon fish, and lived much by fishing, Num. 11.5. Esay 19.8. and they by Pharao-Necho much infested this people, 2 King. 23.29, 33. the Chaldeans termed *hunters;* for their tyranny and fierceness: as Nimrod, Gen. 10.8, 9. See Ezek. 19.4, 8, 9. But this prophecy seems of a later date, than that action of Necho, nor do we read of any great havoc that he made of the people; he fleeced them only by Jehojakim of some part of their wealth, 2 King. 23.25. Others therefore, and so the Jewish commenters, understand both of the Chaldeans; who having enclosed them as fish in a net, by the siege of the city, did first sweep them away, at the surprisal of it, by slaying multitudes of them; compared in that regard to *fishers,* that take fish only to kill them, it being the nature of fish to die, when they are out of their own element: and did afterward make search after them that either lay hid in the city, or were fled, and had betaken themselves for security to some secret places; and fetched them out of their lurking holes to make captives of them; compared therefore to *hunters,* that follow fowls and beasts (for the word here used includes *fowling* also, Lev. 17.13.) in the woods, and in the mountains, to catch them, not to kill them only, and make meat of them, but for other uses also. See 1 Sam. 24.11, 14. & 26.18, 20. Psal. 90.3. and of the Chaldeans dealing in this kind with this people, see 2 King. 25.5. Lam. 3.52. & 4.18. and this latter seems the right; though some of those Rabbinical niceties intermingled with it may seem needless. But there want not of our writers and others, that understand these words, not as a menace, but as a promise: and these again are divided: for some conceive these *fishers* and *fowlers,* to be the Medes and Persians serving under Cyrus, who should make search for, and gather the Jewish people, after Babylon's downfall, out of all those regions into which they had been dispersed: and they parallel this with that, Esay 27.12, 13. Another sort would have the ministers of the Gospel to be here meant: by *fishers,* the Apostles, who being formerly by trade *fishermen,* were made *fishers of men,* Mat. 4.18, 19. Luk. 5.10. by *hunters,* their successors, that were sent abroad into all parts of the world for to catch souls for Christ, Rom. 10.15, 18. and some of these go yet further, the Apostles, say they, were as *fishermen,* that cast in the net, and bring up abundance of fish at one draught, Luk. 5.6, 7. Joh. 21.6, 8. So did Peter, who by the net of the Gospel, caught 3000. at one draught, Acts 2.41. and 2000. if not more, at another, Act. 4.4. the modern ministers, as *hunters,* that run up & down all day long with much noise and cry, and it may be scarce get one poor hare or deer ere night; with much toil and defatigation they weary out themselves, and scarce catch a soul or two, gain at least very few, it may be, all their life long, and may therefore justly complain as the Prophet does, Esay 49.4. & 53.1. those of the latter age shall be as *harvest men,* to bring in God's harvest, Joh. 4.35, 38. Rev. 14.14, 19. But these things, I suppose, are all wide from the genuine sense of the text.

*{the mountains and hills}* Whither they supposed the enemy could hardly follow them, Esay 22.5. Mat. 24.16.

*{the holes of the rocks}* Where they might not easily be discovered. See Esay 2.19, 21. and 7.19.

**V. 17.** *{For mine eyes are upon all their ways; they are not hid from my face, neither is their iniquity hid from mine eyes.}* Heb. *concealed from before mine eyes;* from lying open to my view; as Amos 9.3. Jon. 1.5. Both they themselves and all their wicked courses lie open to mine eye, Job 34.21, 22. Prov. 5.21. & 15.3, 11. Psal. 119.168. & 139.2–12. chap. 13.27. & 32.19. Amos 9.1, 3. Heb. 4.12, 13. howsoever they imagine that I see them not, and little think that I take any notice, either of the one or the other, Psal. 10.4, 11, 13, 14. and 64.5. and 94.7, 10. Esay 29.15. and 66.18. chap. 13.27. and 17.9, 10. Hos. 7.2.

**V. 18.** *{And first I will recompence their sin and their iniquity double,}* First, that is, before I restore the remainder of them, and receive them into grace and favor again, ver. 15. for I conceive those to mistake, that refer this *first,* to the captivity under Jeconiah, 2 Kin. 24.14. as so termed here in regard of that second under Zedekiah, 2 Kin. 25.11. there being nothing in the text to lead thereunto. Nor do I concur with those, who render it, *from the beginning,* from the first to the last, their ancestors' sins and their own; as Esay 65.7. Mat. 23.34, 35. the words of the text will hardly bear it.

*{recompence their iniquity}* Render unto them the wrath and penalty deservedly due unto them for their sins, Esay 59.18. and 65.6, 7. So chap. 14.16.

*{double}* That is, abundantly; as Esay 40.2. & 61.7. chap. 17.18. Rev. 18.6. not as some of Jewish Doctors, first for their forefathers' sins, and then for their own, Esay 65.7.

*{because they have defiled my land}* See chap. 3.1, 2. Psal. 106.38.

*{they have filled mine inheritance with the carcasses of their detestable and abominable things}* They have filled that land, which I counted as *mine inheritance,* chap. 2.7. *with the carcasses* (Heb. *carcasse;* but collectively taken: as Psal. 79.2.) *of their detestable things,* (chap. 4.1. and 7.30. both of men, Psal. 106.38. chap. 7.31. & 19.5. Ezek. 16.20. and of vile and unclean creatures, which they sacrificed to their idols, Deut. 12.17. Esay 65.4. and 66.17. called *the carcasses of their idols,* Lev. 26.30. wherewith they caused God *to abhor his own inheritance,* Psal. 106.40.) *and with their abominations;* that is, the idols themselves, unto whom they sacrificed them, so termed, Deut. 7.25. and 27.15. 2 King. 23.13.

**V. 19.** *{O LORD, my strength and my fortress, my refuge in the day of affliction}* An acknowledgment of God as the only stay and strength of his, and on whom alone they depended for relief and deliverance in times of trouble and distress, Psal. 18.1, 2. and 46.1. chap. 17.17.

*{the Gentiles shall come unto thee from the ends of the earth}* A prophecy of the coming in of the Gentiles to God, being convinced of his power and majesty manifestly discovered in his admirable works wrought for the deliverance and restitution of his people; that which some understand of such, as upon the dissolution of the Babylonian captivity, embraced the service of the true God, and joined themselves unto his people. See Ezr. 6.21. and the like, Esth. 8.17. Others, of those that should out of all parts be brought in unto Christ by the ministry of the Gospel, chap. 5.2. Mal. 1.11. Some of both, the one being as a type and forerunner of the other.

*{and shall say, Surely our Fathers have inherited lies, vanity and things wherein there is no profit.}* Some expound this of the Jewish people, returning from those remote regions, into which they had been dispersed, Deut. 30.4. and whose ancestors in former times had been idolaters, Josh. 24.2, 3. but the most rather of the Gentiles, acknowledging, that their forefathers had fondly served, and set their hearts and hopes on vain idols that were not able to do them any good, or to stand them in any stead, and by the service of whom they had gained nothing but loss, shame and sorrow; and it were extreme folly therefore for them their children to persist and tread still in their steps. See chap. 3.24, 25. and 14.20, 22.

*{inherited}* Got or *gained;* as Prov. 11.29. *he that troubleth his own house, shall inherit wind:* and, *the silly inherit folly,* Prov. 14.18. and, *the upright shall inherit good,* Prov. 28.10. for I conceive their conceit to be over-nice, who suppose in this term, an eye to be had unto their receiving their superstitions and idolatries, as *an inheritance* from their ancestors, chap. 44.17. 1 Pet. 1.18.

*{lies}* Heb. *a lye,* or, *falsehood,* Esay 44.20. chap. 10.14.

*{vanity}* Such as are their idols themselves, and endow those with that follow them, Esay 41.29. chap. 2.5. and 10.3, 8, 15.

*{and things wherein there is no profit}* Heb. *and in them there is not that profiteth: and in them,* for, *wherein:* as, *and they,* for, *who,* Esay 37.27. and 46.11. *there is not that profiteth;* nothing that can profit, or is good for ought, Esay 44.10. Howbeit, some render it, *and there is none among them* (that is, among their false gods) *that profiteth;* that can do any good, or avails ought, chap. 10.5. Nor is this version improbable.

**V. 20.** *{Should a man make gods to himself, and they are no Gods?}* Some suppose these words to be spoken by God in indignation, that his people who had so great, and so long experience of his power and deity, should not yet discover the vanity of idols made with men's hands, which the Heathen themselves should some of them see and acknowledge. See Esay 42.17–19. and 44.20, 21. chap. 10.1. And this seems very probable, for the inference that seems hereupon grounded, ver. 21. Howbeit, the most interpreters go another way; conceiving them to be meant of the convert Heathens' confession, further acknowledging with some detestation, the extreme folly of their forefathers, that could be so sottish, as to believe, that such idols made by man's hand should be gods, Act. 17.29. Some render the words; *can a man* (the indicative in a potential notion; as chap. 12.23.) *make him gods?* (either, *make for himself,* to worship, Esay 2.20. or, *make him;* by an elegant redundancy; as Esay 31.8.) *yet they are no Gods.* Others, *can,* or, *should a man make him gods, which are no gods? and they,* for, *which;* as chap. 17.6. Mal. 3.1. and the pronoun demonstrative for the verb substantive; as chap. 10.3, 8. Can any man endued with reason, be so silly and sottish, as to deem that his god, which either himself has made, or some other man for him; whereas thereby he may know it not so to be, because it is the work of man's hands: Psal. 115.14. Esay 2.8. chap. 10.3, 9. Hos. 8.6. or, that he can so change the nature of things, as to make that God, which by nature is nothing less than God? or that he should attempt so to do? Isaiah 44.16, 17. chap. 2.11. Gal. 4.8. But an interpreter of prime note rejecting all these, as but cold notions, thus renders and expounds the text; *Can any man* (or, *men,* the word collectively taken) *make them Gods, when as they themselves are no Gods;* but men? Can he that is no God, make a god? give that to another which he has not himself: the words may well bear it; but I leave it to the judgment of others.

**V. 21.** *{Therefore behold I will for this once, cause them to know}* Heb. *behold I am making them for this time,* or *turn, to know.*

*{Therefore}* Because this people persist in their obstinacy, say some: others rather, because they are so addicted to idolatry, a sin so palpable, and in them wholly inexcusable, ver. 18, 20. Esay 2.8, 9.

*{I will cause them to know}* I will teach them another lesson, by those evils, that I will inflict upon them, Esa. 28.19.

*{them}* This people the Jews, v. 5, 18.

*{this once}* Or, *once for all;* as Judg. 15.3. chap. 10.18. not by divers petty or lighter evils, but by one that shall serve for all.

*{I will make them to know my hand and my might,}* The heaviness of my hand, and what I am able to do, (Psalm 90.11.) by the sight and sense of those dreadful judgments now denounced, but not believed, when the same shall be inflicted upon them, ver. 18. for they seem to go out of the way here, both that understand the place, of God's power to be manifested in the deliverance and restitution of the Jewish people, ver. 15. and those also, that expound it of God's might and majesty to be made known unto the convert Gentiles together with the Jews, Isaiah 66.19. as if the *them* here mentioned, were not the same with the *them* in the foregoing branch.

*{and they shall know that my name is the LORD.}* Or, *that Jehovah is my name,* Psalm 83.18. Isaiah 42.8. another manner of God than any of your idols are, Isaiah 43.11. one that can make my word good, Exod. 6.2. Isa. 43.12, 13. See Ezek. 6.10, 14. & 7.17. chap. 23.20. & 30.24.

## CHAPTER 17

**V. 1.** *{The sin of Judah is written with a pen of iron, and with the point of a diamond, it is graven upon the table of their heart, and upon the horns of their altars:}* Whether the four first verses of this chapter (which in the Greek version are wanting) depend upon the chapter foregoing, as I conceive them to do; or the whole chapter so do, as some suppose: or whether it be an entire sermon of itself, as some would have it; or contain the sum of some several sermons, as some others are of opinion, with whom I concur, are matters neither very certain, nor much material. Certain it is, that in these four first verses, the former denunciation of wrath and judgment delivered, chap. 16.13, 16, 21. is again renewed, ver. 3, 4. and the ground of it, to wit, their idolatry, there pointed to, ver. 18, 20. here pressed and aggravated by their extreme pertinacy therein, the notoriousness of it, and their inward and entire affection unto it. The first whereof is in the former part of the verse laid down, and illustrate by a resemblance taken from some characters, cut or carved with iron or steel, or other strong tool, in marble-stone, or the like hard matter, so deep, that they cannot easily, if at all, be done out again: thereby intimating, that in like manner, this evil of idolatry was so deeply riveted into their souls, and had made so deep an impression in their minds and memories, that it was not possible to get or raze it out thence, to work it out of their hearts, or to make them leave minding & remembering it. The same pertinacy in evil in them, see set forth by other expressions and resemblances, chap. 2.22. & 6.29, 30. & 13.23. For I cannot concur with those, who would have the words rendered, *The sin of Judah* shall be *written with a pen of iron, and an adamantine claw;* that is, say they, the guilt and penalty of it shall be so set on with them, that they shall not be able in haste to forget it.

*{sin}* Their idolatry, by way of eminency, for the heinousness of it here, so termed, (see Exo. 32.31.) as appears both by the close of this verse, and by what follows, ver. 2, 3.

*{written}* That is, *cut,* or *engraven:* for so the Hebrew word is commonly used, not only for to *write* in a book, Deut. 29.20. chap. 32.10. but to *engrave* also in stone, or other like material, Exod. 24.12. & 34.1.

*{with a pen of iron}* Such an iron tool as men use to carve or engrave with: as Job 19.24. Of the word rendered *pen,* signifying first *a pen* to write with, Psal. 45.2. then *a tool* to grave with, see on chap. 8.8.

*{and with the point of a diamond}* The former word here used, signifies properly the *claw* of a fowl; for from *a bird,* or *fowl,* it has its name: but it is used also for the *nail* of man or woman, Deut. 21.12. Dan. 4.33. and because the claws of fowls, birds of prey especially, are strong and sharp: Hence by resemblance, such iron tools also, as artificers that work in hard matter, such as masons or smiths engrave with, are so termed, as by some places by the Jewish Scholiast here, and by others elsewhere, out of the Talmudists' writings produced, may appear. So that by the word here, rendered *point,* there seems no other to be intended, than what was rendered *a pen* before; at least, that they were both names, if not of one and the same tool, of two tools not unlike the one to the other; the one, resembling the *pen* of a fowl; the other, the *claw,* and both, as may seem also, among workmen, much of the same use. And hence, as here, *a pen of iron;* so out of the Midras, *a claw of iron.* But of the other word there is not a little difficulty; for some of the Jewish critics would have it to signify any hard matter in general: and here, to signify *hard iron,* or *steel;* supplying the word *iron* from the former member; as, say they, the Chaldee Paraphrast uses it for an *hard-stone,* joining *stone* and it together, Deut. 32.13. and that it signifies not *an adamant* alone, (the point whereof, I suppose, was never in common use thus to grave with) but any hard rocky, or flinty stone, appears by the common use of it in the Chaldee, Deut. 8.15. Job 28.10. Psal. 114.8. and it is strange, if this term signify *a diamond,* how it came to miss a place in the stones of the Ephod; for another word is deemed to go for *a diamond* there, Exod. 28.18. I will not make use of that Talmudical tale, (which yet some of the Jewish Scholiasts, on Esa. 5.6. follow) to wit, that this *Shamir* should signify a worm, that Moses made use of, to cut those precious stones with; and Solomon, to cut out the stones for the Temple, being taught the use of it by Asmodeus the devil, and fetched out of Paradise by an eagle: this were to confute, a mistake at most, by a more frivolous fable: but that it signifies a very hard stone, so called from its own lasting, and the sure and long *keeping* of things therein cut and engraved, is evident by those two places, where in this notion it is found used, Ezek. 3.9. & Zach. 7.12. in the former place, whereof it is said, *shamir, harder than the rock.* But what use is there ordinarily, save among savage people, where iron tools are wanting, of flints or stone to carve with in hard matter? Some therefore of the Jewish writers would have the words read, *with a pen of iron, and with a claw in an hard stone;* such as marble, or the like: and thereby to be meant, what by further explication follows, *upon the table of their hearts;* for their hearts, say they, are elsewhere called *hearts of stone,* Ezek. 36.26. and said to be as this *hard stone,* Zach. 7.12. But because this seems an overhard construction, I adhere rather to that learned writer, who by the *claw,* or *iron tool of the hard stone,* or *long-lasting stone,* understands a tool not made of such a stone, but wherewith in such stones, not soft, but hard marble, or rocky stones, things are wont to be cut and engraven: the rather, for that I find *a furnace of iron,* not for a furnace made of iron, but for a furnace, wherein iron is melted and wrought, Deut. 4.20. See on chap. 11.4.

*{it is graven upon the table of their heart.}* Heb. *engraven,* or, *being engraved.* The word here used, answers precisely to the Latin *exarata:* for it arises as that also does, from a root that signifies *to plow;* whence the *plow-share,* that enters and cuts the ground, 1 Sam. 13.21. and a term for notion parallel to it, and in one radical letter only differing, is found, Exod. 32.16. and as that only there, (where it is used of God's Law engraven on the two Tables of stone) so this, in that notion alone here: Of the phrase of *the table of the heart,* and ought be written and engraven there, see 2 Cor. 3.3. Their sin, a transgression of God's Law, 1 John 3.4. is engraven and stamped upon their hearts, and that in such manner, as was before said, where the Law of God was sometime, Rom. 2.15. and ought still to be written, Ezek. 31.33. Some think there is an allusion to those superstitious tablets, which idolatrous people used to wear next their hearts, with the name, mark, or number, of that god, whom they were most addicted to, engraven thereon; or to the common practice of such persons as used to carry about them, the effigies, or names of those, whom they did in special manner affect, either drawn upon such tablets, or engraved upon some agate, or the like stone in their rings, or seals. See on Esay 49.16. But hereof let the learned judge. Some other suppose, that the meaning should be, that the guilt of their sin stuck so fast to their conscience, that all they could do, would not be able to raze it out, but that it would stand forever firm and fresh, as upon record, there, Deut. 32.34. Esa. 65.6. But of this before.

*{and upon the horns of your altars.}* In the former words was intimated their pertinacious disposition, in regard of their sin: in this clause, the notoriousness of it; as if he had said, You will ask me, peradventure, how I can come to know, or tell what is in your hearts. God, from whom I have it, sees and knows it well enough, ver. 10. But I need not have recourse to any such special revelations, your outward courses and practices do openly publish and proclaim it: as it is enstamped upon the tables of your hearts, so is it likewise portrayed upon the horns of your altars. In which term, there is by most writers deemed an allusion to be unto the blood of beasts offered in sacrifices, which was usually sprinkled upon the horns of the altar, a rite enjoined by God, and imitated by idolaters in the service of their false gods: For God's altar was foursquare, and at each of the four corners of it, was fixed a rising of brass, to some height, in the fashion of an horn, to keep from falling over such things as were laid to be burnt upon the altar, Exo. 27.1, 2. Ezek. 43.15, 16. Now upon these, for expiation, was the blood of the sacrifice part of it put, Exod. 29.12. Levit. 4.7. & 16.18. The like rite whereunto being used by these idolaters, was an open profession of their idolatrous services, and is here produced as a pregnant proof and evidence against them. Now this being the meaning of the text, the word of *engraving,* must be taken here in a double notion, as if it were said, *engraven upon the tables of your hearts,* (for the terms are collective) *and* painted (for of blood that is most proper) *upon the horns of your altars.* It is not unlike those speeches of Moses, *The people saw the thunderings and lightnings;* saw the one, heard the other, Exod. 20.18. & Deut. 4.12. *Ye saw*

*no similitude, a voice only* heard you: as also to that of the Apostle, *I made you to drink milk, not to eat meat;* or fed you *not with meat,* 1 Cor. 3.2. But this double notion, some avoid, supposing this clause to have respect not to the blood put, or sprinkled upon the altars; but to the names of those gods, that at them were worshipped, inscribed, or engraved, upon the altars: Of which, see Act. 17.23. and that in the term of *horns* is intimated, that by, and for those, their abominable practices, they should be gored, as with horns, unto their utter destruction. See 1 King. 22.11. But the former seems the more probable, and is admitted by the most. Howsoever it be taken, there is in the text, the particle *unto,* for *upon,* as Psa. 9.4. chap. 15.8. and a passage from person to person, from the third to the second; as Esay 1.29. chap. 16.12.

**V. 2.** *{While their children remember their altars and their groves, by the greene trees upon the high hills.}* According to this version, which the old Latin holds forth, the meaning should be, that the children took after their parents, treading in their idolatrous steps, while they kept in, or called to mind their courses of that kind, and the places wherein they usually exercised the same. See chap. 7.18. But the Chaldee Paraphrast, whom both the Jewish commenters, and some of ours, follow, render the words; *As they remember their children,* (Heb. *according to the remembring,* or, *remembrance of their children*) so remember they *their altars and their groves;* that is, as men are wont to mind their children, the daily remembrance of whom, being most dear and precious to them, is very pleasing and delightful; so are these men wont to mind and think upon continually with much pleasure and delight, the places wherein they do service to their idols, being far dearer to them, than their children themselves. See chap. 7.31, 32. & 19.5. See for the form of speech, Psa. 106.4. Esay 1.7. and for the supply of the verb from the former branch, Gen. 1.16. 2 Chr. 10.11. Esay 10.5. chap. 8.10. Thus read, (which I conceive to be the genuine sense) it implies the great love and affection that they bare unto their idols. See Esay 57.5, 8. For that seems too much forced, which some Jewish ones suggest, of making *memorials* of their children, by burning them in fire to their idols; according to that, Lev. 2.9. Esay 66.3. as also that of those who expound it, that they shall for a long time *remember* these their practices, when the evils that they suffer for them, shall stick close to them.

*{groves}* Set apart for, and abused unto idolatrous services, Judg. 3.7. Esay 1.29. See Esay 27.9.

*{by the green trees}* Or, *beside;* as chap. 32.20. or, *with the green trees;* (Heb. *green tree;* but taken collectively) the *groves* set with, or consisting of such. So is the particle used, Gen. 32.11. Exod. 35.22. 1 Sam. 1.24. for they needlessly wring the text, that by a trajection would refer, *beside the green trees,* not to the *groves,* but to the *altars;* or that instead of, *upon the green trees,* as the particle most commonly signifies, render it, *under the green tree;* because it is so, chap. 2.20. for this particle is never that I can find, used in so cross a sense.

*{upon the high hills.}* The usual places of their idol-services; whence the term of *high places,* chap. 2.20. & 3.2.

**V. 13.** *{O my mountain in the field, I will give thy substance, and all thy treasures to the spoil; and thy high places for sin, in all thy borders.}* The fruit and effect of these their idolatrous courses follows, to wit, the exposing of their substance and wealth to direption, and their persons to deportation and servitude, ver. 4.

*{O my mountain in the field}* The city of Jerusalem, and Sion more especially, God's holy hill, Psal. 68.15. & 133.3. because the city stood, though in the midst of a plain, Psal. 125.1, 2. yet upon a rising all of it, and that upper part of it, upon an eminent hill; with many rich and pleasant fields round about it: for the Rabbine seems here to sit besides the cushion, who would have the name of *a mountain* to be given here to the Jewish people; because on the *mountains* they usually exercised their idolatry, Esay 65.4. Ezek. 18.6. nor seem they to have hit the nail on the head, who render the words, *O thou mountain,* you people of Judah and Jerusalem, that dwell on and amidst the mountains, and trust much to the strength of them, as if you were therefore impregnable, chap. 21.13. you shall be no more safe, than as if you were seated *in the open field,* exposed to prey and spoil: or, come down *into the field,* or you shall be brought down *into the field;* for your enemies shall pull you down, lay you low, and make you level with the plain, Luk. 19.44. as also those no less miss the mark, who by a trajection would render the words; *thy wealth in the fields will I give for a prey.* None of these (save the first, which the words may well bear) but seem to force the text too much. Those I conceive to come nearest to the genuine sense of the place, who thus read it; *My mountains, with the fields, thy wealth and all thy treasures, will I expose to spoil.* Heb. *My mountain,* and *field;* but taken collectively; as *heart,* for, *hearts,* ver. 1. *tree,* for *trees,* ver. 2. the mountains of Judah, being much of it hilly, Psal. 125.2. Luk. 1.39. (which God calls by a specialty, *his mountains,* Esay 14.26. & 65.9.) and the whole territory divided into *mountain* and *field,* or plain, as Ezek. 6.3. *with the fields.* So is the particle rendered, chap. 11.19. Deut. 6.7. Psal. 35.16. 1 Sam. 1.24. Hos. 5.6. *thy wealth,* that lies abroad in the field; and *all thy treasures,* (the copulative supplied from chap. 15.13.) whether abroad in the field; as chap. 41.8. or laid up in your storehouses and treasuries, chap. 15.13. Esay 39.6. *will I expose to prey.* Heb. *give to,* or, *for, prey;* that is, give up to be preyed upon, or made a prey, chap. 9.10.

*{and thy high places for sin, in all thy borders.}* The former member is diversely read and expounded. Some understand it of their high places to be given up to the spoil with the rest, *for the sin* therein committed. See Ezek. 6.6. Others, *the high-places* erected *for sin;* for sinful and idolatrous practices, chap. 7.31. Others, *thy high places* are *sin;* as the calf is called *their sin,* Deut. 9.21. the particle redundant; as Job 18.8. See Esay 26.4. & 40.10. ver. 4. Others, and so some of the Jewish critics, by a trajection, *thy high places for sin;* that is, *for the sin of thine high places:* as, *after and build,* for, *and build afterward,* Prov. 24.27. and, *a place there of sepulture,* for, *a place of sepulture there,* Ezek. 39.11. and, *wailing to such as are skillfull in lamentation,* for, *such as are skillfull in lamentation to wailing,* Amos 5.16. and this in effect does come home to the first; save that the one makes the *high places* the common subject matter of direption with the rest; the other makes them the subject place of their sin: the last clause may have reference, either unto their *wealth* and *treasure,* that they should in all places be stripped of, chap. 4.20. or unto their high places, that the whole land was filled with in all parts of it, and the sins therein committed, chap. 3.2. & 16.18. See the same with this, chap. 15.13.

**V. 4.** *{And thou, even thyself, shalt discontinue from thy heritage, that I gave thee}* Heb. *And thou, and in thee, shall intermit,* or *discontinue.* Which some expound; *And thou, even* (as chap. 15.13.) *thou;* the other particle being redundant, as ver. 3. Others, *And thou* yourself, *and* those that are *in thee:* all the inhabitants of the land. Others, *Then* (as chap. 16.11. to wit, when you have been thus stripped) *shalt thou, and* that (as ver. 10. chap. 20.5.) *for,* or, *through, thy self,* (that is, *for,* or, *through,* your own default: as chap. 15.13. Esay 47.9. & 57.17.) *discontinue,* or, *intermit from thine heritage:* cease from, and forbear to till the land, that you now possess; there is in this term an allusion to that law, by which they were enjoined to intermit the tillage of their land in certain years, called therefore Sabbatical years, because the land in them rested, as men did on the *Sabbath.* See Exod. 23.10, 11. (where the word here used is found) and to that intermination of such a cessation or intermission, while they should abide in captivity abroad, Lev. 26.34. which the words next following do evidently evince: and a learned Scholiast therefore supposes, that there should be here a supply of the word *hand,* because he finds it subjoined there to the very here used, rendering the text, *thou shalt be compelled to omit,* or, *withhold thine hand from thy possession;* but he might have observed, that the verb is there in an active form; here in a neuter: and it may well therefore be rendered, *thou shalt cease from* (as the like, Esay 2.22.) *thine heritage,* or, *possession* (to wit, from tilling, or earing and enjoying of it) *which I had given thee,* to possess, Psal. 135.12.

*{and I will cause thee to serve thine enemies in the land that thou knowest not}* Or, *while* (so is the copulative taken, 1 Kin. 11.25. and so rendered, Esth. 2.21. Psal. 146.2.) *I cause thee to serve thine enemies in a land that thou knowest not,* or, *in the land* (as particularly pointing at Babylon) *which thou hast not known,* formerly, save by hearsay only; that is, during the time of your absence from your own land, and of your servitude in a strange country. See Lev. 26.34, 35. Of the divers reading here, see on chap. 15.14. where the other is in the text; which if we admit, the words must be rendered, *and I will cause,* or, *when* (as chap. 34.1. Zach. 12.2.) *I shall cause thee to pass with thine enemies into a land that thou knowest not.*

*{for ye have kindled a fire in mine anger, which shall burn for ever.}* See chap. 15.14. a want of the relative is there in the former branch, as here in the latter.

*{for ever.}* That is, for a long time; as Exod. 21.6. Deut. 15.17. 1 Sam. 1.22. & 27.12. Psal. 89.1. Esay 34.10.

**V. 5.** *{Thus saith the LORD;}* Here seems to begin a short sum of another sermon; though most conceive it to have dependence upon the former; as holding out a second sin after their idolatry, ver. 1, 4. to wit, confidence in an arm of flesh, and worldly wealth, for which also they were to suffer. It begins with a curse denounced against all that withdraw their hearts from God, ver. 5, 6. and a blessing to all that constantly depend upon him, ver. 7, 8.

*{Cursed be the man, that trusteth in man, and maketh flesh his arm, and whose heart departeth from the LORD}* A corruption that this people were ever over-prone to, seeking unto, and relying upon, foreign aids from time to time with a neglect of God, and refusal to rest upon him. See 2 Chron. 16.7. and 28.16, 20. Esay 30.1, 2. & 31.1, 2. & 36.6. chap. 35.5, 7. Ezek. 29.6, 7, 16.

*{Cursed be the man,}* Or, *is the man:* as the like, ver. 7.

*{trusteth in man}* Relies upon him, as his absolute support and firm stay, Psal. 146.3, 4.

*{in man}* Heb. *in Adam; a man of earth,* or *dirt,* of *clay,* or *dust;* so the name imports, Gen. 2.7. & 3.19. Psal. 103.14. See on Esay 2.9.

*{maketh flesh his arm}* *Flesh,* for, *man;* a feeble, frail and corruptible creature, exposed to casualty, and subject to mortality, Psal. 103.15, 16. and 144.4. and 146.4. Esay 2.22. and 51.3. So Psal. 78.39. Esay 40.6, 7. *arm,* for, might and strength; as 1 Sam. 2.31. Psal. 10.15. and for support, Esay 33.2. Hence, *an arm of flesh,* 2 Chron. 32.8. as if one would say, of mere flesh, without bone or sinew, without strength or firmness, (for in the bone and sinew, not in the *flesh,* does the strength and firmness of the body consist, Psal. 24.7. Job 40.18.) an infirm and feeble thing, unable to bear up itself, and much less able to sustain or bear up ought else; and *flesh,* for, a man that is nothing but *flesh;* as Gen. 6.3. and in the places before pointed to, Psa. 78.19. Esa. 40.6. and such and no better is the mightiest man without God's support, even as a mere *fleshy arm,* without any nerve or bone at all in it; and a mere folly and madness for any man to rely on such a piece of infirm and feeble stuff, Esay 31.1, 3.

*{whose heart departeth from God}* Though he make show still outwardly of continuance with him. See Esa. 29.13. & 48.2. & 58.2. chap. 12.2. Ezek. 14.4. & 33.30, 32.

**V. 3.** *{For he shall be like the heath in the desert}* Heb. *And;* as Psal. 1.3. How uncertain the great masters in Israel are, and how far to seek in their own language, concerning the names as well of birds, and beasts, as of trees and plants, mentioned in Scripture, has in part been already showed, for the former, on Esa. 13.21, 22. & 34.14, 15. for the latter, on Isa. 41.19. and we shall here make further to appear. The Hebrew *Arar* here, or *Aroar,* as it is found written, chap. 48.6. some of them affirm to be the same with *dardar,* Gen. 3.18. Hos. 10.8. which some render *a thistle,* some *a bramble,* some *a briar.* See the parallel place, Heb. 6.8. which seems to carry it to the last. Others say, it is a kind of *thistle,* that is prickly without, but eatable within. And the like is said of the term that the Chaldee Paraphrast gives it; so it might be our *artichoke.* Another tells us, that it is in some barbarous tongues called *joncier,* so it should be *a bulrush,* according to the Latin *juncus.* Another, that it is that which the Arabians call *bahal,* by which name are the *Juniper-berries* said to be termed: yea, some tell us, that the *juniper* bush itself is in the Arabian tongue called by the very name here used. Which it is marvel then how it escaped that Jewish Doctor that gave this interpretation of it, by the name of the *berry,* rather than of the *bush.* Others of them say, it is a plant that in foreign languages is termed *myrice;* and so the old Latin renders it. Now under this appellation, are two sorts of plants comprehended, both with the Greeks, and with the Latins; the one called *the tamarisk,* that loves watery places, and grows usually near the brinks of brooks and rivers; the other called also *erice,* and with us *heath,* a shrub lower than the former, that affects dry grounds and waste places; which from it therefore we usually term *heaths,* whether heath grow on them, or no. Now of this latter sort our English version, (wherein many other interpreters concur with it) understands the word here used to be meant; as also some say, that the word used by the Chaldee, does signify the same. But of this plant or shrub, and the several sorts of it, see Dioscorides, l. 1. c. 117. Basil in his *six days work,* Sermon 5. Pliny, l. 13. c. 21. & l. 16. c. 26. & l. 24. c. 9. in which two latter places he tells us, that this sort of plant is reckoned among those that were counted *unlucky,* or *unhappy,* and *damned* ones; such as might not be admitted into any religious rite, and that were therefore so termed, because they bare neither fruit nor seed, nor were wont at all to be planted or set: of which sort this being one, was deemed good for nothing, save to make *besoms,* or *brooms,* such as are with us known commonly by the name of *heath-brooms;* that which suits passing well with the use of the word in this place. Howbeit, Pliny in those places seems to confound those two plants; which Basil well distinguishes, applying that to the former sort, that is peculiar to the latter; because the common sort of people in his time used to give the name of the former to the latter. Which error also, it seems, the Italian and some others also following him, are not free from, who render the word here *tamarice,* or *tamarisk;* the Italian note adding, that it is a bastard plant (which what it should mean, I wot not well, unless it be, as *bastard-saffron,* for *saffron,* falsely so termed: and so *bastard-tamarisk,* for, *tamarisk;* for likeness of it to the right *tamarisk,* so commonly called) of no use but for the fire: for of the former, both Dioscorides and others affirm, that it is planted, and does bear fruit, and is very useful in physic: and well the Greek therefore here, to take away all ambiguity, expresses it by a term that signifies *wild-myrice;* that kind of it (as the text says) that grows *in the wilderness.* Howbeit, in the last place, another of them directly crossing this opinion, yea, and himself too elsewhere, tells us, it is *a great tree,* that grows in the wilderness; but what tree he says not, relating only what some other say of it. Thus these; agreeing, as we say, like harp and harrow, yet all taking it for some peculiar kind of plant. But some late writers are herein of another mind; for they conceive it not to design any special sort or kind of plant; but an attribute only of some plant, tree, or shrub in general: and with these I concur, for two causes; first, because in the opposite branch, ver. 7. there is no mention of any particular plant, but *a tree* only, at large: and secondly, because I find it used, as an attribute, not of a plant, but of a person, Psal. 102.17. where some expound the word *solitary,* as here, ver. 7. from a word that signifies, *barren, childless,* without issue, Gen. 15.2. Lev. 20.20, 21. chap. 22.30. and so it might here signify a tree that stands *alone* by itself on the waste; or *a barren* tree, such as the Eunuch is compared unto, Isa. 56.3. but these both, are afterward expressed. Others, *low,* or, *lowly,* or *dejected;* from a root that signifies *to throw,* or, *pull down,* chap. 51.58. and so it might here be, *a low* shrub: but that seems not to suit so well with the root, whence it should come, used of pulling down walls and buildings only, as the word *to raze,* with us. Others lastly, render it *destitute;* as those, Heb. 11.37. or, *despoiled, left naked, made bare:* as Job 1.21. from a verb that signifies *to strip, to make naked,* or, *bare,* Isa. 32.11. Habb. 3.9. and accordingly some render it, *a bare,* or, *naked tree:* without any furniture of fruit or leaf. See Isaiah 1.30. a defect of the subject; as, *vile,* for, *vile grapes,* Isaiah 5.4. *a fading,* for, *a fading* plant, Isaiah 28.4. *untempered,* for, *untempered* mortar, Ezek. 13.11. and the word being of a doubled form, may well be deemed to signify *most bare:* which I conceive to be the genuine sense of the word.

*{in the desert}* As, *in the wilderness,* Isa. 48.6. but there is here an elegant consonancy, between the term intimating the condition of the tree, and that designing the place of its abode: as if it were said, *an exceeding bare tree in an extreme barren soil.*

*{and shall not see when good cometh.}* Or, *that seeth not;* that is, enjoys it not, partakes not of it, has not any share in it; (as the word is used, Job 9.25. Psa. 34.12. chap. 29.32.) when any rain from heaven, or other benefit or blessing falls upon, or befalls other places, Isa. 5.6. Amos 4.7. for that learned late writer seems here to have strayed, who does thus paraphrase these words; it shall not bring forth any fruit fit for food, when the time of so doing shall with other trees be.

*{but shall inhabit the parched places in the wilderness}* Or, *but* (Heb. *and;* as chap. 15.19.) *is situate* (as Josh. 22.19.) *in some parched,* or, *extreme dry* place, (Heb. *parched places,* for some *parched place:* as, *sepulchers,* for, *any one sepulcher,* Gen. 23.6. *cities,* for, *one of the cities,* Judg. 12.7. *streams,* for, *some one stream,* Psal. 1.3. and a defect of the subject; as in the foregoing branch: or, a place of *parchedness,* or, *drynesses,* for, *a most dry,* or, *parched* place: as, a place of *drought,* for, *a dry* place, Isa. 25.5. & 32.2. a land of *drought,* for, *a dry* land, Isaiah 35.1. and, a land of *droughts,* for, *an extreme dry* land, Psalm 105.41.) *in the wilderness:* where such places are most frequent, chap. 2.6. & 51.43. in such a land of soil, as can afford it no moisture: and consequently, that cannot thrive, receiving neither rain from above, nor moisture from beneath. See Ezek. 19.13.

*{in a salt land,}* Or, *a salt ground.* Heb. *a land,* or, *ground, of saltness:* as, a land of *saltness,* Job 39.6. Psal. 107.34. such as are altogether barren and unfruitful, Deut. 29.23. to which purpose also were places sometime *sowed with salt,* on purpose to make them such, Judg. 9.45.

*{and not inhabited}* Or, *which is not inhabited;* the copulative for the relative: as chap. 14.18. Heb. *inhabiteth,* for, *is inhabited:* the neuter in a passive notion; as Isa. 13.20. where is no inhabitant to manure or dress it, Gen. 2.5, 15. Isa. 5.6. Luk. 13.8. or where for the barrenness of the soil, no man dwells, chap. 2.6, 15. I am not ignorant, that some writers of great note, understand both this similitude and the next, as intending, not external prosperity and success, but spiritual graces, and the exercise of them: the latter, as that also, Psal. 1.3. of regeneration by insition into Christ; production of good works, and perseverance in well-doing: that which the course of the context there does abundantly refel: and so this former accordingly of the want of all these; he shall not partake in the grace of regeneration, nor be manured and dressed by God's Word in his Church; nor bear any fruit of good works: but these things seem wholly beside the intent of the Prophet; which is to show such as trusted to human helps, how they should not only miss of that benefit, good, prosperity, and safety, which by those means they made account to attain; but should also bring upon themselves those evils, which thereby they sought and thought to escape and avoid.

**V. 7.** *{Blessed is the man that trusteth in the LORD, and whose hope the LORD is.}* From the cursed condition of all those, that withdraw their trust from God, to repose it on the creature; he passes to the blessed and happy estate of all those that continue loyal to God, and depend wholly for support and safety upon him, who alone is able to support and to save. See the like blessedness promised and assured unto such, Psal. 2.12. & 40.4. & 125.1. & 146.5. Prov. 16.20. Isa. 26.3, 4. and 30.18.

*{and whose hope the LORD is.}* Heb. *and the Lord is his trust,* or, *confidence:* for the word is a verbal, derived from the foregoing verb: *and his,* for, *whose;* as chap. 5.22. & 15.19. and *trust,* or, *confidence,* for person trusted on, or confided in. So Psal. 40.4. and 65.4.

**V. 8.** *{For he shall be as a tree planted by the waters, and that spreadeth out her roots by the river;}* See the like description of the godly man's prosperous thriving and flourishing condition, Psalm 1.3. and the like resemblance, Job 8.16, 17. Ezek. 19.10. and 31.4.

*{For he shall be}* As Psal. 1.3. ver. 6.

*{as a tree}* See Isa. 65.22.

*{planted by the waters}* Or, *planted* (as Psalm 1.3. and 92.13.) *by the water side;* as Isa. 32.20. & 55.1. of which care has been taken, to set it in some rich and well watered soil, Isa. 5.1, 2. Ezek. 19.10.

*{and that spreadeth out her roots by the river}* Where it may freely and constantly *drink water;* as the Prophet speaks, Ezek. 31.4. See Job 8.17. and 29.19. Ezek. 31.4, 5, 7. Heb.

*sendeth out* (as Psalm 80.11. Ezek. 17.7. & 31.5.) *his roots;* as Job 8.17.

*{and shall not see when heat cometh}* Or, *and doth not see;* that is, *feel, suffer,* or sustain any damage or annoyance by any parching or scorching heat, when such comes at some time of the year, because it draws moisture sufficient from the streams of the neighboring river, that run round about its roots, Ezek. 31.4. *to see,* for, *to suffer;* as chap. 5.12. & 42.14. & 44.17.

*{but her leaf shall be green}* Or, *but* (Heb. *and;* as v. 6.) *its leaf* (Heb. *his;* as, *his roots* before) *is* (that is, continues; as Dan. 1.21.) *green;* neither failing, nor fading, Psal. 1.3. but retaining its verdure, notwithstanding any scorching heat of the sun. So Job 8.17. *he is green before the sun.*

*{and shall not be careful in the year of drought;}* Or, *Nor taketh thought,* or, *needeth to take thought;* as Mark 6.25. to think what may become of it (a figurative speech like that, Jonah 1.4. *the ship thought to be drown'd,* see chap. 15.18.) *in the year of drought.* Heb. *of restraint;* as chap. 14.1. when the showers are restrained, chap. 3.3. and no rain comes from above, 1 Kin. 17.1.

*{neither shall cease from yielding fruit.}* Or, *nor ceaseth from yielding fruit.* Heb. *making fruit;* as Gen. 1.12. Esa. 37.31. In the foregoing branch was an allusion to those trees that have their leaves continually green, such as are the palm, the olive, the myrtle, the laurel: Whereof see Theophrast, l. 1. c. 15. Pliny, l. 16. c. 20, 21. So Psal. 1.3. & 37.35. & 52.8. & 92.12. in this latter, to those that have fruit on them all the year long; such as are the orange, the lemon, the pine: Whereof see Theophrast in his *story of plants,* l. 4. c. 4. and in his *causes,* l. 1. c. 11. Pliny, l. 12. c. 3. l. 16. c. 24. So Psal. 1.3. & 92.14. Ezek. 27.12. Rev. 22.2.

**V. 9.** *{The heart of man is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked; who can know it?}* A lively and pregnant description of the great pravity, and deep corruption of man's heart, very hard and difficult to be discovered by others. That which some suppose here to have reference to those that withdrawing their hearts from God, put their confidence in man, ver. 6. Others, to those whom such persons rely upon, and are prone to deceive, sure to fail, those that rely on them, Prov. 25.19. the former seems the right: whereof see more on the next verse.

*{heart}* For *soul,* or, *mind;* as most frequently, chap. 4.4. & 5.24. ver. 5.

*{deceitful}* The word here used is a very pregnant term; and is diversely rendered; by some, *wily, fraudulent, prone* (properly) *to supplant,* to circumvent and deceive. So it is said of Jehu, by a term thence deduced, 2 King. 10.19. when he made a show, as if he meant to serve Baal; *he did it subtilly,* or, *in subtilty;* to deceive and destroy the servants of that idol; and chap. 9.3. *every brother will supplant,* or, *deceive,* will undermine, go beyond, circumvent his brother: word for word, *trip up his heels;* for thence had *Jacob* his name, Gen. 25.26. & 27.36. Hos. 12.3. Others render it *perverse,* full of *pravity,* so the old Latin: or *crooked,* and *uneven;* as the word is used of ways, Esay 40.5. Luk. 3.5. that have many windings and turnings in them, and are hard therefore to find: and so is it with *man's heart;* full of windings and turnings, and nooks and corners, and wiles and flights, Esay 29.15, 16. intending one thing, when it pretends another, and inwardly purposing the clean contrary unto that which by the tongue and outward carriage it pretends and promises, Psalm 41.6. and 55.13, 14, 20, 21. in regard whereof some render the word here *unsearchable;* (as the old Latin does the next word; and one of our ancienter editions, this) and the ancient Greek, *deep,* according to that, Psalm 64.5, 6. Esay 29.15. See Prov. 26.24, 26. The Chaldee gives it, *hard;* and one of our editions *stubborn:* for which I see no ground, save that pravity and perverseness has stubbornness commonly joined with it. The first and second seem the best, because having some ground in the root and stock of the term, and the notion and use of either.

*{above all things}* Heb. *From all,* that is, *above ought.* No creature so sly or wily, as is man's heart: No creature in wicked subtlety and dissembling can go beyond him. See Eccl. 7.26, 29. *from,* for, *before,* or, *above;* a particle much so used in a comparative notion; as Prov. 22.1. Eccl. 7.1. chap. 5.3. and *all,* for, *ought;* as Job 1.11. chap. 32.23.

*{and desperately wicked}* This word also (for it is but one in the text) is diversely rendered; some render it, *desperate;* some, *deadly.* Others joining both together, *desperately* bent unto, and set upon *deadly* mischief: wholly given deceitfully to destroy, and to do mischief, 2 Sam. 20.9, 10. Psalm 64.5. whereof see a pregnant proof in the demeanor of this people toward this our Prophet, chap. 11.18, 19. & 12.6. as also in some other towards Gedaliah, chap. 40.14, 16. & 41.1, 2. Of the word, see on Esa. 17.11. chap. 15.18. & 30.12, 15. and hereafter, v. 16. in which place, as also in this, some, instead of *anush,* by a mistake of the vowel-points read *enosh,* and render it *a man;* whereof more on the next clause. But here the words run *desperate,* or, *deadly* it; the pronoun for the verb substantive: as Eccl. 1.5. chap. 10.2, 8.

*{who can know it?}* Heb. *who knoweth it?* but the verb is taken potentially: as chap. 2.23. so Job 22.13. *how doth God know?* for, *how can God know?* and, *who seeth them,* for, *seeth us?* Psal. 64.5. & Esa. 29.15. *Who sees us?* or, *Who knoweth us?* that is, *who can see,* or *know,* what we do? So close and unsearchable is man's heart, so full of shifts and fetches, that no man can know what is in it but himself, 1 Cor. 2.11. yea, so full of guile, that a man cannot fully know himself, Psal. 19.12. that oft-times it even gulls and beguiles a man's own self, Gal. 6.3. Jam. 1.22. The Greek here renders the text, joining this and the former words together, *and he is a man, and who knoweth him?* and this divers expositors apply unto Christ, and his human nature: but the ground of this mistake we pointed to before; and shall again meet with the like, v. 16.

**V. 10.** *{I the LORD search the heart, I try the reins, even to give every man according to his ways, and according to his doings.}* Because he had spoken before of *withdrawing the heart from God,* ver. 5. and they, it may be, would pretend, as Esay 48.2. what the godly do sincerely profess, Psal. 44.17, 18. that their heart was not turned away from God, and would not stick herein to bear down God's Prophets to their faces, when they charged them with it, and reproved them for it, chap. 2.23, 35.
