God therefore here tells them, that though they might delude men, and blind or blear their eyes, by raising many such mists of goodly pretenses before them, that they could hardly, if at all, be able to discover what lay hid in their hearts; having so many flights and shifts to conceal and color it withal; yet they could not beguile God, who had an eye, that was able to pierce and pry into every nook and corner of their souls, and through all those cloudy mists, and colorable pretenses, descry the inwardest motions, and secretest intentions of their hearts, and accordingly deal with them, as they justly deserved, 1 Sam. 16.7. 1 Chron. 28.9. 2 Chron. 6.30. Psalm 7.9. and 94.9, 11. Prov. 15.11. chap. 11.20. and 20.11. Acts 1.24. and 15.9. Heb. 4.12. Rev. 2.23. Heb. *searching,* and *trying,* or *exploring:* and so both the Greek and Latin render it, which may two ways be expressed; either, *I the Lord am he that doth search and explore.* So our version; or, as in way of answer to the former question, ver. 9. who knows it? *I the Lord, who search and explore.* I that can so do, or do so, know it: Either of both may well stand: *heart* and *reins;* for the inwardest motions, intentions, devices, affections, dispositions, and desires of the soul, Psa. 16.7. & 26.2. & 51.6. & 139.23. chap. 12.2. and in the places before pointed to.

*{to give to every man according to his ways, and according to the fruit of his doings}* Weighing as well the inward disposition and affection of the heart, as the outward act and work of the hand, 1 Kin. 15.14. 2 Kin. 14.3. 2 Chr. 15.17. & 25.2. Psa. 9.8, 10. & 18.23, 28. chap. 3.10. Prov. 16.2. & 21.2.

*{even}* Or, *and that:* as ver. 4.

*{to give unto every man according to his ways}* So 1 King. 8.32, 39. Psalm 62.12. Rom. 2.6. Rev. 22.12. *ways,* that is, tenor, or course of life and carriage: as Psalm 1.6. & 119.1. Ezek. 7.3, 4, 27.

*{according to the fruit of his doings}* That is, the reward either of mercy by promise, Psal. 62.12. Mat. 5.12. or in strict justice due to them, Rom. 2.7, 16. & 3.23. So is the word *fruit* used, Prov. 1.31. & 31.31. chap. 21.14. & 32.19. Mic. 7.13.

**V. 11.** *{As the partridge sitteth on eggs, and hatcheth them not; so he that getteth riches, and not by right, shall leave them in the midst of his days; and at his end shall be a fool.}* This people, as they relied much upon foreign forces, an arm of flesh; which the Prophet met with, ver. 5. so they trusted not a little to their wealth and treasure, and that much of it gotten by wicked courses, either fraud or oppression, whereby they made account that they should be able to hire foreign forces enough for their defense, or by means thereof, otherwise, shift well enough for themselves. See Esay 28.15. & 30.6. and this the Prophet seems here to meet with, telling them, that this their wealth so gotten, wherein they put so much confidence, Psalm 49.6. and 52.7. Prov. 18.11. Eccl. 7.12. shall not avail them, nor be able to protect and secure them, Esay 28.17, 18. for they shall be stripped of it, or have it taken from them sooner than they expect, Prov. 23.5. Luk. 12.15. and shall at length prove fools, Luk. 12.20. as finding themselves to have labored for the wind, Psal. 39.6. Eccl. 5.13, 16. and this he illustrates, by the similitude of a fowl, that sits upon strange eggs, which being hatched, leave her; or having laid eggs, has them broken by one means or other, so that she never comes to hatch them.

*{As}* Both the notes of similitude, *as,* and *so,* are here wanting; as also, Prov. 26.7, 9, 14, 21. and 27.17, 21. save that there the latter is supplied by the copulative, but is wholly wanting, Proverbs 26.11.

*{the partridge,}* Heb. *kore;* and so is this fowl also called, 1 Sam. 26.20. the word imports *a caller,* or, *a cryer,* Esay 40.3. which name might seem to be given her, from her manner, as some write, of *calling* her young after her, when having deluded the fowler, by her flights, she has drawn herself away from the place of her nest. See Ælian, l. 3. c. 16. But one of the Jewish masters, in his annotations on this place, tells us, that this *kore* is that which the French (for in those parts he lived) call a *cuckow:* and that indeed is a more clamorous fowl than any other so commonly and ordinarily is: but the *hunting* of this *kore on the mountains,* 1 Sam. 26.20. seems to agree better to *the partridge,* than to the *cuckow,* which few, I suppose, in that manner follow: the ancient Greek respecting the notation of the word, renders it, as if they had read it doubled, the *partridge cryeth.*

*{sitteth on eggs, and hatcheth them not}* Or, as some, *gathereth eggs together, but* (Heb. *and;* as ver. 6.) *hatcheth them not: gathereth together;* as, say they, the word signifies, Esa. 34.15. and in the Talmudists' writings, seems sometime to be taken: and, *gathereth them together;* to sit on, and to hatch, but hatches them not; her eggs either proving windy and addle, as oft it falls out, with those especially that have been produced without the company of the male, which with the partridge is said to be frequent. See Aristotle, l. 5. c. 5. & l. 6. c. 2. Pliny, l. 10. c. 32. & 58. or otherwise miscarrying, either by means of those that take them away, Deut. 22.6. Esa. 10.14. or of beasts that trample casually upon them, Job 39.15. or of her own mate, the male; that which as of the partridge reported, that the female uses not to sit on her eggs where she lays them, but to remove them from place to place, where the male may not find them, because being a very lustful bird, he will be disturbing, and breaking of them, that he may have the company of the dam: Of which, see Aristotle, l. 9. c. 8. & Pliny, l. 10. c. 32. but the word here rendered *hatcheth,* is, in the Hebrew, *bringeth forth,* used commonly of *birth,* and that not in womankind only, but in the female of other creatures, chap. 14.5. Job 39.13. and they confess it therefore thus taken, as they would have it, to be *a catachrestical,* or a far-fetched metaphorical kind of speech. The most therefore render it, some, *gather together;* (of which before) others, *sitteth on eggs, which she hath not brought forth;* and the former verb, indeed, signifies, *to sit upon,* or, *to brood;* either eggs to hatch them, as the Chaldee uses it, Job 39.14. and the Talmudists very frequently; or young ones already hatched; as Esay 34.15. for of the proper signification of the latter, there can be no question; and that the copulative coming between them, is frequently put for the relative, appears by Esay 3.6. & 5.4. & 44.7, 14. chap. 4.16. & 14.18. compared with, chap. 17.4. in all which places, and many more it is found so used. Now those that go this way, some expound it of the male partridges sitting on the young, which not he, but the female brought forth: and to this purpose, Aristotle indeed reports of them, l. 6. c. 8. that having divided their eggs into several nests, they sit on them apart. But neither does this (were it granted to be so) any way well suit with the drift of the text, or that whereunto it is here applied; for as for the masculine form here used, see on chap. 2.23, 24. Others therefore rejecting this, say, some, that the partridge having lost her own young, gets some other partridges' eggs, and sits upon them, which when they are hatched, hearing their own dam's note, and by a natural kind of instinct discerning it, run away from this their nurse, and go after her. So Ambrose, in his *six days work,* l. 6. c. 3. and Jerome, referring us to Aristotle, Pliny, and others; in whom yet I find it not. Others, that the *kore* here mentioned, is a bird that gets together the eggs of fowls, and is wont to sit on them as her own, until they be hatched, which then leave her, and keep with those of their own kind. So the Rabbines, some of them, and some other obscure writers, say of the partridge; which if it can be made good, will very well suit, both with the terms, and drift of the text: And some such thing certainly, either as this, or the first, to me seems undoubtedly here to be intimated: For as for the *cuckow,* whom some Jewish Doctors would have to be this *Kore,* she is so far from filching, and sitting on the eggs of other birds, that she usually lays her own in the nests of others, to be sat upon, and hatched by them. So Aristotle, l. 6. c. 7. & l. 9. c. 29. Pliny, lib. 10. cap. 9.

*{he that getteth riches, and not by right}* Heb. *making,* or, *he that maketh* (as *searching,* ver. 10.) *riches,* (as, *to make wealth,* for, to *get* it, Deut. 8.18.) *and,* or, *and that,* (as ver. 4, 10. for there is no certainty even of goods lawfully gotten, Psal. 62.10. Prov. 23.5. 1 Tim. 6.17. and much less of those that are by unlawful courses compassed, Prov. 21.6.) *not by judgment,* that is, either without *discretion* and due consideration; as the word is used, Psal. 112.5. without any regard of right or wrong, as it is with those that set this down with themselves, that they will be rich, by what means soever it be, 1 Tim. 6.10. or *not by right* (for so also is the word used, Ezek. 18.5, 19, 21.) that is, by unjust and injurious courses, *wrongfully,* as it is rendered, Ezek. 22.29.

*{shall leave them}* Either having them taken from him, Esay 8.4. & 10.13, 14. Eccl. 5.14. ver. 3. Matt. 6.19. or being taken away from them, Psalm 49.10, 12, 17. & 52.5, 7. Eccles. 5.15, 16. Luke 12.20.

*{in the midst of his days}* Coming to some untimely end, and not lengthening his life above half that time, which in course of nature he might have attained unto. See Job 15.31, 33. & 22.16. Psal. 55.23. & 102.24.

*{at his end shall be a fool.}* Heb. *at,* or, *in* (wanting as chap. 5.7. & 11.23.) *his last* (as Num. 23.10. chap. 12.4.) *he shall be a nabal,* or, *a fool,* 1 Sam. 25.25, 26. he shall appear so to be, Psal. 49.13. Luk. 12.20. See the like, Joh. 15.8.

**V. 12.** *{A glorious high Throne from the beginning is the place of our Sanctuary.}* In these words themselves, there is no great difficulty; but about the connection or coherence of this passage with the rest of the context, there is among interpreters much dissension. A learned late writer deems, that this is here noted, as the fourth vain confidence, that this people were wont to trust unto: the first whereof was their strength, ver. 3. the second, their foreign forces, ver. 5. the third, their human policy, ver. 9. the fourth here, the Temple, which they relied upon as a fortress impregnable, chap. 7.4. Zeph. 3.11. So should these words be rather a speech of the people, than of the Prophet; that which to me seems very improbable, finding in the text nothing that should so make or hold it out; nor any other that herein accords with him. Howsoever, some think that the Prophet, whose own words they make them, might have some privy nip at that their vain presumption. Among the Jewish Doctors, some conceive it to have reference to what was before said, concerning trust in human helps, ver. 5. as if it were said, Let them trust in man, we will trust in him whose throne is aloft in heaven, and his Sanctuary here on earth, as Psal. 20.7. but there is too far a distance between these two, than to be brought thus together, and to be made cohere the one with the other. Others of them would have it referred to God's *sight and exploration of the heart and reins,* ver. 10. which might appear, as well by his looking down from his palace in heaven, Psalm 11.4. & 33.14, 15. & 113.5, 6. as by his sitting on his throne, to wit, his Ark, in his Temple situate here upon earth, Psal. 80.1. and that in the very midst of all the earth, Psal. 74.12. for the earth, say they, stands in the middle of the whole world, and the land of Judah in the middle of the earth, and Jerusalem in the middle of Judea, and the Temple in the middle of Jerusalem, and the Ark in the middle of the Temple: but not to stand upon examination of the exactness of these vain niceties; this coherence seems to be no less far-fetched than the former. Others of them would have it depend upon the last branch of the foregoing verse, *he shall in his latter end be,* or be found *a fool,* being cast out of that *glorious high Throne, the place of the Sanctuary:* from which, by means of such injurious carriages, he shall come to be secluded. But this seems yet more forced, than either of those before mentioned. Others of them refer it to that which follows, as if it were said, O you whose *glorious high throne, the place of our Sanctuary is, Jehovah, the hope of Israel.* And this seems most probable of any that I find by any produced. Only some of our best & soundest interpreters, reading it without such precise connection, (which some also of those Jewish that go this way, regard not, nor is indeed so needful) as an entire sentence of itself, as our version yields it, do add, That this is by the Prophet prefixed before his ensuing speech directed unto God; partly, to show the singular favor of God unto his people, who had settled the place of his special residence, as in his palace, among them: and thus pointing to him, whom thus dwelling among them, they ought to have trusted unto, Psal. 68.28, 29. and partly; also, to tax the ingratitude and folly of them, who notwithstanding that thereby he had manifested to them his forwardness to protect and secure them, would leave him, and seek after others for protection and safeguard, which were not able to afford it, that which is intimated in the latter part of verse 13. See Ezek. 7.20. The words some read as our version exhibits, taking *throne,* and *sanctuary,* for one and the same. See chap. 3.17. & 14.21. Others distinguish them, and make *heaven* the one, Psalm 11.4. Esay 66.1. the *Temple* the other, Exod. 15.17. 2 Chr. 20.8. and they render the words, with a note of similitude prefixed; *As* the *glorious and high throne* (to wit, in heaven) *is the place of our Sanctuary.* But the former is the plainer, and seems the righter.

*{A glorious and high throne}* Heb. *A throne of glory* (as Esay 22.23.) *high,* or, *of heighth;* which some render with repetition, a throne of height. Others, *of the high one,* that is, of God: and the word being as well of an adjective, as of a substantive notion, will admit either: but the latter is the rather here to be refused; nor need the other to be received: but that of our version retained instead of either, because of that parallel place, Esa. 6.1. *a throne high and lifted up;* where the former term coming from the same root with this here, is adjective only.

*{from the beginning}* Heb. *from the first;* from the first foundation of it: and this the pauses or points in the original, join unto the word, *high:* in regard whereof, the text would thus be rendered, *A glorious throne,* (for there is a stop) *high* (or *lofty*) *from the beginning;* in regard of God's presence and residence in it, 1 King. 8.12, 13, 27. & 9.3. For frivolous and ridiculous is that figment of the Rabbines, who to that purpose abusing that place, Exod. 15.17. and this, reckon *the place of the Temple* among those *seven* things, which God, say they, made before the creation of the world. But a late learned writer conceives, that this clause may be rendered, *an heighth,* or *celsitude, far above the chief;* that is, far in height and loftiness, surpassing any earthly or worldly height and dignity; and such use, indeed, of the particle, in comparisons, is frequent: as Gen. 3.1. chap. 17.9. See ver. 16. and of the height of God's house, see on Esay 2.2. But this I leave to the judgment of others. Only I suppose it hard to find, where the word, *first,* is, in Hebrew, found for *chief;* that Esa. 41.27. is questionable.

**V. 13.** *{O LORD, the hope of Israel,}* Or, *expectation:* See chap. 14.8.

*{all that forsake thee shall be ashamed}* Or, *confounded;* as it is rendered, Psal. 97.7. ver. 18. or, *abashed;* as word for word it sounds: see on chap. 8.9. as in way of prediction, or denunciation, telling what the end of such will be; as v. 11. So Psal. 73.27. Isa. 1.28. Howbeit, some take it as spoken in way of supplication and prayer, rendering the words, *Let* them be *confounded,* or, *abashed,* as Psa. 35.4, 26. & 40.14. and so in the latter part of the next branch, *Let* them *be written;* as Psal. 69.28. but that which our version yields, seems herein the better.

*{and they that depart from thee}* The words, *from thee,* are not in the original: and there is a fourfold reading of the Hebrew text: for some read it *vesure,* which our version follows, supposing the form contracted to be put for the entire; as chap. 22.14. and the words, *from thee,* to be supplied from ver. 5. the term is so found, Esay 49.21. Some, *vesuri,* that *shall depart:* a defect of the relative; as chap. 14.18. Others, *vesurai, that depart from me;* that is, from the doctrine by me delivered to them: *from me;* as Josh. 1.7. *depart,* or, *turn not aside from him;* that is, say they, from Moses: Heb. *that depart me,* for, *that depart from me:* the preposition, swallowed up between the verb and the pronoun affixed to it; as, *that rise me,* for, *that rise against me,* Lam. 3.62. and, which comes in form near to this, *that contend me,* for, *contend with me,* Psal. 35.1. chap. 18.19. Others lastly, *vesurai; my castigations:* whereof more anon; for the former three will in effect come to one; but the first of them is most received.

*{shall be written in the earth}* Such as so do, shall not be written *in heaven;* as Luk. 16.20. where *the book of life* eternal is under safe custody kept, Rev. 13.8. & 20.12, 15. but here *on earth;* as Matth. 6.19. where their hopes and happiness wholly consists, Psal. 17.14. grounded upon such fickle and uncertain things like themselves, ver. 11. Prov. 23.5. Mat. 6.19, 21. 1 Tim. 6.17. or, as some of the Rabbines, they *shall be written in the earth;* that is, they shall be *laid in the dust,* Psalm 7.5. die like brute beasts, be laid in the grave, and there go to dust, Psalm 49.12, 14. Eccl. 3.20. or lastly, it may well be a proverbial speech, *shall be written on the earth;* they shall not be written in brass, or marble, in some durable matter for long continuance: as Job 19.24. on which therefore men use to engrave their names, and memorials, to be transmitted to posterity; but as such things, as being of little regard, are written, or drawn upon the ground, or *on the earth,* or *in the dust;* (*earth,* for, *dust;* because *dust* is but *earth* with dryness dissolved, and *earth* so dissolved falls into *dust,* Gen. 2.7. & 3.19. Psal. 22.15. Eccl. 12.7.) and things *written in the dust,* are with every puff of wind blown away, dissipated, and done out: *to write in dust,* a proverbial form, with the Hebrews; as to write ought *in the wind,* or, *in running water,* with the Greeks and Latins: and this last seems most likely; they shall be of no continuance, see ver. 11. Howbeit, a learned late writer, following the last of the readings before-mentioned, and conceiving the word here rendered, *depart,* to rise from another root, that signifies, *to chastise,* or, *to instruct,* whereof see on chap. 6.8. and the word therefore to import *castigation,* and *instruction;* as he deems one not unlike it to do, Job 39.35. thus renders the words. *Let my castigations,* or, *reproofs, be written in the earth;* that is, Let my sermons, and reproofs, whereby I have laboriously, from time to time, endeavored to reclaim this revolted people, be entered here on earth in your presence, to remain, as upon record, in some book or monument, for my justification, and their conviction. See the like, Deut. 31.19, 21. Job 19.23, 24. & 31.35, 36. Esa. 30.8. But herein, for ought I find, he goes alone, few sure, if any, following him: nor seems this notion of the word to have place here: beside that the word, in Job, referred unto, is very questionable, whether it be a noun, or a verb.

*{because they have forsaken the LORD, the fountain of living waters}* *Living water,* for, *spring-water,* Gen. 26.19. not rainwater that comes by times, either certain, or uncertain, with intervals and intermissions, and that sometime very long ones, 1 King. 17.1. chap. 3.3. and 14.1. ver. 8. or pond-water, that may soon be drained or dried up, Esay 19.6, 8. or land-floods, that swell up and run swiftly in winter, but fall again, and fail, when most need is of them, in heat of summer; and such are all human helps and stays, creature-comforts and contentments, Job 6.15, 21. But *spring-water,* and such *a fountain* therefore, as runs incessantly, and never fails, for the support, refreshing, and affording a competent supply of all necessary good unto all those that be his, and continue faithful to him, Psal. 36.8, 9. & 84.11. See chap. 2.13.

**V. 14.** *{Heal me, O LORD, and I shall be healed; save me, and I shall be saved;}* The Prophet here again renews his suit unto God for himself; for consolation and confirmation, preservation and protection, amidst those manifold difficulties, dangers and distresses, that he was exposed unto, and assaulted with, for the faithful discharge of his duty in the work of his ministry, ver. 14, 17, 18. which he had not taken up of himself, but had entered upon at his command, v. 16. complaining of his people's contempt of it, and scoffing at it, ver. 15. and requiring to be righted on them for their wicked demeanor towards him, ver. 18.

*{Heal me, O LORD, and I shall be healed; save me, and I shall be saved:}* *heal me;* by freeing me from that affliction and grief of heart and mind, that I continually sustain at the hands of this malicious people. See chap. 15.16. which place illustrates this: and *save me,* or preserve and deliver me, from the pits that they dig, and snares that they set for me, from those plots and projects, whereby they seek to take my life away from me. See chap. 11.19, 21. Some read the words, *If thou Lord heal me, I shall be healed; if thou save me, I shall be saved:* as they also read that, Psal. 5.7. as if he should say, those means of relief and safety that others leaving you rely upon, v. 5, 11, 13. cannot answer their expectation; but you Lord are able to afford what they cannot: they are sure to do well, whom you undertake the cure of; to be safe, whom you undertake the charge of, Matth. 8.2, 8. Luke 5.16, 18. A good notion, and a sound consequence; but an harsh construction. Those that expound it of spiritual healing and preservation, from being infected with the corruptions of the times, John 17.15. as some also do that, chap. 11.17. and of eternal salvation, which he should pray to be preserved unto, 2 Tim. 4.18. seem to have strayed from the genuine sense of the text.

*{for thou art my praise.}* *Praise;* for the subject matter, or the object of praise; or the person praised, Esay 60.18. & 61.7. chap. 5.1, 41. as, *trust,* for, the object of trust, the thing trusted in, and relied upon, ver. 5. you are he, whom I praise incessantly for the favors that you are pleased to afford unto me, ascribing them to you alone, Psal. 40.3. & 65.1. or, *praise,* for the ground and procuring cause of praise; you alone are he that does minister occasions of praise and thanksgiving to me, by your mercies, for which I depend upon you alone, and no other, Exo. 15.2. Psa. 22.2. & 44.8. & 109.1. Howbeit, it may well be rendered, which some of the Jewish commenters also suggest, in the future: *thou* shall be *my praise;* you shall give me abundant cause and matter of praising you for your mercy, when you shall have delivered me out of their hands, Psa. 18. title, v. 1, 2. & 32.7. & 37.1, 2. Esay 25.1. & 38.19, 20.

**V. 15.** *{Behold they say unto me, Where is the Word of the LORD? let it come now.}* Heb. *they are saying;* it is their common speech to me in way of derision, chap. 20.7. to ask, *where is the word of the Lord?* as, *where is the promise of his coming?* 2 Pet. 3.4. so, where is the destruction that you have so long threatened us with, as from God? why does it not come? we would fain see it once, Esa. 5.19. Amos 5.18. the pronoun demonstrative for the verb substantive; as chap. 10.15. & 14.15. & 32.36, 43.

**V. 16.** *{I have not hastened from being a Pastor before thee; neither have I desired the woeful day.}* Because the people and false Prophets would not stick to tell the Prophet, that he complained much of evil usage, of derision and vexation, but he might thank himself for it; he had pulled it unadvisedly upon himself, by thrusting himself upon such an employment, and taking upon him to be a Prophet, out of either a mad or ambitious humor, chap. 29.26, 27. and telling them tales of his own forging, which he never had from God, chap. 5.13. the Prophet therefore appeals unto God, who could bear witness for him, that as he had not pressed himself in to be discharged of this so troublesome and thankless an employment, since that it stood not with his duty to God so to do; so he had not sought or desired to be put at first thereupon; as well knowing, and then foreseeing, when God at first called him thereunto, how troublesome an employment it was like in all probability to prove, as also that he was able to testify for him, with what faithfulness and integrity he had carried himself in the discharge of his duty therein.

*{I have not hastened from being a Pastor}* The word indeed here used, signifies commonly *to hasten,* or run headlong; as Josh. 17.13. Prov. 19.2. & 21.8. & 28.20. & 29.19. and hence divers interpreters render it, *I hastened not to be a Pastor;* that is, a Prophet; for he was, as a Priest, a Pastor before, chap. 1.1. but this is directly contrary to the terms of the text; which are expressly, not, *to be a Pastor,* but, *from being a Pastor:* which is rather as much as *not to be a Pastor:* as, *from* being a *King,* for to be *no more a King,* 1 Sam. 15.22. *from* being a *Priest,* for, to be *no longer a Priest,* Hos. 4.6. *from being an harlot,* for, *to play the harlot no more,* or, *to cease* from *playing the harlot,* Ezek. 16.41. and some other therefore render the word; *I hastened not from* being *a Pastor;* that is, an ordinary Priest, as before I was, to become an extraordinary Prophet: *from a Pastor,* for, *from* being *a Pastor:* a defect of the verb substantive; as 1 Sam. 15.22. before alleged: and *from a city,* for, *from* being *a city;* Esa. 17.1. and, *from a nation,* for, *from* being *a nation,* chap. 48.2. But this will hardly here hold; for Jeremy ceased not then to be a Pastor, when he was to be a Prophet, any more than when he was a Priest before. Others therefore again go another way to work: and because the particle here used, is of frequent use, not in way of deprivation only, but in way of comparison, as Gen. 19.9. *we will do evil unto thee from* them, or, *in comparison of* them: the Latins, *præ illis;* that is, *we will do worse unto thee than to* them: and so also, *A name* (that is, a good name, a good note, a good repute, a good report) *is good* (*pra*) *above,* or, *in comparison of, a good* (that is, a sweet, or precious) *oil,* or *ointment;* that is, the one is better than the other: and the like, Prov. 22.1. as also Esa. 54.1. *the children of the desolate are many in comparison of the children of the married;* that is, the one are in number more than the other; hence therefore they thus render the text; *I pressed not more than a Pastor;* I pressed not upon this prophetical office more than was meet for a Pastor, that is, a teacher, to do, such, as I was already, being a Priest, chap. 1.6. But this seems somewhat forced; and has found therefore few favorites. Howbeit, from it an hint may be taken of that, which with some others, I conceive to be the genuine sense of the place: the word here used signifies, not *to hasten* only, but *to press,* and *to urge:* as Gen. 19.15. *they pressed upon the Angels:* and, *the Task-masters urged,* or, *pressed* them, Exo. 5.13. the word then may well be rendered; *I have not urged,* or, *pressed, from* being *a Pastor;* not to be a Pastor: that which some apply to the time of the Prophet's first calling, when howsoever at first he excused himself in regard of his want of years, chap. 1.6. yet he neither sought by flight to avoid, as Jonas did, Jon. 1.3. nor refused to undertake the employment, when God further pressed it on him. But I suppose it rather to be spoken by him of his carriage after his entrance upon it: that albeit, he had found it to be a very troublesome, and difficult work, through the malice and obstinacy of those, whom he was sent unto: yet he had not been earnest with God in soliciting and pressing him, to discharge him of that service. For as for that which the ancient Greek exhibits, *I have not been weary following thee:* and the old Latin, *I have not been troubled following thee my Shepherd:* the one leaves out somewhat that is in the text; the other puts in that which is not in the text: the words of the text will by no means admit either.

*{I have not}* Or, as some render it, *As for me, I have not urged,* or, *pressed;* the nominative put absolutely; as 1 Chr. 28.2. *I,* (that is, *As for me*) *it was in my heart;* and, *I,* (or, *as for me*) *this shall be my covenant with them,* Esay 59.21. as opposed to their mockery, ver. 15. which he had not so far prevailed with him, as to move God for a discharge of his prophetical ministry, though it went much to the heart with him.

*{after thee}* That is, as some render it, walking *after thee;* or, *following thee,* simply: either in obedience to you, or to do you service: as 1 Sam. 11.17. 1 King. 2.25. yet a defect of some verb, as 1 Sam. 7.2.

*{neither have I desired the woeful day,}* Or, *neither did I desire the doleful,* or, (as some) *the deadly day.* See of the word, chap. 15.18. as I do not now press you to be rid of mine office: howsoever I solicit you for right against those that thus wrong me: so I did not at first desire, much less seek or sue for the employment, offer myself to it, or put myself upon it; but excused myself rather, as not so fit for it, chap. 1.6. as forecasting what opposition and affliction I must look to sustain from those that I was to be sent unto, with such distasteful and unpleasing messages, chap. 1.15, 19. Howbeit, some understand by *deadly,* or, *doleful, day,* the denunciation of such sad and sore evils, as he was enjoined by God to denounce: but this seems somewhat too far fetched. More probable is that of some others, who by *the doleful day,* understand the execution of those judgments which from God he had denounced; for they suppose, that he alludes unto the carriage of Jonas, who at first fled out of the way, that he might not go on God's errand to denounce destruction against Nineveh; and yet was afterward vexed, because the judgment denounced was not put in execution, Jon. 1.3. and 4.1. whereas Jeremy had neither withdrawn himself from the one, nor desired the other. See chap. 15.16. & 18.10. Some read and render it, *the day of man.* So the ancient Greek and old Latin. Which some expound one way, and some another. Some, of some such things as worldly men seek after, in undertaking offices, honor or gain: others, of men's censures of him, which he regarded not with the Apostle, 1 Cor. 4.3. but of this mistake, see on ver. 9.

*{thou knowest,}* Or, *thou knowest it;* a defect of the pronoun, as Psal. 40.9. this may be referred, as the most, to the words foregoing, concerning his manner of entrance into his prophetical employment; or, as others, to that which follows, concerning his carriage in the exercise and execution of it; as I conceive, to both. See his like appeal to God, chap. 12.3. & 15.15. and the Apostle Paul's in the like case, 2 Cor. 1.12.

*{that which came out of my lips was right before thee}* Heb. *the outgoing,* or, *the thing gone out of my lips* (as Num. 30.13. Deut. 23.24.) *hath been before thy face;* or, simply, *before thee;* as Ezek. 14.3, 6. Lam. 2.19. such as has been well known to you, and such therefore as you are able to attest: or, as some render it, which comes home to our English, according to *the rightness of thy face;* that is, sincere and upright, such as I needed not to fear the laying of it open to your sight; but it may as well be rendered to the same effect without any such supply, or circumlocution, *was before thy face,* or, *before thee:* as, *to walk before God,* is to walk sincerely and uprightly, Gen. 17.1. Esay 57.2. I have delivered nothing to them, but your truth, and that with a sincere heart; you who search the heart, and try the reins, ver. 10. know it. So chap. 15.15. to somewhat the like purpose, some render it, *was before thy face;* that is, *came from thy face,* or, *from thee;* as Psal. 17.3. *let my judgment proceed,* or, *come forth from thy face,* or, *from before thee:* but there is that there, that is not here; and this seems to be of larger extent: Some also restrain it, to his former profession, as they take it, that he had not desired, either to be an instrument of denouncing the ruin of that state, or to have what he had denounced, to be accordingly accomplished, for fear of being deemed a false Prophet; Jonas had done, Jon. 4.1. that which God was able to testify for him, whom he had at sundry times earnestly solicited for the revoking of that heavy doom, chap. 10.24, 25. & 4.7, 9, 19, 20. See chap. 18.19. But this seems narrower than the Prophet's intent; nor to be the genuine sense of the foregoing branch.

**V. 17.** *{Be not a terror unto me; thou art my hope in the day of evil.}* Having appealed to God as a witness of his integrity and uprightness, ver. 16. he now sues to him, and solicits him, to be his patron and protector, whom he had made choice of, to repair unto him in times of distress.

*{Be not a terror unto me;}* Heb. *for a terror;* as chap. 48.39. or, as some of the Rabbines render it, *unto contrition,* or, *destruction:* and so the word is used, Psal. 89.40. Prov. 10.14, 29. & 13.3. Howsoever wicked men deal rigorously with me, yet do not you in your indignation handle me roughly, or destroy me, as Psal. 6.1. chap. 10.24. or do not cause or suffer me to live in fear and terror, exposed to their might and malice, for want of relief and support. See chap. 15.15. and for the manner of speech, Esay 63.17. Yet some others, *Be not thou a fear to me;* and then I fear not ought that they can do to me: as Psal. 27.1. but this seems not so freely or fairly to flow from the text.

*{thou art my hope in the day of evil}* Or, be *thou my hope,* or, *refuge,* (as the word is well rendered, Psal. 46.1. & 104.18.) or, adjoining it to the former, *be not, thou my refuge,* (or, who *art my refuge*) *for a terror,* unto me: *hope,* or, *refuge,* for the party hoped in, or the place repaired unto, for relief, succor and safety, Esay 4.6. See Psal. 31.1, 3. & 42.5. and 143.9.

*{in the day of evil}* That is, *of affliction,* chap. 16.19. So Psal. 49.5.

**V. 18.** *{Let them be confounded that persecute me; but let me not be confounded: let them be dismayed; but let not me be dismayed:}* Or, *Let my persecutors be abashed; but* (Heb. *and;* as ver. 6. and so in the next) *let not me be abashed;* (see ver. 13.) *let them be dismayed,* or, *destroyed,* Heb. *terrified,* or, *affrighted;* as Deut. 1.21. Joh. 1.9. or, *broken to pieces,* as 2 Sam. 2.25. Psal. 18.34.) *but* (Heb. *and;* as before) *let not me be affrighted,* or, *broken to pieces.* So Psal. 25.2, 3. & 35.4. & 40.14.

*{bring upon them the day of evil}* As, *the time of evil,* Eccl. 9.12. of affliction, misery, or destruction. So ver. 17.

*{and destroy them with double destruction.}* Heb. *break them with a double breach;* that is, *with breach upon breach;* or, *destruction upon destruction;* as chap. 4.20. or, *with full, abundant, utter,* destruction. So is *double* commonly taken in Scripture, chap. 16.18. Rev. 18.6. Of these and the like prayers or imprecations, see chap. 11.20.

**V. 19.** *{Thus saith the LORD unto me;}* This seems to be the sum of a new sermon diverse from that foregoing; to which the rather he prefixes God's particular charge, for the publishing of it, in regard of the place where he was enjoined to publish it, and of the persons therein principally concerned. See chap. 7.2.

*{Go and stand in the gate of the children of the people, whereby the Kings of Judah come in, and by which they go out; and in all the gates of Jerusalem.}* *Go and stand.* Heb. *Going* (that is, *going go,* be sure to go; as Judg. 4.9. a defect of the verb finite; or, *going,* simply, for, *go,* the infinitive for the imperative. See chap. 2.2. & 13.1.) *and stand.* Heb. *and thou shalt stand:* as, *thou shalt publish,* chap. 2.2. and, *thou shalt say,* chap. 34.2.

*{in the gate of the children of the people, whereby the Kings of Judah come in, and by the which they go out,}* That the usual manner of Prophets was to publish their prophecies in the gates, either of the Temple, or of the city; because the greatest concourse of people was most commonly there, is apparent. See chap. 7.2. & 19.2. & 26.10. as also that some one gate among the rest is here designed, does as plainly appear; but what gate that was, is not so certain. Some would have it to be the *sheep-gate;* whereof, Neh. 3.1, 32. & 12.39. called, say they, here, the *gate of the children of the people;* as Cant. 7.4. the *gate daughter of many;* or the gate most frequented: because the greatest confluence of people, by reason of the great sheep-market there kept, was thither: but neither does it appear that the gate in the Canticles mentioned, is *the sheep-gate,* nor that it was any gate of more frequency than any other. Many take the word rather for the proper name of a place called *Bath-rabbim.* Nor again is the gate here designed, called *the gate of the children of the people;* because either the most of them went out and in that way; or because it was usually more frequented than any other: for, the term is no other than what agrees unto any other gate of the city, that people ordinarily went in and out by: *the children of the people,* being no other than *the people* themselves; as the Greeks use to say, *the children of the Physicians,* for, *the Physicians* themselves: and *the children of the Achaians,* for, *the Achaians* themselves. See chap. 5.7. So, *the children of thy people,* for, your people, simply, and generally, whether young or old, parents or children, Ezek. 3.11. & 33.2, 12, 17, 30. & 37.18. the particular designation of it is from the words following. Whence some other conceive it to be the *water-gate;* whereof, Neh. 3.26. & 8.3, 16. 2 Chron. 29.3, 4. & 32.6. by which places it appears, that it was situate on the east side of the city, and that the street it opened upon, was one of the eminentest, and of greatest receipt in the city, deemed to be that of Millo, which lay between the Temple and the palace, by which the king and his courtiers therefore did usually pass to and fro.

*{the gate of the children of the people}* Not the court-gate, but one of the city-gates, one of those nearest the palace, by which the people of the land, as well as the king and his followers, had ordinary passage, ver. 2.

*{the Kings of Judah}* Either successively in their several times and reigns; or, as the Rabbine here, the king's children that were to reign after him, 2 King. 3.27. or the princes rather and rulers that frequented the king's court; as chap. 19.3. & 20.5.

*{and in all the gates of Jerusalem.}* In that first, of most eminency, or most made use of, near the court; because those of the court were therein principally concerned: then in the rest of the gates round about the city, that all might take notice of it, the gates of the city, being the places whereunto for civil affairs of several kinds, the people used to resort, Ruth 4.1, 2. 2 Sam. 19.8. chap. 38.7.

**V. 20.** *{Hear ye the word of the LORD, ye Kings of Judah, and all Judah, and all the Inhabitants of Jerusalem, that enter in by these gates.}* As chap. 7.2. & 22.2. but here more especially the kings and rulers: as ver. 19. in the first place; because they stood bound, not only to observe the Sabbath themselves, but to cause it to be kept by others: so the tenor of the commandment runs, Exod. 20.8, 10. See Neh. 13.16, 18. then all *Judah;* that is, the inhabitants, who were wont from all parts to repair unto Jerusalem, as a principal market, and the head city, both for judicature, and for God's solemn service, Psal. 122.4, 5. See ver. 25, 26.

**V. 21.** *{Thus saith the LORD}* As ver. 5.

*{Take heed to yourselves,}* Heb. *to your souls;* as, *to your selves,* Deut. 4.15. Josh. 23.11. implying the importance and weight of the duty required of them: a matter that no less than their lives lay upon, and that concerned the eternal welfare of their souls, Deut. 32.47. See Exod. 31.14, 15. Num. 15.32, 35. for that of the learned Scholiast, who renders it, *Take heed in your souls,* or, *in your hearts;* that is, *take diligent heed;* seems overharsh, and suits not so well with those places pointed to, where himself renders it, *Take heed to your selves.*

*{and bear no burden on the Sabbath day, nor bring it in by the gates of Jerusalem.}* Or, *that* (as chap. 4.4. and 14.19.) *ye bear no burden,* (so the Hebrew) or, *any burden* (so rather, than *burdens,* as some; *any* supplied: Job 16.17. Esay 53.9.) *on the Sabbath day,* (Heb. *the day of rest,* Exod. 20.8, 11.) *or* (Heb. *and;* as chap. 16.1, 7.) *bring* it, (a defect of the participle: as chap. 12.11.) or, any (supplied as before) *in* (supplied from the opposite, *carry out,* ver. 22. Heb. *make to go,* or, *come*) *by the gates of Jerusalem.* See Neh. 13.15, 16, 19.

**V. 22.** *{Neither carry forth a burden out of your houses upon the Sabbath day}* Or, *And that* (as ver. 21.) *ye carry not out* (Heb. *make to go out,* as Ezek. 12.7.) *from your houses any* (as ver. 24.) *burden on the Sabbath day;* as ver. 21. not out by the gates of the city only, but out of your houses within the city. Where it may be demanded why he says, *bring out of your houses,* rather than *bring into your houses:* to which some answer, that by *carrying out a burden;* is meant the casting out the dust, or dirt and soil of their houses contracted the week past: but that seems over-narrow, nor very proper. Others would have it so said, because the gates of the city were on the Sabbath day shut, Neh. 13.19. and they could not therefore bring in ought to be bestowed in their houses: but that seems no satisfactory answer; for neither does it appear that that provision of shutting the gates, was constantly continued, in such corrupt times especially as these were: and notwithstanding it, they might as well bring wares or other burdens from other places within the city into their houses, as carry out of them to other places: but the better answer is, that the one by analogy, and just consequence, comprehends both. See the like, ver. 24. and as for our Savior's act, willing the man healed at the pool of Bethesda, to carry his bed home, Joh. 5.8, 11. which the Jews so much caviled at, it no way either infringed the Law of the Sabbath, or crossed this inhibition: for what should the man do with his bed there then, when as there was no need or use either of his bed there, or of his stay there to keep it? it was fitter and better for him to get home with it, and to the Temple thence, to praise God there with Ezekiah for his recovery, Esay 38.22. than stay idling at the pool among other cripples with his couch: nor need we with some to say, that being done by Christ's command who was God, it was no sin nor violation of the Sabbath, though the Law were otherwise; ranking it with Abraham's sacrificing of Isaac in resolution and purpose, Gen. 22. and the Hebrews' spoiling of the Egyptians, Exod. 11.2. and 12.35, 36. for to say nothing of them; little did the man at that time dream of Christ's deity; nor was that which the man then did any other, than what any man lying abroad on his couch, being suddenly so cured, whether by miracle, or by some special providence, might lawfully, without breach of that commandment concerning the Sabbath, have done.

*{neither do ye any work, but hallow ye the Sabbath;}* Or, *nor do* (to carry it on in one tenor with the former) *any work,* to wit, any such work as in the Law is forbidden to be done on that day. Heb. *all work: all,* for, *any;* as Lev. 3.17. So Exod. 20.10.

*{as I commanded your fathers}* Exod. 20.8. and 23.12. and 31.14, 15. Lev. 19.4. and 23.3. Deut. 5.12, 15. Exod. 20.12, 20. and you also in them, Exod. 31.13, 16, 17. the observation of the Sabbath, pressed here, as much neglected; and put for all religious duties and offices, Esay 56.2.

**V. 23.** *{But they obeyed not, neither inclined their ear;}* See chap. 7.24, 26. So chap. 19.15. in general: and of this precept in particular, Ezek. 20.21.

*{but hardened their necks that they might not hear, nor receive instruction.}* See chap. 7.26. and 16.12. Zach. 7.11, 12. and of the last clause, chap. 2.30. and 5.3. and 7.28.

**V. 24.** *{And it shall come to pass,}* Or, *Yet;* the copulative for the discretive: as chap. 14.9, 15. *it shall come to pass.* Heb. *it shall be,* as chap. 5.19. Their pollution of my day shall not be punished in you, if you keep free from it yourselves, or, reform it in yourselves, Ezek. 18.14, 17.

*{if ye diligently hearken unto me, saith the LORD}* Heb. *hearkening hearken;* as Exod. 15.26. and 19.5.

*{to bring no burden through the gates of the city on the Sabbath day:}* Or, *to bring in:* as before, ver. 21. neither bring in, nor bear out: the one comprehended under the other, as ver. 22.

*{but hallow the Sabbath day to do no work therein}* Or, *by doing no work therein;* as the particle with the infinitive is used, Deut. 9.18. & 17.2. & 22.21. & 28.63. See before, ver. 21.

**V. 25.** *{Then shall there enter into the gates of this city}* *Then,* as having reference to the condition, *if,* ver. 14. Heb. *And;* as chap. 16.11. but, *That,* rather here; as chap. 5.19. & 7.32. & 9.25. for it answers not to the conditional, but to the words, *it shall be,* where the promise made upon that condition, begins after the condition itself there inserted, here prosecuted. See the like promise, chap. 22.4.

*{Kings and Princes}* See ver. 19.

*{sitting upon the Throne of David}* As chap. 13.13.

*{riding in chariots, and on horses,}* Riding out and in, in royal state and pomp, 2 King. 10.15, 16. Psal. 45.4.

*{they and their Princes, the men of Judah, and the Inhabitants of Jerusalem}* For the gates of the city were common to either, ver. 20. the latter is omitted, where the palace gates are intended, chap. 22.4. Heb. *man of Judah,* for, *men;* as Esay 5.3.

*{and this city shall remain for ever.}* Heb. *shall sit;* as Lev. 14.8. chap. 40.6. or, *be inhabited* (as ver. 6. Zach. 12.6. & 14.11.) *for ever;* which has reference to the establishment of David's throne in much prosperity, and the continuance of state and city, 2 Sam. 7.16. Psal. 132.12, 14, 17. 2 King. 21.7, 8. chap. 7.3, 5, 7.

**V. 26.** *{And they shall come from the cities of Judah, and from the places about Jerusalem, and from the land of Benjamin, and from the plain, and from the mountains, and from the South, bringing burnt offerings, and sacrifices, and meat offerings, and incense, & bringing sacrifices of praise, unto the house of the LORD.}* The city and Temple shall both stand, and be both frequented, from all parts of the kingdom, as formerly they have been.

*{from the land of Benjamin,}* Which continued firm to Judah, when the other tribes fell from her, 2 King. 12.21. 2 Chr. 11.12. & 15.2, 8, 9. and so still did, chap. 6.1. See chap. 32.44. & 33.13.

*{and from the plain, and from the mountains, and from the South}* *And,* or, *both;* as the copulative is rendered, Gen. 36.24. Psal. 76.6. chap. 5.24. & 44.25. for the copulative does not knit this branch to the former, as if the places ensuing were not within the land of Judah and Benjamin, and the territory about Jerusalem, but in other regions elsewhere abroad; but it refers to the latter, distinguishing the places in the former branch mentioned, and therein laid out according to their limits, and the tribes or principal parts of them, whereunto they appertained; and here further ranking them according to the divers condition of them, some of each sort being found in each of those parts: nor is therefore this distribution (the like whereunto, see chap. 32.44. and 33.13.) to be restrained (as some do it) to Judah only, as if proper to that tribe alone, Josh. 15. and not common to the rest; but respects the land of Benjamin as well as that of Judah. See chap. 33.13.

*{from the plain}* Or, as it is rendered, chap. 34.44. *the valley,* and chap. 33.13. *the vale,* and so would be here, for another word the Hebrews have for *the plain,* chap. 21.13. where *the vale* and it are distinguished, and the term *plain* better agrees to the last, Heb. *the low* land, or, ground, a defect of the subject; as *dry;* for *dry* land, Esay 44.3. Jon. 1.9, 13. & 2.11. opposed there to the *sea;* as this here to the *mountain,* for so is the word here singular, though used collectively.

*{from the South}* Or, *the upland;* the word indeed here found, is used commonly for the *South,* in bounding of places especially, as Josh. 15.1, 2, 4. in regard whereof that learned writer, who restrains the word here unto Judah, would have it to be here so taken, affirming from that place of Joshuah, the land belonging to that tribe, to be there divided into *Southerly* land, *mountain,* and *vale,* but there is no such division found there, the *South* is mentioned only as in all entire divisions of lands, and of the other tribes also there, Josh. 17.9, 10. & 18.13, 14. & 19.8. nor was the Southern part of Judah, or of any other tribe, without mountain, or vale, more than the Eastern, Western, or Northern part of the same, but the word that does first properly signify *South,* where opposed to, or distinguished from, East, West, or North, has a diverse notion, where it is opposed to, or distinguished from *mountain* and *low-land,* or, *vale;* as here and in that place of Joshua afterward, and signifies a middle sort of land, between *mountain* and *vale;* such as we use to term *heaths,* and *plains,* and *downs;* as we when, say, *New-market-heath, Salisbury-plain,* and *Banbury Downs;* which are neither *mountainy* places, nor *valleys,* properly so called: and such places in the Hebrew have this name given them; because they are dryer commonly than the vales, as the Southern parts are ordinarily, being nearer to the sun, and more exposed to its parching heat. See Achsah's request to her father Caleb, Josh. 15.19. Judg. 1.15. See also Zach. 7.7. where this and the *low-ground,* are expressly distinguished.

*{burnt offerings, and sacrifices, and meat offerings, and incense.}* Of these, see on Esay 1.11, 13.

*{bringing sacrifices of praise.}* Heb. *bringing praise,* or, *thanksgiving,* or, *confession.* So Psal. 50.14, 23. as *sin,* for, a *sin-sacrifice,* Lev. 4.24. 2 Cor. 5.21. or, a sacrifice for *sin,* Rom. 8.3. Heb. 10.6, 8. so, *praise,* for a sacrifice of *praise,* or thankful acknowledgment.

This is mentioned apart, because it should be most frequent, while God by his mercies should give frequent occasions of such. See chap. 33.11.

**V. 27.** *{But if ye will not hearken unto me, to hallow the Sabbath day, and not to bear burdens, even entering in at the gates of Jerusalem on the Sabbath day}* Heb. *And,* as ver. 23. See for the next words, ver. 21, 24. the latter, some read, *as you enter,* or, *while you pass thorow, the gates of Jerusalem,* as the copulative is used, 1 King. 11.25. but I suppose may rather be rendered jointly with the former, thus, *to sanctify the Sabbath-day, both by not bearing any burthen,* or, (Heb. *and,* as ver. 21.) *going,* or, *passing,* in and out, (as Esay 25.1. & 24.10.) *thorow the gates of Jerusalem,* for by needless passing to and fro, as well without burden, as with burden, might they violate the Sabbath, Exod. 16.29.

*{then will I kindle a fire in the gates thereof; and it shall devour the palaces of Jerusalem, and shall not be quenched.}* Or, *Then,* (Heb. *And* as chap. 16.11.) *I will kindle a fire,* (as chap. 21.14. & 43.12. & 50.2.) *in the gates thereof,* (in those gates thus abused. See Neh. 1.3. & 2.13.) *which* (as chap. 9.22.) *shall devour,* (as Esay 9.18.) *the palaces of Jerusalem;* (the lofty and stately buildings of it, as chap. 49.27. See it fulfilled, 2 King. 25.9. chap. 52.13.) *and shall not be quenched,* until it have consumed both the one and the other, as did those Chaldean forces, 2 Chr. 36.19. Psal. 74.7, 8.

## CHAPTER 18

**Verse 1.** *{The word came to Jeremiah from the LORD, saying;}* Heb. *Was to Jeremiah* from the Lord, as chap. 7.1. The sermon in this chapter contained, consists of two principal parts, a prophecy, and a complaint. In the prophecy is contained; 1. A demonstration by a type, what God is able to do either with the Jewish people, or any other, ver. 1, 6. 2. A declaration of God's meaning and intent, as well in his menaces, as in his promises, ver. 7, 10. 3. An exhortation to repentance and amendment of life, ver. 11. 4. A relation of their obstinacy, notwithstanding mercy offered them, ver. 12. 5. A redargution of their extreme folly therein, ver. 13, 14. 6. A denunciation of destruction to befall them for the same, ver. 15, 17. The complaint follows to the end of the chapter.

**V. 2.** *{Arise}* See chap. 1.17. & 13.4, 6.

*{and go down}* Or, *go;* simply: as also, chap. 22.1. See Esay 38.8. *go down from the Temple,* say some, beneath which, the potter's workhouse was, Mat. 27.10. but neither does it appear by the one text, that Jeremy was then in the temple, when God spoke this to him; nor by the other, that the potter's workhouse stood either beneath the Temple, or near unto it: and of the use of the word *descending,* see on the place of Esay pointed to.

*{to the Potters house,}* This with the fields belonging to it, seem to have been situate without the gates, on the south side of the city. See chap. 19.2. & 31.40.

*{and there will I cause thee to hear my words.}* There I will further acquaint you with my mind, and the message that I mean to send by you, upon that which there you shall see. So, *to make,* or, *cause, to hear,* for, *to tell,* chap. 4.15.

**V. 3.** *{Then I went down to the Potters house;}* Or, *So,* (Heb. *And;* as 2 King. 9.4. Esay 37.5. according as was commanded) *I went.* See ver. 2.

*{and behold he wrought a work on the wheels}* Or, *he was working* (Heb. *making*) some *work upon the frames,* or, *seat;* as the Chaldee gives it: and ours render the same word, *stools,* Exod. 1.16. The word is of a dual form; as that of *a mill;* whereof see on Esay 47.2. and by the notation of it may seem to have consisted of *two stones:* as the dual, though irregular of *Eben,* which signifies *a stone;* and so the Greek renders it *upon the stones.* Howbeit, most interpreters render it *a wheel,* or, as ours, *wheels:* and howsoever one of the Rabbines tells us it was but one *wheel,* on which the potter used to work: yet another of them informs us, that in the Eastern parts the frame that they wrought on, consisted of *two wheels,* a bigger and a less; that uppermost, this lower, or within that: and would have it by change of a letter to come of the word *Ophan,* that signifies *a wheel.* But I suppose the word to come neither from *Eben,* a *stone;* or, *Ophan, a wheel:* but either to be, or to have, a peculiar root of itself, or its own; as the word for *heaven,* and that for *loins,* chap. 13.1. whose originals are now unknown.

**V. 4.** *{And the vessel which he made of clay was marred in the hand of the potter}* Or, *the vessel which he* was *making,* (as ver. 3.) *miscarried,* as *clay in the potters hand.* But here comes in a doubt which none of the Jewish commenters seem to take notice of. That which we render *of clay,* is constantly in our Hebrew Bibles, *as clay;* that which is also exhibited in the margin of our last version, (howsoever most interpreters take no notice at all of it) with the same particle prefixed to it, that is afterward used, ver. 6. where neither of the sense or reading any doubt is or can be made. So that according to this reading, the meaning might seem to be, *while it was yet clay;* (as *when* it was *budding,* Gen. 40.10.) that is, moist and soft, as one of the Jewish Doctors interprets the word *clay,* here; before it was nealed & hardened, while he was yet framing and fashioning it; as both the word *making,* not *made,* and the clause *in his hand,*) or, *hands,* collectively taken; for he makes use of both, in giving it the fashion) is implied. Howbeit, both he also with the rest, says, that the particle here used is put for *mem,* or, *min,* designing the matter. Where it may be conjectured; that they read it not with *caph,* the usual note of similitude; but with *beth:* and yet I nowhere find *beth* so used, save Exod. 38.8. where it is said that the laver of brass was made *of,* or, *with the womens mirrors,* or *looking-brasses,* rather than *glasses.* Where yet no good parallel is brought of this use of that particle: only one of them tells us, that such use of it is frequent in the Ishmaelitish tongue. So that whether *caph,* were here, by some slip, written for *beth,* the letters being very like the one to the other; and *beth,* be the right, as most seem to have taken it, may justly require further consideration, which I leave therefore to the learned.

*{in the hand of the potter}* That is, *in his hand;* (as also some render it) whom he had before named, ver. 3. the noun for the pronoun: as Esay 33.2. & 35.8. chap. 10.3, 4. and so in the close of this verse: and *hand,* for, *hands,* taken collectively; as also afterward, ver. 6.

*{So he made it again another vessel, as it seemed good to the potter to make it}* Or, *so he made of it again another vessel, such as he thought good to make.*

*{So}* Heb. *and;* as ver. 3.

*{he made it again}* Or, *of it,* as Exod. 32.4. Judg. 17.4. Heb. *he returned and made:* as, *returned and digged,* for, *digged again,* Gen. 26.18. See Esay 6.13.

*{as it seemed good to the potter}* Heb. *as was right in the eyes of the Potter:* as chap. 27.5. *the Potter,* for, *him,* or, *himself:* as before.

**V. 5.** *{Then came the word of the LORD unto me, saying,}* Heb. *And:* as chap. 17.27. the rest, as ver. 1.

**V. 6.** *{O house of Israel, cannot I do with you, as this Potter? saith the LORD.}* The Lord in these words shows the reason why he had enjoined Jeremy to meet him at the potter's workhouse; to wit, there by a pregnant demonstration to show him how he was able without further ado to deal with this people; he was able to destroy them, and might well so do without further warning; and it was his mere mercy, if he gave them any warning, having so ill deserved of him, before he so did: and that as he had framed them, and made them a people, a nation, a church, a state formerly, Esay 43.1. & 44.2. & 64.8. so he could again mar them, especially since that they had first so corrupted and marred themselves by their sins, Deut. 32.5, 6. Esay 1.4. unmake them either people, or nation, or church, or state; and either remake or frame them again such as before they were, Esay 1.25, 26. chap. 33.7. Rom. 11.23, 24. or make others such in their room. See Num. 14.12. Mat. 3.9. Rom. 11.11, 17. and they had no just cause to complain, if he should so do, Esay 45.9. Rom. 9.20.

*{O house of Israel,}* The people of the Jews; as chap. 2.26.

*{as this Potter doth}* To wit, with his clay, ver. 4.

*{as the clay is in the Potters hand, so are ye in my hand, O house of Israel.}* I have as much power over you, as the potter over the clay, that he works upon; and as much both might and right also to dispose of you at my pleasure, as he to deal as seems good to him with his own work, Esay 29.15, 16. and 49.5.

**V. 7.** *{At what instant I shall speak against a nation, and concerning a Kingdom, to pluck up, and to pull down, and to destroy it;}* Whensoever I shall by my Prophets threaten destruction to any people or state; that which in mercy he usually does before he come to destroy, Amos 3.7. & 4.12. and for that very end also that he may not destroy, chap. 6.8. & 36.2. Ezek. 3.18.

*{At what instant I shall speak}* Or, *Let me speak suddenly;* as Job 34.20. Psal. 6.10. or there may be a trajection in the text, as there is apparently in the next verse, and then the words may be thus rendered; *Let me speak concerning a nation—suddenly—to destroy it;* that it shall in an instant, without any long delay be destroyed; as with Nineveh he did, Jon. 3.4. and to this I much incline.

*{against a nation, and concerning a Kingdom}* Or, *concerning* any *nation,* (as chap. 17.21.) *or* (as chap. 15.1, 7.) *concerning* any *Kingdome;* for the particle is the same in either member, and ought to be alike expressed in either. So chap. 16.3. and in the parallel, ver. 9.

*{to pluck up, and pull down, and to destroy it}* The copulative may here also be well rendered, as before by the disjunctive, that I intend, or am about so to do. See chap. 1.10. a defect of the pronoun, *it:* as chap. 3.7. and 4.28. So ver. 9.

**V. 8.** *{If that nation against whom I have pronounced, turn from their evil, I will repent of the evil, that I thought to do unto them.}* Or, *If that nation concerning whom I* so (supplied, as the like, ver. 23.) *spake, shall return from its evil, I also will repent concerning the evil that I thought to do unto it.* Thus repentance in man produces repentance with God. When people or persons repent of the evil of sin, for which God had denounced a doom of penalty against them, God stays his hand, revokes the doom, and reprieves such people or persons. So Judg. 10.13, 16. 1 King. 21.20. Jon. 3.10. Not that God repents as man through oversight, or want of forecast and foresight, or out of fickleness and mutability of mind; for such grounds of repentance are imperfections in man, and cannot befall him who is perfection itself, Num. 23.19. 1 Sam. 15.29. Mal. 3.6. Jam. 1.17. but God is said then to repent, when he does as men use to do when they repent, 1 Sam. 25.33, 34. when he undoes what he had done before, revokes a doom that he had past before, stays the execution of a sentence that formerly he had denounced, Gen. 6.6, 7. 1 Sam. 15.11, 28. which as it was denounced because of man's sin, so is it reversed, when man ceases so to do; the end being accomplished for which it was denounced, to wit, that it might not be inflicted. See on ver. 7. So that, as the Schoolmen well say, Repentance in man is a change of the mind, or will; repentance with God, is the willing of a change, his mind and purpose abiding still the same, chap. 20.16. There is in the text a trajection of the words; as ver. 7. for in the text they thus lie; *and let that nation return from its evil, concerning which I spake.* See the like, chap. 11.16. and an elegant *antanaclasis* between *evil* and *evil; sin* meant by the one, and *penalty* by the other. So Jon. 3.10.

*{If}* Heb. *And;* as chap. 16.10. Amos 3.4. Yet may the copulative be retained, reading the text as before, ver. 7. *Let me speak concerning a nation———And let that nation turn———and I will repent.*

*{that nation}* Or, *kingdom,* v. 7.

*{against whom}* Or, *concerning whom:* as v. 7. Heb. *whom against it:* an usual redundancy in the Hebrew; as Psal. 1.4.

*{I have pronounced}* Or, *I so spake;* as v. 7.

*{return}* A necessary companion of true repentance, Act. 3.19. & 26.20. whereby therefore repentance is frequently described, Isa. 55.7. chap. 26.3. & 36.7. Jon. 3.10.

*{I will repent}* Or, *I will also repent.* Heb. *and I will repent: and,* for, *also;* chap. 14.5. or the copulative may stand, if we read the former branch, as was before hinted; *Let that nation return,———and I will repent.*

*{I purposed}* Or, *thought,* or, *had devised,* chap. 11.19. See ver. 11.

**V. 9.** *{And at what instant I shall speak concerning a nation, and concerning a Kingdom, to build and to plant it}* Or, *Let me speak in like manner* (the copulative for the redditive note of similitude: as Isa. 10.26. & 33.7.) *concerning a nation, or concerning a kingdom, suddenly to build* or *to plant it:* acquainting them by my Prophets what I intend to do for them, and what good is coming to them. See v. 7. & chap. 1.10.

**V. 10.** *{If it do evil in my sight, that it obey not my voice, then will I repent of the good wherewith I said I would benefit them.}* Or, *and let it* (that nation or kingdom, whereof ver. 9.) *do* that which is *evil in my sight,* (Heb. *in mine eyes;* that is, offensive and displeasing to me; as 2 Sam. 11.27.) *in not hearkening to my voice,* (as chap. 16.12. & 17.23.) *I shall then* (Heb. *and;* as chap. 4.1, 2. & 8.9.) *repent concerning the good wherein I said I would do them good.* See before, ver. 8. As God's menaces are denounced with a condition, if not expressed, yet secretly implied and intended, of repentance; so are his promises of the like nature propounded unto persons and people, though in absolute terms oft-times conceived, yet with the like reservation, not to take place, but upon their continuance and perseverance in well-doing, unto whom the same are made. So Deut. 28.1, 10. 1 Sam. 2.30. & 15.1, 2.

**V. 11.** *{Now therefore, go to, speak to the men of Judah, and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, saying, thus saith the LORD;}* From the former declaration of God's intentions and courses, concerning both his righteous menaces and gracious promises in general: The Lord now proceeds and descends to an application thereof in particular unto the Jewish people, and the message that his Prophet was now enjoined to deliver to them from him.

*{Now therefore}* Heb. *And now,* as chap. 15.6.

*{go to, speak}* Heb. *speak now;* for the latter particle is commonly also so rendered, but it has withal a notion; sometime of entreating, as Isa. 36.11. sometime of inciting, as Isa. 36.8. See there, and so here; and again in the close of the verse.

*{men}* Heb. *man,* as chap. 11.22.

*{Behold, I frame evil against you, and devise a device against you:}* Heb. *I am framing* (as the potter frames a vessel; so the word properly signifies: used also, Gen. 2.7. And the very same word is used commonly for *a potter,* as v. 3, 4.) *against you, and* am *devising a device* (to wit, of evil, as before) *against you.* So chap. 48.2. & 49.30. it is a borrowed speech from that model that the workman or artist conceives in his mind, according to which he afterward fashions his work, Exod. 35.33. 2 Chr. 2.13.

*{return ye now every one from his evil ways, and make your ways and your doings good.}* Take notice of the evil that will otherwise befall you, and take the course above-mentioned, for the preventing of it, by sincere repentance, and serious reformation and amendment of your lives: by these means alone yet may you escape, v. 7, 8. 2 King. 17.13. chap. 3.12. & 7.3. & 25.5. & 35.15. Ezek. 18.21. & 33.11.

*{every one}* Heb. *a man;* as chap. 5.8. & 12.15.

**V. 12.** *{And they said, There is no hope; but we will walk after our own devices, and we will do every one the imagination of his evil heart.}* *And* (or, *But;* as chap. 17.23.) *they said,* or, *they have said,* or, *say:* this has been their former saying, and still is; and this answer, I know, they will now give you again. The effect, or sum of the answer, either that the people did return to God's admonition delivered to them by the Prophet, as some; or that God beforehand knew that they would return, as formerly they oft had done: so not improbably one of the Jewish commenters; or, as some other, thus they say, or think still with themselves: And it is as if in a manner they had said; It is to no purpose to speak to us, or to deal and strive further with us; (whence God's resolution, Gen. 6.3.) there is no possibility of reclaiming or reducing us: (see the like desperate return, chap. 2.25. & 13.9.) we are fully and firmly fixed upon it, and resolved to take those courses that we are pitched upon, and to live as we list ourselves. See chap. 13.10. and 16.20. and 44.16. and hence it appears, that the words rendered *device,* and *imagination,* are much at one the same: and *man* here for *every one:* as ver. 12.

*{his evil heart}* Or, *his own evil heart:* as Isa. 53.6. *evil* is inserted, not as if they themselves would so speak, unless it were in way of derision, as you account it, or use to call it: for they would never themselves acknowledge their hearts to be such: but thereby intimating what indeed they were; whatsoever conceit themselves had of them, Prov. 16.2.

**V. 13.** *{Therefore thus saith the LORD}* Upon this their desperate obstinacy, and refusal of God's gracious offers; after some amplification of their strange carriage and extreme folly therein, v. 13, 14. God proceeds to the passing of a peremptory sentence upon them, ver. 15, 16.

*{Ask ye among the Heathen, who hath heard such a thing?}* See the like contestation, chap. 2.10.

*{the Virgin of Israel}* Or, *the Virgin Israel.* See Isaiah 17.8. Israel termed *a Virgin;* as other states. See Esa. 23.12. & 47.1. though some suppose a further emphasis here; as if it were said, She that should have kept herself a pure Virgin for God, who had espoused her to himself, Ezek. 16.8. 2 Cor. 11.2.

*{hath done a very horrible thing.}* Or, *committed a very vile thing.* See chap. 5.30. So chap. 23.14. See also chap. 24.2. what this *vile thing* is, see ver. 15.

**V. 14.** *{Will a man leave the snow of Lebanon, which cometh from the rock of the field?}* Or, *Shall the snow of Lebanon be left coming down from the rock in the fields?* for the verb is indefinite; and may be therefore be rendered by the passive: as chap. 10.3, 4. or, as some again render it, *Shall water* like the *snow* (that is, as cold as the snow) *of Lebanon* issuing *from a rock in the field be left?* the word *water,* supplied from the clause ensuing, and the note of similitude, as Psalm 11.1. Esa. 21.8. The meaning of the words either of these ways thus read, is, that neither any traveler in the heat of the day, meeting in the field with a spring, whose water issues from some rock having the head of it fed with the snow of mount Lebanon, where it has its first rise, being at time of year dissolved, will pass by it, and go on looking for some other elsewhere; or no wise man having such a spring at hand in his field, will, when he has use and need thereof, refuse it, and go to seek water in some pond or pool, puddle much less, elsewhere. For as for the Chaldee, Greek and Latin versions, who render it to this effect; *Will,* or, *Can,* the water *fail from the rock in the field?* or, as the Greek by mistake of a point, *the teats from the rock,* or, *the snow from Libanus?* But this the text will not well bear, the verb of *leaving,* or *forsaking,* being hardly found so used, as they take it. Howbeit, to remove that difficulty, a learned late writer thus renders the text; *Doth the snow of Lebanon from the rock leave,* or, *forsake, my field?* that is, does the snow that is perpetually on the mountains and rocks of Lebanon, ever leave running down, as it melts, into my fields? as God thereby intimating the care that he had of making a constant provision of water for the land of his people lying below that mount. Which though it seem not so well to fit here, no more than what concerning the next branch he suggests, yet may for sense seem to come home to the former; implying, that God, whom his people left to look after idols and strangers, was as a wellspring of water that never fails, but runs continually, either gushing out of some rock, or descending from mount Lebanon, from whence many constant streams ran down to the fields and places near about it; whom yet this people left, to seek relief and refreshment where it was not to be found. So it parallels well with chap. 2.13. & 17.13. And this way the most go, both Jews and others; but rendering the words the former way. Howbeit, some late writers of special note render the words far otherwise, thus; *Will* a traveler *leave my fields,* (as one of them) *the fields* (as another, supposing no affix pronoun here; but such an irregular form as in some words and places is found; as Psal. 50.11. & 96.12. & 104.11. Esay 56.9. Lam. 4.9. Hos. 10.4.) *for a rock,* and for the *snow of Lebanon;* that is, for *the snowy Lebanon?* whereto, see Esay 2.13. and this is from them exhibited in the margin of our Bibles. So the meaning should be; Will any traveler be so foolish or mad, as to leave the plain, where he has a fair, even, free, and clear way before him, without let or impediment, and instead thereof take his way over craggy and rocky hills through bushes and briars, and thickets covered over with snow, no less dangerous than difficult? as implying, that this people foolishly and unadvisedly left God's service, that was easy and free, Matth. 11.29. to run after idols, who required of them other manner of service, far more hard and harsh than any that he did, Deut. 12.30, 31. 1 King. 18.28. chap. 19.5. ver. 15. And this should I incline to, in regard of the next verse's close, that may seem to hint some such matter, did I find the particle *min* here found, to be anywhere used in the notion of *for,* or, *instead of:* it oft indeed answers the Latin *præ;* and they so express it. Which turned into English, imports not *for,* or, *instead of;* but *before,* or, *rather than;* being much used in comparisons, as the Hebrew particle also is: and being so here Englished, would make the text sound clean contrary to what they would have it speak; to wit, *Will* any traveler *leave the plain before the rock,* or, *rather than the rock; and before,* or, *rather than the snowy Lebanon?* when as they would have the meaning to be, that no wise man, or in his wits, will choose the rocky and snowy way before the plain; or will not leave that, to betake himself to this. So their version and their intention do directly cross the one the other. The Italian version renders it; *Should snowy Lebanon be left for a stone of the field?* implying as great an inequality between God the rock and strength of all ages, Deut. 32.4. Esa. 26.4. and idols; as there is between mount Lebanon and some stone in the field. See Deut. 32.31. But to pass by the unusualness of the word here used to signify *a stone:* the same incongruity is here also that was in the former.

*{or shall the cold flowing waters that come from another place be forsaken?}* About this latter branch here is no less difficulty and diversity among interpreters, than about the former. The text is, word for word, or (supplied, as chap. 11.19.) *shall strange, cool, flowing, waters be forsaken;* or, *fail?* which the most thus expound; Will men, though they have not such a spring of water as was before said, yet if they have fresh conduit water with them at home, derived and brought to them by pipes, channels, or other means of conveyance for that purpose contrived, from some place more remote, so long as it is cool, and flows clear, refuse to make use of it, and content themselves with it, rather than trouble themselves with running abroad to seek for other elsewhere; and that in some pond or standing pool, which neither runs fresh, nor is so cool, being constantly exposed to the heat of the sun? for such supply the opposite attributes require: that which in effect for the application comes home to the same with the former. See Prov. 5.15. And that learned man before alleged, taking the term in a notion of *failing;* *shall* such *waters fail?* expounds it of the waters of Euphrates and Nilus, which though rising in foreign parts, yet watered the land of his people; as if God had said, when as hence it appears that I forget not my people, in that I furnish them with water both springing up in their own land from mount Lebanon; and such also, as those of Euphrates and Nilus, that have their rise in regions more remote: what reason is it that my people should forget me? But how these two great rivers should water the land of Judah, (to say nothing of Lebanon) I see not: and the seeking after these waters is expressly objected to them, and charged as a crime upon them, chap. 2.18. nor does this therefore seem so well to suit with the drift of the place. Those other worthies above mentioned, do here also go a way out of the common road by themselves; thus rendering the words, *Shall the running waters be left for strange cold waters?* or, for *waters strangely cold?* that is, is any man so foolish, as that when he is athirst, having wholesome running water by him, he will leave that, and seek elsewhere for water extremely cold and unwholesome? But sure it is a commendation of water to be cool. See Prov. 25.25. nor is there any more than so in the text: for that which another has of *waters corrupted with ice,* seems not to satisfy: and if I could go this way therefore, I should choose rather to render it; *shall the running waters be left* for *strange* ones? But neither is the particle *min* here at all in the text; as in the former branch it was: though not in that notion or use as they here take it; nor were it put in, would the text afford that sense that they would give it; as in the former branch was evidently showed.

*{cold}* The same word with that, Prov. 25.25. though some of the Jewish critics would refer it to another root that signifies *digging,* for water especially, Esa. 37.25. as if the meaning were, water by digging procured: but the ready sense is here needlessly rejected, for one without due analogy further fetched.

*{that come from another place}* Heb. *Strange.* For the meaning whereof, some of the Jewish writers refer us to 2 King. 19.24. where the same term is used of waters: but there of waters digged and delved for, where none appeared, nor were ever before known to be. Which they press to confirm that formerly delivered concerning the meaning of that word from the same place, and Esa. 37.25. But other of them go the way before mentioned, understanding it of water brought from remote places, as before: for as for their curious application of it unto God, as being in some sort remote from them; because dwelling in heaven, Esay 63.15. and yet near unto them in regard of his Temple with them, and in his continual beneficence to them, 1 King. 8.13, 27. I let pass: nor are those criticisms of some of them worthy debate, that from a term used Esay 1.6. would have the word signify *medicinal* waters, like those, Ezek. 47.8, 9. or that would derive it from another term that signifies *an inundation,* or *a storm,* Esay 25.4. and 32.2. as noting the abundance of them: which I therefore also so leave: for of that which draws the term out to Euphrates and Nilus, see before.

*{be forsaken}* So the most of the Jewish interpreters; yet withal observing, that this is not the ordinary signification of the word; but that by change of a letter of like sound, *samec* for *teth,* it comes to signify as here it is rendered. Howbeit, the old Latin retaining the ordinary use of the word, renders the text, *can such waters be pulled out,* or, *plucked up?* but the insolency of the phrase is such, as enforces recourse to the former acception.
