Howsoever our Romanists to maintain the authority of that version, which the Council of Trent has made authentic, endeavor to strain some convenient sense out of it.

**V. 15.** *{Because my people hath forgotten me;}* Or, *That* (as chap. 2.5.) *my people hath forgotten me:* as making application of what was before spoken, ver. 14. to the practice of his people: they have so forsaken me, that they have even forgotten me too: for one may forsake a person, whom yet he does not, nor can forget. See chap. 2.13, 32. and 17.13.

*{they have burnt incense to vanity;}* Performed religious worship (as chap. 7.9. & 11.17.) to idols, chap. 2.5. & 10.2, 15. An interpreter of great note, following the old Latin, thus renders this branch, as in coherence with the former, *Because my people have forgotten me; they burn incense in vain* to me. See Esa. 1.13. & 66.3. which I leave to the judgment of others, adhering rather to the former.

*{and they have caused them to stumble in their ways from the ancient paths, to walk in paths in a way not cast up.}* Or, *while* (as the copulative is used, 1 Kin. 11.25.) *they* (that is, their false Prophets, say some; their idols, say others) *cause them to stumble in their ways,* (as the corrupt Priests are said to do the like, partly, by their corrupt doctrine, and partly, by their bad lives and evil example, Mal. 2.8.) by leaving (a defect of the verb, as the Jewish critic observes; like that, Psal. 89.29.) *the ancient paths,* (as Psal. 77.19. a word in this notion nowhere else found. Heb. *the paths of eternity;* as some, what is tending to life eternal: or, *of antiquity,* as the most; which God anciently in his Law by Moses prescribed them; and that Moses himself, Joshua, David, and other the faithful walked in before them, chap. 6.16. Deut. 4.1. & 6.1. & 28.9.) *to walk* (as Prov. 2.13.) or, *by walking* (as Lev. 18.4.) *paths,* or, *in* (as Exo. 13.18.) *paths* (the common word for such passages) *of a way not cast up;* or, where there is *no way cast up:* where there is no causey; no way fitted and accommodated for passage, the contrary whereunto is the way of God, that the godly and faithful walk in, said to be, Prov. 15.19. Esay 35.8. See on ver. 14.

**V. 16.** *{To make their land desolate, and a perpetual hissing;}* Not that this was the thing they aimed at, but that this must needs, and would undoubtedly prove the issue and effect of it. See Esa. 3.8. chap. 7.18. nor could they take a readier way to bring such evils upon their land, if they desired and should study so to do. See the like, Prov. 13.24. and 14.1. Heb. *To put their land into desolation,* (as chap. 4.7.) or, *astonishment,* (such a desolation as may make any one astonished to behold it, see the next branch) *an hissing of perpetuity:* this and desolation are joined usually together, 2 Chr. 29.8. chap. 19.8. and 25.9.

*{every one that passeth by it, shall be astonished, and wag his head.}* Or, *So that* (as Esay 58.6. and 63.13.) *every one that passeth over it shall be astonished,* (the verb from which the noun before comes) *and wag his head:* in way, either of admiration, wondering to see so strange an alteration; or of indignation and vexation, to see such spoil and havoc made of all things; or of scorn and derision, as enemies and ill-willers are in such case wont to do, Psalm 22.7. Esay 37.22. Matth. 27.39. See chap. 19.8. and 50.13.

**V. 17.** *{I will scatter them as with an East wind before the enemy;}* Or, *That* (as before) *I should scatter them;* that is, cause them to flee every way, glad to take any way to shift for themselves, and (if it be possible) to make any escapes, (as with armies routed by some fierce overpowering enemy it usually falls out) Deut. 28.25, 64. like chaff or dust before the wind, Psalm 18.43. chap. 4.11. & 15.7. the *East-wind* especially, that is wont to be most violent, and furious in those parts, carrying all away before it, Job 27.21. Psal. 48.7. Esay 27.8.

*{I will shew them the back and not the face, in the day of their calamity.}* Or, *that* (as before) *I should shew them the back* (Heb. *the neck*, or *back-part of the neck*. See on Esay 66.3. Exod. 23.27. Josh. 7.8, 12. chap. 48.39.) *and not the face in the day,* or, *time of their calamity;* as chap. 46.21. To make me turn my face away from them, and turn my back toward them, not enduring to hear or behold them, when being in distress, they shall seek unto me for succor, Esay 1.15. dealing then with them, as they now deal with me, 2 Chron. 29.6. chap. 2.27. and 32.33. Ezek. 8.16.

**V. 18.** *{Then said they, Come let us devise devices against Jeremiah;}* Heb. *And they said;* as chap. 17.27. This verse holds out to us the ground of the Prophet's ensuing complaint; to wit, the people's malicious and mischievous plotting against him for the faithful delivery of God's message.

*{let us devise devices}* Contrive some device or other to do him a mischief: so the plural is oft used; as Gen. 23.6. Judg. 12.7. Psalm 1.3. See chap. 17.5.

*{for the Law shall not perish from the Priest, nor counsel from the wise, nor the word from the Prophet.}* The Priests cannot but conceive and teach the Law aright; nor can the sages, being men of understanding, fail of giving good advice; and the word that our Prophets do so unanimously deliver, can be no other than God's Word, Mal. 2.7. Joh. 7.48, 49. but this Jeremy in his preaching dissents from them all; and must needs therefore be in the wrong; and we have no cause then to regard what he says: So fared it with Micah, 1 King. 22.13, 24. See chap. 7.4. and 5.12, 31. and 26.8. This is just like the Papists' plea, the Church, or the Pope, and his conclave (for he is virtually the Church) cannot err. But see the contrary to which they here presume of, by God himself threatened, Esay 29.14. Ezek. 7.26. *to perish,* for, *to fail,* as Psal. 142.4. chap. 49.7. Amos 2.14.

*{Come, let us smite him with the tongue;}* Let us inform, and by informing, incense the higher powers against him, chap. 20.10. & 26.11. or, as others render it, *let us smite him in the tongue;* let us cause his mouth to be stopped, that he may preach no more on this fashion, Tit. 1.11. or, as others, *for the tongue;* for his preaching in this manner, as the particle is used, Gen. 18.28. See chap. 26.11. and 38.4, 6.

*{and let us give heed unto any of his words.}* For they are not God's, but his own. So chap. 5.12, 13. & 43.2. Heb. *all his words: all* for, *any;* as Job 1.11. & 8.12.

**V. 19.** *{Give heed to me, O LORD:}* Though they heed not my words, that I deliver to them from you; yet do you vouchsafe to heed my words, wherewith I complain to you of them.

*{and hearken to the voice of them that contend with me.}* Or rather, *hear the voice of them that contend with me* (Heb. *of my contenders;* as Psal. 35.1. Esay 49.25.) *hear* their words to take notice of them, and to punish them for them; as Esa. 37.4, 17. not *hearken* to them, to grant their desires, Psal. 140.8. for the particle is here redundant and vacant, as oft elsewhere, Gen. 29.13. 1 Sam. 10.4. Job 8.8. Esay 37.22. chap. 40.2.

**V. 20.** *{Shall evil be recompensed for good?}* Or, *Should;* as chap. 16.20. Should men be so wicked and so maliciously minded, as to plot evil against, and seek to mischief those, that desire and endeavor nothing but, or more than, their good? The common complaint and lot of God's Prophets and people, 1 Sam. 24.17. Psalm 35.12. and 109.5.

*{for they have digged a pit for my soul;}* Or, *that* (as before ver. 15.) *they should dig a pit for my soul?* that they should seek to destroy me, and to take my life away from me, who have by all means that I could endeavored to do them good: *my soul,* for, *me;* or, *my life;* as Psalm 35.7. and 56.6. and there is in the words a speech borrowed from the practice of those that dig pits, or pitfalls, to take wild beasts, or to catch birds in. So Psalm 9.15. & 35.7. & 94.13. Prov. 16.27. and 26.27. Eccl. 10.8. Ezek. 19.4, 8. So ver. 22.

*{remember that I stood before thee to speak good for them, and to turn away thy wrath from them.}* He appeals to God himself, as able to testify, how he had from time to time labored with him, to pacify his wrath incensed against them, and to obtain favor and mercy for them. So chap. 15.15. & 17.16. Heb. *remember my standing before thee.* See chap. 15.1.

*{to speak good for them}* See chap. 14.11.

*{to turn away thy wrath}* As Psal. 106.23.

**V. 21.** *{Wherefore deliver up their children to the famine;}* Of these & the like imprecations, see chap. 11.20. & 15.15. & 17.18. Heb. *Give* (as chap. 34.18.) *their sons* (including both sexes, as afterward) *to the famine;* that which did befall this people, Lam. 1.11, 12. See Psalm 109.10.

*{and pour out their blood by the force of the sword:}* Heb. *pour them out by the hands of the sword.* See the like defect, Ezek. 35.5. and the like phrase also, Psalm 63.10. This seems spoken of the persons themselves, or the parents; as the former of the children: let that befall them, that they intend against me, ver. 20, 23. chap. 11.22.

*{and let their wives be bereaved of their children, and be widows, and let their men be put to death.}* Or, *that* (as chap. 14.19.) *their wives may be left childless, and widows, their husbands* (as chap. 44.19.) *being taken away by death.* Heb. *slain of death;* as, *slain of the sword,* and, *of hunger,* chap. 14.18. Lam. 4.9. slain by one means or other, enough to make their wives widows. Howbeit, by *death* here, some of the Rabbines not amiss understand some one particular kind of it, the *pestilence;* as chap. 15.2. where it is expressly distinguished from the *famine,* and the *sword:* the like whereunto, see also Rev. 6.8. So it may be rendered, their husbands being taken *away by the pestilence;* as were multitudes of them no doubt in the siege of the city, chap. 14.12. & 21.6.

*{let their young men be slain by the sword in battle.}* The usual lot of such in war, because fittest for service in the field; whence the Greek proverb, *Young men for arms, and old men for advice;* and the speech of the Heathen king, that *Peace was to be preferred before War, because in times of war parents bury their children; children their parents, in times of peace:* the old, the young in the one; the young, the old in the other; a thing more agreeable to the course of nature. So 2 King. 8.12. 2 Chr. 36.17. chap. 11.22. Heb. *smitten of the sword:* *to smite,* for, *to slay;* as Num. 25.14. chap. 21.6. & 40.14, 15. the form of speech, as before.

**V. 22.** *{Let a cry be heard from their houses, when thou shalt bring a troop suddenly upon them.}* Such an outcry as people are wont to make, when military persons break in upon them, to plunder all with them, and so surprise or destroy them, chap. 20.16. So should it be with them, when the troops of the Chaldeans, and their complices, should surprise and sack their dwellings, 2 Kin. 24.2.

*{for}* Or, *because;* as chap. 10.21.

*{they have digged a pit for me}* As ver. 20. Psal. 57.6.

*{and hid snares for my feet.}* A borrowed speech, as the former, from the practice of those that set gins, or snares, to catch beasts or fowl with. So Psalm 35.7, 8. & 64.5. & 141.9. & 142.3. chap. 5.6.

**V. 23.** *{Yet LORD thou knowest all their counsel against me to slay me.}* *Yet* (Heb. *And;* but so also, chap. 14.9, 11. and then it must have reference to ver. 20. though I have sought their good, yet you know they seek my life) or *yea* (as Esay 44.15. & 59.15. for it seems to be here rather in an affirmative, than in a discretive notion) *thou Lord.* (so the words lie in the text; as Psal. 55.23.) *knowest all their consultations,* or *devices,* (ver. 18. See Esay 7.5. & 14.24, 25.) *against me to slay me.* Heb. *for death:* to destroy, and make me away, by one means or other; as if he had said, this is no bare suspicion, or groundless surmise of mine own, concerning their mischievous plots and projects against me, but that which the Lord himself is privy to, and knows to be true. See chap. 11.18, 19.

*{forgive not their iniquity, neither blot out their sin from thy sight;}* See the like imprecations, Neh. 4.4, 5. Psal. 59.5. & 109.14, 15. a form of speech borrowed from those that keep debt-books, to demand and require their debts by, which they continue undefaced, until they be paid, or they please to discharge the debtors of them, and do then either blot them out, or cross the book. See Psal. 51.1. Esay 43.25.

*{but let them be overthrown before thee;}* Heb. *and* (as Esa. 29.13.) *let them be made to stumble;* as ver. 15. See chap. 6.15. & 8.12. *before thee;* when you pursue them with your wrath. See Psal. 35.6. & 83.15.

*{deal thus with them in the time of thine anger.}* Heb. *in the time of thine anger do to them;* as Psal. 83.9. the particle *thus,* is wanting, and may well be supplied; as that, or the like, ver. 8.

## CHAPTER 19

**Verse 1.** *{Thus saith the LORD,}* As chap. 17.5, 21. or, *Thus said the Lord;* to wit, sometime to me, as chap. 17.19. The present prophecy contains a threatening of destruction to the Jewish state, and a confounding of all those courses, whereby they should endeavor to avert or avoid it, resembled by the breaking of an earthen vessel in Tophet, enjoined by God, and effected by the Prophet, as for their idolatry in general, so more specially for the same in that place committed.

*{Go and get a potters earthen bottle}* Heb. *Going,* or, *Go, and thou shalt buy,* or *get* (as chap. 13.1.) *a bottle of the framer of earthen stuff;* an earthen bottle of the potter's framing, such an one as is easily broken, Psal. 2.9. Esay 30.19. Howbeit, the Jewish critics suggest unto us another syntax of the place, rendering the text, *Go and get,* or *buy, of,* or from, *the framer of earthen stuff, a bottle,* or from the *potter an earthen bottle:* a defect, say they, of the particle *of,* or *from;* as the like, 2 Sam. 23.24. *Dodo Bethlehem,* for, *Dodo of,* or from *Bethlehem:* and this is much more probable, than that which the old Latin translator exhibits, who having jumbled together the two branches of the verse, renders the words, *Go and take an earthen bottle from the Elders of the people, and of the Priests;* and would consequently have this earthen pot, or bottle, not to have been bought or brought by Jeremy from the potter, but to have been demanded of, and received from, those ancients or elders of the people, or the priests.

*{a bottle}* Heb. *bakbuk:* a word nowhere found in Scripture, but here, and 1 King. 14.3. and it is said by the Jewish commenter here, to signify a vessel with a big belly, but narrow mouth or neck: so called from the *bubbling* sound that it makes, when it is dipped in the water, or liquor, either poured forth, or drunk out of it; and he adds withal, that the same is both in the Greek, and other languages, termed *bocal;* wherein howsoever a learned writer control him, both affirming, that no such term as that is found in Greek, or that comes anything near it, save *bikos,* which the Greek version here makes use of, and that the vessel in Spain and Italy, so termed, is not of that making: Yet herein, for the former, he bewrays his own ignorance; for Athenæus in his *Supper-sophisters,* l. 11. out of ancient Greek authors mentions it, adding withal, that it was at Alexandria much used, and made sometime curiously, with images upon it, of glass. And Nicephorus also in his *Ecclesiastical Story,* l. 8. c. 5. tells of a Presbyter at Alexandria, who was commonly called *Baucalis,* in allusion to the vessel so termed, which he says was such an earthen vessel, as the Jewish critic here describes; and for the same reason so termed, to wit, in regard of the *bubbling,* or *guggling* sound that it made, either in taking in of liquor, or in the voiding of it again: whereof Alexander the Greek-questionist, (or, as some will have it, Trallian) renders a reason in his problems, lib. 1. quest. 94. and for the latter exception, that the pot, or *vessel,* in those places now commonly so called, was of another fashion than is here described: whereunto might be added, that such a narrow-necked vessel is not so fit to put or carry *honey* in; of which use of this *bakbuk,* see 1 King. 14.3. the answer is not difficult, that the same name may comprehend vessels of divers sorts, and differing in fashion, though at first appropriated unto some one kind of them; as also that names borrowed from foreign languages may, in time, much alter from that notion and use of them, which in their native at first they had: for so we use the term *a vial;* for some small glass only of such a fashion as has here been mentioned; albeit the word *phiala,* from whence we have it, did both with the Greeks and Latins, from whom we received it, signify *a drinking cup;* as by the frequent use of authors, in either language, appears. See Rev. 15.7. with chap. 14.10. And also again the Hebrew *sephel,* from which their *phiala* is not amiss deemed to have descended, did with the Jews signify, neither *a vial,* as with us, or *a drinking cup,* as with them; but *a dish* for butter, Judg. 5.25. or *a bowl* to hold water, Judg. 6.37. But howsoever it were for the shape or fashion of it, that an earthen vessel it was, appears by the word following, whereof see Esa. 45.9. Nor can I concur with that learned commenter here, who to comply with the vicious Latin version, would have it to have been one of those pots, wherein by way of balloting (as the ancient both Greeks and Romans, and some states also at this day, so the Jews also, and those ancients from whom Jeremy had it) in their places of judicature, when they sat on the bench, used to give and gather up their votes. But of the sandy ground of that conceit, see before.

*{and take of the ancients of the people, and of the ancients of the Priests.}* Some of the elders of either sort, (for of both these the Jewish consistory consisted, 2 Chr. 19.8. Act. 4.5, 6, 23.) to go along with you, that they may be eyewitnesses of what you do, and take special notice of what thereupon you say. See somewhat the like, Esay 8.2.

**V. 2.** *{And go forth unto the valley of the son of Hinnom}* A valley near to Jerusalem: whereof see on Esay 30.33. and chap. 7.31.

*{which is by the entry of the East gate;}* What gate this was, or why so called, is not so certain. Some affirm it to have been *the dung-gate,* mentioned, Neh. 2.13. & 3.12. & 12.31. So the Chaldee, and after him, those of the Rabbines, upon this place: one of whom tells us, that this gate had seven several names; and that it is here called the *Sun gate,* from a word that signifies *the Sun,* Judg. 8.13. & 14.18. Job 9.7. because it looked Eastward toward the sunrising, whence some also would have it to be *the East-gate,* mentioned, Neh. 3.29. Others render it, *the Pot-sherd-gate;* as the word is used, Job 2.8. or, *the Earthen-vessel-gate;* as ver. 1. so the old Latin renders it: and it is so called, say some, in part concurring with the former; because together with the filth of the city, and the Temple, the broken potsherds of earthen vessels used in the Temple, or in other places thereabout, used to be there cast out: or, say others, with more probability, because the potters' fields, whence they had the clay that they wrought with, and their workhouses wherein they wrought it, being not far distant from thence, the ways thereabout could not want store of that, in the drying and making of it up much of course necessarily miscarrying. See chap. 18.1, 2. I suppose therefore, that it is not likely to have been either *the dung-gate,* which stood farther out of the way; nor yet *the East-gate,* if from the *Sun* it be so termed; but *the South-gate* rather, declining somewhat from the east side of the city, so called, because the sun lay most upon it, in regard whereof it was the more useful to the potters, for the drying and hardening of their ware. And again, by it was the way to the valley of Hinnom, which lay Southward from Jerusalem, Josh. 15.8. See Esay 16.7.

*{and proclaim there the words that I shall tell thee}* Heb. *and thou shalt proclaim* (as ver. 1. *thou shalt get,* or *buy*) to wit, in the presence of those ancients, v. 2.

*{there}* In that place, where such horrible abominations are committed, v. 4.

*{I shall tell thee.}* When you come thither; as chap. 18.2. whereby it appears that God's messages many times were not revealed to the Prophets, before the very instant of time, wherein they were to deliver them.

**V. 3.** *{And say,}* Or, *Then say;* as chap. 18.18. Heb. *thou shalt say;* and so also, ver. 11.

*{Hear the word of the LORD, O Kings of Judah, and inhabitants of Jerusalem:}* He speaks to them as present, in the hearing of those that might relate them unto them; and yet not unlikely but many of the people would for novelty flock after them, seeing the Prophet with those ancients going solemnly that way out of the city, and taking from the potter such a vessel to carry along with him. So chap. 17.20.

*{Kings}* That is, King and Queen-mother, say some, chap. 13.18. or, as others, King and his Council, or Princes and Rulers. See chap. 17.20.

*{Thus saith the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel}* He that is able to do whatsoever he menaces, and will do it, just cause being given him, even to those, that call him their God, and profess to be his Israel, Esa. 48.1. So chap. 7.21.

*{Behold I will bring evil upon this place,}* Heb. *Behold I am bringing evil* (as chap. 6.10. & 11.11.) *upon this place:* not that particular place where the Prophet stood, but upon the neighbor-city, upon the state of Judah and Jerusalem.

*{the which whosoever heareth his ears shall tingle.}* So hideous, that whosoever, not sees it, but hears of it, hears only the bare report of it, shall have his ears stricken with horror and astonishment of it. So 1 Sam. 3.11. 2 King. 21.12. he shall not easily get his ears rid of it again, Job 15.21.

**V. 4.** *{Because they have forsaken me}* Chap. 16.11.

*{and estranged this place}* Or, *have strangely abused;* as the word seems to be taken, Deut. 32.27. So abused this city contrary to what should have been practiced in it, and so polluted and profaned it, that I can no longer own it. See Esa. 1.4, 11, 12. Psal. 58.3. Eph. 4.18. Col. 1.21.

*{and burnt incense to other gods, whom neither they, nor their fathers, have known, nor the Kings of Judah;}* Or, *while they burn incense,* (so the copulative is used, 1 Kin. 11.25.) or, *in that they have burnt incense,* (as Esa. 37.24.) to idols, to strange gods, such as neither they, nor their ancestors, kings or others, had ever any experimental knowledge or proof of, for their good, as from time to time, they had of him, whom for these vanities they leave. See Deut. 32.17. Judg. 5.8. chap. 1.16. & 44.3.

*{and have filled this place with the blood of innocents.}* Both the city of Jerusalem by oppression and murder, 1 Kin. 21.16. & 24.4. See chap. 7.6. & 22.3. and this place in particular where we now are, by sacrificing of poor infants to their abominable idols, Psal. 106.37, 38. See v. 5. but the former principally here intended, as also, chap. 2.34. for of the latter apart afterward, ver. 5.

**V. 5.** *{They have built also the high places of Baal to burn their sons with fire for burnt offerings unto Baal, which I commanded not, nor spake it, neither came it into my mind.}* Heb. *And have built,* which may well be here retained. See chap. 7.31. & 32.35. 2 Kin. 23.10. What is here said *to Baal,* is in these two latter places said *to Moloch:* but *Baal* and *Moloch,* were two terms very generally and promiscuously used of their idols; the one signifying *a Lord,* or *Owner;* the other *a King;* whence also *Baalim* oft, in the plural number. See chap. 2.23. & 7.9.

**V. 6.** *{Therefore behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that this place shall no more be called Tophet, nor the valley of the son of Hinnom, but the valley of slaughter.}* See chap. 7.32.

**V. 7.** *{And I will make void the counsel of Judah and Jerusalem in this place,}* *In this place,* is in Jerusalem especially, as before, ver. 4. though some would have it spoken by the pointing to the king's palace, situate not far from thence, on the south side of the city: but that may be deemed somewhat over-curious. The plain meaning is, I will frustrate all your plots and projects, (as chap. 18.23.) whereby you think to escape, and to secure yourselves, (see Esa. 30.13. & 31.1, 3. chap. 37.7, 8.) and make them as vain and empty as this earthen bottle is: for unto the name thereof in this word he alludes, which some therefore would have to be so named, not from the sound it makes in filling or emptying, but from the term of emptying only, here used: but that is not necessary; for in Scripture allusion is oft made to the vicinity of sound in some term, from which yet the word never had its original. So Mic. 1.10, 14.

*{and I will cause them to fall by the sword before their enemies,}* *To fall,* for, *to be foiled,* or, *to be slain,* or, *to fall down,* being slain: as 1 Sam. 4.10. & 31.1. chap. 20.4. Ezek. 6.4.

*{and by the hands of them that seek their lives:}* Heb. *their souls;* as chap. 4.30. & 18.20. So v. 9.

*{and their carcasses will I give to be meat for the fowls of heaven, and the beasts of the field.}* See chap. 7.33. & 16.4.

**V. 8.** *{And I will make this city desolate, and an hissing; every one that passeth thereby shall be astonished and hiss, because of all the plagues thereof.}* Heb. *strokes thereof;* as Deut. 28.59. & 29.22. See the same before, chap. 18.16.

**V. 9.** *{And I will cause them to eat the flesh of their sons, and the flesh of their daughters, and they shall eat every one the flesh of his friend, in the siege and straitness, wherewith their enemies and they that seek their lives shall straiten them.}* Before threatened, Lev. 26.29. Deut. 28.23. and in the siege of the city accomplished, Lam. 4.10.

*{every one the flesh of his friend}* Or, *neighbour;* they shall feed one upon another, (as chap. 46.16.) without regard had to any bonds of vicinity or amity. See Esay 9.20.

*{———straiten them.}* Or, *distress them.* See Esay 29.2.

**V. 10.** *{Then shalt thou break the bottle;}* Or, *Then* (Heb. *And,* as chap. 18.18.) *break* (as ver. 1. *get,* or, *buy*) *the bottle:* which he had bought or took along with him; thereby, as by a visible type, representing and consigning what before he had said, that it might make a deeper impression in the minds of those that behold it.

*{in the sight of them that go with thee.}* See ver. 1. Heb. *to the eyes of them:* as chap. 28.1, 5, 11.

**V. 11.** *{And shalt say unto them;}* Or, *And say unto them;* as ver. 3.

*{Thus saith the LORD of Hosts; Even so will I break this people, and this city, as one breaketh a potters vessel, that cannot be made whole again;}* Before, he compared this people and state to moist and soft clay, which though it miscarry in the framing, yet may, with no great ado, be made up again, in some other fashion, to the mind of the maker, chap. 18.4, 6. Now, to an earthen vessel, dried and hardened, which being broken in pieces, cannot be made up, and set together again. So Esa. 30.14. and somewhat the like, chap. 48.12.

*{as one breaketh a potters vessel}* Or, *as a potters vessel is broken;* as chap. 16.6.

*{made whole}* Heb. *cured.* as chap. 15.18. Deut. 28.27, 35.

*{and they shall bury them in Tophet till there be no place else to bury.}* Or rather, *they shall bury in Tophet* (for *them* is not in the text) *for want of room to bury* elsewhere. See chap. 7.32.

**V. 12.** *{Thus will I do unto this place, saith the LORD, and to the Inhabitants thereof,}* *this place;* this city, ver. 11.

*{and even make their city as Tophet}* Where you had wont to slaughter and sacrifice your children, ver. 5. I will fill the whole city with the carcasses of slaughtered ones, as you filled it before with innocent blood, 2 King. 21.16. & 24.4. chap. 32.29. so that it shall be all like another Tophet, ver. 13. not unlike that Isa. 29.2. that the whole city should be as another *Ariel.* See there. Heb. *and* (or *even,* as chap. 15.13.) *to give* (for *to make:* as chap. 25.18. Dan. 12.11.) *this city,* (so is the text) *as Tophet.*

**V. 13.** *{And the houses of Jerusalem, and the houses of the Kings of Judah shall be defiled as the place of Tophet;}* The houses and palaces being filled also as well as the streets, with abundance of dead corpses, lying without sepulture in them, for want either of persons or place to bury them. See of Josias his defiling Tophet, 2 King. 23.10. Howbeit, some read the words, *the houses of Jerusalem, and of the Kings of Judah, which are defiled,* (to wit, with those abominations exercised in them, and upon them, hereafter mentioned) *shall be as Tophet;* and the words may very well bear it: *Kings,* as before, ver. 3.

*{because of all the houses upon whose roofs they have burnt incense unto the host of heaven, and have poured out drink offerings unto other gods}* Or rather *with all the houses* (so is the particle frequently used Ezra. 1.5. & 2.63. Neh. 7.65.) *upon whose roofs;* for their houses being flat-roofed, Deut. 22.8. they used on the tops of them to serve their idols, & to sacrifice to them, to the celestial bodies especially, as being in regard of the height of their houses nearer there to them, and having them more conspicuous there to their eye. See 2 King. 23.12. Isa. 65.3. chap. 32.29. Zeph. 1.5.

**V. 14.** *{Then came Jeremiah from Tophet, whither the LORD had sent him to prophesy, and he stood in the Court of the Lords house, and said to all the people;}* Heb. *And;* as ver. 10. Having dispatched his errand by God enjoined him at Tophet, he returns to the Temple, from whence in likelihood he took those ancients along with him, ver. 1. and there in the court, whereunto the people had access as well as the priests, 2 Chr. 23. he delivered in their hearing the sum of that which at Tophet had before denounced.

**V. 15.** *{Thus saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel;}* See the same proem, ver. 3.

*{Behold, I will bring upon this city, and upon all her Towns, all the evil that I have pronounced against it,}* Heb. *Behold I am bringing* (as ver. 3.) *unto* (or *upon;* as chap. 4.3. & 11.7.) *this city, and upon her cities,* (the inferior cities, and lesser towns belonging to Jerusalem as the mother-city. See chap. 15.8. & 34.1.) *all the evil that I have spoken against it,* or *concerning it;* as chap. 18.7, 9.

*{because they have hardened their necks,}* Their extreme obstinacy the main cause of their ruin. See chap. 7.26. and 17.23.

*{that they might not hear my words.}* That is, yield obedience thereunto, Deut. 6.3. & 28.1. Psal. 81.11. Zach. 7.12.

## CHAPTER 20

**Verse 1.** *{Now Pashur, &c.}* This chapter has a manifest dependence upon the former, containing a relation of the evil usage of Jeremy by one of the principal priests, for his plain and faithful delivery of God's message before-mentioned, ver. 1, 6. together with a grievous complaint made to God by the Prophet; wherein a strange mixture of contrary affections and passions is manifested; not free from some tang and taint of human frailty, ver. 7, 18.

*{Now Pashur the son of Immer the Priest, who was also chief Governor in the house of the LORD, heard that Jeremiah prophesied these things,}* Or, *Now when Pashur heard Jeremy prophesying these things; Pashur smote Jeremy,* &c. This syntax is very common, chap. 2.7, 10. & 5.7. & 6.9, 10.

*{Pashur}* Heb. *Pashhur,* or *Pashchur:* as *Ahaz,* or *Achaz.* See Isaiah 1.1.

*{the son of Immer}* Not that this Immer was Pashur's immediate parent, but his progenitor; this Pashur being a priest of the sixteenth course, whereof Immer at first constitution of them was chief head, 1 Chr. 24.14. and this seems added to distinguish this *Pashur* from one of the same name, that was of another course, chap. 21.1.

*{who was also chief Governor in the house of the LORD.}* Heb. *and he,* for, *who;* as chap. 15.19. & 17.7. unless we read it by way of parenthesis, (*now he was principal ruler in the house of the Lord*) for *also* is not in the text. As for the style here given him, in the original they are two several substantives, whereof the one signifies *a prefect,* (rendered *an officer,* chap. 29.26. and *an overseer,* Neh. 11.9, 14, 22.) the other *a Prince,* or *Ruler,* used of Temple-officers, 1 Chro. 9.20. & 26.24. 2 Chr. 31.12. the head it may be he was of that course whereunto he belonged, the priests whereof were then in their course attending the Temple-service: or as some suppose, the *second,* next under the high priest; who upon any occasional disability betiding the high priest, was to perform offices in his place, Numb. 3.32. 2 King. 25.18. chap. 52.24. called, say they, the *principal;* because divers other rulers were under this *second,* 2 Chr. 35.8. chap. 35.4. Others again suppose him to have been the *Captain of the Temple;* who had power to apprehend such as committed any disorder in the Temple, Act. 4.1. See chap. 29.26. the thing, being uncertain, I shall leave to the consideration of the learned. I concur with the first; for they that would have this Pashur to be high priest, are easily answered; since, that besides that he was one of the 24. courses, whereas the high priest was of none (that which proves Zachary also not to have been high priest, as the ancients most of them imagined, Luk. 1.5.) in the continued list of the high priests, from Aaron to past his time, we find none such mentioned, 1 Chr. 6.4, 15.

*{heard that Jeremiah prophesied these things.}* Or rather, *heard Jeremiah prophesying these things;* for so the words run in the text: he heard not of it by information from some other; but he himself heard him in the Temple delivering this prophecy. Heb. *these words,* for *these things;* as chap. 11.6. and 16.10.

**V. 2.** *{Then Pashur smote Jeremiah the Prophet}* Or, *when Pashur heard Jeremiah the Prophet* thus *prophesying, he smote him;* (the nouns for pronouns; as Isa. 64.2. chap. 4.4. 2 Tim. 1.18.) to wit, in likelihood with his hand, or fist, as Zedekiah smote Micaiah, 1 King. 22.24. and as they our Savior, Matth. 26.67. And that, as may seem, interrupting him, while he was yet speaking, so that he could not proceed. Thus this presumptuous priest, for ought we find, was the first that offered such an affront unto the Prophet, as none either of the greater or more powerful, or the meaner and ruder sort had hitherto done. Nor can I agree to that learned annotator, who would have it to import no more than that he *apprehended* him, or laid hands on him; because it is said, Ezek. 33.21. & 40.1. *the city is smitten,* for *the city is taken:* for even there also is more than so implied; not *taken* barely, but *stormed,* or *taken by storming:* besides, that *apprehending,* or *attaching* and *smiting,* are two distinct things, and diversely expressed, chap. 37.14, 15.

*{and put him in the stocks}* Heb. *gave him.* as Gen. 39.20. chap. 37.15. but for the word following, there is no small doubt concerning the right signification of it: nor does the original of it afford us any sure ground to build on therein: it signifies properly *subversion,* or *turning upside downward,* Isa. 1.7. and 13.19. chap. 49.18. and 50.40. our translators are not constant to themselves about it: they render it here *stocks,* elsewhere *prison,* chap. 29.26. and 2 Chr. 16.10. where the word *house,* or *place* is joined with it: as with the like, 1 Kin. 22.27. 2 King. 17.4. And for the Jewish Doctors, some of them also so take it: but others then tell us that it was a wooden engine, that they used to fasten men with in the prison; and some of these, that it was an engine made of two boards, wherein they were held fast by the neck; such as our pillory. Whereunto also some add, that it had three holes in it, one for the neck, and two for the hands. Others, that it was such an one wherein they held men fast by the legs, which in foreign languages, say they, is called *cippus:* from whence the Chaldee swerves very little; (though some give the word used by him another notation) and so should it be the same with our *stocks,* such as Job speaks of, Job 13.27. (but there is another word there) and such as Paul and Silas were laid in, Act. 16.24. Some of the Greek versions render it in general, *an engine of torture.* Among this variety to deliver mine opinion; I suppose it rather to signify the *prison-house,* than any engine for surer custody, or torture therein used; to which purpose, see further on chap. 29.26.

*{that were in the high gate of Benjamin, which was by the house of the LORD.}* Or, *that was;* if the word be taken for a prison: which from hence also it may seem to be; because it is said to have been situate *in the high-gate,* or *upper-gate of Benjamin,* where it is more probable that a prison was, than such an engine for any such use without it: But about this *upper gate of Benjamin,* there is again some question, whether it were one of the gates of the Temple, or one of the gates of the city. The Rabbines, and those that therein follow them, go the former way, and the words of the text seem so to carry it, (for that is the most general notion of the particle here used) *in the house of the Lord:* not the Temple itself alone, but the courts also and other buildings about them, coming within the name of God's house. See chap. 7.2, 10, 11. Matth. 21.12, 13. Joh. 2.14, 16. and 10.23, 24. and this gate, say they, is called *the gate of Benjamin,* because it stood on that side of the Temple that belonged to the tribe of Benjamin; the city of Jerusalem, and the ground also whereon the Temple was built, being part of it within the lot of Benjamin, and part within the lines of Judah. That which seems true indeed concerning the city, Josh. 15.63. compared with Judg. 1.21. but for the other concerning the Temple, though a learned late writer of ours has endeavored by a line drawn from east to west through, or outright to an hair, assigning just the one half of it, to wit, the north side to Benjamin, and the other precise half of it on the south side to Judah; yet in the sacred records does no such thing appear; nor is ought produced for the proof thereof, save some places out of Jacob's & Moses his blessing of Benjamin, Gen. 49.27. & Deut. 33.12. by the Chaldee Paraphrast, & some Talmudists frivolously forced that way: which Talmudists also cut us out the Temple another way than this learned man does, assigning to Judah the Eastern part unto the altar of burnt-offerings, and to Benjamin thence the Western part; grounding likewise this their division on the same places as before abused. But taking for granted, that the Temple stood part of it within Benjamin's lot, the fore-mentioned interpreters further add, that on the Benjamin-side of the Temple there were two gates, an upper and a lower; that this was *the upper,* so called, not in regard of the loftier structure of it; but in regard of the situation of it, because it stood nearer to the innermost part of the Temple, the Holy of Holies: and that in this gate there was a prison, to commit such unto, of the priests or Levites especially, as did carry themselves amiss in the Temple. Thus they. But others, whom our version follows, suppose this *gate* to be one of the gates of the city. Howbeit, among these also I find some diversity. For some would have it to be a gate within the city. So a learned interpreter, affirming it to be a gate in the wall of the city, that divided Judah's part of the city from Benjamin's part of it, called therefore *the gate of Benjamin;* because by it they passed out of Judah, into Benjamin's quarter. But others, and so the most of this way, conceive it to have been a gate situate in the outer wall; so called, because it looked toward the lot and land of that tribe: (as *the Gate of Ephraim,* 2 King. 14.23. that opened that way) and it may well be also that it was situate on that part of the city wherein that tribe had interest, called either *the high-gate,* as some, for the stateliness of it, (as 2 Chr. 23.20.) or, as others, *the upper-gate,* (as, *the utter pool,* Esay 7.3.) to distinguish it from another that stood lower then it on the same side: and this the rather they are induced to admit, because they find elsewhere *the gate of Benjamin,* so used and taken, for one of the gates of the city, as twice in this prophecy, chap. 37.12. & 31.7. and Zach. 14.10. but nowhere any of the Temple-gates so termed: all the difficulty here is in the last clause, wherein of this gate it is said, that it was *in the house of the Lord:* which to remove, our version renders it, *by the house of the Lord:* and this version is herein well justifiable; for the particle here used does oft import, not the comprehension of the thing spoken of in the place mentioned, but the vicinity of it thereunto. So Num. 33.37. *they pitched in* (that is, *by,* or *near to*) *mount Hor.* See there ver. 38. and, *Joshouah stood, in* (for, *by;* or *near to,*) *Jericho.* Josh. 5.13. So also Josh. 24.25, 26. Joshua is said to have *made a covenant* between God and the people, *in Sechem,* setting up *a stone* for a monument thereof, *under an oak,* that stood *in,* or *by the Sanctuary of the Lord;* that is, *near to Sechem,* where that *oak stood,* Gen. 35.4. not in the Sanctuary, but near unto it: as also in the same chapter, ver. 32. *Josephs bones* are said to have been *buried in Sechem;* that is also, *near unto* it. Yea, so chap. 13.5. *I hid the girdle in Euphrates;* that is, *by it, near unto* it, in the cleft of a rock: and chap. 32.7. *my field in Anathoth,* for, *beside* it, or, *near unto* it. And it is probable enough, that this gate of Benjamin was not far from the Temple. See further on chap. 37.12.

**V. 3.** *{And it came to pass on the morrow, that Pashur brought forth Jeremiah out of the stocks; Then said Jeremiah unto him;}* Or, *And so it was* (as chap. 3.9.) *on the morrow, when Pashur brought Jeremiah out of the prison, that Jeremiah said unto him.* Of the syntax, see on ver. 1. Of the word *prison,* on ver. 2.

*{on the morrow Pashur brought forth Jeremiah}* Not to bring him to some public hearing, as they did the Apostles, whom they had overnight clapped up in prison, Act. 4.3, 7. but to let him go again, whether admonished so to do by some other more considerate than himself, or imagining this restraint and disgraceful usage of him in public would stop his mouth for time to come, or for what other reason thereunto moving him, uncertain. But howsoever it was in this regard, this contumelious carriage toward the Prophet, no more daunted him, or damped his spirits, than Zedekiah's like presumptuous demeanor did Micaiah; for at his parting with him, the Prophet freely delivers him the like message here, that Micaiah did to Zedekiah there, 1 King. 22.25. confirming what he tells him concerning himself, by a new name, and that such an one, as not man, but God should give him; (see somewhat of the like kind in Paul to Ananias, Act. 23.3, 4.) and withal renews again his former denunciations against the whole land and the city, ver. 4, 5.

*{The LORD hath not called thy name Pashur, but Magor-missabib.}* Together with the change of men's conditions are their names oftentimes altered; and names are imposed oft to intimate as much: So was *Abrams* name changed to *Abraham;* Sarai's to *Sarah,* Gen. 17.5, 15. *Jacobs* to *Israel,* Gen. 32.28. *Josephs* by Pharaoh to *Zaphnath-Paaneah,* Gen. 41.45. and hence Naomi at her return out of Moab, *Call me not Naomi, but call me Marah,* Ruth 1.20. and such or such a name is God said to impose on a person, not intending or importing simply that in ordinary compellation or communication, he should be commonly so called or styled; but thereby intimating & assuring, that such should be the condition and state of that party, as that he might well deserve such a name, and might justly so be styled. See hereof on Esay 7. & 14. & 9.6. & 62.4. chap. 23.6. & 33.16. In like manner here the Prophet tells this proud & godless priest, that God, instead of *Pashur,* had named him *Magor-missabib;* thereby to assure him, that so dreadful should his state and condition ere long be, that in regard thereof he should justly bear that name, and have it on good ground commonly given him by others. What the notation or signification of his native name *Pashur,* or *Pashchur,* was, is uncertain: nor is it greatly material. Some make it a compound, consisting of two terms, whereof the one signifies *a growing up,* Mal. 4.2. the other *a noble,* Eccl. 10.17. & so would have it to import *a growing up Prince,* or *Noble.* Others, of a word used commonly for *the mouth;* and another that signifies *black;* whereof Nilus has its name *Shichor,* chap. 2.18. And others, of a word that signifies *to diffuse,* Lev. 13.5, 7. And another that imports *paleness,* Esay 29.22. as signifying one that by his authority and stern carriage, makes men look pale; which the rather pleases the author of it, because it sorts well with the name now given him; as if it were said, he that is now *Pashchur,* one that by his sternness makes men pale for fear on every side, shall hereafter become *Magor-missabib,* one beset with terrors on every side himself. But these far-fetched and forced notations are of little weight, and of less need or use here. Whatsoever it were that that term did or might import, God here gives him another name, which to that needs have no relation; for the signification thereof is well enough known, and it is word for word, *Terror round about,* or *Fear on every side;* and it may well be deemed by the frequent use of it, to have been a proverbial form of speech, used of persons in extreme distress, so beset with difficulties and dangers, that they are at their wits' end, not knowing which way to escape or to shift for themselves. See Psal. 31.13. chap. 6.25. & 49.5. & 46.29. Lam. 2.22.

*{hath called thy name}* Or, *calleth thy name;* that is, *calleth thee:* as *call his name,* that is, *call him,* Isa. 8.3.

**V. 4.** *{For thus saith the LORD,}* He that gives you this name, (whereof the reason here follows) and will make it good upon you.

*{Behold, I will make thee be a terror to thyself, and to all thy friends}* Heb. *I am giving thee for a terror: giving,* as *bringing,* chap. 19.19. *to give for a terror,* for *to make* one matter *of terror:* as *to give for an astonishment,* for *to make* one matter *of astonishment,* chap. 25.18. I will inflict such evils upon you, as shall affright not you alone, but all those that have any special relation to you, or interest in you, Psal. 31.31. or as some render it, *I will expose thee to terror, thee and thy friends.* I will surround and environ both you and them with frights and fears; according to which version, the particle here used should be vacant and redundant; as chap. 18.19. & 40.2. or as others again, *I will put a terror into thee, into thee and thy friends:* *thee* unto *a terror;* by a trajection, for *a terror into thee:* as *they cast the city into fire,* for *they set on fire the city,* Josh. 1.8. But the former seems the more familiar, and the better.

*{and they shall fall by the sword of their enemies, and thine eyes shall behold it;}* Or, *and* (as chap. 17.4.) *in thy sight.* Heb. *and thine eyes seeing;* as Deut. 28.32. Your friends, on whom at present you rely, and to whose support, it may be, trusting, you now carry yourself so presumptuously, shall be slain (as chap. 19.7.) and so taken from you by the enemy, that you shall be deprived of all hope of relief or succor from them; and this, to enhance your grief, and augment your terror, shall be done in your presence, while you stand by looking on, neither able to afford any help unto them, nor to expect any from them. See the like aggravations, Deut. 28.29, 34. 1 Sam. 2.33. and the like judgment executed on King Zedekiah himself, chap. 39.6, 7.

*{and I will give all Judah into the hand of the King of Babylon, and he shall carry them captive into Babylon, and shall slay them with the sword.}* I will deliver the whole country and people of it into Nebuchadnezzar's power, to dispose, either for captivity, or for slaughter at his pleasure, who shall also accordingly slay some, and enslave others of them, chap. 25.9. & 29.6, 9. *hand* for *power,* as chap. 27.6. Psal. 22.20. & 49.15. So also ver. 5.

*{and shall slay}* *And* for *or;* as chap. 18.7. Heb. *smite;* as chap. 18.21.

**V. 5.** *{Moreover I will deliver all the strength of this city, and all the labour thereof, and all the precious things thereof, and all the treasures of the Kings of Judah will I give into the hand of their enemies, which shall spoil them, and take them, and carry them to Babylon.}* Or, *I will also deliver,* or *give up,* Heb. *And* (as chap. 1.3.) *I will give;* and the same word is again repeated.

*{strength}* So the word is used, Isa. 33.6. but here rather *wealth;* so called, because by industry and exercise of strength ordinarily attained. So Prov. 15.6. & 27.24. See Deut. 8.18.

*{the labours thereof}* Heb. *labour;* put here for the fruit of their labor, their goods thereby gotten: as Psal. 128.2. chap. 3.24. & 5.17.

*{all the precious things}* Heb. *each precious thing;* as intimating, that nothing of price or worth should escape their hands. See Isa. 39.2. Lam. 1.10.

*{the treasures of the Kings}* Both of the King himself, and of his Princes, 2 Chron. 36.18. See chap. 17.20. & 19.3. or gathered together, and stored up by many Kings successively, 2 King. 20.17. Isa. 39.6. where this also was all foretold. See chap. 15.13. & 17.3.

*{will I give into the hand of their enemies}* The Chaldeans, chap. 37.10. So 2 Chron. 36.17. *God gave all into his hand.*

*{and they shall spoil them}* Not mar them, as we use the word *spoil;* though they did make foul spoil and havoc of many matters of much worth, because they could not transport them whole and entire, chap. 52.17. but the word here used is of another notion, and may well be rendered, *shall prey on them,* or *shall make prey of them;* as 2 Chron. 14.14. and 25.13.

*{and carry them to Babylon}* 2 King. 25.13, 16. 2 Chron. 36.18.

**V. 6.** *{And thou Pashur, and all that dwell in thine house shall go into captivity, and thou shalt come to Babylon, and there shalt thou die, and shalt be buried there, thou and all thy friends, to whom thou hast prophesied lies.}* You and your family shall partake in the miseries and calamities, howsoever you will not now endure to hear of them, that shall befall this place and people in either kind, both in the siege and surprisal of the city at home, and in captivity also, and thraldom abroad: your life shall for no other end be lengthened, but that you may survive to see and suffer the more misery, both in your own person, and in those that have special relation to you.

*{there shalt thou be buried}* Though not debarred of burial; as against some other is denounced, chap. 22.19. & 34.20. yet interred in a foreign land, out of the land of Israel, where to have their corpse laid up, in regard of that peculiar interest that God's people by his assignment had in that land, was in those times counted a favor, Gen. 50.5, 25. Josh. 24.32. and the contrary threatened as a penalty, Isa. 22.16, 18. chap. 22.10.

*{thou and thy friends}* You, together with them that have been seduced and deluded by you, faring both of you alike. See chap. 14.15, 16.

*{to whom thou hast prophesied lies}* Heb. *whom to them:* an usual redundancy; as Psal. 1.4. *thou hast prophesied by,* or *with a lie,* or *a falsehood;* as the article in the particle included here carries it: so chap. 5.32. & 23.14. and so chap. 13.25. as more particularly pointing to the present message from God by his lying prophecy, and presumptuous contradiction of it, opposed: otherwise without the article, with the particle alone, it might well be rendered as some here do, *in,* or *with falsehood;* that is, *falsely,* as chap. 3.10. & 29.9. but that is not so full here.

**V. 7.** *{O LORD, thou hast deceived me, and I was deceived:}* The ensuing part of this chapter is wholly spent in a discourse of the Prophet's own concerning himself; supposed by some to have been used by him, while he was under restraint in the prison, as the 57. Psalm, to have been composed by David when he was in the cave: and that of Jonas, chap. 2. while he was in the whale's belly. But of this there is no certainty. But whether then, or afterward, which to me seems more likely: it is of an abrupt frame, having much of man in it, consisting of a medley of passions and expressions of diverse nature, some pious, courageous, confident and comfortable, some savoring of discontent and distemper, whereby it may appear to have proceeded from an eager combat and conflict between two contrary principles within him, and altering therefore otherwhiles (as it fared in the fight between Amelek and Israel, Exod. 17.11.) as the one or other for the present either prevailed, or was foiled: the like see before, chap. 11.20. & 15.15, 18. and 17.14, 18. & 18.19, 23. He begins with a complaint, wherein he complains not unto God only, but even of God himself, and his dealing with him. The like fits of infirmity whereunto, see in Jonas, Jon. 4.1, 2. yea in Moses himself, Exod. 5.22, 23. Num. 11.11, 15. yet as Jonas his contestation with God, Jonas 4.9. might well be somewhat mollified by a justifiable version, as the margin there shows; so may Jeremy's complaint have the harshness of it, in part, helped by a favorable reddition of it in some milder terms, which the words may well admit. For instead of that which our version exhibits, following the old Greek and Latin, *O Lord, thou hast deceived me, and I was deceived:* And others, with some little allay, *Thou hast enticed me, and I was enticed:* the text may well be rendered, *O Lord, thou persuadedst me, and I was persuaded;* to wit, by you. You did persuade me to undertake this prophetical employment, when I was of myself nothing forward, but averse rather thereunto, and desired to be excused from being engaged therein, chap. 1.6. Howsoever by your injunction and encouragement, upon your pressing it upon me, chap. 1.7, 8. I was persuaded and induced willingly to condescend thereunto, chap. 17.16. but I find it now far more troublesome than at first I did or could expect. True it is, that the word here found, is ordinarily used for by smooth and colorable insinuations to *entice* and *seduce* simple and silly creatures, (thence in Hebrew also denominated, because prone to give heed to, and be taken with fair shows, and flattering language, Prov. 14.15. and 21.11. Hos. 7.11. Rom. 16.18.) and consequently by such cunning carriage to *deceive* and *beguile.* So is it taken, Exod. 22.16. 1 King. 22.19, 22. Job 31.9. Prov. 16.29. and 20.19. and so hereafter, ver. 10. but the word in his first notion signifies more largely, *to persuade* in general and simply, and by persuasion (as it is opposed to a violent impulsion) to induce and allure unto the doing of ought good or evil, without any special connotation of *fraud* or *guile.* So is it used, Prov. 25.15. and is attributed to God himself by Noah, Gen. 9.27. in allusion to Japhet's name; and by God himself used of himself, Hos. 2.14. Those that render it, as our version does, seek divers ways to salve it; some supposing, that Jeremy should complain that God had deceived him, when he told him, that he had *set him over nations and kingdoms, to pull down and destroy,* chap. 1.10. which he conceived to have been meant of foreign nations and kingdoms, the enemies of God's people, to whom he was willing enough to go with such messages; but he found it after to be otherwise, being sent on such errands to his own people. Others, that God had failed in the promise made him of protection, chap. 1.8. by exposing and leaving him to such contumelious usages, as he had lately endured. See chap. 15.18. and the like, Psal. 89.39. Others, that he had sent him to threaten judgments, but had not hitherto inflicted them; by occasion whereof, he had exposed him to derision, and caused him to be deemed a false Prophet, chap. 17.15. Jonas his case, Jon. 4.1, 2. But of this, see on chap. 15.15. Others lastly, which would do well, if the sequel would well admit it, *Lord, thou hast deceived me, if I be deceived;* for I have delivered nothing but what you have enjoined me: and the copulative indeed sometime seems put for the conditional; as chap. 18.8. Amos 3.4. and we speak sometime in the same manner, *The Prophet is mistaken, and I be mistaken; for I say nothing but what he saith.* But the context of the Prophet's discourse seems to bend another way: and I adhere to the version before delivered, as most fitly, in mine opinion, expressing the Prophet's mind and intent here.

*{thou art stronger than I, and hast prevailed;}* Or, *thou wast too strong for me, and prevailedst* with me: supplied as before. Heb. *thou wast strong from me;* as Psal. 18.17. *they were strong from me;* well rendered there, *they were too strong for me:* save that here the particle expressed, which here is suppressed, as included in the verb: the like syntax, see, Isa. 65.5. You did by your persuasions and encouragements prevail with me, and put me upon it, when I had no mind or inclination of myself thereunto, chap. 1.6, 7, 8.

*{I am in derision daily, every one mocketh me.}* Or, *I am had in derision all the day-long;* as Psal. 44.15, 22. Esay 62.6. & 65.2, 6. *each of* them; to wit, of this people; (Heb. *all he,* as chap. 8.10. *mocketh me.* I am incessantly and universally derided. See the like complaints of other God's servants, Job 12.4. Psal. 22.7. Lam. 3.14. But here the Prophet complains to God of his continual and general derision; as an effect and fruit of the execution his office by God imposed on him, ver. 8.

**V. 8.** *{For since I spake, I cried out, I cried violence and spoil; because the word of the LORD was made a reproach unto me and a derision daily.}* In these words the Prophet relates the cause why he was thus derided by his people.

*{For}* Or, *Because;* as chap. 3.21, 25. Or, *For Because;* for the particle is oft used in a double notion: as Exod. 18.16. Deut. 31.20.

*{since I spake}* So most render the particle here: as also, chap. 31.20. *since I spake* of him, and so the meaning should be, ever since I began to prophesy. But the Jewish critics, and others, treading in their steps, render it, *So oft as I speak;* so oft as I prophesy, and so the term is used, 1 Sam. 17.28. 18.29. 1 King. 14.28. Isa. 28.19.

*{I spake, I cried out,}* Or, *I speak crying out:* as God in such case would have his Prophets to do, Esay 58.1. Heb. *I spake, cryed* for *spake crying:* as, *cry fill,* for, *cry* with *full* mouth, chap. 4.5. though some disjoin them, thus reading the text, *since I began to speak,* or, *so oft as I speak—I cry out.* I am enforced by the evil usage of those that hear me, to cry out and complain of them; but this seems somewhat forced: rather, as before, *Because when I speak,* (that is, so oft as I speak) *I cry out.* So the text runs most freely.

*{I cried violence and spoil}* Or, *I cry,* or, *proclaim violence and spoil:* this clause some knit to the former branch, some refer to what follows: and by *violence and spoil* here, some understand the violence and wrong, which himself was therefore enforced to complain of, because he was so reproachfully entertained for it; but of that before. Others understand it of the wicked injurious courses of his people, which in his prophecy he still cried out of, and inveighed against, chap. 6.6, 7. Others again, of the spoil and rapine that should from the enemy befall them; which in his sermons he was frequently foretelling. See on ver. 5. and this unpleasing matter was that indeed that made the Prophet so odious among them: to which sense of the words I the rather incline; because the term of *proclaiming* (chap. 3.12. Dan. 3.4.) seems to carry it that way.

*{because the word of the LORD was made a reproach unto me, and a derision daily.}* The words thus rendered seem to render a reason why he was constrained thus to cry out of violence and spoil; because so oft as he prophesied, he found continually such contumelious and reproachful entertainment. Howbeit, the words may well be read on this manner with good coherence to the former; *For when,* or, *For as oft as I speak crying out,* (in way of admonition and reproof) and *proclaim violence and spoil,* ready to fall upon them for their wickedness and obstinacy) *surely,* (so is the particle oft used. See Esay 60.9. & 63.16.) *the word of the Lord becometh a reproch unto me,* (see chap. 6.10.) or, *For because, when,* or, *so oft as I speak crying out, I proclaim violence and spoil, therefore* (for this cause, because I preach in this manner; as the particle is used, Psal. 116.10. See chap. 9.20. & 16.5. as also, Gen. 22.12. where the particle is also repeated in a twofold distinct notion, as here) *doth the word become a reproch unto me, and a derision all day long:* incessantly; as before v. 7. not as some, because what I speak is not presently executed; as if that were the ground of the Prophet's complaint, and the occasion of his present distemper and grievance, though that were one main cause, that made many of them so presumptuous and insolent in opposing the Prophet, imagining his words were but wind; and that what he said would never be effected, chap. 5.12, 13. & 17.15. but simply, that this was the continual issue of his teaching, as he had before hinted, ver. 7. nothing but continual reproach and mockage; that which therefore made him weary of his employment, ver. 9.

**V. 9.** *{Then I said, I will not make mention of him; nor speak any more in his name.}* Heb. *And I said;* as chap. 19.14. or, *Therefore,* (as chap. 16.13.) *I said;* I began hereupon to think or resolve with myself, (as Psal. 32.5. & 39.1.) to forbear prophesying any more; to silence myself, considering what manner of success I had with it, and to leave mentioning the Lord, and delivering any message unto them as from him: *him,* for, *the Lord;* the pronoun for the noun: as Gen. 15.13. Exod. 34.28. I supposed it better to hold my peace; since that I saw nothing to accrue by my speaking, either to God or myself, but dishonor and disgrace, Amos 5.13.

*{But his word was in mine heart, as a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I was weary with forbearing, and I could not stay.}* Or, *But* (Heb. *and;* as chap. 18.27.) *there was,* or, *but* that *there was in mine heart as a burning fire shut up in my bones; while I was weary with holding, and* not able to keep in: or, as some render the last clause, *and I laboured to sustain it;* but *could not:* the former verb signifies precisely *to be weary,* Esay 1.14. chap. 15.6. the latter either *to contain,* as 1 King. 8.27. chap. 2.12. or, *to sustain,* as chap. 10.10. Amos 7.10. but I follow rather here the former: for that parallel place, chap. 6.11. the substantive is impersonal; nor is, *his word,* in the text; which should therefore have had a different letter: though the Rabbines expound it of the word of prophecy; and might better be deemed the word of charge: but neither is in the text; and the copulative for the relative is frequent: as chap. 14.18. & 17.6. The meaning is, I was so inwardly pained and tormented, while I did awhile strive to forbear, as if I had had a glowing fire enclosed within me, in my bowels and my bones, so that I was not able to contain myself, but must of necessity fall to my former employment again. See the like, chap. 6.11. Psal. 39.3. Job 32.18, 19. See also, 1 Cor. 9.17.

**V. 10.** *{For I heard the defaming of many, fear on every side.}* These words are taken from Psal. 31.13. and are applied by the Prophet here to his own present occasion and condition; if we take them simply (which our version does) as they are in the Psalm, and as the latter branch is used, in some of those other places above produced, on ver. 3. there is no great difficulty in the text: for the meaning is plain enough, having reference to what the Prophet had before said, of thoughts rising within him of relinquishing his employment, and rendering the reason of such his thoughts; to wit, because he had notice given him of slanderous reports and treacherous devices of many, that combined and consulted together, how by false suggestions and malicious informations against him, they might work his ruin; in regard whereof, he perceived that from all sides there was much danger towards him, and matter consequently of affrightment: for so with David it was when he uttered those words; and so with Jeremy at the present. Howbeit, some interpreters here suppose the latter branch to be spoken of Pashur and his complices; whereof more anon.

*{For I heard}* Or, *I had heard,* (Gen. 12.1. *God had said*) or, *I had heard of:* a report had come to mine ears of it: for it is not likely that these contrivers of mischief would openly in the Prophet's own hearing relate, what they intended to charge him with.

*{the defaming}* Or, *defamation,* or, *detraction,* or, *slander,* as it is not amiss rendered, Num. 14.36. Psal. 31.13. Prov. 10.18. for the word seems properly to signify, to wit, a false report tending to the discredit of the party or thing, whereof it is reported, Numb. 13.32. & 14.36, 37. and the Jewish critics' observation of it is both frivolous and groundless, to wit, that where it is joined to the word *jotsi,* it should signify a *false report;* as Prov. 10.18. Num. 13. & 14. where with the word *hebi,* a *true:* as Gen. 37.2. for those two verbs signifying, the one *to produce,* and the other *to bring,* do alter nothing at all in the nature of the word; a slander may as well be produced, as brought; and brought, as produced: and for that place of Genesis, though Joseph's report made to his father concerning his brethren might be true, as in likelihood it was; yet that which he complained of to his father concerning them, (if it were, as I conceive it to have been, their opprobrious language, and bad terms given him) might as well for the matter thereof be false as true: (emulation and spitefulness seldom speaking otherwise) or if it were not matter of speech, but evil and scandalous carriage, as some would have it, whereby they brought *infamy* and shame upon themselves; (for so also is the word sometime used; because *infamy* is a brat of slanders breeding, Prov. 25.10. Ezek. 36.3.) then the place makes nothing at all to the purpose for the founding or grounding of the distinction concerning reports, true or false, by this term signified: which questionless is used as by David before concerning those false reports that were suggested to Saul against him, 1 Sam. 24.9. So by Jeremy here, concerning those false aspersions, and unjust charges, whereby his persecutors conspired together, to incense King and State against him. See chap. 38.4.

*{Of many, fear on every side}* Or, as some, *the defamation of many, the terrors on every side,* of those that say, such things as follow in the text: or, as others, *the defamation of many,* from whom *terror is on every side;* by reason of the multitude that thus combine against me: a defect of the relative: as chap. 15.14, 18. and of the particle *from;* as chap. 10.20. & 18.1. But some interpreters of note retain the Hebrew term here, taking the word for a proper name, some of them rendering the text; *I heard the defamation of many Magor-missabibs;* that is, of many such as this Pashur. Others, *of many, of Magor-missabib,* (that is, of Pashur, and of the false Prophets, such as are after here described.) Others again, *I have heard a report* from many, concerning *Magor-Missabib;* that is, concerning this Pashur, how he has set others on work to raise and bring in false reports and charges against me. But I rather incline to take the words here, as I find them in the Psalm, from whence they are taken.

*{Report, say they, and we will report it:}* These some make the words of Pashur, which those many before-mentioned should hear him speak; and they therefore infer, *how he should say, Report ye to us,* &c. Others, of him and his complices, or, his instruments, those of his house, ver. 6. others, indefinitely, of those *many,* before spoken of; which seems most both safe and probable; and with our version well agrees: for I cannot accord with that learned interpreter, who (going herein, I suppose, alone) would have it to be a description of the false Prophets, thus rendering the text, of those that say, *Tell us what we shall tell:* that demand of the people what they will have told or taught them, and accordingly tell them, what they best like to hear. But the words seem rather the speech of those, who desirous to get somewhat whereof to accuse the Prophet unto the King and State, set others on work to watch him, and if they can catch hold of ought that slips from him, and that by misrelating and misconstruing, may make any way against him, to bring it to them, that they may accordingly make use of it against him: and this suits well with the words ensuing. See chap. 18.18. See also the like practices against our Savior Christ, when he taught here upon earth, Mat. 22.16, 17. Mar. 12.13, 14. Luk. 11.53, 54. & 20.21.

*{all my familiars watched for my halting;}* Heb. *every man of my peace:* as chap. 38.22. Even those that pretended kindness, and made show of good affection to me, carrying themselves outwardly towards me, as if they intended me no evil, but were desirous of my welfare; yet did generally lie in wait to take me tripping in ought if they could, that might give mine adversaries any advantage against me. See the like perfidiousness complained of, Job 19.19. Psal. 14.9. & 55.13. and warning given of it, chap. 9.4, 6. & 12.6. and the like lying in wait, with the term of *halting* here used, Psal. 35.15. & 38.16. See also chap. 5.26. That learned interpreter before-mentioned, does hitherto carry on the whole foregoing passage of this verse in one continued tenor, on this wise; *For I heard the infamous speech of many, of Magor-missabib,* of those that say, *Tell us what we shall tell you, of every one that should have been at peace with me, of those that watch for my halting.* But it goes better in parts asunder; as our version exhibits it.

*{saying, Peradventure, he will be enticed; and we shall prevail against him; and we will take our revenge on him.}* It may be by closing and glozing with him, we may draw something from him; whereby having overreached him, we may prevail against him, and work our own ends. See of the term here used on ver. 7. Of such snares to catch and entrap persons, chap. 5.26. & 18.20, 22. Esay 29.21. See also the like defects of, *say they,* and *saying,* chap. 2.25. & 3.22. Psal. 27.8. and 115.15. Act. 15.5.

**V. 11.** *{But the LORD is with thee, as a mighty terrible one:}* After the former storm of discontent and misdoubt, arising from the apprehension and consideration of the general conspiracy, and banding together of persons maliciously and mischievously disposed against him, which seemed shrewdly to have staggered him, ver. 9, 10. the Prophet in the next passage here begins to recover himself, and to strengthen his faith against all oppositions, by assurance of God's constant presence with him, and powerful protection of him, according to his promise, chap. 1.19. & 15.20, 21. *But,* or, *Howbeit,* or, *Notwithstanding;* Heb. *And;* as chap. 35.14. *the Lord is with me,* as Psal. 46.7. Rom. 8.31. *as a mighty terrible one:* one of infinite might; and able to terrify the most terrible among them, that thus plot together, and set themselves against me, thereby thinking to affright and daunt me, chap. 11.21.

*{therefore my persecutors shall stumble}* They that thus pursue me, shall themselves be overthrown, chap. 18.23. Psal. 27.2.

*{and they shall not prevail}* They must prevail against God, ere they prevail against me. See chap. 1.19.

*{they shall be greatly ashamed;}* Or, *abashed,* chap. 17.18. Psal. 70.2, 3.

*{for they shall not prosper,}* Or, *they deal not prudently,* or, *skillfully:* for thence our English word *skill.* See of the use of the word on Esay 52.13. they take a very unwise course by opposing God in his Prophet, Act. 5.39.

*{their everlasting confusion shall never be forgotten.}* Heb. *ignominy of perpetuity.* So chap. 23.40. a defect of the pronoun: as chap. 17.21. or, as some, referring these words to the first member, *they shall be greatly abashed* (because *they shall not prosper*) *with an everlasting infamy, that shall never be forgotten:* a defect of the relative: as chap. 50.5.

**V. 12.** *{But, O LORD of hosts, that triest the righteous, and seest the reins, and the heart: let me see thy vengeance on them; for unto thee have I opened my cause.}* See the same in effect before, chap. 11.20. See also chap. 17.10.

*{triest the just}* And by trying of them, know them, take notice of them, and approve them, Psal. 11.5, 7.

**V. 13.** *{Sing unto the LORD, praise ye the LORD;}* From the before professed assurance of God's presence with him, and protection of him, the Prophet here rises higher, raising up his soul from his former damped and dumpish disposition, to no small degree of lightsomeness and alacrity of spirit, expressed in an enticement of himself to sing praises to God for his goodness showed toward him, in delivering him out of the hand of Pashur and his complices, and restoring him to his liberty again. See the like, Psal. 42.5, 11. & 43.5. or it may be deemed, as some take it, to respect future deliverances, praising God for them, before he receive them, out of an hopeful and assured expectation of them, as if already he had received them, like that of David, Psal. 13.6.

*{for he hath delivered the soul of the poor from the hand of evil doers.}* Or, *because* (as chap. 14.5, 6.) *he hath delivered the soul of the poor* (that is, *the poor* simply; as, *to my soul,* for, *to me,* Psal. 3.2. or, *the life of the poor:* the poor man being in danger of losing his life; as Psal. 30.3. & 116.8. and his meaning is, my poor soul, my poor self, Psal. 34.6. *out of the hand* (that is, *the power;* as chap. 15.21. Psal. 89.48.) *of evil-doers.* So Psal. 20.5. and 109.31.

**V. 14.** *{Cursed be the day wherein I was born}* A strange alteration and sudden downfall from such a strength of confidence before professed, ver. 12. and height of joy in the very next foregoing words manifested, to such a low dejection of mind, and such an uncouth distemper of spirit, as inconsiderately to curse the day of his nativity, and the persons themselves that brought his father the report of his birth. Wherein is represented unto us a very lively pattern of human imbecility, remaining even in the best, who in regard thereof therefore have need of an incessant assistance and support from above, to carry them on inoffensively through the cross occurrents of this present wicked world. See the like weakness in Job, Job 3.3, 16. a tang hereof we had before, chap. 15.10. Howbeit, some, to take away the strangeness of this sudden change, suppose these execrations not to have fallen from the Prophet at this present, but that in these ensuing verses is contained a relation only of what had slipped from him, during the time of his restraint and distress: and they render the text with a connection of these words to the former, in this manner; *he hath delivered out of the hand of evil doers the soul of the poor,* who said, *Cursed be the day wherein I was born,* &c. that is, who out of impatience and impotency of spirit, while he was yet in distress, cursed his birthday in this manner: and this may seem to carry some show of probability with it. Let the learned judge of it.

*{let not the day wherein my mother bare me be blessed.}* The same in other terms with the former.

**V. 15.** *{Cursed be the man who brought tidings to my father, saying, A man child is born unto thee, making him very glad.}* So our Savior, for joy that *a man* (that is, a male) *is brought forth,* Joh. 16.21. Heb. *by gladding gladding him:* as the like, Esay 6.10. Thus are parents much gladded oft at the birth of their children, who if they did foresee what misery they are born to, would lament many times as much over them, as they are wont to rejoice for them.

**Verse 16.** *{And let that man be as the cities, which the LORD overthrew and repented not.}* Let him perish as did Sodom and Gomorrah, (Deut. 29.23. Amos 4.11.) which God destroyed without recovery, or without revocation of the doom passed upon them, Zeph. 2.9. which concerning Zoar was reversed, Gen. 19.21.22.

*{and let him hear the cry in the morning, and the shouting at noontide:}* The shouting of enemies breaking in, and the outcries of people surprised by them, chap. 4.19. & 15.8. & 18.22. & 49.2. Zeph. 1.16. Let him live in continual terror and trouble, Job 15.21.

**Verse 17.** *{Because he slew me not from the womb:}* Or, *why was I not slain from the womb?* that is, so soon as I came out of it, so soon as I was born, Job 3.10. & 10.18,19. Hos. 9.11. for *in the womb*, which a late learned annotator suggests, will not do well here. Heb. *he did not cause me to die;* that is, God, say some, which the Italian version puts in the text: he that brought my father news of my birth; as the most: but the verb seems indefinite, and is best rendered by the passive: as ch. 18.14.

*{or that my mother might have been my grave, and her womb to be always great with me}* Heb. *and:* but here in a disjunctive notion; as v. 4. or *was not* (the negative supplied from the former branch: as Psal. 9.18.) *my mother made my grave, and her womb ever great?* being never delivered of that she went with. Heb. *her womb going great of perpetuity;* or, *an everlasting going great;* that she had never been delivered of me; that I had never come to light; like those, Psal. 68.8. Eccl. 6.3.

**Verse 18.** *{Wherefore came I forth out of the womb to see labour and sorrow,}* So Job 3.10. *to see*, that is, to sustain and suffer: as ch. 5.12. & 14.13. Lam. 3.1. *labour and sorrow;* or *vexation and grief;* that which man is born to, Job 5.6,7.

*{that my days should be consumed with shame?}* That my whole life should be thus spent, and myself wasted away, through the ignominious and contumelious usage of my adversaries, v. 7,8.
